Summary: Secreted, propeptide‑processed cysteine‑rich mini‑domains: compact extracellular segments immediately downstream of a signal peptide that contain clustered cysteines forming multiple disulfide bonds (defensin/CSαβ, WAP four‑disulfide core, cystine‑knot/knottin, CHH‑like, evasin‑like, and related small CRP scaffolds), often flanked by dibasic convertase sites and enriched in Lys/Arg
Activation pattern: Regional activation on short segments (≈20–60 aa) right after the signal peptide; strong peaks on cysteines and nearby basic residues, frequently overlapping proprotein convertase (dibasic) processing motifs; may recur for multi‑domain or repeat CRP proteins
Exemplars: - WAP/four‑disulfide core protease inhibitors (SLPI/elafin/WFDC): activation on the WAP domain’s Cys framework following the signal/propeptide
- Plant defensin‑like peptides (DEFL/LURE/ESF) and thionins: activation on the mature antimicrobial CSαβ cysteine motif
- Venom cystine‑knot peptides (conotoxins/knottins, mini‑toxins): activation on the canonical Cys frameworks in the mature toxin region of prepropeptides
- Tick evasins (chemokine‑binding CRPs): activation on the Cys‑rich chemokine‑binding domain
- Crustacean CHH/MIH neuropeptide precursors: activation on the mature hormone core with conserved six‑Cys motif adjacent to dibasic cleavage
- Fungal GPI‑anchored cell‑wall adhesins/stress proteins: activation on extracellular Cys‑rich segments just after secretion signals
- Small plant CRP protease inhibitors: activation on the disulfide‑stabilized inhibitory mini‑domain

Summary: Extracellular secreted precursors and ectodomains with disulfide-bonded cysteine-rich loops/domains (cystine-stabilized scaffolds), and a subset of secreted neuropeptide precursors whose activation concentrates on flexible, processing-rich segments even without dense cysteine content. Common in proteins with signal peptides, glycosylation, and proteolytic processing.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks on cysteines and adjacent positions (often Gly/Pro and basic Lys/Arg) within extracellular regions; regional activation over cysteine-rich loops or repeats; also highlights Gly/Pro and Lys/Arg flanking propeptide cleavage motifs in cysteine-poor neuropeptide precursors; absent in transmembrane helices and cytosolic tails; strongest in low-to-moderate order ectodomain segments, sometimes near N-glycosylation and cleavage sites.
Exemplars:
- Chemokines (especially CXC): activation on conserved disulfide-forming cysteine motifs.
- Defensins/plant CRPs and knottin-like/trypsin inhibitor peptides (CSαβ/ICK scaffolds): activation across disulfide-bonded loops.
- WFDC, Kunitz, and Kazal protease inhibitors: activation on disulfide-stabilized inhibitor domains.
- Venom toxins (e.g., Kunitz-type, ShK, disintegrins): activation on clustered cysteines defining the scaffold.
- Viral envelope glycoproteins (class I/II/III): activation in cysteine-rich ectodomains near disulfide networks and glycosylation sites.
- Extracellular receptor/adhesion and metalloprotease proteins: activation on EGF-like, disintegrin, and other cysteine-rich modules.
- DEG/ENaC family channels: activation in the extracellular cysteine-rich loop.
- Neuropeptide hormone precursors (e.g., small cardioactive peptides): activation around flexible, dibasic cleavage-rich segments even with low cysteine content.
- Apicomplexan AMA1 invasion protein: activation confined to ectodomain cysteine-rich segments, absent from TM/cytosolic regions.

Summary: Sequence contexts marking disulfide-bonded cysteines in secreted/extracellular proteins—cysteine pairs/clusters (often flanked by Gly/Pro) that form stabilizing disulfide frameworks typical of toxins, antimicrobial peptides, protease inhibitors, neuropeptide/hormone/pheromone peptides, and viral envelope ectodomains.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks at or immediately adjacent to disulfide-bonded cysteines; compact, contiguous activation across the cystine framework in short disulfide-rich peptides; multiple peaks scattered across ectodomains of large secreted glycoproteins; minimal activation in signal peptides, transmembranes, or cytosolic regions.
Exemplars: - AB toxins (pertussis toxin B subunit): peaks next to disulfide-forming cysteines within the mature chain.
- Venom disulfide-rich toxins (conotoxins; scorpion α/β-toxins; spider ω/κ-toxins): activation tracks the canonical Cys frameworks.
- Defensins and other CSαβ antimicrobial peptides: activation on the conserved disulfide pairs.
- Kunitz- and Kazal-type serine protease inhibitors: peaks around the conserved disulfide-bonded cysteines stabilizing the inhibitory fold.
- Neuropeptide hormones/pheromones with intrachain/interchain disulfides (e.g., insulin family, oxytocin/vasopressin): activation at the disulfide-forming Cys and neighboring Gly/Pro.
- Viral envelope glycoproteins: multiple peaks across ectodomain cysteine clusters and Cys–Gly/Pro motifs.
- Secreted nematode extracellular/ECM-associated cysteine-rich proteins: activation over disulfide-stabilized modules.

Summary: Short linear segments in intrinsically disordered or otherwise low-structure-confidence regions, often at N-termini and within signal peptides/propeptides of secreted and regulatory proteins (including viral accessory proteins and small ORF microproteins), enriched in small/basic residues (G, P, S, A, R; often with Cys), rather than in well-folded catalytic cores.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks scattered across IDRs and low-confidence coils/short helices; frequently clustered near the N-terminus, in signal peptides, propeptides, and disordered tails; little to no activation in well-structured domains; occasional activation in low-confidence transmembrane/signal-anchor helices.
Exemplars: - Viral accessory protein (HIV-1 Vif): peaks throughout low-pLDDT coils, especially the disordered N-terminal region.
- Neuropeptide precursor (Drosophila Amnesiac): activation in the N-terminal signal peptide and multiple mature peptide segments with very low pLDDT.
- Secreted serine carboxypeptidase: activation confined to disordered C-terminal tail, annotated disordered segment, the signal peptide, and a low-confidence C-terminal transmembrane helix; absent from the structured catalytic domain.
- Disordered human tumor-suppressor–associated protein (ST20): scattered peaks within predicted helices in a globally disordered chain, including the N-terminus.
- lncRNA/sORF-derived microprotein (IGF2 antisense protein): multiple peaks across annotated disordered regions rich in Arg/Pro/Gly.

Summary: Short residue windows in mixed-composition regions of diverse proteins, frequently in N-terminal or non-catalytic portions of enzymes, transmembrane-adjacent stretches, and small secreted peptides.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks concentrated in short 3–7 residue windows, often clustered with several nearby peaks. Activated residues are chemically diverse (including hydrophobic, polar, and charged residues) and can occur in helical transmembrane segments, disordered linkers, or globular regions outside annotated catalytic/binding sites.
Exemplars:
- Bacterial DNA ligase: clusters of peaks in the N-terminal region upstream of the catalytic and BRCT domains.
- Viral integrase homolog: short peaks within the chain including a GPAYGRP-containing segment.
- Peroxisomal biogenesis factor 9 (Pex9): peaks overlapping helical transmembrane segments and an adjacent disordered/polar region.
- Small secreted peptides (e.g., Califin-B large subunit): short peaks within the mature peptide.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, Lys/Arg‑rich low‑complexity segments—typically long terminal tails, often containing RG/RGG/GAR motifs—that mediate electrostatic binding to nucleic acids (especially rRNA/RNA) and promote association with ribonucleoprotein assemblies such as the nucleolus and ribosome
Activation pattern: Strong regional activation across long contiguous stretches of disordered sequence, most often at C‑termini (sometimes N‑termini); local peaks coincide with polybasic clusters and RG/RGG motifs; minimal activation within folded catalytic or recognition domains
Exemplars: - Nucleolar biogenesis factors (e.g., NOP12): activation on C‑terminal Lys/Arg‑rich disordered tails, not on folded RRMs
- RRP12-like ribosome assembly proteins: strongest at terminal disordered segments with basic compositional bias, especially the C‑tail
- DEAD-box RNA helicases (e.g., SrmB): activation confined to C‑terminal basic low‑complexity extensions outside the helicase core
- 3′–5′ exoribonucleases (RNase R family): disordered C‑terminal Lys/Arg‑rich tails
- Kinetoplast-associated small basic proteins: broad activation across disordered, low‑complexity basic C‑terminal halves
- Linker histones H1/H1‑like: Lys‑rich disordered C‑terminal tails that bind DNA
- Ribosomal proteins (small and large subunits): basic, often terminal extensions that contact rRNA
- SRP72 subunit: GAR/RGG‑rich basic segment
- Nucleolar/ribosome‑associated GTPases and membrane biogenesis/transport factors: cytosolic polybasic loops/tails

Summary: The feature recognizes cationic, amphipathic, low-complexity segments that mediate targeting or membrane/lipid association—classically N‑terminal signal/transit/leader-like regions of secreted, mitochondrial, and viral proteins—and frequently the propeptide/mature regions of toxin and neuropeptide precursors; it can also highlight short basic/hydrophobic helices or redox-active motifs within structured domains.
Activation pattern: Predominantly long, continuous activation over N‑terminal, low‑pLDDT leader/propeptide regions enriched in Lys/Arg, Ser/Pro and hydrophobic/aromatic residues; with occasional residue-level peaks within well-structured helices (e.g., specific positions in thioredoxin CGHC motifs or matrix-exposed helices of membrane proteins).
Exemplars: 
- Venom phospholipase A2 precursors (activation on signal/propeptide segments and conserved cationic patches).
- Apolipoproteins (N‑terminal signal peptide and amphipathic helical stretches).
- Protein kinases with disordered/basic N‑termini (e.g., cyclin-dependent and PRK family N‑tails).
- Thioredoxin-fold protein disulfide-isomerases (peak at the CGHC active-site helix).
- Mitochondrial calcium uniporter (selected residues in a matrix-exposed helix).
- Conotoxin and other secreted toxin precursors; neuropeptide prepropeptides (activation across pro/mature peptide regions).
- Viral silencing suppressors and small membrane/morphogenesis proteins (basic, hydrophobic leader-like segments).
- Kinetochore coiled-coil scaffold proteins (basic low-complexity regions).
- FYVE-domain endosomal adaptors (basic, membrane/PIP-interacting low-complexity segments).
- RNA-modifying enzymes with basic N‑terminal tails (e.g., tRNA methyltransferases).

Summary: Short, low‑complexity, intrinsically disordered proteins and modules that encode targeting/processing signals—often but not always secretory—combining hydrophobic signal peptides, double‑Gly bacteriocin leaders, or polybasic/NLS‑like segments, frequently adjacent to Ser/Thr/Pro‑rich stretches and basic clusters (e.g., RXLR, KR/RR)—common in micropeptides, toxins/secreted precursors, viral accessory proteins, keratin‑associated and testis‑specific low‑complexity proteins across taxa
Activation pattern: Regional activation across short proteins, spanning hydrophobic/targeting segments and Ser/Thr/Pro‑rich low‑complexity tracts with peaks on basic motifs such as RXLR, dibasic KR/RR, or double‑Gly leader junctions
Exemplars:
- Oomycete RxLR effectors: activation on the N‑terminal signal peptide and the RXLR/EER host‑targeting motif immediately downstream.
- Secreted peptide hormone/venom/toxin precursors: activation on the signal peptide and basic prohormone convertase cleavage motifs (KR/RR) within the propeptide region.
- Class II bacteriocins: activation on the N‑terminal double‑Gly leader and adjacent cationic tract recognized by ABC exporters.
- Viral accessory/regulatory proteins (e.g., small disordered regulators): activation across S/T/P‑rich low‑complexity disordered segments containing polybasic/NLS‑like clusters.
- Keratin‑associated proteins (KRTAPs): activation over short, repetitive low‑complexity regions (Ser/Pro‑rich and basic tracts) typical of hair shaft proteins.
- Cancer/testis antigens and testis‑associated proteins: activation on Lys/Arg‑ and Pro/Ser‑rich low‑complexity stretches in very short proteins.
- Short uncharacterized micropeptides/antisense products: broad activation across their low‑complexity/basic segments.
- Enzymes that carry secretory leaders or short disordered/basic tails (including some cytosolic enzymes lacking signal peptides): activation limited to the disordered tail, not the catalytic core.

Summary: Low-complexity, intrinsically disordered segments—often at protein N-termini—such as mucin-like/propeptide regions or flexible linkers adjacent to signal/transit peptides, common in small secreted or membrane-associated proteins and also as disordered extensions in diverse enzymes (broad taxonomic coverage, including viral, bacterial, and eukaryotic proteins).
Activation pattern: Regional activation over short to moderate stretches, frequently in disordered or polar/low-complexity segments; in longer proteins, multiple low-complexity patches can activate; in micropeptides, activation can span much of the sequence. Residue-level peaks can fall on Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly within polar-residue stretches but also on basic or hydrophobic residues within the same disordered context.
Exemplars:
- Viral envelope/accessory microproteins: activation on N-terminal Ser/Thr/Pro-rich disordered segments (often mucin-like or regulatory tails).
- Secreted eukaryotic effectors (e.g., oomycete RxLR effectors): activation on the low-complexity region flanking the signal peptide/RxLR motif.
- Human testis-biased and lncRNA-derived micropeptides: activation across intrinsically disordered peptide regions.
- Secreted precursors/propeptides: activation on N-terminal regions following the signal peptide.
- Membrane-associated single-pass proteins: activation on luminal or cytosolic tails flanking the transmembrane helix.
- Bacterial/archaeal metabolic enzymes: activation on disordered, low-complexity N-terminal extensions/linkers enriched in Ser/Thr/Gly/Pro.

Summary: Broad, regional recognition of helical and hydrophobic/amphipathic segments, including contiguous hydrophobic alpha-helical transmembrane segments and proline/glycine-rich low-complexity stretches; the feature also fires across large internal regions of soluble enzymes and effector proteins, with a bias toward hydrophobic and helix-favoring residues and proline/glycine context.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over stretches: contiguous activation across single-pass or multi-pass transmembrane alpha-helices and amphipathic helical motifs; broad, distributed activation across internal regions of soluble proteins; sparser peaks within short secreted, low-complexity segments; overall bias toward hydrophobic and helix-favoring residues with enrichment for proline and glycine context.
Exemplars:
- Fibrillar collagens: strong activation along the triple-helical G–X–Y domain, peaking at X/Y positions (especially proline/hydroxyproline-like Y), with minimal signal on G.
- Light-harvesting complex alpha subunits (photosynthetic bacteria): activation along their single transmembrane alpha-helix.
- YhhN/TMEM86 lysoplasmalogenases: activation across multiple transmembrane segments.
- Viral accessory proteins (including non-membrane factors like replication enhancers), envelope proteins, and viroporins: activation on short hydrophobic or amphipathic helical motifs (membrane-anchored or not).
- Single-pass small integral membrane proteins: activation on the transmembrane helix.
- Plant CLE/CLAVATA/ESR peptide precursors: activation on the conserved proline-rich mature peptide region and adjacent low-complexity stretches.
- Oomycete RxLR effectors: activation across the mature effector region including the RxLR-dEER motif and adjacent low-complexity repeats.
- Fungal secreted/surface-associated effectors (e.g., hydrophobin-like): activation on hydrophobic, repetitive patches outside core cystine motifs.
- Small cysteine-rich toxins/defensin-like peptides: activation on hydrophobic patches within or adjacent to the disulfide-stabilized core.
- Soluble cytosolic enzymes/regulators: broad, distributed activation across internal regions, including disordered and low-complexity stretches.

Summary: Feature fires broadly across short proteins and small peptides, often covering most of the chain, with a preference for low-complexity, Pro/Gly-rich and polybasic segments but also extending into adjacent structured regions of short polypeptides.
Activation pattern: Broad, near-whole-protein activation in short (~50-200 aa) precursors and microproteins, with local maxima on Pro-rich tracts (including poly-P), GP/GG-containing stretches, and basic clusters; activation is not restricted to disordered patches and can extend into folded domains in short proteins.
Exemplars:
- Class II bacteriocin/lantibiotic precursors: broad activation across the short precursor chain, including mature regions containing GG and GW motifs.
- Secreted peptide/toxin and prohormone precursors (e.g., cholecystokinin): activation spread across the precursor chain.
- Sperm protamine precursors: concentrated on disordered propeptides and at propeptide–mature boundaries; minimal on highly basic mature cores.
- Viral accessory/regulatory microproteins (e.g., Vpx, Vif): activation across the short viral protein, with strong peaks on poly-P / GP-rich low-complexity patches when present.
- lncRNA-encoded micropeptides and very small uncharacterized proteins (e.g., RUSC1-AS1, N-cym): activation on Pro/Gly-rich disordered segments and across much of the chain.
- Plant transcription factors with WG/GW- and GP-rich low-complexity regions: activation on those patches.
- ATP synthase epsilon subunits: signal on short GP-rich linkers or terminal low-complexity tails.
- Large enzymes (e.g., DDX11 helicase, acyl-CoA synthetase): activation on disordered N/C-terminal low-complexity regions or basic/GP-rich insertions.
- Small mitochondrial membrane proteins (ATP8): signal on short basic matrix-exposed loops or termini flanking TM helices.
- Short proteolytic chains of secreted enzymes (e.g., snake venom metalloproteinase fragments, acrosin chain fragments): broad activation across the short mature chain, including within structured peptidase/disintegrin regions.

Summary: Residue-level detector that activates broadly at sparse positions across diverse protein contexts, with notable preference for disordered/low-complexity regions, mature secreted peptides, and short helical segments (including transmembrane helices and helix-prone regions inside intrinsically disordered stretches). It does not appear to track a single specific motif.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks, typically one to a few strong peaks per protein with additional weaker peaks scattered along the sequence. Strong activation is observed within intrinsically disordered regions (including Gly-rich and polar/charged compositionally biased segments), within short transmembrane helices, and within mature processed peptides. Activation is also seen scattered within globular enzyme domains.
Exemplars:
- Small integral membrane proteins: single strong peak within a short transmembrane helix.
- Secretory preprohormones (e.g., cholecystokinin): multiple peaks within the mature processed peptide regions.
- Homeobox/disordered regulators (e.g., Rhox5): multiple peaks throughout disordered Gly-rich and basic/acidic compositionally biased segments.
- CaMKII inhibitor peptides: peaks at the start of the inhibitory domain and at Pro-rich positions.
- Viral accessory/integrase-like proteins: multiple short peaks scattered across the chain, including disordered C-terminal segments.
- Bacterial/yeast enzymes (e.g., beta-lactamase, aspartyl-tRNA synthetase, imidazolonepropionase, peroxin-9): scattered peaks within N-terminal or globular regions.

Summary: Short residue windows in mixed-composition regions of diverse proteins, frequently in N-terminal or non-catalytic portions of enzymes, transmembrane-adjacent stretches, and small secreted peptides.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks concentrated in short 3–7 residue windows, often clustered with several nearby peaks. Activated residues are chemically diverse (including hydrophobic, polar, and charged residues) and can occur in helical transmembrane segments, disordered linkers, or globular regions outside annotated catalytic/binding sites.
Exemplars:
- Bacterial DNA ligase: clusters of peaks in the N-terminal region upstream of the catalytic and BRCT domains.
- Viral integrase homolog: short peaks within the chain including a GPAYGRP-containing segment.
- Peroxisomal biogenesis factor 9 (Pex9): peaks overlapping helical transmembrane segments and an adjacent disordered/polar region.
- Small secreted peptides (e.g., Califin-B large subunit): short peaks within the mature peptide.

Summary: Secreted, propeptide‑processed cysteine‑rich mini‑domains: compact extracellular segments immediately downstream of a signal peptide that contain clustered cysteines forming multiple disulfide bonds (defensin/CSαβ, WAP four‑disulfide core, cystine‑knot/knottin, CHH‑like, evasin‑like, and related small CRP scaffolds), often flanked by dibasic convertase sites and enriched in Lys/Arg
Activation pattern: Regional activation on short segments (≈20–60 aa) right after the signal peptide; strong peaks on cysteines and nearby basic residues, frequently overlapping proprotein convertase (dibasic) processing motifs; may recur for multi‑domain or repeat CRP proteins
Exemplars: - WAP/four‑disulfide core protease inhibitors (SLPI/elafin/WFDC): activation on the WAP domain’s Cys framework following the signal/propeptide
- Plant defensin‑like peptides (DEFL/LURE/ESF) and thionins: activation on the mature antimicrobial CSαβ cysteine motif
- Venom cystine‑knot peptides (conotoxins/knottins, mini‑toxins): activation on the canonical Cys frameworks in the mature toxin region of prepropeptides
- Tick evasins (chemokine‑binding CRPs): activation on the Cys‑rich chemokine‑binding domain
- Crustacean CHH/MIH neuropeptide precursors: activation on the mature hormone core with conserved six‑Cys motif adjacent to dibasic cleavage
- Fungal GPI‑anchored cell‑wall adhesins/stress proteins: activation on extracellular Cys‑rich segments just after secretion signals
- Small plant CRP protease inhibitors: activation on the disulfide‑stabilized inhibitory mini‑domain

Summary: Secreted, short cysteine-rich peptides and small extracellular cysteine-rich domains stabilized by multiple disulfide bonds (CRPs), spanning venom toxins, disintegrins, defensins/hepcidin, Kunitz/Kazal/hevein-like inhibitors/defense peptides, and related cystine‑knotted or cysteine‑stabilized folds. The feature captures the mature, proteolytically processed peptide/module characterized by clustered Cys (often CC motifs) and basic residues.
Activation pattern: Regional activation confined to short mature peptide segments (tens of residues) following the signal peptide and propeptides; minimal/absent on signal/pro-regions. Strong residue-level peaks on cysteines and frequent secondary peaks on Lys/Arg and Gly. Activation spans mixed secondary structure (β-strands, coils, short helices) and can include key functional loops (e.g., RGD in disintegrins).
Exemplars: - Plant cyclotides (cystine-knot cyclopeptides, e.g., chassatide): activation across the cyclic cystine‑knot core of the mature peptide after processing.
- Snake venom disintegrins: activation across the disintegrin domain, including the RGD integrin-binding loop and adjacent cysteine-dense core.
- Inhibitor cystine-knot (ICK) venom toxins from spiders, cone snails, centipedes, and sea anemones: activation on the disulfide‑knotted toxin core.
- Kunitz/BPTI- and Kazal-type serine protease inhibitors (including tick chemokine/complement inhibitors): activation on the small disulfide‑rich inhibitor domain.
- Hevein-like/seed defense peptides: activation on the cysteine-rich chitin‑binding hevein domain.
- Defensins (plant/fungal/animal CSαβ peptides) and vertebrate hepcidin: activation on the cysteine‑stabilized mature AMP region.
- Euplotes ciliate mating pheromones: activation on the secreted disulfide‑rich pheromone core.
- Cysteine-rich modules within large extracellular/mucin-like proteins: activation on the short, cysteine‑dense repeat/subdomain embedded in the larger precursor.

Summary: Folded extracytoplasmic luminal domains of secretory or organellar precursors—i.e., the mature globular regions (and, when present as independent folds, structured inhibitory propeptides) that lie immediately downstream of signal/transit peptides—common in plant/apoplastic and other lumenal proteins (secreted, vacuolar, chloroplast/thylakoid) and spanning diverse families (proteases, expansins, phytocyanins, SCP/CAP toxins, GDSL lipases), often disulfide‑stabilized and glycosylated; targeting peptides and low‑complexity linkers are de-emphasized.
Activation pattern: Domain-level, long continuous activation that switches on sharply after the signal/transit peptide cleavage site (or at the start of a folded pro/mature domain), remains high across well-structured secondary elements, and drops in signal/transit peptides, low-complexity/disordered tails, and small auxiliary motifs (e.g., ShKT). Within catalytic domains the feature does not focus on active-site residues and can dip at catalytic positions.

Summary: Conserved N-terminal segment of EGF-like repeats, recognizing the cysteine framework that initiates the EGF fold in extracellular, disulfide-rich proteins.
Activation pattern: Localized, repeat-wise activation at the starts of individual EGF-like domains; sharp residue-level peaks within the first disulfide loop (often on His/Val/Asn/Tyr/Thr residues adjacent to the conserved cysteines), with variable signal on nearby cysteines; repeats across tandem arrays; minimal in signal peptides and non-EGF modules (e.g., MAM), with occasional buildup in the short linker immediately preceding the first repeat.
Exemplars: - EGFR ligands (epiregulin): activation across the N-terminal portion of the single EGF-like growth-factor domain, including residues around the first disulfide.
- Fibulin family (ECM proteins with EGF-like repeats): strong, repeated peaks at the N-terminus of each repeat within the cysteine-flanked region; inactive in signal peptide and distal non-EGF regions.
- EGFL proteins (e.g., EGFL6): high, localized peaks within specific N-terminal EGF-like repeats; no activation in the intervening disordered segment or the C-terminal MAM domain.

Summary: Short, disulfide‑bonded extracellular cysteine‑rich repeat modules—especially EGF‑like (including cbEGF and laminin‑type LE) and LDL receptor class A (LDLa) domains, but also von Willebrand type C (CR) and other disulfide‑rich repeats—detected via acidic/polar loop motifs flanked by conserved cysteines (including Ca2+-binding Dx[D/N] motifs when present); broadly marks ectodomains of secreted proteins and single‑pass receptors.
Activation pattern:
- Strong activation confined to extracellular regions; absent in transmembrane helices and cytoplasmic tails.
- Repeated peaks aligning with tandem repeats; long activation tracts across multi‑repeat proteins.
- LDLa repeats: maxima over the central acidic DxSDE/DxD… segment; flanking cysteines variably engaged.
- EGF‑like repeats (cbEGF and LE): highest in the C‑terminal half containing the D/N‑x‑D/N‑x(4)‑Y/F motif when present, near the last cysteines.
- Also activates analogous acidic/polar loops in other cysteine‑rich repeats (e.g., VWC/CR, TIL/Kunitz, TSR); preference for D/E/S/T/N/Q/G and Y with nearby Cys; modest activation in short acidic linkers between repeats.
Exemplars:
- LDL receptor family (LDLR/LRP1/LRP4): LDLa repeat Ca2+-binding loops and cbEGF/LE segments across the ectodomain.
- Notch receptors and ligands (Notch, Delta/Jagged): tandem EGF‑like repeats with peaks at Ca2+-binding loops.
- Coagulation/complement components (e.g., Factors VII/IX/X, protein C/S, C1r/C1s modules): cbEGF domains.
- ECM scaffolds and glycoproteins (fibrillins, fibulins, LTBPs, laminins, tenascins, matrilins): arrays of EGF‑like/LE repeats.
- Chordin‑like/BMP modulators (BMPER/Crossveinless‑2, chordin): arrays of VWC/CR repeats.
- Cell‑adhesion receptors (selectins, integrin β I‑EGF modules) and extracellular metalloproteases/modulators (ADAM/ADAMTS): EGF‑like/cysteine‑rich repeats.
- Disulfide‑rich protease inhibitors and invertebrate toxins (e.g., Kunitz/TIL‑type).
- Plant receptor‑like proteins/kinases (e.g., WAKs, vacuolar sorting receptors): ectodomains with EGF‑like repeats.

Summary: Short, cationic, amphipathic peptide segments—typically the mature cores of secreted antimicrobial/cytolytic peptides and analogous AMP‑like helices embedded in larger proteins. These regions are Lys/Arg‑rich with interspersed hydrophobes, often form (or have propensity for) an amphipathic α‑helix, and are used for membrane interaction/disruption or other bioactive signaling; they are usually produced by proteolytic processing from precursor proteins and can include RiPP cores despite post‑translational crosslinks.
Activation pattern: Regional activation on short contiguous blocks (∼15–40 aa, sometimes shorter), with sharp on/off at the boundaries of mature peptide segments; minimal activation in signal peptides and propeptides. Peaks often coincide with hydrophobic residues along an amphipathic face and clusters of Lys/Arg. Frequently at N‑ or C‑terminal helices or short internal helices with low-to-moderate pLDDT.
Exemplars: - Amphibian helical antimicrobial peptides (e.g., aureins): activation precisely on the mature AMP helix, not on signal/propeptide.
- Hymenopteran venom cytolysins (e.g., myrmeciitoxins): strong activation across the mature toxin’s amphipathic α‑helix.
- Lantibiotic RiPPs (e.g., lacticin 3147 A2): activation on the modified mature lantibiotic core despite lanthionine/beta‑methyllanthionine crosslinks.
- Phage/bacterial holins: activation on the N‑terminal amphipathic helix adjacent to the first transmembrane segment; little/no activation in TM or periplasmic domains.
- Crustacean anti‑lipopolysaccharide factors (ALFs): activation on the N‑terminal cationic LPS‑binding helix of the mature peptide.
- Plant NLR immune receptors (coiled‑coil N‑termini): activation on the N‑terminal CC helix implicated in membrane permeabilization/channel activity.
- Insect stress-response secreted proteins (Turandot family): activation on a C‑terminal amphipathic α‑helix of the mature chain.
- Outer membrane polysaccharide export proteins (CtrA family): activation on a short periplasmic C‑terminal helical tail with amphipathic character.
- Kininogen‑derived peptides (bradykinin variants): activation on the short, basic bioactive peptide released from a disordered region.

Summary: Membrane-interacting helical modules: cationic, Gly/Ala-rich amphipathic α-helices and short transmembrane hairpins/fusogenic segments that mediate lipid binding, insertion, or pore formation in toxins, secretion/translocation factors, and viral/secreted proteins; typically low-confidence/disordered in isolation and become helical upon membrane contact.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long, contiguous helical stretches; strongest over amphipathic or hydrophobic helices (including TM segments), with peaks on small hydrophobics (A/V/L/I/G) and frequent Lys/Arg; tends to avoid structured catalytic cores, instead marking N- or C‑terminal delivery/membrane-interaction regions; often coincides with low pLDDT and predicted helices or annotated transmembranes; in peptides, activates on the mature membrane-active helix rather than the signal peptide.
Exemplars: - Cry-family insecticidal δ-endotoxins: activation on the N‑terminal pore-forming helical bundle (domain I) of Cry13Aa.
- Cationic antimicrobial peptide (moricin): activation across the mature α‑helical AMP, not the signal peptide.
- Type VI secretion effector VasX: activation over the C‑terminal membrane-inserting module comprising multiple transmembrane helices.
- LXG polymorphic toxin (YqcG): activation on a long C‑terminal, low‑pLDDT disordered segment following the LXG export domain (a membrane/translocation-prone tail-like region).
- T6SS ADP‑ribosyltransferase (mART) effector (Tre1): activation on N‑terminal glycine‑rich, low‑confidence helical regions flanking PAAR and outside the catalytic core, consistent with delivery/membrane-targeting helices.

Summary: Short hydrophobic membrane-inserting alpha-helices and related fusion/pore-forming segments (15–40 aa) used as single-pass transmembrane anchors or membrane-penetrating peptides; enriched in small hydrophobics with interspersed Ser/Thr and glycine motifs (e.g., GxxxG/glycine-zipper) that promote helix insertion/packing, common in toxins, secretion pores, viral fusion proteins, and other membrane-associated factors.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over contiguous hydrophobic segments, often helical or coil-to-helix; sharp residue-level peaks frequently at Gly or Ser/Thr near helix starts, within TM cores, or immediately after cleavage sites that expose fusion peptides; multiple activated segments can occur per protein; frequently low pLDDT due to membrane context or intrinsic flexibility; near termini in small precursors and internal in larger proteins.
Exemplars: - Type III secretion translocon (SctE): strong activation across two annotated transmembrane helices, peaking at residues whose mutation disrupts helix formation.
- Paramyxovirus fusion glycoprotein F: activation spanning the furin cleavage and N-terminus of the F1 fusion peptide (membrane-penetrating segment).
- Bacteriocin/antimicrobial peptide (Pumilarin): activation on a hydrophobic, helix-forming membrane-active segment within the mature toxin peptide.
- Membrane-anchored toxin (double-stranded DNA deaminase toxin A): primary activation on the N-terminal transmembrane helix; weaker activation on a short disordered hydrophobic segment.
- Magnetosome membrane protein (MamG): localized activation within the single-pass transmembrane helix, peaking at the helix start following an LG motif.

Summary: Membrane‑active amphipathic α‑helices enriched in small hydrophobic residues (A/V/L/I/G) that insert into, line, or associate with lipid bilayers—i.e., the pore‑forming/translocation helices of toxins and translocons and analogous lipid‑binding/stress‑sensing helices in other membrane proteins
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long, contiguous helical segments (often single helices or helical hairpins), with sparse charges and frequent Gly/Ala runs; peaks track α‑helical stretches that often fold upon membrane contact (low pLDDT in isolation). Activation typically avoids catalytic motifs and generic signal peptides/TM anchors, instead favoring amphipathic or pore‑lining helices (including lipid‑binding helices) within toxin, antimicrobial, and membrane‑associated domains.
Exemplars: - Pore-forming colicins: strong activation on the C‑terminal pore‑forming transmembrane/helical hairpin region.
- Bacillus thuringiensis Cry (δ‑endotoxins): activation on the N‑terminal pore‑forming helical bundle (domain I) with peaks in membrane‑inserting helices.
- Cationic antimicrobial peptides (e.g., Styelin‑D): activation confined to the mature amphipathic α‑helix; absent on the signal peptide and propeptide.
- Mitochondrial inner‑membrane protease OMA1: activation on amphipathic helices within the peptidase domain, including a cardiolipin‑binding/stress‑sensor region; little to no activation on the N‑terminal propeptide or the single‑pass TM anchor.

Summary: Detector of cationic, hydrophobic amphipathic alpha‑helical membrane‑interacting segments (including short transmembrane helices with basic flanks and pore‑forming amphipathic helices), with secondary emphasis on the maturation junctions of secreted membrane‑active peptides (notably C‑terminal amidation/cleavage sites).
Activation pattern: Predominantly long, contiguous activation across small helical membrane‑active peptides; in larger proteins, strong regional activation on specific alpha‑helical segments that contact or insert into membranes (TMs and adjacent basic loops, amphipathic helices), often near termini. In peptide precursors, sharp peaks at processing boundaries, especially at the C‑terminus of the mature peptide and adjacent Gly/Lys residues used for amidation. Residue preference is for basic (K/R) and hydrophobic (I/L/V/F/W/Y/A) content arranged in helical contexts; non‑amphipathic helices or acidic/disordered stretches are weak.
Exemplars: - Bacteriophage holins/antiholins: activation across N‑terminal transmembrane helices and cytoplasmic basic loops; decreased signal in non‑matching TM segments.
- Filamentous phage major coat proteins: strong activation on the short TM and adjacent amphipathic helical region used for membrane insertion/assembly.
- Adenovirus membrane‑active factors (e.g., preprotein VI/E1B Bcl‑2‑like): selective activation on amphipathic helices implicated in membrane binding/disruption; other helices remain low.
- Bcl‑2 family proteins: activation on the C‑terminal membrane‑anchoring helix and amphipathic BH‑region helices involved in membrane interaction.
- Peroxisomal membrane proteins (PEX11/PEX16): activation on amphipathic helices/hairpins that remodel or anchor to membranes.
- Lipid‑droplet surface proteins/perilipins: activation on amphipathic helices that target neutral‑lipid surfaces.
- Organelle membrane import/fission components (mitochondrial/chloroplast/plasma membrane): activation on amphipathic targeting or curvature‑sensing helices.
- Antimicrobial and venom peptides: near‑continuous activation across the mature cationic helical peptide; in precursors, sharp peaks at N‑ and C‑terminal cleavage sites and at C‑terminal amidation motifs (e.g., Gly/Lys donors).
- Bacteriocins (including helical and circular classes): strong activation across the membrane‑active helical segments with isolated dips at non‑matching residues.
- Globins (non‑membrane control): sparse residue‑level peaks limited to hydrophobic/basic helical faces, illustrating sequence‑composition specificity rather than generic helix detection.

Summary: Short, cationic, amphipathic peptide segments—typically the mature cores of secreted antimicrobial/cytolytic peptides and analogous AMP‑like helices embedded in larger proteins. These regions are Lys/Arg‑rich with interspersed hydrophobes, often form (or have propensity for) an amphipathic α‑helix, and are used for membrane interaction/disruption or other bioactive signaling; they are usually produced by proteolytic processing from precursor proteins and can include RiPP cores despite post‑translational crosslinks.
Activation pattern: Regional activation on short contiguous blocks (∼15–40 aa, sometimes shorter), with sharp on/off at the boundaries of mature peptide segments; minimal activation in signal peptides and propeptides. Peaks often coincide with hydrophobic residues along an amphipathic face and clusters of Lys/Arg. Frequently at N‑ or C‑terminal helices or short internal helices with low-to-moderate pLDDT.
Exemplars: - Amphibian helical antimicrobial peptides (e.g., aureins): activation precisely on the mature AMP helix, not on signal/propeptide.
- Hymenopteran venom cytolysins (e.g., myrmeciitoxins): strong activation across the mature toxin’s amphipathic α‑helix.
- Lantibiotic RiPPs (e.g., lacticin 3147 A2): activation on the modified mature lantibiotic core despite lanthionine/beta‑methyllanthionine crosslinks.
- Phage/bacterial holins: activation on the N‑terminal amphipathic helix adjacent to the first transmembrane segment; little/no activation in TM or periplasmic domains.
- Crustacean anti‑lipopolysaccharide factors (ALFs): activation on the N‑terminal cationic LPS‑binding helix of the mature peptide.
- Plant NLR immune receptors (coiled‑coil N‑termini): activation on the N‑terminal CC helix implicated in membrane permeabilization/channel activity.
- Insect stress-response secreted proteins (Turandot family): activation on a C‑terminal amphipathic α‑helix of the mature chain.
- Outer membrane polysaccharide export proteins (CtrA family): activation on a short periplasmic C‑terminal helical tail with amphipathic character.
- Kininogen‑derived peptides (bradykinin variants): activation on the short, basic bioactive peptide released from a disordered region.

Summary: Short helical/loop segments adjacent to membrane domains in membrane-associated proteins, including cytoplasmic helices flanking transmembrane anchors and lumenal/extracytoplasmic loops between transmembrane helices.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over contiguous short stretches of roughly 10-25 residues, with residue-level peaks on a mixture of hydrophobic/aromatic anchors (L, I, V, F, W) and interfacial basic residues (Arg/Lys), with tolerance for Gly/Pro. The activated stretch is typically positioned just outside an annotated transmembrane helix rather than within it; non-activated soluble tails far from the membrane domain are silent.
Exemplars:
- Sec61 γ subunits (translocon): activation on the N-terminal cytoplasmic amphipathic helix preceding the single TM anchor, peaking around a conserved Arg.
- Chloride channel CLIC-like protein 1 (ERAC1) across vertebrates: activation on a conserved lumenal loop region between transmembrane helices.
- Membrane metalloproteases of the S2P/RseP family (e.g., ARASP, ARASP2, MmpA): activation on a conserved soluble helical stretch flanking the catalytic membrane domain.

Summary: Membrane‑active amphipathic α‑helices enriched in small hydrophobic residues (A/V/L/I/G) that insert into, line, or associate with lipid bilayers—i.e., the pore‑forming/translocation helices of toxins and translocons and analogous lipid‑binding/stress‑sensing helices in other membrane proteins
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long, contiguous helical segments (often single helices or helical hairpins), with sparse charges and frequent Gly/Ala runs; peaks track α‑helical stretches that often fold upon membrane contact (low pLDDT in isolation). Activation typically avoids catalytic motifs and generic signal peptides/TM anchors, instead favoring amphipathic or pore‑lining helices (including lipid‑binding helices) within toxin, antimicrobial, and membrane‑associated domains.
Exemplars: - Pore-forming colicins: strong activation on the C‑terminal pore‑forming transmembrane/helical hairpin region.
- Bacillus thuringiensis Cry (δ‑endotoxins): activation on the N‑terminal pore‑forming helical bundle (domain I) with peaks in membrane‑inserting helices.
- Cationic antimicrobial peptides (e.g., Styelin‑D): activation confined to the mature amphipathic α‑helix; absent on the signal peptide and propeptide.
- Mitochondrial inner‑membrane protease OMA1: activation on amphipathic helices within the peptidase domain, including a cardiolipin‑binding/stress‑sensor region; little to no activation on the N‑terminal propeptide or the single‑pass TM anchor.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered post-signal/TM prohormone regions of secreted short-peptide precursors—i.e., the segments that encode mature neuropeptides/hormones or toxin/antimicrobial peptides and their flanking propeptides—characterized by Lys/Arg-rich convertase cleavage motifs and frequent support for C‑terminal amidation
Activation pattern: Domain-level: inactive on signal peptides and transmembrane helices; strongly active across the luminal propeptide from signal/TM cleavage to the C-terminus. Regional: sustained high activation over mature peptide blocks and adjacent propeptides, often spanning multiple peptides in one precursor; activation typically drops immediately after the last processed peptide. Residue-level: peaks over peptide cores and nearby linkers; selective dips at the second residue of dibasic Lys/Arg cleavage pairs; enrichment around basic clusters and glycine positions associated with amidation.
Exemplars: - Dermaseptin antimicrobial peptide precursor: high on the mature dermaseptin and both flanking propeptides; off on the N‑terminal signal peptide; all activated regions are disordered.
- Insect prokineticin/hugin precursor: strong activation across the region containing Hug‑gamma and PK‑2 peptides and linker/C‑terminal propeptide; inactive on the signal peptide; disordered.
- Tachykinin/protachykinin (neurokinin family): activated across the neurokinin peptide (e.g., Neurokinin‑B) and propeptide segments; sharp local drop at a dibasic cleavage Arg; disordered.
- Neuropeptide F precursor: moderate to strong activation on the mature NPF and the C‑terminal propeptide; signal peptide unactivated; disordered.
- Insect diuretic hormone class 2 precursor: maximal activation across the mature diuretic hormone peptide; off on the signal peptide; disordered.
- Proenkephalin (opioid peptide precursor): broadly activated over enkephalin copies and intervening prosegments; recurrent dip at the second basic residue of dibasic cleavage motifs; disordered.
- Gonadoliberin (GnRH) precursor: high activation across the GnRH peptide and the associated peptide; inactive on the signal peptide; disordered.
- Gastrin prohormone: strong activation over “Big gastrin”/“Gastrin” region and C‑terminal propeptide where amidation/cleavage motifs occur; off on the signal peptide; disordered.
- Pigment-dispersing factor (PDF) precursor: activated on the mature PDF chain; signal peptide not activated; disordered.
- Membrane-anchored secretory peptide-like precursor (e.g., Frey): inactive on the N‑terminal transmembrane helix; strong activation on the disordered luminal C‑terminal region consistent with a processed propeptide segment.

Summary: Low-complexity, intrinsically disordered, cysteine-poor segments enriched in small/polar and charged residues (G, A, S, T, K, E, D) that act as surface‑active, lipid‑interface–binding regions (amphipathic/helix‑forming “hydrophilin/apolipoprotein‑like” tracts). These occur broadly across taxa, often at N‑termini or luminal/cytosolic tails of secreted or membrane‑associated proteins, including stress‑protective hydrophilins/LEA proteins, apolipoproteins, ATG2 lipid‑transfer tethers, and cationic antimicrobial/venom peptides.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over long low‑complexity stretches (frequently N‑terminal), with diffuse highlighting and occasional peaks on glycine/threonine repeats or short amphipathic helix motifs; spans entire sequence for small AMPs/venom peptides; in large proteins (e.g., ATG2) covers extended acidic/polar IDRs flanking or preceding hydrophobic cores but not the transmembrane segments.
Exemplars: - Apolipoproteins (e.g., ApoC/ApoA/ApoE families): activation on amphipathic helix repeats and adjacent polar low‑complexity segments that coat lipid particles.
- Plant LEA/hydrophilin proteins (LEA4/LEA5, dehydrins, Hsp12‑like): activation across glycine/threonine/serine‑rich, charged repeats conferring stress‑protective, membrane‑associating properties.
- Autophagy‑related protein 2 (ATG2 family): activation over long acidic/polar IDRs and N‑terminal amphipathic membrane‑tethering segments used at ER–mitochondria/phagophore contact sites.
- Lipid‑droplet/oil‑body scaffolds (oleosins, perilipins, apolipoprotein‑like droplet proteins): activation on low‑complexity polar tails and amphipathic segments surrounding the hydrophobic hairpin/core.
- Cationic antimicrobial and venom peptides (melittin/cecropin/magainin/mastoparan‑like): activation across the whole cationic amphipathic segment that binds membranes.
- Membrane proteins with long disordered N‑ or luminal regions (mitochondrial/ER/PM): activation on polar/charged low‑complexity tails used as flexible linkers or membrane‑proximal surface‑binders.
- Viral matrix/core/viroporin‑associated proteins: activation on low‑complexity, amphipathic, membrane‑interacting stretches.
- Bacterial low‑complexity scaffold/toxin repeats: activation on glycine/threonine‑rich polar segments used for surface association or scaffolding.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity polybasic segments—stretches enriched in Lys/Arg (often with His) and sometimes interspersed with Ser and acidic residues (RS/KE‑rich patterns). These tracts are typically long tails (frequently C‑terminal) found in nuclear/RNA‑associated proteins and serve as generic basic, nucleic‑acid–contacting or localization‑prone regions.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across extended disordered segments with strong residue‑level peaks at the densest K/R/H clusters; little to no activation in folded domains. Frequently concentrated in C‑terminal low‑complexity regions.
Exemplars: - Spliceosome-associated RP9: strong activation on a C‑terminal Lys/Arg/His‑rich disordered tail.
- G‑patch RNA‑binding proteins (e.g., GPATCH8): long C‑terminal basic low‑complexity regions.
- Uncharacterized pxr1-like protein: disordered C‑terminal basic/charge‑mixed tract with helical propensity.
- TFIID subunit 2 (TAF2): C‑terminal His/Lys‑biased intrinsically disordered region.
- Cyclophilin-type peptidyl‑prolyl isomerase G (PPIG): extended RS/K‑rich disordered C‑terminal tail; no activation in the structured PPIase domain.
- Yeast TMA23 ribosome‑biogenesis/nucleolar factor: long Lys‑rich disordered C‑terminal tail.

Summary: Low-complexity, intrinsically disordered or signal/transmembrane–proximal segments—often N‑terminal—commonly enriched in H/Q/Y/W but not exclusively, acting as generic interaction/activation modules in small regulatory/viral proteins and in secreted/membrane-linked precursors
Activation pattern: Regional activation across extended low‑complexity stretches or N‑terminal signal/TM-adjacent regions; per‑residue preference for H/Q with contributions from Y/W, but tolerant of basic- or serine‑rich tracts found in viral accessory proteins and secreted precursors
Exemplars:
- Viral accessory/regulatory proteins (e.g., Rex, agnoproteins): activation over N‑terminal basic/low‑complexity tails (may lack H/Q bias)
- Eukaryotic sORF/micropeptides and apoptosis/testis-linked proteins: activation across low‑complexity IDRs, often H/Q/Y‑rich when present
- Secreted precursors and extracellular peptides (e.g., plant SCOOPs, protease propeptides): activation on signal peptides/propeptides or serine‑rich low‑complexity regions
- Small membrane proteins/channels (e.g., FluC) and proteolipids (e.g., neuronatin): activation at N‑terminal low‑complexity loops or signal/TM-proximal regions
- Histidine‑rich metal‑binding/antimicrobial tracts: activation on poly‑His/His‑biased regions when present

Summary: The feature recognizes cationic, amphipathic, low-complexity segments that mediate targeting or membrane/lipid association—classically N‑terminal signal/transit/leader-like regions of secreted, mitochondrial, and viral proteins—and frequently the propeptide/mature regions of toxin and neuropeptide precursors; it can also highlight short basic/hydrophobic helices or redox-active motifs within structured domains.
Activation pattern: Predominantly long, continuous activation over N‑terminal, low‑pLDDT leader/propeptide regions enriched in Lys/Arg, Ser/Pro and hydrophobic/aromatic residues; with occasional residue-level peaks within well-structured helices (e.g., specific positions in thioredoxin CGHC motifs or matrix-exposed helices of membrane proteins).
Exemplars: 
- Venom phospholipase A2 precursors (activation on signal/propeptide segments and conserved cationic patches).
- Apolipoproteins (N‑terminal signal peptide and amphipathic helical stretches).
- Protein kinases with disordered/basic N‑termini (e.g., cyclin-dependent and PRK family N‑tails).
- Thioredoxin-fold protein disulfide-isomerases (peak at the CGHC active-site helix).
- Mitochondrial calcium uniporter (selected residues in a matrix-exposed helix).
- Conotoxin and other secreted toxin precursors; neuropeptide prepropeptides (activation across pro/mature peptide regions).
- Viral silencing suppressors and small membrane/morphogenesis proteins (basic, hydrophobic leader-like segments).
- Kinetochore coiled-coil scaffold proteins (basic low-complexity regions).
- FYVE-domain endosomal adaptors (basic, membrane/PIP-interacting low-complexity segments).
- RNA-modifying enzymes with basic N‑terminal tails (e.g., tRNA methyltransferases).

Summary: Short, low‑complexity, intrinsically disordered proteins and modules that encode targeting/processing signals—often but not always secretory—combining hydrophobic signal peptides, double‑Gly bacteriocin leaders, or polybasic/NLS‑like segments, frequently adjacent to Ser/Thr/Pro‑rich stretches and basic clusters (e.g., RXLR, KR/RR)—common in micropeptides, toxins/secreted precursors, viral accessory proteins, keratin‑associated and testis‑specific low‑complexity proteins across taxa
Activation pattern: Regional activation across short proteins, spanning hydrophobic/targeting segments and Ser/Thr/Pro‑rich low‑complexity tracts with peaks on basic motifs such as RXLR, dibasic KR/RR, or double‑Gly leader junctions
Exemplars:
- Oomycete RxLR effectors: activation on the N‑terminal signal peptide and the RXLR/EER host‑targeting motif immediately downstream.
- Secreted peptide hormone/venom/toxin precursors: activation on the signal peptide and basic prohormone convertase cleavage motifs (KR/RR) within the propeptide region.
- Class II bacteriocins: activation on the N‑terminal double‑Gly leader and adjacent cationic tract recognized by ABC exporters.
- Viral accessory/regulatory proteins (e.g., small disordered regulators): activation across S/T/P‑rich low‑complexity disordered segments containing polybasic/NLS‑like clusters.
- Keratin‑associated proteins (KRTAPs): activation over short, repetitive low‑complexity regions (Ser/Pro‑rich and basic tracts) typical of hair shaft proteins.
- Cancer/testis antigens and testis‑associated proteins: activation on Lys/Arg‑ and Pro/Ser‑rich low‑complexity stretches in very short proteins.
- Short uncharacterized micropeptides/antisense products: broad activation across their low‑complexity/basic segments.
- Enzymes that carry secretory leaders or short disordered/basic tails (including some cytosolic enzymes lacking signal peptides): activation limited to the disordered tail, not the catalytic core.

Summary: Short linear motifs centered on serine/threonine within intrinsically disordered regions that correspond to eukaryotic Ser/Thr phosphorylation sites (often SP/TP or basic R/K-flanked motifs), used for regulatory control across diverse proteins including viral proteins
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks on single S/T or 1–3 aa motifs, punctate and distributed across proteins; strongly enriched in low-pLDDT coils and low-complexity segments; depleted in folded domains and transmembrane helices; occasional peaks at edges of low-confidence helices; context frequently includes nearby proline and/or basic residues
Exemplars: - PH plus RapGAP scaffold proteins: activation on S/T residues in disordered linkers; minimal signal in folded PH and GAP domains
- Chromatin regulator Spt21: multiple peaks in disordered C-terminal regions; includes a known phosphoserine site
- TORC1 subunit Tco89: peaks at/near an annotated phosphothreonine and other disordered segments
- Large transmembrane receptor with long cytosolic tail (stum): activation confined to disordered cytosolic regions; none in transmembrane helices
- Developmental cytoskeletal regulator (bottleneck): clusters on S/T within low-complexity, basic-enriched disordered C-terminus
- Small GTPase regulators (e.g., RhoGAPs, RasGEFs, ARF GEFs) and protein kinases: signal found in regulatory low-complexity regions and termini rather than catalytic cores, consistent with phosphorylation-prone SLiMs

Summary: Short, intrinsically disordered C‑terminal tails of secreted or membrane‑associated proteins (from microproteins to larger multi‑pass enzymes) and viral accessory microproteins, typically low‑complexity and enriched in proline and basic residues, often immediately downstream of a hydrophobic signal/transmembrane segment; can include cysteine‑rich patches in secreted/toxin peptides.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over contiguous 10–30 aa windows, most frequently at the extreme C‑terminus; often spans a brief helix that transitions into coil with peak signal in the disordered coil; commonly adjacent to a hydrophobic (signal/TM) segment and characterized by low pLDDT; can also occur in short cytosolic juxtamembrane loops of larger multi‑pass proteins.
Exemplars:
- Oomycete RxLR secreted effectors: activation on the C‑terminal tail immediately following a predicted hydrophobic segment, in a low‑confidence helix/coil region.
- Human ST20 (apoptosis/stress‑related microprotein): activation on a short C‑terminal helix‑to‑coil, highly disordered stretch.
- Small uncharacterized microproteins: activation confined to the last ~10–15 residues forming a disordered coil tail.
- Viral accessory/viroporin‑like proteins: activation on basic/proline‑rich cytosolic C‑tails adjacent to a single‑pass TM helix; also applies to non‑TM viral accessory proteins with disordered C‑tails (e.g., Vif).
- Small secreted cysteine‑rich toxins/defensin‑like peptides: activation on short cationic/cysteine‑biased segments within the mature or processing tail.
- ATP synthase epsilon subunits: activation on a conserved, short, disordered C‑terminal regulatory segment in these small mitochondrial/bacterial proteins.
- Multi‑pass membrane enzymes (e.g., phytoene dehydrogenase): activation on short cytosolic C‑terminal or juxtamembrane tails adjacent to TM helices.

Summary: Residue-level detector that activates broadly at sparse positions across diverse protein contexts, with notable preference for disordered/low-complexity regions, mature secreted peptides, and short helical segments (including transmembrane helices and helix-prone regions inside intrinsically disordered stretches). It does not appear to track a single specific motif.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks, typically one to a few strong peaks per protein with additional weaker peaks scattered along the sequence. Strong activation is observed within intrinsically disordered regions (including Gly-rich and polar/charged compositionally biased segments), within short transmembrane helices, and within mature processed peptides. Activation is also seen scattered within globular enzyme domains.
Exemplars:
- Small integral membrane proteins: single strong peak within a short transmembrane helix.
- Secretory preprohormones (e.g., cholecystokinin): multiple peaks within the mature processed peptide regions.
- Homeobox/disordered regulators (e.g., Rhox5): multiple peaks throughout disordered Gly-rich and basic/acidic compositionally biased segments.
- CaMKII inhibitor peptides: peaks at the start of the inhibitory domain and at Pro-rich positions.
- Viral accessory/integrase-like proteins: multiple short peaks scattered across the chain, including disordered C-terminal segments.
- Bacterial/yeast enzymes (e.g., beta-lactamase, aspartyl-tRNA synthetase, imidazolonepropionase, peroxin-9): scattered peaks within N-terminal or globular regions.

Summary: Targeting/processing segments of secretory and organellar proteins—especially N‑terminal signal peptides, secretory propeptides, and mitochondrial/chloroplast transit peptides—together with nearby protease‑cleavage motifs (signal peptidase −3/−1 small‑residue rule, dibasic KR/RR, furin RXXR, caspase DXXD); more generally, low‑complexity S/T/E/D/A/G‑rich disordered stretches (with occasional polybasic clusters) in diverse proteins
Activation pattern: Predominantly regional activation spanning short N‑terminal targeting/propeptide regions or other low‑complexity segments; superimposed residue‑level peaks at canonical cleavage motifs (Ala‑X‑Ala signal peptidase sites, KR/RR convertase or RXXR furin sites, DXXD caspase sites); occasional activation at C‑terminal Type IX secretion signals and internal S/T‑rich acidic linkers
Exemplars: Viral envelope/egress glycoproteins: activation on N‑terminal signal peptides and polybasic furin cleavage sites, plus S/T‑rich lumenal loops; Plant virus RNA‑silencing suppressors (e.g., HC‑Pro/P19): activation on disordered acidic/serine‑rich N‑terminal segments; Animal neuropeptide/prohormone precursors (POMC, tachykinins, etc.): activation on signal peptides and dibasic prohormone convertase sites; Human micropeptides/lncRNA‑derived and testis/sperm‑associated secreted microproteins: activation on short signal peptides or acidic low‑complexity regions; Yeast mitochondrial proteins: activation on N‑terminal transit peptides (Ser/Thr/Ala‑rich, Arg‑enriched, low in hydrophobic/acidic residues) and their MPP cleavage vicinity; Chloroplast/archaeal tRNA/RNA‑processing enzymes and bacterial transporters: activation on acidic/polar low‑complexity N/C‑terminal tails or linkers; Porphyromonas gingivalis gingipain cysteine proteases: activation on N‑terminal signal/propeptide and C‑terminal Type IX secretion CTD; Human apoptosis/stress‑related proteins: peaks at caspase DXXD cleavage motifs within acidic/disordered regions

Summary: Hydrophobic residues (often Ile, Leu, Met, Ala, Trp) in non-catalytic regions flanking structured catalytic cores, including N-terminal extensions, cytoplasmic tails, and transmembrane segments of membrane/secreted and viral proteins; largely absent from folded catalytic domains.

Activation pattern: Sharp residue-level peaks centered on hydrophobic/aromatic residues, often clustered in short stretches; located in N-terminal regulatory extensions, flexible/coil regions adjacent to structured domains, and within transmembrane helices; minimal to none within well-folded catalytic domains such as PPM phosphatase or PARP catalytic folds.

Exemplars:
- PPM/PP2C phosphatases: activation confined to the N-terminal regulatory extension; no activation in the metal-binding PPM catalytic domain.
- PARP family: peaks in the N-terminal region upstream of the WGR and PARP catalytic domains.
- HIV accessory proteins (Vpr, Vif): peaks on hydrophobic residues in functional/interaction regions (e.g., APOBEC3F F1-box, SOCS box-like region).
- GPCRs and related membrane receptors: activation on hydrophobic residues within transmembrane helices and adjacent cytoplasmic segments.
- Sperm/testis proteins: scattered peaks on hydrophobic and Thr/Pro residues outside annotated acidic/basic low-complexity stretches.
- Protein kinases: disordered N- or C-terminal regulatory tails rather than the conserved kinase fold.
- Plastid-encoded RNA polymerase subunits (PEP): acidic/disordered N- or C-terminal extensions.
- Prokaryotic metabolic/cofactor enzymes: only in short low-complexity insertions or termini, not in the structured catalytic cores.

Summary: Short linear segments in intrinsically disordered or otherwise low-structure-confidence regions, often at N-termini and within signal peptides/propeptides of secreted and regulatory proteins (including viral accessory proteins and small ORF microproteins), enriched in small/basic residues (G, P, S, A, R; often with Cys), rather than in well-folded catalytic cores.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks scattered across IDRs and low-confidence coils/short helices; frequently clustered near the N-terminus, in signal peptides, propeptides, and disordered tails; little to no activation in well-structured domains; occasional activation in low-confidence transmembrane/signal-anchor helices.
Exemplars: - Viral accessory protein (HIV-1 Vif): peaks throughout low-pLDDT coils, especially the disordered N-terminal region.
- Neuropeptide precursor (Drosophila Amnesiac): activation in the N-terminal signal peptide and multiple mature peptide segments with very low pLDDT.
- Secreted serine carboxypeptidase: activation confined to disordered C-terminal tail, annotated disordered segment, the signal peptide, and a low-confidence C-terminal transmembrane helix; absent from the structured catalytic domain.
- Disordered human tumor-suppressor–associated protein (ST20): scattered peaks within predicted helices in a globally disordered chain, including the N-terminus.
- lncRNA/sORF-derived microprotein (IGF2 antisense protein): multiple peaks across annotated disordered regions rich in Arg/Pro/Gly.

Summary: Residue-level detector that activates broadly at sparse positions across diverse protein contexts, with notable preference for disordered/low-complexity regions, mature secreted peptides, and short helical segments (including transmembrane helices and helix-prone regions inside intrinsically disordered stretches). It does not appear to track a single specific motif.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks, typically one to a few strong peaks per protein with additional weaker peaks scattered along the sequence. Strong activation is observed within intrinsically disordered regions (including Gly-rich and polar/charged compositionally biased segments), within short transmembrane helices, and within mature processed peptides. Activation is also seen scattered within globular enzyme domains.
Exemplars:
- Small integral membrane proteins: single strong peak within a short transmembrane helix.
- Secretory preprohormones (e.g., cholecystokinin): multiple peaks within the mature processed peptide regions.
- Homeobox/disordered regulators (e.g., Rhox5): multiple peaks throughout disordered Gly-rich and basic/acidic compositionally biased segments.
- CaMKII inhibitor peptides: peaks at the start of the inhibitory domain and at Pro-rich positions.
- Viral accessory/integrase-like proteins: multiple short peaks scattered across the chain, including disordered C-terminal segments.
- Bacterial/yeast enzymes (e.g., beta-lactamase, aspartyl-tRNA synthetase, imidazolonepropionase, peroxin-9): scattered peaks within N-terminal or globular regions.

Summary: Short segments within disordered and compositionally biased stretches of diverse proteins, particularly regions enriched in basic and acidic residues. Activations are also seen in non-disordered contexts across proteins of varied function, suggesting the feature captures a relatively broad local sequence pattern rather than a tight structural motif.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks with small clusters, distributed throughout the length of the protein. Peaks frequently overlap annotated disordered regions and basic/acidic compositionally biased segments, but also occur at isolated positions within structured chains; occurs in both helical and coil contexts.
Exemplars: - Oomycete RxLR secreted effectors: peaks within the mature effector chain, with occasional spikes in the signal peptide.
- Plant CLE peptide precursors: localized peaks within the C-terminal CLE motif corresponding to the mature signaling peptide.
- Cholecystokinin prohormone: peaks at or immediately adjacent to the N-termini of mature neuropeptides generated by proteolytic processing.
- Herpesvirus ICP47-like small accessory proteins: multiple peaks in the N-terminal active helical region and in polar, disordered C-terminal stretches.
- Keratin-associated proteins: activation across cysteine/proline/serine-rich, low-complexity repeat regions.
- Phosphodiesterase and fungal/bacterial enzymes with disordered N- or internal stretches: peaks within basic-and-acidic compositionally biased segments.

Summary: Low-complexity, intrinsically disordered segments—often at protein N-termini—such as mucin-like/propeptide regions or flexible linkers adjacent to signal/transit peptides, common in small secreted or membrane-associated proteins and also as disordered extensions in diverse enzymes (broad taxonomic coverage, including viral, bacterial, and eukaryotic proteins).
Activation pattern: Regional activation over short to moderate stretches, frequently in disordered or polar/low-complexity segments; in longer proteins, multiple low-complexity patches can activate; in micropeptides, activation can span much of the sequence. Residue-level peaks can fall on Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly within polar-residue stretches but also on basic or hydrophobic residues within the same disordered context.
Exemplars:
- Viral envelope/accessory microproteins: activation on N-terminal Ser/Thr/Pro-rich disordered segments (often mucin-like or regulatory tails).
- Secreted eukaryotic effectors (e.g., oomycete RxLR effectors): activation on the low-complexity region flanking the signal peptide/RxLR motif.
- Human testis-biased and lncRNA-derived micropeptides: activation across intrinsically disordered peptide regions.
- Secreted precursors/propeptides: activation on N-terminal regions following the signal peptide.
- Membrane-associated single-pass proteins: activation on luminal or cytosolic tails flanking the transmembrane helix.
- Bacterial/archaeal metabolic enzymes: activation on disordered, low-complexity N-terminal extensions/linkers enriched in Ser/Thr/Gly/Pro.

Summary: Short residue windows in mixed-composition regions of diverse proteins, frequently in N-terminal or non-catalytic portions of enzymes, transmembrane-adjacent stretches, and small secreted peptides.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks concentrated in short 3–7 residue windows, often clustered with several nearby peaks. Activated residues are chemically diverse (including hydrophobic, polar, and charged residues) and can occur in helical transmembrane segments, disordered linkers, or globular regions outside annotated catalytic/binding sites.
Exemplars:
- Bacterial DNA ligase: clusters of peaks in the N-terminal region upstream of the catalytic and BRCT domains.
- Viral integrase homolog: short peaks within the chain including a GPAYGRP-containing segment.
- Peroxisomal biogenesis factor 9 (Pex9): peaks overlapping helical transmembrane segments and an adjacent disordered/polar region.
- Small secreted peptides (e.g., Califin-B large subunit): short peaks within the mature peptide.

Summary: Generic detector of low-complexity or low-structure segments, with a bias toward the N-terminal portion of proteins, including secretory signal peptides, disordered N-terminal stretches, and short membrane-embedded helical regions.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks; sparse, isolated activations often concentrated within the first ~100 residues (frequently within the first 30), though peaks can also appear in mid-protein membrane or low-complexity stretches. Peaks occur within signal peptides, low-pLDDT disordered coils, and short helices, including transmembrane helical segments; rarely form contiguous runs.
Exemplars: - Secreted serpin (antithrombin): peak in the N‑terminal signal peptide and additional peaks in a longer disordered N‑terminal segment.
- Antimicrobial peptide precursor (lumbricin): strong peaks confined to the N‑terminal signal peptide; minimal activation in the mature peptide.
- Secreted bacterial catalase–peroxidase (KatG): minor peaks in the signal peptide and immediately at the start of the mature chain.
- Poxvirus accessory protein: multiple peaks across low-confidence, disordered regions near the N‑terminus.
- Retroviral integrase homolog: peaks near the N‑terminus and at residues just before an annotated disordered linker.
- p53-induced DNA-binding protein (Killin): peaks on basic residues within a low‑pLDDT, N‑terminal DNA-binding region.
- Small membrane protein (ATP synthase subunit 8): peaks within an N-terminal transmembrane helix.

Summary: Low-complexity, compositionally biased segments in intrinsically disordered regions, typically enriched in Gly and/or Pro and frequently punctuated by aromatic residues (Tyr/Phe/Trp). YG/YGG/GYG motifs are common but not required. These tracts are common in secreted/extracellular proteins, antimicrobial/allergen precursors, and prion-like or reproductive IDRs.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across low-pLDDT coil-rich tracts with short Gly/Pro runs and intermittent aromatics; local peaks at Gly, Pro, and aromatic residues. Strongly off in well-structured helices/strands, transmembranes, and folded domains; activation often concentrates in N-terminal low-complexity leaders or propeptides.
Exemplars:
- Peroxisomal membrane protein PEX13: N-terminal Gly/Pro- and Tyr/Phe-punctuated low-complexity coil; off in TM and SH3 domain.
- Small heat shock protein (Hsp42): N-terminal IDR with Y/F/G/P motifs; off over the alpha-crystallin domain.
- Keratin-associated proteins and other extracellular structural proteins (e.g., caseins, chorion components): activation on Gly/Pro/Tyr-rich repeats.
- Plant HIPPs: activation on Pro/Tyr/Gly-rich low-complexity segments.
- Antimicrobial peptide precursors (e.g., clavanin) and allergens: activation on low-complexity signal/propeptides or IDRs that can be Pro/His-rich with occasional aromatics.
- Proline-rich salivary proteins (e.g., opiorphin/PRP1 precursors): activation on basic Pro-rich low-complexity stretches.
- Reproductive proteins including protamine/protamine-like: activation on simple Arg/Lys-rich low-complexity segments or cleaved propeptides when present.

Summary: Arg/Lys-rich, intrinsically disordered low‑complexity tails that mediate electrostatic binding and condensation of nucleic acids—found in histones (esp. H1 and core histone N‑terminal tails), protamines, viral nucleoproteins/capsid cores, and bacterial/archaeal nucleoid proteins; enriched for interspersed Ser/Pro/Gly and dipeptide/repeat patterns such as SP/TP, RS/SR, and RG/RGG
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long polybasic IDRs; strong, contiguous activation on entire very short basic polypeptides (e.g., protamines, viral basic cores) and on specific basic segments within larger proteins, especially N‑terminal histone tails and Lys/Arg‑rich low‑complexity tracts; residue‑level peaks over runs of R/K and RS/SR, SP/TP, RGG motifs
Exemplars: - Protamines and protamine‑like sperm nuclear proteins — activation spans the whole Arg/Lys‑rich, low‑complexity chain used for genome hyper‑condensation.
- Linker histone H1 family (including testis/oocyte‑specific variants) — activation on the long Lys/Ser/Pro‑rich C‑terminal tail and basic N‑terminal segment that contact linker DNA.
- Core histones and centromeric histone variants (e.g., CENP‑A) — activation on the N‑terminal basic tails that interact with DNA and are sites of proline‑directed phosphorylation (SP/TP).
- High mobility group/AT‑hook proteins (HMGA/HMGN) — activation over clusters of AT‑hooks (RGRP‑like) and adjacent Lys/Arg‑rich low‑complexity tracts.
- Bacterial/chlamydial/archaeal nucleoid‑associated or histone‑like proteins (e.g., HU/IHF, HctA/B, archaeal histones) — activation on basic tails and Lys/Arg‑rich segments that compact the chromosome.
- Kinetoplastid histone H1‑like (kinetoplast‑associated proteins) — activation across Lys/Ser/Pro‑rich disordered regions that package kDNA.
- Viral nucleocapsid/core and histone‑like proteins — activation on protamine‑like basic regions that nonspecifically coat and condense viral RNA/DNA.

Summary: Glycine-rich low‑complexity, intrinsically disordered repeat segments, especially those containing glycine–aromatic dipeptides (FG, GY) and related small‑residue motifs (G/S/P with optional C enrichment), as found in FG‑nucleoporins and in structural/adhesive proteins of metazoan integuments (keratin‑associated, cuticle/eggshell, epidermal) and other glycine‑rich biomaterials
Activation pattern: Long, contiguous activation across disordered low‑complexity regions; strongest residue‑level peaks on glycine and aromatic positions within FG/GY repeats; tolerates S/P/C within G‑rich tracts; little to no activation in folded helical/strand domains
Exemplars: - FG‑nucleoporins (e.g., Nup54/Nup62/Nup98): activation on the FG‑repeat IDRs (e.g., N‑terminal FG blocks), absent from structured C‑terminal domains.
- Keratin‑associated proteins (KAPs; high‑GY and high‑sulfur/cysteine‑rich types): activation across GY‑rich or C/G‑rich low‑complexity stretches in hair/wool matrix proteins.
- Intermediate filament proteins (keratins, vimentin, beaded filament proteins): activation on Gly/Ser‑rich head and tail IDRs that modulate filament assembly.
- Arthropod cuticle/eggshell structural proteins: activation on glycine‑ and aromatic‑rich repetitive low‑complexity segments involved in exoskeletal matrices.
- Extracellular adhesive/biomaterial proteins (silk‑like, mussel/barnacle/caddisfly adhesives): activation on G/Y‑rich repetitive blocks in secreted biomaterials.
- Short secreted peptides (neuropeptides, toxins, antimicrobial peptides): activation on short repetitive G/Y‑motif segments (often low complexity).
- Plant glycine‑rich and proline‑rich cell wall/epidermal proteins: activation on glycine‑rich or P/G/S low‑complexity tracts.

Summary: Low-complexity segments, most commonly in extracellular/cell-surface proteins, comprising two frequently co-occurring subclasses: (a) aromatic–glycine–rich repeats enriched in G/Y with WG/WGY and His/Pro interspersed, and (b) cysteine-rich tracts and micropeptides (often disulfide-stabilized) that may lack GY but are strongly Cys-punctuated. These also appear as shorter motifs or isolated His/Cys peaks in other proteins (e.g., metallothioneins) and in intracellular structural LCRs (e.g., neurofilament/protamine tails) where sparse His and occasional aromatic–glycine micro-motifs are embedded in basic/acidic repeats.
Activation pattern: Primarily regional activation across these LCRs; residue-level peaks at aromatic–glycine dipeptides and histidines, and at cysteine clusters/disulfide motifs; signal often spans disordered coils and can extend into an adjacent α-helix at a coil–helix boundary; in intracellular scaffolds, activation may be limited to short His/aromatic–Gly micro-motifs within long basic/acidic tails.
Exemplars: - Keratin-associated proteins (high glycine–tyrosine and/or high sulfur types): activation over GY- and Cys-rich low-complexity repeats.
- Fungal cell-wall/GPI-anchored glycoproteins (e.g., SPI1, CPP3): activation on extracellular low-complexity segments with GY/WG motifs and/or Cys-rich patches.
- Prion family (PrP central region, Shadoo): strong activation across low-complexity aromatic–glycine/H-containing tracts near coil–helix boundaries.
- Disulfide-rich antimicrobial peptides (e.g., tachyplesins/defensins): activation over short Cys-clustered segments lacking extended GY repeats.
- Metallothioneins and other Cys-dense proteins: localized/regional activation on cysteine clusters.
- Neuropeptide/antimicrobial precursors with GY-rich tracts: activation on GY/YG/WG repeats within propeptide regions.
- Cytoskeletal intermediate filaments (e.g., neurofilaments): activation on disordered head/tail regions via sparse His and occasional aromatic–glycine micro-motifs embedded in basic/acidic repeats.
