Summary: Extracellular/periplasmic low-complexity linear segments—typically intrinsically flexible N-terminal tails, periplasmic loops, or secreted propeptide regions—enriched in metal-contacting residues (Cys/His/Met) or other compositionally biased motifs (Pro/Gly- and acidic/cationic repeats), used for transition‑metal capture/sensing (Cu/Zn), envelope‑stress/quality‑control interactions, and bioactive peptide stretches in secreted precursors.
Activation pattern: Primarily regional activation across disordered or compositionally biased segments with superimposed residue‑level peaks: strong on Cys clusters (metallothioneins), Met‑rich motifs (CTR N‑termini), and His patches; additional hotspots in Pro/Gly tracts and Arg/Lys‑rich segments within AMP/kinin/neuropeptide precursors. Activation is biased to extracellular/periplasmic regions (often N‑terminal), including sensor loops and secreted propeptides; it is weak/absent in signal peptides and well‑ordered transmembrane or globular cores.
Exemplars:
- CTR-family copper transporters: N‑terminal extracellular Met‑rich, disordered metal‑binding domains.
- Metallothioneins: pervasive activation on Cys arrays across the chain for metal sequestration.
- Periplasmic Zn/Cu-handling proteins: zinc chaperones (AztD/AztC) and multicopper oxidases (CueO) with metal‑interacting flexible segments.
- Two‑component sensor histidine kinases: flexible periplasmic sensory loops adjacent to transmembranes.
- Periplasmic stress-response accessory proteins (CpxP-like): disordered, compositionally biased periplasmic regions mediating envelope stress signaling.
- Secreted salivary proline‑rich proteins: long proline‑rich tandem‑repeat regions in disordered central segments.
- Antimicrobial and neuropeptide precursors: residues within annotated bioactive peptide blocks (AMPs/kinins/neuropeptides).
- Biomineralization proteins (magnetosome membrane proteins): low‑complexity, metal‑contacting luminal loops associated with mineral handling.

Summary: Gly/Thr/Ser/Pro–rich low-complexity segments and flexible linker/tail regions—including cleavage-derived peptides with GG/GT repeats—in structural assemblies and stress/cytoskeletal proteins
Activation pattern: Regional activation across contiguous segments, frequently C-terminal or flanking protease cleavage sites, sometimes extending into adjacent structured elements at domain boundaries
Exemplars: - Adenovirus capsid linker (protein VIII): strong, sustained activation across the C-terminal hexon-linking peptide produced by proteolysis, spanning unstructured coil and a short terminal helix.
- Cilia/flagella-associated scaffold (CFAP96): activation confined to annotated disordered coil regions; absent from long stable alpha-helices.
- Plant LEA/dehydrin: high activation on an N-terminal glycine/polar-rich low-complexity tract within a fully disordered region.
- ARF-GAP regulators: broad activation over the C-terminal disordered, polar/basic tail; no activation in the folded N-terminal GAP domain.
- Ribosomal protein uS19: activation on the flexible, low-confidence C-terminal tail with minor nearby peaks.
- Viral structural proteins (capsid/tail/core, including phage tape measure proteins): long flexible segments, cleavage-flanking peptides, and linker peptides between assembly domains show strong activation, often with GG/GT-rich context.
- Rare outlier: metabotropic glutamate receptor 1 shows a single peak within a structured helix, consistent with occasional boundary/sequence-composition matches.

Summary: G/A/S/T/P/Q/N-biased, glycine-rich low-complexity and disordered segments — including flexible tails, linkers, and propeptides — in extracellular/virion-associated proteins (assembly, entry, secretion), with the feature also tolerating small-residue beta-strand/coil stretches in beta-rich assembly factors.
Activation pattern: Broad regional activation across contiguous stretches enriched in small residues (often including short Gly runs), frequently covering most or all of small virion proteins; residue-level peaks fall within these low-complexity or small-residue segments and can localize to either terminus or to internal small-residue tracts; in some beta-rich extracellular assemblies (e.g., CsgF) the signal maps to compact beta-strand/coil subregions; in non-viral enzymes, activation can narrow to isolated glycine-rich or polar disordered loops.
Exemplars: - Viral capsid and envelope proteins (e.g., adenovirus minor capsid proteins IIIa/VIII/VI; plant virus coat/movement/readthrough proteins; bacteriophage portal/tail/core/ejection proteins): activation on gly/ser-rich low-complexity tails and linkers used in assembly and entry.
- Bacteriophage muralytic enzymes (endolysins/transglycosylases): activation on gly/ser-rich linkers or N-terminal prosegments connecting catalytic and cell wall–binding domains.
- Type III secretion system components (needle/translocon/pilin) and extracellular assembly factors: activation on low-complexity tails or small-residue beta-strand/coil segments involved in secretion/assembly.
- Curli biogenesis factor CsgF: activation over the C-terminal beta-sheet domain (beta-strands and connecting coils enriched in small residues).
- Retroviral/endogenous retroviral envelope glycoproteins: activation on low-complexity, Asn/Ser/Thr/Gly-rich loops and N-terminal segments associated with processing and host interaction.
- Small secreted antimicrobial and toxin peptides: activation on N-terminal leader/propeptides and glycine-rich low-complexity regions that mediate secretion/processing.

Summary: Glycine-biased, low-complexity coil/linker segments—often containing GG or small-residue motifs—that mark flexible junctions and proteolytic processing sites (leaders/propeptides, viral protease cuts), and that in NTPases coincide with the glycine-rich Walker A phosphate-binding loop
Activation pattern: - Predominantly regional activation across disordered, glycine/serine/threonine-rich stretches; enriched for G and R with interspersed E/D
- Sharp residue-level peaks at GG motifs and at helix–coil junctions
- Frequently near N-termini (leaders/propeptides and NBD/P-loop regions)
- In P-loop NTPases, concentrates on the glycine-rich Walker A (GxxxxGKT) loop
Exemplars: - Adenoviral structural proteins (e.g., hexon-linking protein VIII): GG motifs and adjacent residues in disordered regions flanking viral protease cleavage sites
- Viral capsid/tail proteins (including bacteriophage tape measure): glycines in flexible loops and helix–loop transitions
- Peptide hormone/neuropeptide precursors (e.g., KiSS-1): N-terminal disordered propeptides/leader regions around processing sites
- RiPP/bacteriocin precursors: N-terminal double-glycine leader cleavage motifs recognized by ABC transporter peptidases
- ABC transporter ATP-binding/NBD proteins (P-loop NTPases): glycine-rich Walker A phosphate-binding loop, often near the N-terminus of the domain
- Carbohydrate-active enzymes (glycoside hydrolases): glycine/threonine-rich interdomain linkers connecting catalytic and binding modules
- Sperm/protamine family proteins: arginine/glycine-rich low-complexity tracts
- Microtubule-associated Jupiter proteins: basic, low-complexity flexible segments
- Purine biosynthesis and tRNA/rRNA-modifying enzymes: glycine-rich loops/flexible hinges adjacent to functional motifs

Summary: Membrane‑active amphipathic α‑helices enriched in small hydrophobic residues (A/V/L/I/G) that insert into, line, or associate with lipid bilayers—i.e., the pore‑forming/translocation helices of toxins and translocons and analogous lipid‑binding/stress‑sensing helices in other membrane proteins
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long, contiguous helical segments (often single helices or helical hairpins), with sparse charges and frequent Gly/Ala runs; peaks track α‑helical stretches that often fold upon membrane contact (low pLDDT in isolation). Activation typically avoids catalytic motifs and generic signal peptides/TM anchors, instead favoring amphipathic or pore‑lining helices (including lipid‑binding helices) within toxin, antimicrobial, and membrane‑associated domains.
Exemplars: - Pore-forming colicins: strong activation on the C‑terminal pore‑forming transmembrane/helical hairpin region.
- Bacillus thuringiensis Cry (δ‑endotoxins): activation on the N‑terminal pore‑forming helical bundle (domain I) with peaks in membrane‑inserting helices.
- Cationic antimicrobial peptides (e.g., Styelin‑D): activation confined to the mature amphipathic α‑helix; absent on the signal peptide and propeptide.
- Mitochondrial inner‑membrane protease OMA1: activation on amphipathic helices within the peptidase domain, including a cardiolipin‑binding/stress‑sensor region; little to no activation on the N‑terminal propeptide or the single‑pass TM anchor.

Summary: Arg/Lys-rich, low-complexity, intrinsically disordered basic segments (often S/T-interspersed) that mediate electrostatic binding to polyanions—primarily nucleic acids (DNA/RNA) in chromatin, ribosomes, and viral genomes—and, in some cases, other anionic targets; typically realized as long polybasic tails or entire small basic proteins
Activation pattern: Regional activation over long stretches of K/R-rich sequence, frequently covering N- or C-terminal tails or the entirety of small basic proteins; strongest in predicted-disordered/coil regions with compositional bias for basic residues and often enriched in Ser/Thr; in multi-domain proteins, activation is confined to flexible basic segments rather than structured cores
Exemplars: - Linker histones H1/H5 and H1-like proteins: activation on the Lys/Arg-rich, disordered C-terminal tails that compact chromatin (e.g., histone-like protein 18C C-terminal tail).
- Sperm nuclear proteins (protamines and transition proteins): activation across the whole, highly basic, disordered proteins that neutralize and condense DNA.
- Archaeal chromatin proteins (histone HMf/HMz, H1-like): activation on basic DNA-binding tails/segments.
- Ribosomal proteins (various small/acidic-binding subunits): activation on Lys-rich terminal extensions that contact rRNA.
- Small acid-soluble spore proteins (SASPs): full-length activation of their highly basic DNA-binding polypeptides.
- Viral DNA-condensing/packaging and core DNA-binding proteins (e.g., adenovirus/phage basic proteins, terminal proteins): activation on polybasic segments used for genome binding/packaging.
- Cationic antimicrobial/bacteriocin peptides: activation on Lys/Arg-rich, low-complexity cationic stretches.
- Plant RALF-like secreted peptides: activation on polybasic stretches within the propeptide/mature region.
- Viral serine/threonine kinases: activation on polybasic, disordered segments (often NLS-like regions).
- Mollusk sperm H1/protamine-like proteins: activation on extended Lys/Arg-rich tails or entire basic proteins involved in DNA compaction.

Summary: Short, intrinsically disordered C‑terminal tails of secreted or membrane‑associated proteins (from microproteins to larger multi‑pass enzymes) and viral accessory microproteins, typically low‑complexity and enriched in proline and basic residues, often immediately downstream of a hydrophobic signal/transmembrane segment; can include cysteine‑rich patches in secreted/toxin peptides.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over contiguous 10–30 aa windows, most frequently at the extreme C‑terminus; often spans a brief helix that transitions into coil with peak signal in the disordered coil; commonly adjacent to a hydrophobic (signal/TM) segment and characterized by low pLDDT; can also occur in short cytosolic juxtamembrane loops of larger multi‑pass proteins.
Exemplars:
- Oomycete RxLR secreted effectors: activation on the C‑terminal tail immediately following a predicted hydrophobic segment, in a low‑confidence helix/coil region.
- Human ST20 (apoptosis/stress‑related microprotein): activation on a short C‑terminal helix‑to‑coil, highly disordered stretch.
- Small uncharacterized microproteins: activation confined to the last ~10–15 residues forming a disordered coil tail.
- Viral accessory/viroporin‑like proteins: activation on basic/proline‑rich cytosolic C‑tails adjacent to a single‑pass TM helix; also applies to non‑TM viral accessory proteins with disordered C‑tails (e.g., Vif).
- Small secreted cysteine‑rich toxins/defensin‑like peptides: activation on short cationic/cysteine‑biased segments within the mature or processing tail.
- ATP synthase epsilon subunits: activation on a conserved, short, disordered C‑terminal regulatory segment in these small mitochondrial/bacterial proteins.
- Multi‑pass membrane enzymes (e.g., phytoene dehydrogenase): activation on short cytosolic C‑terminal or juxtamembrane tails adjacent to TM helices.

Summary: Single-pass alpha-helical transmembrane signal-anchor segments in small membrane proteins across taxa; a 15–25-residue hydrophobic helix used to anchor proteins in lipid bilayers, enriched in Leu/Ile/Val/Phe with internal aromatics and glycines, few charges, occasional cysteines, and rare internal prolines.
Activation pattern: Strong regional activation over a single, contiguous hydrophobic helix (typically 15–25 residues), with residue-level peaks in the hydrophobic/aromatic core and minimal activation in flanking cytosolic/periplasmic/luminal regions; often near the N-terminus (signal-anchor) but can occur mid-sequence; coincides with annotated/predicted alpha-helical transmembrane segments.
Exemplars: - Bacteriophage lysis proteins — activation on their sole membrane-spanning anchor helix.
- Virion membrane proteins (e.g., poxvirus/orthopox orthologs) — activation on the N-terminal helical signal-anchor.
- Plant viral movement proteins — activation on the single transmembrane helix.
- Photosystem II assembly factor Psb34 — activation on its thylakoid single-pass transmembrane helix.
- Cytochrome bd ubiquinol oxidase small accessory subunit (CydX) — activation on its single membrane-spanning helix.
- Endoregulin-like micropeptide regulators — activation on their single, helical membrane anchor.

Summary: Short hydrophobic alpha-helical segments enriched in small aliphatic residues (A, V, I, L with frequent T/G), depleted of charged/aromatic residues—commonly the h‑region of Sec signal peptides, short transmembrane helices, and internal helix-forming hydrophobic patches in both membrane and soluble proteins; often N‑terminal but also internal/C‑terminal.
Activation pattern: Regional activation on contiguous hydrophobic clusters predicted as alpha‑helix, with sharp residue‑level peaks at A/V/I/L/T (often with G); observed in signal peptides, TM segments, and internal helices; occurs in both structured and disordered contexts (not restricted to low pLDDT).
Exemplars: Adenovirus E4‑ORF4 and HCV ARFP: internal hydrophobic helix‑prone stretches in small viral proteins; Oomycete RxLR effectors and yeast killer toxin precursors: strong activation on N‑terminal Sec signal peptides; Bacterial cytochrome c oxidase subunit 2 and DHHC palmitoyltransferases: activation on short transmembrane helices; Kdo transferase and OMA hydratase: activation on internal hydrophobic helices within soluble/peripheral membrane enzymes.

Summary: Short hydrophobic targeting helices and cationic amphipathic motifs that mediate membrane/organellar targeting or unconventional secretion—encompassing classical N‑terminal signal peptides, internal signal‑anchor helices, C‑terminal tail‑anchors, mitochondrial targeting helices, and CPP‑like basic/aromatic motifs. Enriched for Leu/Phe with Tyr/Trp at helix boundaries; Arg/His frequent; acidic residues (D/E) scarce. In very small secreted/toxin-like proteins, activation can extend into cysteine/proline‑rich mature regions; in soluble enzymes/regulators it may mark short amphipathic or hydrophobic helices.

Activation pattern: Predominantly regional activation over 15–30 aa hydrophobic segments (whether N‑terminal signal peptides/signal anchors or C‑terminal tail‑anchors); in microproteins, activation can span most of the sequence; in large soluble proteins, limited residue‑level peaks over short amphipathic/basic or hydrophobic helices (e.g., DNA/RNA‑binding or coiled‑coil segments).

Exemplars:
- Viral envelope/accessory and regulatory proteins — activation on N‑terminal signal/signal‑anchor helices or on CPP‑like Arg/Trp‑enriched motifs (e.g., Tat‑like proteins) enabling leaderless export/cellular entry.
- Secreted peptide precursors (hormones, antimicrobial peptides, venom toxins, immune effectors) — activation on the signal peptide; in very short precursors, also across the cysteine/proline‑rich mature region.
- Oomycete RxLR effectors — activation on the N‑terminal signal peptide immediately upstream of the RxLR motif.
- Human microproteins/lncRNA‑derived peptides — activation across a single hydrophobic TM helix acting as a signal anchor or tail‑anchor, or short amphipathic targeting motifs.
- Mitochondrial nucleus‑encoded proteins (e.g., mitochondrial ribosomal proteins; ATP synthase-associated subunits) — activation on N‑terminal mitochondrial targeting helices or short hydrophobic segments.
- Bacterial/archaeal enzymes and phage integrases — isolated peaks over internal hydrophobic or amphipathic helices (e.g., helix‑turn‑helix/coiled‑coil regions) without spanning whole domains.
- Tail‑anchored SNAREs and other vesicle proteins — activation on the C‑terminal transmembrane tail‑anchor.

Summary: N-terminal intrinsically disordered, low-complexity tails (typically 10–70 residues) enriched in polar/charged and Pro/Gly/Ser/Thr residues that often contain a short helix; these segments act as generic targeting/interaction modules (short linear motifs) for assembly, translocation, or compartment/complex association across diverse proteins.
Activation pattern: Regional activation confined to the extreme N-terminus: a single contiguous cluster with a peak within the first ~10–40 residues, coincident with IDR/low-complexity annotations and low pLDDT; activation falls off before the folded core and is largely absent from structured domains; can appear as multiple short N-terminal clusters in repeat-rich proteins.
Exemplars: - GrpE (Hsp70 co-chaperone): disordered N-terminal tail with mixed charged composition and short helix propensity.
- SRP receptor FtsY: acidic, low-complexity A-domain at the N-terminus (disordered helix-prone segment).
- Gas vesicle protein O: charged low-complexity N-terminus containing a short disordered helix.
- Carboxysome maintenance protein McdB: N-terminal IDR required for McdA:DNA complex interaction.
- Magnetosome-associated MamJ: glycine-biased, disordered N-terminal tail preceding acidic repeats.
- Bacterial microcompartment enzyme EutE: short N-terminal BMC-targeting helix within an IDR.
- Prokaryotic ubiquitin-like protein Pup: short disordered N-terminal segment adjacent to the ARC/Mpa ATPase-binding site.
- Specialized prokaryotic organelle proteins (gas vesicle, carboxysome, magnetosome): shared use of N-terminal low-complexity IDRs as assembly/targeting segments.

Summary: Low-complexity, intrinsically disordered segments—often at protein N-termini—such as mucin-like/propeptide regions or flexible linkers adjacent to signal/transit peptides, common in small secreted or membrane-associated proteins and also as disordered extensions in diverse enzymes (broad taxonomic coverage, including viral, bacterial, and eukaryotic proteins).
Activation pattern: Regional activation over short to moderate stretches, frequently in disordered or polar/low-complexity segments; in longer proteins, multiple low-complexity patches can activate; in micropeptides, activation can span much of the sequence. Residue-level peaks can fall on Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly within polar-residue stretches but also on basic or hydrophobic residues within the same disordered context.
Exemplars:
- Viral envelope/accessory microproteins: activation on N-terminal Ser/Thr/Pro-rich disordered segments (often mucin-like or regulatory tails).
- Secreted eukaryotic effectors (e.g., oomycete RxLR effectors): activation on the low-complexity region flanking the signal peptide/RxLR motif.
- Human testis-biased and lncRNA-derived micropeptides: activation across intrinsically disordered peptide regions.
- Secreted precursors/propeptides: activation on N-terminal regions following the signal peptide.
- Membrane-associated single-pass proteins: activation on luminal or cytosolic tails flanking the transmembrane helix.
- Bacterial/archaeal metabolic enzymes: activation on disordered, low-complexity N-terminal extensions/linkers enriched in Ser/Thr/Gly/Pro.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low-complexity segments enriched in serine/threonine/proline/glycine and often basic (lysine/arginine), typically found in flexible N- or C-terminal tails and loops; highlights IDRs that may harbor short linear motifs (e.g., basic NLS patches) rather than structured domain cores.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long disordered stretches with additional sparse residue-level peaks in low-confidence loops; often N-terminal-biased in short/viral proteins; rarely within well-folded cores.
Exemplars: Retroviral accessory proteins (e.g., HTLV-1 p30): activation on central and C-terminal IDRs including a basic nuclear localization signal; p53-regulated apoptosis-inducing microprotein: widespread activation across a globally disordered protein; Bacterial DNA ligase: scattered activation in an annotated disordered linker and flexible loops within the ligase domain; Uncharacterized human microprotein: multiple peaks throughout a low-pLDDT, disordered sequence irrespective of predicted secondary structure.

Summary: Residue-level detector that activates broadly at sparse positions across diverse protein contexts, with notable preference for disordered/low-complexity regions, mature secreted peptides, and short helical segments (including transmembrane helices and helix-prone regions inside intrinsically disordered stretches). It does not appear to track a single specific motif.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks, typically one to a few strong peaks per protein with additional weaker peaks scattered along the sequence. Strong activation is observed within intrinsically disordered regions (including Gly-rich and polar/charged compositionally biased segments), within short transmembrane helices, and within mature processed peptides. Activation is also seen scattered within globular enzyme domains.
Exemplars:
- Small integral membrane proteins: single strong peak within a short transmembrane helix.
- Secretory preprohormones (e.g., cholecystokinin): multiple peaks within the mature processed peptide regions.
- Homeobox/disordered regulators (e.g., Rhox5): multiple peaks throughout disordered Gly-rich and basic/acidic compositionally biased segments.
- CaMKII inhibitor peptides: peaks at the start of the inhibitory domain and at Pro-rich positions.
- Viral accessory/integrase-like proteins: multiple short peaks scattered across the chain, including disordered C-terminal segments.
- Bacterial/yeast enzymes (e.g., beta-lactamase, aspartyl-tRNA synthetase, imidazolonepropionase, peroxin-9): scattered peaks within N-terminal or globular regions.

Summary: The feature recognizes cationic, amphipathic, low-complexity segments that mediate targeting or membrane/lipid association—classically N‑terminal signal/transit/leader-like regions of secreted, mitochondrial, and viral proteins—and frequently the propeptide/mature regions of toxin and neuropeptide precursors; it can also highlight short basic/hydrophobic helices or redox-active motifs within structured domains.
Activation pattern: Predominantly long, continuous activation over N‑terminal, low‑pLDDT leader/propeptide regions enriched in Lys/Arg, Ser/Pro and hydrophobic/aromatic residues; with occasional residue-level peaks within well-structured helices (e.g., specific positions in thioredoxin CGHC motifs or matrix-exposed helices of membrane proteins).
Exemplars: 
- Venom phospholipase A2 precursors (activation on signal/propeptide segments and conserved cationic patches).
- Apolipoproteins (N‑terminal signal peptide and amphipathic helical stretches).
- Protein kinases with disordered/basic N‑termini (e.g., cyclin-dependent and PRK family N‑tails).
- Thioredoxin-fold protein disulfide-isomerases (peak at the CGHC active-site helix).
- Mitochondrial calcium uniporter (selected residues in a matrix-exposed helix).
- Conotoxin and other secreted toxin precursors; neuropeptide prepropeptides (activation across pro/mature peptide regions).
- Viral silencing suppressors and small membrane/morphogenesis proteins (basic, hydrophobic leader-like segments).
- Kinetochore coiled-coil scaffold proteins (basic low-complexity regions).
- FYVE-domain endosomal adaptors (basic, membrane/PIP-interacting low-complexity segments).
- RNA-modifying enzymes with basic N‑terminal tails (e.g., tRNA methyltransferases).

Summary: Short, low‑complexity, intrinsically disordered proteins and modules that encode targeting/processing signals—often but not always secretory—combining hydrophobic signal peptides, double‑Gly bacteriocin leaders, or polybasic/NLS‑like segments, frequently adjacent to Ser/Thr/Pro‑rich stretches and basic clusters (e.g., RXLR, KR/RR)—common in micropeptides, toxins/secreted precursors, viral accessory proteins, keratin‑associated and testis‑specific low‑complexity proteins across taxa
Activation pattern: Regional activation across short proteins, spanning hydrophobic/targeting segments and Ser/Thr/Pro‑rich low‑complexity tracts with peaks on basic motifs such as RXLR, dibasic KR/RR, or double‑Gly leader junctions
Exemplars:
- Oomycete RxLR effectors: activation on the N‑terminal signal peptide and the RXLR/EER host‑targeting motif immediately downstream.
- Secreted peptide hormone/venom/toxin precursors: activation on the signal peptide and basic prohormone convertase cleavage motifs (KR/RR) within the propeptide region.
- Class II bacteriocins: activation on the N‑terminal double‑Gly leader and adjacent cationic tract recognized by ABC exporters.
- Viral accessory/regulatory proteins (e.g., small disordered regulators): activation across S/T/P‑rich low‑complexity disordered segments containing polybasic/NLS‑like clusters.
- Keratin‑associated proteins (KRTAPs): activation over short, repetitive low‑complexity regions (Ser/Pro‑rich and basic tracts) typical of hair shaft proteins.
- Cancer/testis antigens and testis‑associated proteins: activation on Lys/Arg‑ and Pro/Ser‑rich low‑complexity stretches in very short proteins.
- Short uncharacterized micropeptides/antisense products: broad activation across their low‑complexity/basic segments.
- Enzymes that carry secretory leaders or short disordered/basic tails (including some cytosolic enzymes lacking signal peptides): activation limited to the disordered tail, not the catalytic core.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity polybasic segments—stretches enriched in Lys/Arg (often with His) and sometimes interspersed with Ser and acidic residues (RS/KE‑rich patterns). These tracts are typically long tails (frequently C‑terminal) found in nuclear/RNA‑associated proteins and serve as generic basic, nucleic‑acid–contacting or localization‑prone regions.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across extended disordered segments with strong residue‑level peaks at the densest K/R/H clusters; little to no activation in folded domains. Frequently concentrated in C‑terminal low‑complexity regions.
Exemplars: - Spliceosome-associated RP9: strong activation on a C‑terminal Lys/Arg/His‑rich disordered tail.
- G‑patch RNA‑binding proteins (e.g., GPATCH8): long C‑terminal basic low‑complexity regions.
- Uncharacterized pxr1-like protein: disordered C‑terminal basic/charge‑mixed tract with helical propensity.
- TFIID subunit 2 (TAF2): C‑terminal His/Lys‑biased intrinsically disordered region.
- Cyclophilin-type peptidyl‑prolyl isomerase G (PPIG): extended RS/K‑rich disordered C‑terminal tail; no activation in the structured PPIase domain.
- Yeast TMA23 ribosome‑biogenesis/nucleolar factor: long Lys‑rich disordered C‑terminal tail.

Summary: Alpha-helical segments embedded in low-complexity/disordered contexts, including short amphipathic helical peptides and longer helix-prone stretches (enriched in Q/A/L/S with tolerated P/G), often near termini or proteolytic cleavage sites; the feature highlights the helix-like portions of low-complexity blocks while avoiding well-folded domains and non‑helical glycine-repeat coils.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across contiguous helix-length stretches (typically 10–30 aa, sometimes forming longer runs) that align with predicted alpha-helices even when structural confidence is low; sharp onset/offset at peptide or boundary edges; low or absent in structured globular domains (e.g., RRMs), signal peptides, and purely coil-like glycine-rich repeats; frequent bias toward terminal regions.
Exemplars: - Prohormone/prokineticin precursors: activation on a C-terminal helical stretch within the propeptide immediately before the bioactive peptide; minimal signal on the signal peptide and processed peptides.
- Vespid venom chemotactic peptides: strong activation across the entire mature amphipathic helical peptide, but not on the signal peptide or preceding prosegment.
- Yeast nuclear RNA-binding/splicing factors (RRM-containing RBPs): activation on low-complexity, helical-prone segments in disordered tails and linker regions; no activation in the folded RRM domains.
- Plant-pathogen harpin (HrpZ) effectors: activation on specific alpha-helical segments (including within peptide-binding regions) and in low-confidence flexible helices; absent on glycine-rich coil repeats.
- Viral structural proteins (capsid/nucleocapsid/readthrough proteins): activation on low-complexity helical arms or termini implicated in assembly/packaging.
- Drosophila eggshell/glue proteins and plant low-complexity/storage proteins: activation along long, low-complexity helical stretches near termini within secretion-associated proteins.

Summary: Long, low‑complexity Q/N‑rich tracts (poly‑asparagine and poly‑glutamine) in eukaryotic proteins—typically intrinsically disordered terminal or linker regions and compositionally biased coiled‑coil segments—lying outside structured catalytic/recognition domains; especially prevalent in Dictyostelium (and similar N‑rich proteomes).
Activation pattern: Regional activation across extended, compositionally biased blocks with dense N (and Q) runs; sustained high activation over tens of residues with residue‑level peaks on homopolymeric N/Q. Little to no activation in well‑folded domains (kinase cores, DNA‑binding folds, TM helices, ABC NBDs, zinc fingers); when present within a domain boundary, it coincides with a low‑confidence, low‑complexity insert. Often concentrated in N/C‑terminal tails and inter‑domain linkers; can include Q/N‑rich coiled‑coil segments.
Exemplars: - Alpha‑type protein kinase with Arf‑GAP regulator: strong activation on multiple polyQ and polyN tracts (including Q‑rich coiled‑coils) outside the Arf‑GAP and kinase domains.
- Hybrid histidine kinase (PAS–HisKA–RR two‑component‑like): activation on N‑ and Q‑rich disordered linkers; absent from PAS, HisKA, and response‑regulator domains.
- Homeobox transcription factor: activation confined to N‑rich low‑complexity segments; absent from the folded homeobox DNA‑binding domain.
- Rho GTPase‑activating protein (RhoGAP): activation on asparagine‑rich low‑complexity regions (notably a C‑terminal polyN tract); no activation in the MYND zinc finger or RhoGAP catalytic domain.
- Sirtuin (NAD‑dependent deacetylase): activation on extensive C‑terminal N‑rich disordered regions and a short N‑run insert with low structural confidence; not on the structured catalytic core.
- Diacylglycerol kinase: activation on asparagine‑rich disordered segments in the C‑terminus; not in C1 zinc fingers or the DAGK catalytic domain.
- ABC transporter (ABCB7‑like): activation on N‑rich disordered N‑ and C‑terminal tails; absent from transmembrane helices and the cytosolic ABC nucleotide‑binding domain.

Summary: Short, glycine/alanine-rich hydrophobic alpha-helices that insert into or span membranes—including single-pass transmembrane anchors, fusion peptides, and pore/translocation helices—frequently containing GxxxG/glycine‑zipper motifs used for helix packing.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over contiguous 15–25-residue hydrophobic segments, with residue-level peaks on small residues (especially glycine and alanine) within the helix. Activations typically coincide with annotated/predicted transmembrane helices or membrane-inserting amphipathic helices, and can appear as multiple short activated segments in multi-pass or multi-helical proteins; N-terminal signal peptides are generally not favored relative to internal or transmembrane helices.
Exemplars: Viral envelope/fusion glycoproteins (paramyxovirus F, coronavirus spike, retroviral Env): activation on hydrophobic membrane-active helical regions; paramyxovirus F also activates on the N-terminal fusion peptide; Baculovirus per os infectivity factor 5: activation on the single-pass TM helix; Toxoplasma dense granule proteins: activation on the C-terminal tail-anchor TM helix; Magnetospirillum magnetosome proteins (e.g., Mms6): activation across the single transmembrane helix and immediate lumenal flank; Bacteriocins/pyocins/colicins: activation within the hydrophobic membrane-inserting/translocation or pore-forming helix; Big defensin antimicrobial peptides: activation on the N-terminal amphipathic membrane-active helix; Human interferon-inducible small membrane proteins and ApoL family: activation on short TM or membrane-inserting helices; Bacteriophage tail structural proteins (including tape measure proteins): activation on short hydrophobic helical segments within tail/tip assemblies.

Summary: Short hydrophobic/amphipathic segments enriched in Gly/Ala and interfacial Trp/Tyr, flanked by basic residues, that occur either immediately N-terminal to a transmembrane helix (signal-anchor–like) or within translocation/insertion domains of secreted bacterial proteins. These stretches frequently show coil→helix propensity and can adopt helical structure upon membrane or partner engagement.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over contiguous hydrophobic/aromatic segments (typically ~10–25 aa); local maxima at aromatic residues (Trp/Phe/Tyr) within the segment; activation often begins at or just after a basic cluster (Lys-rich) and extends toward an adjacent helical or TM region. Multiple nonadjacent activated segments per protein are common, with secondary peaks in TM-proximal regions.
Exemplars:
- Influenza hemagglutinin‑esterase‑fusion glycoprotein: strong activation at the HEF2 N‑terminus (canonical fusion peptide immediately post‑cleavage), plus a secondary peak near the TM start.
- HIV‑1 envelope (gp160/gp41): peak across the SU–TM cleavage and N‑terminus of the gp41 fusion peptide; minor activation in TM‑proximal/cytoplasmic segments.
- ISG12/IFI6 family (interferon‑inducible small membrane proteins): activation on the loop between TM1–TM2 extending into the N‑terminus of TM2, the membrane‑anchoring helix.
- Baculovirus per os infectivity factors (e.g., PIF5): activation across the basic-residue cluster leading into the C-terminal TM helix.
- E-group colicins (E2/E3/E7) and cloacin: activation on a conserved KGPFKF(GLW) aromatic motif within the translocation (T) domain.
- Peroxisome biogenesis factor PEX3: activation across the N‑terminal peroxisomal targeting/signal‑anchor segment and the initial part of the first TM helix.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, Lys/Arg‑rich low‑complexity segments—typically long terminal tails, often containing RG/RGG/GAR motifs—that mediate electrostatic binding to nucleic acids (especially rRNA/RNA) and promote association with ribonucleoprotein assemblies such as the nucleolus and ribosome
Activation pattern: Strong regional activation across long contiguous stretches of disordered sequence, most often at C‑termini (sometimes N‑termini); local peaks coincide with polybasic clusters and RG/RGG motifs; minimal activation within folded catalytic or recognition domains
Exemplars: - Nucleolar biogenesis factors (e.g., NOP12): activation on C‑terminal Lys/Arg‑rich disordered tails, not on folded RRMs
- RRP12-like ribosome assembly proteins: strongest at terminal disordered segments with basic compositional bias, especially the C‑tail
- DEAD-box RNA helicases (e.g., SrmB): activation confined to C‑terminal basic low‑complexity extensions outside the helicase core
- 3′–5′ exoribonucleases (RNase R family): disordered C‑terminal Lys/Arg‑rich tails
- Kinetoplast-associated small basic proteins: broad activation across disordered, low‑complexity basic C‑terminal halves
- Linker histones H1/H1‑like: Lys‑rich disordered C‑terminal tails that bind DNA
- Ribosomal proteins (small and large subunits): basic, often terminal extensions that contact rRNA
- SRP72 subunit: GAR/RGG‑rich basic segment
- Nucleolar/ribosome‑associated GTPases and membrane biogenesis/transport factors: cytosolic polybasic loops/tails

Summary: Arg/Lys-rich, low-complexity, intrinsically disordered basic segments (often S/T-interspersed) that mediate electrostatic binding to polyanions—primarily nucleic acids (DNA/RNA) in chromatin, ribosomes, and viral genomes—and, in some cases, other anionic targets; typically realized as long polybasic tails or entire small basic proteins
Activation pattern: Regional activation over long stretches of K/R-rich sequence, frequently covering N- or C-terminal tails or the entirety of small basic proteins; strongest in predicted-disordered/coil regions with compositional bias for basic residues and often enriched in Ser/Thr; in multi-domain proteins, activation is confined to flexible basic segments rather than structured cores
Exemplars: - Linker histones H1/H5 and H1-like proteins: activation on the Lys/Arg-rich, disordered C-terminal tails that compact chromatin (e.g., histone-like protein 18C C-terminal tail).
- Sperm nuclear proteins (protamines and transition proteins): activation across the whole, highly basic, disordered proteins that neutralize and condense DNA.
- Archaeal chromatin proteins (histone HMf/HMz, H1-like): activation on basic DNA-binding tails/segments.
- Ribosomal proteins (various small/acidic-binding subunits): activation on Lys-rich terminal extensions that contact rRNA.
- Small acid-soluble spore proteins (SASPs): full-length activation of their highly basic DNA-binding polypeptides.
- Viral DNA-condensing/packaging and core DNA-binding proteins (e.g., adenovirus/phage basic proteins, terminal proteins): activation on polybasic segments used for genome binding/packaging.
- Cationic antimicrobial/bacteriocin peptides: activation on Lys/Arg-rich, low-complexity cationic stretches.
- Plant RALF-like secreted peptides: activation on polybasic stretches within the propeptide/mature region.
- Viral serine/threonine kinases: activation on polybasic, disordered segments (often NLS-like regions).
- Mollusk sperm H1/protamine-like proteins: activation on extended Lys/Arg-rich tails or entire basic proteins involved in DNA compaction.

Summary: Asparagine/serine/threonine–enriched low-complexity, disordered tracts, including Asn-rich tandem repeats and S/T-rich mucin-like regions typical of secreted and surface proteins; more generally, polar N/S/T-biased compositionally biased segments in diverse proteins, with occasional firing on Lys-containing repeated tripeptides in venom precursors.
Activation pattern: Predominantly long regional activation across low-complexity segments; strong residue-level peaks at asparagines within Asn-rich repeats and polar disordered tracts; extended activation over S/T-rich repeats in surface/secreted proteins.
Exemplars:
- Viral envelope/membrane glycoproteins: activation on N/S/T-rich loops
- Secreted adhesins and mucin-like cell-surface proteins: activation over S/T-rich repeats and embedded polar tracts
- Parasite surface/antigenic proteins (e.g., Plasmodium repeat proteins): activation across long Asn-rich low-complexity regions
- Dictyostelium low-complexity proteins: activation on NST-rich compositionally biased segments
- Neuropeptide and toxin precursors: activation on Asn-rich repeated prodomains and on Lys-centered repeated tripeptides
- Secreted carbohydrate-active enzymes (glycosidases/lyases): activation at luminal/extracellular N/S/T-rich segments
- Nuclear regulators (transcription factors, kinases, phosphatases; zinc-finger proteins): activation on N/S/T-biased low-complexity linkers

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low-complexity segments used as extracellular stalks/linkers and nuclear/regulatory IDRs. These segments are typically either polyampholyte tracts enriched in acidic and basic residues (E/D with K/R/H; often E–x–K repeats) or mucin-/extensin-like Pro/Thr/Ser-rich O-glycosylation tracts; they are common in secreted/adhesive proteins, peptide/venom/neuropeptide precursors, viral/apicomplexan low-complexity proteins, and some germ cell/testis antigens.

Activation pattern: Regional activation across long disordered low-complexity tracts; frequent periodic residue-level peaks on charged residues (E/D and K/R/H) when present. In S/T/P-rich mucin/extensin-like segments, activation is broad/regional and may highlight nearby acidic residues; little or no activation in folded domains, signal peptides, or short structured modules, though low-complexity propeptides of precursors can activate.

Exemplars:
- Fungal cell-wall adhesins and signaling mucins: central low-complexity stalks (K/E-rich or Ser/Thr/Pro-rich glycostalks) are activated; signal peptides and structured domains are not.
- Plant extensins (hydroxyproline/proline-rich glycoproteins): activation along long S/T/P-rich repeats with acidic patches in disordered tails.
- Germ cell/testis antigens and chromatin remodeler subunits: EK-repeat polyampholyte IDRs with sharp peaks on E/K and suppression on intervening spacers.
- Viral regulatory proteins (e.g., EBNA-LP) and apicomplexan exported proteins (e.g., RESA): long acidic/basic low-complexity repeats with periodic peaks on charged residues.
- Secreted matrix/adhesion glycoproteins (e.g., MAdCAM-1 mucin-like stalk, ovocleidin-116): disordered low-complexity extracellular regions (acidic and/or S/T/P-rich) show regional activation.
- Peptide/venom/neuropeptide precursors: low-complexity, often acidic/basic-rich propeptide segments can activate.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low-complexity proline-rich tandem-repeat tracts (typically enriched in P/S/T and often Q/H) found predominantly in secreted/extracellular proteins and viral surface proteins; the feature marks conserved proline positions within repeat units that form mucin-like stalks, adhesin/cell-wall repeats, or Hyp/O-glycosylation scaffolds, and it also occurs in intracellular repeat-rich proteins such as nuclear regulators and cytoskeletal/testis-specific proteins.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long disordered repeat domains with sharp residue-level peaks mainly on prolines at fixed positions in each repeat unit (e.g., second P in PP; the P in DPxG, NANP/NVDP, or PAA-PEA motifs). Outside these tracts, activation is low, including in structured domains (signal peptides, transmembranes, enzyme cores, or GPI-anchor/propeptide segments); however, short P-rich low-complexity inserts/propeptides within secretory-pathway glycoproteins can also activate.
Exemplars:
- Fungal GPI-anchored adhesins/flocculins: strong activation on prolines within central Ser/Thr/Pro-rich tandem repeats that form the extracellular stalk.
- Plant arabinogalactan proteins/extensins: activation on PP motifs, biased to the second P that is hydroxylated to Hyp and O-glycosylated.
- Viral envelope proteins (e.g., herpesvirus gC; Plasmodium CSP): activation on prolines within repetitive, disordered external repeats (e.g., P-D-P-A-V-A-P, NANP/NVDP).
- Mucin-like secreted proteins: activation across disordered 10–15 aa repeat arrays (e.g., DPxG-containing repeats).
- Testis-specific/cytoskeletal repeat proteins (e.g., outer dense fiber proteins): activation on prolines anchoring short tandem repeats in disordered segments.
- Nuclear transcriptional regulators with Pro-rich low-complexity regions (e.g., REST): activation over Pro-rich tracts.
- Bacterial autotransporters/actin modulators (e.g., BimA): activation on surface-exposed Pro-rich repeats.
- Secretory/vacuolar glycoproteins with short low-complexity inserts: activation confined to Pro-rich inserts, not the folded enzyme core.

Summary: Short, positively charged (Lys/Arg-rich) basic patches at coil→helix transitions, including the N-region/N-cap of signal peptides and signal anchors but also analogous basic-rich segments elsewhere in the protein (propeptide–mature peptide boundaries, internal basic linkers, C-proximal basic tails).
Activation pattern: Regional activation on short contiguous patches (~5–20 aa) with residue-level peaks on or adjacent to Lys/Arg residues, typically flanked by Gly/Pro/Ser/Ala at a coil→helix onset; frequently just upstream of the first transmembrane helix in signal-anchor proteins, and also at internal or terminal basic low-complexity segments.
Exemplars:
- Single-pass cysteine-rich membrane proteins: activation in the short N-terminal segment immediately preceding the first transmembrane helix (signal anchor)
- Viral envelope and small accessory proteins (including polyomavirus agnoproteins): activation on basic leaders adjacent to a signal-anchor helix
- Bacteriocins and small ribosomally synthesized peptides (e.g., lasso peptides such as microcin J25): activation on basic patches within the propeptide leader
- Secreted bombesin-like peptide precursors: activation at the basic propeptide/mature peptide junction
- Cytoplasmic/nuclear proteins with internal Lys/Arg-rich low-complexity stretches: activation on those basic segments rather than on canonical N-terminal targeting leaders
- Secreted pathogenesis-related protein precursors (e.g., PR-4 family): activation within the N-terminal signal peptide
- Bacterial penicillin-binding proteins and other periplasmic enzymes: activation on Sec signal peptides
- Holins and membrane transporters: activation at the basic N-proximal stretch just before the first transmembrane helix
- Mitochondrial/chloroplast-targeted preproteins: activation on amphipathic transit peptides enriched in Arg/Ser/Pro near the N-terminus
- RNA-binding proteins (e.g., ribosomal proteins) and nucleic-acid enzymes (e.g., RNase HII, tRNA-modification enzymes): activation on short basic, low-complexity N-terminal tails that share the same composition/features as targeting leaders

Summary: Polybasic, low-complexity segments—often intrinsically disordered—and K/R-rich polyanion-binding modules (including protamine/histone-like regions, surface-attachment/GW repeats, and exported S/T-rich repeats in secreted proteins).
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long contiguous tracts; tracks K/R-rich low-complexity regions, frequently in disordered or amphipathic segments; falls off sharply in folded catalytic cores and does not mark active-site residues; signal peptides themselves are typically not marked.
Exemplars: - Gram-positive cell-wall enzymes (autolysins, amidases, peptidoglycan deacetylases, glycosidases): activation on cationic surface-attachment/wall-binding repeats; not on catalytic domains.
- Surface adhesins, S-layer proteins, and serine-rich repeat glycoproteins: long activation across exported low-complexity tracts and GW cell-wall-anchoring repeats.
- Bacteriophage endolysins/lytic enzymes: activation on cationic wall-binding regions.
- Antimicrobial/host-defense peptides and small secreted cationic proteins: activation spanning the whole polybasic amphipathic peptide.
- Reproductive protamines/transition proteins and viral histone-like core proteins: activation across K/R-rich DNA-binding regions.
- Secreted proteases with disordered C-terminal tails: activation across the basic/disordered tail rather than the peptidase domain.

Summary: Polybasic, lysine‑rich low‑complexity intrinsically disordered segments (acidic‑poor and often N/T/S‑rich), frequently located near protein N‑termini; the feature highlights short basic patches/tracts rather than structured domains
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks on Lys that coalesce into short regional activation across disordered/basic patches; strongest in low‑pLDDT coils or low‑confidence helices, often near the N‑terminus, with neighboring N/T/S also elevated
Exemplars: - Viral accessory proteins (e.g., agnoproteins): strong peaks at terminal K and adjacent N in unstructured tails.
- Antimicrobial peptide precursors (e.g., Ixosin): activation within the mature cationic peptide on K/N, with weaker signals in the propeptide.
- ABC transporters: concentrated activation in an N‑terminal disordered, lysine‑rich segment immediately preceding the structured transporter domain.
- Telomere‑associated proteins: scattered peaks on K/N within low‑pLDDT coils across the sequence.
- Human intrinsically disordered regulatory proteins: multiple K‑centered peaks distributed across low‑confidence helices/coils.

Summary: Extreme N-terminal basic, low-complexity initiation segments that serve as generic localization/processing leaders: includes the n-region of ER signal peptides, mitochondrial/chloroplast transit peptides, short propeptides, and signal anchors of membrane proteins, as well as analogous basic N-termini in viral and nuclear/cytosolic microproteins.
Activation pattern: Strong, localized activation confined to the first ~5–20 residues at the extreme N-terminus, with sharp peaks around positions 2–10; overlaps disordered/low-confidence coil that can include a short initial helix; activation rapidly decays after this segment with only rare internal/C-terminal stray peaks.
Exemplars:
- Neuropeptide precursors (galanin family): activation at the start of the secreted peptide segment within a short disordered N-terminus.
- Oomycete RxLR secreted effectors: activation within the N-terminal signal peptide n-region/early helix (~1–12).
- Secreted fungal multicopper oxidases (laccases): activation in the first residues of the signal peptide n-region, tapering across the leader.
- Plant ribosome-inactivating proteins (type 1 RIPs): activation across the N-terminal propeptide preceding the mature enzyme.
- Viral regulatory proteins (e.g., adenoviral E4-ORF6): activation at a basic, low-complexity extreme N-terminus used for subcellular targeting.
- Human microproteins/lncRNA-derived peptides (e.g., PINT87aa): activation over an N-terminal basic, low-complexity tract even without a classical signal peptide.
- Bacterial enzymes with N-terminal signal anchors or basic tails (e.g., membrane-associated carotenoid pathway enzymes): activation at the extreme N-terminus.

Summary: Extracellular secreted precursors and ectodomains with disulfide-bonded cysteine-rich loops/domains (cystine-stabilized scaffolds), and a subset of secreted neuropeptide precursors whose activation concentrates on flexible, processing-rich segments even without dense cysteine content. Common in proteins with signal peptides, glycosylation, and proteolytic processing.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks on cysteines and adjacent positions (often Gly/Pro and basic Lys/Arg) within extracellular regions; regional activation over cysteine-rich loops or repeats; also highlights Gly/Pro and Lys/Arg flanking propeptide cleavage motifs in cysteine-poor neuropeptide precursors; absent in transmembrane helices and cytosolic tails; strongest in low-to-moderate order ectodomain segments, sometimes near N-glycosylation and cleavage sites.
Exemplars:
- Chemokines (especially CXC): activation on conserved disulfide-forming cysteine motifs.
- Defensins/plant CRPs and knottin-like/trypsin inhibitor peptides (CSαβ/ICK scaffolds): activation across disulfide-bonded loops.
- WFDC, Kunitz, and Kazal protease inhibitors: activation on disulfide-stabilized inhibitor domains.
- Venom toxins (e.g., Kunitz-type, ShK, disintegrins): activation on clustered cysteines defining the scaffold.
- Viral envelope glycoproteins (class I/II/III): activation in cysteine-rich ectodomains near disulfide networks and glycosylation sites.
- Extracellular receptor/adhesion and metalloprotease proteins: activation on EGF-like, disintegrin, and other cysteine-rich modules.
- DEG/ENaC family channels: activation in the extracellular cysteine-rich loop.
- Neuropeptide hormone precursors (e.g., small cardioactive peptides): activation around flexible, dibasic cleavage-rich segments even with low cysteine content.
- Apicomplexan AMA1 invasion protein: activation confined to ectodomain cysteine-rich segments, absent from TM/cytosolic regions.

Summary: Short, cationic, amphipathic peptide segments—typically the mature cores of secreted antimicrobial/cytolytic peptides and analogous AMP‑like helices embedded in larger proteins. These regions are Lys/Arg‑rich with interspersed hydrophobes, often form (or have propensity for) an amphipathic α‑helix, and are used for membrane interaction/disruption or other bioactive signaling; they are usually produced by proteolytic processing from precursor proteins and can include RiPP cores despite post‑translational crosslinks.
Activation pattern: Regional activation on short contiguous blocks (∼15–40 aa, sometimes shorter), with sharp on/off at the boundaries of mature peptide segments; minimal activation in signal peptides and propeptides. Peaks often coincide with hydrophobic residues along an amphipathic face and clusters of Lys/Arg. Frequently at N‑ or C‑terminal helices or short internal helices with low-to-moderate pLDDT.
Exemplars: - Amphibian helical antimicrobial peptides (e.g., aureins): activation precisely on the mature AMP helix, not on signal/propeptide.
- Hymenopteran venom cytolysins (e.g., myrmeciitoxins): strong activation across the mature toxin’s amphipathic α‑helix.
- Lantibiotic RiPPs (e.g., lacticin 3147 A2): activation on the modified mature lantibiotic core despite lanthionine/beta‑methyllanthionine crosslinks.
- Phage/bacterial holins: activation on the N‑terminal amphipathic helix adjacent to the first transmembrane segment; little/no activation in TM or periplasmic domains.
- Crustacean anti‑lipopolysaccharide factors (ALFs): activation on the N‑terminal cationic LPS‑binding helix of the mature peptide.
- Plant NLR immune receptors (coiled‑coil N‑termini): activation on the N‑terminal CC helix implicated in membrane permeabilization/channel activity.
- Insect stress-response secreted proteins (Turandot family): activation on a C‑terminal amphipathic α‑helix of the mature chain.
- Outer membrane polysaccharide export proteins (CtrA family): activation on a short periplasmic C‑terminal helical tail with amphipathic character.
- Kininogen‑derived peptides (bradykinin variants): activation on the short, basic bioactive peptide released from a disordered region.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered post-signal/TM prohormone regions of secreted short-peptide precursors—i.e., the segments that encode mature neuropeptides/hormones or toxin/antimicrobial peptides and their flanking propeptides—characterized by Lys/Arg-rich convertase cleavage motifs and frequent support for C‑terminal amidation
Activation pattern: Domain-level: inactive on signal peptides and transmembrane helices; strongly active across the luminal propeptide from signal/TM cleavage to the C-terminus. Regional: sustained high activation over mature peptide blocks and adjacent propeptides, often spanning multiple peptides in one precursor; activation typically drops immediately after the last processed peptide. Residue-level: peaks over peptide cores and nearby linkers; selective dips at the second residue of dibasic Lys/Arg cleavage pairs; enrichment around basic clusters and glycine positions associated with amidation.
Exemplars: - Dermaseptin antimicrobial peptide precursor: high on the mature dermaseptin and both flanking propeptides; off on the N‑terminal signal peptide; all activated regions are disordered.
- Insect prokineticin/hugin precursor: strong activation across the region containing Hug‑gamma and PK‑2 peptides and linker/C‑terminal propeptide; inactive on the signal peptide; disordered.
- Tachykinin/protachykinin (neurokinin family): activated across the neurokinin peptide (e.g., Neurokinin‑B) and propeptide segments; sharp local drop at a dibasic cleavage Arg; disordered.
- Neuropeptide F precursor: moderate to strong activation on the mature NPF and the C‑terminal propeptide; signal peptide unactivated; disordered.
- Insect diuretic hormone class 2 precursor: maximal activation across the mature diuretic hormone peptide; off on the signal peptide; disordered.
- Proenkephalin (opioid peptide precursor): broadly activated over enkephalin copies and intervening prosegments; recurrent dip at the second basic residue of dibasic cleavage motifs; disordered.
- Gonadoliberin (GnRH) precursor: high activation across the GnRH peptide and the associated peptide; inactive on the signal peptide; disordered.
- Gastrin prohormone: strong activation over “Big gastrin”/“Gastrin” region and C‑terminal propeptide where amidation/cleavage motifs occur; off on the signal peptide; disordered.
- Pigment-dispersing factor (PDF) precursor: activated on the mature PDF chain; signal peptide not activated; disordered.
- Membrane-anchored secretory peptide-like precursor (e.g., Frey): inactive on the N‑terminal transmembrane helix; strong activation on the disordered luminal C‑terminal region consistent with a processed propeptide segment.

Summary: Arg/Lys-rich, low-complexity, intrinsically disordered basic segments (often S/T-interspersed) that mediate electrostatic binding to polyanions—primarily nucleic acids (DNA/RNA) in chromatin, ribosomes, and viral genomes—and, in some cases, other anionic targets; typically realized as long polybasic tails or entire small basic proteins
Activation pattern: Regional activation over long stretches of K/R-rich sequence, frequently covering N- or C-terminal tails or the entirety of small basic proteins; strongest in predicted-disordered/coil regions with compositional bias for basic residues and often enriched in Ser/Thr; in multi-domain proteins, activation is confined to flexible basic segments rather than structured cores
Exemplars: - Linker histones H1/H5 and H1-like proteins: activation on the Lys/Arg-rich, disordered C-terminal tails that compact chromatin (e.g., histone-like protein 18C C-terminal tail).
- Sperm nuclear proteins (protamines and transition proteins): activation across the whole, highly basic, disordered proteins that neutralize and condense DNA.
- Archaeal chromatin proteins (histone HMf/HMz, H1-like): activation on basic DNA-binding tails/segments.
- Ribosomal proteins (various small/acidic-binding subunits): activation on Lys-rich terminal extensions that contact rRNA.
- Small acid-soluble spore proteins (SASPs): full-length activation of their highly basic DNA-binding polypeptides.
- Viral DNA-condensing/packaging and core DNA-binding proteins (e.g., adenovirus/phage basic proteins, terminal proteins): activation on polybasic segments used for genome binding/packaging.
- Cationic antimicrobial/bacteriocin peptides: activation on Lys/Arg-rich, low-complexity cationic stretches.
- Plant RALF-like secreted peptides: activation on polybasic stretches within the propeptide/mature region.
- Viral serine/threonine kinases: activation on polybasic, disordered segments (often NLS-like regions).
- Mollusk sperm H1/protamine-like proteins: activation on extended Lys/Arg-rich tails or entire basic proteins involved in DNA compaction.

Summary: Extracellular secreted precursors and ectodomains with disulfide-bonded cysteine-rich loops/domains (cystine-stabilized scaffolds), and a subset of secreted neuropeptide precursors whose activation concentrates on flexible, processing-rich segments even without dense cysteine content. Common in proteins with signal peptides, glycosylation, and proteolytic processing.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks on cysteines and adjacent positions (often Gly/Pro and basic Lys/Arg) within extracellular regions; regional activation over cysteine-rich loops or repeats; also highlights Gly/Pro and Lys/Arg flanking propeptide cleavage motifs in cysteine-poor neuropeptide precursors; absent in transmembrane helices and cytosolic tails; strongest in low-to-moderate order ectodomain segments, sometimes near N-glycosylation and cleavage sites.
Exemplars:
- Chemokines (especially CXC): activation on conserved disulfide-forming cysteine motifs.
- Defensins/plant CRPs and knottin-like/trypsin inhibitor peptides (CSαβ/ICK scaffolds): activation across disulfide-bonded loops.
- WFDC, Kunitz, and Kazal protease inhibitors: activation on disulfide-stabilized inhibitor domains.
- Venom toxins (e.g., Kunitz-type, ShK, disintegrins): activation on clustered cysteines defining the scaffold.
- Viral envelope glycoproteins (class I/II/III): activation in cysteine-rich ectodomains near disulfide networks and glycosylation sites.
- Extracellular receptor/adhesion and metalloprotease proteins: activation on EGF-like, disintegrin, and other cysteine-rich modules.
- DEG/ENaC family channels: activation in the extracellular cysteine-rich loop.
- Neuropeptide hormone precursors (e.g., small cardioactive peptides): activation around flexible, dibasic cleavage-rich segments even with low cysteine content.
- Apicomplexan AMA1 invasion protein: activation confined to ectodomain cysteine-rich segments, absent from TM/cytosolic regions.

Summary: Polycationic, low‑complexity disordered segments in secreted or periplasmic proteins—typically Lys/Arg/His‑rich patches (often interspersed with Pro/Gly) found in propeptides, flexible linkers, and low‑confidence tails rather than in folded catalytic domains.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across extended basic, repeat‑rich blocks; often multiple patches per precursor; strongest in disordered/propeptide regions with low predicted structure confidence; little to no activation on signal peptides or well‑structured domains.
Exemplars: - Secreted metalloprotease precursors (M12A/ADAMTS/tolloid‑like): activation on basic, disordered propeptide segments and C‑terminal low‑complexity tails.
- Mating pheromone precursors (e.g., ciliate/fungal pheromones): activation confined to the N‑terminal propeptide; not on the signal peptide or the mature pheromone.
- Cationic antimicrobial peptides and toxin precursors (e.g., magainin/cecropin‑like, histidine‑rich peptides, venom peptides): activation across the polybasic, low‑complexity cationic segment or basic prodomain patches.
- Fungal secreted CAZymes (glycoside hydrolases/oxidoreductases): activation on Lys/Arg‑rich disordered linkers and/or basic prosegments between catalytic and accessory modules.
- Plant small secreted peptides and lysine‑rich arabinogalactan proteins: activation on Lys‑rich repetitive extracellular regions.
- Bacterial TonB and TonB‑like periplasmic proteins: activation along long, basic low‑complexity periplasmic stretches.
- Host–pathogen interaction and some viral secreted proteins: activation on surface‑exposed basic low‑complexity repeat patches used for extracellular interactions.

Summary: Arg/Lys-rich, low-complexity, intrinsically disordered basic segments (often S/T-interspersed) that mediate electrostatic binding to polyanions—primarily nucleic acids (DNA/RNA) in chromatin, ribosomes, and viral genomes—and, in some cases, other anionic targets; typically realized as long polybasic tails or entire small basic proteins
Activation pattern: Regional activation over long stretches of K/R-rich sequence, frequently covering N- or C-terminal tails or the entirety of small basic proteins; strongest in predicted-disordered/coil regions with compositional bias for basic residues and often enriched in Ser/Thr; in multi-domain proteins, activation is confined to flexible basic segments rather than structured cores
Exemplars: - Linker histones H1/H5 and H1-like proteins: activation on the Lys/Arg-rich, disordered C-terminal tails that compact chromatin (e.g., histone-like protein 18C C-terminal tail).
- Sperm nuclear proteins (protamines and transition proteins): activation across the whole, highly basic, disordered proteins that neutralize and condense DNA.
- Archaeal chromatin proteins (histone HMf/HMz, H1-like): activation on basic DNA-binding tails/segments.
- Ribosomal proteins (various small/acidic-binding subunits): activation on Lys-rich terminal extensions that contact rRNA.
- Small acid-soluble spore proteins (SASPs): full-length activation of their highly basic DNA-binding polypeptides.
- Viral DNA-condensing/packaging and core DNA-binding proteins (e.g., adenovirus/phage basic proteins, terminal proteins): activation on polybasic segments used for genome binding/packaging.
- Cationic antimicrobial/bacteriocin peptides: activation on Lys/Arg-rich, low-complexity cationic stretches.
- Plant RALF-like secreted peptides: activation on polybasic stretches within the propeptide/mature region.
- Viral serine/threonine kinases: activation on polybasic, disordered segments (often NLS-like regions).
- Mollusk sperm H1/protamine-like proteins: activation on extended Lys/Arg-rich tails or entire basic proteins involved in DNA compaction.

Summary: A charge-rich, low-complexity, intrinsically flexible signal that marks solvent-exposed coils, linkers, repeats, and N‑terminal targeting peptides. It tends to highlight long, disordered or poorly packed regions enriched in E/D/K/R/S/T (often with glycine within repeat motifs) and is broadly active over such segments; in enzymes it can peak on charged residues in active-site/metal-coordination loops.
Activation pattern: Primarily regional/domain-level activation over long contiguous segments (IDRs, flexible subdomains, and transit peptides), with residue-level peaks on glycine and exposed charged sites within low-complexity repeats.
Exemplars: - LEA/EM-like stress proteins: strong activation across low-complexity tandem repeats, with peak residues frequently on glycines within the conserved PGGTGG-like motif.
- Urease beta/gamma fusions: domain-level activation spanning the urease beta subunit region (lower structural confidence), absent over the well-packed gamma domain.
- Acyl-CoA-binding proteins: elevated activation in loops and helix termini; minimal activation within the stable helical core and at substrate-contacting residues.
- Superoxide reductases: peaks on coil/turn segments harboring iron-binding His/Glu and adjacent charged residues, including short β segments containing these sites.
- Organelle-targeted enzyme precursors (e.g., methionine sulfoxide reductases): activation on N‑terminal mitochondrial/chloroplast transit peptides.
- Nucleic-acid–binding proteins (histone H2A, ribosomal L31/L33/eL42): activation on basic, low-complexity tails that contact RNA/DNA.
- DNA repair factors (Ku, LigD) and other redox/metal enzymes (e.g., nitrile hydratase): activation across the 3'-phosphoesterase / Ku domains, including turns and short strands near metal-coordination and active-site residues.

Summary: A broadly distributed feature that activates across small proteins and selected α-helical/charged segments in larger proteins; it shows up in short bacterial toxins (CbtA/YkfI/YpjF family), small viral/phage regulators, apoptotic peptides, and on discrete helical or disordered segments of larger enzymes and chromatin/regulatory proteins.

Activation pattern: In short proteins (<150 aa) the feature is active over essentially the entire chain with relatively uniform signal and peaks typically in the N-terminal half on charged/α-helical stretches. In larger multidomain proteins activation is sparse, restricted to one short block — often an N-terminal disordered/basic-acidic region or a localized α-helical segment late in the chain — with the catalytic core and most binding sites silent.

Exemplars:
- Bacterial toxin family CbtA/YkfI/YpjF: broad activation across the toxin chain with strongest peaks in the central "HYGLT" motif region implicated in FtsZ/MreB interaction.
- Phage T4 late transcription coactivator gp33: strong activation on the annotated α-helix (residues 37-50) preceding the host RNAP-interaction region.
- Drosophila Reaper: dense activation across the entire short pro-apoptotic peptide.
- Bacterial phosphomethylpyrimidine synthases: localized activation on a C-terminal segment (~residues 583-595) downstream of the catalytic core.
- Plant regulatory/chromatin proteins (e.g. SUVR1, LPA1): activation on N-terminal disordered/basic-acidic stretches, with catalytic SET or NTPase domains silent.
- Mycobacterial envelope-preserving protein Rv2742c: a single internal block of activation around an aromatic/hydrophobic patch.

Summary: Disordered terminal/linker segments — especially N-terminal tails — that act as flexible interaction modules common in viral structural/nucleoproteins and in nucleic-acid–related enzymes and bacterial toxin/effectors; occasionally extends to compact terminal patches even when locally structured.
Activation pattern: Predominantly regional activation over long continuous stretches with low predicted structure quality, most often at the N-terminus and sometimes the C-terminus; minimal activation in well-folded catalytic cores, with rare activation of compact terminal segments.
Exemplars: - Phage minor capsid proteins: strong activation on the short, disordered N-terminal tail/propeptide immediately after the initiator Met.
- Phage peptidoglycan hydrolases/autolysins: activation on the disordered N-terminal segment and on additional low-confidence terminal regions, with no activation across the structured catalytic core.
- Rhabdovirus nucleoproteins: a focused peak on the basic N-terminal tail (e.g., around K18) within the flexible N-core region.
- CRISPR-Cas13a endoribonucleases: activation on disordered insertions and the C-terminal tail within/adjacent to HEPN-like domains; the structured central body is inactive.
- LXG family polymorphic toxins: activation at the extreme C-terminus outside the N-terminal LXG targeting domain, marking a terminal patch within the toxic effector region (even when locally structured).

Summary: Amphipathic alpha-helical segments in structured regions that serve as interaction surfaces—covering helical cores of nuclear/viral protein domains (e.g., coronavirus N CTD dimerization helices) and the helical cores of compact, disulfide-stabilized secreted peptides (toxins/AMPs)—typically enriched in small aliphatic and charged residues and often forming extended helical tracts.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across one or more contiguous helices; low/absent in disordered regions, signal peptides, or short coil tails. Residue-level peaks favor helix-forming small/aliphatic residues (A, L, V, I, G) and, in cysteine-rich peptides, the cysteines that form disulfide bonds; activation frequently coincides with validated protein–target interaction helices.
Exemplars: - Coronavirus nucleoproteins: activation on C-terminal alpha-helical patches within the N CTD/dimerization domain, peaking on small aliphatic residues (Ala) and avoiding disordered/RNA-binding N-terminal segments.
- Scorpion kappa-KTx potassium-channel toxins: activation confined to the mature toxin's helical core with strongest signal on disulfide-bonded cysteines and adjacent helix residues; inactive over the signal peptide/propeptide.
- Plant YABBY transcription factors: activation on the C-terminal YABBY DNA-binding domain, spanning two alpha helices and their loop, including residues known to affect developmental function when mutated.

Summary: Secreted, short cysteine-rich peptides and small extracellular cysteine-rich domains stabilized by multiple disulfide bonds (CRPs), spanning venom toxins, disintegrins, defensins/hepcidin, Kunitz/Kazal/hevein-like inhibitors/defense peptides, and related cystine‑knotted or cysteine‑stabilized folds. The feature captures the mature, proteolytically processed peptide/module characterized by clustered Cys (often CC motifs) and basic residues.
Activation pattern: Regional activation confined to short mature peptide segments (tens of residues) following the signal peptide and propeptides; minimal/absent on signal/pro-regions. Strong residue-level peaks on cysteines and frequent secondary peaks on Lys/Arg and Gly. Activation spans mixed secondary structure (β-strands, coils, short helices) and can include key functional loops (e.g., RGD in disintegrins).
Exemplars: - Plant cyclotides (cystine-knot cyclopeptides, e.g., chassatide): activation across the cyclic cystine‑knot core of the mature peptide after processing.
- Snake venom disintegrins: activation across the disintegrin domain, including the RGD integrin-binding loop and adjacent cysteine-dense core.
- Inhibitor cystine-knot (ICK) venom toxins from spiders, cone snails, centipedes, and sea anemones: activation on the disulfide‑knotted toxin core.
- Kunitz/BPTI- and Kazal-type serine protease inhibitors (including tick chemokine/complement inhibitors): activation on the small disulfide‑rich inhibitor domain.
- Hevein-like/seed defense peptides: activation on the cysteine-rich chitin‑binding hevein domain.
- Defensins (plant/fungal/animal CSαβ peptides) and vertebrate hepcidin: activation on the cysteine‑stabilized mature AMP region.
- Euplotes ciliate mating pheromones: activation on the secreted disulfide‑rich pheromone core.
- Cysteine-rich modules within large extracellular/mucin-like proteins: activation on the short, cysteine‑dense repeat/subdomain embedded in the larger precursor.

Summary: Secreted, propeptide‑processed cysteine‑rich mini‑domains: compact extracellular segments immediately downstream of a signal peptide that contain clustered cysteines forming multiple disulfide bonds (defensin/CSαβ, WAP four‑disulfide core, cystine‑knot/knottin, CHH‑like, evasin‑like, and related small CRP scaffolds), often flanked by dibasic convertase sites and enriched in Lys/Arg
Activation pattern: Regional activation on short segments (≈20–60 aa) right after the signal peptide; strong peaks on cysteines and nearby basic residues, frequently overlapping proprotein convertase (dibasic) processing motifs; may recur for multi‑domain or repeat CRP proteins
Exemplars: - WAP/four‑disulfide core protease inhibitors (SLPI/elafin/WFDC): activation on the WAP domain’s Cys framework following the signal/propeptide
- Plant defensin‑like peptides (DEFL/LURE/ESF) and thionins: activation on the mature antimicrobial CSαβ cysteine motif
- Venom cystine‑knot peptides (conotoxins/knottins, mini‑toxins): activation on the canonical Cys frameworks in the mature toxin region of prepropeptides
- Tick evasins (chemokine‑binding CRPs): activation on the Cys‑rich chemokine‑binding domain
- Crustacean CHH/MIH neuropeptide precursors: activation on the mature hormone core with conserved six‑Cys motif adjacent to dibasic cleavage
- Fungal GPI‑anchored cell‑wall adhesins/stress proteins: activation on extracellular Cys‑rich segments just after secretion signals
- Small plant CRP protease inhibitors: activation on the disulfide‑stabilized inhibitory mini‑domain

Summary: Short, disulfide‑bonded extracellular cysteine‑rich repeat modules—especially EGF‑like (including cbEGF and laminin‑type LE) and LDL receptor class A (LDLa) domains, but also von Willebrand type C (CR) and other disulfide‑rich repeats—detected via acidic/polar loop motifs flanked by conserved cysteines (including Ca2+-binding Dx[D/N] motifs when present); broadly marks ectodomains of secreted proteins and single‑pass receptors.
Activation pattern:
- Strong activation confined to extracellular regions; absent in transmembrane helices and cytoplasmic tails.
- Repeated peaks aligning with tandem repeats; long activation tracts across multi‑repeat proteins.
- LDLa repeats: maxima over the central acidic DxSDE/DxD… segment; flanking cysteines variably engaged.
- EGF‑like repeats (cbEGF and LE): highest in the C‑terminal half containing the D/N‑x‑D/N‑x(4)‑Y/F motif when present, near the last cysteines.
- Also activates analogous acidic/polar loops in other cysteine‑rich repeats (e.g., VWC/CR, TIL/Kunitz, TSR); preference for D/E/S/T/N/Q/G and Y with nearby Cys; modest activation in short acidic linkers between repeats.
Exemplars:
- LDL receptor family (LDLR/LRP1/LRP4): LDLa repeat Ca2+-binding loops and cbEGF/LE segments across the ectodomain.
- Notch receptors and ligands (Notch, Delta/Jagged): tandem EGF‑like repeats with peaks at Ca2+-binding loops.
- Coagulation/complement components (e.g., Factors VII/IX/X, protein C/S, C1r/C1s modules): cbEGF domains.
- ECM scaffolds and glycoproteins (fibrillins, fibulins, LTBPs, laminins, tenascins, matrilins): arrays of EGF‑like/LE repeats.
- Chordin‑like/BMP modulators (BMPER/Crossveinless‑2, chordin): arrays of VWC/CR repeats.
- Cell‑adhesion receptors (selectins, integrin β I‑EGF modules) and extracellular metalloproteases/modulators (ADAM/ADAMTS): EGF‑like/cysteine‑rich repeats.
- Disulfide‑rich protease inhibitors and invertebrate toxins (e.g., Kunitz/TIL‑type).
- Plant receptor‑like proteins/kinases (e.g., WAKs, vacuolar sorting receptors): ectodomains with EGF‑like repeats.

Summary: Extracellular secreted precursors and ectodomains with disulfide-bonded cysteine-rich loops/domains (cystine-stabilized scaffolds), and a subset of secreted neuropeptide precursors whose activation concentrates on flexible, processing-rich segments even without dense cysteine content. Common in proteins with signal peptides, glycosylation, and proteolytic processing.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks on cysteines and adjacent positions (often Gly/Pro and basic Lys/Arg) within extracellular regions; regional activation over cysteine-rich loops or repeats; also highlights Gly/Pro and Lys/Arg flanking propeptide cleavage motifs in cysteine-poor neuropeptide precursors; absent in transmembrane helices and cytosolic tails; strongest in low-to-moderate order ectodomain segments, sometimes near N-glycosylation and cleavage sites.
Exemplars:
- Chemokines (especially CXC): activation on conserved disulfide-forming cysteine motifs.
- Defensins/plant CRPs and knottin-like/trypsin inhibitor peptides (CSαβ/ICK scaffolds): activation across disulfide-bonded loops.
- WFDC, Kunitz, and Kazal protease inhibitors: activation on disulfide-stabilized inhibitor domains.
- Venom toxins (e.g., Kunitz-type, ShK, disintegrins): activation on clustered cysteines defining the scaffold.
- Viral envelope glycoproteins (class I/II/III): activation in cysteine-rich ectodomains near disulfide networks and glycosylation sites.
- Extracellular receptor/adhesion and metalloprotease proteins: activation on EGF-like, disintegrin, and other cysteine-rich modules.
- DEG/ENaC family channels: activation in the extracellular cysteine-rich loop.
- Neuropeptide hormone precursors (e.g., small cardioactive peptides): activation around flexible, dibasic cleavage-rich segments even with low cysteine content.
- Apicomplexan AMA1 invasion protein: activation confined to ectodomain cysteine-rich segments, absent from TM/cytosolic regions.
