Activation pattern: Domain-level activation across extracellular repeat modules with sharp residue-level peaks on conserved cysteines (and adjacent prolines); in small toxins/AMPs only a few core Cys/Pro positions spike, whereas in large multidomain ectoproteins many sites across N‑terminal/extracellular repeats are activated.
Exemplars: - Cysteine‑knot toxins and antimicrobial peptides (defensins, plant cyclotides/knottins, cone/snail/scorpion toxins) — peaks on the conserved cystine‑knot cysteine framework.
- Protease inhibitors (Kunitz, Kazal, WAP/four‑disulfide core) — activation on the disulfide scaffold and the reactive‑site loop (often including Pro).
- EGF‑like and LDLR class A repeats of extracellular receptors (LDLR/LRP, Notch/coagulation/selectins) — activation on the repeat’s conserved cysteines (and Ca2+‑binding loop in LDLR‑A).
- Thrombospondin type‑1 repeat (TSR/TSP1)–containing proteins (thrombospondins, ADAMTS/ECM proteins) — peaks on TSR disulfide‑bonded cysteines flanking the WxxW ladder.
- Adhesion GPCR ectodomains — activation across their long N‑terminal cysteine‑rich modules preceding the GPS/GAIN site.
- Chemokines (CC/CXC/CX3C) and other immune complement‑related extracellular proteins — peaks on the defining cysteine motifs in the N‑terminal/loop regions.
- Viral envelope/membrane glycoproteins — activation on disulfide‑stabilized cysteine‑rich loops in ectodomains.
- Secreted serine proteases — broader activation over disulfide cysteines in the catalytic domain and associated propeptides.

Summary: Secreted, propeptide‑processed cysteine‑rich mini‑domains: compact extracellular segments immediately downstream of a signal peptide that contain clustered cysteines forming multiple disulfide bonds (defensin/CSαβ, WAP four‑disulfide core, cystine‑knot/knottin, CHH‑like, evasin‑like, and related small CRP scaffolds), often flanked by dibasic convertase sites and enriched in Lys/Arg
Activation pattern: Regional activation on short segments (≈20–60 aa) right after the signal peptide; strong peaks on cysteines and nearby basic residues, frequently overlapping proprotein convertase (dibasic) processing motifs; may recur for multi‑domain or repeat CRP proteins
Exemplars: - WAP/four‑disulfide core protease inhibitors (SLPI/elafin/WFDC): activation on the WAP domain’s Cys framework following the signal/propeptide
- Plant defensin‑like peptides (DEFL/LURE/ESF) and thionins: activation on the mature antimicrobial CSαβ cysteine motif
- Venom cystine‑knot peptides (conotoxins/knottins, mini‑toxins): activation on the canonical Cys frameworks in the mature toxin region of prepropeptides
- Tick evasins (chemokine‑binding CRPs): activation on the Cys‑rich chemokine‑binding domain
- Crustacean CHH/MIH neuropeptide precursors: activation on the mature hormone core with conserved six‑Cys motif adjacent to dibasic cleavage
- Fungal GPI‑anchored cell‑wall adhesins/stress proteins: activation on extracellular Cys‑rich segments just after secretion signals
- Small plant CRP protease inhibitors: activation on the disulfide‑stabilized inhibitory mini‑domain

Summary: Secreted, short cysteine-rich peptides and small extracellular cysteine-rich domains stabilized by multiple disulfide bonds (CRPs), spanning venom toxins, disintegrins, defensins/hepcidin, Kunitz/Kazal/hevein-like inhibitors/defense peptides, and related cystine‑knotted or cysteine‑stabilized folds. The feature captures the mature, proteolytically processed peptide/module characterized by clustered Cys (often CC motifs) and basic residues.
Activation pattern: Regional activation confined to short mature peptide segments (tens of residues) following the signal peptide and propeptides; minimal/absent on signal/pro-regions. Strong residue-level peaks on cysteines and frequent secondary peaks on Lys/Arg and Gly. Activation spans mixed secondary structure (β-strands, coils, short helices) and can include key functional loops (e.g., RGD in disintegrins).
Exemplars: - Plant cyclotides (cystine-knot cyclopeptides, e.g., chassatide): activation across the cyclic cystine‑knot core of the mature peptide after processing.
- Snake venom disintegrins: activation across the disintegrin domain, including the RGD integrin-binding loop and adjacent cysteine-dense core.
- Inhibitor cystine-knot (ICK) venom toxins from spiders, cone snails, centipedes, and sea anemones: activation on the disulfide‑knotted toxin core.
- Kunitz/BPTI- and Kazal-type serine protease inhibitors (including tick chemokine/complement inhibitors): activation on the small disulfide‑rich inhibitor domain.
- Hevein-like/seed defense peptides: activation on the cysteine-rich chitin‑binding hevein domain.
- Defensins (plant/fungal/animal CSαβ peptides) and vertebrate hepcidin: activation on the cysteine‑stabilized mature AMP region.
- Euplotes ciliate mating pheromones: activation on the secreted disulfide‑rich pheromone core.
- Cysteine-rich modules within large extracellular/mucin-like proteins: activation on the short, cysteine‑dense repeat/subdomain embedded in the larger precursor.

Summary: Mature soluble extracellular domains of secreted precursor proteins: the feature turns on immediately after signal peptide (and any propeptide) cleavage and spans the processed secreted chain across diverse folds and taxa.
Activation pattern: Domain-level, long continuous activation starting near the canonical signal-peptide cleavage site (~positions 18–35) and covering most or all of the mature chain; minimal to absent on the hydrophobic signal peptide and propeptides. Activation occurs across helices, strands, and coils, in both ordered and intrinsically disordered secreted proteins, with occasional local peaks but no single motif.
Exemplars: Cytokines: interferon-gamma and a viral interleukin-6 mimic show strong activation across the mature cytokine domain, none on the signal peptide; Lipid transport: insect apolipophorin-3 activates across the mature helical apolipoprotein domain, not on signal peptide/propeptide; Odorant/pheromone-binding proteins: insect OBP/PBP family activates across the mature cysteine-rich secreted domain; Antimicrobial peptides: microplusin activates across the mature disulfide-rich peptide, not on the signal peptide; Allergens: major allergen I activates across the processed allergen chain including disulfide-bonded cysteines and glycosylation site; Secreted structural proteins: alpha-S2-casein activates across the mature, largely disordered secreted chain.

Summary: Conserved N-terminal segment of EGF-like repeats, recognizing the cysteine framework that initiates the EGF fold in extracellular, disulfide-rich proteins.
Activation pattern: Localized, repeat-wise activation at the starts of individual EGF-like domains; sharp residue-level peaks within the first disulfide loop (often on His/Val/Asn/Tyr/Thr residues adjacent to the conserved cysteines), with variable signal on nearby cysteines; repeats across tandem arrays; minimal in signal peptides and non-EGF modules (e.g., MAM), with occasional buildup in the short linker immediately preceding the first repeat.
Exemplars: - EGFR ligands (epiregulin): activation across the N-terminal portion of the single EGF-like growth-factor domain, including residues around the first disulfide.
- Fibulin family (ECM proteins with EGF-like repeats): strong, repeated peaks at the N-terminus of each repeat within the cysteine-flanked region; inactive in signal peptide and distal non-EGF regions.
- EGFL proteins (e.g., EGFL6): high, localized peaks within specific N-terminal EGF-like repeats; no activation in the intervening disordered segment or the C-terminal MAM domain.

Summary: N-terminal, immediately post–signal peptide pro-regions of secreted/luminal proteins: intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity segments enriched in acidic and Ser/Thr/Pro residues that frequently harbor proteolytic processing motifs and embedded bioactive peptides (common in prohormones/toxin precursors, ECM and exocrine secretions).
Activation pattern: Regional activation forming long, contiguous stretches that begin right after the signal peptide; minimal on the signal peptide itself and on structured C‑terminal domains. Peaks can coincide with embedded peptide segments and/or clusters of basic residues typical of proprotein convertase/kallikrein cleavage sites; overall low-to-moderate structure confidence (often coil with occasional short helices).
Exemplars: - Neuroendocrine granule proproteins (e.g., chromogranins): activation over N‑terminal peptide segments that are processed into bioactive peptides (Peptide I/II), not on the signal peptide.
- Kininogen/bradykinin precursors: activation across the N‑terminal region containing the bradykinin segment and adjacent helical stretch, immediately post–signal peptide.
- Bone/ECM phosphoproteins (e.g., MEPE/SIBLING family): activation over the disordered, compositionally biased N‑terminal region after the signal peptide.
- Salivary proline-rich proteins: activation on the P‑rich, disordered N‑terminal segment following the signal peptide.
- Plant small secreted peptide precursors (e.g., GLV/RGF/CLE-type): activation on the N‑terminal pro-region of the preproprotein; little/no activation on the short mature peptide.
- Acrosomal/other luminal secreted glycoproteins: activation at the N‑terminus of the mature chain after the signal peptide, including low‑complexity/coil segments with glycosylation sites.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low-complexity segments enriched in serine/threonine/proline/glycine and often basic (lysine/arginine), typically found in flexible N- or C-terminal tails and loops; highlights IDRs that may harbor short linear motifs (e.g., basic NLS patches) rather than structured domain cores.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long disordered stretches with additional sparse residue-level peaks in low-confidence loops; often N-terminal-biased in short/viral proteins; rarely within well-folded cores.
Exemplars: Retroviral accessory proteins (e.g., HTLV-1 p30): activation on central and C-terminal IDRs including a basic nuclear localization signal; p53-regulated apoptosis-inducing microprotein: widespread activation across a globally disordered protein; Bacterial DNA ligase: scattered activation in an annotated disordered linker and flexible loops within the ligase domain; Uncharacterized human microprotein: multiple peaks throughout a low-pLDDT, disordered sequence irrespective of predicted secondary structure.

Summary: Short residue windows in mixed-composition regions of diverse proteins, frequently in N-terminal or non-catalytic portions of enzymes, transmembrane-adjacent stretches, and small secreted peptides.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks concentrated in short 3–7 residue windows, often clustered with several nearby peaks. Activated residues are chemically diverse (including hydrophobic, polar, and charged residues) and can occur in helical transmembrane segments, disordered linkers, or globular regions outside annotated catalytic/binding sites.
Exemplars:
- Bacterial DNA ligase: clusters of peaks in the N-terminal region upstream of the catalytic and BRCT domains.
- Viral integrase homolog: short peaks within the chain including a GPAYGRP-containing segment.
- Peroxisomal biogenesis factor 9 (Pex9): peaks overlapping helical transmembrane segments and an adjacent disordered/polar region.
- Small secreted peptides (e.g., Califin-B large subunit): short peaks within the mature peptide.

Summary: Single-pass alpha-helical transmembrane signal-anchor segments in small membrane proteins across taxa; a 15–25-residue hydrophobic helix used to anchor proteins in lipid bilayers, enriched in Leu/Ile/Val/Phe with internal aromatics and glycines, few charges, occasional cysteines, and rare internal prolines.
Activation pattern: Strong regional activation over a single, contiguous hydrophobic helix (typically 15–25 residues), with residue-level peaks in the hydrophobic/aromatic core and minimal activation in flanking cytosolic/periplasmic/luminal regions; often near the N-terminus (signal-anchor) but can occur mid-sequence; coincides with annotated/predicted alpha-helical transmembrane segments.
Exemplars: - Bacteriophage lysis proteins — activation on their sole membrane-spanning anchor helix.
- Virion membrane proteins (e.g., poxvirus/orthopox orthologs) — activation on the N-terminal helical signal-anchor.
- Plant viral movement proteins — activation on the single transmembrane helix.
- Photosystem II assembly factor Psb34 — activation on its thylakoid single-pass transmembrane helix.
- Cytochrome bd ubiquinol oxidase small accessory subunit (CydX) — activation on its single membrane-spanning helix.
- Endoregulin-like micropeptide regulators — activation on their single, helical membrane anchor.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity segments (often serine/proline‑rich) that serve as phosphorylation‑ and partner‑binding platforms in large eukaryotic scaffold/adaptor and signaling proteins; the feature highlights SLiM‑bearing IDRs and avoids well‑folded catalytic or recognition domains.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across extended IDRs with many discrete residue‑level peaks; peaks frequently occur in low‑pLDDT coil/incipient‑helix segments and near annotated interaction regions or PTM sites; little to no activation in structured domains.
Exemplars: - Tensin (focal adhesion adaptor): activation across the unstructured N‑terminal scaffold; absent from folded SH2/PTB domains.
- Multi‑domain RhoGEF/FYVE/PH regulators: activation confined to disordered N‑terminal/linker regions; no activation in DH, PH, or FYVE domains.
- Inositol polyphosphate 5‑phosphatases: activation in the long disordered N‑terminal region with discrete peaks in coil/transient helices.
- Vacuolar transport adaptor Vac17: strong activation within disordered VAC8‑binding C‑terminus and MYO2‑binding region (SLiM‑mediated PPIs).
- Centromeric chaperone HJURP: localized peaks in low‑confidence helical/isoform‑variable segments adjacent to SUMOylation sites.
- RGS signaling proteins with GoLoco motif: activation throughout disordered C‑terminal tails, including the GoLoco SLiM; absent from PDZ/PID/RGS folded domains.

Summary: Generic detector of low-complexity or low-structure segments, with a bias toward the N-terminal portion of proteins, including secretory signal peptides, disordered N-terminal stretches, and short membrane-embedded helical regions.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks; sparse, isolated activations often concentrated within the first ~100 residues (frequently within the first 30), though peaks can also appear in mid-protein membrane or low-complexity stretches. Peaks occur within signal peptides, low-pLDDT disordered coils, and short helices, including transmembrane helical segments; rarely form contiguous runs.
Exemplars: - Secreted serpin (antithrombin): peak in the N‑terminal signal peptide and additional peaks in a longer disordered N‑terminal segment.
- Antimicrobial peptide precursor (lumbricin): strong peaks confined to the N‑terminal signal peptide; minimal activation in the mature peptide.
- Secreted bacterial catalase–peroxidase (KatG): minor peaks in the signal peptide and immediately at the start of the mature chain.
- Poxvirus accessory protein: multiple peaks across low-confidence, disordered regions near the N‑terminus.
- Retroviral integrase homolog: peaks near the N‑terminus and at residues just before an annotated disordered linker.
- p53-induced DNA-binding protein (Killin): peaks on basic residues within a low‑pLDDT, N‑terminal DNA-binding region.
- Small membrane protein (ATP synthase subunit 8): peaks within an N-terminal transmembrane helix.

Summary: Low-complexity, intrinsically disordered segments—often at protein N-termini—such as mucin-like/propeptide regions or flexible linkers adjacent to signal/transit peptides, common in small secreted or membrane-associated proteins and also as disordered extensions in diverse enzymes (broad taxonomic coverage, including viral, bacterial, and eukaryotic proteins).
Activation pattern: Regional activation over short to moderate stretches, frequently in disordered or polar/low-complexity segments; in longer proteins, multiple low-complexity patches can activate; in micropeptides, activation can span much of the sequence. Residue-level peaks can fall on Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly within polar-residue stretches but also on basic or hydrophobic residues within the same disordered context.
Exemplars:
- Viral envelope/accessory microproteins: activation on N-terminal Ser/Thr/Pro-rich disordered segments (often mucin-like or regulatory tails).
- Secreted eukaryotic effectors (e.g., oomycete RxLR effectors): activation on the low-complexity region flanking the signal peptide/RxLR motif.
- Human testis-biased and lncRNA-derived micropeptides: activation across intrinsically disordered peptide regions.
- Secreted precursors/propeptides: activation on N-terminal regions following the signal peptide.
- Membrane-associated single-pass proteins: activation on luminal or cytosolic tails flanking the transmembrane helix.
- Bacterial/archaeal metabolic enzymes: activation on disordered, low-complexity N-terminal extensions/linkers enriched in Ser/Thr/Gly/Pro.

Summary: Short linear motifs centered on serine/threonine within intrinsically disordered regions that correspond to eukaryotic Ser/Thr phosphorylation sites (often SP/TP or basic R/K-flanked motifs), used for regulatory control across diverse proteins including viral proteins
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks on single S/T or 1–3 aa motifs, punctate and distributed across proteins; strongly enriched in low-pLDDT coils and low-complexity segments; depleted in folded domains and transmembrane helices; occasional peaks at edges of low-confidence helices; context frequently includes nearby proline and/or basic residues
Exemplars: - PH plus RapGAP scaffold proteins: activation on S/T residues in disordered linkers; minimal signal in folded PH and GAP domains
- Chromatin regulator Spt21: multiple peaks in disordered C-terminal regions; includes a known phosphoserine site
- TORC1 subunit Tco89: peaks at/near an annotated phosphothreonine and other disordered segments
- Large transmembrane receptor with long cytosolic tail (stum): activation confined to disordered cytosolic regions; none in transmembrane helices
- Developmental cytoskeletal regulator (bottleneck): clusters on S/T within low-complexity, basic-enriched disordered C-terminus
- Small GTPase regulators (e.g., RhoGAPs, RasGEFs, ARF GEFs) and protein kinases: signal found in regulatory low-complexity regions and termini rather than catalytic cores, consistent with phosphorylation-prone SLiMs

Summary: Small, often poorly characterized or compositionally biased proteins, including viral accessory proteins, cancer/testis and germline-associated proteins, antisense-ORF microproteins, and short secreted/surface peptides; activation is broadly distributed across the polypeptide rather than focused on a single structured domain
Activation pattern: Regional/distributed activation spread across much of the protein with sparse residue-level peaks; often includes early N-terminal residues and disordered segments; variable coverage from short patches to most of the protein
Exemplars:
- Viral non-structural/accessory proteins: activation distributed through the protein, including basic/Arg-rich motifs such as nuclear localization signals.
- Cancer/testis antigens and germline-associated proteins: activation on long disordered low-complexity regions, often at N-termini.
- Small uncharacterized microproteins/antisense ORFs: activation spanning most of the polypeptide.
- Short secreted peptides and toxin precursors: activation across both signal/propeptide and mature regions.
- Compact cytosolic proteins with disordered N- or C-terminal extensions: activation enriched on the disordered tails.

Summary: Broadly distributed activation across small secreted peptides, processed protein fragments, and various polar/charged residues in short proteins, with frequent firing in viral, venom, and signaling-peptide contexts.

Activation pattern: Sparse residue-level peaks scattered across the protein, with no strong preference for structured versus unstructured regions; peaks occur on a mix of polar (Asn, Asp, Ser, Gln), basic (Arg, Lys), and hydrophobic (Leu, Val, Ala) residues, and can fall within transmembrane helices, disordered stretches, or short folded chains alike.

Exemplars:
- Secreted peptide hormones (cholecystokinin, kisspeptin/metastin): multiple peaks across the processed peptide chain.
- Snake venom metalloproteinase/disintegrin fragment: distributed peaks across the short chain.
- Viral hexon-linking precursor proteins: weak peaks distributed across the chain including propeptide and cleaved segments.
- Peroxisomal biogenesis factors: peaks within transmembrane helices and other regions of the membrane protein.
- Bacterial methyltransferases: activation localized to C-terminal disordered extension while the catalytic core is inactive.
- Antithrombin/serpin precursor: peaks spanning the signal peptide and mature chain.

Summary: Short proteins (microproteins, secreted peptide precursors, and small viral regulatory proteins), with activation favoring signal peptide, propeptide, and disordered stretches but also extending into the body of small mature peptides.
Activation pattern: Residue-level, multi-site peaks distributed across short sequences; frequently concentrated in N-terminal signal peptides, adjacent prosegments, and intrinsically disordered C-terminal tails, but also seen within compact mature peptide chains when the protein itself is small.
Exemplars: - Conotoxin-like peptide precursors (venom prepropeptides): activation on the signal peptide and propeptides, peaking near cleavage boundaries, with little on the mature disulfide-rich toxin.
- cAMP-dependent protein kinase inhibitors (PKI isoforms): scattered peaks across intrinsically disordered regions of these short inhibitory microproteins.
- Viral accessory/regulatory proteins (e.g., Vpr, agnoprotein, nuclear egress protein): peaks over short N-terminal and C-terminal disordered/low-complexity stretches, occasionally extending into adjacent structured segments.
- Short secreted peptide/hormone/toxin precursors broadly: signal peptides and pro-sequences highlighted, with activation sometimes also present across small mature peptide chains.
- Human testis-associated or lncRNA-derived microproteins: activation across Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly–enriched disordered stretches.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity, charge‑biased tails (long N- or C‑terminal IDRs enriched in Lys/Arg and/or Asp/Glu, often with K–A–P repeats and Ser/Thr phosphorylation sites). The feature primarily recognizes the sequence/structural property of these polyelectrolyte IDRs—which are especially common in chromatin/nuclear proteins—while excluding folded domains.
Activation pattern: Extended regional activation across long IDRs with low predicted structure (coil, low pLDDT); strongest over compositionally biased blocks (polybasic or polyacidic, low complexity, Ser/Thr‑rich), with sharp loss of activation inside structured domains (e.g., histone fold, PHD finger, enzymatic cores). Frequently starts near a domain boundary and continues through the terminal tail.
Exemplars: Linker histone H1 family: broad activation on Lys‑rich C‑terminal tails with K–A–P motifs (dominant overall among strongest activators); Protamine‑like sperm nuclear proteins: continuous activation across Arg/Lys‑rich disordered sequences; HMG/FACT subunit SSRP1: activation begins near the end of the HMG box and intensifies across the long disordered, charge‑biased, phospho‑rich C‑terminal tail; Histone H2B variants: activation confined to the basic, disordered N‑terminal tail and excluded from the histone‑fold domain; FKBP immunophilin (FKBP4): long C‑terminal low‑complexity, charged IDR is activated, while PPIase domains are not; DNA polymerase delta subunit 3: extensive activation over the disordered, low‑complexity C‑terminal region, absent from structured parts; ING/YNG (NuA4/ING) PHD‑finger chromatin factors: activation on disordered regions flanking the PHD finger, with the folded PHD domain excluded.

Summary: Polyanionic, intrinsically disordered low‑complexity tracts enriched in Asp/Glu and S/T/P/G repeats that function as flexible, modification‑rich scaffold/matrix regions—frequent in secreted/ECM and cell‑wall proteins as well as cytoskeletal/nuclear scaffolds—often mediating Ca2+ binding/sequestration, biomineralization nucleation, and/or dense O‑glycosylation/phosphorylation
Activation pattern: Strong regional activation across long contiguous low‑complexity segments (often N‑ or C‑terminal tails or large internal tracts), rather than sharp residue‑level motifs
Exemplars: - Biomineralization matrix proteins (dentin phosphoprotein from DSPP, osteopontin, bone sialoprotein, enamelin/amelogenin): activation on acidic, phospho‑Ser–rich disordered repeats that bind Ca2+ and nucleate hydroxyapatite.
- Caseins and secreted acidic phosphoproteins (alpha/beta‑caseins, chromogranins/secretogranins): activation on long polyanionic, phospho‑Ser clusters that sequester Ca2+ and form micellar/condensed phases.
- ECM proteoglycan core proteins and mucin‑like scaffolds (aggrecan, versican, perlecan, salivary proline‑rich proteins): activation on Ser‑Gly and S/T‑P–rich O‑glycosylated low‑complexity regions.
- Cornified envelope/keratinocyte proteins (involucrin, filaggrin, loricrin, SPRR/LCE families): activation on Glu/Ser/Pro‑rich disordered repeats serving as crosslinkable structural matrices.
- Microtubule/actin‑associated scaffolds and neurofilaments (MAP2/tau, NEFH/NEFM, spectraplakin side arms): activation on acidic, Pro‑rich projection domains that are extended and highly disordered.
- Sperm/testis peri‑axonemal scaffolds (AKAPs, outer dense fiber/fibrous sheath proteins): activation on long acidic Ser/Pro‑rich low‑complexity regions used as flexible tethers/scaffolds.
- Neuropeptide/prohormone precursors and secretory granule matrix proteins (POMC/proenkephalin/prodynorphin; chromogranins): activation on acidic low‑complexity pro‑segments involved in granule condensation and processing.
- Plant cell‑wall extensins and proline‑/glycine‑rich proteins (extensins, PRPs, GRPs) and LEA/dehydrin proteins: activation on S/T–P (Hyp) repeats and low‑complexity acidic tracts that are O‑glycosylated/crosslinked or act as disordered stress‑response matrices.
- Nuclear/nucleolar acidic low‑complexity scaffolds (nucleolin/nucleophosmin‑like, chromatin‑associated IDRs): activation on Glu/Asp‑rich disordered tails that interact with basic proteins and RNA.

Summary: Eukaryote‑specific detector of the first structured module of a protein: the feature activates on the N‑terminal initiation segment of a folded domain or repeat (e.g., the first helix/strand unit or the first WD blade), which often forms interaction/assembly surfaces in multi‑subunit complexes; these N‑terminal stretches are commonly charged/Gly‑rich and can include Lys clusters.
Activation pattern: Regional activation focused on a long, contiguous N‑terminal segment (typically the first ~20–60 residues) corresponding to the N‑terminal half of a domain or the first repeat/blade; strongest on the initial helix/strand(s) and adjacent loop; little to no activation in later repeats/C‑terminal halves or in disordered tails.
Exemplars: - NTF2‑like nuclear transport factors: activation on the N‑terminal helix plus adjoining beta‑strand that forms the N‑terminal subdomain and dimer/interface region.
- WD40 beta‑propeller scaffolds: activation restricted to the first WD blade (Velcro/closure blade) at the N‑terminus, not on subsequent blades.
- Ubiquitin/ubiquitin‑like pathway components (e.g., SUMO and UBL‑domain shuttles): activation on the N‑terminal portion of the UBL fold or an N‑terminal UBL domain.
- Core Sm/LSM splicing ring subunits: activation on the N‑terminal segment of the Sm fold that mediates subunit contacts/RNA engagement.
- Ribosomal proteins, including ubiquitin–ribosomal fusion precursors and P‑stalk proteins: activation on basic N‑terminal stretches or the N‑terminal helical dimerization domain (not the acidic C‑terminal tail).
- EF‑hand calcium‑binding and actin‑associated proteins: activation on the N‑terminal helix/loop that seeds the first EF‑hand or interaction surface.
- Co‑chaperones/proteostasis adaptors and AN1/A20 zinc‑finger proteins: activation on N‑terminal interaction modules (e.g., UBL/UBA/ZnF‑adjacent regions).
- Vesicle trafficking/tethering factors: activation on N‑terminal repeat/blade elements that initiate scaffold assembly.

Summary: Long, low-complexity intrinsically disordered regions enriched in acidic residues (E/D) with Ser/Thr/Pro and Lys (PEST-like, poly-E/K polyampholyte tracts) that function as phosphorylation-regulated tails/linkers in large scaffolding proteins; these segments are depleted of hydrophobics and lie outside folded domains (also including the acidic A-domain of bacterial FtsY).
Activation pattern: Extended regional activation across entire disordered segments; little to none in structured/coiled-coil core domains; suppressed on hydrophobic residues and pure Lys-only repeats; strongest over S/T-rich, compositionally biased stretches with many phosphosites.
Exemplars: - Plant LEA/dehydrin proteins: activation on the N-terminal disordered, P/E/S/T-rich segment; reduced in Lys-only repeat blocks and at hydrophobic residues.
- Intermediate filament (neurofilament) proteins: strong, continuous activation across the C-terminal intrinsically disordered, highly phosphorylated tail; no activation in the N-terminal coiled-coil rod.
- ERM/4.1 family membrane–cytoskeleton adaptors: activation throughout the disordered C-terminal spectrin–actin-binding/CTD region; N-terminal FERM domain inactive.
- SRP receptor FtsY (bacteria): activation on the acidic, low-complexity N-terminal A-domain.

Summary: Charged, composition-biased interaction segments: long E/D/K/R-rich stretches that form extended alpha-helices (often coiled-coils or helical bundles) or acidic intrinsically disordered tails, used as electrostatic interfaces in eukaryotic macromolecular assemblies (chromatin/RNA-associated and cytoskeletal/coat complexes).
Activation pattern: Long, contiguous regional or domain-level activation; strongest across charged helices/coiled-coils and acidic IDRs, with local peaks at clusters of Lys/Arg or acidic blocks; can span entire charged helical bundles (e.g., BAG domain); weak on neutral, hydrophobic globular domains.
Exemplars: - Translation initiation factor eIF3 subunit J: activation on a long charged helix and adjacent low-complexity region that mediates eIF3 interactions, not on the compact C-terminal domain.
- HIRA-interacting protein 3: activation of the C-terminal acidic disordered motif that binds the histone H2A-H2B complex.
- Radial spoke head protein 3 (axonemal): activation across a central long coiled-coil alpha-helix, not in flanking disordered termini.
- BAG family Hsp70 co-chaperone: activation over the charged three-helix BAG domain that contacts Hsp70, with inactive N-terminal low-complexity region.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low-complexity segments enriched in serine/threonine/proline/glycine and often basic (lysine/arginine), typically found in flexible N- or C-terminal tails and loops; highlights IDRs that may harbor short linear motifs (e.g., basic NLS patches) rather than structured domain cores.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long disordered stretches with additional sparse residue-level peaks in low-confidence loops; often N-terminal-biased in short/viral proteins; rarely within well-folded cores.
Exemplars: Retroviral accessory proteins (e.g., HTLV-1 p30): activation on central and C-terminal IDRs including a basic nuclear localization signal; p53-regulated apoptosis-inducing microprotein: widespread activation across a globally disordered protein; Bacterial DNA ligase: scattered activation in an annotated disordered linker and flexible loops within the ligase domain; Uncharacterized human microprotein: multiple peaks throughout a low-pLDDT, disordered sequence irrespective of predicted secondary structure.

Summary: Low-complexity, intrinsically disordered segments—often at protein N-termini—such as mucin-like/propeptide regions or flexible linkers adjacent to signal/transit peptides, common in small secreted or membrane-associated proteins and also as disordered extensions in diverse enzymes (broad taxonomic coverage, including viral, bacterial, and eukaryotic proteins).
Activation pattern: Regional activation over short to moderate stretches, frequently in disordered or polar/low-complexity segments; in longer proteins, multiple low-complexity patches can activate; in micropeptides, activation can span much of the sequence. Residue-level peaks can fall on Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly within polar-residue stretches but also on basic or hydrophobic residues within the same disordered context.
Exemplars:
- Viral envelope/accessory microproteins: activation on N-terminal Ser/Thr/Pro-rich disordered segments (often mucin-like or regulatory tails).
- Secreted eukaryotic effectors (e.g., oomycete RxLR effectors): activation on the low-complexity region flanking the signal peptide/RxLR motif.
- Human testis-biased and lncRNA-derived micropeptides: activation across intrinsically disordered peptide regions.
- Secreted precursors/propeptides: activation on N-terminal regions following the signal peptide.
- Membrane-associated single-pass proteins: activation on luminal or cytosolic tails flanking the transmembrane helix.
- Bacterial/archaeal metabolic enzymes: activation on disordered, low-complexity N-terminal extensions/linkers enriched in Ser/Thr/Gly/Pro.

Summary: N‑terminal start and proteolytic maturation junction detector: activates on the initiator methionine or the first residue of a newly formed mature peptide after signal peptide/propeptide cleavage, typically within low‑complexity, disordered segments enriched in Ser/Pro/Gly/Arg; most prominent in secreted and membrane precursors and small peptides, but also marking N‑termini of diverse proteins (including many viral proteins) across taxa.
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks at the exact boundary (the first residue of the mature peptide and/or the immediately preceding residue), with short flanking N‑terminal stretches in low‑complexity IDRs; occasional weaker N‑terminal peaks elsewhere; broad, low‑specificity activation across taxa.
Exemplars: Plant PROPEP/Pep danger‑peptide precursors: strong peak at the N‑terminal boundary of the mature Pep within a disordered, acidic/basic‑biased prodomain; Viral envelope glycoproteins (e.g., class I fusion proteins): activation at signal peptide cleavage and/or polybasic convertase junctions, and at the extreme N‑terminus; Secreted hormone/neuropeptide and growth factor precursors: activation at propeptide removal sites that define the N‑terminus of the active peptide; Type I membrane receptors and secretory pathway glycoproteins: initiator Met and signal peptide region/cleavage site highlighted; lncRNA‑encoded micropeptides/smORFs: activation at Met1 and adjacent low‑complexity N‑terminal residues; Sperm/testis secreted or acrosomal proteins: activation on N‑terminal signal/pro‑region cleavage junctions; Bacterial/archaeal metabolic enzymes: weaker, generic N‑terminal activation at the start of disordered/low‑complexity tails; p53/apoptosis‑related proteins: N‑terminal disordered domains (e.g., transactivation/pro‑segments) show start‑proximal peaks.

Summary: Detector of compositionally biased, low‑complexity segments—predominantly intrinsically disordered Ser/Thr‑rich (often RS-/Pro‑containing) tracts—with a strong N‑terminal bias; it also flags the extreme N‑terminus including signal peptides of secreted precursors.
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks clustered within long disordered/low‑complexity regions (often spanning tens to hundreds of residues), with strongest peaks on Ser/Thr and nearby polar/basic residues; broad regional activation across such IDRs and minimal signal in well‑folded domains or transmembranes; additional discrete peaks frequently occur at residues 1–10, including within N‑terminal signal peptides.
Exemplars: - Transcriptional regulator (CROC-4): multiple peaks across a central low‑complexity disordered segment (S/T/R/P‑rich), with minor N‑terminal peaks.
- Mechanosensory receptor (Stum): numerous high peaks on serines dispersed through annotated disordered, low‑complexity/polar regions.
- Yeast RNA/chromatin‑associated factor (REF2‑interacting protein): peaks within disordered, compositionally biased tracts; strongest at a threonine in an S/T‑rich context, near (but not exactly on) annotated phosphosites.
- Secreted antimicrobial peptide precursor (lumbricin): strongest activation on the N‑terminal signal peptide helix; weaker peaks just after the signal peptide preceding a long disordered pro‑region.
- Yeast HPH2 regulatory protein: activation confined to disordered, low‑complexity regions in the N‑terminal two‑thirds; absent from the structured C‑terminal domain and its transmembrane helix.

Summary: Feature fires broadly across short proteins and small peptides, often covering most of the chain, with a preference for low-complexity, Pro/Gly-rich and polybasic segments but also extending into adjacent structured regions of short polypeptides.
Activation pattern: Broad, near-whole-protein activation in short (~50-200 aa) precursors and microproteins, with local maxima on Pro-rich tracts (including poly-P), GP/GG-containing stretches, and basic clusters; activation is not restricted to disordered patches and can extend into folded domains in short proteins.
Exemplars:
- Class II bacteriocin/lantibiotic precursors: broad activation across the short precursor chain, including mature regions containing GG and GW motifs.
- Secreted peptide/toxin and prohormone precursors (e.g., cholecystokinin): activation spread across the precursor chain.
- Sperm protamine precursors: concentrated on disordered propeptides and at propeptide–mature boundaries; minimal on highly basic mature cores.
- Viral accessory/regulatory microproteins (e.g., Vpx, Vif): activation across the short viral protein, with strong peaks on poly-P / GP-rich low-complexity patches when present.
- lncRNA-encoded micropeptides and very small uncharacterized proteins (e.g., RUSC1-AS1, N-cym): activation on Pro/Gly-rich disordered segments and across much of the chain.
- Plant transcription factors with WG/GW- and GP-rich low-complexity regions: activation on those patches.
- ATP synthase epsilon subunits: signal on short GP-rich linkers or terminal low-complexity tails.
- Large enzymes (e.g., DDX11 helicase, acyl-CoA synthetase): activation on disordered N/C-terminal low-complexity regions or basic/GP-rich insertions.
- Small mitochondrial membrane proteins (ATP8): signal on short basic matrix-exposed loops or termini flanking TM helices.
- Short proteolytic chains of secreted enzymes (e.g., snake venom metalloproteinase fragments, acrosin chain fragments): broad activation across the short mature chain, including within structured peptidase/disintegrin regions.

Summary: Extracellular/mature segments of secreted proteins — the bioactive peptide or ectodomain of secreted precursors — including toxins, chemokines/peptide hormones/neuropeptides, antimicrobial peptides, protease inhibitors, extracellular matrix modules, viral envelope ectodomains, bacterial toxins/lipoproteins, fungal/oomycete effectors, and secretory granule proteins. These segments are typically cationic and often cysteine‑rich/disulfide‑stabilized, but can also be disulfide‑poor (e.g., certain neuropeptides); the feature tracks mature peptides/ectodomains rather than signal peptides or cytosolic tails.

Activation pattern: Regional activation within extracellular/mature segments with residue‑level peaks, especially at basic residues (Lys/Arg; including prohormone convertase sites) and, when present, cysteines; strongest over well‑structured extracellular cores or compact mature peptides; minimal to absent in signal peptides and often lower in low‑complexity pro‑segments.

Exemplars: - Disulfide‑rich venom peptides (e.g., kappa‑/scorpion/centipede toxins, conotoxins): activation on the mature toxin’s folded core; in kappa‑scoloptoxin, strongest on the C‑terminal helical/disulfide region.
- Chemokines and peptide hormones/neuropeptides (e.g., CXCLs; natriuretic peptides, oxytocin/vasopressin‑like, insulin‑like; and disulfide‑poor peptides such as SIFamide): activation on the mature peptide/core, not on the signal/propeptide.
- Antimicrobial peptides (defensins and other cationic AMPs): activation across the extracellular peptide core.
- Protease inhibitors (Kunitz, Kazal, plant cystine‑knot/knottins): activation on the inhibitory domain.
- Extracellular matrix/serum glycoproteins with cysteine‑patterned modules (EGF/TSR/Ig‑like, albumin family): activation on extracellular repeats/domains.
- Viral envelope glycoproteins: activation on luminal ectodomain loops.
- Bacterial secreted toxins and lipoproteins: activation on secreted extracellular segments (including lipobox‑proximal Cys and mature toxin domains).
- Fungal/oomycete small secreted effectors: activation on compact extracellular cores.
- Secretory pathway enzymes/chaperones (PDI/Ero1/QSOX) and granule proteins (e.g., 7B2): activation on luminal Cys motifs or basic, structured regions within the secretory lumen.

Summary: Secreted/processed peptides and extracellular or luminal domains of membrane proteins. The feature reads the prepropeptide architecture of small secreted hormones/neuropeptides, defense peptides and toxins, as well as disulfide-stabilized domains of extracellular receptors/ligands and viral envelope glycoproteins.

Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks concentrated within the mature secreted peptide or extracellular/luminal domain, often on residues in the structured (helical/strand) core of the processed peptide, with additional peaks on nearby basic residues and on Gly/Pro in flexible loop regions; these peaks aggregate into regional activation over the mature peptide or ectodomain. Activation is variable in extent across proteins.

Exemplars:
- Invertebrate venom peptides (knottins/conotoxins/spider and sea anemone toxins): activation across the mature toxin, with additional support on basic residues near propeptide cleavage sites.
- Antimicrobial/defense peptides (animal defensins, plant thionins/defensins): activation across conserved disulfide-stabilized frameworks and Gly/Pro-rich loop residues.
- Neuropeptide/hormone precursors (e.g., calcitonin/CGRP/amylin-like, adrenomedullin): activation concentrated on the structured core of the mature hormone within the PEPTIDE region.
- Amidated, cysteine-poor neuropeptides (e.g., FMRFamide/SIFamide-like): activation across the mature peptide and clustered convertase sites.
- Plant secreted cysteine-rich signaling peptides and protease inhibitors (CRPs, Kunitz/Bowman–Birk): activation across the secreted domain and processing motifs.
- Viral envelope/secreted glycoproteins (e.g., HA/gp120-like ectodomains): broad activation across the ectodomain, including loop and cleavage-junction residues.
- Metazoan extracellular receptor/ligand systems (disulfide-stabilized ectodomains such as EGF-like/lectin/similar Cys-rich modules): activation across the ligand-binding domains.
- Extracellular/luminal loops of multi-pass membrane proteins with small Cys clusters (e.g., receptor-transporting proteins): activation on luminal segments.
- Prokaryotic secreted/surface or secretion-system-associated proteins: activation on periplasmic/extracellular segments.
- Occasional chromatin/DNA-binding and histone-modifying proteins (Cys-rich Zn-binding or catalytic motifs): weaker activation driven by clustered Cys and basic residues that resemble the extracellular motif pattern.

Summary: Short, low‑complexity, intrinsically disordered proteins and modules that encode targeting/processing signals—often but not always secretory—combining hydrophobic signal peptides, double‑Gly bacteriocin leaders, or polybasic/NLS‑like segments, frequently adjacent to Ser/Thr/Pro‑rich stretches and basic clusters (e.g., RXLR, KR/RR)—common in micropeptides, toxins/secreted precursors, viral accessory proteins, keratin‑associated and testis‑specific low‑complexity proteins across taxa
Activation pattern: Regional activation across short proteins, spanning hydrophobic/targeting segments and Ser/Thr/Pro‑rich low‑complexity tracts with peaks on basic motifs such as RXLR, dibasic KR/RR, or double‑Gly leader junctions
Exemplars:
- Oomycete RxLR effectors: activation on the N‑terminal signal peptide and the RXLR/EER host‑targeting motif immediately downstream.
- Secreted peptide hormone/venom/toxin precursors: activation on the signal peptide and basic prohormone convertase cleavage motifs (KR/RR) within the propeptide region.
- Class II bacteriocins: activation on the N‑terminal double‑Gly leader and adjacent cationic tract recognized by ABC exporters.
- Viral accessory/regulatory proteins (e.g., small disordered regulators): activation across S/T/P‑rich low‑complexity disordered segments containing polybasic/NLS‑like clusters.
- Keratin‑associated proteins (KRTAPs): activation over short, repetitive low‑complexity regions (Ser/Pro‑rich and basic tracts) typical of hair shaft proteins.
- Cancer/testis antigens and testis‑associated proteins: activation on Lys/Arg‑ and Pro/Ser‑rich low‑complexity stretches in very short proteins.
- Short uncharacterized micropeptides/antisense products: broad activation across their low‑complexity/basic segments.
- Enzymes that carry secretory leaders or short disordered/basic tails (including some cytosolic enzymes lacking signal peptides): activation limited to the disordered tail, not the catalytic core.

Summary: Short, intrinsically disordered, charge-biased N-terminal motifs at domain edges, including Cys-containing metal-coordination micro-motifs (notably adjacent to Fe-S cluster-binding Cys residues) and acidic/basic patches that serve as regulatory/nucleic-acid-interacting elements (transactivation segments, RNA/DNA-binding patches, or auto-inhibitory/interface loops).
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks within 8-20 aa windows, frequently in coils or short helix/loop segments with low structure confidence; often immediately N-terminal to or within small metal-coordination cores; can extend across longer low-complexity acidic (E/D, sometimes glycine-rich) blocks or basic Lys/Arg clusters; enriched near N-termini and domain boundaries.
Exemplars:
- Cytosolic Fe-S cluster assembly factors (NBP35/Nubp1 family): activation on the N-terminal disordered segment containing the conserved HCPGxESE motif immediately upstream of and including the first [4Fe-4S]-coordinating Cys.
- Plant NAC transcription factors: activation on the N-terminal disordered transactivation segment immediately upstream of the NAC DNA-binding domain.
- RIG-I-like helicase (MDA5/IFIH1): activation on short, flexible helix/loop elements in the C-terminal regulatory RNA-binding/auto-inhibitory domain.
- Zinc-finger/PR/SET chromatin regulators: activation on Cys/His-rich coordination loops and flanking low-complexity regulatory segments used for transcriptional modulation.
- RNA polymerase/RNP and small ribosomal proteins: activation on short acidic or Lys/Arg-rich low-complexity tails that contact nucleic acids.
- Viral transcription/oncoproteins: activation on acidic, disordered transactivation regions.

Summary: Short linear segments in intrinsically disordered or otherwise low-structure-confidence regions, often at N-termini and within signal peptides/propeptides of secreted and regulatory proteins (including viral accessory proteins and small ORF microproteins), enriched in small/basic residues (G, P, S, A, R; often with Cys), rather than in well-folded catalytic cores.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks scattered across IDRs and low-confidence coils/short helices; frequently clustered near the N-terminus, in signal peptides, propeptides, and disordered tails; little to no activation in well-structured domains; occasional activation in low-confidence transmembrane/signal-anchor helices.
Exemplars: - Viral accessory protein (HIV-1 Vif): peaks throughout low-pLDDT coils, especially the disordered N-terminal region.
- Neuropeptide precursor (Drosophila Amnesiac): activation in the N-terminal signal peptide and multiple mature peptide segments with very low pLDDT.
- Secreted serine carboxypeptidase: activation confined to disordered C-terminal tail, annotated disordered segment, the signal peptide, and a low-confidence C-terminal transmembrane helix; absent from the structured catalytic domain.
- Disordered human tumor-suppressor–associated protein (ST20): scattered peaks within predicted helices in a globally disordered chain, including the N-terminus.
- lncRNA/sORF-derived microprotein (IGF2 antisense protein): multiple peaks across annotated disordered regions rich in Arg/Pro/Gly.

Summary: Short, cationic, amphipathic peptide segments—typically the mature cores of secreted antimicrobial/cytolytic peptides and analogous AMP‑like helices embedded in larger proteins. These regions are Lys/Arg‑rich with interspersed hydrophobes, often form (or have propensity for) an amphipathic α‑helix, and are used for membrane interaction/disruption or other bioactive signaling; they are usually produced by proteolytic processing from precursor proteins and can include RiPP cores despite post‑translational crosslinks.
Activation pattern: Regional activation on short contiguous blocks (∼15–40 aa, sometimes shorter), with sharp on/off at the boundaries of mature peptide segments; minimal activation in signal peptides and propeptides. Peaks often coincide with hydrophobic residues along an amphipathic face and clusters of Lys/Arg. Frequently at N‑ or C‑terminal helices or short internal helices with low-to-moderate pLDDT.
Exemplars: - Amphibian helical antimicrobial peptides (e.g., aureins): activation precisely on the mature AMP helix, not on signal/propeptide.
- Hymenopteran venom cytolysins (e.g., myrmeciitoxins): strong activation across the mature toxin’s amphipathic α‑helix.
- Lantibiotic RiPPs (e.g., lacticin 3147 A2): activation on the modified mature lantibiotic core despite lanthionine/beta‑methyllanthionine crosslinks.
- Phage/bacterial holins: activation on the N‑terminal amphipathic helix adjacent to the first transmembrane segment; little/no activation in TM or periplasmic domains.
- Crustacean anti‑lipopolysaccharide factors (ALFs): activation on the N‑terminal cationic LPS‑binding helix of the mature peptide.
- Plant NLR immune receptors (coiled‑coil N‑termini): activation on the N‑terminal CC helix implicated in membrane permeabilization/channel activity.
- Insect stress-response secreted proteins (Turandot family): activation on a C‑terminal amphipathic α‑helix of the mature chain.
- Outer membrane polysaccharide export proteins (CtrA family): activation on a short periplasmic C‑terminal helical tail with amphipathic character.
- Kininogen‑derived peptides (bradykinin variants): activation on the short, basic bioactive peptide released from a disordered region.

Summary: Membrane‑active amphipathic α‑helices enriched in small hydrophobic residues (A/V/L/I/G) that insert into, line, or associate with lipid bilayers—i.e., the pore‑forming/translocation helices of toxins and translocons and analogous lipid‑binding/stress‑sensing helices in other membrane proteins
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long, contiguous helical segments (often single helices or helical hairpins), with sparse charges and frequent Gly/Ala runs; peaks track α‑helical stretches that often fold upon membrane contact (low pLDDT in isolation). Activation typically avoids catalytic motifs and generic signal peptides/TM anchors, instead favoring amphipathic or pore‑lining helices (including lipid‑binding helices) within toxin, antimicrobial, and membrane‑associated domains.
Exemplars: - Pore-forming colicins: strong activation on the C‑terminal pore‑forming transmembrane/helical hairpin region.
- Bacillus thuringiensis Cry (δ‑endotoxins): activation on the N‑terminal pore‑forming helical bundle (domain I) with peaks in membrane‑inserting helices.
- Cationic antimicrobial peptides (e.g., Styelin‑D): activation confined to the mature amphipathic α‑helix; absent on the signal peptide and propeptide.
- Mitochondrial inner‑membrane protease OMA1: activation on amphipathic helices within the peptidase domain, including a cardiolipin‑binding/stress‑sensor region; little to no activation on the N‑terminal propeptide or the single‑pass TM anchor.

Summary: Detector of cationic, hydrophobic amphipathic alpha‑helical membrane‑interacting segments (including short transmembrane helices with basic flanks and pore‑forming amphipathic helices), with secondary emphasis on the maturation junctions of secreted membrane‑active peptides (notably C‑terminal amidation/cleavage sites).
Activation pattern: Predominantly long, contiguous activation across small helical membrane‑active peptides; in larger proteins, strong regional activation on specific alpha‑helical segments that contact or insert into membranes (TMs and adjacent basic loops, amphipathic helices), often near termini. In peptide precursors, sharp peaks at processing boundaries, especially at the C‑terminus of the mature peptide and adjacent Gly/Lys residues used for amidation. Residue preference is for basic (K/R) and hydrophobic (I/L/V/F/W/Y/A) content arranged in helical contexts; non‑amphipathic helices or acidic/disordered stretches are weak.
Exemplars: - Bacteriophage holins/antiholins: activation across N‑terminal transmembrane helices and cytoplasmic basic loops; decreased signal in non‑matching TM segments.
- Filamentous phage major coat proteins: strong activation on the short TM and adjacent amphipathic helical region used for membrane insertion/assembly.
- Adenovirus membrane‑active factors (e.g., preprotein VI/E1B Bcl‑2‑like): selective activation on amphipathic helices implicated in membrane binding/disruption; other helices remain low.
- Bcl‑2 family proteins: activation on the C‑terminal membrane‑anchoring helix and amphipathic BH‑region helices involved in membrane interaction.
- Peroxisomal membrane proteins (PEX11/PEX16): activation on amphipathic helices/hairpins that remodel or anchor to membranes.
- Lipid‑droplet surface proteins/perilipins: activation on amphipathic helices that target neutral‑lipid surfaces.
- Organelle membrane import/fission components (mitochondrial/chloroplast/plasma membrane): activation on amphipathic targeting or curvature‑sensing helices.
- Antimicrobial and venom peptides: near‑continuous activation across the mature cationic helical peptide; in precursors, sharp peaks at N‑ and C‑terminal cleavage sites and at C‑terminal amidation motifs (e.g., Gly/Lys donors).
- Bacteriocins (including helical and circular classes): strong activation across the membrane‑active helical segments with isolated dips at non‑matching residues.
- Globins (non‑membrane control): sparse residue‑level peaks limited to hydrophobic/basic helical faces, illustrating sequence‑composition specificity rather than generic helix detection.

Summary: Disordered/low-complexity module: broadly activates over intrinsically disordered, low-complexity, and polar/Pro/Gly/Gln-rich segments — including secretory or export/membrane-targeting segments (classical signal peptides, signal anchors, transit peptides, and non-classical low-complexity export signals), adjacent propeptide tails, and internal or C-terminal disordered regions. Mature folded cores are typically not activated. Active in plant secreted/storage proteins, bacterial type III effectors, and prion/disordered cytosolic proteins.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over disordered and low-complexity stretches, including N-terminal signal peptides or signal anchors (hydrophobic h-helix/cleavage vicinity), immediately following low-complexity/disordered tails, internal Q/N/G-rich disordered domains, and C-terminal propeptide/GPI signal regions. Deactivation over compact, well-folded cores. Peaks enriched in low-pLDDT, small/polar/Pro-rich segments and hydrophobic signal/SP-anchor helices.
Exemplars:
- Plant nsLTPs (incl. GPI-anchored): N-terminal SP and C-terminal propeptide/disordered tail; low on cysteine-stabilized core.
- Cereal prolamins/2S albumins: SP plus disordered N-/C-termini; low on structured central core.
- Streptomycete rodlin/chaplin surface proteins: N-terminal SP; low on amyloid-forming core.
- Antimicrobial/toxin precursors: SP and removable propeptides.
- Type III secretion components/effectors (e.g., Harpins, PopA): unstructured, low-complexity N-termini as export signals plus internal disordered repeats.
- Viral membrane-lytic/entry proteins: amphipathic N-terminal segments.
- ER/peroxisomal membrane proteins (e.g., EMC3, Pex13): N-terminal signal-anchor/targeting segments and adjacent disordered regions.
- Plant dehydrins and nodulin-related disordered proteins: strongly disordered, low-complexity segments despite lack of secretion.
- Q/N-rich prion domains (e.g., RNQ1): internal disordered low-complexity stretches.

Summary: Membrane-interacting helical modules: cationic, Gly/Ala-rich amphipathic α-helices and short transmembrane hairpins/fusogenic segments that mediate lipid binding, insertion, or pore formation in toxins, secretion/translocation factors, and viral/secreted proteins; typically low-confidence/disordered in isolation and become helical upon membrane contact.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long, contiguous helical stretches; strongest over amphipathic or hydrophobic helices (including TM segments), with peaks on small hydrophobics (A/V/L/I/G) and frequent Lys/Arg; tends to avoid structured catalytic cores, instead marking N- or C‑terminal delivery/membrane-interaction regions; often coincides with low pLDDT and predicted helices or annotated transmembranes; in peptides, activates on the mature membrane-active helix rather than the signal peptide.
Exemplars: - Cry-family insecticidal δ-endotoxins: activation on the N‑terminal pore-forming helical bundle (domain I) of Cry13Aa.
- Cationic antimicrobial peptide (moricin): activation across the mature α‑helical AMP, not the signal peptide.
- Type VI secretion effector VasX: activation over the C‑terminal membrane-inserting module comprising multiple transmembrane helices.
- LXG polymorphic toxin (YqcG): activation on a long C‑terminal, low‑pLDDT disordered segment following the LXG export domain (a membrane/translocation-prone tail-like region).
- T6SS ADP‑ribosyltransferase (mART) effector (Tre1): activation on N‑terminal glycine‑rich, low‑confidence helical regions flanking PAAR and outside the catalytic core, consistent with delivery/membrane-targeting helices.

Summary: Short residue windows in mixed-composition regions of diverse proteins, frequently in N-terminal or non-catalytic portions of enzymes, transmembrane-adjacent stretches, and small secreted peptides.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks concentrated in short 3–7 residue windows, often clustered with several nearby peaks. Activated residues are chemically diverse (including hydrophobic, polar, and charged residues) and can occur in helical transmembrane segments, disordered linkers, or globular regions outside annotated catalytic/binding sites.
Exemplars:
- Bacterial DNA ligase: clusters of peaks in the N-terminal region upstream of the catalytic and BRCT domains.
- Viral integrase homolog: short peaks within the chain including a GPAYGRP-containing segment.
- Peroxisomal biogenesis factor 9 (Pex9): peaks overlapping helical transmembrane segments and an adjacent disordered/polar region.
- Small secreted peptides (e.g., Califin-B large subunit): short peaks within the mature peptide.

Summary: Small, often poorly characterized or compositionally biased proteins, including viral accessory proteins, cancer/testis and germline-associated proteins, antisense-ORF microproteins, and short secreted/surface peptides; activation is broadly distributed across the polypeptide rather than focused on a single structured domain
Activation pattern: Regional/distributed activation spread across much of the protein with sparse residue-level peaks; often includes early N-terminal residues and disordered segments; variable coverage from short patches to most of the protein
Exemplars:
- Viral non-structural/accessory proteins: activation distributed through the protein, including basic/Arg-rich motifs such as nuclear localization signals.
- Cancer/testis antigens and germline-associated proteins: activation on long disordered low-complexity regions, often at N-termini.
- Small uncharacterized microproteins/antisense ORFs: activation spanning most of the polypeptide.
- Short secreted peptides and toxin precursors: activation across both signal/propeptide and mature regions.
- Compact cytosolic proteins with disordered N- or C-terminal extensions: activation enriched on the disordered tails.

Summary: Serine/threonine‑rich, low‑complexity intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs)—often containing RS dipeptides and proline‑directed S/T‑P motifs, with frequent glycine/proline (and occasional poly‑Q/polar) bias—used as regulatory and interaction tracts in eukaryotic nuclear and scaffold/cytoskeletal proteins; activation is largely absent from folded domains.
Activation pattern: Broad regional activation over long IDRs with multiple segments per protein; strong enrichment in S/T/G/P‑heavy low‑complexity stretches with local peaks over RS, S/T‑P and Pro/Gly‑rich subsequences; minimal to no activation within structured domains (e.g., zinc fingers, WH1, GYF, HTH/HARE, DEUBAD, PHD).
Exemplars: - P‑TEFb Cyclin T: C‑terminal disordered low‑complexity tail (basic/acidic, polar, glycine‑biased) strongly activated; structured N‑terminus not.
- GLI3 zinc‑finger transcription factor: multiple disordered segments (including DZIP1‑binding region) activated; zinc‑finger cores not.
- BCL9‑like coactivator: broad disordered region required for β‑catenin (CTNNB1) binding and other low‑complexity tracts activated.
- Mastermind coactivator: several low‑complexity disordered segments highlighted; no specific structured sites targeted.
- ASXL2 (Polycomb‑associated): disordered PTM‑rich segments (includes nearby Ser phosphorylation/Arg methylation) activated; HTH/HARE, DEUBAD, and PHD domains not.
- GRB10‑interacting GYF scaffold: disordered linkers and C‑terminal IDRs activated; folded GYF domain and long high‑confidence helices not.
- Ena/VASP actin regulator: Pro/Gly‑rich repeats and disordered EVH2 region activated; folded WH1 domain not.

Summary: Detector of compositionally biased, low‑complexity segments—predominantly intrinsically disordered Ser/Thr‑rich (often RS-/Pro‑containing) tracts—with a strong N‑terminal bias; it also flags the extreme N‑terminus including signal peptides of secreted precursors.
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks clustered within long disordered/low‑complexity regions (often spanning tens to hundreds of residues), with strongest peaks on Ser/Thr and nearby polar/basic residues; broad regional activation across such IDRs and minimal signal in well‑folded domains or transmembranes; additional discrete peaks frequently occur at residues 1–10, including within N‑terminal signal peptides.
Exemplars: - Transcriptional regulator (CROC-4): multiple peaks across a central low‑complexity disordered segment (S/T/R/P‑rich), with minor N‑terminal peaks.
- Mechanosensory receptor (Stum): numerous high peaks on serines dispersed through annotated disordered, low‑complexity/polar regions.
- Yeast RNA/chromatin‑associated factor (REF2‑interacting protein): peaks within disordered, compositionally biased tracts; strongest at a threonine in an S/T‑rich context, near (but not exactly on) annotated phosphosites.
- Secreted antimicrobial peptide precursor (lumbricin): strongest activation on the N‑terminal signal peptide helix; weaker peaks just after the signal peptide preceding a long disordered pro‑region.
- Yeast HPH2 regulatory protein: activation confined to disordered, low‑complexity regions in the N‑terminal two‑thirds; absent from the structured C‑terminal domain and its transmembrane helix.

Summary: Short, low‑complexity, intrinsically disordered proteins and modules that encode targeting/processing signals—often but not always secretory—combining hydrophobic signal peptides, double‑Gly bacteriocin leaders, or polybasic/NLS‑like segments, frequently adjacent to Ser/Thr/Pro‑rich stretches and basic clusters (e.g., RXLR, KR/RR)—common in micropeptides, toxins/secreted precursors, viral accessory proteins, keratin‑associated and testis‑specific low‑complexity proteins across taxa
Activation pattern: Regional activation across short proteins, spanning hydrophobic/targeting segments and Ser/Thr/Pro‑rich low‑complexity tracts with peaks on basic motifs such as RXLR, dibasic KR/RR, or double‑Gly leader junctions
Exemplars:
- Oomycete RxLR effectors: activation on the N‑terminal signal peptide and the RXLR/EER host‑targeting motif immediately downstream.
- Secreted peptide hormone/venom/toxin precursors: activation on the signal peptide and basic prohormone convertase cleavage motifs (KR/RR) within the propeptide region.
- Class II bacteriocins: activation on the N‑terminal double‑Gly leader and adjacent cationic tract recognized by ABC exporters.
- Viral accessory/regulatory proteins (e.g., small disordered regulators): activation across S/T/P‑rich low‑complexity disordered segments containing polybasic/NLS‑like clusters.
- Keratin‑associated proteins (KRTAPs): activation over short, repetitive low‑complexity regions (Ser/Pro‑rich and basic tracts) typical of hair shaft proteins.
- Cancer/testis antigens and testis‑associated proteins: activation on Lys/Arg‑ and Pro/Ser‑rich low‑complexity stretches in very short proteins.
- Short uncharacterized micropeptides/antisense products: broad activation across their low‑complexity/basic segments.
- Enzymes that carry secretory leaders or short disordered/basic tails (including some cytosolic enzymes lacking signal peptides): activation limited to the disordered tail, not the catalytic core.

Summary: The feature recognizes cationic, amphipathic, low-complexity segments that mediate targeting or membrane/lipid association—classically N‑terminal signal/transit/leader-like regions of secreted, mitochondrial, and viral proteins—and frequently the propeptide/mature regions of toxin and neuropeptide precursors; it can also highlight short basic/hydrophobic helices or redox-active motifs within structured domains.
Activation pattern: Predominantly long, continuous activation over N‑terminal, low‑pLDDT leader/propeptide regions enriched in Lys/Arg, Ser/Pro and hydrophobic/aromatic residues; with occasional residue-level peaks within well-structured helices (e.g., specific positions in thioredoxin CGHC motifs or matrix-exposed helices of membrane proteins).
Exemplars: 
- Venom phospholipase A2 precursors (activation on signal/propeptide segments and conserved cationic patches).
- Apolipoproteins (N‑terminal signal peptide and amphipathic helical stretches).
- Protein kinases with disordered/basic N‑termini (e.g., cyclin-dependent and PRK family N‑tails).
- Thioredoxin-fold protein disulfide-isomerases (peak at the CGHC active-site helix).
- Mitochondrial calcium uniporter (selected residues in a matrix-exposed helix).
- Conotoxin and other secreted toxin precursors; neuropeptide prepropeptides (activation across pro/mature peptide regions).
- Viral silencing suppressors and small membrane/morphogenesis proteins (basic, hydrophobic leader-like segments).
- Kinetochore coiled-coil scaffold proteins (basic low-complexity regions).
- FYVE-domain endosomal adaptors (basic, membrane/PIP-interacting low-complexity segments).
- RNA-modifying enzymes with basic N‑terminal tails (e.g., tRNA methyltransferases).

Summary: Low-complexity, intrinsically disordered, cysteine-poor segments enriched in small/polar and charged residues (G, A, S, T, K, E, D) that act as surface‑active, lipid‑interface–binding regions (amphipathic/helix‑forming “hydrophilin/apolipoprotein‑like” tracts). These occur broadly across taxa, often at N‑termini or luminal/cytosolic tails of secreted or membrane‑associated proteins, including stress‑protective hydrophilins/LEA proteins, apolipoproteins, ATG2 lipid‑transfer tethers, and cationic antimicrobial/venom peptides.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over long low‑complexity stretches (frequently N‑terminal), with diffuse highlighting and occasional peaks on glycine/threonine repeats or short amphipathic helix motifs; spans entire sequence for small AMPs/venom peptides; in large proteins (e.g., ATG2) covers extended acidic/polar IDRs flanking or preceding hydrophobic cores but not the transmembrane segments.
Exemplars: - Apolipoproteins (e.g., ApoC/ApoA/ApoE families): activation on amphipathic helix repeats and adjacent polar low‑complexity segments that coat lipid particles.
- Plant LEA/hydrophilin proteins (LEA4/LEA5, dehydrins, Hsp12‑like): activation across glycine/threonine/serine‑rich, charged repeats conferring stress‑protective, membrane‑associating properties.
- Autophagy‑related protein 2 (ATG2 family): activation over long acidic/polar IDRs and N‑terminal amphipathic membrane‑tethering segments used at ER–mitochondria/phagophore contact sites.
- Lipid‑droplet/oil‑body scaffolds (oleosins, perilipins, apolipoprotein‑like droplet proteins): activation on low‑complexity polar tails and amphipathic segments surrounding the hydrophobic hairpin/core.
- Cationic antimicrobial and venom peptides (melittin/cecropin/magainin/mastoparan‑like): activation across the whole cationic amphipathic segment that binds membranes.
- Membrane proteins with long disordered N‑ or luminal regions (mitochondrial/ER/PM): activation on polar/charged low‑complexity tails used as flexible linkers or membrane‑proximal surface‑binders.
- Viral matrix/core/viroporin‑associated proteins: activation on low‑complexity, amphipathic, membrane‑interacting stretches.
- Bacterial low‑complexity scaffold/toxin repeats: activation on glycine/threonine‑rich polar segments used for surface association or scaffolding.

Summary: Short helical/loop segments adjacent to membrane domains in membrane-associated proteins, including cytoplasmic helices flanking transmembrane anchors and lumenal/extracytoplasmic loops between transmembrane helices.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over contiguous short stretches of roughly 10-25 residues, with residue-level peaks on a mixture of hydrophobic/aromatic anchors (L, I, V, F, W) and interfacial basic residues (Arg/Lys), with tolerance for Gly/Pro. The activated stretch is typically positioned just outside an annotated transmembrane helix rather than within it; non-activated soluble tails far from the membrane domain are silent.
Exemplars:
- Sec61 γ subunits (translocon): activation on the N-terminal cytoplasmic amphipathic helix preceding the single TM anchor, peaking around a conserved Arg.
- Chloride channel CLIC-like protein 1 (ERAC1) across vertebrates: activation on a conserved lumenal loop region between transmembrane helices.
- Membrane metalloproteases of the S2P/RseP family (e.g., ARASP, ARASP2, MmpA): activation on a conserved soluble helical stretch flanking the catalytic membrane domain.

Summary: Short helical patches (often amphipathic and enriched in basic/aromatic residues) embedded within intrinsically disordered linkers or tails, typically positioned immediately C-terminal to signal/translocation motifs, adjacent to transmembrane segments, or at the edge of folded domains/coiled-coils. These helices mediate membrane association or adaptor docking in secretion, trafficking, and virulence contexts.
Activation pattern: Regional activation on contiguous 20–40 aa stretches with low predicted structure confidence but helix propensity; strongest residue-level peaks on hydrophobic/aromatic positions within the helix. Frequently located just downstream of motifs (e.g., RxLR-dEER), at domain termini (e.g., WD40, UBX), or proximal to transmembrane helices/coiled-coil boundaries.
Exemplars:
- Oomycete RxLR effectors: N-terminal segment immediately after RxLR-dEER used for host entry/membrane interaction.
- Autophagy PROPPINs (Atg18/Atg21): disordered C-terminal tail with a short amphipathic helix for membrane/adaptor contacts.
- Membrane-embedded autophagy receptors (Atg39/Atg40): cytosolic amphipathic/basic helical patches adjacent to hairpin TMs for ER-phagy machinery engagement.
- UBX-domain proteins: disordered C-terminal extension after the UBX fold containing a short helix for partner interactions.
- Clathrin assembly/adaptor proteins (epsins/ENTH/ANTH/AP180/AP-2): N-terminal insertion amphipathic helices that bind acidic membranes.
- Viral coat/membrane proteins and replicase polyproteins: TM-proximal amphipathic/basic helices or basic tails that anchor or organize membranes (e.g., filamentous phage coat G8P) and amphipathic helices in replicases.
- Bacterial pathogen effectors/toxins: basic/aromatic amphipathic helices for host membrane interaction/translocation.
- LEA proteins: Lys-rich amphipathic “K-segment” helices that form upon stress and associate with membranes.
- Nuclear envelope SUN/LEM proteins: basic helical patches/linker helices near the membrane that mediate partner or membrane contacts.
- Coiled-coil scaffold proteins (e.g., TRIMs): short basic helical patches at coiled-coil termini that mediate partner docking.

Summary: Serine/threonine‑rich, low‑complexity intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs)—often containing RS dipeptides and proline‑directed S/T‑P motifs, with frequent glycine/proline (and occasional poly‑Q/polar) bias—used as regulatory and interaction tracts in eukaryotic nuclear and scaffold/cytoskeletal proteins; activation is largely absent from folded domains.
Activation pattern: Broad regional activation over long IDRs with multiple segments per protein; strong enrichment in S/T/G/P‑heavy low‑complexity stretches with local peaks over RS, S/T‑P and Pro/Gly‑rich subsequences; minimal to no activation within structured domains (e.g., zinc fingers, WH1, GYF, HTH/HARE, DEUBAD, PHD).
Exemplars: - P‑TEFb Cyclin T: C‑terminal disordered low‑complexity tail (basic/acidic, polar, glycine‑biased) strongly activated; structured N‑terminus not.
- GLI3 zinc‑finger transcription factor: multiple disordered segments (including DZIP1‑binding region) activated; zinc‑finger cores not.
- BCL9‑like coactivator: broad disordered region required for β‑catenin (CTNNB1) binding and other low‑complexity tracts activated.
- Mastermind coactivator: several low‑complexity disordered segments highlighted; no specific structured sites targeted.
- ASXL2 (Polycomb‑associated): disordered PTM‑rich segments (includes nearby Ser phosphorylation/Arg methylation) activated; HTH/HARE, DEUBAD, and PHD domains not.
- GRB10‑interacting GYF scaffold: disordered linkers and C‑terminal IDRs activated; folded GYF domain and long high‑confidence helices not.
- Ena/VASP actin regulator: Pro/Gly‑rich repeats and disordered EVH2 region activated; folded WH1 domain not.

Summary: Immunoglobulin-superfamily (Ig-like) domains—especially C2-set repeats—predominantly in extracellular ectodomains of metazoan cell-adhesion and receptor proteins, with recognition also of standalone cytosolic Ig-like modules (e.g., telokin-like) and viral Ig-like mimics; generally avoids non-Ig modules such as FNIII cores and transmembrane helices, but can also engage the short flexible N-terminal linkers immediately adjacent to Ig-like domains (including in some adhesion GPCR N-termini lacking explicit Ig annotation).
Activation pattern: Regional/domain-boundary activation repeated across long Ig arrays: peaks begin in the short linker immediately preceding an Ig-like domain and extend into the first ~15–40 residues of the domain (often at strand-edge/loop regions with moderate confidence), sometimes spreading across the entire Ig module; minimal in enzymatic cores and TM segments; activation centers on Ig-like folds and their adjacent flexible linkers rather than being strictly confined inside the Ig core.
Exemplars:
- Neuronal contactins (GPI-anchored IgCAMs with multiple IgC2 domains): repeated peaks at the start of each Ig-like domain and preceding linkers.
- Receptor-type protein tyrosine phosphatases (LAR/PTPR families): strong activation across N-terminal Ig-like domains; little in downstream FNIII repeats or cytoplasmic phosphatase domains.
- Receptor tyrosine kinases with Ig-like ectodomains (e.g., VEGFR/KDR family): activation on Ig-like domains; none in kinase/cytosolic regions.
- IL-1/18 receptor family: activation across the trio of extracellular Ig-like C2 domains; none in the intracellular TIR domain.
- Adhesion GPCR N-termini with Ig-like modules or proximal linkers (e.g., ADGRA/GPR124; ADGRF3/GPR113): focused activation in the Ig-like region or immediately adjacent linker; none in 7TM/cytosolic regions.
- Viral envelope Ig-like proteins (e.g., herpesvirus gD): activation across the Ig-like core.
- Cytosolic telokin/Ig-like modules in myosin-associated kinases (e.g., smMLCK): activation across the telokin Ig-like domain; none in the catalytic kinase region.

Summary: Low-complexity terminal and internal segments enriched in Thr (often interleaved with His and short runs of branched hydrophobics like Ile/Val/Leu/Ala/Met), most commonly found in disordered C-terminal tails of membrane and cytoplasmic proteins, with occasional firing on N-terminal signal/transit peptide regions.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over short stretches dominated by clustered Thr in repetitive HTHTHT-like or T/I/V-rich low-complexity tracts; peaks land on Thr and on neighboring Ile/Val/Leu/Ala/Met residues; usually located in disordered C-terminal cytoplasmic tails outside annotated structured domains, and sometimes within N-terminal signal-peptide-spanning low-complexity segments; rarely within well-folded domains; typically low-confidence/disordered structure.
Exemplars:
- Membrane receptors with long cytoplasmic tails (e.g., FGF receptor-like, beta-adrenergic receptor): activation on Thr-rich low-complexity stretches in the cytoplasmic C-terminal tail.
- Gap junction/connexin family: activation in the cytoplasmic C-terminal tail on hydrophobic/Thr-containing low-complexity regions.
- Mitochondrial/organellar proteases (e.g., YME1-like): activation on C-terminal Thr-rich low-complexity tail.
- Plant secreted precursors: activation across the signal peptide region in low-complexity hydrophobic/aromatic repeats.
- Axonemal/structural proteins with internal disordered Thr-rich repeats: activation on extended HTHTHT-type tracts.
- Small uncharacterized/regulatory proteins: activation on internal Thr/hydrophobic low-complexity segments adjacent to disordered, charge-biased regions.
