Summary: Feature fires broadly across short proteins and small peptides, often covering most of the chain, with a preference for low-complexity, Pro/Gly-rich and polybasic segments but also extending into adjacent structured regions of short polypeptides.
Activation pattern: Broad, near-whole-protein activation in short (~50-200 aa) precursors and microproteins, with local maxima on Pro-rich tracts (including poly-P), GP/GG-containing stretches, and basic clusters; activation is not restricted to disordered patches and can extend into folded domains in short proteins.
Exemplars:
- Class II bacteriocin/lantibiotic precursors: broad activation across the short precursor chain, including mature regions containing GG and GW motifs.
- Secreted peptide/toxin and prohormone precursors (e.g., cholecystokinin): activation spread across the precursor chain.
- Sperm protamine precursors: concentrated on disordered propeptides and at propeptide–mature boundaries; minimal on highly basic mature cores.
- Viral accessory/regulatory microproteins (e.g., Vpx, Vif): activation across the short viral protein, with strong peaks on poly-P / GP-rich low-complexity patches when present.
- lncRNA-encoded micropeptides and very small uncharacterized proteins (e.g., RUSC1-AS1, N-cym): activation on Pro/Gly-rich disordered segments and across much of the chain.
- Plant transcription factors with WG/GW- and GP-rich low-complexity regions: activation on those patches.
- ATP synthase epsilon subunits: signal on short GP-rich linkers or terminal low-complexity tails.
- Large enzymes (e.g., DDX11 helicase, acyl-CoA synthetase): activation on disordered N/C-terminal low-complexity regions or basic/GP-rich insertions.
- Small mitochondrial membrane proteins (ATP8): signal on short basic matrix-exposed loops or termini flanking TM helices.
- Short proteolytic chains of secreted enzymes (e.g., snake venom metalloproteinase fragments, acrosin chain fragments): broad activation across the short mature chain, including within structured peptidase/disintegrin regions.

Summary: The feature recognizes cationic, amphipathic, low-complexity segments that mediate targeting or membrane/lipid association—classically N‑terminal signal/transit/leader-like regions of secreted, mitochondrial, and viral proteins—and frequently the propeptide/mature regions of toxin and neuropeptide precursors; it can also highlight short basic/hydrophobic helices or redox-active motifs within structured domains.
Activation pattern: Predominantly long, continuous activation over N‑terminal, low‑pLDDT leader/propeptide regions enriched in Lys/Arg, Ser/Pro and hydrophobic/aromatic residues; with occasional residue-level peaks within well-structured helices (e.g., specific positions in thioredoxin CGHC motifs or matrix-exposed helices of membrane proteins).
Exemplars: 
- Venom phospholipase A2 precursors (activation on signal/propeptide segments and conserved cationic patches).
- Apolipoproteins (N‑terminal signal peptide and amphipathic helical stretches).
- Protein kinases with disordered/basic N‑termini (e.g., cyclin-dependent and PRK family N‑tails).
- Thioredoxin-fold protein disulfide-isomerases (peak at the CGHC active-site helix).
- Mitochondrial calcium uniporter (selected residues in a matrix-exposed helix).
- Conotoxin and other secreted toxin precursors; neuropeptide prepropeptides (activation across pro/mature peptide regions).
- Viral silencing suppressors and small membrane/morphogenesis proteins (basic, hydrophobic leader-like segments).
- Kinetochore coiled-coil scaffold proteins (basic low-complexity regions).
- FYVE-domain endosomal adaptors (basic, membrane/PIP-interacting low-complexity segments).
- RNA-modifying enzymes with basic N‑terminal tails (e.g., tRNA methyltransferases).

Summary: Low-complexity, intrinsically disordered segments—often at protein N-termini—such as mucin-like/propeptide regions or flexible linkers adjacent to signal/transit peptides, common in small secreted or membrane-associated proteins and also as disordered extensions in diverse enzymes (broad taxonomic coverage, including viral, bacterial, and eukaryotic proteins).
Activation pattern: Regional activation over short to moderate stretches, frequently in disordered or polar/low-complexity segments; in longer proteins, multiple low-complexity patches can activate; in micropeptides, activation can span much of the sequence. Residue-level peaks can fall on Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly within polar-residue stretches but also on basic or hydrophobic residues within the same disordered context.
Exemplars:
- Viral envelope/accessory microproteins: activation on N-terminal Ser/Thr/Pro-rich disordered segments (often mucin-like or regulatory tails).
- Secreted eukaryotic effectors (e.g., oomycete RxLR effectors): activation on the low-complexity region flanking the signal peptide/RxLR motif.
- Human testis-biased and lncRNA-derived micropeptides: activation across intrinsically disordered peptide regions.
- Secreted precursors/propeptides: activation on N-terminal regions following the signal peptide.
- Membrane-associated single-pass proteins: activation on luminal or cytosolic tails flanking the transmembrane helix.
- Bacterial/archaeal metabolic enzymes: activation on disordered, low-complexity N-terminal extensions/linkers enriched in Ser/Thr/Gly/Pro.

Summary: Short residue windows in mixed-composition regions of diverse proteins, frequently in N-terminal or non-catalytic portions of enzymes, transmembrane-adjacent stretches, and small secreted peptides.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks concentrated in short 3–7 residue windows, often clustered with several nearby peaks. Activated residues are chemically diverse (including hydrophobic, polar, and charged residues) and can occur in helical transmembrane segments, disordered linkers, or globular regions outside annotated catalytic/binding sites.
Exemplars:
- Bacterial DNA ligase: clusters of peaks in the N-terminal region upstream of the catalytic and BRCT domains.
- Viral integrase homolog: short peaks within the chain including a GPAYGRP-containing segment.
- Peroxisomal biogenesis factor 9 (Pex9): peaks overlapping helical transmembrane segments and an adjacent disordered/polar region.
- Small secreted peptides (e.g., Califin-B large subunit): short peaks within the mature peptide.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low-complexity segments enriched in serine/threonine/proline/glycine and often basic (lysine/arginine), typically found in flexible N- or C-terminal tails and loops; highlights IDRs that may harbor short linear motifs (e.g., basic NLS patches) rather than structured domain cores.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long disordered stretches with additional sparse residue-level peaks in low-confidence loops; often N-terminal-biased in short/viral proteins; rarely within well-folded cores.
Exemplars: Retroviral accessory proteins (e.g., HTLV-1 p30): activation on central and C-terminal IDRs including a basic nuclear localization signal; p53-regulated apoptosis-inducing microprotein: widespread activation across a globally disordered protein; Bacterial DNA ligase: scattered activation in an annotated disordered linker and flexible loops within the ligase domain; Uncharacterized human microprotein: multiple peaks throughout a low-pLDDT, disordered sequence irrespective of predicted secondary structure.

Summary: Short, low‑complexity, intrinsically disordered proteins and modules that encode targeting/processing signals—often but not always secretory—combining hydrophobic signal peptides, double‑Gly bacteriocin leaders, or polybasic/NLS‑like segments, frequently adjacent to Ser/Thr/Pro‑rich stretches and basic clusters (e.g., RXLR, KR/RR)—common in micropeptides, toxins/secreted precursors, viral accessory proteins, keratin‑associated and testis‑specific low‑complexity proteins across taxa
Activation pattern: Regional activation across short proteins, spanning hydrophobic/targeting segments and Ser/Thr/Pro‑rich low‑complexity tracts with peaks on basic motifs such as RXLR, dibasic KR/RR, or double‑Gly leader junctions
Exemplars:
- Oomycete RxLR effectors: activation on the N‑terminal signal peptide and the RXLR/EER host‑targeting motif immediately downstream.
- Secreted peptide hormone/venom/toxin precursors: activation on the signal peptide and basic prohormone convertase cleavage motifs (KR/RR) within the propeptide region.
- Class II bacteriocins: activation on the N‑terminal double‑Gly leader and adjacent cationic tract recognized by ABC exporters.
- Viral accessory/regulatory proteins (e.g., small disordered regulators): activation across S/T/P‑rich low‑complexity disordered segments containing polybasic/NLS‑like clusters.
- Keratin‑associated proteins (KRTAPs): activation over short, repetitive low‑complexity regions (Ser/Pro‑rich and basic tracts) typical of hair shaft proteins.
- Cancer/testis antigens and testis‑associated proteins: activation on Lys/Arg‑ and Pro/Ser‑rich low‑complexity stretches in very short proteins.
- Short uncharacterized micropeptides/antisense products: broad activation across their low‑complexity/basic segments.
- Enzymes that carry secretory leaders or short disordered/basic tails (including some cytosolic enzymes lacking signal peptides): activation limited to the disordered tail, not the catalytic core.

Summary: Secreted, propeptide‑processed cysteine‑rich mini‑domains: compact extracellular segments immediately downstream of a signal peptide that contain clustered cysteines forming multiple disulfide bonds (defensin/CSαβ, WAP four‑disulfide core, cystine‑knot/knottin, CHH‑like, evasin‑like, and related small CRP scaffolds), often flanked by dibasic convertase sites and enriched in Lys/Arg
Activation pattern: Regional activation on short segments (≈20–60 aa) right after the signal peptide; strong peaks on cysteines and nearby basic residues, frequently overlapping proprotein convertase (dibasic) processing motifs; may recur for multi‑domain or repeat CRP proteins
Exemplars: - WAP/four‑disulfide core protease inhibitors (SLPI/elafin/WFDC): activation on the WAP domain’s Cys framework following the signal/propeptide
- Plant defensin‑like peptides (DEFL/LURE/ESF) and thionins: activation on the mature antimicrobial CSαβ cysteine motif
- Venom cystine‑knot peptides (conotoxins/knottins, mini‑toxins): activation on the canonical Cys frameworks in the mature toxin region of prepropeptides
- Tick evasins (chemokine‑binding CRPs): activation on the Cys‑rich chemokine‑binding domain
- Crustacean CHH/MIH neuropeptide precursors: activation on the mature hormone core with conserved six‑Cys motif adjacent to dibasic cleavage
- Fungal GPI‑anchored cell‑wall adhesins/stress proteins: activation on extracellular Cys‑rich segments just after secretion signals
- Small plant CRP protease inhibitors: activation on the disulfide‑stabilized inhibitory mini‑domain

Summary: Secreted, short cysteine-rich peptides and small extracellular cysteine-rich domains stabilized by multiple disulfide bonds (CRPs), spanning venom toxins, disintegrins, defensins/hepcidin, Kunitz/Kazal/hevein-like inhibitors/defense peptides, and related cystine‑knotted or cysteine‑stabilized folds. The feature captures the mature, proteolytically processed peptide/module characterized by clustered Cys (often CC motifs) and basic residues.
Activation pattern: Regional activation confined to short mature peptide segments (tens of residues) following the signal peptide and propeptides; minimal/absent on signal/pro-regions. Strong residue-level peaks on cysteines and frequent secondary peaks on Lys/Arg and Gly. Activation spans mixed secondary structure (β-strands, coils, short helices) and can include key functional loops (e.g., RGD in disintegrins).
Exemplars: - Plant cyclotides (cystine-knot cyclopeptides, e.g., chassatide): activation across the cyclic cystine‑knot core of the mature peptide after processing.
- Snake venom disintegrins: activation across the disintegrin domain, including the RGD integrin-binding loop and adjacent cysteine-dense core.
- Inhibitor cystine-knot (ICK) venom toxins from spiders, cone snails, centipedes, and sea anemones: activation on the disulfide‑knotted toxin core.
- Kunitz/BPTI- and Kazal-type serine protease inhibitors (including tick chemokine/complement inhibitors): activation on the small disulfide‑rich inhibitor domain.
- Hevein-like/seed defense peptides: activation on the cysteine-rich chitin‑binding hevein domain.
- Defensins (plant/fungal/animal CSαβ peptides) and vertebrate hepcidin: activation on the cysteine‑stabilized mature AMP region.
- Euplotes ciliate mating pheromones: activation on the secreted disulfide‑rich pheromone core.
- Cysteine-rich modules within large extracellular/mucin-like proteins: activation on the short, cysteine‑dense repeat/subdomain embedded in the larger precursor.

Summary: Folded extracytoplasmic luminal domains of secretory or organellar precursors—i.e., the mature globular regions (and, when present as independent folds, structured inhibitory propeptides) that lie immediately downstream of signal/transit peptides—common in plant/apoplastic and other lumenal proteins (secreted, vacuolar, chloroplast/thylakoid) and spanning diverse families (proteases, expansins, phytocyanins, SCP/CAP toxins, GDSL lipases), often disulfide‑stabilized and glycosylated; targeting peptides and low‑complexity linkers are de-emphasized.
Activation pattern: Domain-level, long continuous activation that switches on sharply after the signal/transit peptide cleavage site (or at the start of a folded pro/mature domain), remains high across well-structured secondary elements, and drops in signal/transit peptides, low-complexity/disordered tails, and small auxiliary motifs (e.g., ShKT). Within catalytic domains the feature does not focus on active-site residues and can dip at catalytic positions.

Summary: Disulfide-stabilized extracellular β‑strand modules, most prominently thrombospondin type‑1 repeats (TSR), but also related small cystine‑rich domains (Kunitz/BPTI inhibitors, EGF‑like repeats, lectin CRDs, defensin/toxin folds) in secreted or surface proteins involved in adhesion, protease regulation, and host–pathogen interaction.
Activation pattern: Domain- and residue-level: repeated activation bands across tandem extracellular modules; sharp peaks on β‑strand cores and adjacent short connectors, emphasizing disulfide‑forming cysteines and nearby basic/aromatic residues (Arg/Lys, Trp/Tyr) characteristic of TSR/Kunitz/EGF motifs; minimal activation in signal peptides, helices, and unrelated domains (e.g., Ig‑like C2, PLAC).
Exemplars: - TSR-containing ECM/axon-guidance proteins (thrombospondins, ADAMTS-like/madd-4): activation on β‑strands within TSRs, including conserved cysteines and basic/tryptophan motifs; neighboring Ig-like/PLAC segments remain low.
- Kunitz-type serine protease inhibitors and extracellular protease regulators (e.g., coagulation/complement inhibitors): activation on the central β‑strand and disulfide cysteines of Kunitz repeats; helices are unactivated.
- Apicomplexan adhesins with TSR-like modules (TRAP/CTRP/MIC families): activation along TSR-like β‑strand elements mediating host binding.
- Integrin β subunits and other EGF-repeat proteins: activation on β‑strands of EGF-like cysteine‑rich repeats.
- Lectin-like extracellular receptors and plant lectins: activation on β‑sheets within disulfide-stabilized carbohydrate-recognition domains.
- Small disulfide-rich toxins and defensins: activation on short β‑strand segments and the disulfide‑forming cysteines.

Summary: Plant P/S/T–rich low-complexity glycomodules (HRGP-like), predominantly found as long, intrinsically disordered regions in secreted and cell-surface proteins (AGPs/EXT/PRPs, GPI-anchored proteins) and as mucin-like linkers/tails appended to extracellular domains; can also occur in other plant proteins that harbor similar Ser/Pro-rich disordered segments outside the cell wall context.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across contiguous IDRs enriched in P/S/T repeats; typically turns on after signal peptides in secretory proteins, peaks along Pro-rich/disordered stretches, and often tapers near the GPI ω-site. Activation is minimal over signal peptides, transmembrane helices, GPI propeptides, and well-folded domains (e.g., FAS1 cores, blue-copper phytocyanin folds, β/α elements, cytosolic kinase domains). Occasionally marks analogous P/S/T-rich low-complexity segments irrespective of subcellular location, while still avoiding structured domains.
Exemplars: - Classical arabinogalactan proteins (AGPs): strong activation on the central Ser/Pro/Thr‑rich disordered AGP glycomodule; not on the N‑terminal signal peptide or the C‑terminal GPI‑signal propeptide.
- Fasciclin‑like AGPs (FLAs): high activation on the Pro‑rich disordered C‑terminal tail and inter‑domain linker; suppressed in the structured FAS1 domain cores; modest at the GPI ω‑site.
- Phytocyanins/early nodulin‑like blue copper proteins: low in the copper‑binding domain and signal peptide; strong across the long P/S/T‑rich disordered segment immediately preceding the GPI anchor; low in the helical GPI propeptide.
- Proline‑rich proteins/extensins: maximal activation across repetitive Pro‑rich coil regions; absent in intervening ordered β/helix blocks.
- Receptor‑like kinases/proteins: activation on extracellular Pro‑rich, low‑confidence N‑terminal stretches and coil linkers; not on the transmembrane helix or the cytoplasmic kinase domain; reduced in more ordered extracellular β segments.
- Seed storage/allergen proteins (e.g., 2S albumins): occasional activation on low‑complexity propeptides or tails; low on compact disulfide-stabilized cores.
- Cytosolic/membrane E3 RING proteins: occasional activation on Ser/Pro‑rich low‑complexity regions; not on folded RING domains or transmembrane helices.

Summary: Secreted, propeptide‑processed cysteine‑rich mini‑domains: compact extracellular segments immediately downstream of a signal peptide that contain clustered cysteines forming multiple disulfide bonds (defensin/CSαβ, WAP four‑disulfide core, cystine‑knot/knottin, CHH‑like, evasin‑like, and related small CRP scaffolds), often flanked by dibasic convertase sites and enriched in Lys/Arg
Activation pattern: Regional activation on short segments (≈20–60 aa) right after the signal peptide; strong peaks on cysteines and nearby basic residues, frequently overlapping proprotein convertase (dibasic) processing motifs; may recur for multi‑domain or repeat CRP proteins
Exemplars: - WAP/four‑disulfide core protease inhibitors (SLPI/elafin/WFDC): activation on the WAP domain’s Cys framework following the signal/propeptide

- Tick evasins (chemokine‑binding CRPs): activation on the Cys‑rich chemokine‑binding domain
- Crustacean CHH/MIH neuropeptide precursors: activation on the mature hormone core with conserved six‑Cys motif adjacent to dibasic cleavage
- Fungal GPI‑anchored cell‑wall adhesins/stress proteins: activation on extracellular Cys‑rich segments just after secretion signals
- Small plant CRP protease inhibitors: activation on the disulfide‑stabilized inhibitory mini‑domain

Summary: Secreted, short cysteine-rich peptides and small extracellular cysteine-rich domains stabilized by multiple disulfide bonds (CRPs), spanning venom toxins, disintegrins, defensins/hepcidin, Kunitz/Kazal/hevein-like inhibitors/defense peptides, and related cystine‑knotted or cysteine‑stabilized folds. The feature captures the mature, proteolytically processed peptide/module characterized by clustered Cys (often CC motifs) and basic residues.
Activation pattern: Regional activation confined to short mature peptide segments (tens of residues) following the signal peptide and propeptides; minimal/absent on signal/pro-regions. Strong residue-level peaks on cysteines and frequent secondary peaks on Lys/Arg and Gly. Activation spans mixed secondary structure (β-strands, coils, short helices) and can include key functional loops (e.g., RGD in disintegrins).
Exemplars: - Plant cyclotides (cystine-knot cyclopeptides, e.g., chassatide): activation across the cyclic cystine‑knot core of the mature peptide after processing.
- Snake venom disintegrins: activation across the disintegrin domain, including the RGD integrin-binding loop and adjacent cysteine-dense core.
- Inhibitor cystine-knot (ICK) venom toxins from spiders, cone snails, centipedes, and sea anemones: activation on the disulfide‑knotted toxin core.
- Kunitz/BPTI- and Kazal-type serine protease inhibitors (including tick chemokine/complement inhibitors): activation on the small disulfide‑rich inhibitor domain.
- Hevein-like/seed defense peptides: activation on the cysteine-rich chitin‑binding hevein domain.
- Defensins (plant/fungal/animal CSαβ peptides) and vertebrate hepcidin: activation on the cysteine‑stabilized mature AMP region.
- Euplotes ciliate mating pheromones: activation on the secreted disulfide‑rich pheromone core.
- Cysteine-rich modules within large extracellular/mucin-like proteins: activation on the short, cysteine‑dense repeat/subdomain embedded in the larger precursor.

Summary: Short, disulfide‑bonded extracellular cysteine‑rich repeat modules—especially EGF‑like (including cbEGF and laminin‑type LE) and LDL receptor class A (LDLa) domains, but also von Willebrand type C (CR) and other disulfide‑rich repeats—detected via acidic/polar loop motifs flanked by conserved cysteines (including Ca2+-binding Dx[D/N] motifs when present); broadly marks ectodomains of secreted proteins and single‑pass receptors.
Activation pattern:
- Strong activation confined to extracellular regions; absent in transmembrane helices and cytoplasmic tails.
- Repeated peaks aligning with tandem repeats; long activation tracts across multi‑repeat proteins.
- LDLa repeats: maxima over the central acidic DxSDE/DxD… segment; flanking cysteines variably engaged.
- EGF‑like repeats (cbEGF and LE): highest in the C‑terminal half containing the D/N‑x‑D/N‑x(4)‑Y/F motif when present, near the last cysteines.
- Also activates analogous acidic/polar loops in other cysteine‑rich repeats (e.g., VWC/CR, TIL/Kunitz, TSR); preference for D/E/S/T/N/Q/G and Y with nearby Cys; modest activation in short acidic linkers between repeats.
Exemplars:
- LDL receptor family (LDLR/LRP1/LRP4): LDLa repeat Ca2+-binding loops and cbEGF/LE segments across the ectodomain.
- Notch receptors and ligands (Notch, Delta/Jagged): tandem EGF‑like repeats with peaks at Ca2+-binding loops.
- Coagulation/complement components (e.g., Factors VII/IX/X, protein C/S, C1r/C1s modules): cbEGF domains.
- ECM scaffolds and glycoproteins (fibrillins, fibulins, LTBPs, laminins, tenascins, matrilins): arrays of EGF‑like/LE repeats.
- Chordin‑like/BMP modulators (BMPER/Crossveinless‑2, chordin): arrays of VWC/CR repeats.
- Cell‑adhesion receptors (selectins, integrin β I‑EGF modules) and extracellular metalloproteases/modulators (ADAM/ADAMTS): EGF‑like/cysteine‑rich repeats.
- Disulfide‑rich protease inhibitors and invertebrate toxins (e.g., Kunitz/TIL‑type).
- Plant receptor‑like proteins/kinases (e.g., WAKs, vacuolar sorting receptors): ectodomains with EGF‑like repeats.

Summary: Short, structured beta-strand segments at or near domain termini in extracellular proteins/domains—most prominently the conserved C-terminal strand of C-type lectin-like domains (CTLD)—often bearing closely spaced, disulfide-forming cysteines and flanked by aromatic/basic residues; analogous terminal strands in other adhesin/receptor-binding ectodomains and in compact disulfide-rich secreted toxins/antimicrobial peptides also trigger.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks on 8–20 aa stretches at ectodomain or domain termini; highest on cysteines within a beta-strand (often terminal) and immediate neighbors; repeats once per CTLD module in multi-CTLD proteins; occasionally extends just beyond the annotated CTLD into a short structured island; also marks the terminal beta-strand at the ends of viral/bacteriophage receptor-binding fibers and short strands within disulfide-rich peptide toxins.
Exemplars:
- Selectins: activation at the CTLD C-terminus at the CTLD–EGF boundary, mapping to a short beta-strand.
- NK/killer cell lectin-like receptors: activation on the CTLD terminal beta-strand, peaking on paired cysteines implicated in disulfides.
- Invertebrate C-type lectins (e.g., echinoidin): activation confined to the CTLD C-terminal beta-strand.
- Echinoderm spicule matrix CTLD proteins: activation on a short beta-strand immediately C-terminal to the CTLD within an otherwise disordered tail.
- Bacteriophage long-tail fiber proteins: activation on the extreme C-terminal beta-strand of the fiber tip/knob domain.
- Cysteine-rich peptide toxins (e.g., sea anemone sodium-channel toxins): activation on a short beta-strand around paired cysteines, typically near a terminus.

Summary: Secreted, cysteine-rich disulfide‑bonded mini-domains of extracellular proteins—compact folds such as Kunitz, WAP/four‑disulfide core, knottin/cystine‑knot, and colipase‑like—found in protease inhibitors, venom toxins, and antimicrobial/immune modulators across diverse taxa; the feature recognizes the mature extracellular cysteine‑patterned domain rather than the signal peptide.
Activation pattern: Strong domain-level activation over the mature disulfide-stabilized extracellular domain; low-to-moderate in signal peptides and unrelated regions, rising sharply at the maturation site. Within the domain, activation is broadly distributed across cysteine-rich motif segments, with peaks frequently falling on or immediately adjacent to disulfide-bonding cysteines and the short basic/Gly/Pro-containing spacers between them; in some precursors, activation can extend into short hydrophobic propeptides.
Exemplars: - Kunitz-type serine protease inhibitors and Kunitz-type venom toxins: activation over the single Kunitz fold of the mature inhibitor/toxin.
- WAP/WFDC (four-disulfide core) protease inhibitors/antimicrobials (e.g., SLPI/elafin/WFDC family): activation on the WAP domain(s) in the secreted region.
- Knottin/cystine-knot peptides (conotoxins, spider toxins, plant cyclotides/trypsin inhibitors): activation on the cystine‑knot core of the mature peptide.
- Dickkopf (Dkk) family Wnt modulators: strong activation across the DKK-type Cys-1 and Cys-2 disulfide-rich regions of the mature chain.
- Colipase-like secreted proteins: activation across the mature colipase-like domain with low activation on the signal peptide.
- Metallocarboxypeptidase inhibitors (small disulfide‑rich inhibitors): activation across the mature inhibitory domain including enzyme-interaction loops, with occasional carryover into a short hydrophobic propeptide.
- Dictyostelium secreted spore/adhesion cysteine-rich proteins: activation on their extracellular cysteine‑rich modules.

Summary: Secreted, cysteine-rich disulfide‑bonded mini-domains of extracellular proteins—compact folds such as Kunitz, WAP/four‑disulfide core, knottin/cystine‑knot, and colipase‑like—found in protease inhibitors, venom toxins, and antimicrobial/immune modulators across diverse taxa; the feature recognizes the mature extracellular cysteine‑patterned domain rather than the signal peptide.
Activation pattern: Strong domain-level activation over the mature disulfide-stabilized extracellular domain; low-to-moderate in signal peptides and unrelated regions, rising sharply at the maturation site. Within the domain, activation is broadly distributed across cysteine-rich motif segments, with peaks frequently falling on or immediately adjacent to disulfide-bonding cysteines and the short basic/Gly/Pro-containing spacers between them; in some precursors, activation can extend into short hydrophobic propeptides.
Exemplars: - Kunitz-type serine protease inhibitors and Kunitz-type venom toxins: activation over the single Kunitz fold of the mature inhibitor/toxin.
- WAP/WFDC (four-disulfide core) protease inhibitors/antimicrobials (e.g., SLPI/elafin/WFDC family): activation on the WAP domain(s) in the secreted region.
- Knottin/cystine-knot peptides (conotoxins, spider toxins, plant cyclotides/trypsin inhibitors): activation on the cystine‑knot core of the mature peptide.
- Dickkopf (Dkk) family Wnt modulators: strong activation across the DKK-type Cys-1 and Cys-2 disulfide-rich regions of the mature chain.
- Colipase-like secreted proteins: activation across the mature colipase-like domain with low activation on the signal peptide.
- Metallocarboxypeptidase inhibitors (small disulfide‑rich inhibitors): activation across the mature inhibitory domain including enzyme-interaction loops, with occasional carryover into a short hydrophobic propeptide.
- Dictyostelium secreted spore/adhesion cysteine-rich proteins: activation on their extracellular cysteine‑rich modules.

Summary: Disulfide-rich extracellular modules in secreted proteins and receptors, prominently including thrombospondin type-1 repeats (TSR/TSP1) but also related small cysteine/tryptophan-rich modules such as somatomedin-B, chordin/VWC (von Willebrand factor type C), follistatin-like/SPARC, thyroglobulin type-1, and select metalloprotease disintegrin/cysteine-rich segments.
Activation pattern: Domain-level activation across these compact extracellular modules; arrays yield long activation tracts. Residue-level peaks tend to fall just upstream of the conserved aromatic core of TSRs (in the vicinity of the WxxW motif), with broad coverage of the surrounding disulfide-bonded scaffold. Minimal signal in transmembrane and cytoplasmic regions; in proteins like UNC5, activation is confined to the extracellular TSRs.
Exemplars: 
- ADAMTS metalloproteases: activation across TSR arrays and the disintegrin/cysteine-rich segments; low on catalytic metalloprotease cores.
- UNC5/netrin receptors and spondins: activation on extracellular TSRs and somatomedin-B where present.
- ADAM sheddases (e.g., ADAM10): activation over disintegrin/cysteine-rich extracellular segments.
- Chordin-like proteins: activation on repeated VWC (chordin) cysteine-rich domains.
- Follistatin-like/SPARC family: activation on the follistatin-like/SPARC cysteine-rich module.
- IGF-binding proteins: activation on the cysteine-rich C-terminal thyroglobulin-like repeat.
- Complement/MACPF proteins: activation on embedded small cysteine-rich accessory domains (including TSR where present).

Summary: Short, disulfide‑bonded extracellular cysteine‑rich repeat modules—especially EGF‑like (including cbEGF and laminin‑type LE) and LDL receptor class A (LDLa) domains, but also von Willebrand type C (CR) and other disulfide‑rich repeats—detected via acidic/polar loop motifs flanked by conserved cysteines (including Ca2+-binding Dx[D/N] motifs when present); broadly marks ectodomains of secreted proteins and single‑pass receptors.
Activation pattern:
- Strong activation confined to extracellular regions; absent in transmembrane helices and cytoplasmic tails.
- Repeated peaks aligning with tandem repeats; long activation tracts across multi‑repeat proteins.
- LDLa repeats: maxima over the central acidic DxSDE/DxD… segment; flanking cysteines variably engaged.
- EGF‑like repeats (cbEGF and LE): highest in the C‑terminal half containing the D/N‑x‑D/N‑x(4)‑Y/F motif when present, near the last cysteines.
- Also activates analogous acidic/polar loops in other cysteine‑rich repeats (e.g., VWC/CR, TIL/Kunitz, TSR); preference for D/E/S/T/N/Q/G and Y with nearby Cys; modest activation in short acidic linkers between repeats.
Exemplars:
- LDL receptor family (LDLR/LRP1/LRP4): LDLa repeat Ca2+-binding loops and cbEGF/LE segments across the ectodomain.
- Notch receptors and ligands (Notch, Delta/Jagged): tandem EGF‑like repeats with peaks at Ca2+-binding loops.
- Coagulation/complement components (e.g., Factors VII/IX/X, protein C/S, C1r/C1s modules): cbEGF domains.
- ECM scaffolds and glycoproteins (fibrillins, fibulins, LTBPs, laminins, tenascins, matrilins): arrays of EGF‑like/LE repeats.
- Chordin‑like/BMP modulators (BMPER/Crossveinless‑2, chordin): arrays of VWC/CR repeats.
- Cell‑adhesion receptors (selectins, integrin β I‑EGF modules) and extracellular metalloproteases/modulators (ADAM/ADAMTS): EGF‑like/cysteine‑rich repeats.
- Disulfide‑rich protease inhibitors and invertebrate toxins (e.g., Kunitz/TIL‑type).
- Plant receptor‑like proteins/kinases (e.g., WAKs, vacuolar sorting receptors): ectodomains with EGF‑like repeats.

Summary: Disulfide-braced loops of extracellular cysteine-rich modules, most prominently the C2–C3 loop of EGF-like domains that carries the O-fucosylation site and (in cbEGF modules) Ca2+-binding determinants; peaks center on the third conserved cysteine and nearby S/T, Asp/Asn, Gly/Pro, or His residues; repeated across tandem EGF repeats, with similar signal also occurring in other compact disulfide-rich scaffolds (e.g., Kunitz/Kazal, TIL, cyclotides) and occasional weaker matches in CCP/Sushi modules and in disulfide-bonded beta-sandwich domains (e.g., Ig-like, CUB)
Activation pattern: Repeated short regional activations within each EGF-like repeat (10–15 residues), with residue-level peaks at conserved cysteines (often C3) and the intervening C2–C3 loop; minimal signal in signal peptides, transmembranes, or cytosolic tails; the same cysteine-centered 8–15-residue motif can recur in non-EGF disulfide-rich scaffolds (toxins/protease inhibitors), occasional single-residue hits at a conserved aromatic in CCP/Sushi repeats, and rare activations adjacent to the conserved disulfide in Ig-like/CUB domains
Exemplars:
- Notch ligands (Delta/Serrate): strong, periodic activation in each EGF-like domain, centered on the C2–C3 loop; enhanced in calcium-binding EGF repeats
- ECM glycoproteins with tandem EGF repeats (e.g., nidogens, matrilins): activation spans the loop between conserved cysteines of each EGF-like module, peaking on a disulfide-forming cysteine
- Selectins and LDL receptor family members: dominant peaks within EGF-like domains, plus weaker periodic hits in successive CCP/Sushi repeats
- EGF-repeat–containing secreted regulators (e.g., WIF1, cbEGF-bearing developmental modulators): localized activation at the N-terminal end of cbEGF modules including paired cysteines and nearby His/Asp residues
- Small cysteine-rich toxins and protease inhibitors (e.g., cyclotides, Kunitz/Kazal/TIL inhibitors): activation on short disulfide-braced loops centered on conserved cysteines
- Ig-superfamily/FNIII adhesion proteins and CUB-domain proteases: occasional activation adjacent to the conserved disulfide within Ig-like or CUB domains

Summary: Secreted, short cysteine-rich peptides and small extracellular cysteine-rich domains stabilized by multiple disulfide bonds (CRPs), spanning venom toxins, disintegrins, defensins/hepcidin, Kunitz/Kazal/hevein-like inhibitors/defense peptides, and related cystine‑knotted or cysteine‑stabilized folds. The feature captures the mature, proteolytically processed peptide/module characterized by clustered Cys (often CC motifs) and basic residues.
Activation pattern: Regional activation confined to short mature peptide segments (tens of residues) following the signal peptide and propeptides; minimal/absent on signal/pro-regions. Strong residue-level peaks on cysteines and frequent secondary peaks on Lys/Arg and Gly. Activation spans mixed secondary structure (β-strands, coils, short helices) and can include key functional loops (e.g., RGD in disintegrins).
Exemplars: - Plant cyclotides (cystine-knot cyclopeptides, e.g., chassatide): activation across the cyclic cystine‑knot core of the mature peptide after processing.
- Snake venom disintegrins: activation across the disintegrin domain, including the RGD integrin-binding loop and adjacent cysteine-dense core.
- Inhibitor cystine-knot (ICK) venom toxins from spiders, cone snails, centipedes, and sea anemones: activation on the disulfide‑knotted toxin core.
- Kunitz/BPTI- and Kazal-type serine protease inhibitors (including tick chemokine/complement inhibitors): activation on the small disulfide‑rich inhibitor domain.
- Hevein-like/seed defense peptides: activation on the cysteine-rich chitin‑binding hevein domain.
- Defensins (plant/fungal/animal CSαβ peptides) and vertebrate hepcidin: activation on the cysteine‑stabilized mature AMP region.
- Euplotes ciliate mating pheromones: activation on the secreted disulfide‑rich pheromone core.
- Cysteine-rich modules within large extracellular/mucin-like proteins: activation on the short, cysteine‑dense repeat/subdomain embedded in the larger precursor.

Summary: Short amphipathic, positively biased membrane-proximal segments that drive organelle/inner-membrane targeting and topology—most commonly N-terminal mitochondrial/peroxisomal targeting or PEX19-binding regions and the short cytosolic/intermembrane-space loops that cap or connect transmembrane helices (positive-inside–type motifs).
Activation pattern: Broad activation across membrane-associated proteins, with residue-level peaks concentrated at N-terminal coils/helices and at helix ends, interhelical loops, and helix-capping positions flanking or within transmembrane segments. Activated segments are enriched in Leu/Ile/Val/Ala/Gly with clustered Lys/Arg and often show lower predicted structure confidence when they are transit peptides.
Exemplars: Phosphatidylserine decarboxylase (inner-membrane lipid enzyme): activation on an N-terminal Arg/Lys-rich amphipathic segment, not at the autocatalytic site; Mitochondrial pyruvate carrier 1 (small inner-membrane transporter): activation on the matrix-facing N-terminus, the intermembrane-space loop connecting its two TMs, and a short matrix segment after the second TM; Complex I assembly factor DMAC1: activation centered on the loop between its two TMs and adjacent helix caps; Peroxisomal ABC transporter (ABCD1/ALDP): activation on the N-terminal amphipathic coil/helix consistent with a peroxisomal membrane targeting/PEX19-binding region; Mitochondrial rhomboid intramembrane protease: activation at TM termini and adjacent loops flanking the active site; Mitochondrial nuclease EXOG: activation confined to the cleavable N-terminal mitochondrial transit peptide, absent in the structured nuclease domain.

Summary: Hydrophobic alpha‑helical topogenic segments used for membrane insertion/localization—i.e., single‑pass transmembrane helices and signal peptides—with a strong bias toward C‑terminal tail‑anchors across organelles and viruses; enriched in L/V/I/A/G, often containing small‑residue motifs (e.g., GxxxG/AxxxA) and flanked by basic residues (positive‑inside).
Activation pattern: Regional activation over single contiguous 15–25 aa hydrophobic runs; peaks within glycine/alanine clusters inside the helix. Frequently at the extreme C‑terminus (tail‑anchors), at N‑termini for signal peptides, and repeated across sequences in multi‑pass proteins. Activated regions often show lower predicted structural confidence than adjacent soluble domains and may be bordered by basic residues.
Exemplars: - Peroxisome assembly proteins (e.g., PEX22‑type): activation on the single N‑terminal transmembrane helix.
- Peroxisomal tail‑anchored adaptors (e.g., PEX26‑like): activation on the C‑terminal membrane anchor.
- Mitochondrial apoptosis regulators (BCL‑2/BAX families and viral Bcl‑2 homologs): activation on the C‑terminal tail‑anchor helix.
- Mitochondrial import/organization complexes (TOM/SAM/TIM subunits; OXPHOS assembly factors): activation on their membrane‑spanning helices, often with GxxxG motifs.
- Mitochondrial dynamics proteins (Fis1, mitofusins): activation on C‑terminal TM anchor(s).
- Chloroplast outer‑envelope single‑pass proteins (OEP7‑like): activation on the C‑terminal tail‑anchor.
- Bacterial magnetosome membrane proteins (Mam family): activation on one or more hydrophobic TM helices, including small‑residue–rich segments.
- Secretory/lumenal precursors: activation on N‑terminal signal peptides.
- Multi‑pass transporters/channels: multiple activated segments corresponding to each transmembrane helix.

Summary: Single-pass alpha-helical transmembrane signal-anchor segments in small membrane proteins across taxa; a 15–25-residue hydrophobic helix used to anchor proteins in lipid bilayers, enriched in Leu/Ile/Val/Phe with internal aromatics and glycines, few charges, occasional cysteines, and rare internal prolines.
Activation pattern: Strong regional activation over a single, contiguous hydrophobic helix (typically 15–25 residues), with residue-level peaks in the hydrophobic/aromatic core and minimal activation in flanking cytosolic/periplasmic/luminal regions; often near the N-terminus (signal-anchor) but can occur mid-sequence; coincides with annotated/predicted alpha-helical transmembrane segments.
Exemplars: - Bacteriophage lysis proteins — activation on their sole membrane-spanning anchor helix.
- Virion membrane proteins (e.g., poxvirus/orthopox orthologs) — activation on the N-terminal helical signal-anchor.
- Plant viral movement proteins — activation on the single transmembrane helix.
- Photosystem II assembly factor Psb34 — activation on its thylakoid single-pass transmembrane helix.
- Cytochrome bd ubiquinol oxidase small accessory subunit (CydX) — activation on its single membrane-spanning helix.
- Endoregulin-like micropeptide regulators — activation on their single, helical membrane anchor.

Summary: Short hydrophobic/amphipathic segments enriched in Gly/Ala and interfacial Trp/Tyr, flanked by basic residues, that occur either immediately N-terminal to a transmembrane helix (signal-anchor–like) or within translocation/insertion domains of secreted bacterial proteins. These stretches frequently show coil→helix propensity and can adopt helical structure upon membrane or partner engagement.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over contiguous hydrophobic/aromatic segments (typically ~10–25 aa); local maxima at aromatic residues (Trp/Phe/Tyr) within the segment; activation often begins at or just after a basic cluster (Lys-rich) and extends toward an adjacent helical or TM region. Multiple nonadjacent activated segments per protein are common, with secondary peaks in TM-proximal regions.
Exemplars:
- Influenza hemagglutinin‑esterase‑fusion glycoprotein: strong activation at the HEF2 N‑terminus (canonical fusion peptide immediately post‑cleavage), plus a secondary peak near the TM start.
- HIV‑1 envelope (gp160/gp41): peak across the SU–TM cleavage and N‑terminus of the gp41 fusion peptide; minor activation in TM‑proximal/cytoplasmic segments.
- ISG12/IFI6 family (interferon‑inducible small membrane proteins): activation on the loop between TM1–TM2 extending into the N‑terminus of TM2, the membrane‑anchoring helix.
- Baculovirus per os infectivity factors (e.g., PIF5): activation across the basic-residue cluster leading into the C-terminal TM helix.
- E-group colicins (E2/E3/E7) and cloacin: activation on a conserved KGPFKF(GLW) aromatic motif within the translocation (T) domain.
- Peroxisome biogenesis factor PEX3: activation across the N‑terminal peroxisomal targeting/signal‑anchor segment and the initial part of the first TM helix.

Summary: Short juxta-membrane/anchor-flanking segments at the boundary of single-pass transmembrane helices, with peaks centered on aromatic + basic residues (Y/F/W flanked by K/R) immediately at or just past the TM end on the lumenal or cytoplasmic side; also fires on short basic/aromatic-rich motifs in disordered or low-complexity regions of some soluble proteins.
Activation pattern: Sharp local peaks (3–7 residues wide) at the TM-helix terminus and the first residues of the adjacent topological domain; little activation in deeply buried TM cores or in well-folded soluble domains such as TPR repeats; occasional firing on disordered basic/aromatic clusters with similar local sequence character.
Exemplars: - Mitochondrial outer membrane anchors (OM45, TOM70): peaks at the cytoplasmic end of the N-terminal TM, on aromatic + basic flanking residues.
- Magnetosome membrane proteins (MamD, Mms5, Mms6): peaks just past the TM helix in the adjacent lumenal/cytoplasmic domain, on Y/M/K-containing motifs.
- Pyocin S1/S2: peaks on an internal aromatic/basic motif (YSSRT-AEQW) within the chain.
- Plant abscisic stress-ripening proteins (ASR1, ASR5): peaks on a disordered His/Lys-rich motif (AFHEHHEKK).

Summary: Low-complexity, polybasic segments enriched for Lys interleaved with small residues (A/P/T/S/V/G)—typically intrinsically disordered tails or repeat tracts—most prominently in linker histone H1/H1-like proteins and other nucleic acid–associated proteins; the feature tends to score the small/nonbasic positions within these repeats and, in unrelated proteins, can collapse to a single flexible glycine in a conserved loop.
Activation pattern: Primarily long regional activation across low-complexity/basic tails and repeats; silent in compact globular domains (e.g., H15). Within Lys-interleaved repeats, activation is periodic and centers on the nonbasic small residues rather than on Lys/Arg. Occasionally presents as a sharp single-residue peak at a conserved Gly in flexible loops (e.g., P-type ATPases). Can extend across ordered segments if they share the same small-residue/low-aromatic composition (e.g., TBCC C-terminal half).
Exemplars: - Linker histone H1: strong activation on the disordered, basic C-terminal (and weaker N-terminal) tails; no activation over the structured H15 globular domain.
- Sperm-specific H1/protamine-like histones: sustained activation on the Lys-rich disordered C-terminal tail; weak at the N-terminus; absent in the globular core.
- Histone H1-like HC2 repeats: periodic activation on V/A/S/T/Pro positions within Lys/Arg-interleaved low-complexity repeats; Lys/Arg themselves are not activated.
- Ribosomal protein L21 (bL21): activation confined to the disordered, compositionally biased C-terminal tail that contacts rRNA.
- P-type cation-transporting ATPases: isolated, high peak on a single conserved glycine in a flexible cytosolic loop near a helix terminus.
- Tubulin-specific chaperone C (TBCC/cofactor C): continuous activation across the C-terminal half of the cofactor C-like domain spanning multiple secondary-structure elements, consistent with the feature’s small-residue/low-aromatic preference.

Summary: Arg/Lys-rich, intrinsically disordered low‑complexity tails that mediate electrostatic binding and condensation of nucleic acids—found in histones (esp. H1 and core histone N‑terminal tails), protamines, viral nucleoproteins/capsid cores, and bacterial/archaeal nucleoid proteins; enriched for interspersed Ser/Pro/Gly and dipeptide/repeat patterns such as SP/TP, RS/SR, and RG/RGG
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long polybasic IDRs; strong, contiguous activation on entire very short basic polypeptides (e.g., protamines, viral basic cores) and on specific basic segments within larger proteins, especially N‑terminal histone tails and Lys/Arg‑rich low‑complexity tracts; residue‑level peaks over runs of R/K and RS/SR, SP/TP, RGG motifs
Exemplars: - Protamines and protamine‑like sperm nuclear proteins — activation spans the whole Arg/Lys‑rich, low‑complexity chain used for genome hyper‑condensation.
- Linker histone H1 family (including testis/oocyte‑specific variants) — activation on the long Lys/Ser/Pro‑rich C‑terminal tail and basic N‑terminal segment that contact linker DNA.
- Core histones and centromeric histone variants (e.g., CENP‑A) — activation on the N‑terminal basic tails that interact with DNA and are sites of proline‑directed phosphorylation (SP/TP).
- High mobility group/AT‑hook proteins (HMGA/HMGN) — activation over clusters of AT‑hooks (RGRP‑like) and adjacent Lys/Arg‑rich low‑complexity tracts.
- Bacterial/chlamydial/archaeal nucleoid‑associated or histone‑like proteins (e.g., HU/IHF, HctA/B, archaeal histones) — activation on basic tails and Lys/Arg‑rich segments that compact the chromosome.
- Kinetoplastid histone H1‑like (kinetoplast‑associated proteins) — activation across Lys/Ser/Pro‑rich disordered regions that package kDNA.
- Viral nucleocapsid/core and histone‑like proteins — activation on protamine‑like basic regions that nonspecifically coat and condense viral RNA/DNA.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, Lys/Arg‑rich low‑complexity segments—typically long terminal tails, often containing RG/RGG/GAR motifs—that mediate electrostatic binding to nucleic acids (especially rRNA/RNA) and promote association with ribonucleoprotein assemblies such as the nucleolus and ribosome
Activation pattern: Strong regional activation across long contiguous stretches of disordered sequence, most often at C‑termini (sometimes N‑termini); local peaks coincide with polybasic clusters and RG/RGG motifs; minimal activation within folded catalytic or recognition domains
Exemplars: - Nucleolar biogenesis factors (e.g., NOP12): activation on C‑terminal Lys/Arg‑rich disordered tails, not on folded RRMs
- RRP12-like ribosome assembly proteins: strongest at terminal disordered segments with basic compositional bias, especially the C‑tail
- DEAD-box RNA helicases (e.g., SrmB): activation confined to C‑terminal basic low‑complexity extensions outside the helicase core
- 3′–5′ exoribonucleases (RNase R family): disordered C‑terminal Lys/Arg‑rich tails
- Kinetoplast-associated small basic proteins: broad activation across disordered, low‑complexity basic C‑terminal halves
- Linker histones H1/H1‑like: Lys‑rich disordered C‑terminal tails that bind DNA
- Ribosomal proteins (small and large subunits): basic, often terminal extensions that contact rRNA
- SRP72 subunit: GAR/RGG‑rich basic segment
- Nucleolar/ribosome‑associated GTPases and membrane biogenesis/transport factors: cytosolic polybasic loops/tails

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, polybasic Lys/Arg-rich low-complexity tracts (often KA/KP/KK repeats) that create nonspecific electrostatic cationic patches engaging polyanionic partners—DNA/RNA, acidic protein surfaces, and anionic membranes—used for genome association/packaging, rRNA–protein interfaces, ribosome/protein interactions, and membrane association.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long unstructured basic stretches with repeating KK/KKK and K–A/P/S/T/G patterns; strong residue-level peaks on K and R; typically in N- or C-terminal tails and other disordered regions; depleted in bulky hydrophobics/aromatics and cysteine; little activation in folded cores; also seen in cytosolic/peripheral loops/tails of membrane and translation-associated proteins.
Exemplars:
- Linker histones (H1/H5): activation on Lys-rich disordered C-terminal tails that compact chromatin.
- Archaeal/bacterial histone-like proteins (e.g., HU/Lsr2-like): activation on polybasic arms that wrap DNA.
- Viral nucleoproteins/histone-like genome-packaging proteins: activation on basic RNA/DNA-binding tails.
- Ribosomal proteins with rRNA-binding extensions: activation on Lys/Arg-rich low-complexity tails contacting rRNA.
- Translation-associated factors and chaperones (e.g., ribosome-binding regions of Trigger factor): activation on polybasic patches that bind acidic ribosomal surfaces.
- Membrane proteins with polybasic cytosolic tails/loops (e.g., small inner-membrane subunits, signaling/pheromone-regulated membrane proteins): activation on basic low-complexity segments mediating membrane proximity or partner binding.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity, charge‑biased tails (long N- or C‑terminal IDRs enriched in Lys/Arg and/or Asp/Glu, often with K–A–P repeats and Ser/Thr phosphorylation sites). The feature primarily recognizes the sequence/structural property of these polyelectrolyte IDRs—which are especially common in chromatin/nuclear proteins—while excluding folded domains.
Activation pattern: Extended regional activation across long IDRs with low predicted structure (coil, low pLDDT); strongest over compositionally biased blocks (polybasic or polyacidic, low complexity, Ser/Thr‑rich), with sharp loss of activation inside structured domains (e.g., histone fold, PHD finger, enzymatic cores). Frequently starts near a domain boundary and continues through the terminal tail.
Exemplars: Linker histone H1 family: broad activation on Lys‑rich C‑terminal tails with K–A–P motifs (dominant overall among strongest activators); Protamine‑like sperm nuclear proteins: continuous activation across Arg/Lys‑rich disordered sequences; HMG/FACT subunit SSRP1: activation begins near the end of the HMG box and intensifies across the long disordered, charge‑biased, phospho‑rich C‑terminal tail; Histone H2B variants: activation confined to the basic, disordered N‑terminal tail and excluded from the histone‑fold domain; FKBP immunophilin (FKBP4): long C‑terminal low‑complexity, charged IDR is activated, while PPIase domains are not; DNA polymerase delta subunit 3: extensive activation over the disordered, low‑complexity C‑terminal region, absent from structured parts; ING/YNG (NuA4/ING) PHD‑finger chromatin factors: activation on disordered regions flanking the PHD finger, with the folded PHD domain excluded.

Summary: Short linear segments in intrinsically disordered or otherwise low-structure-confidence regions, often at N-termini and within signal peptides/propeptides of secreted and regulatory proteins (including viral accessory proteins and small ORF microproteins), enriched in small/basic residues (G, P, S, A, R; often with Cys), rather than in well-folded catalytic cores.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks scattered across IDRs and low-confidence coils/short helices; frequently clustered near the N-terminus, in signal peptides, propeptides, and disordered tails; little to no activation in well-structured domains; occasional activation in low-confidence transmembrane/signal-anchor helices.
Exemplars: - Viral accessory protein (HIV-1 Vif): peaks throughout low-pLDDT coils, especially the disordered N-terminal region.
- Neuropeptide precursor (Drosophila Amnesiac): activation in the N-terminal signal peptide and multiple mature peptide segments with very low pLDDT.
- Secreted serine carboxypeptidase: activation confined to disordered C-terminal tail, annotated disordered segment, the signal peptide, and a low-confidence C-terminal transmembrane helix; absent from the structured catalytic domain.
- Disordered human tumor-suppressor–associated protein (ST20): scattered peaks within predicted helices in a globally disordered chain, including the N-terminus.
- lncRNA/sORF-derived microprotein (IGF2 antisense protein): multiple peaks across annotated disordered regions rich in Arg/Pro/Gly.

Summary: Small, often poorly characterized or compositionally biased proteins, including viral accessory proteins, cancer/testis and germline-associated proteins, antisense-ORF microproteins, and short secreted/surface peptides; activation is broadly distributed across the polypeptide rather than focused on a single structured domain
Activation pattern: Regional/distributed activation spread across much of the protein with sparse residue-level peaks; often includes early N-terminal residues and disordered segments; variable coverage from short patches to most of the protein
Exemplars:
- Viral non-structural/accessory proteins: activation distributed through the protein, including basic/Arg-rich motifs such as nuclear localization signals.
- Cancer/testis antigens and germline-associated proteins: activation on long disordered low-complexity regions, often at N-termini.
- Small uncharacterized microproteins/antisense ORFs: activation spanning most of the polypeptide.
- Short secreted peptides and toxin precursors: activation across both signal/propeptide and mature regions.
- Compact cytosolic proteins with disordered N- or C-terminal extensions: activation enriched on the disordered tails.

Summary: Short segments within disordered and compositionally biased stretches of diverse proteins, particularly regions enriched in basic and acidic residues. Activations are also seen in non-disordered contexts across proteins of varied function, suggesting the feature captures a relatively broad local sequence pattern rather than a tight structural motif.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks with small clusters, distributed throughout the length of the protein. Peaks frequently overlap annotated disordered regions and basic/acidic compositionally biased segments, but also occur at isolated positions within structured chains; occurs in both helical and coil contexts.
Exemplars: - Oomycete RxLR secreted effectors: peaks within the mature effector chain, with occasional spikes in the signal peptide.
- Plant CLE peptide precursors: localized peaks within the C-terminal CLE motif corresponding to the mature signaling peptide.
- Cholecystokinin prohormone: peaks at or immediately adjacent to the N-termini of mature neuropeptides generated by proteolytic processing.
- Herpesvirus ICP47-like small accessory proteins: multiple peaks in the N-terminal active helical region and in polar, disordered C-terminal stretches.
- Keratin-associated proteins: activation across cysteine/proline/serine-rich, low-complexity repeat regions.
- Phosphodiesterase and fungal/bacterial enzymes with disordered N- or internal stretches: peaks within basic-and-acidic compositionally biased segments.

Summary: Detector of compositionally biased, low‑complexity segments—predominantly intrinsically disordered Ser/Thr‑rich (often RS-/Pro‑containing) tracts—with a strong N‑terminal bias; it also flags the extreme N‑terminus including signal peptides of secreted precursors.
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks clustered within long disordered/low‑complexity regions (often spanning tens to hundreds of residues), with strongest peaks on Ser/Thr and nearby polar/basic residues; broad regional activation across such IDRs and minimal signal in well‑folded domains or transmembranes; additional discrete peaks frequently occur at residues 1–10, including within N‑terminal signal peptides.
Exemplars: - Transcriptional regulator (CROC-4): multiple peaks across a central low‑complexity disordered segment (S/T/R/P‑rich), with minor N‑terminal peaks.
- Mechanosensory receptor (Stum): numerous high peaks on serines dispersed through annotated disordered, low‑complexity/polar regions.
- Yeast RNA/chromatin‑associated factor (REF2‑interacting protein): peaks within disordered, compositionally biased tracts; strongest at a threonine in an S/T‑rich context, near (but not exactly on) annotated phosphosites.
- Secreted antimicrobial peptide precursor (lumbricin): strongest activation on the N‑terminal signal peptide helix; weaker peaks just after the signal peptide preceding a long disordered pro‑region.
- Yeast HPH2 regulatory protein: activation confined to disordered, low‑complexity regions in the N‑terminal two‑thirds; absent from the structured C‑terminal domain and its transmembrane helix.

Summary: Broad, regional recognition of helical and hydrophobic/amphipathic segments, including contiguous hydrophobic alpha-helical transmembrane segments and proline/glycine-rich low-complexity stretches; the feature also fires across large internal regions of soluble enzymes and effector proteins, with a bias toward hydrophobic and helix-favoring residues and proline/glycine context.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over stretches: contiguous activation across single-pass or multi-pass transmembrane alpha-helices and amphipathic helical motifs; broad, distributed activation across internal regions of soluble proteins; sparser peaks within short secreted, low-complexity segments; overall bias toward hydrophobic and helix-favoring residues with enrichment for proline and glycine context.
Exemplars:
- Fibrillar collagens: strong activation along the triple-helical G–X–Y domain, peaking at X/Y positions (especially proline/hydroxyproline-like Y), with minimal signal on G.
- Light-harvesting complex alpha subunits (photosynthetic bacteria): activation along their single transmembrane alpha-helix.
- YhhN/TMEM86 lysoplasmalogenases: activation across multiple transmembrane segments.
- Viral accessory proteins (including non-membrane factors like replication enhancers), envelope proteins, and viroporins: activation on short hydrophobic or amphipathic helical motifs (membrane-anchored or not).
- Single-pass small integral membrane proteins: activation on the transmembrane helix.
- Plant CLE/CLAVATA/ESR peptide precursors: activation on the conserved proline-rich mature peptide region and adjacent low-complexity stretches.
- Oomycete RxLR effectors: activation across the mature effector region including the RxLR-dEER motif and adjacent low-complexity repeats.
- Fungal secreted/surface-associated effectors (e.g., hydrophobin-like): activation on hydrophobic, repetitive patches outside core cystine motifs.
- Small cysteine-rich toxins/defensin-like peptides: activation on hydrophobic patches within or adjacent to the disulfide-stabilized core.
- Soluble cytosolic enzymes/regulators: broad, distributed activation across internal regions, including disordered and low-complexity stretches.

Summary: Short segments within disordered and compositionally biased stretches of diverse proteins, particularly regions enriched in basic and acidic residues. Activations are also seen in non-disordered contexts across proteins of varied function, suggesting the feature captures a relatively broad local sequence pattern rather than a tight structural motif.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks with small clusters, distributed throughout the length of the protein. Peaks frequently overlap annotated disordered regions and basic/acidic compositionally biased segments, but also occur at isolated positions within structured chains; occurs in both helical and coil contexts.
Exemplars: - Oomycete RxLR secreted effectors: peaks within the mature effector chain, with occasional spikes in the signal peptide.
- Plant CLE peptide precursors: localized peaks within the C-terminal CLE motif corresponding to the mature signaling peptide.
- Cholecystokinin prohormone: peaks at or immediately adjacent to the N-termini of mature neuropeptides generated by proteolytic processing.
- Herpesvirus ICP47-like small accessory proteins: multiple peaks in the N-terminal active helical region and in polar, disordered C-terminal stretches.
- Keratin-associated proteins: activation across cysteine/proline/serine-rich, low-complexity repeat regions.
- Phosphodiesterase and fungal/bacterial enzymes with disordered N- or internal stretches: peaks within basic-and-acidic compositionally biased segments.

Summary: Detector of compositionally biased, low‑complexity segments—predominantly intrinsically disordered Ser/Thr‑rich (often RS-/Pro‑containing) tracts—with a strong N‑terminal bias; it also flags the extreme N‑terminus including signal peptides of secreted precursors.
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks clustered within long disordered/low‑complexity regions (often spanning tens to hundreds of residues), with strongest peaks on Ser/Thr and nearby polar/basic residues; broad regional activation across such IDRs and minimal signal in well‑folded domains or transmembranes; additional discrete peaks frequently occur at residues 1–10, including within N‑terminal signal peptides.
Exemplars: - Transcriptional regulator (CROC-4): multiple peaks across a central low‑complexity disordered segment (S/T/R/P‑rich), with minor N‑terminal peaks.
- Mechanosensory receptor (Stum): numerous high peaks on serines dispersed through annotated disordered, low‑complexity/polar regions.
- Yeast RNA/chromatin‑associated factor (REF2‑interacting protein): peaks within disordered, compositionally biased tracts; strongest at a threonine in an S/T‑rich context, near (but not exactly on) annotated phosphosites.
- Secreted antimicrobial peptide precursor (lumbricin): strongest activation on the N‑terminal signal peptide helix; weaker peaks just after the signal peptide preceding a long disordered pro‑region.
- Yeast HPH2 regulatory protein: activation confined to disordered, low‑complexity regions in the N‑terminal two‑thirds; absent from the structured C‑terminal domain and its transmembrane helix.

Summary: Alpha-helix boundary/capping motif (helix starts, N-caps, and helix kinks/hinges), especially at protein N-termini and within transmembrane helices; favors small/polar helix-friendly residues (S/T/A/G/P) with nearby charged residues (E/D/R), and often marks signal-peptide starts or conserved glycine kinks adjacent to functional acidic sites.
Activation pattern: Mixed: (1) regional activation across N-terminal low-complexity segments that contain short predicted helices, and (2) sharp single-residue peaks at conserved small residues that introduce kinks/hinges within helices (notably in TM helices). Typically weak or absent in well-folded catalytic cores; number of activated positions varies with the count of helix starts/hinges.
Exemplars: - Aspartyl-tRNA synthetase family: strong activation across the disordered N-terminal extension with helix/coil patches; no activation in the structured catalytic domain.
- Oomycete RxLR effectors: activation on the N-terminal signal peptide helix and the first helix of the mature effector (e.g., M56–T57–L58), plus adjacent N-terminal coil.
- Coronavirus non-structural proteins: peaks on S/T/R within and at the boundary of a disordered functional region, consistent with helix initiation/capping; minor peaks on short predicted helices.
- ATP synthase c subunit: a single sharp peak at a conserved glycine immediately C-terminal to the proton-binding glutamate within a TM helix, marking a helix kink/hinge site.
- ClC chloride channels: activation at a conserved glycine in an internal TM helix that creates a gating/kink position.
- Other bacterial respiratory-chain membrane proteins: isolated single-residue peaks at small residues marking TM helix hinge/kink points.
- Viral early proteins (e.g., adenovirus E4): identical N-terminal triplets and S/T-rich starts highlighted, consistent with helix N-cap preferences.
- Small human micropeptides: N-terminal activation over their principal amphipathic helix.

Summary: Low-complexity, intrinsically disordered segments with a bias for serine/threonine (often with proline and nearby basic/acidic residues) that encode short linear motifs for regulation or targeting (e.g., phosphosite motifs, RxLR-dEER), found in flexible regulatory tails, disordered viral protein regions, and short secreted peptide precursors.
Activation pattern: Predominantly regional activation across disordered, low-pLDDT stretches with many sites per segment; superimposed residue-level peaks on S/T and adjacent charged/proline residues. Also active in short, low-complexity transmembrane/peptide precursors; minimal in well-folded globular domains.
Exemplars: - Coronavirus nucleocapsid proteins: central low-complexity, disordered regions enriched in Ser/Thr with known phosphosites, plus disordered C-terminal tails.

Summary: Serine/threonine–rich, low‑complexity intrinsically disordered segments (often N‑terminal), frequently containing proline/glycine, occurring in a subset of viral accessory/immune‑evasion proteins and secreted/extracellular or regulatory tails; these tracts act as flexible linkers and common modification hotspots (e.g., O‑glycosylation in secreted regions or phosphorylation in cytosolic tails). Presence depends on local S/T enrichment and disorder, not on protein class per se.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across short-to-long low‑complexity stretches with residue‑level peaks on S/T (often adjacent to P/G); strong N‑terminal bias; suppressed in well‑folded domains, cysteine‑rich defensins, and transmembrane helices; appears only when S/T‑rich LCRs are present and may be absent elsewhere in the same protein.
Exemplars: - Viral accessory/immune‑evasion proteins with cytosolic tails: activation on S/T/P‑rich disordered segments (e.g., EBV BNLF2a); many viral polyprotein/membrane regions without such tracts show no activation.

- Testis/spermatogenesis‑associated proteins that carry S/T/P‑rich disordered N‑terminal tails: activated; those lacking such tracts are not.
- lncRNA‑derived micropeptides: activation only in S/T/G‑rich disordered sequences; those without S/T enrichment may not activate.
- Host immune/stress-response factors: activation on S/T‑rich regulatory IDRs; structured kinases without S/T‑rich tails show little to no activation.
- Bacterial/archaeal surface or secreted proteins: activation on S/T‑rich low‑complexity linkers between domains; absent otherwise.
- Core metabolic enzymes: rare activation, confined to S/T‑rich unstructured loops or termini; many enzymes show none.

Summary: Often fires within intrinsic disorder/low-complexity segments—especially terminal or propeptide regions enriched in Pro/Ser/Thr/Gly—that serve as flexible carriers of short linear motifs; the feature highlights unstructured tails/loops across diverse proteins (including secreted precursors, viral regulators, membrane-protein tails, and micropeptides), sometimes coinciding with proteolytic processing and PTM sites, but also produces residue-level peaks within some short folded enzymes/fragments.

- Mycobacterial cell-envelope–associated proteins: single-residue/short-segment peaks within UniProt-annotated disordered coil regions.
- p53-inducible regulatory proteins: sparse peaks across N-terminal and central intrinsically disordered regions, including isoform-variable segments.
- Alternative reading frame micropeptides: activation across low-complexity, disordered coils.

Summary: N‑terminal start and proteolytic maturation junction detector: activates on the initiator methionine or the first residue of a newly formed mature peptide after signal peptide/propeptide cleavage, typically within low‑complexity, disordered segments enriched in Ser/Pro/Gly/Arg; most prominent in secreted and membrane precursors and small peptides, but also marking N‑termini of diverse proteins (including many viral proteins) across taxa.
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks at the exact boundary (the first residue of the mature peptide and/or the immediately preceding residue), with short flanking N‑terminal stretches in low‑complexity IDRs; occasional weaker N‑terminal peaks elsewhere; broad, low‑specificity activation across taxa.
Exemplars: Plant PROPEP/Pep danger‑peptide precursors: strong peak at the N‑terminal boundary of the mature Pep within a disordered, acidic/basic‑biased prodomain; Viral envelope glycoproteins (e.g., class I fusion proteins): activation at signal peptide cleavage and/or polybasic convertase junctions, and at the extreme N‑terminus; Secreted hormone/neuropeptide and growth factor precursors: activation at propeptide removal sites that define the N‑terminus of the active peptide; Type I membrane receptors and secretory pathway glycoproteins: initiator Met and signal peptide region/cleavage site highlighted; lncRNA‑encoded micropeptides/smORFs: activation at Met1 and adjacent low‑complexity N‑terminal residues; Sperm/testis secreted or acrosomal proteins: activation on N‑terminal signal/pro‑region cleavage junctions; Bacterial/archaeal metabolic enzymes: weaker, generic N‑terminal activation at the start of disordered/low‑complexity tails; p53/apoptosis‑related proteins: N‑terminal disordered domains (e.g., transactivation/pro‑segments) show start‑proximal peaks.

Summary: Short linear segments in intrinsically disordered or otherwise low-structure-confidence regions, often at N-termini and within signal peptides/propeptides of secreted and regulatory proteins (including viral accessory proteins and small ORF microproteins), enriched in small/basic residues (G, P, S, A, R; often with Cys), rather than in well-folded catalytic cores.

Summary: Residue-level detector that fires sparsely in small proteins, peptide precursors, and disordered/loosely structured regions, often in propeptide or disordered C-/N-terminal segments; avoids structured catalytic cores and binding sites.

Exemplars: - tRNA (pseudouridine(54)-N1)-methyltransferase: activation restricted to the disordered N-terminal extension (e.g., a peak in a short transient helix), absent from the SAM-dependent catalytic domain
- Secreted bacterial protease: strong activation in disordered N- and C-terminal tails, none across the structured protease core

Summary: Methionine residue identity, with a strong bias toward the N‑terminal initiator Met and early hydrophobic N‑terminal segments; generally fires on Met in diverse structural/functional contexts and is largely structure-agnostic.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks centered on Met; often includes the initiator Met at position 1 and occasionally nearby bulky hydrophobic/aromatic residues (W, V, L, I; sometimes T, C). Typically only a few residues per protein are active, with a tendency to cluster near the N-terminus but also occurring on internal Met.
Exemplars: - cAMP-specific phosphodiesterase (PDE4A) fragment: exclusive activation on multiple internal Met residues independent of secondary structure or disorder.
- Secreted precursors (hormones, toxins, bacteriocins): activation on the initiator Met of the signal peptide/propeptide.
- Viral accessory/immune-modulatory proteins: short, N-terminally focused activation on M1 and occasional internal Met.
- Membrane-associated proteins (signal anchors/transmembrane leaders): activation on the N-terminal Met and Met within early hydrophobic segments.
- Human microproteins and testis/spermatogenesis-related proteins: sparse activation on M1 and any internal Met in short proteins.
- Glycoprotein precursors: activation on the initiator Met at the start of signal peptides.

Summary: Broad, regional recognition of helical and hydrophobic/amphipathic segments, including contiguous hydrophobic alpha-helical transmembrane segments and proline/glycine-rich low-complexity stretches; the feature also fires across large internal regions of soluble enzymes and effector proteins, with a bias toward hydrophobic and helix-favoring residues and proline/glycine context.

Exemplars:
- Fibrillar collagens: strong activation along the triple-helical G–X–Y domain, peaking at X/Y positions (especially proline/hydroxyproline-like Y), with minimal signal on G.

- Plant CLE/CLAVATA/ESR peptide precursors: activation on the conserved proline-rich mature peptide region and adjacent low-complexity stretches.
- Oomycete RxLR effectors: activation across the mature effector region including the RxLR-dEER motif and adjacent low-complexity repeats.
- Fungal secreted/surface-associated effectors (e.g., hydrophobin-like): activation on hydrophobic, repetitive patches outside core cystine motifs.
- Small cysteine-rich toxins/defensin-like peptides: activation on hydrophobic patches within or adjacent to the disulfide-stabilized core.
- Soluble cytosolic enzymes/regulators: broad, distributed activation across internal regions, including disordered and low-complexity stretches.
