The feature captures the mature, proteolytically processed peptide/module characterized by clustered Cys (often CC motifs) and basic residues.
Activation pattern: Regional activation confined to short mature peptide segments (tens of residues) following the signal peptide and propeptides; minimal/absent on signal/pro-regions. Strong residue-level peaks on cysteines and frequent secondary peaks on Lys/Arg and Gly. Activation spans mixed secondary structure (β-strands, coils, short helices) and can include key functional loops (e.g., RGD in disintegrins).
Exemplars: - Plant cyclotides (cystine-knot cyclopeptides, e.g., chassatide): activation across the cyclic cystine‑knot core of the mature peptide after processing.
- Snake venom disintegrins: activation across the disintegrin domain, including the RGD integrin-binding loop and adjacent cysteine-dense core.
- Inhibitor cystine-knot (ICK) venom toxins from spiders, cone snails, centipedes, and sea anemones: activation on the disulfide‑knotted toxin core.
- Kunitz/BPTI- and Kazal-type serine protease inhibitors (including tick chemokine/complement inhibitors): activation on the small disulfide‑rich inhibitor domain.
- Hevein-like/seed defense peptides: activation on the cysteine-rich chitin‑binding hevein domain.
- Defensins (plant/fungal/animal CSαβ peptides) and vertebrate hepcidin: activation on the cysteine‑stabilized mature AMP region.
- Euplotes ciliate mating pheromones: activation on the secreted disulfide‑rich pheromone core.
- Cysteine-rich modules within large extracellular/mucin-like proteins: activation on the short, cysteine‑dense repeat/subdomain embedded in the larger precursor.

Summary: Folded extracytoplasmic luminal domains of secretory or organellar precursors—i.e., the mature globular regions (and, when present as independent folds, structured inhibitory propeptides) that lie immediately downstream of signal/transit peptides—common in plant/apoplastic and other lumenal proteins (secreted, vacuolar, chloroplast/thylakoid) and spanning diverse families (proteases, expansins, phytocyanins, SCP/CAP toxins, GDSL lipases), often disulfide‑stabilized and glycosylated; targeting peptides and low‑complexity linkers are de-emphasized.
Activation pattern: Domain-level, long continuous activation that switches on sharply after the signal/transit peptide cleavage site (or at the start of a folded pro/mature domain), remains high across well-structured secondary elements, and drops in signal/transit peptides, low-complexity/disordered tails, and small auxiliary motifs (e.g., ShKT). Within catalytic domains the feature does not focus on active-site residues and can dip at catalytic positions.

Summary: Disulfide-stabilized extracellular β‑strand modules, most prominently thrombospondin type‑1 repeats (TSR), but also related small cystine‑rich domains (Kunitz/BPTI inhibitors, EGF‑like repeats, lectin CRDs, defensin/toxin folds) in secreted or surface proteins involved in adhesion, protease regulation, and host–pathogen interaction.
Activation pattern: Domain- and residue-level: repeated activation bands across tandem extracellular modules; sharp peaks on β‑strand cores and adjacent short connectors, emphasizing disulfide‑forming cysteines and nearby basic/aromatic residues (Arg/Lys, Trp/Tyr) characteristic of TSR/Kunitz/EGF motifs; minimal activation in signal peptides, helices, and unrelated domains (e.g., Ig‑like C2, PLAC).
Exemplars: - TSR-containing ECM/axon-guidance proteins (thrombospondins, ADAMTS-like/madd-4): activation on β‑strands within TSRs, including conserved cysteines and basic/tryptophan motifs; neighboring Ig-like/PLAC segments remain low.
- Kunitz-type serine protease inhibitors and extracellular protease regulators (e.g., coagulation/complement inhibitors): activation on the central β‑strand and disulfide cysteines of Kunitz repeats; helices are unactivated.
- Apicomplexan adhesins with TSR-like modules (TRAP/CTRP/MIC families): activation along TSR-like β‑strand elements mediating host binding.
- Integrin β subunits and other EGF-repeat proteins: activation on β‑strands of EGF-like cysteine‑rich repeats.
- Lectin-like extracellular receptors and plant lectins: activation on β‑sheets within disulfide-stabilized carbohydrate-recognition domains.
- Small disulfide-rich toxins and defensins: activation on short β‑strand segments and the disulfide‑forming cysteines.

Summary: Post–signal peptide bioactive segments of small secreted peptide precursors—especially plant peptide hormones (CLE, CIF, SCOOP, IDA, RALF, CEP, PSY, EPF/EPFL) and related cysteine-rich/pheromonal or inhibitory peptides (e.g., SFTI)—i.e., the propeptide/mature peptide region that carries receptor-binding motifs and processing/PTM signals (e.g., sulfotyrosine, hydroxyproline), typically flexible/disordered. Occasional weaker activation can occur in non-secreted proteins with short basic/proline-rich disordered segments due to compositional similarity.
Activation pattern: Regional activation that switches on just after the N-terminal signal peptide (≈residue 20–40) and spans a short-to-moderate C-terminal stretch corresponding to the propeptide and/or mature peptide; peaks over receptor-binding and processing motifs (e.g., SxS, sulfated Tyr, dibasic/basic clusters) within largely low-pLDDT coils with occasional short helices/strands; minimal on the signal peptide and often lower on rigid disulfide-bonding cysteines.
Exemplars: - CLE peptide precursors: activation across the disordered C-terminal region encompassing the mature CLE peptides.
- Casparian strip integrity factors (CIF): strong activation over the sulfated-tyrosine/hydroxyproline-modified C-terminal receptor-binding segment.
- CEP and PSY families: activation on the post–signal peptide pro/mature regions bearing Hyp/sulfated motifs.
- SCOOP and IDA/IDL peptides: activation across the disordered C-terminal mature chain following the signal peptide.
- RALF-like peptides: activation across the propeptide and into the N-terminus of the mature RALF, peaking at the short helical/receptor-interacting region.
- EPF/EPFL cysteine-rich peptides: activation over the mature ligand with reduced signal on disulfide-forming cysteines.
- PAMP-induced secreted peptides (PIP): activation spans the entire mature peptide, not the signal peptide.
- Animal peptide hormones (e.g., apelin) and small plant inhibitory peptides (e.g., SFTI): activation on the processed bioactive segment with lower signal on disulfide-bonding cysteines.
- Note: rare off-target activation may occur in non-secreted, short disordered/basic regions (e.g., SMR-like proteins) and is typically weaker.

Summary: Membrane‑active amphipathic α‑helices enriched in small hydrophobic residues (A/V/L/I/G) that insert into, line, or associate with lipid bilayers—i.e., the pore‑forming/translocation helices of toxins and translocons and analogous lipid‑binding/stress‑sensing helices in other membrane proteins
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long, contiguous helical segments (often single helices or helical hairpins), with sparse charges and frequent Gly/Ala runs; peaks track α‑helical stretches that often fold upon membrane contact (low pLDDT in isolation). Activation typically avoids catalytic motifs and generic signal peptides/TM anchors, instead favoring amphipathic or pore‑lining helices (including lipid‑binding helices) within toxin, antimicrobial, and membrane‑associated domains.
Exemplars: - Pore-forming colicins: strong activation on the C‑terminal pore‑forming transmembrane/helical hairpin region.
- Bacillus thuringiensis Cry (δ‑endotoxins): activation on the N‑terminal pore‑forming helical bundle (domain I) with peaks in membrane‑inserting helices.
- Cationic antimicrobial peptides (e.g., Styelin‑D): activation confined to the mature amphipathic α‑helix; absent on the signal peptide and propeptide.
- Mitochondrial inner‑membrane protease OMA1: activation on amphipathic helices within the peptidase domain, including a cardiolipin‑binding/stress‑sensor region; little to no activation on the N‑terminal propeptide or the single‑pass TM anchor.

Summary: Membrane-interacting helical modules: cationic, Gly/Ala-rich amphipathic α-helices and short transmembrane hairpins/fusogenic segments that mediate lipid binding, insertion, or pore formation in toxins, secretion/translocation factors, and viral/secreted proteins; typically low-confidence/disordered in isolation and become helical upon membrane contact.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long, contiguous helical stretches; strongest over amphipathic or hydrophobic helices (including TM segments), with peaks on small hydrophobics (A/V/L/I/G) and frequent Lys/Arg; tends to avoid structured catalytic cores, instead marking N- or C‑terminal delivery/membrane-interaction regions; often coincides with low pLDDT and predicted helices or annotated transmembranes; in peptides, activates on the mature membrane-active helix rather than the signal peptide.
Exemplars: - Cry-family insecticidal δ-endotoxins: activation on the N‑terminal pore-forming helical bundle (domain I) of Cry13Aa.
- Cationic antimicrobial peptide (moricin): activation across the mature α‑helical AMP, not the signal peptide.
- Type VI secretion effector VasX: activation over the C‑terminal membrane-inserting module comprising multiple transmembrane helices.
- LXG polymorphic toxin (YqcG): activation on a long C‑terminal, low‑pLDDT disordered segment following the LXG export domain (a membrane/translocation-prone tail-like region).
- T6SS ADP‑ribosyltransferase (mART) effector (Tre1): activation on N‑terminal glycine‑rich, low‑confidence helical regions flanking PAAR and outside the catalytic core, consistent with delivery/membrane-targeting helices.

Summary: Short hydrophobic membrane-inserting alpha-helices and related fusion/pore-forming segments (15–40 aa) used as single-pass transmembrane anchors or membrane-penetrating peptides; enriched in small hydrophobics with interspersed Ser/Thr and glycine motifs (e.g., GxxxG/glycine-zipper) that promote helix insertion/packing, common in toxins, secretion pores, viral fusion proteins, and other membrane-associated factors.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over contiguous hydrophobic segments, often helical or coil-to-helix; sharp residue-level peaks frequently at Gly or Ser/Thr near helix starts, within TM cores, or immediately after cleavage sites that expose fusion peptides; multiple activated segments can occur per protein; frequently low pLDDT due to membrane context or intrinsic flexibility; near termini in small precursors and internal in larger proteins.
Exemplars: - Type III secretion translocon (SctE): strong activation across two annotated transmembrane helices, peaking at residues whose mutation disrupts helix formation.
- Paramyxovirus fusion glycoprotein F: activation spanning the furin cleavage and N-terminus of the F1 fusion peptide (membrane-penetrating segment).
- Bacteriocin/antimicrobial peptide (Pumilarin): activation on a hydrophobic, helix-forming membrane-active segment within the mature toxin peptide.
- Membrane-anchored toxin (double-stranded DNA deaminase toxin A): primary activation on the N-terminal transmembrane helix; weaker activation on a short disordered hydrophobic segment.
- Magnetosome membrane protein (MamG): localized activation within the single-pass transmembrane helix, peaking at the helix start following an LG motif.

Summary: Short, cationic, amphipathic peptide segments—typically the mature cores of secreted antimicrobial/cytolytic peptides and analogous AMP‑like helices embedded in larger proteins. These regions are Lys/Arg‑rich with interspersed hydrophobes, often form (or have propensity for) an amphipathic α‑helix, and are used for membrane interaction/disruption or other bioactive signaling; they are usually produced by proteolytic processing from precursor proteins and can include RiPP cores despite post‑translational crosslinks.
Activation pattern: Regional activation on short contiguous blocks (∼15–40 aa, sometimes shorter), with sharp on/off at the boundaries of mature peptide segments; minimal activation in signal peptides and propeptides. Peaks often coincide with hydrophobic residues along an amphipathic face and clusters of Lys/Arg. Frequently at N‑ or C‑terminal helices or short internal helices with low-to-moderate pLDDT.
Exemplars: - Amphibian helical antimicrobial peptides (e.g., aureins): activation precisely on the mature AMP helix, not on signal/propeptide.
- Hymenopteran venom cytolysins (e.g., myrmeciitoxins): strong activation across the mature toxin’s amphipathic α‑helix.
- Lantibiotic RiPPs (e.g., lacticin 3147 A2): activation on the modified mature lantibiotic core despite lanthionine/beta‑methyllanthionine crosslinks.
- Phage/bacterial holins: activation on the N‑terminal amphipathic helix adjacent to the first transmembrane segment; little/no activation in TM or periplasmic domains.
- Crustacean anti‑lipopolysaccharide factors (ALFs): activation on the N‑terminal cationic LPS‑binding helix of the mature peptide.
- Plant NLR immune receptors (coiled‑coil N‑termini): activation on the N‑terminal CC helix implicated in membrane permeabilization/channel activity.
- Insect stress-response secreted proteins (Turandot family): activation on a C‑terminal amphipathic α‑helix of the mature chain.
- Outer membrane polysaccharide export proteins (CtrA family): activation on a short periplasmic C‑terminal helical tail with amphipathic character.
- Kininogen‑derived peptides (bradykinin variants): activation on the short, basic bioactive peptide released from a disordered region.

Summary: Amphipathic, membrane-active insertion/oligomerization segments (typically short helical or pre-stem peptides) used for pore formation, membrane lysis or fusion; enriched for K/R with interspersed hydrophobics (L/I/V) and some E/D and S/T; characteristic of secreted toxins, bacteriocins/microcins, viral fusion/capsid proteins, and ApoL pore-formers, and also captured in Lys/Glu-rich coiled-coil heptads
Activation pattern: Regional activation on contiguous 15–40 aa windows corresponding to amphipathic helices or pre-insertion stems; frequently near the N-terminus in Cry toxins and bacteriocins; occasional longer C-terminal Lys/Glu-rich coiled-coil stretches; residue-level peaks align with alternating basic/hydrophobic positions in a heptad/amphipathic pattern rather than whole-domain activation
Exemplars: - Bacillus thuringiensis Cry insecticidal toxins: activation on N-terminal helical bundle hairpins that insert into membranes to form pores
- Staphylococcus aureus pore-forming toxins (alpha-hemolysin, leukocidins): activation on the pre-stem/insertion segment that becomes the membrane-embedded pore
- Aerolysin/hemolysin beta-pore-formers (Gram-negative): activation on amphipathic pre-insertion loops/stems used during pore assembly
- Bacteriocins and microcins: activation on N-terminal cationic amphipathic helices that permeabilize bacterial membranes
- Invertebrate hemolysins/actinoporins: activation on the N-terminal amphipathic insertion helix used for lysis
- Viral fusion/spike proteins: activation on fusion peptides and heptad-repeat amphipathic segments mediating membrane fusion/oligomerization
- Viral capsid proteins: activation on short membrane-penetrating/basic amphipathic segments used during entry or assembly
- Human apolipoprotein L family: activation on amphipathic, pH-dependent membrane-inserting/pore-forming helices
- Magnetosome small membrane proteins: activation on short amphipathic helices adjacent to TM/signal regions that interface with the inner membrane
- Dictyostelium Ca2+-upregulated secreted proteins: activation on basic/hydrophobic amphipathic stretches predicted to bind/perturb membranes
- Fungal secreted LysM/chitinase effectors: activation on long Lys/Glu-rich amphipathic/coiled-coil-like C-terminal segments mediating oligomerization or host-membrane interaction
- Coiled-coil proteins with Lys/Glu-rich heptads: activation on amphipathic oligomerization helices sharing the same charge/hydrophobic pattern

Summary: Short linear segments in intrinsically disordered or otherwise low-structure-confidence regions, often at N-termini and within signal peptides/propeptides of secreted and regulatory proteins (including viral accessory proteins and small ORF microproteins), enriched in small/basic residues (G, P, S, A, R; often with Cys), rather than in well-folded catalytic cores.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks scattered across IDRs and low-confidence coils/short helices; frequently clustered near the N-terminus, in signal peptides, propeptides, and disordered tails; little to no activation in well-structured domains; occasional activation in low-confidence transmembrane/signal-anchor helices.
Exemplars: - Viral accessory protein (HIV-1 Vif): peaks throughout low-pLDDT coils, especially the disordered N-terminal region.
- Neuropeptide precursor (Drosophila Amnesiac): activation in the N-terminal signal peptide and multiple mature peptide segments with very low pLDDT.
- Secreted serine carboxypeptidase: activation confined to disordered C-terminal tail, annotated disordered segment, the signal peptide, and a low-confidence C-terminal transmembrane helix; absent from the structured catalytic domain.
- Disordered human tumor-suppressor–associated protein (ST20): scattered peaks within predicted helices in a globally disordered chain, including the N-terminus.
- lncRNA/sORF-derived microprotein (IGF2 antisense protein): multiple peaks across annotated disordered regions rich in Arg/Pro/Gly.

Summary: Short, intrinsically disordered C‑terminal tails of secreted or membrane‑associated proteins (from microproteins to larger multi‑pass enzymes) and viral accessory microproteins, typically low‑complexity and enriched in proline and basic residues, often immediately downstream of a hydrophobic signal/transmembrane segment; can include cysteine‑rich patches in secreted/toxin peptides.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over contiguous 10–30 aa windows, most frequently at the extreme C‑terminus; often spans a brief helix that transitions into coil with peak signal in the disordered coil; commonly adjacent to a hydrophobic (signal/TM) segment and characterized by low pLDDT; can also occur in short cytosolic juxtamembrane loops of larger multi‑pass proteins.
Exemplars:
- Oomycete RxLR secreted effectors: activation on the C‑terminal tail immediately following a predicted hydrophobic segment, in a low‑confidence helix/coil region.
- Human ST20 (apoptosis/stress‑related microprotein): activation on a short C‑terminal helix‑to‑coil, highly disordered stretch.
- Small uncharacterized microproteins: activation confined to the last ~10–15 residues forming a disordered coil tail.
- Viral accessory/viroporin‑like proteins: activation on basic/proline‑rich cytosolic C‑tails adjacent to a single‑pass TM helix; also applies to non‑TM viral accessory proteins with disordered C‑tails (e.g., Vif).
- Small secreted cysteine‑rich toxins/defensin‑like peptides: activation on short cationic/cysteine‑biased segments within the mature or processing tail.
- ATP synthase epsilon subunits: activation on a conserved, short, disordered C‑terminal regulatory segment in these small mitochondrial/bacterial proteins.
- Multi‑pass membrane enzymes (e.g., phytoene dehydrogenase): activation on short cytosolic C‑terminal or juxtamembrane tails adjacent to TM helices.

Summary: Small, often poorly characterized or compositionally biased proteins, including viral accessory proteins, cancer/testis and germline-associated proteins, antisense-ORF microproteins, and short secreted/surface peptides; activation is broadly distributed across the polypeptide rather than focused on a single structured domain
Activation pattern: Regional/distributed activation spread across much of the protein with sparse residue-level peaks; often includes early N-terminal residues and disordered segments; variable coverage from short patches to most of the protein
Exemplars:
- Viral non-structural/accessory proteins: activation distributed through the protein, including basic/Arg-rich motifs such as nuclear localization signals.
- Cancer/testis antigens and germline-associated proteins: activation on long disordered low-complexity regions, often at N-termini.
- Small uncharacterized microproteins/antisense ORFs: activation spanning most of the polypeptide.
- Short secreted peptides and toxin precursors: activation across both signal/propeptide and mature regions.
- Compact cytosolic proteins with disordered N- or C-terminal extensions: activation enriched on the disordered tails.

Summary: Residue-level detector that activates broadly at sparse positions across diverse protein contexts, with notable preference for disordered/low-complexity regions, mature secreted peptides, and short helical segments (including transmembrane helices and helix-prone regions inside intrinsically disordered stretches). It does not appear to track a single specific motif.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks, typically one to a few strong peaks per protein with additional weaker peaks scattered along the sequence. Strong activation is observed within intrinsically disordered regions (including Gly-rich and polar/charged compositionally biased segments), within short transmembrane helices, and within mature processed peptides. Activation is also seen scattered within globular enzyme domains.
Exemplars:
- Small integral membrane proteins: single strong peak within a short transmembrane helix.
- Secretory preprohormones (e.g., cholecystokinin): multiple peaks within the mature processed peptide regions.
- Homeobox/disordered regulators (e.g., Rhox5): multiple peaks throughout disordered Gly-rich and basic/acidic compositionally biased segments.
- CaMKII inhibitor peptides: peaks at the start of the inhibitory domain and at Pro-rich positions.
- Viral accessory/integrase-like proteins: multiple short peaks scattered across the chain, including disordered C-terminal segments.
- Bacterial/yeast enzymes (e.g., beta-lactamase, aspartyl-tRNA synthetase, imidazolonepropionase, peroxin-9): scattered peaks within N-terminal or globular regions.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low-complexity regulatory segments in nuclear proteins—long tracts enriched in charged/polar residues (Ser/Pro with Lys/Arg and/or acidic E/D), often containing short basic patches (NLS/AT-hook–like) and phospho-Ser/Thr motifs; these simple-sequence tails/linkers occur in transcription/chromatin and RNA-processing regulators (and viral regulators) and are largely absent from folded domains.
Activation pattern: Domain-level off on structured domains (e.g., BTB, PWWP); regional on in extended IDRs with low pLDDT; localized peaks over short basic clusters (often NLS-like), Ser-rich/Pro-rich or acidic patches, and phospho-motifs (e.g., ETPS), sometimes selecting only a subsegment within a larger disordered region.
Exemplars: - Mediator complex subunit tail (MED19): activation confined to the C-terminal disordered tail, peaking over an ETPS phospho-motif, a Lys/Arg-rich patch, and a Ser-rich low-complexity stretch; silent across the more structured N-terminus.
- BTB transcription factor (Lola): off across the folded BTB domain; on across the central low-complexity/disordered linker, with a pronounced peak in a short Ser-rich segment; minimal signal in helical C-terminal regions.
- Hepatoma-derived growth factor (HDGF): off on the N-terminal PWWP domain; strong activation on a C-terminal disordered segment overlapping a bipartite nuclear localization signal and adjacent mixed basic/acidic low-complexity sequence, with a peak at a Lys-rich patch.

Summary: Short linear segments in intrinsically disordered or otherwise low-structure-confidence regions, often at N-termini and within signal peptides/propeptides of secreted and regulatory proteins (including viral accessory proteins and small ORF microproteins), enriched in small/basic residues (G, P, S, A, R; often with Cys), rather than in well-folded catalytic cores.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks scattered across IDRs and low-confidence coils/short helices; frequently clustered near the N-terminus, in signal peptides, propeptides, and disordered tails; little to no activation in well-structured domains; occasional activation in low-confidence transmembrane/signal-anchor helices.
Exemplars: - Viral accessory protein (HIV-1 Vif): peaks throughout low-pLDDT coils, especially the disordered N-terminal region.
- Neuropeptide precursor (Drosophila Amnesiac): activation in the N-terminal signal peptide and multiple mature peptide segments with very low pLDDT.
- Secreted serine carboxypeptidase: activation confined to disordered C-terminal tail, annotated disordered segment, the signal peptide, and a low-confidence C-terminal transmembrane helix; absent from the structured catalytic domain.
- Disordered human tumor-suppressor–associated protein (ST20): scattered peaks within predicted helices in a globally disordered chain, including the N-terminus.
- lncRNA/sORF-derived microprotein (IGF2 antisense protein): multiple peaks across annotated disordered regions rich in Arg/Pro/Gly.

Summary: Small, often poorly characterized or compositionally biased proteins, including viral accessory proteins, cancer/testis and germline-associated proteins, antisense-ORF microproteins, and short secreted/surface peptides; activation is broadly distributed across the polypeptide rather than focused on a single structured domain
Activation pattern: Regional/distributed activation spread across much of the protein with sparse residue-level peaks; often includes early N-terminal residues and disordered segments; variable coverage from short patches to most of the protein
Exemplars:
- Viral non-structural/accessory proteins: activation distributed through the protein, including basic/Arg-rich motifs such as nuclear localization signals.
- Cancer/testis antigens and germline-associated proteins: activation on long disordered low-complexity regions, often at N-termini.
- Small uncharacterized microproteins/antisense ORFs: activation spanning most of the polypeptide.
- Short secreted peptides and toxin precursors: activation across both signal/propeptide and mature regions.
- Compact cytosolic proteins with disordered N- or C-terminal extensions: activation enriched on the disordered tails.

Summary: Short, low‑complexity, intrinsically disordered proteins and modules that encode targeting/processing signals—often but not always secretory—combining hydrophobic signal peptides, double‑Gly bacteriocin leaders, or polybasic/NLS‑like segments, frequently adjacent to Ser/Thr/Pro‑rich stretches and basic clusters (e.g., RXLR, KR/RR)—common in micropeptides, toxins/secreted precursors, viral accessory proteins, keratin‑associated and testis‑specific low‑complexity proteins across taxa
Activation pattern: Regional activation across short proteins, spanning hydrophobic/targeting segments and Ser/Thr/Pro‑rich low‑complexity tracts with peaks on basic motifs such as RXLR, dibasic KR/RR, or double‑Gly leader junctions
Exemplars:
- Oomycete RxLR effectors: activation on the N‑terminal signal peptide and the RXLR/EER host‑targeting motif immediately downstream.
- Secreted peptide hormone/venom/toxin precursors: activation on the signal peptide and basic prohormone convertase cleavage motifs (KR/RR) within the propeptide region.
- Class II bacteriocins: activation on the N‑terminal double‑Gly leader and adjacent cationic tract recognized by ABC exporters.
- Viral accessory/regulatory proteins (e.g., small disordered regulators): activation across S/T/P‑rich low‑complexity disordered segments containing polybasic/NLS‑like clusters.
- Keratin‑associated proteins (KRTAPs): activation over short, repetitive low‑complexity regions (Ser/Pro‑rich and basic tracts) typical of hair shaft proteins.
- Cancer/testis antigens and testis‑associated proteins: activation on Lys/Arg‑ and Pro/Ser‑rich low‑complexity stretches in very short proteins.
- Short uncharacterized micropeptides/antisense products: broad activation across their low‑complexity/basic segments.
- Enzymes that carry secretory leaders or short disordered/basic tails (including some cytosolic enzymes lacking signal peptides): activation limited to the disordered tail, not the catalytic core.

Summary: Residue-level detector that activates broadly at sparse positions across diverse protein contexts, with notable preference for disordered/low-complexity regions, mature secreted peptides, and short helical segments (including transmembrane helices and helix-prone regions inside intrinsically disordered stretches). It does not appear to track a single specific motif.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks, typically one to a few strong peaks per protein with additional weaker peaks scattered along the sequence. Strong activation is observed within intrinsically disordered regions (including Gly-rich and polar/charged compositionally biased segments), within short transmembrane helices, and within mature processed peptides. Activation is also seen scattered within globular enzyme domains.
Exemplars:
- Small integral membrane proteins: single strong peak within a short transmembrane helix.
- Secretory preprohormones (e.g., cholecystokinin): multiple peaks within the mature processed peptide regions.
- Homeobox/disordered regulators (e.g., Rhox5): multiple peaks throughout disordered Gly-rich and basic/acidic compositionally biased segments.
- CaMKII inhibitor peptides: peaks at the start of the inhibitory domain and at Pro-rich positions.
- Viral accessory/integrase-like proteins: multiple short peaks scattered across the chain, including disordered C-terminal segments.
- Bacterial/yeast enzymes (e.g., beta-lactamase, aspartyl-tRNA synthetase, imidazolonepropionase, peroxin-9): scattered peaks within N-terminal or globular regions.

Summary: Short, linear, compositionally biased motifs—often the hydrophobic core of signal peptides or signal-anchor helices (positions ~10–20), and downstream host-targeting motifs—together with sensitivity to the 'X' position of Gly–X–Y collagen repeats; the feature can also fire broadly across small/disordered or membrane-associated proteins.
Activation pattern: A mix of focused residue-level peaks and broader distributed activation. Focused peaks frequently land in the first 10–30 residues (especially ~10–20) within alpha-helical signal peptides or signal-anchor transmembranes; sparse, periodic single-residue peaks every third position across collagen Gly–X–Y repeats; short clusters over linear motifs (e.g., RxLR–dEER); additional peaks distributed across cytoplasmic and disordered segments of small membrane or regulatory proteins.
Exemplars: - Collagen alpha chains (extracellular matrix): activates on the 'X' position within Gly–X–Y collagen repeats across the collagenous domain.
- Scorpion alpha-KTx potassium-channel toxins (secreted peptides): single-residue peak in the N-terminal signal peptide helix (~position 10).
- Mammalian alpha-defensins (antimicrobial peptides): single hydrophobic residue in the N-terminal signal peptide helix (~position 15).
- Oomycete RxLR effectors (secreted host-targeting proteins): residues within the RxLR–dEER motif and additional peaks in the preceding signal peptide.
- Bacterial TonB (inner-membrane/periplasmic): leucine near the boundary of the N-terminal signal-anchor transmembrane helix.
- Plant arabinogalactan protein precursors (secreted glycoproteins): short two-residue patch in the N-terminal signal peptide helix.
- Small viral suppressors and crustacean antimicrobial peptide precursors: peaks in low-confidence disordered regions and in the hydrophobic core of N-terminal signal peptides.

Summary: Short linear segments in intrinsically disordered or otherwise low-structure-confidence regions, often at N-termini and within signal peptides/propeptides of secreted and regulatory proteins (including viral accessory proteins and small ORF microproteins), enriched in small/basic residues (G, P, S, A, R; often with Cys), rather than in well-folded catalytic cores.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks scattered across IDRs and low-confidence coils/short helices; frequently clustered near the N-terminus, in signal peptides, propeptides, and disordered tails; little to no activation in well-structured domains; occasional activation in low-confidence transmembrane/signal-anchor helices.
Exemplars: - Viral accessory protein (HIV-1 Vif): peaks throughout low-pLDDT coils, especially the disordered N-terminal region.
- Neuropeptide precursor (Drosophila Amnesiac): activation in the N-terminal signal peptide and multiple mature peptide segments with very low pLDDT.
- Secreted serine carboxypeptidase: activation confined to disordered C-terminal tail, annotated disordered segment, the signal peptide, and a low-confidence C-terminal transmembrane helix; absent from the structured catalytic domain.
- Disordered human tumor-suppressor–associated protein (ST20): scattered peaks within predicted helices in a globally disordered chain, including the N-terminus.
- lncRNA/sORF-derived microprotein (IGF2 antisense protein): multiple peaks across annotated disordered regions rich in Arg/Pro/Gly.

Summary: The feature recognizes cationic, amphipathic, low-complexity segments that mediate targeting or membrane/lipid association—classically N‑terminal signal/transit/leader-like regions of secreted, mitochondrial, and viral proteins—and frequently the propeptide/mature regions of toxin and neuropeptide precursors; it can also highlight short basic/hydrophobic helices or redox-active motifs within structured domains.
Activation pattern: Predominantly long, continuous activation over N‑terminal, low‑pLDDT leader/propeptide regions enriched in Lys/Arg, Ser/Pro and hydrophobic/aromatic residues; with occasional residue-level peaks within well-structured helices (e.g., specific positions in thioredoxin CGHC motifs or matrix-exposed helices of membrane proteins).
Exemplars: 
- Venom phospholipase A2 precursors (activation on signal/propeptide segments and conserved cationic patches).
- Apolipoproteins (N‑terminal signal peptide and amphipathic helical stretches).
- Protein kinases with disordered/basic N‑termini (e.g., cyclin-dependent and PRK family N‑tails).
- Thioredoxin-fold protein disulfide-isomerases (peak at the CGHC active-site helix).
- Mitochondrial calcium uniporter (selected residues in a matrix-exposed helix).
- Conotoxin and other secreted toxin precursors; neuropeptide prepropeptides (activation across pro/mature peptide regions).
- Viral silencing suppressors and small membrane/morphogenesis proteins (basic, hydrophobic leader-like segments).
- Kinetochore coiled-coil scaffold proteins (basic low-complexity regions).
- FYVE-domain endosomal adaptors (basic, membrane/PIP-interacting low-complexity segments).
- RNA-modifying enzymes with basic N‑terminal tails (e.g., tRNA methyltransferases).

Summary: Polybasic, lysine‑rich low‑complexity intrinsically disordered segments (acidic‑poor and often N/T/S‑rich), frequently located near protein N‑termini; the feature highlights short basic patches/tracts rather than structured domains
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks on Lys that coalesce into short regional activation across disordered/basic patches; strongest in low‑pLDDT coils or low‑confidence helices, often near the N‑terminus, with neighboring N/T/S also elevated
Exemplars: - Viral accessory proteins (e.g., agnoproteins): strong peaks at terminal K and adjacent N in unstructured tails.
- Antimicrobial peptide precursors (e.g., Ixosin): activation within the mature cationic peptide on K/N, with weaker signals in the propeptide.
- ABC transporters: concentrated activation in an N‑terminal disordered, lysine‑rich segment immediately preceding the structured transporter domain.
- Telomere‑associated proteins: scattered peaks on K/N within low‑pLDDT coils across the sequence.
- Human intrinsically disordered regulatory proteins: multiple K‑centered peaks distributed across low‑confidence helices/coils.

Summary: Short, low‑complexity, intrinsically disordered proteins and modules that encode targeting/processing signals—often but not always secretory—combining hydrophobic signal peptides, double‑Gly bacteriocin leaders, or polybasic/NLS‑like segments, frequently adjacent to Ser/Thr/Pro‑rich stretches and basic clusters (e.g., RXLR, KR/RR)—common in micropeptides, toxins/secreted precursors, viral accessory proteins, keratin‑associated and testis‑specific low‑complexity proteins across taxa
Activation pattern: Regional activation across short proteins, spanning hydrophobic/targeting segments and Ser/Thr/Pro‑rich low‑complexity tracts with peaks on basic motifs such as RXLR, dibasic KR/RR, or double‑Gly leader junctions
Exemplars:
- Oomycete RxLR effectors: activation on the N‑terminal signal peptide and the RXLR/EER host‑targeting motif immediately downstream.
- Secreted peptide hormone/venom/toxin precursors: activation on the signal peptide and basic prohormone convertase cleavage motifs (KR/RR) within the propeptide region.
- Class II bacteriocins: activation on the N‑terminal double‑Gly leader and adjacent cationic tract recognized by ABC exporters.
- Viral accessory/regulatory proteins (e.g., small disordered regulators): activation across S/T/P‑rich low‑complexity disordered segments containing polybasic/NLS‑like clusters.
- Keratin‑associated proteins (KRTAPs): activation over short, repetitive low‑complexity regions (Ser/Pro‑rich and basic tracts) typical of hair shaft proteins.
- Cancer/testis antigens and testis‑associated proteins: activation on Lys/Arg‑ and Pro/Ser‑rich low‑complexity stretches in very short proteins.
- Short uncharacterized micropeptides/antisense products: broad activation across their low‑complexity/basic segments.
- Enzymes that carry secretory leaders or short disordered/basic tails (including some cytosolic enzymes lacking signal peptides): activation limited to the disordered tail, not the catalytic core.

Summary: Short linear motifs centered on serine/threonine within intrinsically disordered regions that correspond to eukaryotic Ser/Thr phosphorylation sites (often SP/TP or basic R/K-flanked motifs), used for regulatory control across diverse proteins including viral proteins
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks on single S/T or 1–3 aa motifs, punctate and distributed across proteins; strongly enriched in low-pLDDT coils and low-complexity segments; depleted in folded domains and transmembrane helices; occasional peaks at edges of low-confidence helices; context frequently includes nearby proline and/or basic residues
Exemplars: - PH plus RapGAP scaffold proteins: activation on S/T residues in disordered linkers; minimal signal in folded PH and GAP domains
- Chromatin regulator Spt21: multiple peaks in disordered C-terminal regions; includes a known phosphoserine site
- TORC1 subunit Tco89: peaks at/near an annotated phosphothreonine and other disordered segments
- Large transmembrane receptor with long cytosolic tail (stum): activation confined to disordered cytosolic regions; none in transmembrane helices
- Developmental cytoskeletal regulator (bottleneck): clusters on S/T within low-complexity, basic-enriched disordered C-terminus
- Small GTPase regulators (e.g., RhoGAPs, RasGEFs, ARF GEFs) and protein kinases: signal found in regulatory low-complexity regions and termini rather than catalytic cores, consistent with phosphorylation-prone SLiMs

Summary: Broad, regional recognition of helical and hydrophobic/amphipathic segments, including contiguous hydrophobic alpha-helical transmembrane segments and proline/glycine-rich low-complexity stretches; the feature also fires across large internal regions of soluble enzymes and effector proteins, with a bias toward hydrophobic and helix-favoring residues and proline/glycine context.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over stretches: contiguous activation across single-pass or multi-pass transmembrane alpha-helices and amphipathic helical motifs; broad, distributed activation across internal regions of soluble proteins; sparser peaks within short secreted, low-complexity segments; overall bias toward hydrophobic and helix-favoring residues with enrichment for proline and glycine context.
Exemplars:
- Fibrillar collagens: strong activation along the triple-helical G–X–Y domain, peaking at X/Y positions (especially proline/hydroxyproline-like Y), with minimal signal on G.
- Light-harvesting complex alpha subunits (photosynthetic bacteria): activation along their single transmembrane alpha-helix.
- YhhN/TMEM86 lysoplasmalogenases: activation across multiple transmembrane segments.
- Viral accessory proteins (including non-membrane factors like replication enhancers), envelope proteins, and viroporins: activation on short hydrophobic or amphipathic helical motifs (membrane-anchored or not).
- Single-pass small integral membrane proteins: activation on the transmembrane helix.
- Plant CLE/CLAVATA/ESR peptide precursors: activation on the conserved proline-rich mature peptide region and adjacent low-complexity stretches.
- Oomycete RxLR effectors: activation across the mature effector region including the RxLR-dEER motif and adjacent low-complexity repeats.
- Fungal secreted/surface-associated effectors (e.g., hydrophobin-like): activation on hydrophobic, repetitive patches outside core cystine motifs.
- Small cysteine-rich toxins/defensin-like peptides: activation on hydrophobic patches within or adjacent to the disulfide-stabilized core.
- Soluble cytosolic enzymes/regulators: broad, distributed activation across internal regions, including disordered and low-complexity stretches.

Summary: Small, often poorly characterized or compositionally biased proteins, including viral accessory proteins, cancer/testis and germline-associated proteins, antisense-ORF microproteins, and short secreted/surface peptides; activation is broadly distributed across the polypeptide rather than focused on a single structured domain
Activation pattern: Regional/distributed activation spread across much of the protein with sparse residue-level peaks; often includes early N-terminal residues and disordered segments; variable coverage from short patches to most of the protein
Exemplars:
- Viral non-structural/accessory proteins: activation distributed through the protein, including basic/Arg-rich motifs such as nuclear localization signals.
- Cancer/testis antigens and germline-associated proteins: activation on long disordered low-complexity regions, often at N-termini.
- Small uncharacterized microproteins/antisense ORFs: activation spanning most of the polypeptide.
- Short secreted peptides and toxin precursors: activation across both signal/propeptide and mature regions.
- Compact cytosolic proteins with disordered N- or C-terminal extensions: activation enriched on the disordered tails.

Summary: Short residue windows in mixed-composition regions of diverse proteins, frequently in N-terminal or non-catalytic portions of enzymes, transmembrane-adjacent stretches, and small secreted peptides.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks concentrated in short 3–7 residue windows, often clustered with several nearby peaks. Activated residues are chemically diverse (including hydrophobic, polar, and charged residues) and can occur in helical transmembrane segments, disordered linkers, or globular regions outside annotated catalytic/binding sites.
Exemplars:
- Bacterial DNA ligase: clusters of peaks in the N-terminal region upstream of the catalytic and BRCT domains.
- Viral integrase homolog: short peaks within the chain including a GPAYGRP-containing segment.
- Peroxisomal biogenesis factor 9 (Pex9): peaks overlapping helical transmembrane segments and an adjacent disordered/polar region.
- Small secreted peptides (e.g., Califin-B large subunit): short peaks within the mature peptide.

Summary: Low-complexity, intrinsically disordered segments—often at protein N-termini—such as mucin-like/propeptide regions or flexible linkers adjacent to signal/transit peptides, common in small secreted or membrane-associated proteins and also as disordered extensions in diverse enzymes (broad taxonomic coverage, including viral, bacterial, and eukaryotic proteins).
Activation pattern: Regional activation over short to moderate stretches, frequently in disordered or polar/low-complexity segments; in longer proteins, multiple low-complexity patches can activate; in micropeptides, activation can span much of the sequence. Residue-level peaks can fall on Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly within polar-residue stretches but also on basic or hydrophobic residues within the same disordered context.
Exemplars:
- Viral envelope/accessory microproteins: activation on N-terminal Ser/Thr/Pro-rich disordered segments (often mucin-like or regulatory tails).
- Secreted eukaryotic effectors (e.g., oomycete RxLR effectors): activation on the low-complexity region flanking the signal peptide/RxLR motif.
- Human testis-biased and lncRNA-derived micropeptides: activation across intrinsically disordered peptide regions.
- Secreted precursors/propeptides: activation on N-terminal regions following the signal peptide.
- Membrane-associated single-pass proteins: activation on luminal or cytosolic tails flanking the transmembrane helix.
- Bacterial/archaeal metabolic enzymes: activation on disordered, low-complexity N-terminal extensions/linkers enriched in Ser/Thr/Gly/Pro.

Summary: Short linear motifs in low-complexity or flexible loops—often near the N-terminus and at coil↔helix or strand↔helix boundaries—that include polybasic patches such as RxLR but also small/polar and occasional acidic residues, mediating targeting or transient interactions across secreted, membrane, viral/regulatory, and soluble enzymes.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks clustered in short (2–8 aa) stretches or single spikes; enriched for R/L/S/T/P/A with context-dependent D/E (notably in loops of membrane enzymes); frequent near N-termini or after signal peptides but also in internal surface loops; occurs in IDRs (low pLDDT) and modest-confidence loops at secondary-structure junctions.
Exemplars:
- Oomycete RxLR effectors: strong activation over RxLR and adjacent basic/proline-rich disordered segments; additional peaks on arginine-rich patches within helical regions.
- Viral regulatory/accessory proteins and envelope glycoproteins: peaks in basic/disordered regions (e.g., cytosolic tails or low-structure segments) supporting interaction/trafficking roles.
- Chitin synthase-like and membrane acyltransferases: short loop motifs at structure transitions with peaks on K/R as well as D/E in adjacent flexible loops.
- Large eukaryotic regulators (kinases, RalGAP, formins): activation in N-terminal/basic or proline-rich low-complexity segments and at helix/loop boundaries.
- Soluble bacterial enzymes (e.g., ITPase, glutamate 5-kinase): isolated peaks on small/polar/basic residues within flexible surface loops.
