Summary: N-terminal secretory leader/proregion of peptide precursors and effectors—short, charged, often S/T-rich, mostly disordered/helix–coil segments that lie at or just after the signal peptide and carry export/processing/translocation motifs (e.g., double‑glycine bacteriocin leaders, RxLR–dEER). These regions function during secretion or maturation and are typically removed or not part of the mature active domain.
Activation pattern: Regional activation on a single contiguous 20–60 aa stretch at the extreme N-terminus, usually overlapping the C-terminal tail of the signal peptide and/or the immediate post-signal leader. Strongest on conserved charged motifs (e.g., GG leaders, polybasic/acidic clusters, RxLR–dEER). Activation drops to near-zero in the mature peptide/domain.
Exemplars: - Lantibiotic/lantipeptide precursors: activation on the N-terminal leader peptide that is cleaved before the mature lantipeptide (e.g., Flv-type lantipeptides).
- Bacteriocin/glycocin Sublancin-168: activation confined to the annotated propeptide (double‑glycine–type leader), not the mature toxin.
- Lasso peptide (Microcin J25) precursor: activation on the N-terminal leader required for biosynthetic processing; no activation on the mature lasso core.
- Thiopeptide (Thiocillin) precursor: activation on the leader region removed in the mature antibiotic.
- ComX bacterial pheromone precursor: activation across the N-terminal propeptide preceding the mature pheromone.
- Conotoxin precursor: activation spanning the C-terminal portion of the signal peptide into the N-terminal propeptide; absent on the mature toxin.
- Plant secreted peptide precursor (e.g., SCOOP-type): activation over the late signal-peptide tail and adjacent pro-region; not on the mature motif.
- Secreted protease inhibitor (Marinostatin): activation on the signal peptide that targets secretion; absent on the mature inhibitor.
- Oomycete RxLR effectors: activation on the post-signal translocation region containing the RxLR–dEER motif; no activation on the C-terminal effector domain.

Summary: Mature bioactive segments of secreted peptides and peptide-derived natural products—especially RiPP cores (lantibiotics, class II bacteriocins, lasso peptides)—and analogous extracellular toxin/effector regions that lie C-terminal to leaders/signal peptides; these regions are often enriched in small/processable residues (G/S/T/C, Gly–Gly) or in cationic/hydrophobic content typical of antimicrobial, pheromonal, amyloid, and effector peptides.
Activation pattern: Primarily regional/domain-level activation that sharply rises after leader/signal-peptide cleavage sites and runs contiguously across the mature/functional chain; leaders and signal peptides are largely inactive. Activation tolerates mixed secondary structure and frequently occurs in low-structure-confidence segments. In large nonsecreted proteins, the feature collapses to isolated residue-level peaks, often on Gly/Ser/Cys (e.g., near metal-binding motifs), rather than extended regions.
Exemplars: - Lantipeptide/lantibiotic precursors: strong, continuous activation over the lanthipeptide core, including Ser/Thr/Cys that become dehydrated or form lanthionines; leader region silent.
- Class II bacteriocins (e.g., lactococcin A): high activation across the mature bacteriocin, including its membrane-acting helix; no activation in the N-terminal propeptide.
- Lasso peptides (Microcin J25): activation confined to the mature lasso core, including residues forming the isopeptide ring; leader off.
- Functional amyloid system (Pseudomonas FapE): inactive on the signal peptide, strongly active across the secreted mature amyloid subunit.
- ComX pheromone precursors: activation on the mature isoprenylated-tryptophan pheromone and extending into the adjacent C-terminal tail/propeptide.
- Oomycete RxLR effectors: low/absent on signal peptide and RxLR-dEER motif; peaks on the C-terminal, Lys/Arg-rich helical effector domain.
- Venom/antimicrobial helical peptides (e.g., IsCT precursors): peaks at the C-terminus of the mature peptide and into the adjacent propeptide at a helix–coil boundary.
- Housekeeping/cytosolic proteins (e.g., deubiquitinases, coiled-coil subunits): only sparse, low-level hits on individual Gly/Ser/Cys residues within structured regions.

Summary: Short processing/cleavage motifs marking secretion or autoproteolytic boundaries, covering double-glycine leaders of bacteriocin/microcin/lantibiotic (RiPP) precursors, the RxLR-EER host-entry region of oomycete effectors, the Type VII secretion signal at the end of mycobacterial PE domains, and the C-terminal cleavage/processing region preceding toxin cargo in polymorphic toxins (Rhs/CDI/T6SS) and analogous proteins bearing inteins/homing endonucleases.
Activation pattern: Focal activation (~5-10 aa) on a conserved DPxG[L/M] / DPDGxA-type motif in large toxins, typically located in the distal C-terminal segment at or immediately adjacent to an autoproteolytic cleavage site; in small precursors activation lies at the N-terminal leader spanning the signal/chain boundary. Peaks sit at or just beyond cleavage/recognition motifs.
Exemplars: - RiPP bacteriocins/lantibiotics/microcins: activation on the N-terminal double-glycine leader recognized by ABC exporters/C39 peptidases (cleavage/processing signal).
- Enterobacterial colicins/microcins: activation on leader/translocation regions.
- Oomycete RxLR effectors: activation on the RxLR followed by the acidic EER tract immediately after the signal peptide (host-targeting/export module).
- Mycobacterial PE/PPE (Type VII secretion) proteins: activation at the C-terminal end of the PE domain and adjacent helix bearing the secretion signal (YxxxD/E-like), as seen in PE_PGRS family.
- Polymorphic toxins (Rhs/CDI/T6SS): activation on a conserved DPxGL-like motif in the distal C-terminal region at or near the autoproteolytic cleavage site that releases the toxin cargo (e.g. YenC1/YenC2, Tse5, DddA, RhsB/RhsC).
- Intein/homing endonuclease–containing proteins (including archaeal/phage): activation on short linkers near intein junctions or homing endonuclease motifs that flank processing/splicing sites.

Summary: Low-complexity repetitive/disordered segments in secreted and extracellular proteins, often associated with fibrillar/amyloid-like or biomaterial assemblies and surface layers; also includes N-terminal double-glycine leader regions of secreted bacteriocins, the glycine-rich PGRS repeats of mycobacterial PE/PPE proteins, acidic Asp/Ser-rich extracellular matrix phosphoproteins, and certain outer surface lipoproteins where activation occurs within the signal/lipobox region and the adjacent low-complexity stretch.
Activation pattern: Broad regional activation across low-complexity tracts, frequently covering signal peptides and their adjacent mature N-terminal regions; strong peaks occur on Pro-, acidic-, Ser-, and Gly-biased low-complexity stretches; weak/absent outside these low-complexity segments.
Exemplars:
- Mycobacterial PE/PGRS and PPE surface proteins: activation on the PGRS glycine-rich GGX-type repeats.
- Keratin-associated/cornified envelope proteins of hair/skin: activation across long low-complexity stretches.
- Insect chorion eggshell and cuticle proteins: activation on glycine–tyrosine-rich repetitive arrays.
- Plant glycine-rich cell wall proteins and small secreted peptides: activation across the low-complexity region following the signal peptide.
- Silk/fibroin/spidroin-like biomaterial proteins: activation across the central GA/GY-rich repetitive core.
- Bacterial amyloid/rodlet-forming matrix proteins (e.g., chaplins, rodlins): broad activation across the signal peptide and disordered low-complexity core, including Pro-, acidic-, and Gly-biased stretches.
- Class II bacteriocins/microcins: activation at the N-terminal double-glycine leader cleavage motif and adjacent G-rich segment.
- Small cysteine-rich antimicrobial/toxin peptides: localized activation on short glycine patches within the mature peptides.
- SIBLING family extracellular matrix phosphoproteins (e.g., DMP1): activation across Asp/Ser-rich acidic low-complexity tracts.
- Spirochaete outer surface lipoproteins (e.g., OspC): activation at the N-terminus of the mature lipoprotein near the signal peptide/lipobox within a low-complexity stretch.

Summary: N-terminal prepro-regions of secreted/extracellular proteins: classical signal peptides and the adjacent inhibitory propeptides that are proteolytically removed to generate the mature chain (covering toxins/antimicrobial peptides, secreted hydrolases and protease inhibitors, cell-wall enzymes, and virulence factors).
Activation pattern: Domain-level, contiguous N-terminal activation beginning at the initiator methionine. The block spans the signal peptide and often extends through the propeptide, with activation frequently strongest in the propeptide. Activation drops sharply at the signal peptidase/proprotein convertase cleavage site that marks the start of the mature chain and remains off over the folded catalytic/toxin domains. In some cases it marks only the signal peptide, or only the propeptide; boundaries often align with small/polar residues at the cleavage site.
Exemplars: - Cathepsin-like cysteine proteases: activation confined to the inhibitory propeptide (prodomain), not the signal peptide or mature enzyme.
- Secreted bacterial proteases: activation over the signal peptide plus propeptide, off in the mature catalytic domain.
- TIMP family protease inhibitors: activation restricted to the N-terminal signal peptide; mature inhibitor off.
- Fungal defensin precursors (e.g., plectasin): strong activation across signal peptide and propeptide; mature cysteine-rich AMP off.
- Yeast killer toxin precursors: activation on signal peptide and propeptide; mature toxin off.
- Ribotoxins (alpha-sarcin): activation on the signal peptide only; mature RNase off.
- Resuscitation-promoting factor (Rpf) family cell-wall enzymes: activation across signal peptide and disordered N-terminal segment; catalytic domain off.
- Secreted esterases/lipases: activation on the signal peptide; mature hydrolase off.
- Fungal hydrophobins: activation on the signal peptide; mature secreted protein off.
- Venom peptide precursors (conotoxin/hexatoxin-like): strong activation on signal peptide plus propeptide; mature toxin off.

Summary: Low-complexity, intrinsically disordered segments—often at protein N-termini—such as mucin-like/propeptide regions or flexible linkers adjacent to signal/transit peptides, common in small secreted or membrane-associated proteins and also as disordered extensions in diverse enzymes (broad taxonomic coverage, including viral, bacterial, and eukaryotic proteins).
Activation pattern: Regional activation over short to moderate stretches, frequently in disordered or polar/low-complexity segments; in longer proteins, multiple low-complexity patches can activate; in micropeptides, activation can span much of the sequence. Residue-level peaks can fall on Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly within polar-residue stretches but also on basic or hydrophobic residues within the same disordered context.
Exemplars:
- Viral envelope/accessory microproteins: activation on N-terminal Ser/Thr/Pro-rich disordered segments (often mucin-like or regulatory tails).
- Secreted eukaryotic effectors (e.g., oomycete RxLR effectors): activation on the low-complexity region flanking the signal peptide/RxLR motif.
- Human testis-biased and lncRNA-derived micropeptides: activation across intrinsically disordered peptide regions.
- Secreted precursors/propeptides: activation on N-terminal regions following the signal peptide.
- Membrane-associated single-pass proteins: activation on luminal or cytosolic tails flanking the transmembrane helix.
- Bacterial/archaeal metabolic enzymes: activation on disordered, low-complexity N-terminal extensions/linkers enriched in Ser/Thr/Gly/Pro.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low-complexity segments enriched in serine/threonine/proline/glycine and often basic (lysine/arginine), typically found in flexible N- or C-terminal tails and loops; highlights IDRs that may harbor short linear motifs (e.g., basic NLS patches) rather than structured domain cores.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long disordered stretches with additional sparse residue-level peaks in low-confidence loops; often N-terminal-biased in short/viral proteins; rarely within well-folded cores.
Exemplars: Retroviral accessory proteins (e.g., HTLV-1 p30): activation on central and C-terminal IDRs including a basic nuclear localization signal; p53-regulated apoptosis-inducing microprotein: widespread activation across a globally disordered protein; Bacterial DNA ligase: scattered activation in an annotated disordered linker and flexible loops within the ligase domain; Uncharacterized human microprotein: multiple peaks throughout a low-pLDDT, disordered sequence irrespective of predicted secondary structure.

Summary: Short linear segments in intrinsically disordered or otherwise low-structure-confidence regions, often at N-termini and within signal peptides/propeptides of secreted and regulatory proteins (including viral accessory proteins and small ORF microproteins), enriched in small/basic residues (G, P, S, A, R; often with Cys), rather than in well-folded catalytic cores.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks scattered across IDRs and low-confidence coils/short helices; frequently clustered near the N-terminus, in signal peptides, propeptides, and disordered tails; little to no activation in well-structured domains; occasional activation in low-confidence transmembrane/signal-anchor helices.
Exemplars: - Viral accessory protein (HIV-1 Vif): peaks throughout low-pLDDT coils, especially the disordered N-terminal region.
- Neuropeptide precursor (Drosophila Amnesiac): activation in the N-terminal signal peptide and multiple mature peptide segments with very low pLDDT.
- Secreted serine carboxypeptidase: activation confined to disordered C-terminal tail, annotated disordered segment, the signal peptide, and a low-confidence C-terminal transmembrane helix; absent from the structured catalytic domain.
- Disordered human tumor-suppressor–associated protein (ST20): scattered peaks within predicted helices in a globally disordered chain, including the N-terminus.
- lncRNA/sORF-derived microprotein (IGF2 antisense protein): multiple peaks across annotated disordered regions rich in Arg/Pro/Gly.

Summary: N‑terminal start and proteolytic maturation junction detector: activates on the initiator methionine or the first residue of a newly formed mature peptide after signal peptide/propeptide cleavage, typically within low‑complexity, disordered segments enriched in Ser/Pro/Gly/Arg; most prominent in secreted and membrane precursors and small peptides, but also marking N‑termini of diverse proteins (including many viral proteins) across taxa.
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks at the exact boundary (the first residue of the mature peptide and/or the immediately preceding residue), with short flanking N‑terminal stretches in low‑complexity IDRs; occasional weaker N‑terminal peaks elsewhere; broad, low‑specificity activation across taxa.
Exemplars: Plant PROPEP/Pep danger‑peptide precursors: strong peak at the N‑terminal boundary of the mature Pep within a disordered, acidic/basic‑biased prodomain; Viral envelope glycoproteins (e.g., class I fusion proteins): activation at signal peptide cleavage and/or polybasic convertase junctions, and at the extreme N‑terminus; Secreted hormone/neuropeptide and growth factor precursors: activation at propeptide removal sites that define the N‑terminus of the active peptide; Type I membrane receptors and secretory pathway glycoproteins: initiator Met and signal peptide region/cleavage site highlighted; lncRNA‑encoded micropeptides/smORFs: activation at Met1 and adjacent low‑complexity N‑terminal residues; Sperm/testis secreted or acrosomal proteins: activation on N‑terminal signal/pro‑region cleavage junctions; Bacterial/archaeal metabolic enzymes: weaker, generic N‑terminal activation at the start of disordered/low‑complexity tails; p53/apoptosis‑related proteins: N‑terminal disordered domains (e.g., transactivation/pro‑segments) show start‑proximal peaks.

Summary: Short segments within disordered and compositionally biased stretches of diverse proteins, particularly regions enriched in basic and acidic residues. Activations are also seen in non-disordered contexts across proteins of varied function, suggesting the feature captures a relatively broad local sequence pattern rather than a tight structural motif.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks with small clusters, distributed throughout the length of the protein. Peaks frequently overlap annotated disordered regions and basic/acidic compositionally biased segments, but also occur at isolated positions within structured chains; occurs in both helical and coil contexts.
Exemplars: - Oomycete RxLR secreted effectors: peaks within the mature effector chain, with occasional spikes in the signal peptide.
- Plant CLE peptide precursors: localized peaks within the C-terminal CLE motif corresponding to the mature signaling peptide.
- Cholecystokinin prohormone: peaks at or immediately adjacent to the N-termini of mature neuropeptides generated by proteolytic processing.
- Herpesvirus ICP47-like small accessory proteins: multiple peaks in the N-terminal active helical region and in polar, disordered C-terminal stretches.
- Keratin-associated proteins: activation across cysteine/proline/serine-rich, low-complexity repeat regions.
- Phosphodiesterase and fungal/bacterial enzymes with disordered N- or internal stretches: peaks within basic-and-acidic compositionally biased segments.

Summary: Glycine- and aromatic-enriched low-complexity segments, predominantly in secreted/extracellular proteins and matrices (including bacterial amyloids), but also present in some intracellular intrinsically disordered proteins and in luminal tails of small membrane proteins; typically cationic/disordered tracts featuring YGG/G–X–G/GGW motifs with interspersed Lys/Arg/His.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long, continuous low-complexity stretches (glycine runs with interleaved Tyr/Trp and basic residues), rather than sharp residue-level peaks.
Exemplars:
- Neuropeptide/opioid prohormones (proenkephalin, prodynorphin, POMC): activation on YGG-containing peptide blocks and adjacent Gly/Aromatic-rich repeats.
- Salivary secreted proteins: histidine-rich peptides (histatins), proline-rich salivary proteins, and statherin with cationic Gly/His/Pro- and aromatic-glycine motifs.
- Antimicrobial peptide precursors (e.g., spider ctenidins, glycine-rich insect AMPs like gloverins/attacins; amphibian skin propeptides): activation on Gly-rich, aromatic-glycine and G–X–G repeat regions in exported segments.
- Extracellular surface/structural proteins (fungal hydrophobins; spore wall/coat proteins; bacterial amyloid subunits such as FapC): activation on Gly/Tyr-rich low-complexity repeat blocks.
- Secreted enzymes/proproteins (e.g., astacin metalloproteases): activation on low-complexity propeptides or repeat-rich inserts within the secreted domains.
- Plant dehydrins/LEA intrinsically disordered proteins: activation on Gly/Lys-rich low-complexity tracts with occasional aromatic-glycine motifs.
- Small cysteine-rich single-pass membrane proteins (e.g., CYSTM family): activation on short luminal extracellular low-complexity segments enriched in Gly/Tyr/His.
- Insect seminal fluid peptides (e.g., sex peptide): activation on exported low-complexity tracts, often with glycine/aromatic motifs.

Summary: A feature that activates at conserved internal sequence motifs in secreted prepropeptides and within specific structural domains of nuclear ATPases. In secreted/secretory granule proteins, the strongest peaks fall within propeptide/activation-peptide regions at or near basic-rich motifs (e.g., "PARRAR"/"PTRRAR" in serglycins) and within the N-terminal peptide segments of neuroendocrine prohormones; weaker peaks occur internally within signal peptides. In MORC family ATPases, peaks localize within the CW-type zinc finger domain.

Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks concentrated at a small number of sites per protein. In propeptide-containing secreted proteins, the dominant peak occurs on or near a basic residue inside the propeptide/activation peptide, with weaker secondary peaks inside signal peptides and disordered C-terminal regions. In MORC-family proteins, peaks cluster on residues within the CW-type zinc finger fold (roughly the first third of the ZF region and around the conserved aromatic positions).

Exemplars:
- Serglycins (mouse, rat, human): strong peaks at the conserved PxRRAR motif within the activation peptide, plus weaker peaks within the signal peptide and disordered C-terminal tail.
- Neuroendocrine protein 7B2 (pig, frog, fly): peaks within the mature N-terminal peptide region, with weaker peaks inside the signal peptide.
- Mycobacterial pilin: peaks within the mature chain.
- MORC family CW-type zinc finger ATPases (MORC1 C. elegans, MORC2B mouse, MORC1 human): peaks within the CW-type zinc finger domain.

Summary: Polycationic, low‑complexity disordered segments in secreted or periplasmic proteins—typically Lys/Arg/His‑rich patches (often interspersed with Pro/Gly) found in propeptides, flexible linkers, and low‑confidence tails rather than in folded catalytic domains.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across extended basic, repeat‑rich blocks; often multiple patches per precursor; strongest in disordered/propeptide regions with low predicted structure confidence; little to no activation on signal peptides or well‑structured domains.
Exemplars: - Secreted metalloprotease precursors (M12A/ADAMTS/tolloid‑like): activation on basic, disordered propeptide segments and C‑terminal low‑complexity tails.
- Mating pheromone precursors (e.g., ciliate/fungal pheromones): activation confined to the N‑terminal propeptide; not on the signal peptide or the mature pheromone.
- Cationic antimicrobial peptides and toxin precursors (e.g., magainin/cecropin‑like, histidine‑rich peptides, venom peptides): activation across the polybasic, low‑complexity cationic segment or basic prodomain patches.
- Fungal secreted CAZymes (glycoside hydrolases/oxidoreductases): activation on Lys/Arg‑rich disordered linkers and/or basic prosegments between catalytic and accessory modules.
- Plant small secreted peptides and lysine‑rich arabinogalactan proteins: activation on Lys‑rich repetitive extracellular regions.
- Bacterial TonB and TonB‑like periplasmic proteins: activation along long, basic low‑complexity periplasmic stretches.
- Host–pathogen interaction and some viral secreted proteins: activation on surface‑exposed basic low‑complexity repeat patches used for extracellular interactions.

Summary: Arg/Lys-rich, intrinsically disordered low‑complexity tails that mediate electrostatic binding and condensation of nucleic acids—found in histones (esp. H1 and core histone N‑terminal tails), protamines, viral nucleoproteins/capsid cores, and bacterial/archaeal nucleoid proteins; enriched for interspersed Ser/Pro/Gly and dipeptide/repeat patterns such as SP/TP, RS/SR, and RG/RGG
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long polybasic IDRs; strong, contiguous activation on entire very short basic polypeptides (e.g., protamines, viral basic cores) and on specific basic segments within larger proteins, especially N‑terminal histone tails and Lys/Arg‑rich low‑complexity tracts; residue‑level peaks over runs of R/K and RS/SR, SP/TP, RGG motifs
Exemplars: - Protamines and protamine‑like sperm nuclear proteins — activation spans the whole Arg/Lys‑rich, low‑complexity chain used for genome hyper‑condensation.
- Linker histone H1 family (including testis/oocyte‑specific variants) — activation on the long Lys/Ser/Pro‑rich C‑terminal tail and basic N‑terminal segment that contact linker DNA.
- Core histones and centromeric histone variants (e.g., CENP‑A) — activation on the N‑terminal basic tails that interact with DNA and are sites of proline‑directed phosphorylation (SP/TP).
- High mobility group/AT‑hook proteins (HMGA/HMGN) — activation over clusters of AT‑hooks (RGRP‑like) and adjacent Lys/Arg‑rich low‑complexity tracts.
- Bacterial/chlamydial/archaeal nucleoid‑associated or histone‑like proteins (e.g., HU/IHF, HctA/B, archaeal histones) — activation on basic tails and Lys/Arg‑rich segments that compact the chromosome.
- Kinetoplastid histone H1‑like (kinetoplast‑associated proteins) — activation across Lys/Ser/Pro‑rich disordered regions that package kDNA.
- Viral nucleocapsid/core and histone‑like proteins — activation on protamine‑like basic regions that nonspecifically coat and condense viral RNA/DNA.

Summary: Extracellular secreted precursors and ectodomains with disulfide-bonded cysteine-rich loops/domains (cystine-stabilized scaffolds), and a subset of secreted neuropeptide precursors whose activation concentrates on flexible, processing-rich segments even without dense cysteine content. Common in proteins with signal peptides, glycosylation, and proteolytic processing.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks on cysteines and adjacent positions (often Gly/Pro and basic Lys/Arg) within extracellular regions; regional activation over cysteine-rich loops or repeats; also highlights Gly/Pro and Lys/Arg flanking propeptide cleavage motifs in cysteine-poor neuropeptide precursors; absent in transmembrane helices and cytosolic tails; strongest in low-to-moderate order ectodomain segments, sometimes near N-glycosylation and cleavage sites.
Exemplars:
- Chemokines (especially CXC): activation on conserved disulfide-forming cysteine motifs.
- Defensins/plant CRPs and knottin-like/trypsin inhibitor peptides (CSαβ/ICK scaffolds): activation across disulfide-bonded loops.
- WFDC, Kunitz, and Kazal protease inhibitors: activation on disulfide-stabilized inhibitor domains.
- Venom toxins (e.g., Kunitz-type, ShK, disintegrins): activation on clustered cysteines defining the scaffold.
- Viral envelope glycoproteins (class I/II/III): activation in cysteine-rich ectodomains near disulfide networks and glycosylation sites.
- Extracellular receptor/adhesion and metalloprotease proteins: activation on EGF-like, disintegrin, and other cysteine-rich modules.
- DEG/ENaC family channels: activation in the extracellular cysteine-rich loop.
- Neuropeptide hormone precursors (e.g., small cardioactive peptides): activation around flexible, dibasic cleavage-rich segments even with low cysteine content.
- Apicomplexan AMA1 invasion protein: activation confined to ectodomain cysteine-rich segments, absent from TM/cytosolic regions.

Summary: Residue-level detector for tryptophan (W) side chains, often firing on multiple W positions within a sequence and with a mild bias toward N‑terminal Ws; broadly applicable across taxa and protein classes, with frequent occurrences in short membrane/secreted proteins but also in diverse enzymes (e.g., ATP synthase ε, proteases) and mitochondrial proteins.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks centered on W; multiple independent peaks per protein; modest enrichment near N‑termini; occasional weak spillover to neighboring residues (C/E/Q/G/K/R) in W‑rich contexts.
Exemplars: - Viral small/accessory membrane proteins (e.g., viroporin-like): activation on Trp residues in short helices/interfacial segments.
- Bacteriocins and peptide toxins: activation on Trp-rich motifs that mediate membrane interaction/disruption.
- ATP synthase subunit ε (F1 epsilon): activation on conserved Trp residue(s) across bacteria/mitochondria.
- Proteases (serine, cysteine, metalloproteases): activation on Trp positions within the enzyme sequence.
- Secreted and transmembrane protein precursors: activation on interfacial/N‑terminal Trp residues around TM regions or signal-proximal segments.
- Mitochondrial proteins: activation on Trp residues, including in membrane-associated components.
- Eukaryotic micropeptides/antisense-encoded small proteins: activation on any Trp present, often near the N‑terminus due to short length.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low-complexity proline-rich tandem-repeat tracts (typically enriched in P/S/T and often Q/H) found predominantly in secreted/extracellular proteins and viral surface proteins; the feature marks conserved proline positions within repeat units that form mucin-like stalks, adhesin/cell-wall repeats, or Hyp/O-glycosylation scaffolds, and it also occurs in intracellular repeat-rich proteins such as nuclear regulators and cytoskeletal/testis-specific proteins.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long disordered repeat domains with sharp residue-level peaks mainly on prolines at fixed positions in each repeat unit (e.g., second P in PP; the P in DPxG, NANP/NVDP, or PAA-PEA motifs). Outside these tracts, activation is low, including in structured domains (signal peptides, transmembranes, enzyme cores, or GPI-anchor/propeptide segments); however, short P-rich low-complexity inserts/propeptides within secretory-pathway glycoproteins can also activate.
Exemplars:
- Fungal GPI-anchored adhesins/flocculins: strong activation on prolines within central Ser/Thr/Pro-rich tandem repeats that form the extracellular stalk.
- Plant arabinogalactan proteins/extensins: activation on PP motifs, biased to the second P that is hydroxylated to Hyp and O-glycosylated.
- Viral envelope proteins (e.g., herpesvirus gC; Plasmodium CSP): activation on prolines within repetitive, disordered external repeats (e.g., P-D-P-A-V-A-P, NANP/NVDP).
- Mucin-like secreted proteins: activation across disordered 10–15 aa repeat arrays (e.g., DPxG-containing repeats).
- Testis-specific/cytoskeletal repeat proteins (e.g., outer dense fiber proteins): activation on prolines anchoring short tandem repeats in disordered segments.
- Nuclear transcriptional regulators with Pro-rich low-complexity regions (e.g., REST): activation over Pro-rich tracts.
- Bacterial autotransporters/actin modulators (e.g., BimA): activation on surface-exposed Pro-rich repeats.
- Secretory/vacuolar glycoproteins with short low-complexity inserts: activation confined to Pro-rich inserts, not the folded enzyme core.

Summary: Tyrosine‑centered aromatic motifs in long, intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity repeat arrays—most often Y followed by Ser within Ser/Pro‑rich repeats—marking the aromatic “sticker”/crosslinking residues (with ancillary recognition of Phe/Trp and occasional His/Cys) that support adhesion, matrix assembly, or multivalent IDR interactions (e.g., CTD- and FG-type repeats).
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks that recur with the periodicity of tandem repeats, strongest on Tyr and also on other aromatics; frequent weak co‑activation on the residue immediately after Tyr (often Ser or His). Activation extends over long coil‑rich, low‑pLDDT repeat regions and is minimal in structured domains or signal peptides.
Exemplars: - Plant extensins/proline‑rich cell‑wall proteins: strong, periodic peaks on the Tyr that starts each Y–S–P/P‑rich repeat; occasional weaker signal on the following Ser/His.
- Vitelline membrane–like extracellular matrix proteins: peaks on the Tyr within each [PS][AS]YSA PA[AS] 8‑mer repeat across a disordered region.
- Fungal cell‑wall adhesins/flocculins (galactose‑binding agglutinins): one highly activated Tyr per repeat across long tandem arrays, with secondary peaks on F/H/W.
- RNA polymerase II C‑terminal domain: peaks on the Tyr in YSPTSPS heptad repeats, with modest co‑activation on adjacent Ser.
- Nuclear pore–associated disordered proteins: activation on cysteines within low‑confidence IDRs; in FG‑nucleoporins, on the Phe of FG repeats.
- Secreted peptide/toxin and fungal RiPP precursors: activation on aromatic‑rich core motifs embedded in disordered, low‑complexity segments.

Summary: Arginine-selective low-complexity/disordered segments—polybasic tracts and RG/RGG-type repeats—often occurring as long, repetitive stretches; includes the Arg residues embedded in repeated neuropeptide/prohormone units (e.g., RFamide-like repeats). The signal tracks local Arg identity/density with a strong preference for Arg over Lys and is largely independent of stable secondary/tertiary structure.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks on Arg that cluster over extended disordered, compositionally biased regions; broad regional activation in Arg-dense tails or repeats; minimal in well-structured domains and transmembrane helices; occasional co-activation of neighboring Gly (RG/RGG) and sometimes Trp within Arg-rich low-complexity segments; Lys generally weak.
Exemplars: - RFamide-family neuropeptide/prohormone precursors: strong peaks on the Arg within repeated peptide units (e.g., PRQFV-/XREFV-amide motifs) and nearby disordered basic-biased segments; little/no signal in the N-terminal signal peptide.
- Vacuolar zinc transporters (multi-pass membrane transporters): concentrated activation on cytosolic, disordered, Arg-rich C-terminal tails; silent across transmembrane helices and luminal loops.
- RNA-binding and chromatin-associated proteins: activation on RGG/RG boxes and poly-Arg low-complexity tracts that mediate nucleic-acid interactions/phase separation.
- Viral regulatory proteins: strong signal on Arg/Gly-rich low-complexity segments.
- Reproductive proteins (e.g., protamines, semenogelins) and long coiled-coil/golgin scaffolds, mucin-like glycoproteins, and disulfide-rich peptide toxins: activation on extended Arg-rich, repetitive low-complexity regions.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity tandem‑repeat regions across diverse taxa, with broad activation over polar/Pro/Ser/Thr/Gln/Lys/Tyr/His‑rich repeat tracts including mucin‑like, adhesive, and extensin‑like sequences. The feature fires in both secreted/extracellular precursors and intracellular disordered LCR proteins.
Activation pattern: Broad activation over long tandemly repetitive low‑complexity segments, with periodic residue‑level peaks tracking the repeat unit. Sharp peaks tend to fall on Gln, Lys, His, Arg, or Pro residues at conserved positions within the repeat, and activation spreads across surrounding Pro/Ser/Thr/Gln/Lys/Tyr‑rich tracts; periodic patterns appear when motifs are regularly spaced.
Exemplars: - Adhesive glycoproteins (e.g., mussel foot proteins): widespread activation over Tyr‑ and Lys‑rich low‑complexity decapeptide repeats, with peaks on conserved Lys residues.
- Plant Pro‑rich extensins: broad activation across Pro‑rich tandem repeats with peaks on His/Lys within the repeat unit.
- Fungal collagen‑like Gly‑Gln‑Xaa repeat proteins: periodic peaks on Gln within G‑Q‑I/R/S repeats.
- Trypanosome surface antigens with LTR tandem repeats: activation along disordered polar repeat regions with peaks on His.
- Polar/Q‑rich disordered repeat regions of intracellular proteins (e.g., dynein heavy chain LCR, spermatogenesis‑associated SPATA31H1 P‑S‑E‑R‑S‑H‑H‑S repeats, Filia, polyamine acetyltransferase disordered Q/S/P tracts): broad activation over disordered repeat tracts and basic/acidic clusters despite lacking secretion, reflecting the general LCR signature.

Summary: Residue-level detector for tryptophan (W) side chains, often firing on multiple W positions within a sequence and with a mild bias toward N‑terminal Ws; broadly applicable across taxa and protein classes, with frequent occurrences in short membrane/secreted proteins but also in diverse enzymes (e.g., ATP synthase ε, proteases) and mitochondrial proteins.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks centered on W; multiple independent peaks per protein; modest enrichment near N‑termini; occasional weak spillover to neighboring residues (C/E/Q/G/K/R) in W‑rich contexts.
Exemplars: - Viral small/accessory membrane proteins (e.g., viroporin-like): activation on Trp residues in short helices/interfacial segments.
- Bacteriocins and peptide toxins: activation on Trp-rich motifs that mediate membrane interaction/disruption.
- ATP synthase subunit ε (F1 epsilon): activation on conserved Trp residue(s) across bacteria/mitochondria.
- Proteases (serine, cysteine, metalloproteases): activation on Trp positions within the enzyme sequence.
- Secreted and transmembrane protein precursors: activation on interfacial/N‑terminal Trp residues around TM regions or signal-proximal segments.
- Mitochondrial proteins: activation on Trp residues, including in membrane-associated components.
- Eukaryotic micropeptides/antisense-encoded small proteins: activation on any Trp present, often near the N‑terminus due to short length.

Outside these tracts, activation is low, including in structured domains (signal peptides, transmembranes, enzyme cores, or GPI-anchor/propeptide segments); however, short P-rich low-complexity inserts/propeptides within secretory-pathway glycoproteins can also activate.

- Mucin-like secreted proteins: activation across disordered 10–15 aa repeat arrays (e.g., DPxG-containing repeats).
- Testis-specific/cytoskeletal repeat proteins (e.g., outer dense fiber proteins): activation on prolines anchoring short tandem repeats in disordered segments.
- Nuclear transcriptional regulators with Pro-rich low-complexity regions (e.g., REST): activation over Pro-rich tracts.
- Bacterial autotransporters/actin modulators (e.g., BimA): activation on surface-exposed Pro-rich repeats.

Activation extends over long coil‑rich, low‑pLDDT repeat regions and is minimal in structured domains or signal peptides.
Exemplars: - Plant extensins/proline‑rich cell‑wall proteins: strong, periodic peaks on the Tyr that starts each Y–S–P/P‑rich repeat; occasional weaker signal on the following Ser/His.

- Fungal cell‑wall adhesins/flocculins (galactose‑binding agglutinins): one highly activated Tyr per repeat across long tandem arrays, with secondary peaks on F/H/W.
- RNA polymerase II C‑terminal domain: peaks on the Tyr in YSPTSPS heptad repeats, with modest co‑activation on adjacent Ser.
- Nuclear pore–associated disordered proteins: activation on cysteines within low‑confidence IDRs; in FG‑nucleoporins, on the Phe of FG repeats.
- Secreted peptide/toxin and fungal RiPP precursors: activation on aromatic‑rich core motifs embedded in disordered, low‑complexity segments.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity tandem‑repeat regions across diverse taxa, with broad activation over polar/Pro/Ser/Thr/Gln/Lys/Tyr/His‑rich repeat tracts including mucin‑like, adhesive, and extensin‑like sequences. The feature fires in both secreted/extracellular precursors and intracellular disordered LCR proteins.
Activation pattern: Broad activation over long tandemly repetitive low‑complexity segments, with periodic residue‑level peaks tracking the repeat unit. Sharp peaks tend to fall on Gln, Lys, His, Arg, or Pro residues at conserved positions within the repeat, and activation spreads across surrounding Pro/Ser/Thr/Gln/Lys/Tyr‑rich tracts; periodic patterns appear when motifs are regularly spaced.
Exemplars: - Adhesive glycoproteins (e.g., mussel foot proteins): widespread activation over Tyr‑ and Lys‑rich low‑complexity decapeptide repeats, with peaks on conserved Lys residues.
- Plant Pro‑rich extensins: broad activation across Pro‑rich tandem repeats with peaks on His/Lys within the repeat unit.
- Fungal collagen‑like Gly‑Gln‑Xaa repeat proteins: periodic peaks on Gln within G‑Q‑I/R/S repeats.
- Trypanosome surface antigens with LTR tandem repeats: activation along disordered polar repeat regions with peaks on His.
- Polar/Q‑rich disordered repeat regions of intracellular proteins (e.g., dynein heavy chain LCR, spermatogenesis‑associated SPATA31H1 P‑S‑E‑R‑S‑H‑H‑S repeats, Filia, polyamine acetyltransferase disordered Q/S/P tracts): broad activation over disordered repeat tracts and basic/acidic clusters despite lacking secretion, reflecting the general LCR signature.

Summary: Arginine-selective low-complexity/disordered segments—polybasic tracts and RG/RGG-type repeats—often occurring as long, repetitive stretches; includes the Arg residues embedded in repeated neuropeptide/prohormone units (e.g., RFamide-like repeats). The signal tracks local Arg identity/density with a strong preference for Arg over Lys and is largely independent of stable secondary/tertiary structure.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks on Arg that cluster over extended disordered, compositionally biased regions; broad regional activation in Arg-dense tails or repeats; minimal in well-structured domains and transmembrane helices; occasional co-activation of neighboring Gly (RG/RGG) and sometimes Trp within Arg-rich low-complexity segments; Lys generally weak.
Exemplars: - RFamide-family neuropeptide/prohormone precursors: strong peaks on the Arg within repeated peptide units (e.g., PRQFV-/XREFV-amide motifs) and nearby disordered basic-biased segments; little/no signal in the N-terminal signal peptide.
- Vacuolar zinc transporters (multi-pass membrane transporters): concentrated activation on cytosolic, disordered, Arg-rich C-terminal tails; silent across transmembrane helices and luminal loops.
- RNA-binding and chromatin-associated proteins: activation on RGG/RG boxes and poly-Arg low-complexity tracts that mediate nucleic-acid interactions/phase separation.
- Viral regulatory proteins: strong signal on Arg/Gly-rich low-complexity segments.
- Reproductive proteins (e.g., protamines, semenogelins) and long coiled-coil/golgin scaffolds, mucin-like glycoproteins, and disulfide-rich peptide toxins: activation on extended Arg-rich, repetitive low-complexity regions.

Summary: Residue-level detector for tryptophan (W) side chains, often firing on multiple W positions within a sequence and with a mild bias toward N‑terminal Ws; broadly applicable across taxa and protein classes, with frequent occurrences in short membrane/secreted proteins but also in diverse enzymes (e.g., ATP synthase ε, proteases) and mitochondrial proteins.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks centered on W; multiple independent peaks per protein; modest enrichment near N‑termini; occasional weak spillover to neighboring residues (C/E/Q/G/K/R) in W‑rich contexts.
Exemplars: - Viral small/accessory membrane proteins (e.g., viroporin-like): activation on Trp residues in short helices/interfacial segments.
- Bacteriocins and peptide toxins: activation on Trp-rich motifs that mediate membrane interaction/disruption.
- ATP synthase subunit ε (F1 epsilon): activation on conserved Trp residue(s) across bacteria/mitochondria.
- Proteases (serine, cysteine, metalloproteases): activation on Trp positions within the enzyme sequence.
- Secreted and transmembrane protein precursors: activation on interfacial/N‑terminal Trp residues around TM regions or signal-proximal segments.
- Mitochondrial proteins: activation on Trp residues, including in membrane-associated components.
- Eukaryotic micropeptides/antisense-encoded small proteins: activation on any Trp present, often near the N‑terminus due to short length.

Summary: Low-complexity, disorder-associated segments enriched in Asp/Asn/His/Tyr and depleted of Lys/Arg—frequently N- or C-terminal propeptides and regulatory tails, and occasionally short polar/acidic stretches within other contexts including amphipathic helices in small viral proteins.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks on D/H/N/Y within low-pLDDT regions that often coalesce into contiguous activation across long terminal IDRs; activation can also appear in shorter polar/acidic loops embedded in folded chains, and within an N-terminal helix when the helix presents an acidic/polar face.
Exemplars: - Fibroblast growth factor propeptides: selective peaks in the disordered N-terminal propeptide (e.g., H/N/D) with no activation in the mature growth factor domain.
- Small viral regulatory proteins (e.g., polyomavirus Agnoprotein, HIV Tat/Vif): peaks on D/N/H/Y in disordered tails and within amphipathic helical segments.
- Uncharacterized eukaryotic microproteins/regulatory peptides: scattered D/H/Y peaks across very low-confidence, disordered regions, often strongest near termini.
- Short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase family enzymes: activation confined to a disordered, acidic/polar C-terminal extension, absent from the structured NAD(P)-binding/catalytic domain.
- DNA-binding apoptosis regulators (Killin-like): largely disordered proteins with highest peaks on D/N and additional H/Y, mostly outside the annotated DNA-binding segment.

Summary: Compositionally biased low-complexity segments, especially N-terminal hydrophobic helices that form the hydrophobic core of signal peptides or membrane-anchoring amphipathic helices, and serine/threonine-rich intrinsically disordered tracts; the feature reflects sequence-composition bias rather than a specific fold or function and commonly occurs at protein termini across taxa
Activation pattern: Regional activation over extended contiguous blocks (typically 8–20 residues), frequently at the N-terminus; strong peaks within hydrophobic cores of signal peptide–like helices or within S/T-rich low-complexity patches; minimal activation in structured catalytic/core domains
Exemplars: - Viral nonstructural/accessory proteins: activation on a short, flexible N-terminal hydrophobic helix (amphipathic/membrane-anchoring segment).
- Plant secreted signaling peptides (SCOOP family): activation on the N-terminal signal peptide hydrophobic core, not on the C-terminal functional motif.
- Eukaryotic transcriptional coactivator scaffolds (Mediator subunit 24): activation on multiple S/T- and Q-rich intrinsically disordered, low-complexity regions.

Summary: Low‑complexity, simple‑sequence tandem‑repeat tracts enriched in small residues (especially A/T/S/P/G; e.g., AAT and TP/PT motifs), characteristic of mucin‑like PTS regions and antifreeze repeats, and more broadly of simple repeat LCRs across diverse proteins (including viral and reproductive proteins; occasionally extending to basic Arg‑rich LCRs such as protamines). These can be disordered tracts or simple alanine‑rich helices (e.g., type I antifreeze proteins).
Activation pattern: Predominantly regional/domain‑level activation across low‑complexity repeat segments, often with periodic residue‑level peaks aligned to specific positions within the repeat (e.g., the first Ala in AAT). Reduced in globular catalytic/zinc‑finger domains and transmembranes, but activation can occur in simple structured repeats (alanine‑rich helices) and appears as scattered peaks in basic Arg/Cys‑rich LCRs.
Exemplars: - Antifreeze/ice‑structuring proteins: strong periodic activation on AAT repeat tracts and on alanine‑rich type I AFP helices, with lower signal in nonrepetitive linkers.
- Mucin family extracellular glycoproteins: broad activation across disordered PTS‑rich tandem repeats with peaks on Ala/Ser/Thr; typically absent from transmembrane helix and cytosolic tail.
- Viral regulatory proteins (e.g., herpesvirus ICP0‑like RING E3s): activation confined to low‑complexity Pro/Ala- and Gly‑rich segments; reduced in the folded RING domain.
- Testis/sperm‑associated low‑complexity proteins (e.g., testis‑specific repeat proteins): continuous activation over annotated tandem‑repeat, low‑complexity regions.
- Protamines and cysteine‑rich basic sperm proteins: context‑dependent peaks on Arg (and some Cys/Lys/Pro) within Arg‑rich low‑complexity tracts.

Summary: Residue-identity detector for glycine (G), largely context-agnostic but with a tendency to fire on glycines in flexible/disordered, often N-terminal or membrane-proximal regions; also active on glycines within transmembrane helices; broadly taxon- and function-independent.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks confined to individual glycine positions; peaks may appear singly (e.g., an N-terminal G) or as clusters in G-rich stretches; little to no activation on other residues; occurs in coils, helices, and beta strands, frequently in low-confidence/disordered segments and sometimes within or adjacent to transmembrane helices.
Exemplars: - Viral K7-like membrane proteins: multiple glycines highlighted in disordered regions and just after/within a transmembrane helix.
- Antimicrobial bacteriocins (enterocin peptides): every glycine across the peptide, independent of local secondary structure.
- Peroxisomal biogenesis factor PEX9 (peroxisomal membrane protein): glycines throughout, including inside predicted transmembrane segments and a disordered C-terminus.
- Octanoyltransferase/lipoyltransferase (LipB-like) enzymes: a single N-terminal glycine in a coil region.
- Tumor suppressor ARF (CDKN2A/p14ARF): glycines within an intrinsically disordered N-terminal interaction region and the disordered C-terminus.

Summary: Compositionally biased, low-complexity flexible segments (often terminal or in loops/propeptides), frequently enriched in Pro/Gly with a common—but not required—positive bias (Arg/Lys), and carrying simple repeats (e.g., RG/RGG, PG/GPG, PxxP or neutral/polar repeats); used for nucleic-acid contacts, SH3-mediated interactions, targeting peptides, or flexible linkers/tails.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long low-complexity tracts or shorter flexible loops/propeptides (avoiding structured catalytic or transmembrane cores), including mitochondrial transit peptides and serpin reactive center loops.
Exemplars: • Viral regulatory/tegument proteins: activation on basic low-complexity arms
• RNA-binding proteins (including bacterial RNase P protein): activation on short basic patches or disordered termini
• Proline-rich adaptor/scaffold regions: activation on PxxP/PG-rich segments
• Enzymes and transporters: activation on compositionally biased linkers, cytosolic/luminal loops, or targeting peptides, not on conserved cores
• Secreted proteases/serpins: activation on flexible propeptides or reactive center loops (not necessarily polybasic)

Summary: Short hydrophobic targeting helices and cationic amphipathic motifs that mediate membrane/organellar targeting or unconventional secretion—encompassing classical N‑terminal signal peptides, internal signal‑anchor helices, C‑terminal tail‑anchors, mitochondrial targeting helices, and CPP‑like basic/aromatic motifs. Enriched for Leu/Phe with Tyr/Trp at helix boundaries; Arg/His frequent; acidic residues (D/E) scarce. In very small secreted/toxin-like proteins, activation can extend into cysteine/proline‑rich mature regions; in soluble enzymes/regulators it may mark short amphipathic or hydrophobic helices.

Activation pattern: Predominantly regional activation over 15–30 aa hydrophobic segments (whether N‑terminal signal peptides/signal anchors or C‑terminal tail‑anchors); in microproteins, activation can span most of the sequence; in large soluble proteins, limited residue‑level peaks over short amphipathic/basic or hydrophobic helices (e.g., DNA/RNA‑binding or coiled‑coil segments).

Exemplars:
- Viral envelope/accessory and regulatory proteins — activation on N‑terminal signal/signal‑anchor helices or on CPP‑like Arg/Trp‑enriched motifs (e.g., Tat‑like proteins) enabling leaderless export/cellular entry.
- Secreted peptide precursors (hormones, antimicrobial peptides, venom toxins, immune effectors) — activation on the signal peptide; in very short precursors, also across the cysteine/proline‑rich mature region.
- Oomycete RxLR effectors — activation on the N‑terminal signal peptide immediately upstream of the RxLR motif.
- Human microproteins/lncRNA‑derived peptides — activation across a single hydrophobic TM helix acting as a signal anchor or tail‑anchor, or short amphipathic targeting motifs.
- Mitochondrial nucleus‑encoded proteins (e.g., mitochondrial ribosomal proteins; ATP synthase-associated subunits) — activation on N‑terminal mitochondrial targeting helices or short hydrophobic segments.
- Bacterial/archaeal enzymes and phage integrases — isolated peaks over internal hydrophobic or amphipathic helices (e.g., helix‑turn‑helix/coiled‑coil regions) without spanning whole domains.
- Tail‑anchored SNAREs and other vesicle proteins — activation on the C‑terminal transmembrane tail‑anchor.

Summary: Short, low‑complexity, charge‑dense intrinsically disordered segments (mixed K/R and E/D with S/T/Q/N/G/P, including polybasic clusters and acidic E/D repeats) that serve as generic electrostatic interaction/targeting motifs—e.g., RNA/DNA‑binding arginine‑rich patches, PIP2/membrane‑binding basic patches, acidic C‑terminal tails, and proprotein convertase (furin‑like) polybasic processing sites—found across cytosolic, membrane, secreted, and viral proteins
Activation pattern: Regional activation on short contiguous windows (≈5–15 residues) enriched for charged/polar residues; occurs at varied positions without strong N/C‑terminal bias
Exemplars: - Voltage‑gated and inward‑rectifier ion channels: activation on cytosolic polybasic clusters that bind PIP2 or modulate gating/trafficking.
- Microtubule α/β‑tubulins and other acidic-tail cytoskeletal proteins: activation on poly‑E/D C‑terminal tails that recruit MAPs and ions.
- Viral nucleocapsid/core/regulatory proteins (e.g., ARM/NLS‑like segments): activation on arginine‑rich RNA‑binding patches and polybasic sites; also on polybasic furin‑cleavage motifs in viral glycoprotein precursors.
- tRNA/rRNA modification and processing enzymes (methyltransferases, pseudouridine synthases, nucleases): activation on flexible Lys/Arg + Asp/Glu loops that contact the nucleic‑acid backbone.
- Secreted precursors and propeptides: activation on convertase recognition motifs (R‑X‑[RK]‑R) and Ser/acidic low‑complexity stretches in pro/secretion regions.
- Membrane transporters/channels more broadly: activation on short charged/polar low‑complexity loops (peri‑/cytosolic) used for regulatory or interaction interfaces.
- Intrinsically disordered low‑complexity tracts across bacterial/eukaryotic/archaeal proteins (including Rickettsia effectors): activation on C‑terminal acidic “E‑blocks” or basic patches implicated in secretion/targeting.

Summary: Ala/Val/Gly–enriched low‑complexity segments, often within intrinsically disordered or low‑confidence regions of small/unstructured proteins (signal peptides, pro‑peptide extensions, regulatory tails, microproteins), characterized by small aliphatic residues interspersed with sparse acidic residues; composition- rather than function-specific.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks land predominantly on V (and A/D/E) residues within low-complexity or disordered tracts; multiple peaks can be distributed across a stretch (regional LCR activation), with reduced signal in well-folded globular domains.
Exemplars: - Oomycete RxLR effectors: activation on alanines/valines and acidic residues flanking the RxLR motif and within adjacent disordered N‑terminal regions (including non-helical segments of annotated signal/TM zones).

- Mammalian unstructured microproteins (e.g., testis-specific proteins) and ST20-like regulators: sparse peaks on V/A residues distributed throughout globally disordered sequences.
- Small viral accessory proteins (e.g., agnoprotein, PB1‑F2): scattered V/D/E peaks across short, largely disordered chains.

Summary: Basic polycationic patches enriched in arginine (often with lysine) within low-complexity/disordered regions, frequently N-terminal. These include classical monopartite NLSs, nucleic acid–binding basic tails, signal peptide n-regions and cytosolic juxtamembrane segments (positive-inside rule), and basic clusters in secreted precursors; typically depleted of acidic residues.
Activation pattern: Regional activation with strong residue-level peaks across contiguous basic runs; N-terminal bias; minimal Asp/Glu, Arg>Lys preference; predominantly in low-pLDDT segments and outside/adjacent to transmembranes on the cytosolic side; observed across viruses, bacteria, plants, and humans.
Exemplars:
- Viral regulators and capsid/accessory proteins: arginine-rich NLSs and nucleic acid–binding basic tails.
- Human regulators (e.g., ARF/Killin): arginine-rich disordered N-termini for targeting/interactions.
- Secreted zymogens and peptides (e.g., trypsinogen/PROPEPs): basic n-regions/dibasic clusters in pre/pro-sequences.
- Membrane proteins (transporters, respiratory chain subunits like ND2, ECF S-components): cytosolic basic patches consistent with the positive-inside rule.

Summary: Low-complexity, intrinsically disordered segments—often at protein N-termini—such as mucin-like/propeptide regions or flexible linkers adjacent to signal/transit peptides, common in small secreted or membrane-associated proteins and also as disordered extensions in diverse enzymes (broad taxonomic coverage, including viral, bacterial, and eukaryotic proteins).
Activation pattern: Regional activation over short to moderate stretches, frequently in disordered or polar/low-complexity segments; in longer proteins, multiple low-complexity patches can activate; in micropeptides, activation can span much of the sequence. Residue-level peaks can fall on Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly within polar-residue stretches but also on basic or hydrophobic residues within the same disordered context.
Exemplars:

Summary: Activation on disordered, low-complexity, and repetitive segments of secreted/extracellular and small regulatory proteins, including collagen-like triple-helix repeats, short flexible peptides, and disordered N-terminal/internal regions.

Exemplars:
- Fibrillar collagens and collagen-like proteins: broad, distributed activation across Gly-X-Y triple-helix repeats and flanking low-complexity regions

- Viral accessory/regulatory proteins: activation on disordered regions, frequently toward the N-terminus

Summary: Short linear motifs centered on serine/threonine within intrinsically disordered regions that correspond to eukaryotic Ser/Thr phosphorylation sites (often SP/TP or basic R/K-flanked motifs), used for regulatory control across diverse proteins including viral proteins
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks on single S/T or 1–3 aa motifs, punctate and distributed across proteins; strongly enriched in low-pLDDT coils and low-complexity segments; depleted in folded domains and transmembrane helices; occasional peaks at edges of low-confidence helices; context frequently includes nearby proline and/or basic residues
Exemplars: - PH plus RapGAP scaffold proteins: activation on S/T residues in disordered linkers; minimal signal in folded PH and GAP domains
- Chromatin regulator Spt21: multiple peaks in disordered C-terminal regions; includes a known phosphoserine site
- TORC1 subunit Tco89: peaks at/near an annotated phosphothreonine and other disordered segments
- Large transmembrane receptor with long cytosolic tail (stum): activation confined to disordered cytosolic regions; none in transmembrane helices
- Developmental cytoskeletal regulator (bottleneck): clusters on S/T within low-complexity, basic-enriched disordered C-terminus
- Small GTPase regulators (e.g., RhoGAPs, RasGEFs, ARF GEFs) and protein kinases: signal found in regulatory low-complexity regions and termini rather than catalytic cores, consistent with phosphorylation-prone SLiMs

Summary: Short linear segments in intrinsically disordered or otherwise low-structure-confidence regions, often at N-termini and within signal peptides/propeptides of secreted and regulatory proteins (including viral accessory proteins and small ORF microproteins), enriched in small/basic residues (G, P, S, A, R; often with Cys), rather than in well-folded catalytic cores.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks scattered across IDRs and low-confidence coils/short helices; frequently clustered near the N-terminus, in signal peptides, propeptides, and disordered tails; little to no activation in well-structured domains; occasional activation in low-confidence transmembrane/signal-anchor helices.
Exemplars: - Viral accessory protein (HIV-1 Vif): peaks throughout low-pLDDT coils, especially the disordered N-terminal region.

- Secreted serine carboxypeptidase: activation confined to disordered C-terminal tail, annotated disordered segment, the signal peptide, and a low-confidence C-terminal transmembrane helix; absent from the structured catalytic domain.
- Disordered human tumor-suppressor–associated protein (ST20): scattered peaks within predicted helices in a globally disordered chain, including the N-terminus.

Summary: Short hydrophobic targeting helices and cationic amphipathic motifs that mediate membrane/organellar targeting or unconventional secretion—encompassing classical N‑terminal signal peptides, internal signal‑anchor helices, C‑terminal tail‑anchors, mitochondrial targeting helices, and CPP‑like basic/aromatic motifs. Enriched for Leu/Phe with Tyr/Trp at helix boundaries; Arg/His frequent; acidic residues (D/E) scarce. In very small secreted/toxin-like proteins, activation can extend into cysteine/proline‑rich mature regions; in soluble enzymes/regulators it may mark short amphipathic or hydrophobic helices.

Activation pattern: Predominantly regional activation over 15–30 aa hydrophobic segments (whether N‑terminal signal peptides/signal anchors or C‑terminal tail‑anchors); in microproteins, activation can span most of the sequence; in large soluble proteins, limited residue‑level peaks over short amphipathic/basic or hydrophobic helices (e.g., DNA/RNA‑binding or coiled‑coil segments).

Exemplars:
- Viral envelope/accessory and regulatory proteins — activation on N‑terminal signal/signal‑anchor helices or on CPP‑like Arg/Trp‑enriched motifs (e.g., Tat‑like proteins) enabling leaderless export/cellular entry.
- Secreted peptide precursors (hormones, antimicrobial peptides, venom toxins, immune effectors) — activation on the signal peptide; in very short precursors, also across the cysteine/proline‑rich mature region.
- Oomycete RxLR effectors — activation on the N‑terminal signal peptide immediately upstream of the RxLR motif.
- Human microproteins/lncRNA‑derived peptides — activation across a single hydrophobic TM helix acting as a signal anchor or tail‑anchor, or short amphipathic targeting motifs.
- Mitochondrial nucleus‑encoded proteins (e.g., mitochondrial ribosomal proteins; ATP synthase-associated subunits) — activation on N‑terminal mitochondrial targeting helices or short hydrophobic segments.
- Bacterial/archaeal enzymes and phage integrases — isolated peaks over internal hydrophobic or amphipathic helices (e.g., helix‑turn‑helix/coiled‑coil regions) without spanning whole domains.
- Tail‑anchored SNAREs and other vesicle proteins — activation on the C‑terminal transmembrane tail‑anchor.

Summary: Residue-level detector for acidic/polar hotspots within intrinsically disordered regions (often N‑terminal), with a strong preference for Asp, Asn, His, and Tyr; highlights acidic low‑complexity stretches and flexible loops rather than structured domains
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks scattered in IDRs (low pLDDT/low-confidence helices or coils), sometimes forming small clusters within acidic compositional-bias segments; minimal activation inside well-structured domains (e.g., zinc fingers, catalytic cores)
Exemplars: - Adenovirus E4-ORF4 regulatory protein: peaks on Tyr/His (and some Asp/Asn) in highly disordered loops outside annotated motifs
- Viral RNA-silencing suppressor with a C4-type zinc-finger: peaks on Asp and Tyr in low-confidence helical regions adjacent to, but not within, the zinc-finger
- Small viral accessory protein (RDUR-like): sparse peaks on Asn/Asp/His/Tyr across predicted disordered segments with no mapped functional sites
- Neuronal EF-hand Ca2+-binding regulator (calsenilin/DREAM/KChIP3): strong peaks on N-terminal Asp residues within an annotated disordered region
- Retrotransposon polyprotein: scattered peaks on Asp/Asn in long, acidic low-complexity, disordered regions

Summary: Residue-level detector for tryptophan (W) side chains, often firing on multiple W positions within a sequence and with a mild bias toward N‑terminal Ws; broadly applicable across taxa and protein classes, with frequent occurrences in short membrane/secreted proteins but also in diverse enzymes (e.g., ATP synthase ε, proteases) and mitochondrial proteins.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks centered on W; multiple independent peaks per protein; modest enrichment near N‑termini; occasional weak spillover to neighboring residues (C/E/Q/G/K/R) in W‑rich contexts.
Exemplars: - Viral small/accessory membrane proteins (e.g., viroporin-like): activation on Trp residues in short helices/interfacial segments.
- Bacteriocins and peptide toxins: activation on Trp-rich motifs that mediate membrane interaction/disruption.
- ATP synthase subunit ε (F1 epsilon): activation on conserved Trp residue(s) across bacteria/mitochondria.
- Proteases (serine, cysteine, metalloproteases): activation on Trp positions within the enzyme sequence.
- Secreted and transmembrane protein precursors: activation on interfacial/N‑terminal Trp residues around TM regions or signal-proximal segments.
- Mitochondrial proteins: activation on Trp residues, including in membrane-associated components.
- Eukaryotic micropeptides/antisense-encoded small proteins: activation on any Trp present, often near the N‑terminus due to short length.

Summary: Asparagine-rich low-complexity intrinsically disordered tracts, often long, occurring at N-termini or internally (including organelle transit peptides in protists), enriched in polar/charged residues (N with Q/K/S/T/D/E); activation is composition-driven and tracks the disordered low-complexity segments rather than folded cores.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over extended low-complexity segments (sometimes multiple per protein), with residue-level peaks on N runs/repeats and sharp drop at the onset of well-structured domains; activation is strongest within disordered/compositionally biased regions and weak or absent in most globular catalytic folds.
Exemplars: - ZDHHC-type palmitoyltransferase: activation on the disordered, low-complexity N-terminal cytosolic tail and additional unstructured low-complexity patches; absent from transmembrane helices and the DHHC catalytic core.
- Serine/threonine protein kinase: activation on N-terminal/internal asparagine-rich disordered inserts, with the structured kinase core largely unmarked.
- Ribonuclease H–like enzyme: activation confined to the N-terminal low-complexity, low-confidence region (often helical propensity but disordered); absent from the C-terminal RNase H–like catalytic domain.
- Apicoplast 2Fe-2S ferredoxin: activation across the apicoplast transit peptide and adjacent disordered N-terminal stretch; terminates at the boundary of the structured ferredoxin domain.

Summary: Low-complexity, disorder-associated segments enriched in Asp/Asn/His/Tyr and depleted of Lys/Arg—frequently N- or C-terminal propeptides and regulatory tails, and occasionally short polar/acidic stretches within other contexts including amphipathic helices in small viral proteins.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks on D/H/N/Y within low-pLDDT regions that often coalesce into contiguous activation across long terminal IDRs; activation can also appear in shorter polar/acidic loops embedded in folded chains, and within an N-terminal helix when the helix presents an acidic/polar face.
Exemplars: - Fibroblast growth factor propeptides: selective peaks in the disordered N-terminal propeptide (e.g., H/N/D) with no activation in the mature growth factor domain.
- Small viral regulatory proteins (e.g., polyomavirus Agnoprotein, HIV Tat/Vif): peaks on D/N/H/Y in disordered tails and within amphipathic helical segments.
- Uncharacterized eukaryotic microproteins/regulatory peptides: scattered D/H/Y peaks across very low-confidence, disordered regions, often strongest near termini.
- Short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase family enzymes: activation confined to a disordered, acidic/polar C-terminal extension, absent from the structured NAD(P)-binding/catalytic domain.
- DNA-binding apoptosis regulators (Killin-like): largely disordered proteins with highest peaks on D/N and additional H/Y, mostly outside the annotated DNA-binding segment.

Summary: Small, often poorly characterized or compositionally biased proteins, including viral accessory proteins, cancer/testis and germline-associated proteins, antisense-ORF microproteins, and short secreted/surface peptides; activation is broadly distributed across the polypeptide rather than focused on a single structured domain
Activation pattern: Regional/distributed activation spread across much of the protein with sparse residue-level peaks; often includes early N-terminal residues and disordered segments; variable coverage from short patches to most of the protein
Exemplars:
- Viral non-structural/accessory proteins: activation distributed through the protein, including basic/Arg-rich motifs such as nuclear localization signals.
- Cancer/testis antigens and germline-associated proteins: activation on long disordered low-complexity regions, often at N-termini.
- Small uncharacterized microproteins/antisense ORFs: activation spanning most of the polypeptide.
- Short secreted peptides and toxin precursors: activation across both signal/propeptide and mature regions.
- Compact cytosolic proteins with disordered N- or C-terminal extensions: activation enriched on the disordered tails.

Summary: Amphipathic, hydrophobic secondary‑structure cores in small proteins—especially alpha‑helical segments and the juxtamembrane/N‑terminal half of signal‑anchor transmembrane helices with a positive‑inside (Lys/Arg) bias; in soluble proteins, the analogous β‑α/helix bundle core often at oligomerization interfaces—while avoiding disordered tails and catalytic/loop regions
Activation pattern: Regional activation over long, contiguous, high‑confidence secondary‑structure elements (helices and β‑α segments); strongest in ordered cores, weak/absent in disordered termini and peripheral loops; in bitopic membrane proteins, peaks at the cytosolic amphipathic helix and the N‑proximal half of the TM helix (positive‑inside), tapering toward the extracytosolic half
Exemplars: - Sec translocon subunit E (bitopic membrane protein): activation on the pre‑TM cytosolic amphipathic helix and the N‑terminal half of the TM helix, consistent with the positive‑inside rule; low on the periplasmic side.
- CRISPR Cas2 endoribonucleases: activation across the central β strands and adjoining α‑helix that form the homodimer core; catalytic Asp and flexible termini are not emphasized.
- Exodeoxyribonuclease VII small subunit: strong signal on the central ordered helix bundle, with little/no activation on disordered N/C‑terminal regions.
- ATP synthase and respiratory chain small membrane subunits: enrichment on N‑terminal amphipathic/juxtamembrane helices and the entry half of signal‑anchor TM segments.
- Small ribosomal proteins and other RNA/protein‑binding regulators: activation on amphipathic helical cores that present Lys/Arg‑rich faces, rather than on flexible/basic tails.
- Archaeal gas vesicle structural proteins: signal on extended hydrophobic/amphipathic helices forming the shell scaffold.
