Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low-complexity segments enriched in serine/threonine/proline/glycine and often basic (lysine/arginine), typically found in flexible N- or C-terminal tails and loops; highlights IDRs that may harbor short linear motifs (e.g., basic NLS patches) rather than structured domain cores.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long disordered stretches with additional sparse residue-level peaks in low-confidence loops; often N-terminal-biased in short/viral proteins; rarely within well-folded cores.
Exemplars: Retroviral accessory proteins (e.g., HTLV-1 p30): activation on central and C-terminal IDRs including a basic nuclear localization signal; p53-regulated apoptosis-inducing microprotein: widespread activation across a globally disordered protein; Bacterial DNA ligase: scattered activation in an annotated disordered linker and flexible loops within the ligase domain; Uncharacterized human microprotein: multiple peaks throughout a low-pLDDT, disordered sequence irrespective of predicted secondary structure.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low-complexity segments enriched in serine/threonine/proline/glycine and often basic (lysine/arginine), typically found in flexible N- or C-terminal tails and loops; highlights IDRs that may harbor short linear motifs (e.g., basic NLS patches) rather than structured domain cores.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long disordered stretches with additional sparse residue-level peaks in low-confidence loops; often N-terminal-biased in short/viral proteins; rarely within well-folded cores.
Exemplars: Retroviral accessory proteins (e.g., HTLV-1 p30): activation on central and C-terminal IDRs including a basic nuclear localization signal; p53-regulated apoptosis-inducing microprotein: widespread activation across a globally disordered protein; Bacterial DNA ligase: scattered activation in an annotated disordered linker and flexible loops within the ligase domain; Uncharacterized human microprotein: multiple peaks throughout a low-pLDDT, disordered sequence irrespective of predicted secondary structure.

Summary: Short linear segments in intrinsically disordered or otherwise low-structure-confidence regions, often at N-termini and within signal peptides/propeptides of secreted and regulatory proteins (including viral accessory proteins and small ORF microproteins), enriched in small/basic residues (G, P, S, A, R; often with Cys), rather than in well-folded catalytic cores.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks scattered across IDRs and low-confidence coils/short helices; frequently clustered near the N-terminus, in signal peptides, propeptides, and disordered tails; little to no activation in well-structured domains; occasional activation in low-confidence transmembrane/signal-anchor helices.
Exemplars: - Viral accessory protein (HIV-1 Vif): peaks throughout low-pLDDT coils, especially the disordered N-terminal region.
- Neuropeptide precursor (Drosophila Amnesiac): activation in the N-terminal signal peptide and multiple mature peptide segments with very low pLDDT.
- Secreted serine carboxypeptidase: activation confined to disordered C-terminal tail, annotated disordered segment, the signal peptide, and a low-confidence C-terminal transmembrane helix; absent from the structured catalytic domain.
- Disordered human tumor-suppressor–associated protein (ST20): scattered peaks within predicted helices in a globally disordered chain, including the N-terminus.
- lncRNA/sORF-derived microprotein (IGF2 antisense protein): multiple peaks across annotated disordered regions rich in Arg/Pro/Gly.

Summary: Short linear motifs centered on serine/threonine within intrinsically disordered regions that correspond to eukaryotic Ser/Thr phosphorylation sites (often SP/TP or basic R/K-flanked motifs), used for regulatory control across diverse proteins including viral proteins
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks on single S/T or 1–3 aa motifs, punctate and distributed across proteins; strongly enriched in low-pLDDT coils and low-complexity segments; depleted in folded domains and transmembrane helices; occasional peaks at edges of low-confidence helices; context frequently includes nearby proline and/or basic residues
Exemplars: - PH plus RapGAP scaffold proteins: activation on S/T residues in disordered linkers; minimal signal in folded PH and GAP domains
- Chromatin regulator Spt21: multiple peaks in disordered C-terminal regions; includes a known phosphoserine site
- TORC1 subunit Tco89: peaks at/near an annotated phosphothreonine and other disordered segments
- Large transmembrane receptor with long cytosolic tail (stum): activation confined to disordered cytosolic regions; none in transmembrane helices
- Developmental cytoskeletal regulator (bottleneck): clusters on S/T within low-complexity, basic-enriched disordered C-terminus
- Small GTPase regulators (e.g., RhoGAPs, RasGEFs, ARF GEFs) and protein kinases: signal found in regulatory low-complexity regions and termini rather than catalytic cores, consistent with phosphorylation-prone SLiMs

Summary: Short, composition-biased linear "edge" segments at structural boundaries—especially C-terminal tails and juxta-membrane helix ends/hinges—often enriched in Pro and/or charge clusters; the same signal extends to long proline-rich repeats (e.g., collagen PPII/triple-helix regions) and short cationic/acidic motifs common in secreted and membrane proteins across taxa.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level hotspots in short spans (≈3–10 aa) at protein edges and within disordered, charge/polar-biased segments: extreme C termini, helix caps/breaks, and immediately cytosolic to a transmembrane exit; suppressed over well-ordered helical cores and catalytic/metal-binding sites. In proline-rich proteins (collagens/collagen-like), activation expands into long continuous runs. Signals frequently coincide with a local drop in structural confidence or a coil interruption, but can also occur in high-confidence juxta-membrane helices.
Exemplars: - Multi-pass membrane proteins/transporters: hinge or helix-break motifs preceding disordered C-tails (short K/R/L hotspots at the first helix interruption).
- Ribosomal P1 acidic stalk proteins: final few residues forming a short, low-confidence C-terminal helix within the disordered tail.
- GPI-anchor remodeling enzyme PGAP3: a cytosolic EDD triad immediately after a transmembrane helix (juxta-membrane helix cap), including a disease-linked Asp.
- Collagens and collagen-like extracellular proteins: long proline-rich Gly-X-Y repeats (PPII/triple-helix segments).
- Oomycete RxLR effectors: short charge-biased segments immediately upstream of and adjacent to the RxLR/EER region.
- Short secreted bioactive peptides and venoms: cationic amphipathic segments and Pro/Gly-mediated kinks in the mature peptide.
- TOM22 (mitochondrial import receptor): cytosolic/juxta-membrane receptor tail that engages targeting peptides.
- Lipid phosphatases/ceramidases and other membrane lipid enzymes: charged juxta-membrane cytosolic loops or helix caps adjacent to TM segments.
- Alternative oxidase/cytochrome b559 components: short interfacial/juxta-membrane segments next to their anchors.
- Coiled-coil/Golgi/cytoskeletal scaffolds and Ripply family: short conserved, composition-biased motif regions within otherwise low-complexity or coiled-coil contexts.

Summary: Low-complexity, intrinsically disordered segments—often at protein N-termini—such as mucin-like/propeptide regions or flexible linkers adjacent to signal/transit peptides, common in small secreted or membrane-associated proteins and also as disordered extensions in diverse enzymes (broad taxonomic coverage, including viral, bacterial, and eukaryotic proteins).
Activation pattern: Regional activation over short to moderate stretches, frequently in disordered or polar/low-complexity segments; in longer proteins, multiple low-complexity patches can activate; in micropeptides, activation can span much of the sequence. Residue-level peaks can fall on Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly within polar-residue stretches but also on basic or hydrophobic residues within the same disordered context.
Exemplars:
- Viral envelope/accessory microproteins: activation on N-terminal Ser/Thr/Pro-rich disordered segments (often mucin-like or regulatory tails).
- Secreted eukaryotic effectors (e.g., oomycete RxLR effectors): activation on the low-complexity region flanking the signal peptide/RxLR motif.
- Human testis-biased and lncRNA-derived micropeptides: activation across intrinsically disordered peptide regions.
- Secreted precursors/propeptides: activation on N-terminal regions following the signal peptide.
- Membrane-associated single-pass proteins: activation on luminal or cytosolic tails flanking the transmembrane helix.
- Bacterial/archaeal metabolic enzymes: activation on disordered, low-complexity N-terminal extensions/linkers enriched in Ser/Thr/Gly/Pro.

Summary: Short, intrinsically disordered C‑terminal tails of secreted or membrane‑associated proteins (from microproteins to larger multi‑pass enzymes) and viral accessory microproteins, typically low‑complexity and enriched in proline and basic residues, often immediately downstream of a hydrophobic signal/transmembrane segment; can include cysteine‑rich patches in secreted/toxin peptides.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over contiguous 10–30 aa windows, most frequently at the extreme C‑terminus; often spans a brief helix that transitions into coil with peak signal in the disordered coil; commonly adjacent to a hydrophobic (signal/TM) segment and characterized by low pLDDT; can also occur in short cytosolic juxtamembrane loops of larger multi‑pass proteins.
Exemplars:
- Oomycete RxLR secreted effectors: activation on the C‑terminal tail immediately following a predicted hydrophobic segment, in a low‑confidence helix/coil region.
- Human ST20 (apoptosis/stress‑related microprotein): activation on a short C‑terminal helix‑to‑coil, highly disordered stretch.
- Small uncharacterized microproteins: activation confined to the last ~10–15 residues forming a disordered coil tail.
- Viral accessory/viroporin‑like proteins: activation on basic/proline‑rich cytosolic C‑tails adjacent to a single‑pass TM helix; also applies to non‑TM viral accessory proteins with disordered C‑tails (e.g., Vif).
- Small secreted cysteine‑rich toxins/defensin‑like peptides: activation on short cationic/cysteine‑biased segments within the mature or processing tail.
- ATP synthase epsilon subunits: activation on a conserved, short, disordered C‑terminal regulatory segment in these small mitochondrial/bacterial proteins.
- Multi‑pass membrane enzymes (e.g., phytoene dehydrogenase): activation on short cytosolic C‑terminal or juxtamembrane tails adjacent to TM helices.

Summary: Low-complexity Pro/Leu/Gln-rich patches in solvent-exposed regions of secreted/effector proteins—often downstream of signal peptides and including basic or aromatic-sprinkled stretches—that mediate adhesion, membrane association, and host–pathogen/immune-modulatory interactions.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks concentrated in short clustered stretches in regions downstream of signal peptides in secreted proteins; can occur in hydrophobic Leu/Pro-rich or basic clusters; weak over hydrophobic signal peptides; variable number of clusters per protein.
Exemplars:
- Serpin antithrombin: activation on the N-terminal basic patch mediating heparin binding; signal peptide shows little activation.
- Viral proteins (envelope and accessory): activation on polybasic PR/QR-rich segments that bind host glycosaminoglycans or acidic membranes (e.g., GP4; ORF9c basic tails).
- Oomycete RxLR effectors: activation around the RxLR motif and downstream Leu/Pro-rich stretches in secreted effector precursors.
- Secreted precursors and micropeptides (chemokines, antimicrobial/cell-penetrating peptides, hormone propeptides; mucin-like caseins): activation on cationic, aromatic-sprinkled low-complexity stretches engaging proteoglycans or acidic membranes.
- DNA/RNA-binding microproteins and enzymes: activation on terminal/basic patches contacting nucleic acids (e.g., killin; bacterial tRNA m7G methyltransferases).
- Soluble metabolic enzymes: occasional activation at exposed basic clusters that bind phosphate-containing ligands (e.g., riboflavin kinase).
- Membrane-associated proteins/receptors: activation on luminal or cytosolic basic patches used for proteoglycan binding or membrane association (e.g., DEspR-like receptors, neuronatin).
- Reproductive/testis-associated proteins: activation on arginine/proline-rich low-complexity regions mediating polyanion-dependent interactions in the reproductive tract.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity, charge‑rich segments with an acidic bias (poly‑E/D), frequently containing histidine and glutamine clusters; the feature also spikes on solitary histidines (often conserved) within otherwise structured or hydrophobic contexts.
Activation pattern: Primarily regional activation across long IDRs enriched in E/D/H/K/R/Q/N (poly‑acidic and mixed charged runs); secondary mode of residue‑level peaks at individual His residues; occasional short‑motif hits within larger proteins.
Exemplars: - Anaphase‑promoting complex subunits: strong activation on annotated disordered, charge‑biased coil linkers.
- Heme A synthase family: sharp single‑residue activation at the conserved histidine.
- Viral accessory/regulatory and structural proteins: activation on acidic/histidine‑rich low‑complexity terminal tails.
- Secreted/extracellular precursors and toxins: activation on acidic, histidine/glutamine‑rich low‑complexity segments.
- Reproductive‑tract secreted proteins: activation on glutamine‑rich, acidic low‑complexity regions.

Summary: Feature fires broadly across short proteins and small peptides, often covering most of the chain, with a preference for low-complexity, Pro/Gly-rich and polybasic segments but also extending into adjacent structured regions of short polypeptides.
Activation pattern: Broad, near-whole-protein activation in short (~50-200 aa) precursors and microproteins, with local maxima on Pro-rich tracts (including poly-P), GP/GG-containing stretches, and basic clusters; activation is not restricted to disordered patches and can extend into folded domains in short proteins.
Exemplars:
- Class II bacteriocin/lantibiotic precursors: broad activation across the short precursor chain, including mature regions containing GG and GW motifs.
- Secreted peptide/toxin and prohormone precursors (e.g., cholecystokinin): activation spread across the precursor chain.
- Sperm protamine precursors: concentrated on disordered propeptides and at propeptide–mature boundaries; minimal on highly basic mature cores.
- Viral accessory/regulatory microproteins (e.g., Vpx, Vif): activation across the short viral protein, with strong peaks on poly-P / GP-rich low-complexity patches when present.
- lncRNA-encoded micropeptides and very small uncharacterized proteins (e.g., RUSC1-AS1, N-cym): activation on Pro/Gly-rich disordered segments and across much of the chain.
- Plant transcription factors with WG/GW- and GP-rich low-complexity regions: activation on those patches.
- ATP synthase epsilon subunits: signal on short GP-rich linkers or terminal low-complexity tails.
- Large enzymes (e.g., DDX11 helicase, acyl-CoA synthetase): activation on disordered N/C-terminal low-complexity regions or basic/GP-rich insertions.
- Small mitochondrial membrane proteins (ATP8): signal on short basic matrix-exposed loops or termini flanking TM helices.
- Short proteolytic chains of secreted enzymes (e.g., snake venom metalloproteinase fragments, acrosin chain fragments): broad activation across the short mature chain, including within structured peptidase/disintegrin regions.

Summary: Low-complexity, disorder-associated segments enriched in Asp/Asn/His/Tyr and depleted of Lys/Arg—frequently N- or C-terminal propeptides and regulatory tails, and occasionally short polar/acidic stretches within other contexts including amphipathic helices in small viral proteins.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks on D/H/N/Y within low-pLDDT regions that often coalesce into contiguous activation across long terminal IDRs; activation can also appear in shorter polar/acidic loops embedded in folded chains, and within an N-terminal helix when the helix presents an acidic/polar face.
Exemplars: - Fibroblast growth factor propeptides: selective peaks in the disordered N-terminal propeptide (e.g., H/N/D) with no activation in the mature growth factor domain.
- Small viral regulatory proteins (e.g., polyomavirus Agnoprotein, HIV Tat/Vif): peaks on D/N/H/Y in disordered tails and within amphipathic helical segments.
- Uncharacterized eukaryotic microproteins/regulatory peptides: scattered D/H/Y peaks across very low-confidence, disordered regions, often strongest near termini.
- Short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase family enzymes: activation confined to a disordered, acidic/polar C-terminal extension, absent from the structured NAD(P)-binding/catalytic domain.
- DNA-binding apoptosis regulators (Killin-like): largely disordered proteins with highest peaks on D/N and additional H/Y, mostly outside the annotated DNA-binding segment.

Summary: Residue-level detector that activates broadly at sparse positions across diverse protein contexts, with notable preference for disordered/low-complexity regions, mature secreted peptides, and short helical segments (including transmembrane helices and helix-prone regions inside intrinsically disordered stretches). It does not appear to track a single specific motif.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks, typically one to a few strong peaks per protein with additional weaker peaks scattered along the sequence. Strong activation is observed within intrinsically disordered regions (including Gly-rich and polar/charged compositionally biased segments), within short transmembrane helices, and within mature processed peptides. Activation is also seen scattered within globular enzyme domains.
Exemplars:
- Small integral membrane proteins: single strong peak within a short transmembrane helix.
- Secretory preprohormones (e.g., cholecystokinin): multiple peaks within the mature processed peptide regions.
- Homeobox/disordered regulators (e.g., Rhox5): multiple peaks throughout disordered Gly-rich and basic/acidic compositionally biased segments.
- CaMKII inhibitor peptides: peaks at the start of the inhibitory domain and at Pro-rich positions.
- Viral accessory/integrase-like proteins: multiple short peaks scattered across the chain, including disordered C-terminal segments.
- Bacterial/yeast enzymes (e.g., beta-lactamase, aspartyl-tRNA synthetase, imidazolonepropionase, peroxin-9): scattered peaks within N-terminal or globular regions.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low-complexity regulatory segments in nuclear proteins—long tracts enriched in charged/polar residues (Ser/Pro with Lys/Arg and/or acidic E/D), often containing short basic patches (NLS/AT-hook–like) and phospho-Ser/Thr motifs; these simple-sequence tails/linkers occur in transcription/chromatin and RNA-processing regulators (and viral regulators) and are largely absent from folded domains.
Activation pattern: Domain-level off on structured domains (e.g., BTB, PWWP); regional on in extended IDRs with low pLDDT; localized peaks over short basic clusters (often NLS-like), Ser-rich/Pro-rich or acidic patches, and phospho-motifs (e.g., ETPS), sometimes selecting only a subsegment within a larger disordered region.
Exemplars: - Mediator complex subunit tail (MED19): activation confined to the C-terminal disordered tail, peaking over an ETPS phospho-motif, a Lys/Arg-rich patch, and a Ser-rich low-complexity stretch; silent across the more structured N-terminus.
- BTB transcription factor (Lola): off across the folded BTB domain; on across the central low-complexity/disordered linker, with a pronounced peak in a short Ser-rich segment; minimal signal in helical C-terminal regions.
- Hepatoma-derived growth factor (HDGF): off on the N-terminal PWWP domain; strong activation on a C-terminal disordered segment overlapping a bipartite nuclear localization signal and adjacent mixed basic/acidic low-complexity sequence, with a peak at a Lys-rich patch.

Summary: Detector of compositionally biased, low‑complexity segments—predominantly intrinsically disordered Ser/Thr‑rich (often RS-/Pro‑containing) tracts—with a strong N‑terminal bias; it also flags the extreme N‑terminus including signal peptides of secreted precursors.
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks clustered within long disordered/low‑complexity regions (often spanning tens to hundreds of residues), with strongest peaks on Ser/Thr and nearby polar/basic residues; broad regional activation across such IDRs and minimal signal in well‑folded domains or transmembranes; additional discrete peaks frequently occur at residues 1–10, including within N‑terminal signal peptides.
Exemplars: - Transcriptional regulator (CROC-4): multiple peaks across a central low‑complexity disordered segment (S/T/R/P‑rich), with minor N‑terminal peaks.
- Mechanosensory receptor (Stum): numerous high peaks on serines dispersed through annotated disordered, low‑complexity/polar regions.
- Yeast RNA/chromatin‑associated factor (REF2‑interacting protein): peaks within disordered, compositionally biased tracts; strongest at a threonine in an S/T‑rich context, near (but not exactly on) annotated phosphosites.
- Secreted antimicrobial peptide precursor (lumbricin): strongest activation on the N‑terminal signal peptide helix; weaker peaks just after the signal peptide preceding a long disordered pro‑region.
- Yeast HPH2 regulatory protein: activation confined to disordered, low‑complexity regions in the N‑terminal two‑thirds; absent from the structured C‑terminal domain and its transmembrane helix.

Summary: Short residue windows in mixed-composition regions of diverse proteins, frequently in N-terminal or non-catalytic portions of enzymes, transmembrane-adjacent stretches, and small secreted peptides.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks concentrated in short 3–7 residue windows, often clustered with several nearby peaks. Activated residues are chemically diverse (including hydrophobic, polar, and charged residues) and can occur in helical transmembrane segments, disordered linkers, or globular regions outside annotated catalytic/binding sites.
Exemplars:
- Bacterial DNA ligase: clusters of peaks in the N-terminal region upstream of the catalytic and BRCT domains.
- Viral integrase homolog: short peaks within the chain including a GPAYGRP-containing segment.
- Peroxisomal biogenesis factor 9 (Pex9): peaks overlapping helical transmembrane segments and an adjacent disordered/polar region.
- Small secreted peptides (e.g., Califin-B large subunit): short peaks within the mature peptide.

Summary: Residue positions that mark polypeptide boundaries—especially the absolute N-terminus (position 1) and the terminal residue of sequence fragments—and, secondarily, isolated boundary-like sites within larger proteins (e.g., short linkers between secondary-structure elements or helix/turn cap-like positions), consistent with proteolytic processing junctions in pre/propeptides.
Activation pattern: Predominantly single-residue peaks at sequence extremities (most often the first residue; also the last residue of fragments); sparse internal single-residue peaks at boundary-like positions (short linkers or transitions between secondary structures). Often coincides with disordered/low-confidence termini; in secreted/toxin precursors a recurring window around residues ~50–70 is consistent with signal/propeptide cleavage. Per-protein activations are usually one or a few sites.
Exemplars: Snake venom serine protease: peaks at the N-terminal first residue and at the C-terminal end of the chain; Nuclear pore complex protein Nup155: isolated peaks on single residues within a helix and a low-confidence turn; U4/U6.U5 tri-snRNP–associated protein 1: single-residue peak at a glycine linker between β-strands; E4 ubiquitin-conjugation factor (UBE4): isolated methionine within a long α-helix; Reelin (fragment): strong activation at the fragment’s C-terminal residue in a disordered region; Glutamate dehydrogenase (fragment): activation marks the truncated C-terminal residue.

Summary: N-terminal leader/targeting signatures and short hydrophobic stretches: signal peptides, transit peptides, or short flexible N-terminal tails (with or without a subsequent transmembrane helix), with additional sensitivity to single hydrophobic signal-anchor/transmembrane helices; also fires at scattered residues within small proteins and disordered segments
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks, often biased toward N-terminal regions but also distributed through small proteins; occasional short contiguous peaks spanning a hydrophobic signal peptide or transmembrane helix
Exemplars: Secreted antimicrobial peptide precursor: activation on the N-terminal signal peptide; Lipid-droplet targeting protein: peak within a single-pass transmembrane helix that mediates organelle targeting; Small disordered/regulatory proteins: scattered peaks across short, low-complexity sequences

Summary: Single conserved residue—often hydrophobic/aromatic but variable (Phe/Tyr/Trp/Leu/Val/Ile, and sometimes His/Thr)—within nucleotide- or ligand-binding pockets and analogous buried sites across diverse folds; in non-nucleotide proteins it maps to an analogous internal pocket- or core-lining position.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks at an internal pocket-lining residue, occasionally with short adjacent clusters; position varies widely with the fold.
Exemplars:
- Protein kinases (including viral/atypical): activation within the kinase domain at a residue near the ATP-binding cleft.
- tRNA (guanine-N7)-methyltransferases (class I SAM MTases): activation on the conserved aromatic that stacks with the SAM adenine and/or the target guanine in the active site.
- UDP-sugar glycosyltransferases for LPS/teichoic acid/lipid A biosynthesis (GT-B fold): activation on the aromatic that stacks with the UDP uracil ring in the donor-binding site.
- NAD(P)-dependent dehydrogenases (Rossmann fold): activation on an adenine-stacking Phe/Tyr in the dinucleotide-binding pocket.
- MurE (UDP-MurNAc-tripeptide synthetase; ATP-grasp ligase): activation on a buried hydrophobe that helps form the adenine-binding cleft for ATP.
- Carbonic anhydrases: activation on a conserved hydrophobic/aromatic residue lining the active-site hydrophobic pocket adjacent to the catalytic zinc.
- Small ribosomal subunit protein S8: activation on an aromatic residue that base-stacks with rRNA or stabilizes the RNA-binding surface.
- MICOS subunit Mic60 (mitofilin): activation on a buried aromatic within the coiled-coil/mitofilin scaffold that stabilizes the membrane-associated core.

Summary: Ala/Val/Gly–enriched low‑complexity segments, often within intrinsically disordered or low‑confidence regions of small/unstructured proteins (signal peptides, pro‑peptide extensions, regulatory tails, microproteins), characterized by small aliphatic residues interspersed with sparse acidic residues; composition- rather than function-specific.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks land predominantly on V (and A/D/E) residues within low-complexity or disordered tracts; multiple peaks can be distributed across a stretch (regional LCR activation), with reduced signal in well-folded globular domains.
Exemplars: - Oomycete RxLR effectors: activation on alanines/valines and acidic residues flanking the RxLR motif and within adjacent disordered N‑terminal regions (including non-helical segments of annotated signal/TM zones).
- OmpR/PhoB-type response regulators (e.g., PfeR): activation confined to the N‑terminal intrinsically disordered extension; absent from the structured receiver and HTH DNA‑binding domains.
- Conotoxin precursors: peaks in the N‑terminal signal peptide (A/V/E sites) and scattered across the low‑confidence mature toxin region.
- Mammalian unstructured microproteins (e.g., testis-specific proteins) and ST20-like regulators: sparse peaks on V/A residues distributed throughout globally disordered sequences.
- Small viral accessory proteins (e.g., agnoprotein, PB1‑F2): scattered V/D/E peaks across short, largely disordered chains.

Summary: Methionine residue identity, with a strong bias toward the N‑terminal initiator Met and early hydrophobic N‑terminal segments; generally fires on Met in diverse structural/functional contexts and is largely structure-agnostic.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks centered on Met; often includes the initiator Met at position 1 and occasionally nearby bulky hydrophobic/aromatic residues (W, V, L, I; sometimes T, C). Typically only a few residues per protein are active, with a tendency to cluster near the N-terminus but also occurring on internal Met.
Exemplars: - cAMP-specific phosphodiesterase (PDE4A) fragment: exclusive activation on multiple internal Met residues independent of secondary structure or disorder.
- Secreted precursors (hormones, toxins, bacteriocins): activation on the initiator Met of the signal peptide/propeptide.
- Viral accessory/immune-modulatory proteins: short, N-terminally focused activation on M1 and occasional internal Met.
- Membrane-associated proteins (signal anchors/transmembrane leaders): activation on the N-terminal Met and Met within early hydrophobic segments.
- Human microproteins and testis/spermatogenesis-related proteins: sparse activation on M1 and any internal Met in short proteins.
- Glycoprotein precursors: activation on the initiator Met at the start of signal peptides.

Summary: Residue-level detector that fires sparsely in small proteins, peptide precursors, and disordered/loosely structured regions, often in propeptide or disordered C-/N-terminal segments; avoids structured catalytic cores and binding sites.
Activation pattern: Sparse residue-level peaks, often in small (sub-200 aa) proteins or within annotated disordered regions of larger proteins; for larger enzymes peaks cluster in the N-terminal extension well away from catalytic/binding residues. Peak residues are heterogeneous (aromatic, charged, and polar residues all occur).
Exemplars: - tRNA (pseudouridine(54)-N1)-methyltransferase: activation restricted to the disordered N-terminal extension (e.g., a peak in a short transient helix), absent from the SAM-dependent catalytic domain
- Secreted bacterial protease: strong activation in disordered N- and C-terminal tails, none across the structured protease core
- Neuropeptide/prohormone precursor (Amnesiac): isolated peak within the disordered C-terminal propeptide region
- Antisense-encoded microprotein (TAR1): peaks including one within the annotated C-terminal disordered region
- Proapoptotic nucleolar protein: peaks within a broad C-terminal IDR, including near a nucleolar localization segment

Summary: Residue positions that mark polypeptide boundaries—especially the absolute N-terminus (position 1) and the terminal residue of sequence fragments—and, secondarily, isolated boundary-like sites within larger proteins (e.g., short linkers between secondary-structure elements or helix/turn cap-like positions), consistent with proteolytic processing junctions in pre/propeptides.
Activation pattern: Predominantly single-residue peaks at sequence extremities (most often the first residue; also the last residue of fragments); sparse internal single-residue peaks at boundary-like positions (short linkers or transitions between secondary structures). Often coincides with disordered/low-confidence termini; in secreted/toxin precursors a recurring window around residues ~50–70 is consistent with signal/propeptide cleavage. Per-protein activations are usually one or a few sites.
Exemplars: Snake venom serine protease: peaks at the N-terminal first residue and at the C-terminal end of the chain; Nuclear pore complex protein Nup155: isolated peaks on single residues within a helix and a low-confidence turn; U4/U6.U5 tri-snRNP–associated protein 1: single-residue peak at a glycine linker between β-strands; E4 ubiquitin-conjugation factor (UBE4): isolated methionine within a long α-helix; Reelin (fragment): strong activation at the fragment’s C-terminal residue in a disordered region; Glutamate dehydrogenase (fragment): activation marks the truncated C-terminal residue.

Summary: Serine residues across a wide range of structural contexts, with a bias toward serine-rich segments in intrinsically disordered or low-complexity regions (often N-terminal tails), but also firing on serines within transmembrane helices and other structured contexts; the feature behaves primarily as a serine detector with some preference for S-rich patches.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks almost exclusively on Ser; many peaks per protein, frequently clustered near termini and in compositionally biased/disordered regions, but also appearing within transmembrane helices, signal peptides, and transit peptides; minor spillover to nearby residues.
Exemplars: Viral accessory proteins (metapneumovirus X): serines in a disordered C-terminal tail; Herpesvirus envelope glycoprotein L: serines across the gH-interacting segment and a disordered C-terminus; Herpesvirus cytoplasmic envelopment proteins: numerous serines in low-pLDDT regions; Plant ribosome-inactivating proteins (dianthin): N-terminal loop/coil serines; Human adaptor/regulatory protein ST20: N-terminal serines in a low-confidence helix/coil; Oomycete RxLR effectors: serines across the signal peptide, core, and disordered C-terminus; Bacteriocins (enterocins): serines in flexible coil segments.

Summary: Low-complexity, intrinsically disordered or signal/transmembrane–proximal segments—often N‑terminal—commonly enriched in H/Q/Y/W but not exclusively, acting as generic interaction/activation modules in small regulatory/viral proteins and in secreted/membrane-linked precursors
Activation pattern: Regional activation across extended low‑complexity stretches or N‑terminal signal/TM-adjacent regions; per‑residue preference for H/Q with contributions from Y/W, but tolerant of basic- or serine‑rich tracts found in viral accessory proteins and secreted precursors
Exemplars:
- Viral accessory/regulatory proteins (e.g., Rex, agnoproteins): activation over N‑terminal basic/low‑complexity tails (may lack H/Q bias)
- Eukaryotic sORF/micropeptides and apoptosis/testis-linked proteins: activation across low‑complexity IDRs, often H/Q/Y‑rich when present
- Secreted precursors and extracellular peptides (e.g., plant SCOOPs, protease propeptides): activation on signal peptides/propeptides or serine‑rich low‑complexity regions
- Small membrane proteins/channels (e.g., FluC) and proteolipids (e.g., neuronatin): activation at N‑terminal low‑complexity loops or signal/TM-proximal regions
- Histidine‑rich metal‑binding/antimicrobial tracts: activation on poly‑His/His‑biased regions when present

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity tandem‑repeat regions across diverse taxa, with broad activation over polar/Pro/Ser/Thr/Gln/Lys/Tyr/His‑rich repeat tracts including mucin‑like, adhesive, and extensin‑like sequences. The feature fires in both secreted/extracellular precursors and intracellular disordered LCR proteins.
Activation pattern: Broad activation over long tandemly repetitive low‑complexity segments, with periodic residue‑level peaks tracking the repeat unit. Sharp peaks tend to fall on Gln, Lys, His, Arg, or Pro residues at conserved positions within the repeat, and activation spreads across surrounding Pro/Ser/Thr/Gln/Lys/Tyr‑rich tracts; periodic patterns appear when motifs are regularly spaced.
Exemplars: - Adhesive glycoproteins (e.g., mussel foot proteins): widespread activation over Tyr‑ and Lys‑rich low‑complexity decapeptide repeats, with peaks on conserved Lys residues.
- Plant Pro‑rich extensins: broad activation across Pro‑rich tandem repeats with peaks on His/Lys within the repeat unit.
- Fungal collagen‑like Gly‑Gln‑Xaa repeat proteins: periodic peaks on Gln within G‑Q‑I/R/S repeats.
- Trypanosome surface antigens with LTR tandem repeats: activation along disordered polar repeat regions with peaks on His.
- Polar/Q‑rich disordered repeat regions of intracellular proteins (e.g., dynein heavy chain LCR, spermatogenesis‑associated SPATA31H1 P‑S‑E‑R‑S‑H‑H‑S repeats, Filia, polyamine acetyltransferase disordered Q/S/P tracts): broad activation over disordered repeat tracts and basic/acidic clusters despite lacking secretion, reflecting the general LCR signature.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low-complexity repeat/linker tracts enriched for polar/charged residues (Q/N/E/D/H/P/R); common in secreted/extracellular or luminal segments and also in cytosolic/nuclear scaffolds; includes His-rich metal-binding patches, Q/N-rich prion-like/repeat modules, and low-complexity propeptides/linkers in secreted enzymes.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long, contiguous low-complexity/repetitive segments; strongest in extracellular/luminal stretches (often following signal peptides) and in flexible linkers or flanking tails of repeat-domain proteins; little or no isolated peaks within structured catalytic cores.
Exemplars:
- Plant hydroxyproline-rich glycoproteins (extensins/PRPs): activation across Tyr/His/Pro-rich repetitive cell-wall regions.
- Histidine-rich secreted proteins and metal-binding patches: activation on His/Gln/Asp/Glu-rich tracts that chelate metals.
- Multi-C2H2 zinc-finger and other His/Cys metal-coordinating proteins: activation on low-complexity His/Gln-rich linkers or repeat arrays adjacent to the fingers rather than the core motifs.
- TALE-like repeat effectors (bacterial): activation along RVD-bearing repeat arrays enriched in polar/acidic residues.
- Plasmodium low-complexity proteins: activation on long Asn/Gln-rich prion-like segments.
- Neuropeptide/peptide-hormone precursors (basal metazoans): activation across Q/R/P-rich low-complexity propeptide regions between cleavage sites.
- Membrane receptors/adhesins and multispan transporters (e.g., MS4A, MFS/FLVCR): activation on luminal/extracellular low-complexity loops.
- Golgi/vesicle-tethering coiled-coil scaffolds (e.g., COG subunits): activation on acidic/Q-rich low-complexity linkers.
- WD-repeat RNA processing/cleavage factors (e.g., WDR33): activation on low-complexity N/C-terminal tails flanking WD propellers.
- Secreted enzymes (e.g., metalloproteinases, acetylcholinesterase): activation on signal-proximal propeptides, glycosylated insertions, or flexible linkers, not the catalytic cores.
- Testis/germline-associated low-complexity proteins: activation on prion-like Q/H/P-rich regions.
- Elastic/repetitive structural proteins (elastin-/resilin-like or repeat-rich linkers): activation on polar/charged, low-complexity repeats.

Summary: Acidic, PEST-like low-complexity stretches and related pre-structured helical linkers that act as flexible, interaction-prone modules (e.g., activation/dimerization/adaptor-contact), most often in mid-to-C-terminal regions; the feature can also mark short loop/strand residues bordering catalytic pockets.
Activation pattern: Primarily regional activation across long, continuous E/D- and P/S/T/G-rich segments with low-to-moderate predicted order (intrinsically disordered or marginally alpha-helical), with occasional isolated residue-level peaks in loops or edge beta-strands near active sites.
Exemplars: - Aerobic cobaltochelatase (CobT): strong activation on a long, acidic, disordered C-terminal tail.
- RFX transcription factors: extended C-terminal alpha-helical region beyond the winged-helix DNA-binding domain (likely activation/dimerization module).
- Lon AAA+ protease: a short portion of the long interdomain helix linking the N-terminal and protease domains.
- Phosphoethanolamine transferase (EptC): a single glutamate in a loop at a beta-to-helix junction.
- FAD-linked oxidoreductases (PCMH-type): a glycine in a short loop within the FAD-binding domain.
- DNA ligase I: a single residue on a beta-strand immediately adjacent to the catalytic lysine/ATP-binding site.

Summary: Small-residue–biased low-complexity repeat regions—typically intrinsically disordered and enriched for Gly and/or Ser/Thr with frequent acidic (Asp/Glu) residues—serving as flexible linkers or mesh-forming domains (e.g., FG repeats in nucleoporins, PTS- or Ser/Thr-rich repeats in mucins/adhesins, glycine-biased linkers of secreted/cell-wall proteins); also includes N/Q-rich LCRs in some taxa (e.g., Apicomplexa) and occasionally captures glycine-periodic repeats such as Gly–X–Y in collagen-like sequences.
Activation pattern: Predominantly domain- or regional-level activation across long low-complexity segments with residue-level peaks centered on glycine or other small/polar residues within repetitive motifs (e.g., FG, PTS, DE-rich, N-rich tracts); minimal to no activation in structured domains or transmembranes.
Exemplars:
- FG-nucleoporins: strong periodic activation on the G of FG dipeptides across intrinsically disordered FG-repeat domains; no activation in structured regions.
- Mucins and fungal adhesins: activation across Ser/Thr-rich tandem repeat LCRs in secreted precursors.
- Secreted enzymes/proteases (e.g., xylanases, subtilisins): activation in disordered low-complexity linkers or propeptides flanking the structured catalytic cores.
- Extracellular matrix/biomineralization acidic/glycine-rich proteins: broad activation across long G/E/D- or S/T-rich LCRs; collagen-like Gly–X–Y repeats show periodic glycine-centered activation.
- Occasional activation in low-complexity transit peptides (mitochondrial/plastid) and in cytosolic/periplasmic low-complexity loops of membrane proteins, consistent with broad taxonomic spread.

Summary: Periodic short-repeat tracts (low-complexity/simple-sequence) in secreted/extracellular and cell-surface proteins, and also in some intracellular structural or repeat-rich proteins; enriched for S/T/P/A/G and/or acidic D/E (often also N/T). These regions act as flexible glycosylated stalks/spacers or exposed repeat blocks; the feature recognizes repeat architecture (disordered or ordered solenoids) rather than a specific domain.
Activation pattern: Domain/regional activation across extended repeat blocks; often (but not always) downstream of signal peptides/propeptides, with little to no activation in the signal peptide itself. Within each short repeat unit, residue-level periodic peaks favor small/polar/acidic positions (S/T/P/A/G/D/E and sometimes V/I), with suppression at basic positions (and often Asn at specific slots); signal weakens where periodicity deteriorates. Activated regions are frequently disordered and O-glycosylated but can also be ordered solenoid repeats (e.g., bacterial ice-nucleation, TALE-like).
Exemplars: - Plant extensins and proline-rich cell wall proteins: activation across PP[V/I][E/Y][K/N]-type blocks.
- Antifreeze glycoproteins: activation on (Ala–Ala–Thr)n O-glycosylated tracts.
- Mucins and mucin-like secreted glycoproteins; hormone/neuropeptide/toxin precursors: activation on Ser/Thr/Pro-rich propeptide regions.
- Fungal cell-wall adhesins/mannoproteins and stress cell-wall proteins: activation on long Ser/Thr-rich low-complexity stalks.
- Molluscan adhesive foot proteins: activation on repetitive P/T/A/W/K motifs, peaking at non-basic positions.
- Plasmodium surface/repeat antigens: activation across central low-complexity repeats.
- Viral proteins with low-complexity repeat blocks: activation across tandem repeat segments (e.g., EBNA-LP).
- Bacterial secreted/cell-surface repeat proteins (including ice-nucleation proteins) and TALE-like effectors.
- Keratin-associated/epidermal repeat proteins and other intracellular low-complexity repeat proteins (e.g., VCX family).

Summary: Methionine residue identity, with a strong bias toward the N‑terminal initiator Met and early hydrophobic N‑terminal segments; generally fires on Met in diverse structural/functional contexts and is largely structure-agnostic.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks centered on Met; often includes the initiator Met at position 1 and occasionally nearby bulky hydrophobic/aromatic residues (W, V, L, I; sometimes T, C). Typically only a few residues per protein are active, with a tendency to cluster near the N-terminus but also occurring on internal Met.

- Human microproteins and testis/spermatogenesis-related proteins: sparse activation on M1 and any internal Met in short proteins.
- Glycoprotein precursors: activation on the initiator Met at the start of signal peptides.

Summary: Position-driven detector of the extreme protein N-terminus—especially residues 2–5—largely independent of amino-acid identity, typically in short, unstructured signal/leader-like segments; also fires on analogous newly formed N-termini within precursors (e.g., mature peptide starts). Common across taxa, with strong representation in viral accessory proteins, secreted precursors, and micropeptides.
Activation pattern: Sharp, residue-level peaks concentrated at the first few residues after initiation (maximal at position 2), with occasional isolated secondary peaks at internal, low-structure sites that often correspond to signal/transit/leader-like segments or putative processed peptide N-termini.
Exemplars: - Coronavirus accessory protein ORF3b: peaks at the disordered N-terminus (positions 2–3) and additional isolated peaks in low-confidence regions, including a predicted targeting segment.
- Secretory membrane protein with an N-terminal signal peptide (hygromycin-B hypersensitivity protein): strongest activation at residue 2 within the signal peptide; minor scattered peaks in TM/loop regions.
- Bacteriocin (enterocin) precursor: isolated internal activation in an unstructured region consistent with the start of the mature bacteriocin peptide within the precursor.
- Testis-specific lncRNA-derived micropeptide: activation at residue 2 of a disordered N-terminus, with additional sparse peaks in low-confidence coil/helix segments.

Summary: Residue-level detector that fires sparsely in small proteins, peptide precursors, and disordered/loosely structured regions, often in propeptide or disordered C-/N-terminal segments; avoids structured catalytic cores and binding sites.
Activation pattern: Sparse residue-level peaks, often in small (sub-200 aa) proteins or within annotated disordered regions of larger proteins; for larger enzymes peaks cluster in the N-terminal extension well away from catalytic/binding residues. Peak residues are heterogeneous (aromatic, charged, and polar residues all occur).

- Secreted bacterial protease: strong activation in disordered N- and C-terminal tails, none across the structured protease core
- Neuropeptide/prohormone precursor (Amnesiac): isolated peak within the disordered C-terminal propeptide region
- Antisense-encoded microprotein (TAR1): peaks including one within the annotated C-terminal disordered region
- Proapoptotic nucleolar protein: peaks within a broad C-terminal IDR, including near a nucleolar localization segment

- Carbonic anhydrases: activation on a conserved hydrophobic/aromatic residue lining the active-site hydrophobic pocket adjacent to the catalytic zinc.
- Small ribosomal subunit protein S8: activation on an aromatic residue that base-stacks with rRNA or stabilizes the RNA-binding surface.

Summary: Short linear segments in intrinsically disordered or otherwise low-structure-confidence regions, often at N-termini and within signal peptides/propeptides of secreted and regulatory proteins (including viral accessory proteins and small ORF microproteins), enriched in small/basic residues (G, P, S, A, R; often with Cys), rather than in well-folded catalytic cores.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks scattered across IDRs and low-confidence coils/short helices; frequently clustered near the N-terminus, in signal peptides, propeptides, and disordered tails; little to no activation in well-structured domains; occasional activation in low-confidence transmembrane/signal-anchor helices.
Exemplars: - Viral accessory protein (HIV-1 Vif): peaks throughout low-pLDDT coils, especially the disordered N-terminal region.
- Neuropeptide precursor (Drosophila Amnesiac): activation in the N-terminal signal peptide and multiple mature peptide segments with very low pLDDT.
- Secreted serine carboxypeptidase: activation confined to disordered C-terminal tail, annotated disordered segment, the signal peptide, and a low-confidence C-terminal transmembrane helix; absent from the structured catalytic domain.
- Disordered human tumor-suppressor–associated protein (ST20): scattered peaks within predicted helices in a globally disordered chain, including the N-terminus.
- lncRNA/sORF-derived microprotein (IGF2 antisense protein): multiple peaks across annotated disordered regions rich in Arg/Pro/Gly.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low-complexity segments enriched in serine/threonine/proline/glycine and often basic (lysine/arginine), typically found in flexible N- or C-terminal tails and loops; highlights IDRs that may harbor short linear motifs (e.g., basic NLS patches) rather than structured domain cores.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long disordered stretches with additional sparse residue-level peaks in low-confidence loops; often N-terminal-biased in short/viral proteins; rarely within well-folded cores.
Exemplars: Retroviral accessory proteins (e.g., HTLV-1 p30): activation on central and C-terminal IDRs including a basic nuclear localization signal; p53-regulated apoptosis-inducing microprotein: widespread activation across a globally disordered protein; Bacterial DNA ligase: scattered activation in an annotated disordered linker and flexible loops within the ligase domain; Uncharacterized human microprotein: multiple peaks throughout a low-pLDDT, disordered sequence irrespective of predicted secondary structure.

Summary: Short segments within disordered and compositionally biased stretches of diverse proteins, particularly regions enriched in basic and acidic residues. Activations are also seen in non-disordered contexts across proteins of varied function, suggesting the feature captures a relatively broad local sequence pattern rather than a tight structural motif.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks with small clusters, distributed throughout the length of the protein. Peaks frequently overlap annotated disordered regions and basic/acidic compositionally biased segments, but also occur at isolated positions within structured chains; occurs in both helical and coil contexts.
Exemplars: - Oomycete RxLR secreted effectors: peaks within the mature effector chain, with occasional spikes in the signal peptide.
- Plant CLE peptide precursors: localized peaks within the C-terminal CLE motif corresponding to the mature signaling peptide.
- Cholecystokinin prohormone: peaks at or immediately adjacent to the N-termini of mature neuropeptides generated by proteolytic processing.
- Herpesvirus ICP47-like small accessory proteins: multiple peaks in the N-terminal active helical region and in polar, disordered C-terminal stretches.
- Keratin-associated proteins: activation across cysteine/proline/serine-rich, low-complexity repeat regions.
- Phosphodiesterase and fungal/bacterial enzymes with disordered N- or internal stretches: peaks within basic-and-acidic compositionally biased segments.

Summary: Broadly distributed activation across small secreted peptides, processed protein fragments, and various polar/charged residues in short proteins, with frequent firing in viral, venom, and signaling-peptide contexts.

Activation pattern: Sparse residue-level peaks scattered across the protein, with no strong preference for structured versus unstructured regions; peaks occur on a mix of polar (Asn, Asp, Ser, Gln), basic (Arg, Lys), and hydrophobic (Leu, Val, Ala) residues, and can fall within transmembrane helices, disordered stretches, or short folded chains alike.

Exemplars:
- Secreted peptide hormones (cholecystokinin, kisspeptin/metastin): multiple peaks across the processed peptide chain.
- Snake venom metalloproteinase/disintegrin fragment: distributed peaks across the short chain.
- Viral hexon-linking precursor proteins: weak peaks distributed across the chain including propeptide and cleaved segments.
- Peroxisomal biogenesis factors: peaks within transmembrane helices and other regions of the membrane protein.
- Bacterial methyltransferases: activation localized to C-terminal disordered extension while the catalytic core is inactive.
- Antithrombin/serpin precursor: peaks spanning the signal peptide and mature chain.

Common across taxa, with strong representation in viral accessory proteins, secreted precursors, and micropeptides.
Activation pattern: Sharp, residue-level peaks concentrated at the first few residues after initiation (maximal at position 2), with occasional isolated secondary peaks at internal, low-structure sites that often correspond to signal/transit/leader-like segments or putative processed peptide N-termini.
Exemplars: - Coronavirus accessory protein ORF3b: peaks at the disordered N-terminus (positions 2–3) and additional isolated peaks in low-confidence regions, including a predicted targeting segment.
- Secretory membrane protein with an N-terminal signal peptide (hygromycin-B hypersensitivity protein): strongest activation at residue 2 within the signal peptide; minor scattered peaks in TM/loop regions.
- Bacteriocin (enterocin) precursor: isolated internal activation in an unstructured region consistent with the start of the mature bacteriocin peptide within the precursor.
- Testis-specific lncRNA-derived micropeptide: activation at residue 2 of a disordered N-terminus, with additional sparse peaks in low-confidence coil/helix segments.

Summary: Short residue windows in mixed-composition regions of diverse proteins, frequently in N-terminal or non-catalytic portions of enzymes, transmembrane-adjacent stretches, and small secreted peptides.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks concentrated in short 3–7 residue windows, often clustered with several nearby peaks. Activated residues are chemically diverse (including hydrophobic, polar, and charged residues) and can occur in helical transmembrane segments, disordered linkers, or globular regions outside annotated catalytic/binding sites.
Exemplars:
- Bacterial DNA ligase: clusters of peaks in the N-terminal region upstream of the catalytic and BRCT domains.
- Viral integrase homolog: short peaks within the chain including a GPAYGRP-containing segment.
- Peroxisomal biogenesis factor 9 (Pex9): peaks overlapping helical transmembrane segments and an adjacent disordered/polar region.
- Small secreted peptides (e.g., Califin-B large subunit): short peaks within the mature peptide.

Summary: Short linear segments in intrinsically disordered or otherwise low-structure-confidence regions, often at N-termini and within signal peptides/propeptides of secreted and regulatory proteins (including viral accessory proteins and small ORF microproteins), enriched in small/basic residues (G, P, S, A, R; often with Cys), rather than in well-folded catalytic cores.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks scattered across IDRs and low-confidence coils/short helices; frequently clustered near the N-terminus, in signal peptides, propeptides, and disordered tails; little to no activation in well-structured domains; occasional activation in low-confidence transmembrane/signal-anchor helices.
Exemplars: - Viral accessory protein (HIV-1 Vif): peaks throughout low-pLDDT coils, especially the disordered N-terminal region.
- Neuropeptide precursor (Drosophila Amnesiac): activation in the N-terminal signal peptide and multiple mature peptide segments with very low pLDDT.
- Secreted serine carboxypeptidase: activation confined to disordered C-terminal tail, annotated disordered segment, the signal peptide, and a low-confidence C-terminal transmembrane helix; absent from the structured catalytic domain.
- Disordered human tumor-suppressor–associated protein (ST20): scattered peaks within predicted helices in a globally disordered chain, including the N-terminus.
- lncRNA/sORF-derived microprotein (IGF2 antisense protein): multiple peaks across annotated disordered regions rich in Arg/Pro/Gly.

Summary: Low-complexity, intrinsically disordered segments—often at protein N-termini—such as mucin-like/propeptide regions or flexible linkers adjacent to signal/transit peptides, common in small secreted or membrane-associated proteins and also as disordered extensions in diverse enzymes (broad taxonomic coverage, including viral, bacterial, and eukaryotic proteins).
Activation pattern: Regional activation over short to moderate stretches, frequently in disordered or polar/low-complexity segments; in longer proteins, multiple low-complexity patches can activate; in micropeptides, activation can span much of the sequence. Residue-level peaks can fall on Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly within polar-residue stretches but also on basic or hydrophobic residues within the same disordered context.
Exemplars:
- Viral envelope/accessory microproteins: activation on N-terminal Ser/Thr/Pro-rich disordered segments (often mucin-like or regulatory tails).
- Secreted eukaryotic effectors (e.g., oomycete RxLR effectors): activation on the low-complexity region flanking the signal peptide/RxLR motif.
- Human testis-biased and lncRNA-derived micropeptides: activation across intrinsically disordered peptide regions.
- Secreted precursors/propeptides: activation on N-terminal regions following the signal peptide.
- Membrane-associated single-pass proteins: activation on luminal or cytosolic tails flanking the transmembrane helix.
- Bacterial/archaeal metabolic enzymes: activation on disordered, low-complexity N-terminal extensions/linkers enriched in Ser/Thr/Gly/Pro.

Summary: Short, low‑complexity, intrinsically disordered proteins and modules that encode targeting/processing signals—often but not always secretory—combining hydrophobic signal peptides, double‑Gly bacteriocin leaders, or polybasic/NLS‑like segments, frequently adjacent to Ser/Thr/Pro‑rich stretches and basic clusters (e.g., RXLR, KR/RR)—common in micropeptides, toxins/secreted precursors, viral accessory proteins, keratin‑associated and testis‑specific low‑complexity proteins across taxa
Activation pattern: Regional activation across short proteins, spanning hydrophobic/targeting segments and Ser/Thr/Pro‑rich low‑complexity tracts with peaks on basic motifs such as RXLR, dibasic KR/RR, or double‑Gly leader junctions
Exemplars:
- Oomycete RxLR effectors: activation on the N‑terminal signal peptide and the RXLR/EER host‑targeting motif immediately downstream.
- Secreted peptide hormone/venom/toxin precursors: activation on the signal peptide and basic prohormone convertase cleavage motifs (KR/RR) within the propeptide region.
- Class II bacteriocins: activation on the N‑terminal double‑Gly leader and adjacent cationic tract recognized by ABC exporters.
- Viral accessory/regulatory proteins (e.g., small disordered regulators): activation across S/T/P‑rich low‑complexity disordered segments containing polybasic/NLS‑like clusters.
- Keratin‑associated proteins (KRTAPs): activation over short, repetitive low‑complexity regions (Ser/Pro‑rich and basic tracts) typical of hair shaft proteins.
- Cancer/testis antigens and testis‑associated proteins: activation on Lys/Arg‑ and Pro/Ser‑rich low‑complexity stretches in very short proteins.
- Short uncharacterized micropeptides/antisense products: broad activation across their low‑complexity/basic segments.
- Enzymes that carry secretory leaders or short disordered/basic tails (including some cytosolic enzymes lacking signal peptides): activation limited to the disordered tail, not the catalytic core.

Summary: Often fires within intrinsic disorder/low-complexity segments—especially terminal or propeptide regions enriched in Pro/Ser/Thr/Gly—that serve as flexible carriers of short linear motifs; the feature highlights unstructured tails/loops across diverse proteins (including secreted precursors, viral regulators, membrane-protein tails, and micropeptides), sometimes coinciding with proteolytic processing and PTM sites, but also produces residue-level peaks within some short folded enzymes/fragments.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks within annotated/predicted disordered coils and low-complexity tracts, frequently enriched toward N-termini; additional scattered peaks can occur within short folded chains.
Exemplars: - Secreted peptide hormone precursors (e.g., cholecystokinin/prohormones): peaks in unstructured propeptide segments at sulfotyrosine, amidation sites, and cleavage boundaries.
- Herpesviral nuclear egress proteins: activation on N-terminal disordered, polar-biased regions; not on the structured zinc-finger domain.
- Integrase-family proteins: peaks include very low-pLDDT loops and annotated disordered segments, with additional scattered peaks elsewhere in the chain.
- Mycobacterial cell-envelope–associated proteins: single-residue/short-segment peaks within UniProt-annotated disordered coil regions.
- p53-inducible regulatory proteins: sparse peaks across N-terminal and central intrinsically disordered regions, including isoform-variable segments.
- Alternative reading frame micropeptides: activation across low-complexity, disordered coils.

Summary: Acidic, PEST-like low-complexity stretches and related pre-structured helical linkers that act as flexible, interaction-prone modules (e.g., activation/dimerization/adaptor-contact), most often in mid-to-C-terminal regions; the feature can also mark short loop/strand residues bordering catalytic pockets.
Activation pattern: Primarily regional activation across long, continuous E/D- and P/S/T/G-rich segments with low-to-moderate predicted order (intrinsically disordered or marginally alpha-helical), with occasional isolated residue-level peaks in loops or edge beta-strands near active sites.
Exemplars: - Aerobic cobaltochelatase (CobT): strong activation on a long, acidic, disordered C-terminal tail.
- RFX transcription factors: extended C-terminal alpha-helical region beyond the winged-helix DNA-binding domain (likely activation/dimerization module).
- Lon AAA+ protease: a short portion of the long interdomain helix linking the N-terminal and protease domains.
- Phosphoethanolamine transferase (EptC): a single glutamate in a loop at a beta-to-helix junction.
- FAD-linked oxidoreductases (PCMH-type): a glycine in a short loop within the FAD-binding domain.
- DNA ligase I: a single residue on a beta-strand immediately adjacent to the catalytic lysine/ATP-binding site.

Summary: Anionic, low‑complexity intrinsically disordered segments (DE‑rich acidic tracts with poly‑E/DE and PE/EK repeats), typically in soluble non‑cytosolic regions (periplasm, extracellular/ER lumen, mitochondrial intermembrane space) of membrane‑associated and scaffold proteins, and in acidic transcriptional activation/linker tails; characterized by enrichment for E/D/S/T/P/G and low predicted structural order.
Activation pattern: Regional, long contiguous stretches that coincide with annotated compositional bias/IDRs and low structure confidence; little to no activation in transmembrane helices or well‑folded globular domains; occasional weak, isolated peaks in helices only when locally acidic.
Exemplars: - Aerobic cobaltochelatase CobT: strong activation on a C‑terminal acidic, intrinsically disordered segment; no activation on the folded VWFA domain.
- GPI transamidase subunit PIG‑S: activation across a lumenal, low‑confidence region (including an N‑glycosylated site); transmembrane helices and the well‑structured lumenal portion remain inactive.
- MICOS/Mitofilin (Mic60) and TIM44 (mitochondrial inner membrane scaffolds/import): activation on acidic low‑complexity linkers/coiled‑coil‑adjacent regions facing the intermembrane space.
- Gram‑negative cell envelope/secretion assemblies (e.g., secretins, LPS/type II/III/VI components): activation on periplasmic acidic low‑complexity linkers and tails.
- Flagellar/ciliary/axonemal proteins: activation on acidic flexible linkers within stator/assembly/scaffold regions.
- Mediator complex subunit 15 (MED15): activation on the acidic low‑complexity transcriptional activation domain.
- Extracellular matrix/proteoglycan/mucin‑like glycoproteins: activation on Ser/Thr‑rich, acidic, glycosylated low‑complexity stretches in lumenal/extracellular regions.
- Viral acidic glycine‑/DE‑rich proteins: activation on flexible anionic tails and repeats.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low-complexity repeat/linker tracts enriched for polar/charged residues (Q/N/E/D/H/P/R); common in secreted/extracellular or luminal segments and also in cytosolic/nuclear scaffolds; includes His-rich metal-binding patches, Q/N-rich prion-like/repeat modules, and low-complexity propeptides/linkers in secreted enzymes.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long, contiguous low-complexity/repetitive segments; strongest in extracellular/luminal stretches (often following signal peptides) and in flexible linkers or flanking tails of repeat-domain proteins; little or no isolated peaks within structured catalytic cores.
Exemplars:
- Plant hydroxyproline-rich glycoproteins (extensins/PRPs): activation across Tyr/His/Pro-rich repetitive cell-wall regions.
- Histidine-rich secreted proteins and metal-binding patches: activation on His/Gln/Asp/Glu-rich tracts that chelate metals.
- Multi-C2H2 zinc-finger and other His/Cys metal-coordinating proteins: activation on low-complexity His/Gln-rich linkers or repeat arrays adjacent to the fingers rather than the core motifs.
- TALE-like repeat effectors (bacterial): activation along RVD-bearing repeat arrays enriched in polar/acidic residues.
- Plasmodium low-complexity proteins: activation on long Asn/Gln-rich prion-like segments.
- Neuropeptide/peptide-hormone precursors (basal metazoans): activation across Q/R/P-rich low-complexity propeptide regions between cleavage sites.
- Membrane receptors/adhesins and multispan transporters (e.g., MS4A, MFS/FLVCR): activation on luminal/extracellular low-complexity loops.
- Golgi/vesicle-tethering coiled-coil scaffolds (e.g., COG subunits): activation on acidic/Q-rich low-complexity linkers.
- WD-repeat RNA processing/cleavage factors (e.g., WDR33): activation on low-complexity N/C-terminal tails flanking WD propellers.
- Secreted enzymes (e.g., metalloproteinases, acetylcholinesterase): activation on signal-proximal propeptides, glycosylated insertions, or flexible linkers, not the catalytic cores.
- Testis/germline-associated low-complexity proteins: activation on prion-like Q/H/P-rich regions.
- Elastic/repetitive structural proteins (elastin-/resilin-like or repeat-rich linkers): activation on polar/charged, low-complexity repeats.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity tandem‑repeat regions across diverse taxa, with broad activation over polar/Pro/Ser/Thr/Gln/Lys/Tyr/His‑rich repeat tracts including mucin‑like, adhesive, and extensin‑like sequences. The feature fires in both secreted/extracellular precursors and intracellular disordered LCR proteins.
Activation pattern: Broad activation over long tandemly repetitive low‑complexity segments, with periodic residue‑level peaks tracking the repeat unit. Sharp peaks tend to fall on Gln, Lys, His, Arg, or Pro residues at conserved positions within the repeat, and activation spreads across surrounding Pro/Ser/Thr/Gln/Lys/Tyr‑rich tracts; periodic patterns appear when motifs are regularly spaced.
Exemplars: - Adhesive glycoproteins (e.g., mussel foot proteins): widespread activation over Tyr‑ and Lys‑rich low‑complexity decapeptide repeats, with peaks on conserved Lys residues.
- Plant Pro‑rich extensins: broad activation across Pro‑rich tandem repeats with peaks on His/Lys within the repeat unit.
- Fungal collagen‑like Gly‑Gln‑Xaa repeat proteins: periodic peaks on Gln within G‑Q‑I/R/S repeats.
- Trypanosome surface antigens with LTR tandem repeats: activation along disordered polar repeat regions with peaks on His.
- Polar/Q‑rich disordered repeat regions of intracellular proteins (e.g., dynein heavy chain LCR, spermatogenesis‑associated SPATA31H1 P‑S‑E‑R‑S‑H‑H‑S repeats, Filia, polyamine acetyltransferase disordered Q/S/P tracts): broad activation over disordered repeat tracts and basic/acidic clusters despite lacking secretion, reflecting the general LCR signature.

Summary: Feature detects intrinsically disordered, low-complexity acidic/polar segments (enriched in E/D/S/T/Q/P/G) and helix-interrupting linkers at coil–helix boundaries, typically in terminal tails or inter-domain linkers; in more structured proteins it often reduces to single-residue peaks at conserved small or acidic residues positioned in flexible hinges or catalytic P-loop motifs.
Activation pattern: Primarily regional activation across long acidic/polar low-complexity tracts (often Pro-/Gly-/Ser-/Thr-/Gln-rich) and at coiled-coil interruptions or helix–coil junctions; minimal signal in well-ordered cores; secondary behavior of isolated peaks at conserved small (G/A/C) or acidic (D/E) residues near termini, in flexible loops, or at catalytic NTPase motifs.
Exemplars: - Mediator subunit 15 (MED15): strong activation on Q-/S/T-/P-rich disordered segments and at kinks/interruptions within a coiled-coil.
- Magnesium chelatase subunit ChlD: activation confined to a C-terminal Pro-rich, acidic low-complexity disordered tail, peaking on acidic residues.
- Dentin phosphoproteins (DSPP/DPP, DMP1): long S-rich acidic intrinsically disordered extracellular regions.
- Plant-pathogen harpins: Gly/Ser/Thr-repetitive low-complexity secreted segments.
- Membrane protein insertases YidC/ALB3 and TIM44: short disordered tails or helix-edge sites with single-site peaks (often a conserved Cys or acidic residue) near the C-terminus.
- RNase E/G endoribonucleases: single-residue activation around a conserved N-terminal glycine in a flexible segment.
- Dynamin-related/Mx P-loop NTPases: peaks on the conserved Walker-B Asp/Glu and nearby acidic loop positions within the NTPase core.
- Exosome 3′–5′ exonucleases (DIS3/Dis3L2): single alanine peaks in flexible C-terminal tails.
- Aconitase enzymes: scattered weak activations in flexible loop regions.
- Ion channels and other large membrane assemblies: acidic low-complexity cytoplasmic/extracellular loops or terminal tails.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity regions enriched in serine, threonine, proline and polar/charged residues—flexible regulatory linkers/tails and propeptide segments that often host short linear motifs (e.g., phosphorylation- and proline‑rich motifs) and proteolytic processing sites; signal is absent from well‑folded catalytic domains and is common across taxa
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long disordered stretches with many sparse residue‑level peaks; avoids structured domains; peaks biased toward S/T/P, glycine, and charged/polar residues; frequently concentrated in N‑ or C‑terminal IDRs and around cleavage/processing sites; can span hundreds of residues in large eukaryotic proteins
Exemplars: - PAK family serine/threonine kinases: activation on the N‑terminal regulatory IDR preceding the kinase domain (including low‑confidence helical propensities), not in the folded kinase domain.
- Rap/Ras GTPase‑activating proteins: activation on disordered, low‑complexity linkers; absent from the structured GAP domain.
- CARMIL (actin/capping protein regulators): activation on a C‑terminal proline/basic‑rich disordered tail.
- Centrosomal/kinetochore and chromosomal scaffold proteins: multiple low‑complexity, disordered tracts with scattered peaks.
- Transcriptional/chromatin regulators: activation on N‑terminal low‑complexity/activation domains and compositionally biased regions.
- Ribonucleotide reductase large subunit‑like proteins: activation on N‑terminal disordered tails, including proline‑rich segments.
- Neuropeptide/prohormone precursors: activation in disordered propeptides and at termini of amidated peptides, often adjacent to cleavage sites.

Summary: Residue positions that mark polypeptide boundaries—especially the absolute N-terminus (position 1) and the terminal residue of sequence fragments—and, secondarily, isolated boundary-like sites within larger proteins (e.g., short linkers between secondary-structure elements or helix/turn cap-like positions), consistent with proteolytic processing junctions in pre/propeptides.
Activation pattern: Predominantly single-residue peaks at sequence extremities (most often the first residue; also the last residue of fragments); sparse internal single-residue peaks at boundary-like positions (short linkers or transitions between secondary structures). Often coincides with disordered/low-confidence termini; in secreted/toxin precursors a recurring window around residues ~50–70 is consistent with signal/propeptide cleavage. Per-protein activations are usually one or a few sites.
Exemplars: Snake venom serine protease: peaks at the N-terminal first residue and at the C-terminal end of the chain; Nuclear pore complex protein Nup155: isolated peaks on single residues within a helix and a low-confidence turn; U4/U6.U5 tri-snRNP–associated protein 1: single-residue peak at a glycine linker between β-strands; E4 ubiquitin-conjugation factor (UBE4): isolated methionine within a long α-helix; Reelin (fragment): strong activation at the fragment’s C-terminal residue in a disordered region; Glutamate dehydrogenase (fragment): activation marks the truncated C-terminal residue.

Summary: Low-complexity, intrinsically disordered or signal/transmembrane–proximal segments—often N‑terminal—commonly enriched in H/Q/Y/W but not exclusively, acting as generic interaction/activation modules in small regulatory/viral proteins and in secreted/membrane-linked precursors
Activation pattern: Regional activation across extended low‑complexity stretches or N‑terminal signal/TM-adjacent regions; per‑residue preference for H/Q with contributions from Y/W, but tolerant of basic- or serine‑rich tracts found in viral accessory proteins and secreted precursors
Exemplars:
- Viral accessory/regulatory proteins (e.g., Rex, agnoproteins): activation over N‑terminal basic/low‑complexity tails (may lack H/Q bias)
- Eukaryotic sORF/micropeptides and apoptosis/testis-linked proteins: activation across low‑complexity IDRs, often H/Q/Y‑rich when present
- Secreted precursors and extracellular peptides (e.g., plant SCOOPs, protease propeptides): activation on signal peptides/propeptides or serine‑rich low‑complexity regions
- Small membrane proteins/channels (e.g., FluC) and proteolipids (e.g., neuronatin): activation at N‑terminal low‑complexity loops or signal/TM-proximal regions
- Histidine‑rich metal‑binding/antimicrobial tracts: activation on poly‑His/His‑biased regions when present

Summary: Short hydrophobic, amphipathic, or basic/proline-rich segments associated with membrane targeting or low-complexity regions in diverse proteins, including Sec-type signal peptides, signal anchors, and transmembrane helices, plus disordered basic/proline-rich stretches in soluble proteins (including viral regulatory and capsid proteins).
Activation pattern: Regional activation can occur on N-terminal signal peptides or signal-anchor helices (often within the first 10-35 residues), on internal or C-terminal transmembrane helices, and on internal or C-terminal disordered segments enriched in proline, polar, or basic residues.
Exemplars:
- Viral envelope glycoproteins and viroporins: activation on N-terminal signal peptides or signal-anchor helices, with additional peaks on internal/C-terminal TM helices.
- Oomycete RxLR effectors: activation on the N-terminal secretory signal peptide upstream of RxLR.
- Plant small secreted defense/signaling peptides (defensins, RALF, CLE/CEP): activation on prepropeptide signal peptides.
- Human germline/testis-associated and cancer–testis antigen membrane/secreted proteins (including GPI precursors): activation on N-terminal signal peptides/signal anchors.
- Immune pathway proteins (cytokines/chemokines, immunoglobulin fragments): activation on secretory signal peptides.
- Mitochondrial/chloroplast precursors: activation on N-terminal transit peptides (Arg-rich amphipathic helices).
- Tail-anchored/peripheral membrane apoptosis factors (e.g., BH3-only like PUMA): activation on C-terminal tail-anchor helices.
- Viral accessory/regulatory and capsid/coating proteins: activation on short basic or proline-rich segments at N-termini or internal disordered regions.
- Bacterial exported proteins and lipoproteins: activation on Sec-type signal peptides.
- Large bacterial enzymes and DNA recombinases: occasional activation on internal low-complexity or polar/acidic stretches.

Summary: Short basic (Lys/Arg-rich) cationic motifs used for protein routing, processing, and nucleic-acid/host targeting — including secretory signal-peptide regions, organellar transit peptides, dibasic propeptide cleavage sites, and NLS-like basic clusters.
Activation pattern: Regional activation centered on Lys/Arg-rich clusters, often flanked by small residues (Ala/Ser/Gly) around processing/cleavage positions. Peaks frequently occur at N-termini but also within internal basic clusters (NLS-like motifs, propeptide processing sites, basic cytoplasmic tails). In very short proteins the activation can span much of the sequence.
Exemplars:
- Secreted hormone/neuropeptide precursors: activation over signal peptide and at dibasic KR/RR processing sites within the propeptide and mature peptide.
- Viral envelope glycoproteins: activation on signal peptide or signal-anchor with a positively charged n-region; can highlight proximal basic proprotein-convertase motifs.
- Viral accessory/regulatory proteins: activation on Lys/Arg-rich basic clusters and NLS-like motifs used for host targeting (often internal, e.g. lentiviral Tat NLS, polyomavirus agnoprotein basic cluster).
- ATP synthase epsilon (mitochondrial forms): activation on the N-terminal mitochondrial targeting presequence.
- tRNA/rRNA m7G methyltransferases and TilS: activation on N-terminal organellar transit peptides in eukaryotes (mitochondria/plastids) or on basic RNA-binding N-terminal tails in prokaryotes.
- Lipoate biosynthesis/lipoylation enzymes: activation on mitochondrial/chloroplast transit peptides directing enzymes to the organelle where lipoylation occurs.
- Membrane transporters and other membrane-associated proteins: activation on signal anchors with positively charged n-regions.
- Plant proteins and plant-pathogen effectors: activation on secretory signal peptides and basic host-targeting motifs (e.g., RxLR-like) located just after the signal peptide.
- Proteases and protease-related secreted proteins: activation on the secretory signal peptide and basic propeptide processing motifs.
- Ribosome-related proteins/modifiers: activation on short basic segments (often nucleic acid-binding/NLS-like).
- Uncharacterized micropeptides/lncRNA-encoded peptides: activation across short basic regions consistent with leader/targeting-like segments.
