Summary: Residue positions that mark polypeptide boundaries—especially the absolute N-terminus (position 1) and the terminal residue of sequence fragments—and, secondarily, isolated boundary-like sites within larger proteins (e.g., short linkers between secondary-structure elements or helix/turn cap-like positions), consistent with proteolytic processing junctions in pre/propeptides.
Activation pattern: Predominantly single-residue peaks at sequence extremities (most often the first residue; also the last residue of fragments); sparse internal single-residue peaks at boundary-like positions (short linkers or transitions between secondary structures). Often coincides with disordered/low-confidence termini; in secreted/toxin precursors a recurring window around residues ~50–70 is consistent with signal/propeptide cleavage. Per-protein activations are usually one or a few sites.
Exemplars: Snake venom serine protease: peaks at the N-terminal first residue and at the C-terminal end of the chain; Nuclear pore complex protein Nup155: isolated peaks on single residues within a helix and a low-confidence turn; U4/U6.U5 tri-snRNP–associated protein 1: single-residue peak at a glycine linker between β-strands; E4 ubiquitin-conjugation factor (UBE4): isolated methionine within a long α-helix; Reelin (fragment): strong activation at the fragment’s C-terminal residue in a disordered region; Glutamate dehydrogenase (fragment): activation marks the truncated C-terminal residue.

Summary: Low-complexity, intrinsically disordered or signal/transmembrane–proximal segments—often N‑terminal—commonly enriched in H/Q/Y/W but not exclusively, acting as generic interaction/activation modules in small regulatory/viral proteins and in secreted/membrane-linked precursors
Activation pattern: Regional activation across extended low‑complexity stretches or N‑terminal signal/TM-adjacent regions; per‑residue preference for H/Q with contributions from Y/W, but tolerant of basic- or serine‑rich tracts found in viral accessory proteins and secreted precursors
Exemplars:
- Viral accessory/regulatory proteins (e.g., Rex, agnoproteins): activation over N‑terminal basic/low‑complexity tails (may lack H/Q bias)
- Eukaryotic sORF/micropeptides and apoptosis/testis-linked proteins: activation across low‑complexity IDRs, often H/Q/Y‑rich when present
- Secreted precursors and extracellular peptides (e.g., plant SCOOPs, protease propeptides): activation on signal peptides/propeptides or serine‑rich low‑complexity regions
- Small membrane proteins/channels (e.g., FluC) and proteolipids (e.g., neuronatin): activation at N‑terminal low‑complexity loops or signal/TM-proximal regions
- Histidine‑rich metal‑binding/antimicrobial tracts: activation on poly‑His/His‑biased regions when present

Summary: Detector of compositionally biased, low‑complexity segments—predominantly intrinsically disordered Ser/Thr‑rich (often RS-/Pro‑containing) tracts—with a strong N‑terminal bias; it also flags the extreme N‑terminus including signal peptides of secreted precursors.
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks clustered within long disordered/low‑complexity regions (often spanning tens to hundreds of residues), with strongest peaks on Ser/Thr and nearby polar/basic residues; broad regional activation across such IDRs and minimal signal in well‑folded domains or transmembranes; additional discrete peaks frequently occur at residues 1–10, including within N‑terminal signal peptides.
Exemplars: - Transcriptional regulator (CROC-4): multiple peaks across a central low‑complexity disordered segment (S/T/R/P‑rich), with minor N‑terminal peaks.
- Mechanosensory receptor (Stum): numerous high peaks on serines dispersed through annotated disordered, low‑complexity/polar regions.
- Yeast RNA/chromatin‑associated factor (REF2‑interacting protein): peaks within disordered, compositionally biased tracts; strongest at a threonine in an S/T‑rich context, near (but not exactly on) annotated phosphosites.
- Secreted antimicrobial peptide precursor (lumbricin): strongest activation on the N‑terminal signal peptide helix; weaker peaks just after the signal peptide preceding a long disordered pro‑region.
- Yeast HPH2 regulatory protein: activation confined to disordered, low‑complexity regions in the N‑terminal two‑thirds; absent from the structured C‑terminal domain and its transmembrane helix.

Summary: Short basic (Lys/Arg-rich) cationic motifs used for protein routing, processing, and nucleic-acid/host targeting — including secretory signal-peptide regions, organellar transit peptides, dibasic propeptide cleavage sites, and NLS-like basic clusters.
Activation pattern: Regional activation centered on Lys/Arg-rich clusters, often flanked by small residues (Ala/Ser/Gly) around processing/cleavage positions. Peaks frequently occur at N-termini but also within internal basic clusters (NLS-like motifs, propeptide processing sites, basic cytoplasmic tails). In very short proteins the activation can span much of the sequence.
Exemplars:
- Secreted hormone/neuropeptide precursors: activation over signal peptide and at dibasic KR/RR processing sites within the propeptide and mature peptide.
- Viral envelope glycoproteins: activation on signal peptide or signal-anchor with a positively charged n-region; can highlight proximal basic proprotein-convertase motifs.
- Viral accessory/regulatory proteins: activation on Lys/Arg-rich basic clusters and NLS-like motifs used for host targeting (often internal, e.g. lentiviral Tat NLS, polyomavirus agnoprotein basic cluster).
- ATP synthase epsilon (mitochondrial forms): activation on the N-terminal mitochondrial targeting presequence.
- tRNA/rRNA m7G methyltransferases and TilS: activation on N-terminal organellar transit peptides in eukaryotes (mitochondria/plastids) or on basic RNA-binding N-terminal tails in prokaryotes.
- Lipoate biosynthesis/lipoylation enzymes: activation on mitochondrial/chloroplast transit peptides directing enzymes to the organelle where lipoylation occurs.
- Membrane transporters and other membrane-associated proteins: activation on signal anchors with positively charged n-regions.
- Plant proteins and plant-pathogen effectors: activation on secretory signal peptides and basic host-targeting motifs (e.g., RxLR-like) located just after the signal peptide.
- Proteases and protease-related secreted proteins: activation on the secretory signal peptide and basic propeptide processing motifs.
- Ribosome-related proteins/modifiers: activation on short basic segments (often nucleic acid-binding/NLS-like).
- Uncharacterized micropeptides/lncRNA-encoded peptides: activation across short basic regions consistent with leader/targeting-like segments.

Summary: Low-complexity Pro/Leu/Gln-rich patches in solvent-exposed regions of secreted/effector proteins—often downstream of signal peptides and including basic or aromatic-sprinkled stretches—that mediate adhesion, membrane association, and host–pathogen/immune-modulatory interactions.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks concentrated in short clustered stretches in regions downstream of signal peptides in secreted proteins; can occur in hydrophobic Leu/Pro-rich or basic clusters; weak over hydrophobic signal peptides; variable number of clusters per protein.
Exemplars:
- Serpin antithrombin: activation on the N-terminal basic patch mediating heparin binding; signal peptide shows little activation.
- Viral proteins (envelope and accessory): activation on polybasic PR/QR-rich segments that bind host glycosaminoglycans or acidic membranes (e.g., GP4; ORF9c basic tails).
- Oomycete RxLR effectors: activation around the RxLR motif and downstream Leu/Pro-rich stretches in secreted effector precursors.
- Secreted precursors and micropeptides (chemokines, antimicrobial/cell-penetrating peptides, hormone propeptides; mucin-like caseins): activation on cationic, aromatic-sprinkled low-complexity stretches engaging proteoglycans or acidic membranes.
- DNA/RNA-binding microproteins and enzymes: activation on terminal/basic patches contacting nucleic acids (e.g., killin; bacterial tRNA m7G methyltransferases).
- Soluble metabolic enzymes: occasional activation at exposed basic clusters that bind phosphate-containing ligands (e.g., riboflavin kinase).
- Membrane-associated proteins/receptors: activation on luminal or cytosolic basic patches used for proteoglycan binding or membrane association (e.g., DEspR-like receptors, neuronatin).
- Reproductive/testis-associated proteins: activation on arginine/proline-rich low-complexity regions mediating polyanion-dependent interactions in the reproductive tract.

Summary: Low-complexity, intrinsically disordered segments—often at protein N-termini—such as mucin-like/propeptide regions or flexible linkers adjacent to signal/transit peptides, common in small secreted or membrane-associated proteins and also as disordered extensions in diverse enzymes (broad taxonomic coverage, including viral, bacterial, and eukaryotic proteins).
Activation pattern: Regional activation over short to moderate stretches, frequently in disordered or polar/low-complexity segments; in longer proteins, multiple low-complexity patches can activate; in micropeptides, activation can span much of the sequence. Residue-level peaks can fall on Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly within polar-residue stretches but also on basic or hydrophobic residues within the same disordered context.
Exemplars:
- Viral envelope/accessory microproteins: activation on N-terminal Ser/Thr/Pro-rich disordered segments (often mucin-like or regulatory tails).
- Secreted eukaryotic effectors (e.g., oomycete RxLR effectors): activation on the low-complexity region flanking the signal peptide/RxLR motif.
- Human testis-biased and lncRNA-derived micropeptides: activation across intrinsically disordered peptide regions.
- Secreted precursors/propeptides: activation on N-terminal regions following the signal peptide.
- Membrane-associated single-pass proteins: activation on luminal or cytosolic tails flanking the transmembrane helix.
- Bacterial/archaeal metabolic enzymes: activation on disordered, low-complexity N-terminal extensions/linkers enriched in Ser/Thr/Gly/Pro.

Summary: Short segments within disordered and compositionally biased stretches of diverse proteins, particularly regions enriched in basic and acidic residues. Activations are also seen in non-disordered contexts across proteins of varied function, suggesting the feature captures a relatively broad local sequence pattern rather than a tight structural motif.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks with small clusters, distributed throughout the length of the protein. Peaks frequently overlap annotated disordered regions and basic/acidic compositionally biased segments, but also occur at isolated positions within structured chains; occurs in both helical and coil contexts.
Exemplars: - Oomycete RxLR secreted effectors: peaks within the mature effector chain, with occasional spikes in the signal peptide.
- Plant CLE peptide precursors: localized peaks within the C-terminal CLE motif corresponding to the mature signaling peptide.
- Cholecystokinin prohormone: peaks at or immediately adjacent to the N-termini of mature neuropeptides generated by proteolytic processing.
- Herpesvirus ICP47-like small accessory proteins: multiple peaks in the N-terminal active helical region and in polar, disordered C-terminal stretches.
- Keratin-associated proteins: activation across cysteine/proline/serine-rich, low-complexity repeat regions.
- Phosphodiesterase and fungal/bacterial enzymes with disordered N- or internal stretches: peaks within basic-and-acidic compositionally biased segments.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low-complexity segments enriched in serine/threonine/proline/glycine and often basic (lysine/arginine), typically found in flexible N- or C-terminal tails and loops; highlights IDRs that may harbor short linear motifs (e.g., basic NLS patches) rather than structured domain cores.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long disordered stretches with additional sparse residue-level peaks in low-confidence loops; often N-terminal-biased in short/viral proteins; rarely within well-folded cores.
Exemplars: Retroviral accessory proteins (e.g., HTLV-1 p30): activation on central and C-terminal IDRs including a basic nuclear localization signal; p53-regulated apoptosis-inducing microprotein: widespread activation across a globally disordered protein; Bacterial DNA ligase: scattered activation in an annotated disordered linker and flexible loops within the ligase domain; Uncharacterized human microprotein: multiple peaks throughout a low-pLDDT, disordered sequence irrespective of predicted secondary structure.

Summary: Small, often poorly characterized or compositionally biased proteins, including viral accessory proteins, cancer/testis and germline-associated proteins, antisense-ORF microproteins, and short secreted/surface peptides; activation is broadly distributed across the polypeptide rather than focused on a single structured domain
Activation pattern: Regional/distributed activation spread across much of the protein with sparse residue-level peaks; often includes early N-terminal residues and disordered segments; variable coverage from short patches to most of the protein
Exemplars:
- Viral non-structural/accessory proteins: activation distributed through the protein, including basic/Arg-rich motifs such as nuclear localization signals.
- Cancer/testis antigens and germline-associated proteins: activation on long disordered low-complexity regions, often at N-termini.
- Small uncharacterized microproteins/antisense ORFs: activation spanning most of the polypeptide.
- Short secreted peptides and toxin precursors: activation across both signal/propeptide and mature regions.
- Compact cytosolic proteins with disordered N- or C-terminal extensions: activation enriched on the disordered tails.

Summary: N‑terminal start and proteolytic maturation junction detector: activates on the initiator methionine or the first residue of a newly formed mature peptide after signal peptide/propeptide cleavage, typically within low‑complexity, disordered segments enriched in Ser/Pro/Gly/Arg; most prominent in secreted and membrane precursors and small peptides, but also marking N‑termini of diverse proteins (including many viral proteins) across taxa.
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks at the exact boundary (the first residue of the mature peptide and/or the immediately preceding residue), with short flanking N‑terminal stretches in low‑complexity IDRs; occasional weaker N‑terminal peaks elsewhere; broad, low‑specificity activation across taxa.
Exemplars: Plant PROPEP/Pep danger‑peptide precursors: strong peak at the N‑terminal boundary of the mature Pep within a disordered, acidic/basic‑biased prodomain; Viral envelope glycoproteins (e.g., class I fusion proteins): activation at signal peptide cleavage and/or polybasic convertase junctions, and at the extreme N‑terminus; Secreted hormone/neuropeptide and growth factor precursors: activation at propeptide removal sites that define the N‑terminus of the active peptide; Type I membrane receptors and secretory pathway glycoproteins: initiator Met and signal peptide region/cleavage site highlighted; lncRNA‑encoded micropeptides/smORFs: activation at Met1 and adjacent low‑complexity N‑terminal residues; Sperm/testis secreted or acrosomal proteins: activation on N‑terminal signal/pro‑region cleavage junctions; Bacterial/archaeal metabolic enzymes: weaker, generic N‑terminal activation at the start of disordered/low‑complexity tails; p53/apoptosis‑related proteins: N‑terminal disordered domains (e.g., transactivation/pro‑segments) show start‑proximal peaks.

Summary: Methionine residue identity, with a strong bias toward the N‑terminal initiator Met and early hydrophobic N‑terminal segments; generally fires on Met in diverse structural/functional contexts and is largely structure-agnostic.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks centered on Met; often includes the initiator Met at position 1 and occasionally nearby bulky hydrophobic/aromatic residues (W, V, L, I; sometimes T, C). Typically only a few residues per protein are active, with a tendency to cluster near the N-terminus but also occurring on internal Met.
Exemplars: - cAMP-specific phosphodiesterase (PDE4A) fragment: exclusive activation on multiple internal Met residues independent of secondary structure or disorder.
- Secreted precursors (hormones, toxins, bacteriocins): activation on the initiator Met of the signal peptide/propeptide.
- Viral accessory/immune-modulatory proteins: short, N-terminally focused activation on M1 and occasional internal Met.
- Membrane-associated proteins (signal anchors/transmembrane leaders): activation on the N-terminal Met and Met within early hydrophobic segments.
- Human microproteins and testis/spermatogenesis-related proteins: sparse activation on M1 and any internal Met in short proteins.
- Glycoprotein precursors: activation on the initiator Met at the start of signal peptides.

Summary: Residue positions that mark polypeptide boundaries—especially the absolute N-terminus (position 1) and the terminal residue of sequence fragments—and, secondarily, isolated boundary-like sites within larger proteins (e.g., short linkers between secondary-structure elements or helix/turn cap-like positions), consistent with proteolytic processing junctions in pre/propeptides.
Activation pattern: Predominantly single-residue peaks at sequence extremities (most often the first residue; also the last residue of fragments); sparse internal single-residue peaks at boundary-like positions (short linkers or transitions between secondary structures). Often coincides with disordered/low-confidence termini; in secreted/toxin precursors a recurring window around residues ~50–70 is consistent with signal/propeptide cleavage. Per-protein activations are usually one or a few sites.
Exemplars: Snake venom serine protease: peaks at the N-terminal first residue and at the C-terminal end of the chain; Nuclear pore complex protein Nup155: isolated peaks on single residues within a helix and a low-confidence turn; U4/U6.U5 tri-snRNP–associated protein 1: single-residue peak at a glycine linker between β-strands; E4 ubiquitin-conjugation factor (UBE4): isolated methionine within a long α-helix; Reelin (fragment): strong activation at the fragment’s C-terminal residue in a disordered region; Glutamate dehydrogenase (fragment): activation marks the truncated C-terminal residue.

Summary: Residue-level detector that fires sparsely in small proteins, peptide precursors, and disordered/loosely structured regions, often in propeptide or disordered C-/N-terminal segments; avoids structured catalytic cores and binding sites.
Activation pattern: Sparse residue-level peaks, often in small (sub-200 aa) proteins or within annotated disordered regions of larger proteins; for larger enzymes peaks cluster in the N-terminal extension well away from catalytic/binding residues. Peak residues are heterogeneous (aromatic, charged, and polar residues all occur).
Exemplars: - tRNA (pseudouridine(54)-N1)-methyltransferase: activation restricted to the disordered N-terminal extension (e.g., a peak in a short transient helix), absent from the SAM-dependent catalytic domain
- Secreted bacterial protease: strong activation in disordered N- and C-terminal tails, none across the structured protease core
- Neuropeptide/prohormone precursor (Amnesiac): isolated peak within the disordered C-terminal propeptide region
- Antisense-encoded microprotein (TAR1): peaks including one within the annotated C-terminal disordered region
- Proapoptotic nucleolar protein: peaks within a broad C-terminal IDR, including near a nucleolar localization segment

Summary: Single conserved residue—often hydrophobic/aromatic but variable (Phe/Tyr/Trp/Leu/Val/Ile, and sometimes His/Thr)—within nucleotide- or ligand-binding pockets and analogous buried sites across diverse folds; in non-nucleotide proteins it maps to an analogous internal pocket- or core-lining position.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks at an internal pocket-lining residue, occasionally with short adjacent clusters; position varies widely with the fold.
Exemplars:
- Protein kinases (including viral/atypical): activation within the kinase domain at a residue near the ATP-binding cleft.
- tRNA (guanine-N7)-methyltransferases (class I SAM MTases): activation on the conserved aromatic that stacks with the SAM adenine and/or the target guanine in the active site.
- UDP-sugar glycosyltransferases for LPS/teichoic acid/lipid A biosynthesis (GT-B fold): activation on the aromatic that stacks with the UDP uracil ring in the donor-binding site.
- NAD(P)-dependent dehydrogenases (Rossmann fold): activation on an adenine-stacking Phe/Tyr in the dinucleotide-binding pocket.
- MurE (UDP-MurNAc-tripeptide synthetase; ATP-grasp ligase): activation on a buried hydrophobe that helps form the adenine-binding cleft for ATP.
- Carbonic anhydrases: activation on a conserved hydrophobic/aromatic residue lining the active-site hydrophobic pocket adjacent to the catalytic zinc.
- Small ribosomal subunit protein S8: activation on an aromatic residue that base-stacks with rRNA or stabilizes the RNA-binding surface.
- MICOS subunit Mic60 (mitofilin): activation on a buried aromatic within the coiled-coil/mitofilin scaffold that stabilizes the membrane-associated core.

Summary: Short stretches within small, often low-complexity or disordered proteins—sometimes in N-terminal or propeptide regions, sometimes in internal segments of mature chains—common across taxa (including viral regulatory proteins and eukaryotic propeptides).
Activation pattern: Sparse residue-level peaks scattered along compact small proteins, frequently in disordered or coil segments but also in interior regions of mature chains; activations are typically a few isolated residues rather than contiguous blocks.
Exemplars: - Viral regulatory proteins: peaks distributed across the chain, including compositionally biased polar/basic patches.
- Small secreted or propeptide-containing factors: clustered peaks within propeptide and adjacent regions.
- Compact, low-complexity uncharacterized proteins: scattered peaks across the chain.

Summary: Residue positions that mark polypeptide boundaries—especially the absolute N-terminus (position 1) and the terminal residue of sequence fragments—and, secondarily, isolated boundary-like sites within larger proteins (e.g., short linkers between secondary-structure elements or helix/turn cap-like positions), consistent with proteolytic processing junctions in pre/propeptides.
Activation pattern: Predominantly single-residue peaks at sequence extremities (most often the first residue; also the last residue of fragments); sparse internal single-residue peaks at boundary-like positions (short linkers or transitions between secondary structures). Often coincides with disordered/low-confidence termini; in secreted/toxin precursors a recurring window around residues ~50–70 is consistent with signal/propeptide cleavage. Per-protein activations are usually one or a few sites.
Exemplars: Snake venom serine protease: peaks at the N-terminal first residue and at the C-terminal end of the chain; Nuclear pore complex protein Nup155: isolated peaks on single residues within a helix and a low-confidence turn; U4/U6.U5 tri-snRNP–associated protein 1: single-residue peak at a glycine linker between β-strands; E4 ubiquitin-conjugation factor (UBE4): isolated methionine within a long α-helix; Reelin (fragment): strong activation at the fragment’s C-terminal residue in a disordered region; Glutamate dehydrogenase (fragment): activation marks the truncated C-terminal residue.

Summary: Ala/Thr-enriched composition feature with a bias for low-complexity intrinsically disordered regions and N-terminal prepro/signal-peptide segments; the feature reflects small-residue (A/T, secondarily S/P) composition often in flexible regions but also appears at A/T residues in some structured contexts.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks on A and T that frequently cluster within coil-rich, disordered regions—often in the first ~30 residues—and can extend across unstructured precursor segments; activation concentrates at or near signal peptide regions when present, but can also occur at A/T residues within folded domains.
Exemplars: - Antimicrobial peptide precursors: strong activation within the N-terminal signal peptide, including the Thr at the signal peptidase cleavage position (-1), and nearby Ala in the nascent mature N-terminus.
- Secreted serine proteases: activation on Ala/Thr residues that can occur both in the unstructured prepro region and within the folded peptidase domain.
- Apoptosis-related regulatory proteins: A/T peaks within N-terminal interaction/regulatory regions.
- Transcriptional regulators (e.g., CROC-4-like): A/T-biased peaks within annotated low-complexity/disordered stretches and adjacent flexible regions.
- Telomere-associated proteins: N-terminal disordered helix/coil segments with clustered Thr peaks and additional A/T peaks in other low-confidence regions.
- Small disordered microproteins: isolated A/T peaks distributed throughout largely disordered sequences, especially in annotated disordered termini.

Summary: Low-complexity and disordered segments including N-terminal targeting/signal peptides and secretory propeptides, as well as small basic/Pro-enriched proteins and surface loops/insertions of larger enzymes
Activation pattern: Regional activation appearing as clusters of residue-level peaks across low-complexity or disordered stretches, including N-terminal targeting/signal peptides and secretory propeptides; also isolated short peaks within surface loops or domain insertions of otherwise structured enzymes
Exemplars: - Viral accessory/membrane proteins (e.g., gN-type): activation on mucin-like, S/T-rich luminal loops flanking a transmembrane helix
- Viral regulatory proteins (e.g., E4-ORF6, ICP47): multiple peaks within intrinsically disordered regulatory segments (often S/T/Pro-enriched)
- Human p53-target/lncRNA-associated proteins (e.g., TP53TG3, CASC2-derived): globally disordered, low-complexity patches highlighted
- Secreted bioactive peptide precursors (e.g., bombesin-type, conotoxin prepropeptides): activation on signal/propeptide low-complexity segments
- Bacterial metabolic enzymes/ligases: sporadic peaks on surface loops or non-catalytic domain insertions

Summary: Short, low‑complexity interaction segments enriched in Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly (often with nearby Lys/Arg), typically intrinsically disordered, frequently near N‑termini and harboring regulatory PTM sites; the feature also highlights analogous short cationic helices used for molecular interactions (e.g., HTH DNA‑binding helices and amphipathic antimicrobial peptides).
Activation pattern: Predominantly sparse, residue‑level peaks within disordered/low‑complexity stretches (often N‑terminal and PTM‑prone), with occasional single‑residue peaks inside short helices involved in DNA binding or membrane‑active peptides; variable extent per protein.
Exemplars: Herpesvirus ICP4–type transcription factors: peaks on Ser/Thr and basic residues within disordered, low‑complexity regions; Homeobox transcription factors (e.g., Nkx6.1): peaks in disordered regulatory tails flanking the homeodomain, including annotated PTM sites; Cancer/testis microproteins (X antigen family): N‑terminal Ser/Thr residues in disordered regions, including a phosphoserine and proximity to a SUMOylation site; ECF sigma factors (SigM): single‑residue peak within the helix‑turn‑helix recognition helix of sigma‑70 domain 4; Antimicrobial peptides (Ixosin): peaks in the mature amphipathic helical peptide, including residues at the helix start and internal S/N positions.

Summary: Short basic (Lys/Arg-rich) cationic motifs used for protein routing, processing, and nucleic-acid/host targeting — including secretory signal-peptide regions, organellar transit peptides, dibasic propeptide cleavage sites, and NLS-like basic clusters.
Activation pattern: Regional activation centered on Lys/Arg-rich clusters, often flanked by small residues (Ala/Ser/Gly) around processing/cleavage positions. Peaks frequently occur at N-termini but also within internal basic clusters (NLS-like motifs, propeptide processing sites, basic cytoplasmic tails). In very short proteins the activation can span much of the sequence.
Exemplars:
- Secreted hormone/neuropeptide precursors: activation over signal peptide and at dibasic KR/RR processing sites within the propeptide and mature peptide.
- Viral envelope glycoproteins: activation on signal peptide or signal-anchor with a positively charged n-region; can highlight proximal basic proprotein-convertase motifs.
- Viral accessory/regulatory proteins: activation on Lys/Arg-rich basic clusters and NLS-like motifs used for host targeting (often internal, e.g. lentiviral Tat NLS, polyomavirus agnoprotein basic cluster).
- ATP synthase epsilon (mitochondrial forms): activation on the N-terminal mitochondrial targeting presequence.
- tRNA/rRNA m7G methyltransferases and TilS: activation on N-terminal organellar transit peptides in eukaryotes (mitochondria/plastids) or on basic RNA-binding N-terminal tails in prokaryotes.
- Lipoate biosynthesis/lipoylation enzymes: activation on mitochondrial/chloroplast transit peptides directing enzymes to the organelle where lipoylation occurs.
- Membrane transporters and other membrane-associated proteins: activation on signal anchors with positively charged n-regions.
- Plant proteins and plant-pathogen effectors: activation on secretory signal peptides and basic host-targeting motifs (e.g., RxLR-like) located just after the signal peptide.
- Proteases and protease-related secreted proteins: activation on the secretory signal peptide and basic propeptide processing motifs.
- Ribosome-related proteins/modifiers: activation on short basic segments (often nucleic acid-binding/NLS-like).
- Uncharacterized micropeptides/lncRNA-encoded peptides: activation across short basic regions consistent with leader/targeting-like segments.

Summary: Residue positions that mark polypeptide boundaries—especially the absolute N-terminus (position 1) and the terminal residue of sequence fragments—and, secondarily, isolated boundary-like sites within larger proteins (e.g., short linkers between secondary-structure elements or helix/turn cap-like positions), consistent with proteolytic processing junctions in pre/propeptides.
Activation pattern: Predominantly single-residue peaks at sequence extremities (most often the first residue; also the last residue of fragments); sparse internal single-residue peaks at boundary-like positions (short linkers or transitions between secondary structures). Often coincides with disordered/low-confidence termini; in secreted/toxin precursors a recurring window around residues ~50–70 is consistent with signal/propeptide cleavage. Per-protein activations are usually one or a few sites.
Exemplars: Snake venom serine protease: peaks at the N-terminal first residue and at the C-terminal end of the chain; Nuclear pore complex protein Nup155: isolated peaks on single residues within a helix and a low-confidence turn; U4/U6.U5 tri-snRNP–associated protein 1: single-residue peak at a glycine linker between β-strands; E4 ubiquitin-conjugation factor (UBE4): isolated methionine within a long α-helix; Reelin (fragment): strong activation at the fragment’s C-terminal residue in a disordered region; Glutamate dehydrogenase (fragment): activation marks the truncated C-terminal residue.

Summary: Methionine residue identity, with a strong bias toward the N‑terminal initiator Met and early hydrophobic N‑terminal segments; generally fires on Met in diverse structural/functional contexts and is largely structure-agnostic.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks centered on Met; often includes the initiator Met at position 1 and occasionally nearby bulky hydrophobic/aromatic residues (W, V, L, I; sometimes T, C). Typically only a few residues per protein are active, with a tendency to cluster near the N-terminus but also occurring on internal Met.
Exemplars: - cAMP-specific phosphodiesterase (PDE4A) fragment: exclusive activation on multiple internal Met residues independent of secondary structure or disorder.
- Secreted precursors (hormones, toxins, bacteriocins): activation on the initiator Met of the signal peptide/propeptide.
- Viral accessory/immune-modulatory proteins: short, N-terminally focused activation on M1 and occasional internal Met.
- Membrane-associated proteins (signal anchors/transmembrane leaders): activation on the N-terminal Met and Met within early hydrophobic segments.
- Human microproteins and testis/spermatogenesis-related proteins: sparse activation on M1 and any internal Met in short proteins.
- Glycoprotein precursors: activation on the initiator Met at the start of signal peptides.

Summary: Position-driven detector of the extreme protein N-terminus—especially residues 2–5—largely independent of amino-acid identity, typically in short, unstructured signal/leader-like segments; also fires on analogous newly formed N-termini within precursors (e.g., mature peptide starts). Common across taxa, with strong representation in viral accessory proteins, secreted precursors, and micropeptides.
Activation pattern: Sharp, residue-level peaks concentrated at the first few residues after initiation (maximal at position 2), with occasional isolated secondary peaks at internal, low-structure sites that often correspond to signal/transit/leader-like segments or putative processed peptide N-termini.
Exemplars: - Coronavirus accessory protein ORF3b: peaks at the disordered N-terminus (positions 2–3) and additional isolated peaks in low-confidence regions, including a predicted targeting segment.
- Secretory membrane protein with an N-terminal signal peptide (hygromycin-B hypersensitivity protein): strongest activation at residue 2 within the signal peptide; minor scattered peaks in TM/loop regions.
- Bacteriocin (enterocin) precursor: isolated internal activation in an unstructured region consistent with the start of the mature bacteriocin peptide within the precursor.
- Testis-specific lncRNA-derived micropeptide: activation at residue 2 of a disordered N-terminus, with additional sparse peaks in low-confidence coil/helix segments.

Summary: Residue-level detector that fires sparsely in small proteins, peptide precursors, and disordered/loosely structured regions, often in propeptide or disordered C-/N-terminal segments; avoids structured catalytic cores and binding sites.
Activation pattern: Sparse residue-level peaks, often in small (sub-200 aa) proteins or within annotated disordered regions of larger proteins; for larger enzymes peaks cluster in the N-terminal extension well away from catalytic/binding residues. Peak residues are heterogeneous (aromatic, charged, and polar residues all occur).
Exemplars: - tRNA (pseudouridine(54)-N1)-methyltransferase: activation restricted to the disordered N-terminal extension (e.g., a peak in a short transient helix), absent from the SAM-dependent catalytic domain
- Secreted bacterial protease: strong activation in disordered N- and C-terminal tails, none across the structured protease core
- Neuropeptide/prohormone precursor (Amnesiac): isolated peak within the disordered C-terminal propeptide region
- Antisense-encoded microprotein (TAR1): peaks including one within the annotated C-terminal disordered region
- Proapoptotic nucleolar protein: peaks within a broad C-terminal IDR, including near a nucleolar localization segment

Summary: Short stretches within small, often low-complexity or disordered proteins—sometimes in N-terminal or propeptide regions, sometimes in internal segments of mature chains—common across taxa (including viral regulatory proteins and eukaryotic propeptides).
Activation pattern: Sparse residue-level peaks scattered along compact small proteins, frequently in disordered or coil segments but also in interior regions of mature chains; activations are typically a few isolated residues rather than contiguous blocks.
Exemplars: - Viral regulatory proteins: peaks distributed across the chain, including compositionally biased polar/basic patches.
- Small secreted or propeptide-containing factors: clustered peaks within propeptide and adjacent regions.
- Compact, low-complexity uncharacterized proteins: scattered peaks across the chain.

Summary: Short, charge-rich patches in intrinsically disordered regions, enriched in Lys/Arg with interspersed Gln/Gly/Ser/Thr and mixed acidic residues, typically of low structural order.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks in very short windows (2–10 aa), tightly clustered around basic K/R-Q-R motifs within disordered segments; multiple short peaks can occur in one protein; peaks coincide with low‑pLDDT, compositionally biased basic-and-acidic patches; activation is largely absent from structured domains.
Exemplars:
- HIV/SIV Virion infectivity factor (Vif): activation on a conserved K-Q-R-G basic patch in the C-terminal disordered region (~190–193).
- Bacterial ABC transporter ATP-binding proteins (e.g., ModC): activation on a polybasic K/R-rich patch within a C-terminal disordered, basic-and-acidic compositionally biased segment.
- Bacterial membrane-insertion sensor proteins (e.g., MifM): activation on an internal short basic K-S-K-R patch.
- Conotoxin precursors: activation on a basic/mixed-charge K-G-Q-R patch within the disordered propeptide region, not on the signal peptide.
- Transcriptional regulators and E3 ubiquitin ligases: activation on short polybasic or mixed-charge patches (NLS-like/basic clusters) in low-complexity disordered regions.
- IMPase/FBPase superfamily phosphatases: occasional internal peaks at conserved Ser/Thr-containing short loops (~85–110), reflecting the feature’s sensitivity to brief polar/charged motifs.

Summary: Short, intrinsically disordered C‑terminal tails of secreted or membrane‑associated proteins (from microproteins to larger multi‑pass enzymes) and viral accessory microproteins, typically low‑complexity and enriched in proline and basic residues, often immediately downstream of a hydrophobic signal/transmembrane segment; can include cysteine‑rich patches in secreted/toxin peptides.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over contiguous 10–30 aa windows, most frequently at the extreme C‑terminus; often spans a brief helix that transitions into coil with peak signal in the disordered coil; commonly adjacent to a hydrophobic (signal/TM) segment and characterized by low pLDDT; can also occur in short cytosolic juxtamembrane loops of larger multi‑pass proteins.
Exemplars:
- Oomycete RxLR secreted effectors: activation on the C‑terminal tail immediately following a predicted hydrophobic segment, in a low‑confidence helix/coil region.
- Human ST20 (apoptosis/stress‑related microprotein): activation on a short C‑terminal helix‑to‑coil, highly disordered stretch.
- Small uncharacterized microproteins: activation confined to the last ~10–15 residues forming a disordered coil tail.
- Viral accessory/viroporin‑like proteins: activation on basic/proline‑rich cytosolic C‑tails adjacent to a single‑pass TM helix; also applies to non‑TM viral accessory proteins with disordered C‑tails (e.g., Vif).
- Small secreted cysteine‑rich toxins/defensin‑like peptides: activation on short cationic/cysteine‑biased segments within the mature or processing tail.
- ATP synthase epsilon subunits: activation on a conserved, short, disordered C‑terminal regulatory segment in these small mitochondrial/bacterial proteins.
- Multi‑pass membrane enzymes (e.g., phytoene dehydrogenase): activation on short cytosolic C‑terminal or juxtamembrane tails adjacent to TM helices.

Summary: Extreme N-terminal basic, low-complexity initiation segments that serve as generic localization/processing leaders: includes the n-region of ER signal peptides, mitochondrial/chloroplast transit peptides, short propeptides, and signal anchors of membrane proteins, as well as analogous basic N-termini in viral and nuclear/cytosolic microproteins.
Activation pattern: Strong, localized activation confined to the first ~5–20 residues at the extreme N-terminus, with sharp peaks around positions 2–10; overlaps disordered/low-confidence coil that can include a short initial helix; activation rapidly decays after this segment with only rare internal/C-terminal stray peaks.
Exemplars:
- Neuropeptide precursors (galanin family): activation at the start of the secreted peptide segment within a short disordered N-terminus.
- Oomycete RxLR secreted effectors: activation within the N-terminal signal peptide n-region/early helix (~1–12).
- Secreted fungal multicopper oxidases (laccases): activation in the first residues of the signal peptide n-region, tapering across the leader.
- Plant ribosome-inactivating proteins (type 1 RIPs): activation across the N-terminal propeptide preceding the mature enzyme.
- Viral regulatory proteins (e.g., adenoviral E4-ORF6): activation at a basic, low-complexity extreme N-terminus used for subcellular targeting.
- Human microproteins/lncRNA-derived peptides (e.g., PINT87aa): activation over an N-terminal basic, low-complexity tract even without a classical signal peptide.
- Bacterial enzymes with N-terminal signal anchors or basic tails (e.g., membrane-associated carotenoid pathway enzymes): activation at the extreme N-terminus.

Summary: Aromatic (phenylalanine/tyrosine) cluster motif: short, hydrophobic low‑complexity segments enriched for F/Y that act as membrane‑interface anchors or aromatic “sticker” patches, most often at N‑termini or adjacent to transmembrane helices; recurrent in small viral/accessory proteins, secreted effectors and toxin/antimicrobial peptides, micropeptides from alt/lncRNA ORFs, and some nucleic‑acid–associated proteins.
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks on F and Y that aggregate into regional clusters (3–20 residues); strongest near the N‑terminus, within signal peptides/signal‑anchors and at TM‑helix boundaries (“aromatic belt”); can cover entire short peptides when densely FY‑rich; weak response to polar/charged residues; W/C contribute occasionally.
Exemplars: - Viral accessory/structural proteins (e.g., viroporins/small membrane proteins): activation on N‑terminal FY clusters flanking or capping a single TM helix.
- Secreted pathogen effectors (oomycete RxLR family): activation on the FY‑rich, disordered pre‑domain immediately after the signal peptide used for translocation/entry.
- Antimicrobial and toxin peptides: activation across short FY‑enriched hydrophobic segments that mediate membrane binding/disruption.
- Membrane receptors/transporters and small hydrophobic proteins: activation on aromatic belts at TM boundaries and on FY‑rich cytosolic/luminal tails.
- Alt‑ORF/lncRNA micropeptides: activation spanning the whole peptide due to dense FY content.
- Nucleic acid–associated proteins (e.g., RRM/IDR‑containing RNA‑binding proteins): activation on FY hotspots in low‑complexity regions or aromatic patches used for base stacking.
- Diverse enzymes: activation on exposed surface FY clusters or N‑terminal aromatic patches not tied to a specific fold.

Summary: The feature recognizes cationic, amphipathic, low-complexity segments that mediate targeting or membrane/lipid association—classically N‑terminal signal/transit/leader-like regions of secreted, mitochondrial, and viral proteins—and frequently the propeptide/mature regions of toxin and neuropeptide precursors; it can also highlight short basic/hydrophobic helices or redox-active motifs within structured domains.
Activation pattern: Predominantly long, continuous activation over N‑terminal, low‑pLDDT leader/propeptide regions enriched in Lys/Arg, Ser/Pro and hydrophobic/aromatic residues; with occasional residue-level peaks within well-structured helices (e.g., specific positions in thioredoxin CGHC motifs or matrix-exposed helices of membrane proteins).
Exemplars: 
- Venom phospholipase A2 precursors (activation on signal/propeptide segments and conserved cationic patches).
- Apolipoproteins (N‑terminal signal peptide and amphipathic helical stretches).
- Protein kinases with disordered/basic N‑termini (e.g., cyclin-dependent and PRK family N‑tails).
- Thioredoxin-fold protein disulfide-isomerases (peak at the CGHC active-site helix).
- Mitochondrial calcium uniporter (selected residues in a matrix-exposed helix).
- Conotoxin and other secreted toxin precursors; neuropeptide prepropeptides (activation across pro/mature peptide regions).
- Viral silencing suppressors and small membrane/morphogenesis proteins (basic, hydrophobic leader-like segments).
- Kinetochore coiled-coil scaffold proteins (basic low-complexity regions).
- FYVE-domain endosomal adaptors (basic, membrane/PIP-interacting low-complexity segments).
- RNA-modifying enzymes with basic N‑terminal tails (e.g., tRNA methyltransferases).

Summary: Secreted, propeptide‑processed cysteine‑rich mini‑domains: compact extracellular segments immediately downstream of a signal peptide that contain clustered cysteines forming multiple disulfide bonds (defensin/CSαβ, WAP four‑disulfide core, cystine‑knot/knottin, CHH‑like, evasin‑like, and related small CRP scaffolds), often flanked by dibasic convertase sites and enriched in Lys/Arg
Activation pattern: Regional activation on short segments (≈20–60 aa) right after the signal peptide; strong peaks on cysteines and nearby basic residues, frequently overlapping proprotein convertase (dibasic) processing motifs; may recur for multi‑domain or repeat CRP proteins
Exemplars: - WAP/four‑disulfide core protease inhibitors (SLPI/elafin/WFDC): activation on the WAP domain’s Cys framework following the signal/propeptide
- Plant defensin‑like peptides (DEFL/LURE/ESF) and thionins: activation on the mature antimicrobial CSαβ cysteine motif
- Venom cystine‑knot peptides (conotoxins/knottins, mini‑toxins): activation on the canonical Cys frameworks in the mature toxin region of prepropeptides
- Tick evasins (chemokine‑binding CRPs): activation on the Cys‑rich chemokine‑binding domain
- Crustacean CHH/MIH neuropeptide precursors: activation on the mature hormone core with conserved six‑Cys motif adjacent to dibasic cleavage
- Fungal GPI‑anchored cell‑wall adhesins/stress proteins: activation on extracellular Cys‑rich segments just after secretion signals
- Small plant CRP protease inhibitors: activation on the disulfide‑stabilized inhibitory mini‑domain

Summary: Secreted, short cysteine-rich peptides and small extracellular cysteine-rich domains stabilized by multiple disulfide bonds (CRPs), spanning venom toxins, disintegrins, defensins/hepcidin, Kunitz/Kazal/hevein-like inhibitors/defense peptides, and related cystine‑knotted or cysteine‑stabilized folds. The feature captures the mature, proteolytically processed peptide/module characterized by clustered Cys (often CC motifs) and basic residues.
Activation pattern: Regional activation confined to short mature peptide segments (tens of residues) following the signal peptide and propeptides; minimal/absent on signal/pro-regions. Strong residue-level peaks on cysteines and frequent secondary peaks on Lys/Arg and Gly. Activation spans mixed secondary structure (β-strands, coils, short helices) and can include key functional loops (e.g., RGD in disintegrins).
Exemplars: - Plant cyclotides (cystine-knot cyclopeptides, e.g., chassatide): activation across the cyclic cystine‑knot core of the mature peptide after processing.
- Snake venom disintegrins: activation across the disintegrin domain, including the RGD integrin-binding loop and adjacent cysteine-dense core.
- Inhibitor cystine-knot (ICK) venom toxins from spiders, cone snails, centipedes, and sea anemones: activation on the disulfide‑knotted toxin core.
- Kunitz/BPTI- and Kazal-type serine protease inhibitors (including tick chemokine/complement inhibitors): activation on the small disulfide‑rich inhibitor domain.
- Hevein-like/seed defense peptides: activation on the cysteine-rich chitin‑binding hevein domain.
- Defensins (plant/fungal/animal CSαβ peptides) and vertebrate hepcidin: activation on the cysteine‑stabilized mature AMP region.
- Euplotes ciliate mating pheromones: activation on the secreted disulfide‑rich pheromone core.
- Cysteine-rich modules within large extracellular/mucin-like proteins: activation on the short, cysteine‑dense repeat/subdomain embedded in the larger precursor.

Summary: Classical cleavable N-terminal Sec signal peptides (type I) of secreted prepropeptides/proteins, especially venom toxins and antimicrobial/defense peptides; the feature captures the positively charged N-region and hydrophobic helical h‑region of the signal sequence, with activation tapering across the C-region/early propeptide and absent from the mature chain.
Activation pattern: Strong, contiguous regional activation confined to the extreme N-terminus (~20–40 residues), highest over a hydrophobic, alpha-helical block enriched in Leu/Ile/Val/Phe/Ala/Met with basic residues in the first few positions; activation drops near the signal peptidase cleavage site and may extend a few residues into the propeptide; negligible across the mature peptide; typically lower pLDDT in the activated segment.
Exemplars: - Scorpion kappa-KTx potassium channel toxin precursors: activation on the N-terminal signal peptide only.
- Conotoxin precursors (cone snail): activation confined to the signal peptide.
- Plant cyclotide/defensin-like precursors (e.g., chassatides): activation on the signal peptide with slight spillover into the propeptide.
- Insect diapause-specific peptide: activation on the signal peptide only.
- Sea anemone actitoxin precursors: activation across the signal peptide and diminishing in the adjacent propeptide.
- Scorpion chlorotoxin-like peptide precursors: activation on the signal peptide.
- Secreted serine protease inhibitor precursors: activation on the signal peptide, fading in early propeptide.
- Bacterial heat-stable enterotoxin: activation on the N-terminal signal peptide only.
- Secreted vanadium-binding protein: activation on the signal peptide and short propeptide.
- Tick evasin (chemokine-binding protein): activation across the N-terminal signal peptide only.

Summary: Short, structured beta-strand segments at or near domain termini in extracellular proteins/domains—most prominently the conserved C-terminal strand of C-type lectin-like domains (CTLD)—often bearing closely spaced, disulfide-forming cysteines and flanked by aromatic/basic residues; analogous terminal strands in other adhesin/receptor-binding ectodomains and in compact disulfide-rich secreted toxins/antimicrobial peptides also trigger.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks on 8–20 aa stretches at ectodomain or domain termini; highest on cysteines within a beta-strand (often terminal) and immediate neighbors; repeats once per CTLD module in multi-CTLD proteins; occasionally extends just beyond the annotated CTLD into a short structured island; also marks the terminal beta-strand at the ends of viral/bacteriophage receptor-binding fibers and short strands within disulfide-rich peptide toxins.
Exemplars:
- Selectins: activation at the CTLD C-terminus at the CTLD–EGF boundary, mapping to a short beta-strand.
- NK/killer cell lectin-like receptors: activation on the CTLD terminal beta-strand, peaking on paired cysteines implicated in disulfides.
- Invertebrate C-type lectins (e.g., echinoidin): activation confined to the CTLD C-terminal beta-strand.
- Echinoderm spicule matrix CTLD proteins: activation on a short beta-strand immediately C-terminal to the CTLD within an otherwise disordered tail.
- Bacteriophage long-tail fiber proteins: activation on the extreme C-terminal beta-strand of the fiber tip/knob domain.
- Cysteine-rich peptide toxins (e.g., sea anemone sodium-channel toxins): activation on a short beta-strand around paired cysteines, typically near a terminus.

Summary: N-terminal prepro regions of secreted peptide precursors: the signal peptide plus especially the adjacent propeptide/prodomain that is removed during maturation in peptide hormones, neuropeptides, venom peptides, and plant small secreted signaling peptides; the feature avoids the final short mature peptide region.
Activation pattern: Regional N-terminal activation. Signal peptide shows low-to-moderate activation, which rises to the highest levels across the following disordered propeptide; activation typically starts near Met-1 and forms a long contiguous block, then drops to zero at or before the cleavage site(s) leading into the mature peptide(s). Activation is largely structure-agnostic but enriched in low-pLDDT/disordered segments; mature peptide regions are minimally or not activated.
Exemplars: - Somatostatin precursor: activation on signal peptide and N-terminal propeptide; off on mature somatostatin.
- Snake venom bradykinin-potentiating peptide/C-type natriuretic peptide precursors: high on the propeptide (including embedded BPPs); off on the C-type natriuretic peptide domain.
- Urotensin II-gamma precursor: on the Urophysin gamma intermediate chain; off on signal peptide and final urotensin II peptide.
- Uroguanylin/guanylin family: on signal peptide and propeptide; off on the mature guanylin/uroguanylin peptides.
- Pro-melanin-concentrating hormone (pro-MCH): on the N-terminal prohormone region; off on MCH and associated short peptides.
- Insect neuropeptide precursors (e.g., dromyosuppressin): on signal peptide and prodomain; off on the mature neuropeptide.
- Plant CLE/CLV3 family: on signal peptide and N-terminal prodomain; off on the C-terminal CLE peptide.
- Plant GOLVEN/RGF (GLV) precursors: on the propeptide region; off on the C-terminal GLV peptide.
- Plant CEP precursors: on signal peptide and propeptide; off on the C-terminal CEP peptide.
- Plant EPF/stomagen family: on the N-terminal prepro segment; off on the C-terminal stomagen peptide.

Summary: A short, Lys/Arg-rich alpha-helix, primarily the initiator (“helix 1”/leader) of helix–turn–helix DNA-binding domains (especially Cro/C1-type repressors and eukaryotic homeobox/POU/CUT homeodomains). The feature favors the very start of the HTH domain (often N-terminal in bacteria/phage, internal in eukaryotes) rather than the DNA-recognition helix, but it can also match analogous N-terminal basic helices in some non-HTH proteins.
Activation pattern:
- Regional, short contiguous stretches (~10–20 aa) centered on the N-terminal end of the first helix of an HTH domain
- Commonly includes the initiator Met and preceding coil; may extend from a short N-terminal strand into helix 1; peaks near residues 5–8 of the helix
- Strong basic enrichment (Lys/Arg); little to no activation over the canonical H–T–H recognition helix or catalytic cores of fused enzymes
- Can recur multiple times in multi-HTH proteins (separate peaks at each HTH domain start)
- Occasional off-target: standalone N-terminal amphipathic basic helices in enzymes lacking an HTH context
Exemplars:
- Cro/C1-type phage repressors: activation on the N-terminal helix 1 at the start of the HTH domain; recognition helix not activated
- Mycobacterial EspR-like HTH regulators: activation on the first N-terminal helix preceding the annotated H–T–H motif
- Type II DNA methyltransferases with an N-terminal Cro/C1-type HTH module: activation confined to the leading HTH helix; the SAM-dependent MTase domain is inactive
- Enzymes fused to HTH regulatory repeats (e.g., dioxygenases with two Cro/C1-type HTH segments): activation at the N-terminal helix of each HTH segment; catalytic core inactive
- Eukaryotic homeobox/POU/CUT (HNF-1, POU/PIT-1, ONECUT): activation on the internal helix 1 of the homeodomain rather than the recognition helix
- HTH-type antitoxin components of toxin–antitoxin systems: activation on the N-terminal helix of the antitoxin HTH domain
- Occasional non-HTH enzymes with basic N-terminal helices (e.g., HppE epoxidase): activation on the N-terminal amphipathic Lys/Arg-rich helix

Summary: N-terminal flexible/basic segments that precede or flank functional cores—most commonly disordered transactivation regions in eukaryotic transcription factors and short N-terminal arms/leader helices adjoining HTH/homeobox DNA-binding modules in bacterial/phage regulators—enriched in Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly and basic residues; occasionally similar N-terminal tails in other proteins (e.g., RNA-binding ribosomal proteins and some metabolic enzymes).
Activation pattern: Regional activation concentrated in long, contiguous stretches near the N-terminus; peaks in coils or the first helix immediately preceding or adjoining a structured core; often multiple N-terminal segments per protein; little/no activation within the folded HTH/homeobox domains themselves.
Exemplars: HTH-type antitoxin regulators (HigA): activation on N-terminal pre-HTH helices/arm; POU/homeobox transcription factors: activation on N-terminal disordered transactivation regions, not on POU-specific/homeobox domains; Bacteriophage Cro/C1-like repressors (lambda cI): activation on the flexible N-terminal arm before the HTH motif; Type II DNA methyltransferases: activation on short basic N-terminal tails preceding the catalytic core; RNA-binding ribosomal protein S4/uS4: activation on N-terminal basic tail; Fosfomycin biosynthesis enzyme HppE: activation on a short N-terminal tail before the catalytic core.

Summary: Short basic helix–loop element that most often maps to the first helix and adjoining turn of HTH DNA-binding modules, but also recurs as an analogous N-terminal helix–loop in non-HTH proteins (enzymes, Fe–S proteins, and intein-bearing archaeal proteins) where it neighbors ligand/metal/substrate-interacting residues.
Activation pattern: Single short block (~10–30 residues) with residue-level peaks in the helix–turn/loop; enriched in Lys/Arg and frequently near the N-terminus in bacterial/phage proteins, but internal within larger multidomain proteins. Peaks can collapse to a few residues in weaker hits.
Exemplars:
- Phage CI/Cro repressors: activation on the first helix and following loop of the Cro/C1-type HTH at the N-terminus.
- Bacterial HTH regulators (e.g., DdrO/DdrOC, SutR, HigA): strong on helix 1 and the turn; diminished on the recognition helix.
- Replication initiator DnaA: localized activation within the C-terminal HTH helix (Domain IV).
- Type II DNA methyltransferases: N-terminal helix–loop–helix consistent with an HTH-like target-recognition element.
- Eukaryotic POU/homeobox TFs: internal activation within the DNA-binding module.
- Archaeal RFC small subunit with intein: activation within/adjacent to an N-terminal basic helix–loop segment of the intein-containing region.
- Metabolic enzymes (e.g., HEPD/HppE/dioxygenases): N-terminal helix–loop adjacent to essential/basic or ligand-binding residues shows strong activation.
- [4Fe–4S] ferredoxins: occasional weak activation near the first cluster-binding cysteine at the N-terminus.

Summary: A detector for short, charged/polar N-terminal pre-domain segments (flexible tails or the first helix/helix N-cap) that immediately precede a structured domain; when the targeted domain lies internally, the activation shifts to that domain’s N-terminus within the sequence. These short leader/linker regions often include turns, helix starts, and frequent PTM sites or metal-liganding residues, and activation drops upon entering the core domain.
Activation pattern: Regional activation of a short (typically 5–20 aa) segment at domain N-termini, most often at the extreme protein N-terminus; sharp peak around the first helix/turn; activation ceases at the annotated domain boundary and does not extend into the folded domain. In multi-domain proteins, multiple such short, non-contiguous pre-domain segments can activate.
Exemplars: - Phage lambda CI repressor (HTH-type): activation on the extreme N-terminal tail and first helix immediately before the HTH cro/C1 domain; no activation on the DNA-binding motif itself.
- Serine/threonine protein kinases (e.g., bacterial PknD-like): activation on the short disordered N-terminal tail just upstream of the kinase catalytic domain, including the processed, N-acetylated first residue.
- DnaJ/Hsp40 co-chaperones: activation on the very first helix directly preceding the J domain.
- Zinc-containing ferredoxins: activation within an N-terminal extension/turn between metal-binding histidines that precedes the 4Fe-4S ferredoxin fold, including a modified lysine site.
- HTH transcriptional regulators and antitoxins: activation at short basic N-termini immediately before their HTH DNA-binding modules.
- Homeobox/POU/ONECUT transcription factors: activation on internal segments corresponding to the N-terminal arm/pre-helix region at the start of the homeodomain (mid-sequence rather than at the protein N-terminus).

Summary: N-terminal intrinsically disordered/low‑complexity leader segments, typically basic and Ser/Thr‑rich, that precede the first stable structural element (e.g., the initial helix, HTH DNA‑binding domain, or a transmembrane helix); the feature marks the flexible N‑tail rather than the downstream structured domain and occurs in many bacterial transcriptional regulators as well as unrelated proteins.
Activation pattern: Strong, localized activation at the extreme N‑terminus in short contiguous blocks (often ~5–20 aa, sometimes extended across longer IDRs), with highest scores in low‑pLDDT coil enriched for Lys/Arg and Ser/Thr; activation drops sharply upon entry into well‑structured helices/domains (HTH motifs, globular cores, transmembranes). Occasional minor secondary bumps appear in other low‑confidence loops; structured cores remain largely silent.
Exemplars: - TetR-like repressors (e.g., KstR): activation on the short unstructured N‑terminal leader immediately before the HTH; the HTH itself is inactive.
- Other HTH-type bacterial regulators (GntR, MarR, LysR, IclR/DeoR, ArsR/SmtB), LexA/phage repressors: activation on basic/Ser‑rich N‑tails upstream of the DNA‑binding helices.
- ECF sigma factors: activation at the extreme N‑terminal flexible segment, not in conserved helical cores.
- Homeobox and plant MYB transcription factors: activation on N‑terminal low‑complexity tails preceding the DNA‑binding domain.
- COQ9 (mitochondrial coenzyme Q biosynthesis): activation across the long N‑terminal disordered segment immediately downstream of the mitochondrial transit peptide; structured core silent.
- ATP synthase subunit b: activation on the short N‑terminal coil just before the transmembrane helix; TM and helical body show no activation.

Summary: Short segments within disordered and compositionally biased stretches of diverse proteins, particularly regions enriched in basic and acidic residues. Activations are also seen in non-disordered contexts across proteins of varied function, suggesting the feature captures a relatively broad local sequence pattern rather than a tight structural motif.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks with small clusters, distributed throughout the length of the protein. Peaks frequently overlap annotated disordered regions and basic/acidic compositionally biased segments, but also occur at isolated positions within structured chains; occurs in both helical and coil contexts.
Exemplars: - Oomycete RxLR secreted effectors: peaks within the mature effector chain, with occasional spikes in the signal peptide.
- Plant CLE peptide precursors: localized peaks within the C-terminal CLE motif corresponding to the mature signaling peptide.
- Cholecystokinin prohormone: peaks at or immediately adjacent to the N-termini of mature neuropeptides generated by proteolytic processing.
- Herpesvirus ICP47-like small accessory proteins: multiple peaks in the N-terminal active helical region and in polar, disordered C-terminal stretches.
- Keratin-associated proteins: activation across cysteine/proline/serine-rich, low-complexity repeat regions.
- Phosphodiesterase and fungal/bacterial enzymes with disordered N- or internal stretches: peaks within basic-and-acidic compositionally biased segments.

Summary: Short, cationic, amphipathic peptide segments—typically the mature cores of secreted antimicrobial/cytolytic peptides and analogous AMP‑like helices embedded in larger proteins. These regions are Lys/Arg‑rich with interspersed hydrophobes, often form (or have propensity for) an amphipathic α‑helix, and are used for membrane interaction/disruption or other bioactive signaling; they are usually produced by proteolytic processing from precursor proteins and can include RiPP cores despite post‑translational crosslinks.
Activation pattern: Regional activation on short contiguous blocks (∼15–40 aa, sometimes shorter), with sharp on/off at the boundaries of mature peptide segments; minimal activation in signal peptides and propeptides. Peaks often coincide with hydrophobic residues along an amphipathic face and clusters of Lys/Arg. Frequently at N‑ or C‑terminal helices or short internal helices with low-to-moderate pLDDT.
Exemplars: - Amphibian helical antimicrobial peptides (e.g., aureins): activation precisely on the mature AMP helix, not on signal/propeptide.
- Hymenopteran venom cytolysins (e.g., myrmeciitoxins): strong activation across the mature toxin’s amphipathic α‑helix.
- Lantibiotic RiPPs (e.g., lacticin 3147 A2): activation on the modified mature lantibiotic core despite lanthionine/beta‑methyllanthionine crosslinks.
- Phage/bacterial holins: activation on the N‑terminal amphipathic helix adjacent to the first transmembrane segment; little/no activation in TM or periplasmic domains.
- Crustacean anti‑lipopolysaccharide factors (ALFs): activation on the N‑terminal cationic LPS‑binding helix of the mature peptide.
- Plant NLR immune receptors (coiled‑coil N‑termini): activation on the N‑terminal CC helix implicated in membrane permeabilization/channel activity.
- Insect stress-response secreted proteins (Turandot family): activation on a C‑terminal amphipathic α‑helix of the mature chain.
- Outer membrane polysaccharide export proteins (CtrA family): activation on a short periplasmic C‑terminal helical tail with amphipathic character.
- Kininogen‑derived peptides (bradykinin variants): activation on the short, basic bioactive peptide released from a disordered region.

Summary: Short linear segments in intrinsically disordered or otherwise low-structure-confidence regions, often at N-termini and within signal peptides/propeptides of secreted and regulatory proteins (including viral accessory proteins and small ORF microproteins), enriched in small/basic residues (G, P, S, A, R; often with Cys), rather than in well-folded catalytic cores.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks scattered across IDRs and low-confidence coils/short helices; frequently clustered near the N-terminus, in signal peptides, propeptides, and disordered tails; little to no activation in well-structured domains; occasional activation in low-confidence transmembrane/signal-anchor helices.
Exemplars: - Viral accessory protein (HIV-1 Vif): peaks throughout low-pLDDT coils, especially the disordered N-terminal region.
- Neuropeptide precursor (Drosophila Amnesiac): activation in the N-terminal signal peptide and multiple mature peptide segments with very low pLDDT.
- Secreted serine carboxypeptidase: activation confined to disordered C-terminal tail, annotated disordered segment, the signal peptide, and a low-confidence C-terminal transmembrane helix; absent from the structured catalytic domain.
- Disordered human tumor-suppressor–associated protein (ST20): scattered peaks within predicted helices in a globally disordered chain, including the N-terminus.
- lncRNA/sORF-derived microprotein (IGF2 antisense protein): multiple peaks across annotated disordered regions rich in Arg/Pro/Gly.

Summary: Short, low‑complexity, intrinsically disordered proteins and modules that encode targeting/processing signals—often but not always secretory—combining hydrophobic signal peptides, double‑Gly bacteriocin leaders, or polybasic/NLS‑like segments, frequently adjacent to Ser/Thr/Pro‑rich stretches and basic clusters (e.g., RXLR, KR/RR)—common in micropeptides, toxins/secreted precursors, viral accessory proteins, keratin‑associated and testis‑specific low‑complexity proteins across taxa
Activation pattern: Regional activation across short proteins, spanning hydrophobic/targeting segments and Ser/Thr/Pro‑rich low‑complexity tracts with peaks on basic motifs such as RXLR, dibasic KR/RR, or double‑Gly leader junctions
Exemplars:
- Oomycete RxLR effectors: activation on the N‑terminal signal peptide and the RXLR/EER host‑targeting motif immediately downstream.
- Secreted peptide hormone/venom/toxin precursors: activation on the signal peptide and basic prohormone convertase cleavage motifs (KR/RR) within the propeptide region.
- Class II bacteriocins: activation on the N‑terminal double‑Gly leader and adjacent cationic tract recognized by ABC exporters.
- Viral accessory/regulatory proteins (e.g., small disordered regulators): activation across S/T/P‑rich low‑complexity disordered segments containing polybasic/NLS‑like clusters.
- Keratin‑associated proteins (KRTAPs): activation over short, repetitive low‑complexity regions (Ser/Pro‑rich and basic tracts) typical of hair shaft proteins.
- Cancer/testis antigens and testis‑associated proteins: activation on Lys/Arg‑ and Pro/Ser‑rich low‑complexity stretches in very short proteins.
- Short uncharacterized micropeptides/antisense products: broad activation across their low‑complexity/basic segments.
- Enzymes that carry secretory leaders or short disordered/basic tails (including some cytosolic enzymes lacking signal peptides): activation limited to the disordered tail, not the catalytic core.

Summary: Low-complexity, intrinsically disordered, cysteine-poor segments enriched in small/polar and charged residues (G, A, S, T, K, E, D) that act as surface‑active, lipid‑interface–binding regions (amphipathic/helix‑forming “hydrophilin/apolipoprotein‑like” tracts). These occur broadly across taxa, often at N‑termini or luminal/cytosolic tails of secreted or membrane‑associated proteins, including stress‑protective hydrophilins/LEA proteins, apolipoproteins, ATG2 lipid‑transfer tethers, and cationic antimicrobial/venom peptides.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over long low‑complexity stretches (frequently N‑terminal), with diffuse highlighting and occasional peaks on glycine/threonine repeats or short amphipathic helix motifs; spans entire sequence for small AMPs/venom peptides; in large proteins (e.g., ATG2) covers extended acidic/polar IDRs flanking or preceding hydrophobic cores but not the transmembrane segments.
Exemplars: - Apolipoproteins (e.g., ApoC/ApoA/ApoE families): activation on amphipathic helix repeats and adjacent polar low‑complexity segments that coat lipid particles.
- Plant LEA/hydrophilin proteins (LEA4/LEA5, dehydrins, Hsp12‑like): activation across glycine/threonine/serine‑rich, charged repeats conferring stress‑protective, membrane‑associating properties.
- Autophagy‑related protein 2 (ATG2 family): activation over long acidic/polar IDRs and N‑terminal amphipathic membrane‑tethering segments used at ER–mitochondria/phagophore contact sites.
- Lipid‑droplet/oil‑body scaffolds (oleosins, perilipins, apolipoprotein‑like droplet proteins): activation on low‑complexity polar tails and amphipathic segments surrounding the hydrophobic hairpin/core.
- Cationic antimicrobial and venom peptides (melittin/cecropin/magainin/mastoparan‑like): activation across the whole cationic amphipathic segment that binds membranes.
- Membrane proteins with long disordered N‑ or luminal regions (mitochondrial/ER/PM): activation on polar/charged low‑complexity tails used as flexible linkers or membrane‑proximal surface‑binders.
- Viral matrix/core/viroporin‑associated proteins: activation on low‑complexity, amphipathic, membrane‑interacting stretches.
- Bacterial low‑complexity scaffold/toxin repeats: activation on glycine/threonine‑rich polar segments used for surface association or scaffolding.

Summary: Activation on disordered, low-complexity, and repetitive segments of secreted/extracellular and small regulatory proteins, including collagen-like triple-helix repeats, short flexible peptides, and disordered N-terminal/internal regions.

Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks distributed across repetitive or disordered stretches; in collagen-like proteins the activation spreads broadly over Gly-X-Y triple-helix tracts and low-complexity regions; in short secreted peptides and viral accessory proteins, activation tends to cluster in disordered segments and sometimes near the N-terminus; in ECF sigma factors, a peak occurs in the mid/C-terminal (~140-170) region between sigma2 and sigma4 domains.

Exemplars:
- Fibrillar collagens and collagen-like proteins: broad, distributed activation across Gly-X-Y triple-helix repeats and flanking low-complexity regions
- Bacterial ECF (alternative) sigma factors: a focal activation in the mid/C-terminal region near the sigma4 domain
- Secreted micropeptides, antimicrobial peptides, and arthropod venom peptides: activation on short disordered/low-complexity stretches
- Viral accessory/regulatory proteins: activation on disordered regions, frequently toward the N-terminus
- Plant small secreted peptides and cell-wall proteins: activation within short motifs and disordered segments
- Structured cytosolic enzymes and regulators: isolated activation at conserved residues in flexible loops/motifs
- Generic secreted precursors/propeptides: activation within low-complexity segments

Summary: Generic detector of low-complexity or low-structure segments, with a bias toward the N-terminal portion of proteins, including secretory signal peptides, disordered N-terminal stretches, and short membrane-embedded helical regions.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks; sparse, isolated activations often concentrated within the first ~100 residues (frequently within the first 30), though peaks can also appear in mid-protein membrane or low-complexity stretches. Peaks occur within signal peptides, low-pLDDT disordered coils, and short helices, including transmembrane helical segments; rarely form contiguous runs.
Exemplars: - Secreted serpin (antithrombin): peak in the N‑terminal signal peptide and additional peaks in a longer disordered N‑terminal segment.
- Antimicrobial peptide precursor (lumbricin): strong peaks confined to the N‑terminal signal peptide; minimal activation in the mature peptide.
- Secreted bacterial catalase–peroxidase (KatG): minor peaks in the signal peptide and immediately at the start of the mature chain.
- Poxvirus accessory protein: multiple peaks across low-confidence, disordered regions near the N‑terminus.
- Retroviral integrase homolog: peaks near the N‑terminus and at residues just before an annotated disordered linker.
- p53-induced DNA-binding protein (Killin): peaks on basic residues within a low‑pLDDT, N‑terminal DNA-binding region.
- Small membrane protein (ATP synthase subunit 8): peaks within an N-terminal transmembrane helix.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity regulatory segments of nuclear proteins—especially transcription factors/cofactors, chromatin regulators, RNA/splicing factors, and nuclear RING‑type E3 ligases—enriched in basic (Lys/Arg) and polar (Ser/Pro/Gln/Glu/Gly/Thr) tracts that serve as activation/repression, partner‑binding, or localization (NLS‑like) regions; typically outside folded DNA‑binding/catalytic domains and often overlapping phosphorylation sites or simple helices within IDRs.
Activation pattern: Predominantly regional activation across long IDRs with multiple sparse residue‑level peaks; strong signal in basic/polar low‑complexity patches and SLiM‑rich interaction zones; little to no activation in well‑folded domains, with occasional peaks in adjacent/peripheral coil or simple poly‑Ala helices.
Exemplars: - Polycomb ASXL family cofactor: activation on disordered regulatory segments including an NLS‑like Lys/Arg patch and a phospho‑adjacent stretch; also a simple poly‑alanine helix within an IDR.
- T‑box transcription factors (Brachyury‑like): activation on C‑terminal low‑complexity, disordered regulatory tails; absent from the folded T‑box DNA‑binding domain.
- Homeobox transcription factors: activation on N‑ and C‑terminal IDRs and basic patches around the homeodomain, with minor peaks in domain‑adjacent coil.
- WTAP (m6A/splicing regulator): activation across the disordered, low‑complexity C‑terminal tail.
- RING‑type nuclear E3 ligases (e.g., Arkadia/RNF111): activation on N‑terminal/central basic IDRs and a partner‑binding region (AXIN1 interface); no activation within the structured RING domain.

Summary: Short, low‑complexity interaction segments enriched in Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly (often with nearby Lys/Arg), typically intrinsically disordered, frequently near N‑termini and harboring regulatory PTM sites; the feature also highlights analogous short cationic helices used for molecular interactions (e.g., HTH DNA‑binding helices and amphipathic antimicrobial peptides).
Activation pattern: Predominantly sparse, residue‑level peaks within disordered/low‑complexity stretches (often N‑terminal and PTM‑prone), with occasional single‑residue peaks inside short helices involved in DNA binding or membrane‑active peptides; variable extent per protein.
Exemplars: Herpesvirus ICP4–type transcription factors: peaks on Ser/Thr and basic residues within disordered, low‑complexity regions; Homeobox transcription factors (e.g., Nkx6.1): peaks in disordered regulatory tails flanking the homeodomain, including annotated PTM sites; Cancer/testis microproteins (X antigen family): N‑terminal Ser/Thr residues in disordered regions, including a phosphoserine and proximity to a SUMOylation site; ECF sigma factors (SigM): single‑residue peak within the helix‑turn‑helix recognition helix of sigma‑70 domain 4; Antimicrobial peptides (Ixosin): peaks in the mature amphipathic helical peptide, including residues at the helix start and internal S/N positions.

Summary: Short hydrophobic alpha-helical segments enriched in small aliphatic residues (A, V, I, L with frequent T/G), depleted of charged/aromatic residues—commonly the h‑region of Sec signal peptides, short transmembrane helices, and internal helix-forming hydrophobic patches in both membrane and soluble proteins; often N‑terminal but also internal/C‑terminal.
Activation pattern: Regional activation on contiguous hydrophobic clusters predicted as alpha‑helix, with sharp residue‑level peaks at A/V/I/L/T (often with G); observed in signal peptides, TM segments, and internal helices; occurs in both structured and disordered contexts (not restricted to low pLDDT).
Exemplars: Adenovirus E4‑ORF4 and HCV ARFP: internal hydrophobic helix‑prone stretches in small viral proteins; Oomycete RxLR effectors and yeast killer toxin precursors: strong activation on N‑terminal Sec signal peptides; Bacterial cytochrome c oxidase subunit 2 and DHHC palmitoyltransferases: activation on short transmembrane helices; Kdo transferase and OMA hydratase: activation on internal hydrophobic helices within soluble/peripheral membrane enzymes.
