Summary: Detector of compositionally biased, low‑complexity segments—predominantly intrinsically disordered Ser/Thr‑rich (often RS-/Pro‑containing) tracts—with a strong N‑terminal bias; it also flags the extreme N‑terminus including signal peptides of secreted precursors.
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks clustered within long disordered/low‑complexity regions (often spanning tens to hundreds of residues), with strongest peaks on Ser/Thr and nearby polar/basic residues; broad regional activation across such IDRs and minimal signal in well‑folded domains or transmembranes; additional discrete peaks frequently occur at residues 1–10, including within N‑terminal signal peptides.
Exemplars: - Transcriptional regulator (CROC-4): multiple peaks across a central low‑complexity disordered segment (S/T/R/P‑rich), with minor N‑terminal peaks.
- Mechanosensory receptor (Stum): numerous high peaks on serines dispersed through annotated disordered, low‑complexity/polar regions.

Summary: Serine residues across a wide range of structural contexts, with a bias toward serine-rich segments in intrinsically disordered or low-complexity regions (often N-terminal tails), but also firing on serines within transmembrane helices and other structured contexts; the feature behaves primarily as a serine detector with some preference for S-rich patches.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks almost exclusively on Ser; many peaks per protein, frequently clustered near termini and in compositionally biased/disordered regions, but also appearing within transmembrane helices, signal peptides, and transit peptides; minor spillover to nearby residues.
Exemplars: Viral accessory proteins (metapneumovirus X): serines in a disordered C-terminal tail; Herpesvirus envelope glycoprotein L: serines across the gH-interacting segment and a disordered C-terminus; Herpesvirus cytoplasmic envelopment proteins: numerous serines in low-pLDDT regions; Plant ribosome-inactivating proteins (dianthin): N-terminal loop/coil serines; Human adaptor/regulatory protein ST20: N-terminal serines in a low-confidence helix/coil; Oomycete RxLR effectors: serines across the signal peptide, core, and disordered C-terminus; Bacteriocins (enterocins): serines in flexible coil segments.

Summary: Single conserved residue—often hydrophobic/aromatic but variable (Phe/Tyr/Trp/Leu/Val/Ile, and sometimes His/Thr)—within nucleotide- or ligand-binding pockets and analogous buried sites across diverse folds; in non-nucleotide proteins it maps to an analogous internal pocket- or core-lining position.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks at an internal pocket-lining residue, occasionally with short adjacent clusters; position varies widely with the fold.
Exemplars:
- Protein kinases (including viral/atypical): activation within the kinase domain at a residue near the ATP-binding cleft.
- tRNA (guanine-N7)-methyltransferases (class I SAM MTases): activation on the conserved aromatic that stacks with the SAM adenine and/or the target guanine in the active site.
- UDP-sugar glycosyltransferases for LPS/teichoic acid/lipid A biosynthesis (GT-B fold): activation on the aromatic that stacks with the UDP uracil ring in the donor-binding site.
- NAD(P)-dependent dehydrogenases (Rossmann fold): activation on an adenine-stacking Phe/Tyr in the dinucleotide-binding pocket.
- MurE (UDP-MurNAc-tripeptide synthetase; ATP-grasp ligase): activation on a buried hydrophobe that helps form the adenine-binding cleft for ATP.
- Carbonic anhydrases: activation on a conserved hydrophobic/aromatic residue lining the active-site hydrophobic pocket adjacent to the catalytic zinc.
- Small ribosomal subunit protein S8: activation on an aromatic residue that base-stacks with rRNA or stabilizes the RNA-binding surface.
- MICOS subunit Mic60 (mitofilin): activation on a buried aromatic within the coiled-coil/mitofilin scaffold that stabilizes the membrane-associated core.

Summary: Detector of compositionally biased, low‑complexity segments—predominantly intrinsically disordered Ser/Thr‑rich (often RS-/Pro‑containing) tracts—with a strong N‑terminal bias; it also flags the extreme N‑terminus including signal peptides of secreted precursors.
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks clustered within long disordered/low‑complexity regions (often spanning tens to hundreds of residues), with strongest peaks on Ser/Thr and nearby polar/basic residues; broad regional activation across such IDRs and minimal signal in well‑folded domains or transmembranes; additional discrete peaks frequently occur at residues 1–10, including within N‑terminal signal peptides.
Exemplars: - Transcriptional regulator (CROC-4): multiple peaks across a central low‑complexity disordered segment (S/T/R/P‑rich), with minor N‑terminal peaks.
- Mechanosensory receptor (Stum): numerous high peaks on serines dispersed through annotated disordered, low‑complexity/polar regions.
- Yeast RNA/chromatin‑associated factor (REF2‑interacting protein): peaks within disordered, compositionally biased tracts; strongest at a threonine in an S/T‑rich context, near (but not exactly on) annotated phosphosites.
- Secreted antimicrobial peptide precursor (lumbricin): strongest activation on the N‑terminal signal peptide helix; weaker peaks just after the signal peptide preceding a long disordered pro‑region.
- Yeast HPH2 regulatory protein: activation confined to disordered, low‑complexity regions in the N‑terminal two‑thirds; absent from the structured C‑terminal domain and its transmembrane helix.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity, serine/threonine- and charge‑rich segments (flexible linkers, targeting regions, and cytosolic/luminal tails), often containing P/G and K/R/E/D, and frequently forming transient/low‑confidence helices; largely absent from well‑folded domain cores and transmembrane helices
Activation pattern: Regional activation across extended IDRs with many residue‑level peaks on S/T and adjacent polar/charged residues; sparse or absent over structured globular domains, coiled‑coils of high confidence, and transmembrane spans; occasional activation on low‑pLDDT helical segments embedded within disordered regions and juxtamembrane basic clusters
Exemplars: - Eisosome/cortical membrane protein (yeast Sle1 family): activation on disordered, polar eisosome‑targeting region and other low‑complexity coils, with strongest peaks in long IDRs.

- ArfGAP regulator with PH and ankyrin repeats (AGAP family): activation on long disordered linkers between domains and basic low‑complexity blocks after the PH domain; off in GLD/PH cores, C4 zinc‑finger catalytic region, and ankyrin repeats.
- TORC1 scaffold subunit (Tco89‑like): strong hotspots in low‑complexity, disordered basic/acidic segments with sporadic peaks at helix edges; does not uniformly track annotated phosphosites.
- Inner nuclear membrane SUN‑domain protein: activation on low‑confidence helical stretches and basic clusters in the post‑TM luminal tail and juxtamembrane region; absent in the coiled‑coil, transmembrane helix, and structured SUN domain.

Summary: Short hydrophobic alpha-helical segments enriched in small aliphatic residues (A, V, I, L with frequent T/G), depleted of charged/aromatic residues—commonly the h‑region of Sec signal peptides, short transmembrane helices, and internal helix-forming hydrophobic patches in both membrane and soluble proteins; often N‑terminal but also internal/C‑terminal.
Activation pattern: Regional activation on contiguous hydrophobic clusters predicted as alpha‑helix, with sharp residue‑level peaks at A/V/I/L/T (often with G); observed in signal peptides, TM segments, and internal helices; occurs in both structured and disordered contexts (not restricted to low pLDDT).
Exemplars: Adenovirus E4‑ORF4 and HCV ARFP: internal hydrophobic helix‑prone stretches in small viral proteins; Oomycete RxLR effectors and yeast killer toxin precursors: strong activation on N‑terminal Sec signal peptides; Bacterial cytochrome c oxidase subunit 2 and DHHC palmitoyltransferases: activation on short transmembrane helices; Kdo transferase and OMA hydratase: activation on internal hydrophobic helices within soluble/peripheral membrane enzymes.

Summary: Composition-driven detection of intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity segments—especially serine/threonine–rich stretches with interspersed Pro/Gly and small hydrophobics, and often including basic (Lys/Arg) residues—commonly found in secreted/extracellular proteins and short basic accessory or micropeptides, rather than a specific motif or domain
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks scattered across long disordered/low‑complexity regions (often near the N‑terminus), with strongest signals on S/T and additional hits on P/G, A/V/I, and sometimes Lys/Arg or Cys; little preference for signal peptides, transmembranes, or catalytic motifs per se
Exemplars: - Fungal GPI-anchored cell-wall adhesins (e.g., AWA1/adhesin-like): peaks on S/T and small hydrophobics within disordered, low‑complexity O‑glycan–prone repeats; not on the signal peptide or GPI site.

Summary: Amphipathic, hydrophobic secondary‑structure cores in small proteins—especially alpha‑helical segments and the juxtamembrane/N‑terminal half of signal‑anchor transmembrane helices with a positive‑inside (Lys/Arg) bias; in soluble proteins, the analogous β‑α/helix bundle core often at oligomerization interfaces—while avoiding disordered tails and catalytic/loop regions

Summary: Short, low‑complexity interaction segments enriched in Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly (often with nearby Lys/Arg), typically intrinsically disordered, frequently near N‑termini and harboring regulatory PTM sites; the feature also highlights analogous short cationic helices used for molecular interactions (e.g., HTH DNA‑binding helices and amphipathic antimicrobial peptides).

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity regulatory segments of nuclear proteins—especially transcription factors/cofactors, chromatin regulators, RNA/splicing factors, and nuclear RING‑type E3 ligases—enriched in basic (Lys/Arg) and polar (Ser/Pro/Gln/Glu/Gly/Thr) tracts that serve as activation/repression, partner‑binding, or localization (NLS‑like) regions; typically outside folded DNA‑binding/catalytic domains and often overlapping phosphorylation sites or simple helices within IDRs.

Exemplars: - Polycomb ASXL family cofactor: activation on disordered regulatory segments including an NLS‑like Lys/Arg patch and a phospho‑adjacent stretch; also a simple poly‑alanine helix within an IDR.

Summary: Activation on disordered, low-complexity, and repetitive segments of secreted/extracellular and small regulatory proteins, including collagen-like triple-helix repeats, short flexible peptides, and disordered N-terminal/internal regions.

Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks distributed across repetitive or disordered stretches; in collagen-like proteins the activation spreads broadly over Gly-X-Y triple-helix tracts and low-complexity regions; in short secreted peptides and viral accessory proteins, activation tends to cluster in disordered segments and sometimes near the N-terminus; in ECF sigma factors, a peak occurs in the mid/C-terminal (~140-170) region between sigma2 and sigma4 domains.

Summary: Short, low‑complexity, intrinsically disordered proteins and modules that encode targeting/processing signals—often but not always secretory—combining hydrophobic signal peptides, double‑Gly bacteriocin leaders, or polybasic/NLS‑like segments, frequently adjacent to Ser/Thr/Pro‑rich stretches and basic clusters (e.g., RXLR, KR/RR)—common in micropeptides, toxins/secreted precursors, viral accessory proteins, keratin‑associated and testis‑specific low‑complexity proteins across taxa

- Lipoate biosynthesis/lipoylation enzymes: activation on mitochondrial/chloroplast transit peptides directing enzymes to the organelle where lipoylation occurs.
- Membrane transporters and other membrane-associated proteins: activation on signal anchors with positively charged n-regions.
- Plant proteins and plant-pathogen effectors: activation on secretory signal peptides and basic host-targeting motifs (e.g., RxLR-like) located just after the signal peptide.
- Proteases and protease-related secreted proteins: activation on the secretory signal peptide and basic propeptide processing motifs.
- Ribosome-related proteins/modifiers: activation on short basic segments (often nucleic acid-binding/NLS-like).
- Uncharacterized micropeptides/lncRNA-encoded peptides: activation across short basic regions consistent with leader/targeting-like segments.

Summary: Detector of compositionally biased, low‑complexity segments—predominantly intrinsically disordered Ser/Thr‑rich (often RS-/Pro‑containing) tracts—with a strong N‑terminal bias; it also flags the extreme N‑terminus including signal peptides of secreted precursors.
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks clustered within long disordered/low‑complexity regions (often spanning tens to hundreds of residues), with strongest peaks on Ser/Thr and nearby polar/basic residues; broad regional activation across such IDRs and minimal signal in well‑folded domains or transmembranes; additional discrete peaks frequently occur at residues 1–10, including within N‑terminal signal peptides.
Exemplars: - Transcriptional regulator (CROC-4): multiple peaks across a central low‑complexity disordered segment (S/T/R/P‑rich), with minor N‑terminal peaks.
- Mechanosensory receptor (Stum): numerous high peaks on serines dispersed through annotated disordered, low‑complexity/polar regions.
- Yeast RNA/chromatin‑associated factor (REF2‑interacting protein): peaks within disordered, compositionally biased tracts; strongest at a threonine in an S/T‑rich context, near (but not exactly on) annotated phosphosites.
- Secreted antimicrobial peptide precursor (lumbricin): strongest activation on the N‑terminal signal peptide helix; weaker peaks just after the signal peptide preceding a long disordered pro‑region.
- Yeast HPH2 regulatory protein: activation confined to disordered, low‑complexity regions in the N‑terminal two‑thirds; absent from the structured C‑terminal domain and its transmembrane helix.

Summary: Amphipathic, hydrophobic secondary‑structure cores in small proteins—especially alpha‑helical segments and the juxtamembrane/N‑terminal half of signal‑anchor transmembrane helices with a positive‑inside (Lys/Arg) bias; in soluble proteins, the analogous β‑α/helix bundle core often at oligomerization interfaces—while avoiding disordered tails and catalytic/loop regions
Activation pattern: Regional activation over long, contiguous, high‑confidence secondary‑structure elements (helices and β‑α segments); strongest in ordered cores, weak/absent in disordered termini and peripheral loops; in bitopic membrane proteins, peaks at the cytosolic amphipathic helix and the N‑proximal half of the TM helix (positive‑inside), tapering toward the extracytosolic half
Exemplars: - Sec translocon subunit E (bitopic membrane protein): activation on the pre‑TM cytosolic amphipathic helix and the N‑terminal half of the TM helix, consistent with the positive‑inside rule; low on the periplasmic side.
- CRISPR Cas2 endoribonucleases: activation across the central β strands and adjoining α‑helix that form the homodimer core; catalytic Asp and flexible termini are not emphasized.
- Exodeoxyribonuclease VII small subunit: strong signal on the central ordered helix bundle, with little/no activation on disordered N/C‑terminal regions.
- ATP synthase and respiratory chain small membrane subunits: enrichment on N‑terminal amphipathic/juxtamembrane helices and the entry half of signal‑anchor TM segments.
- Small ribosomal proteins and other RNA/protein‑binding regulators: activation on amphipathic helical cores that present Lys/Arg‑rich faces, rather than on flexible/basic tails.
- Archaeal gas vesicle structural proteins: signal on extended hydrophobic/amphipathic helices forming the shell scaffold.
- Eukaryotic coiled‑coil proteins: activation along coiled‑coil helical segments constituting the stable structural core.

Summary: Short hydrophobic alpha-helical segments enriched in small aliphatic residues (A, V, I, L with frequent T/G), depleted of charged/aromatic residues—commonly the h‑region of Sec signal peptides, short transmembrane helices, and internal helix-forming hydrophobic patches in both membrane and soluble proteins; often N‑terminal but also internal/C‑terminal.
Activation pattern: Regional activation on contiguous hydrophobic clusters predicted as alpha‑helix, with sharp residue‑level peaks at A/V/I/L/T (often with G); observed in signal peptides, TM segments, and internal helices; occurs in both structured and disordered contexts (not restricted to low pLDDT).
Exemplars: Adenovirus E4‑ORF4 and HCV ARFP: internal hydrophobic helix‑prone stretches in small viral proteins; Oomycete RxLR effectors and yeast killer toxin precursors: strong activation on N‑terminal Sec signal peptides; Bacterial cytochrome c oxidase subunit 2 and DHHC palmitoyltransferases: activation on short transmembrane helices; Kdo transferase and OMA hydratase: activation on internal hydrophobic helices within soluble/peripheral membrane enzymes.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity, serine/threonine- and charge‑rich segments (flexible linkers, targeting regions, and cytosolic/luminal tails), often containing P/G and K/R/E/D, and frequently forming transient/low‑confidence helices; largely absent from well‑folded domain cores and transmembrane helices
Activation pattern: Regional activation across extended IDRs with many residue‑level peaks on S/T and adjacent polar/charged residues; sparse or absent over structured globular domains, coiled‑coils of high confidence, and transmembrane spans; occasional activation on low‑pLDDT helical segments embedded within disordered regions and juxtamembrane basic clusters
Exemplars: - Eisosome/cortical membrane protein (yeast Sle1 family): activation on disordered, polar eisosome‑targeting region and other low‑complexity coils, with strongest peaks in long IDRs.
- 12‑TM solute carrier–type sodium transporter: activation confined to disordered N‑terminal tail and large extramembranous loops; silent across all transmembrane helices.
- ArfGAP regulator with PH and ankyrin repeats (AGAP family): activation on long disordered linkers between domains and basic low‑complexity blocks after the PH domain; off in GLD/PH cores, C4 zinc‑finger catalytic region, and ankyrin repeats.
- TORC1 scaffold subunit (Tco89‑like): strong hotspots in low‑complexity, disordered basic/acidic segments with sporadic peaks at helix edges; does not uniformly track annotated phosphosites.
- Inner nuclear membrane SUN‑domain protein: activation on low‑confidence helical stretches and basic clusters in the post‑TM luminal tail and juxtamembrane region; absent in the coiled‑coil, transmembrane helix, and structured SUN domain.

Summary: Short linear motifs centered on serine/threonine within intrinsically disordered regions that correspond to eukaryotic Ser/Thr phosphorylation sites (often SP/TP or basic R/K-flanked motifs), used for regulatory control across diverse proteins including viral proteins
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks on single S/T or 1–3 aa motifs, punctate and distributed across proteins; strongly enriched in low-pLDDT coils and low-complexity segments; depleted in folded domains and transmembrane helices; occasional peaks at edges of low-confidence helices; context frequently includes nearby proline and/or basic residues
Exemplars: - PH plus RapGAP scaffold proteins: activation on S/T residues in disordered linkers; minimal signal in folded PH and GAP domains
- Chromatin regulator Spt21: multiple peaks in disordered C-terminal regions; includes a known phosphoserine site
- TORC1 subunit Tco89: peaks at/near an annotated phosphothreonine and other disordered segments
- Large transmembrane receptor with long cytosolic tail (stum): activation confined to disordered cytosolic regions; none in transmembrane helices
- Developmental cytoskeletal regulator (bottleneck): clusters on S/T within low-complexity, basic-enriched disordered C-terminus
- Small GTPase regulators (e.g., RhoGAPs, RasGEFs, ARF GEFs) and protein kinases: signal found in regulatory low-complexity regions and termini rather than catalytic cores, consistent with phosphorylation-prone SLiMs

Activation pattern: Regional activation on contiguous hydrophobic clusters predicted as alpha‑helix, with sharp residue‑level peaks at A/V/I/L/T (often with G); observed in signal peptides, TM segments, and internal helices; occurs in both structured and disordered contexts (not restricted to low pLDDT).
Exemplars: Adenovirus E4‑ORF4 and HCV ARFP: internal hydrophobic helix‑prone stretches in small viral proteins; Oomycete RxLR effectors and yeast killer toxin precursors: strong activation on N‑terminal Sec signal peptides; Bacterial cytochrome c oxidase subunit 2 and DHHC palmitoyltransferases: activation on short transmembrane helices; Kdo transferase and OMA hydratase: activation on internal hydrophobic helices within soluble/peripheral membrane enzymes.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity regions enriched in serine, threonine, proline and polar/charged residues—flexible regulatory linkers/tails and propeptide segments that often host short linear motifs (e.g., phosphorylation- and proline‑rich motifs) and proteolytic processing sites; signal is absent from well‑folded catalytic domains and is common across taxa
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long disordered stretches with many sparse residue‑level peaks; avoids structured domains; peaks biased toward S/T/P, glycine, and charged/polar residues; frequently concentrated in N‑ or C‑terminal IDRs and around cleavage/processing sites; can span hundreds of residues in large eukaryotic proteins
Exemplars: - PAK family serine/threonine kinases: activation on the N‑terminal regulatory IDR preceding the kinase domain (including low‑confidence helical propensities), not in the folded kinase domain.
- Rap/Ras GTPase‑activating proteins: activation on disordered, low‑complexity linkers; absent from the structured GAP domain.
- CARMIL (actin/capping protein regulators): activation on a C‑terminal proline/basic‑rich disordered tail.
- Centrosomal/kinetochore and chromosomal scaffold proteins: multiple low‑complexity, disordered tracts with scattered peaks.
- Transcriptional/chromatin regulators: activation on N‑terminal low‑complexity/activation domains and compositionally biased regions.
- Ribonucleotide reductase large subunit‑like proteins: activation on N‑terminal disordered tails, including proline‑rich segments.
- Neuropeptide/prohormone precursors: activation in disordered propeptides and at termini of amidated peptides, often adjacent to cleavage sites.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity regulatory segments of nuclear proteins—especially transcription factors/cofactors, chromatin regulators, RNA/splicing factors, and nuclear RING‑type E3 ligases—enriched in basic (Lys/Arg) and polar (Ser/Pro/Gln/Glu/Gly/Thr) tracts that serve as activation/repression, partner‑binding, or localization (NLS‑like) regions; typically outside folded DNA‑binding/catalytic domains and often overlapping phosphorylation sites or simple helices within IDRs.
Activation pattern: Predominantly regional activation across long IDRs with multiple sparse residue‑level peaks; strong signal in basic/polar low‑complexity patches and SLiM‑rich interaction zones; little to no activation in well‑folded domains, with occasional peaks in adjacent/peripheral coil or simple poly‑Ala helices.
Exemplars: - Polycomb ASXL family cofactor: activation on disordered regulatory segments including an NLS‑like Lys/Arg patch and a phospho‑adjacent stretch; also a simple poly‑alanine helix within an IDR.
- T‑box transcription factors (Brachyury‑like): activation on C‑terminal low‑complexity, disordered regulatory tails; absent from the folded T‑box DNA‑binding domain.
- Homeobox transcription factors: activation on N‑ and C‑terminal IDRs and basic patches around the homeodomain, with minor peaks in domain‑adjacent coil.
- WTAP (m6A/splicing regulator): activation across the disordered, low‑complexity C‑terminal tail.
- RING‑type nuclear E3 ligases (e.g., Arkadia/RNF111): activation on N‑terminal/central basic IDRs and a partner‑binding region (AXIN1 interface); no activation within the structured RING domain.

Summary: A composition/secondary-structure signal for short, hydrophobic, low-basic-content segments with alpha-helix propensity—most strongly the h-region of N-terminal signal peptides and other amphipathic helices (e.g., the recognition helix of HTH regulators)—and, more weakly, compositionally similar stretches within low-complexity or disordered regions.
Activation pattern: Sparse, residue-level peaks in short stretches (often near the N-terminus), enriched for L/V/I/A/S/T/P/G and occasional acidic/polar residues, with few Lys/Arg; strongest when the segment is a short predicted helix, but also appearing on low-pLDDT coil in low-complexity proteins; variable number of peaks per protein.
Exemplars: - HTH-type ArsR transcriptional regulators: peaks in the DNA-binding H-T-H region, especially the recognition helix.
- Secreted venom/chemotactic peptide precursors: single weak peak within the N-terminal signal peptide helix; little to none on the mature peptide.
- Viral chemokine (IL-8) homologs: peaks in the signal peptide h-region, occasionally a weak site in a disordered tail.
- Plant CLE/CLAVATA propeptides: peaks in the signal peptide and a short helical segment of the propeptide; occasional Pro in the mature peptide region.
- Insect adipokinetic hormone precursors: strongest activation in the signal peptide; additional peaks in helical propeptide segments; absent on the mature hormone.
- Milk caseins: multiple weak peaks across low-confidence, low-complexity segments (some transient-helix predictions) within the mature chain.
- Keratin-associated proteins: sparse peaks within Ser/Thr/Gly-rich repeats of low structural confidence, with occasional short helical sites.
- Retroviral accessory proteins (e.g., HTLV p30II): discrete peaks across disordered regions, including near a short helical targeting motif at the C-terminus.

- Yeast RNA/chromatin‑associated factor (REF2‑interacting protein): peaks within disordered, compositionally biased tracts; strongest at a threonine in an S/T‑rich context, near (but not exactly on) annotated phosphosites.
- Secreted antimicrobial peptide precursor (lumbricin): strongest activation on the N‑terminal signal peptide helix; weaker peaks just after the signal peptide preceding a long disordered pro‑region.
- Yeast HPH2 regulatory protein: activation confined to disordered, low‑complexity regions in the N‑terminal two‑thirds; absent from the structured C‑terminal domain and its transmembrane helix.

Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks on single S/T or 1–3 aa motifs, punctate and distributed across proteins; strongly enriched in low-pLDDT coils and low-complexity segments; depleted in folded domains and transmembrane helices; occasional peaks at edges of low-confidence helices; context frequently includes nearby proline and/or basic residues
Exemplars: - PH plus RapGAP scaffold proteins: activation on S/T residues in disordered linkers; minimal signal in folded PH and GAP domains
- Chromatin regulator Spt21: multiple peaks in disordered C-terminal regions; includes a known phosphoserine site
- TORC1 subunit Tco89: peaks at/near an annotated phosphothreonine and other disordered segments

- Developmental cytoskeletal regulator (bottleneck): clusters on S/T within low-complexity, basic-enriched disordered C-terminus

Summary: Serine residues across a wide range of structural contexts, with a bias toward serine-rich segments in intrinsically disordered or low-complexity regions (often N-terminal tails), but also firing on serines within transmembrane helices and other structured contexts; the feature behaves primarily as a serine detector with some preference for S-rich patches.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks almost exclusively on Ser; many peaks per protein, frequently clustered near termini and in compositionally biased/disordered regions, but also appearing within transmembrane helices, signal peptides, and transit peptides; minor spillover to nearby residues.
Exemplars: Viral accessory proteins (metapneumovirus X): serines in a disordered C-terminal tail; Herpesvirus envelope glycoprotein L: serines across the gH-interacting segment and a disordered C-terminus; Herpesvirus cytoplasmic envelopment proteins: numerous serines in low-pLDDT regions; Plant ribosome-inactivating proteins (dianthin): N-terminal loop/coil serines; Human adaptor/regulatory protein ST20: N-terminal serines in a low-confidence helix/coil; Oomycete RxLR effectors: serines across the signal peptide, core, and disordered C-terminus; Bacteriocins (enterocins): serines in flexible coil segments.

Summary: Single conserved residue—often hydrophobic/aromatic but variable (Phe/Tyr/Trp/Leu/Val/Ile, and sometimes His/Thr)—within nucleotide- or ligand-binding pockets and analogous buried sites across diverse folds; in non-nucleotide proteins it maps to an analogous internal pocket- or core-lining position.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks at an internal pocket-lining residue, occasionally with short adjacent clusters; position varies widely with the fold.
Exemplars:
- Protein kinases (including viral/atypical): activation within the kinase domain at a residue near the ATP-binding cleft.
- tRNA (guanine-N7)-methyltransferases (class I SAM MTases): activation on the conserved aromatic that stacks with the SAM adenine and/or the target guanine in the active site.
- UDP-sugar glycosyltransferases for LPS/teichoic acid/lipid A biosynthesis (GT-B fold): activation on the aromatic that stacks with the UDP uracil ring in the donor-binding site.
- NAD(P)-dependent dehydrogenases (Rossmann fold): activation on an adenine-stacking Phe/Tyr in the dinucleotide-binding pocket.
- MurE (UDP-MurNAc-tripeptide synthetase; ATP-grasp ligase): activation on a buried hydrophobe that helps form the adenine-binding cleft for ATP.
- Carbonic anhydrases: activation on a conserved hydrophobic/aromatic residue lining the active-site hydrophobic pocket adjacent to the catalytic zinc.
- Small ribosomal subunit protein S8: activation on an aromatic residue that base-stacks with rRNA or stabilizes the RNA-binding surface.
- MICOS subunit Mic60 (mitofilin): activation on a buried aromatic within the coiled-coil/mitofilin scaffold that stabilizes the membrane-associated core.

Summary: C-terminal catalytic lobe of FAD-dependent flavoproteins: a mixed β–α segment (often a loop–helix block) adjacent to the FAD isoalloxazine that shapes the substrate/oxygen/quinone access channel and caps the cofactor pocket; this region lies downstream of the canonical N-terminal phosphate-binding glycine loop and frequently includes flexible, glycine/acidic-rich loops and a terminal helix
Activation pattern: Regional activation over long, contiguous stretches in the C-terminal portion of the FAD-oxidoreductase domain; peaks commonly occur in flexible loops and neighboring helices flanking the isoalloxazine ring and substrate tunnel; rarely targets the N-terminal Rossmann-like FAD-binding motif
Exemplars: - Quinone-linked glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (anaerobic GlpA-type): activation on the C-terminal catalytic lobe distal to the N-terminal FAD-binding site (β–α elements and intervening loops).
- tRNA modification oxidoreductase MnmC (C-terminal FAD-dependent domain): activation confined to the oxidoreductase domain’s downstream region, strongest in flexible loops.
- Generic FAD oxidoreductase: activation overlapping a C-terminal segment that includes annotated FAD-binding residues, while other FAD-binding sites in the N-terminus are inactive.
- FAD-dependent amine oxidase/demethylase (LSD1/KDM1): activation immediately N-terminal to an annotated FAD-binding Glu within the catalytic domain (loop–helix region bordering the cofactor).
- Sulfide dehydrogenase flavoprotein: activation across the long C-terminal helix and adjacent coil that cap the active-site/cofactor region, with minor signal near a redox-active disulfide.
- GMC oxidoreductase (choline oxidase): strong activation across a large C-terminal block (β-strands, loops, terminal helix) forming the substrate-binding subdomain; distinct from the N-terminal FAD-binding loop.

Summary: C-terminal lid/capping helical subdomain adjacent to the catalytic/cofactor pocket in FAD-dependent oxidative enzymes, including FAD-dependent tRNA oxidoreductases (MnmC) as well as broader FAD/FMN flavoprotein families (amine oxidases, monooxygenases/halogenases, heme-pathway flavoproteins, respiratory flavoproteins) and some carotenoid-processing enzymes with analogous C-terminal caps (e.g., lycopene beta-cyclase). Activation peaks at a conserved C-terminal motif (e.g., (L/N)PNR-W-(R/K)) within this capping subdomain.
Exemplars: MnmC bifunctional tRNA modification protein: activation on the C-terminal FAD-dependent oxidoreductase capping helix; Carotenoid lycopene beta-cyclase: activation on the C-terminal helical cap of the membrane cyclase

Summary: A conserved FAD-binding loop/helix module that cradles the flavin (FAD) cofactor in diverse flavoprotein oxidoreductases, typically the short beta→loop→alpha transition immediately adjacent to annotated FAD-contact residues and often lining the isoalloxazine/active-site pocket; enriched in small/aliphatic and glycine residues and sometimes incorporating substrate-contacting or redox-active residues.
Activation pattern: Regional activation with sharp residue-level peaks over a contiguous 10–30 aa segment at a coil/turn-to-helix (or beta-to-helix) junction within the FAD-binding domain; frequently starts immediately C-terminal to annotated FAD-binding residues and can overlap substrate-contacting positions; occasional weaker secondary patches on neighboring helices.
Exemplars: - Type II NADH:quinone oxidoreductase (NDH-2): peak on the loop/helix segment overlapping FAD-binding residues (e.g., A333–Q334) immediately following a FAD-binding Asp.
- NAD(P)H:rubredoxin oxidoreductase: strong activation on the loop-to-helix linker just C-terminal to the FAD-binding Asp (D260).
- NAD(P)H-dependent nitrite reductase (flavoprotein): dominant peak on a beta–loop–alpha connector within the FAD-binding domain, with a secondary low-level hit at an annotated FAD-binding beta strand.
- Coproporphyrinogen III oxidase (flavoprotein): discrete C‑terminal coil-to-helix segment overlapping annotated FAD-binding residues (I426–V428).
- Digeranylgeranylglycerophospholipid reductase: peak centered on the coil/helix that binds FAD (G300, K301) and contacts the lipid substrate (H297), with weaker signal near a disulfide-forming cysteine on the adjacent helix.

Summary: Active-site–proximal substrate-binding core of FAD-dependent oxidoreductases (flavoproteins)—an aromatic/basic–rich region flanking the FAD isoalloxazine that positions substrate and channels O2/halogen/quinone equivalents, common to FMOs, flavin halogenases, MAO-like amine oxidases/demethylases, quinone-interacting flavoproteins, and isoprenoid/carotenoid redox enzymes; the feature isolates the oxidoreductase module within multidomain proteins
Activation pattern: Regional/domain-level activation: long, contiguous segments in the middle-to-late portion of sequences corresponding to the C-terminal substrate-binding/oxygen or quinone channel region adjacent to FAD; enriched in aromatic (W/F/Y) and basic (K/R) residues; observed in both soluble and membrane/organellar contexts
Exemplars: - Flavin-dependent monooxygenases (bacterial/fungal FMOs, Baeyer–Villiger-type FMOs): activation over the C-terminal substrate pocket and O2 channel contiguous to the FAD
- Flavin-dependent halogenases (e.g., tryptophan/indole/aliphatic halogenases): activation on the Lys/Arg/Tyr-rich catalytic region that delivers HOX from the peroxyflavin near FAD
- Amine oxidase superfamily (MAO, polyamine oxidases, LSD1/KDM1 demethylases): activation on the “aromatic cage” and adjacent loops that bind cationic amines next to FAD N5
- Amino-acid oxidases/dehydrogenases (L-amino acid oxidase, D-amino acid oxidase/dehydrogenase): activation on the FAD-proximal substrate-binding domain
- Quinone-linked flavoproteins (e.g., NQO-like quinone reductases; FAD subunits of respiratory dehydrogenases): activation on the quinone-binding site adjacent to FAD
- Carotenoid/isoprenoid pathway flavoproteins (phytoene/zeta-carotene desaturases; archaeal/bacterial geranylgeranyl or prenyl-lipid reductases): activation over the membrane-proximal FAD active-site region that accommodates polyprenyl chains
- Multidomain/bifunctional enzymes containing an FAD-oxidoreductase module: activation isolates the oxidoreductase catalytic core within the larger polypeptide

Summary: A short, amphipathic helix/loop that lines the substrate-access channel next to the flavin/nicotinamide site in Rossmann-like FAD/NAD(P)H oxidoreductases (pyridine nucleotide–disulfide/quinone/ascorbate/transhydrogenase families). It typically lies just C‑terminal to an FAD-binding stretch and immediately upstream of catalytic or substrate-contacting residues, contributing to substrate recognition/gating rather than cofactor binding; the segment is enriched in small hydrophobics (A/V/I/L) with occasional Lys/Arg and often a C‑terminal Gly.
Activation pattern: Regional hotspot: a single 15–25 aa patch with a sharp rise and tapered fall, usually centered on an α‑helical segment and its immediate flanks. It frequently begins directly after annotated FAD-binding residues and precedes catalytic/substrate-contacting positions; canonical FAD/NAD-binding motifs and redox Cys pairs are largely not activated.
Exemplars: - Dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase (E3 component): activates on a helix (∼315–334) immediately following an FAD-binding residue, consistent with a pocket-lining/gating helix rather than the catalytic disulfide or NAD site.
- Coenzyme A disulfide reductase: activates over a mid-sequence segment (∼292–320) centered on a known substrate-binding His, avoiding the FAD/NADP+ motifs—indicative of a substrate-channel helix/loop.
- Monodehydroascorbate reductase (plant MDAR): activates on 318–333 including an ascorbate-binding Arg, marking the substrate-recognition helix adjacent to the flavin site.
- Soluble pyridine nucleotide transhydrogenase (SthA/UdhA): shared mid-late segment (∼319–342) across Gammaproteobacteria, matching the conserved helix that shapes the nicotinamide/flavin pocket rather than the early FAD-binding region.
- Quinone-/persulfide-processing flavoenzymes (e.g., AIF-like/persulfide oxidoreductases): activates on a short C‑terminal segment directly after FAD-binding residues and just before a catalytic cysteine persulfide, consistent with a gating element of the active-site channel.

Summary: Small, often poorly characterized or compositionally biased proteins, including viral accessory proteins, cancer/testis and germline-associated proteins, antisense-ORF microproteins, and short secreted/surface peptides; activation is broadly distributed across the polypeptide rather than focused on a single structured domain
Activation pattern: Regional/distributed activation spread across much of the protein with sparse residue-level peaks; often includes early N-terminal residues and disordered segments; variable coverage from short patches to most of the protein
Exemplars:
- Viral non-structural/accessory proteins: activation distributed through the protein, including basic/Arg-rich motifs such as nuclear localization signals.
- Cancer/testis antigens and germline-associated proteins: activation on long disordered low-complexity regions, often at N-termini.
- Small uncharacterized microproteins/antisense ORFs: activation spanning most of the polypeptide.
- Short secreted peptides and toxin precursors: activation across both signal/propeptide and mature regions.
- Compact cytosolic proteins with disordered N- or C-terminal extensions: activation enriched on the disordered tails.

Summary: Broadly distributed activation across small secreted peptides, processed protein fragments, and various polar/charged residues in short proteins, with frequent firing in viral, venom, and signaling-peptide contexts.

Activation pattern: Sparse residue-level peaks scattered across the protein, with no strong preference for structured versus unstructured regions; peaks occur on a mix of polar (Asn, Asp, Ser, Gln), basic (Arg, Lys), and hydrophobic (Leu, Val, Ala) residues, and can fall within transmembrane helices, disordered stretches, or short folded chains alike.

Exemplars:
- Secreted peptide hormones (cholecystokinin, kisspeptin/metastin): multiple peaks across the processed peptide chain.
- Snake venom metalloproteinase/disintegrin fragment: distributed peaks across the short chain.
- Viral hexon-linking precursor proteins: weak peaks distributed across the chain including propeptide and cleaved segments.
- Peroxisomal biogenesis factors: peaks within transmembrane helices and other regions of the membrane protein.
- Bacterial methyltransferases: activation localized to C-terminal disordered extension while the catalytic core is inactive.
- Antithrombin/serpin precursor: peaks spanning the signal peptide and mature chain.

Summary: Often fires within intrinsic disorder/low-complexity segments—especially terminal or propeptide regions enriched in Pro/Ser/Thr/Gly—that serve as flexible carriers of short linear motifs; the feature highlights unstructured tails/loops across diverse proteins (including secreted precursors, viral regulators, membrane-protein tails, and micropeptides), sometimes coinciding with proteolytic processing and PTM sites, but also produces residue-level peaks within some short folded enzymes/fragments.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks within annotated/predicted disordered coils and low-complexity tracts, frequently enriched toward N-termini; additional scattered peaks can occur within short folded chains.
Exemplars: - Secreted peptide hormone precursors (e.g., cholecystokinin/prohormones): peaks in unstructured propeptide segments at sulfotyrosine, amidation sites, and cleavage boundaries.
- Herpesviral nuclear egress proteins: activation on N-terminal disordered, polar-biased regions; not on the structured zinc-finger domain.
- Integrase-family proteins: peaks include very low-pLDDT loops and annotated disordered segments, with additional scattered peaks elsewhere in the chain.
- Mycobacterial cell-envelope–associated proteins: single-residue/short-segment peaks within UniProt-annotated disordered coil regions.
- p53-inducible regulatory proteins: sparse peaks across N-terminal and central intrinsically disordered regions, including isoform-variable segments.
- Alternative reading frame micropeptides: activation across low-complexity, disordered coils.

Summary: Low-complexity, intrinsically disordered segments—often at protein N-termini—such as mucin-like/propeptide regions or flexible linkers adjacent to signal/transit peptides, common in small secreted or membrane-associated proteins and also as disordered extensions in diverse enzymes (broad taxonomic coverage, including viral, bacterial, and eukaryotic proteins).
Activation pattern: Regional activation over short to moderate stretches, frequently in disordered or polar/low-complexity segments; in longer proteins, multiple low-complexity patches can activate; in micropeptides, activation can span much of the sequence. Residue-level peaks can fall on Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly within polar-residue stretches but also on basic or hydrophobic residues within the same disordered context.
Exemplars:
- Viral envelope/accessory microproteins: activation on N-terminal Ser/Thr/Pro-rich disordered segments (often mucin-like or regulatory tails).
- Secreted eukaryotic effectors (e.g., oomycete RxLR effectors): activation on the low-complexity region flanking the signal peptide/RxLR motif.
- Human testis-biased and lncRNA-derived micropeptides: activation across intrinsically disordered peptide regions.
- Secreted precursors/propeptides: activation on N-terminal regions following the signal peptide.
- Membrane-associated single-pass proteins: activation on luminal or cytosolic tails flanking the transmembrane helix.
- Bacterial/archaeal metabolic enzymes: activation on disordered, low-complexity N-terminal extensions/linkers enriched in Ser/Thr/Gly/Pro.

Summary: Arginine-selective low-complexity/disordered segments—polybasic tracts and RG/RGG-type repeats—often occurring as long, repetitive stretches; includes the Arg residues embedded in repeated neuropeptide/prohormone units (e.g., RFamide-like repeats). The signal tracks local Arg identity/density with a strong preference for Arg over Lys and is largely independent of stable secondary/tertiary structure.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks on Arg that cluster over extended disordered, compositionally biased regions; broad regional activation in Arg-dense tails or repeats; minimal in well-structured domains and transmembrane helices; occasional co-activation of neighboring Gly (RG/RGG) and sometimes Trp within Arg-rich low-complexity segments; Lys generally weak.
Exemplars: - RFamide-family neuropeptide/prohormone precursors: strong peaks on the Arg within repeated peptide units (e.g., PRQFV-/XREFV-amide motifs) and nearby disordered basic-biased segments; little/no signal in the N-terminal signal peptide.
- Vacuolar zinc transporters (multi-pass membrane transporters): concentrated activation on cytosolic, disordered, Arg-rich C-terminal tails; silent across transmembrane helices and luminal loops.
- RNA-binding and chromatin-associated proteins: activation on RGG/RG boxes and poly-Arg low-complexity tracts that mediate nucleic-acid interactions/phase separation.
- Viral regulatory proteins: strong signal on Arg/Gly-rich low-complexity segments.
- Reproductive proteins (e.g., protamines, semenogelins) and long coiled-coil/golgin scaffolds, mucin-like glycoproteins, and disulfide-rich peptide toxins: activation on extended Arg-rich, repetitive low-complexity regions.

Summary: Hydrophobic alpha-helical membrane-insertion segments: internal transmembrane helices and signal-anchor/signal peptide h-regions that mediate insertion into lipid bilayers, prominently in viral viroporins/envelope anchors, mitochondrial inner-membrane respiratory subunits, multi-pass transporters/channels, and short hydrophobic microproteins; and, at lower confidence, short hydrophobic/amphipathic low-complexity segments in soluble proteins that mimic h-regions.

Activation pattern: Regional activation over long, contiguous hydrophobic runs (≈18–25 aa) characteristic of α-helical transmembrane segments; often multiple separate activation clusters matching individual helices in multi-pass proteins; frequent strong N-terminal activation corresponding to the signal peptide h-region; in very small hydrophobic proteins, activation can span most of the sequence; tolerates glycine/proline interruptions within the hydrophobic helix; weaker, shorter activations can occur on hydrophobic/amphipathic low-complexity patches in otherwise soluble nuclear/cytosolic proteins.

Exemplars: 
- Viroporins (e.g., influenza M2, coronavirus E, HIV Vpu): activation across the single pore-forming transmembrane helix.
- Viral envelope glycoproteins: activation on the C-terminal transmembrane anchor of fusion/envelope subunits (e.g., retroviral gp41 TM, paramyxovirus F TM, coronavirus spike TM).
- Small viral accessory proteins with membrane-associating helices (e.g., birnavirus VP5).
- Mitochondrial respiratory chain subunits (Complex I ND proteins, cytochrome c oxidase subunits, ATP synthase a/6/8): activation on each inner-membrane transmembrane helix.
- Multi-pass transporters and channels (ABC transporters, secondary transporters, ion channels): activation on each membrane-spanning helix.
- GPCRs: activation on the seven hydrophobic transmembrane helices.
- Secreted proteins with N-terminal signal peptides: activation on the signal peptide h-region preceding the cleavage site (e.g., RxLR effectors, small secreted peptides).
- Type I/II single-pass membrane proteins: activation on the signal-anchor/transmembrane helix.
- Yeast/fungal GPI-anchored and cell-wall/membrane proteins: activation on N-terminal signal peptides and/or short C-terminal hydrophobic GPI-signal segments.
- Occasional off-targets: soluble nuclear/cytosolic proteins (e.g., RING E3 ligases, chromatin modifiers, RNA-processing enzymes) via short hydrophobic low-complexity or amphipathic segments.

Summary: Arginine-selective low-complexity/disordered segments—polybasic tracts and RG/RGG-type repeats—often occurring as long, repetitive stretches; includes the Arg residues embedded in repeated neuropeptide/prohormone units (e.g., RFamide-like repeats). The signal tracks local Arg identity/density with a strong preference for Arg over Lys and is largely independent of stable secondary/tertiary structure.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks on Arg that cluster over extended disordered, compositionally biased regions; broad regional activation in Arg-dense tails or repeats; minimal in well-structured domains and transmembrane helices; occasional co-activation of neighboring Gly (RG/RGG) and sometimes Trp within Arg-rich low-complexity segments; Lys generally weak.
Exemplars: - RFamide-family neuropeptide/prohormone precursors: strong peaks on the Arg within repeated peptide units (e.g., PRQFV-/XREFV-amide motifs) and nearby disordered basic-biased segments; little/no signal in the N-terminal signal peptide.
- Vacuolar zinc transporters (multi-pass membrane transporters): concentrated activation on cytosolic, disordered, Arg-rich C-terminal tails; silent across transmembrane helices and luminal loops.
- RNA-binding and chromatin-associated proteins: activation on RGG/RG boxes and poly-Arg low-complexity tracts that mediate nucleic-acid interactions/phase separation.
- Viral regulatory proteins: strong signal on Arg/Gly-rich low-complexity segments.
- Reproductive proteins (e.g., protamines, semenogelins) and long coiled-coil/golgin scaffolds, mucin-like glycoproteins, and disulfide-rich peptide toxins: activation on extended Arg-rich, repetitive low-complexity regions.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low-complexity segments used as extracellular stalks/linkers and nuclear/regulatory IDRs. These segments are typically either polyampholyte tracts enriched in acidic and basic residues (E/D with K/R/H; often E–x–K repeats) or mucin-/extensin-like Pro/Thr/Ser-rich O-glycosylation tracts; they are common in secreted/adhesive proteins, peptide/venom/neuropeptide precursors, viral/apicomplexan low-complexity proteins, and some germ cell/testis antigens.

Activation pattern: Regional activation across long disordered low-complexity tracts; frequent periodic residue-level peaks on charged residues (E/D and K/R/H) when present. In S/T/P-rich mucin/extensin-like segments, activation is broad/regional and may highlight nearby acidic residues; little or no activation in folded domains, signal peptides, or short structured modules, though low-complexity propeptides of precursors can activate.

Exemplars:
- Fungal cell-wall adhesins and signaling mucins: central low-complexity stalks (K/E-rich or Ser/Thr/Pro-rich glycostalks) are activated; signal peptides and structured domains are not.
- Plant extensins (hydroxyproline/proline-rich glycoproteins): activation along long S/T/P-rich repeats with acidic patches in disordered tails.
- Germ cell/testis antigens and chromatin remodeler subunits: EK-repeat polyampholyte IDRs with sharp peaks on E/K and suppression on intervening spacers.
- Viral regulatory proteins (e.g., EBNA-LP) and apicomplexan exported proteins (e.g., RESA): long acidic/basic low-complexity repeats with periodic peaks on charged residues.
- Secreted matrix/adhesion glycoproteins (e.g., MAdCAM-1 mucin-like stalk, ovocleidin-116): disordered low-complexity extracellular regions (acidic and/or S/T/P-rich) show regional activation.
- Peptide/venom/neuropeptide precursors: low-complexity, often acidic/basic-rich propeptide segments can activate.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low-complexity proline-rich tandem-repeat tracts (typically enriched in P/S/T and often Q/H) found predominantly in secreted/extracellular proteins and viral surface proteins; the feature marks conserved proline positions within repeat units that form mucin-like stalks, adhesin/cell-wall repeats, or Hyp/O-glycosylation scaffolds, and it also occurs in intracellular repeat-rich proteins such as nuclear regulators and cytoskeletal/testis-specific proteins.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long disordered repeat domains with sharp residue-level peaks mainly on prolines at fixed positions in each repeat unit (e.g., second P in PP; the P in DPxG, NANP/NVDP, or PAA-PEA motifs). Outside these tracts, activation is low, including in structured domains (signal peptides, transmembranes, enzyme cores, or GPI-anchor/propeptide segments); however, short P-rich low-complexity inserts/propeptides within secretory-pathway glycoproteins can also activate.
Exemplars:
- Fungal GPI-anchored adhesins/flocculins: strong activation on prolines within central Ser/Thr/Pro-rich tandem repeats that form the extracellular stalk.
- Plant arabinogalactan proteins/extensins: activation on PP motifs, biased to the second P that is hydroxylated to Hyp and O-glycosylated.
- Viral envelope proteins (e.g., herpesvirus gC; Plasmodium CSP): activation on prolines within repetitive, disordered external repeats (e.g., P-D-P-A-V-A-P, NANP/NVDP).
- Mucin-like secreted proteins: activation across disordered 10–15 aa repeat arrays (e.g., DPxG-containing repeats).
- Testis-specific/cytoskeletal repeat proteins (e.g., outer dense fiber proteins): activation on prolines anchoring short tandem repeats in disordered segments.
- Nuclear transcriptional regulators with Pro-rich low-complexity regions (e.g., REST): activation over Pro-rich tracts.
- Bacterial autotransporters/actin modulators (e.g., BimA): activation on surface-exposed Pro-rich repeats.
- Secretory/vacuolar glycoproteins with short low-complexity inserts: activation confined to Pro-rich inserts, not the folded enzyme core.

Summary: Compositionally biased low-complexity segments, especially N-terminal hydrophobic helices that form the hydrophobic core of signal peptides or membrane-anchoring amphipathic helices, and serine/threonine-rich intrinsically disordered tracts; the feature reflects sequence-composition bias rather than a specific fold or function and commonly occurs at protein termini across taxa
Activation pattern: Regional activation over extended contiguous blocks (typically 8–20 residues), frequently at the N-terminus; strong peaks within hydrophobic cores of signal peptide–like helices or within S/T-rich low-complexity patches; minimal activation in structured catalytic/core domains
Exemplars: - Viral nonstructural/accessory proteins: activation on a short, flexible N-terminal hydrophobic helix (amphipathic/membrane-anchoring segment).
- Plant secreted signaling peptides (SCOOP family): activation on the N-terminal signal peptide hydrophobic core, not on the C-terminal functional motif.
- Eukaryotic transcriptional coactivator scaffolds (Mediator subunit 24): activation on multiple S/T- and Q-rich intrinsically disordered, low-complexity regions.

The signal tracks local Arg identity/density with a strong preference for Arg over Lys and is largely independent of stable secondary/tertiary structure.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks on Arg that cluster over extended disordered, compositionally biased regions; broad regional activation in Arg-dense tails or repeats; minimal in well-structured domains and transmembrane helices; occasional co-activation of neighboring Gly (RG/RGG) and sometimes Trp within Arg-rich low-complexity segments; Lys generally weak.
Exemplars: - RFamide-family neuropeptide/prohormone precursors: strong peaks on the Arg within repeated peptide units (e.g., PRQFV-/XREFV-amide motifs) and nearby disordered basic-biased segments; little/no signal in the N-terminal signal peptide.
- Vacuolar zinc transporters (multi-pass membrane transporters): concentrated activation on cytosolic, disordered, Arg-rich C-terminal tails; silent across transmembrane helices and luminal loops.
- RNA-binding and chromatin-associated proteins: activation on RGG/RG boxes and poly-Arg low-complexity tracts that mediate nucleic-acid interactions/phase separation.
- Viral regulatory proteins: strong signal on Arg/Gly-rich low-complexity segments.
- Reproductive proteins (e.g., protamines, semenogelins) and long coiled-coil/golgin scaffolds, mucin-like glycoproteins, and disulfide-rich peptide toxins: activation on extended Arg-rich, repetitive low-complexity regions.

Summary: Low-complexity, intrinsically disordered segments—often at protein N-termini—such as mucin-like/propeptide regions or flexible linkers adjacent to signal/transit peptides, common in small secreted or membrane-associated proteins and also as disordered extensions in diverse enzymes (broad taxonomic coverage, including viral, bacterial, and eukaryotic proteins).
Activation pattern: Regional activation over short to moderate stretches, frequently in disordered or polar/low-complexity segments; in longer proteins, multiple low-complexity patches can activate; in micropeptides, activation can span much of the sequence. Residue-level peaks can fall on Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly within polar-residue stretches but also on basic or hydrophobic residues within the same disordered context.
Exemplars:
- Viral envelope/accessory microproteins: activation on N-terminal Ser/Thr/Pro-rich disordered segments (often mucin-like or regulatory tails).
- Secreted eukaryotic effectors (e.g., oomycete RxLR effectors): activation on the low-complexity region flanking the signal peptide/RxLR motif.
- Human testis-biased and lncRNA-derived micropeptides: activation across intrinsically disordered peptide regions.
- Secreted precursors/propeptides: activation on N-terminal regions following the signal peptide.
- Membrane-associated single-pass proteins: activation on luminal or cytosolic tails flanking the transmembrane helix.
- Bacterial/archaeal metabolic enzymes: activation on disordered, low-complexity N-terminal extensions/linkers enriched in Ser/Thr/Gly/Pro.

Summary: Feature fires broadly across short proteins and small peptides, often covering most of the chain, with a preference for low-complexity, Pro/Gly-rich and polybasic segments but also extending into adjacent structured regions of short polypeptides.
Activation pattern: Broad, near-whole-protein activation in short (~50-200 aa) precursors and microproteins, with local maxima on Pro-rich tracts (including poly-P), GP/GG-containing stretches, and basic clusters; activation is not restricted to disordered patches and can extend into folded domains in short proteins.
Exemplars:
- Class II bacteriocin/lantibiotic precursors: broad activation across the short precursor chain, including mature regions containing GG and GW motifs.
- Secreted peptide/toxin and prohormone precursors (e.g., cholecystokinin): activation spread across the precursor chain.
- Sperm protamine precursors: concentrated on disordered propeptides and at propeptide–mature boundaries; minimal on highly basic mature cores.
- Viral accessory/regulatory microproteins (e.g., Vpx, Vif): activation across the short viral protein, with strong peaks on poly-P / GP-rich low-complexity patches when present.
- lncRNA-encoded micropeptides and very small uncharacterized proteins (e.g., RUSC1-AS1, N-cym): activation on Pro/Gly-rich disordered segments and across much of the chain.
- Plant transcription factors with WG/GW- and GP-rich low-complexity regions: activation on those patches.
- ATP synthase epsilon subunits: signal on short GP-rich linkers or terminal low-complexity tails.
- Large enzymes (e.g., DDX11 helicase, acyl-CoA synthetase): activation on disordered N/C-terminal low-complexity regions or basic/GP-rich insertions.
- Small mitochondrial membrane proteins (ATP8): signal on short basic matrix-exposed loops or termini flanking TM helices.
- Short proteolytic chains of secreted enzymes (e.g., snake venom metalloproteinase fragments, acrosin chain fragments): broad activation across the short mature chain, including within structured peptidase/disintegrin regions.

Summary: Activation on disordered, low-complexity, and repetitive segments of secreted/extracellular and small regulatory proteins, including collagen-like triple-helix repeats, short flexible peptides, and disordered N-terminal/internal regions.

Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks distributed across repetitive or disordered stretches; in collagen-like proteins the activation spreads broadly over Gly-X-Y triple-helix tracts and low-complexity regions; in short secreted peptides and viral accessory proteins, activation tends to cluster in disordered segments and sometimes near the N-terminus; in ECF sigma factors, a peak occurs in the mid/C-terminal (~140-170) region between sigma2 and sigma4 domains.

Exemplars:
- Fibrillar collagens and collagen-like proteins: broad, distributed activation across Gly-X-Y triple-helix repeats and flanking low-complexity regions
- Bacterial ECF (alternative) sigma factors: a focal activation in the mid/C-terminal region near the sigma4 domain
- Secreted micropeptides, antimicrobial peptides, and arthropod venom peptides: activation on short disordered/low-complexity stretches
- Viral accessory/regulatory proteins: activation on disordered regions, frequently toward the N-terminus
- Plant small secreted peptides and cell-wall proteins: activation within short motifs and disordered segments
- Structured cytosolic enzymes and regulators: isolated activation at conserved residues in flexible loops/motifs
- Generic secreted precursors/propeptides: activation within low-complexity segments

Summary: Broadly distributed feature that activates across many residues of short proteins, protein fragments, and unstructured tails, with no strong dependence on whether the underlying region is folded or disordered; appears in viral, secreted, enzymatic, and uncharacterized proteins from diverse organisms.
Activation pattern: Diffuse, regional activation covering large fractions of the protein rather than sharp single-residue peaks; peaks occur on a wide variety of residues (hydrophobic, polar, charged) without a strong S/T/P/G bias; activation is often concentrated toward N- or C-terminal segments, including disordered tails, but is also observed within folded catalytic domains.
Exemplars: - Adenovirus E4-ORF6: activation scattered across the protein with peaks in the N-terminal half.
- Plant peroxidase fragment: activation across the N-terminal disordered region.
- Acrosin fragment: activation in both the light chain and within the Peptidase S1 domain of the heavy chain.
- Uncharacterized SLC67A1-AS: activation across the protein including C-terminal disordered regions.

Summary: Low-complexity, intrinsically disordered segments—often at protein N-termini—such as mucin-like/propeptide regions or flexible linkers adjacent to signal/transit peptides, common in small secreted or membrane-associated proteins and also as disordered extensions in diverse enzymes (broad taxonomic coverage, including viral, bacterial, and eukaryotic proteins).
Activation pattern: Regional activation over short to moderate stretches, frequently in disordered or polar/low-complexity segments; in longer proteins, multiple low-complexity patches can activate; in micropeptides, activation can span much of the sequence. Residue-level peaks can fall on Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly within polar-residue stretches but also on basic or hydrophobic residues within the same disordered context.
Exemplars:
- Viral envelope/accessory microproteins: activation on N-terminal Ser/Thr/Pro-rich disordered segments (often mucin-like or regulatory tails).
- Secreted eukaryotic effectors (e.g., oomycete RxLR effectors): activation on the low-complexity region flanking the signal peptide/RxLR motif.
- Human testis-biased and lncRNA-derived micropeptides: activation across intrinsically disordered peptide regions.
- Secreted precursors/propeptides: activation on N-terminal regions following the signal peptide.
- Membrane-associated single-pass proteins: activation on luminal or cytosolic tails flanking the transmembrane helix.
- Bacterial/archaeal metabolic enzymes: activation on disordered, low-complexity N-terminal extensions/linkers enriched in Ser/Thr/Gly/Pro.

Summary: Extracellular/mature segments of secreted proteins — the bioactive peptide or ectodomain of secreted precursors — including toxins, chemokines/peptide hormones/neuropeptides, antimicrobial peptides, protease inhibitors, extracellular matrix modules, viral envelope ectodomains, bacterial toxins/lipoproteins, fungal/oomycete effectors, and secretory granule proteins. These segments are typically cationic and often cysteine‑rich/disulfide‑stabilized, but can also be disulfide‑poor (e.g., certain neuropeptides); the feature tracks mature peptides/ectodomains rather than signal peptides or cytosolic tails.

Activation pattern: Regional activation within extracellular/mature segments with residue‑level peaks, especially at basic residues (Lys/Arg; including prohormone convertase sites) and, when present, cysteines; strongest over well‑structured extracellular cores or compact mature peptides; minimal to absent in signal peptides and often lower in low‑complexity pro‑segments.

Exemplars: - Disulfide‑rich venom peptides (e.g., kappa‑/scorpion/centipede toxins, conotoxins): activation on the mature toxin’s folded core; in kappa‑scoloptoxin, strongest on the C‑terminal helical/disulfide region.
- Chemokines and peptide hormones/neuropeptides (e.g., CXCLs; natriuretic peptides, oxytocin/vasopressin‑like, insulin‑like; and disulfide‑poor peptides such as SIFamide): activation on the mature peptide/core, not on the signal/propeptide.
- Antimicrobial peptides (defensins and other cationic AMPs): activation across the extracellular peptide core.
- Protease inhibitors (Kunitz, Kazal, plant cystine‑knot/knottins): activation on the inhibitory domain.
- Extracellular matrix/serum glycoproteins with cysteine‑patterned modules (EGF/TSR/Ig‑like, albumin family): activation on extracellular repeats/domains.
- Viral envelope glycoproteins: activation on luminal ectodomain loops.
- Bacterial secreted toxins and lipoproteins: activation on secreted extracellular segments (including lipobox‑proximal Cys and mature toxin domains).
- Fungal/oomycete small secreted effectors: activation on compact extracellular cores.
- Secretory pathway enzymes/chaperones (PDI/Ero1/QSOX) and granule proteins (e.g., 7B2): activation on luminal Cys motifs or basic, structured regions within the secretory lumen.

Summary: Secreted/processed peptides and extracellular or luminal domains of membrane proteins. The feature reads the prepropeptide architecture of small secreted hormones/neuropeptides, defense peptides and toxins, as well as disulfide-stabilized domains of extracellular receptors/ligands and viral envelope glycoproteins.

Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks concentrated within the mature secreted peptide or extracellular/luminal domain, often on residues in the structured (helical/strand) core of the processed peptide, with additional peaks on nearby basic residues and on Gly/Pro in flexible loop regions; these peaks aggregate into regional activation over the mature peptide or ectodomain. Activation is variable in extent across proteins.

Exemplars:
- Invertebrate venom peptides (knottins/conotoxins/spider and sea anemone toxins): activation across the mature toxin, with additional support on basic residues near propeptide cleavage sites.
- Antimicrobial/defense peptides (animal defensins, plant thionins/defensins): activation across conserved disulfide-stabilized frameworks and Gly/Pro-rich loop residues.
- Neuropeptide/hormone precursors (e.g., calcitonin/CGRP/amylin-like, adrenomedullin): activation concentrated on the structured core of the mature hormone within the PEPTIDE region.
- Amidated, cysteine-poor neuropeptides (e.g., FMRFamide/SIFamide-like): activation across the mature peptide and clustered convertase sites.
- Plant secreted cysteine-rich signaling peptides and protease inhibitors (CRPs, Kunitz/Bowman–Birk): activation across the secreted domain and processing motifs.
- Viral envelope/secreted glycoproteins (e.g., HA/gp120-like ectodomains): broad activation across the ectodomain, including loop and cleavage-junction residues.
- Metazoan extracellular receptor/ligand systems (disulfide-stabilized ectodomains such as EGF-like/lectin/similar Cys-rich modules): activation across the ligand-binding domains.
- Extracellular/luminal loops of multi-pass membrane proteins with small Cys clusters (e.g., receptor-transporting proteins): activation on luminal segments.
- Prokaryotic secreted/surface or secretion-system-associated proteins: activation on periplasmic/extracellular segments.
- Occasional chromatin/DNA-binding and histone-modifying proteins (Cys-rich Zn-binding or catalytic motifs): weaker activation driven by clustered Cys and basic residues that resemble the extracellular motif pattern.

Summary: Short linear segments in intrinsically disordered or otherwise low-structure-confidence regions, often at N-termini and within signal peptides/propeptides of secreted and regulatory proteins (including viral accessory proteins and small ORF microproteins), enriched in small/basic residues (G, P, S, A, R; often with Cys), rather than in well-folded catalytic cores.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks scattered across IDRs and low-confidence coils/short helices; frequently clustered near the N-terminus, in signal peptides, propeptides, and disordered tails; little to no activation in well-structured domains; occasional activation in low-confidence transmembrane/signal-anchor helices.
Exemplars: - Viral accessory protein (HIV-1 Vif): peaks throughout low-pLDDT coils, especially the disordered N-terminal region.
- Neuropeptide precursor (Drosophila Amnesiac): activation in the N-terminal signal peptide and multiple mature peptide segments with very low pLDDT.
- Secreted serine carboxypeptidase: activation confined to disordered C-terminal tail, annotated disordered segment, the signal peptide, and a low-confidence C-terminal transmembrane helix; absent from the structured catalytic domain.
- Disordered human tumor-suppressor–associated protein (ST20): scattered peaks within predicted helices in a globally disordered chain, including the N-terminus.
- lncRNA/sORF-derived microprotein (IGF2 antisense protein): multiple peaks across annotated disordered regions rich in Arg/Pro/Gly.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low-complexity segments enriched in serine/threonine/proline/glycine and often basic (lysine/arginine), typically found in flexible N- or C-terminal tails and loops; highlights IDRs that may harbor short linear motifs (e.g., basic NLS patches) rather than structured domain cores.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long disordered stretches with additional sparse residue-level peaks in low-confidence loops; often N-terminal-biased in short/viral proteins; rarely within well-folded cores.
Exemplars: Retroviral accessory proteins (e.g., HTLV-1 p30): activation on central and C-terminal IDRs including a basic nuclear localization signal; p53-regulated apoptosis-inducing microprotein: widespread activation across a globally disordered protein; Bacterial DNA ligase: scattered activation in an annotated disordered linker and flexible loops within the ligase domain; Uncharacterized human microprotein: multiple peaks throughout a low-pLDDT, disordered sequence irrespective of predicted secondary structure.

Summary: Residue-level detector for tryptophan (W) side chains, often firing on multiple W positions within a sequence and with a mild bias toward N‑terminal Ws; broadly applicable across taxa and protein classes, with frequent occurrences in short membrane/secreted proteins but also in diverse enzymes (e.g., ATP synthase ε, proteases) and mitochondrial proteins.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks centered on W; multiple independent peaks per protein; modest enrichment near N‑termini; occasional weak spillover to neighboring residues (C/E/Q/G/K/R) in W‑rich contexts.
Exemplars: - Viral small/accessory membrane proteins (e.g., viroporin-like): activation on Trp residues in short helices/interfacial segments.
- Bacteriocins and peptide toxins: activation on Trp-rich motifs that mediate membrane interaction/disruption.
- ATP synthase subunit ε (F1 epsilon): activation on conserved Trp residue(s) across bacteria/mitochondria.
- Proteases (serine, cysteine, metalloproteases): activation on Trp positions within the enzyme sequence.
- Secreted and transmembrane protein precursors: activation on interfacial/N‑terminal Trp residues around TM regions or signal-proximal segments.
- Mitochondrial proteins: activation on Trp residues, including in membrane-associated components.
- Eukaryotic micropeptides/antisense-encoded small proteins: activation on any Trp present, often near the N‑terminus due to short length.

Summary: Short, intrinsically disordered C‑terminal tails of secreted or membrane‑associated proteins (from microproteins to larger multi‑pass enzymes) and viral accessory microproteins, typically low‑complexity and enriched in proline and basic residues, often immediately downstream of a hydrophobic signal/transmembrane segment; can include cysteine‑rich patches in secreted/toxin peptides.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over contiguous 10–30 aa windows, most frequently at the extreme C‑terminus; often spans a brief helix that transitions into coil with peak signal in the disordered coil; commonly adjacent to a hydrophobic (signal/TM) segment and characterized by low pLDDT; can also occur in short cytosolic juxtamembrane loops of larger multi‑pass proteins.
Exemplars:
- Oomycete RxLR secreted effectors: activation on the C‑terminal tail immediately following a predicted hydrophobic segment, in a low‑confidence helix/coil region.
- Human ST20 (apoptosis/stress‑related microprotein): activation on a short C‑terminal helix‑to‑coil, highly disordered stretch.
- Small uncharacterized microproteins: activation confined to the last ~10–15 residues forming a disordered coil tail.
- Viral accessory/viroporin‑like proteins: activation on basic/proline‑rich cytosolic C‑tails adjacent to a single‑pass TM helix; also applies to non‑TM viral accessory proteins with disordered C‑tails (e.g., Vif).
- Small secreted cysteine‑rich toxins/defensin‑like peptides: activation on short cationic/cysteine‑biased segments within the mature or processing tail.
- ATP synthase epsilon subunits: activation on a conserved, short, disordered C‑terminal regulatory segment in these small mitochondrial/bacterial proteins.
- Multi‑pass membrane enzymes (e.g., phytoene dehydrogenase): activation on short cytosolic C‑terminal or juxtamembrane tails adjacent to TM helices.

Summary: Cysteine-centered motifs (single conserved Cys or short CC/CXC/CXXC clusters), often—but not exclusively—found in oxidizing/extracellular or periplasmic contexts, used for disulfide bonding, redox catalysis, metal/Fe–S coordination, or regulatory thiol switches. The feature captures a generic “cysteine presence/cluster” signal near N-termini or in disordered loops across diverse proteins, including cytosolic and nuclear factors.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks centered on cysteines; strongest when two or more Cys occur within 0–2 residues (CC/CXC/CXXC) and frequently just after signal or transit peptide cleavage. Moderate peaks also occur at single conserved cysteines in disordered/low-complexity segments or coiled coils, regardless of subcellular location.
Exemplars:
- Chemokines (CC/CXC): activation on the signature N-terminal CC/CXC motif.
- Defensin-like antimicrobial peptides and disulfide-rich toxins (cystine-knot, conotoxins): activation across tightly clustered cysteines.
- Extracellular disulfide domains (Kazal/Kunitz, EGF-like): activation on paired disulfide-forming cysteines.
- Thiol–disulfide oxidoreductases (DsbA, PDI, thioredoxin): activation on catalytic CXXC motifs.
- Membrane proteins/transporters (ABC transporters, channels): activation on cysteines in luminal/extracytosolic/periplasmic loops or near processed N-termini.
- Fe–S/metal-binding proteins (rubredoxin, assembly factors): activation on closely spaced cysteines that coordinate cofactors.
- Cytosolic/nuclear regulators (e.g., BH3-only proteins like PUMA; viral early proteins such as adenovirus E4-ORF6): activation on a single Cys or short CC/CXC in disordered regions.
- Housekeeping enzymes and ribosomal/translation proteins (e.g., tRNA methyltransferases, FAD synthase, mitochondrial ribosomal proteins): activation on incidental CC/CXC or conserved single cysteines that may mediate local redox/metal interactions.

Summary: Serine residues across a wide range of structural contexts, with a bias toward serine-rich segments in intrinsically disordered or low-complexity regions (often N-terminal tails), but also firing on serines within transmembrane helices and other structured contexts; the feature behaves primarily as a serine detector with some preference for S-rich patches.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks almost exclusively on Ser; many peaks per protein, frequently clustered near termini and in compositionally biased/disordered regions, but also appearing within transmembrane helices, signal peptides, and transit peptides; minor spillover to nearby residues.
Exemplars: Viral accessory proteins (metapneumovirus X): serines in a disordered C-terminal tail; Herpesvirus envelope glycoprotein L: serines across the gH-interacting segment and a disordered C-terminus; Herpesvirus cytoplasmic envelopment proteins: numerous serines in low-pLDDT regions; Plant ribosome-inactivating proteins (dianthin): N-terminal loop/coil serines; Human adaptor/regulatory protein ST20: N-terminal serines in a low-confidence helix/coil; Oomycete RxLR effectors: serines across the signal peptide, core, and disordered C-terminus; Bacteriocins (enterocins): serines in flexible coil segments.

Summary: Residue positions that mark polypeptide boundaries—especially the absolute N-terminus (position 1) and the terminal residue of sequence fragments—and, secondarily, isolated boundary-like sites within larger proteins (e.g., short linkers between secondary-structure elements or helix/turn cap-like positions), consistent with proteolytic processing junctions in pre/propeptides.
Activation pattern: Predominantly single-residue peaks at sequence extremities (most often the first residue; also the last residue of fragments); sparse internal single-residue peaks at boundary-like positions (short linkers or transitions between secondary structures).
