Often coincides with disordered/low-confidence termini; in secreted/toxin precursors a recurring window around residues ~50–70 is consistent with signal/propeptide cleavage. Per-protein activations are usually one or a few sites.
Exemplars: Snake venom serine protease: peaks at the N-terminal first residue and at the C-terminal end of the chain; Nuclear pore complex protein Nup155: isolated peaks on single residues within a helix and a low-confidence turn; U4/U6.U5 tri-snRNP–associated protein 1: single-residue peak at a glycine linker between β-strands; E4 ubiquitin-conjugation factor (UBE4): isolated methionine within a long α-helix; Reelin (fragment): strong activation at the fragment’s C-terminal residue in a disordered region; Glutamate dehydrogenase (fragment): activation marks the truncated C-terminal residue.

Summary: Short, intrinsically disordered C‑terminal tails of secreted or membrane‑associated proteins (from microproteins to larger multi‑pass enzymes) and viral accessory microproteins, typically low‑complexity and enriched in proline and basic residues, often immediately downstream of a hydrophobic signal/transmembrane segment; can include cysteine‑rich patches in secreted/toxin peptides.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over contiguous 10–30 aa windows, most frequently at the extreme C‑terminus; often spans a brief helix that transitions into coil with peak signal in the disordered coil; commonly adjacent to a hydrophobic (signal/TM) segment and characterized by low pLDDT; can also occur in short cytosolic juxtamembrane loops of larger multi‑pass proteins.
Exemplars:
- Oomycete RxLR secreted effectors: activation on the C‑terminal tail immediately following a predicted hydrophobic segment, in a low‑confidence helix/coil region.
- Human ST20 (apoptosis/stress‑related microprotein): activation on a short C‑terminal helix‑to‑coil, highly disordered stretch.
- Small uncharacterized microproteins: activation confined to the last ~10–15 residues forming a disordered coil tail.
- Viral accessory/viroporin‑like proteins: activation on basic/proline‑rich cytosolic C‑tails adjacent to a single‑pass TM helix; also applies to non‑TM viral accessory proteins with disordered C‑tails (e.g., Vif).
- Small secreted cysteine‑rich toxins/defensin‑like peptides: activation on short cationic/cysteine‑biased segments within the mature or processing tail.
- ATP synthase epsilon subunits: activation on a conserved, short, disordered C‑terminal regulatory segment in these small mitochondrial/bacterial proteins.
- Multi‑pass membrane enzymes (e.g., phytoene dehydrogenase): activation on short cytosolic C‑terminal or juxtamembrane tails adjacent to TM helices.

Summary: Residue-level detector for tryptophan (W) side chains, often firing on multiple W positions within a sequence and with a mild bias toward N‑terminal Ws; broadly applicable across taxa and protein classes, with frequent occurrences in short membrane/secreted proteins but also in diverse enzymes (e.g., ATP synthase ε, proteases) and mitochondrial proteins.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks centered on W; multiple independent peaks per protein; modest enrichment near N‑termini; occasional weak spillover to neighboring residues (C/E/Q/G/K/R) in W‑rich contexts.
Exemplars: - Viral small/accessory membrane proteins (e.g., viroporin-like): activation on Trp residues in short helices/interfacial segments.
- Bacteriocins and peptide toxins: activation on Trp-rich motifs that mediate membrane interaction/disruption.
- ATP synthase subunit ε (F1 epsilon): activation on conserved Trp residue(s) across bacteria/mitochondria.
- Proteases (serine, cysteine, metalloproteases): activation on Trp positions within the enzyme sequence.
- Secreted and transmembrane protein precursors: activation on interfacial/N‑terminal Trp residues around TM regions or signal-proximal segments.
- Mitochondrial proteins: activation on Trp residues, including in membrane-associated components.
- Eukaryotic micropeptides/antisense-encoded small proteins: activation on any Trp present, often near the N‑terminus due to short length.

Summary: Polybasic, lysine‑rich low‑complexity intrinsically disordered segments (acidic‑poor and often N/T/S‑rich), frequently located near protein N‑termini; the feature highlights short basic patches/tracts rather than structured domains
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks on Lys that coalesce into short regional activation across disordered/basic patches; strongest in low‑pLDDT coils or low‑confidence helices, often near the N‑terminus, with neighboring N/T/S also elevated
Exemplars: - Viral accessory proteins (e.g., agnoproteins): strong peaks at terminal K and adjacent N in unstructured tails.
- Antimicrobial peptide precursors (e.g., Ixosin): activation within the mature cationic peptide on K/N, with weaker signals in the propeptide.
- ABC transporters: concentrated activation in an N‑terminal disordered, lysine‑rich segment immediately preceding the structured transporter domain.
- Telomere‑associated proteins: scattered peaks on K/N within low‑pLDDT coils across the sequence.
- Human intrinsically disordered regulatory proteins: multiple K‑centered peaks distributed across low‑confidence helices/coils.

Summary: Cysteine-centered motifs (single conserved Cys or short CC/CXC/CXXC clusters), often—but not exclusively—found in oxidizing/extracellular or periplasmic contexts, used for disulfide bonding, redox catalysis, metal/Fe–S coordination, or regulatory thiol switches. The feature captures a generic “cysteine presence/cluster” signal near N-termini or in disordered loops across diverse proteins, including cytosolic and nuclear factors.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks centered on cysteines; strongest when two or more Cys occur within 0–2 residues (CC/CXC/CXXC) and frequently just after signal or transit peptide cleavage. Moderate peaks also occur at single conserved cysteines in disordered/low-complexity segments or coiled coils, regardless of subcellular location.
Exemplars:
- Chemokines (CC/CXC): activation on the signature N-terminal CC/CXC motif.
- Defensin-like antimicrobial peptides and disulfide-rich toxins (cystine-knot, conotoxins): activation across tightly clustered cysteines.
- Extracellular disulfide domains (Kazal/Kunitz, EGF-like): activation on paired disulfide-forming cysteines.
- Thiol–disulfide oxidoreductases (DsbA, PDI, thioredoxin): activation on catalytic CXXC motifs.
- Membrane proteins/transporters (ABC transporters, channels): activation on cysteines in luminal/extracytosolic/periplasmic loops or near processed N-termini.
- Fe–S/metal-binding proteins (rubredoxin, assembly factors): activation on closely spaced cysteines that coordinate cofactors.
- Cytosolic/nuclear regulators (e.g., BH3-only proteins like PUMA; viral early proteins such as adenovirus E4-ORF6): activation on a single Cys or short CC/CXC in disordered regions.
- Housekeeping enzymes and ribosomal/translation proteins (e.g., tRNA methyltransferases, FAD synthase, mitochondrial ribosomal proteins): activation on incidental CC/CXC or conserved single cysteines that may mediate local redox/metal interactions.

Summary: Methionine residue identity, with a strong bias toward the N‑terminal initiator Met and early hydrophobic N‑terminal segments; generally fires on Met in diverse structural/functional contexts and is largely structure-agnostic.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks centered on Met; often includes the initiator Met at position 1 and occasionally nearby bulky hydrophobic/aromatic residues (W, V, L, I; sometimes T, C). Typically only a few residues per protein are active, with a tendency to cluster near the N-terminus but also occurring on internal Met.
Exemplars: - cAMP-specific phosphodiesterase (PDE4A) fragment: exclusive activation on multiple internal Met residues independent of secondary structure or disorder.
- Secreted precursors (hormones, toxins, bacteriocins): activation on the initiator Met of the signal peptide/propeptide.
- Viral accessory/immune-modulatory proteins: short, N-terminally focused activation on M1 and occasional internal Met.
- Membrane-associated proteins (signal anchors/transmembrane leaders): activation on the N-terminal Met and Met within early hydrophobic segments.
- Human microproteins and testis/spermatogenesis-related proteins: sparse activation on M1 and any internal Met in short proteins.
- Glycoprotein precursors: activation on the initiator Met at the start of signal peptides.

Summary: Single-pass hydrophobic alpha-helical transmembrane segments typical of small organelle membrane proteins—especially inner-mitochondrial (and thylakoid) oxidative phosphorylation subunits and their assembly/organization factors—and analogous small eukaryotic/viral membrane proteins; helices are Gly/Ala- and aromatic-rich, often containing glycine-spacing (e.g., GxxxG) helix-packing motifs and flanked by basic residues consistent with the positive-inside rule.
Activation pattern: One short, contiguous block that aligns with a helical transmembrane segment (core ~20–25 aa within a ~30–80 aa window); activation rises entering the helix, peaks in the hydrophobic core (often at bulky hydrophobes like Phe/Ile/Val/Leu), and decays on exit; negligible in soluble regions; typically a single block per protein.
Exemplars: - Complex I accessory subunit NDUFA13 (B16.6): activation on its sole membrane-spanning helix.
- Cytochrome c oxidase small subunit 13: activation across the annotated helix linking matrix and intermembrane-space domains.
- HIV-1 Vpu viroporin: activation on the single membrane-spanning helix.
- ATP synthase Fo subunit k: activation on its helical transmembrane segment.
- TMEM24 (single-pass membrane tether): activation on its transmembrane anchor helix.
- Mitochondrial inner-membrane assembly/insertase complex subunit 22: activation on its transmembrane helix.

Summary: Flexible extramembrane linkers and terminal tails adjacent to transmembrane helices in organellar membrane proteins (mitochondrial/plastid/peroxisomal), especially the inter‑repeat loop regions of SLC25/MCF carriers; the feature avoids the hydrophobic helical cores and concentrates on low‑structure, juxtamembrane segments
Activation pattern: Regional activation with multiple peaks per protein centered on low‑pLDDT coil/helix‑coil segments that connect or cap transmembrane helices (N-/C‑terminal tails and interhelical linkers); minimal to no activation inside the well‑structured transmembrane helices
Exemplars: - Mitochondrial carrier family (SLC25/MCF: ADP/ATP carrier, glutamate carrier, mitoferrin): strong activation on the linker loops between Solcar repeats and the disordered C‑terminal tail; transmembrane helices are largely inactive.
- ATP synthase Fo subunit k (small single‑pass IMM subunit): activation on N‑ and C‑terminal extramembrane tails; the single transmembrane helix shows little to no activation.
- HIG1 domain family (small multipass IMM proteins): highest activation at the C‑terminal tail (and modest at the N‑terminus); transmembrane helical cores are inactive.
- Plant RETICULATA‑related membrane protein: peak activation in a flexible C‑terminal region adjacent to a transmembrane span and extending into a disordered tail.

Summary: N-terminal organellar targeting/addr​essing segments, predominantly mitochondrial targeting sequences (MTS) that are Arg/Ser/Thr-rich, amphipathic, and low in acidic residues; the feature also captures non-cleavable N-terminal topogenic signals of small mitochondrial membrane proteins (including outer membrane TOM subunits like Tom22), and cross-activates on chloroplast transit peptides and basic N-terminal leaders of peroxisomal membrane proteins. It most often marks nucleus-encoded respiratory chain subunits and their assembly/import/organization factors.

Activation pattern: Regional activation focused on the extreme N-terminus (typically first ~20–60 residues), with strongest signal over amphipathic segments (classically basic for cleavable MTS) and near processing-peptidase cleavage sites when present; the feature can also activate on non-cleavable, compositionally biased N-terminal segments (including acidic patches) that act as topogenic signals for mitochondrial outer/inner membrane proteins; occasional secondary internal peaks at amphipathic segments adjacent to transmembrane helices.

Exemplars: - Respiratory chain complex I/III/IV nuclear-encoded subunits (e.g., NDUFA/NDUFB, UQCR subunits, COX5/6/7/8): activation on the N-terminal presequence or topogenic leader preceding the membrane region.
- Respiratory complex assembly/biogenesis factors (e.g., NDUFAF family, COA/SURF1/BCS1L-like): activation on their N-terminal leaders.
- Mitochondrial protein import and membrane organization components (e.g., TIMM subunits, MICOS/mitofilin complex proteins, TOM subunits such as Tom22): activation on MTS-like leaders or non-cleavable N-terminal topogenic segments.
- Mitochondrial calcium uniporter system (MCU, EMRE/SMDT1, MICU1/2/3): activation on their N-terminal mitochondrial targeting sequences.
- Peroxisomal membrane proteins (e.g., PEX3/PEX11/PMP/PEX14): activation on basic N-terminal membrane peroxisomal targeting leaders (mPTS-like).
- Plant chloroplast electron transport/thylakoid components (e.g., cytochrome b6f Rieske/PetC, PSI/PSII subunits): activation on chloroplast transit peptides at the N-terminus.

Summary: C-terminal, intermembrane-space/matrix-facing soluble tails of small mitochondrial inner-membrane proteins, located immediately after the final transmembrane helix. Activation is strongest on the polar/disordered post-TM segment, with the membrane-embedded helices themselves showing little signal. Enriched in respiratory chain subunits and assembly factors (Complexes I, III, IV) and ATP synthase Fo subunits.
Activation pattern: Broad regional activation across most of the mature protein, with the residue-level peaks concentrated in the C-terminal tail beyond the last transmembrane helix. Transmembrane cores carry weak to negligible signal; helix-to-coil transitions and the adjacent IMS/matrix-facing loops carry the strongest activation. Peak residues are sequence-diverse (frequently G, P, E, K, R, and aromatic/aliphatic residues at helix–coil junctions).
Exemplars: - NADH dehydrogenase [ubiquinone] 1 alpha subcomplex subunit 13 (NDUFA13/GRIM-19) across species: strongest at the C-terminal segment (~residues 120–140) well beyond the single TM helix.
- NDUFA3 (Complex I B9): peaks fall in the C-terminal disordered region following the TM helix.
- ATP synthase subunit J (mitochondrial), yeasts: peaks at the C-terminal residues after the TM helix, with low activation in the TM core itself.
- Cytochrome c oxidase subunit 6C-1: strongest activation in the C-terminal IMS-facing tail.
- Small assembly/inner-membrane factors (SMIM20/MITRAC7, UQCC5): peaks in the C-terminal IMS tail after the single TM helix.

Summary: Alpha-helical transmembrane segments of eukaryotic organelle membrane transporters and related multi-pass membrane proteins, with a strong preference for the 6-helix mitochondrial carrier (Solcar/SLC25) architecture but also capturing other inner/envelope membrane carriers (e.g., sideroflexin, mitochondrial pyruvate carrier) and peroxisomal membrane proteins.
Activation pattern: Domain-level, periodic activation across multiple transmembrane helices; sharp regional peaks confined to each alpha-helix with maxima in the central hydrophobic core and minimal signal in inter-helical loops, termini, and disordered regions. Repeats in carriers appear as six peaks (three Solcar repeats). Occasionally extends to adjacent non-spanning amphipathic/re-entrant helices. Residue preferences are hydrophobic with enrichment for small helix-packing residues (e.g., glycine).
Exemplars: - SLC25 mitochondrial carrier family (including peroxisomal-localized members such as adenine nucleotide transporters, citrate/2-oxoglutarate carriers, and glycine transporters): the feature highlights all six transmembrane helices of the three Solcar repeats while skipping loop regions.
- Mitochondrial pyruvate carrier (MPC) subunits: activation on the two membrane-spanning helices and a nearby matrix-facing amphipathic helix; low in disordered tails.
- Sideroflexin family (inner mitochondrial membrane amino acid/serine carriers): strong activation on multiple transmembrane helices with high structural confidence; loops are weak.
- Peroxisomal membrane/biogenesis proteins (e.g., Woronin sorting complex components): activation on annotated transmembrane helices and adjacent structured helices, with little to no activation in disordered termini.

Summary: Short, intrinsically disordered C‑terminal tails of secreted or membrane‑associated proteins (from microproteins to larger multi‑pass enzymes) and viral accessory microproteins, typically low‑complexity and enriched in proline and basic residues, often immediately downstream of a hydrophobic signal/transmembrane segment; can include cysteine‑rich patches in secreted/toxin peptides.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over contiguous 10–30 aa windows, most frequently at the extreme C‑terminus; often spans a brief helix that transitions into coil with peak signal in the disordered coil; commonly adjacent to a hydrophobic (signal/TM) segment and characterized by low pLDDT; can also occur in short cytosolic juxtamembrane loops of larger multi‑pass proteins.
Exemplars:
- Oomycete RxLR secreted effectors: activation on the C‑terminal tail immediately following a predicted hydrophobic segment, in a low‑confidence helix/coil region.
- Human ST20 (apoptosis/stress‑related microprotein): activation on a short C‑terminal helix‑to‑coil, highly disordered stretch.
- Small uncharacterized microproteins: activation confined to the last ~10–15 residues forming a disordered coil tail.
- Viral accessory/viroporin‑like proteins: activation on basic/proline‑rich cytosolic C‑tails adjacent to a single‑pass TM helix; also applies to non‑TM viral accessory proteins with disordered C‑tails (e.g., Vif).
- Small secreted cysteine‑rich toxins/defensin‑like peptides: activation on short cationic/cysteine‑biased segments within the mature or processing tail.
- ATP synthase epsilon subunits: activation on a conserved, short, disordered C‑terminal regulatory segment in these small mitochondrial/bacterial proteins.
- Multi‑pass membrane enzymes (e.g., phytoene dehydrogenase): activation on short cytosolic C‑terminal or juxtamembrane tails adjacent to TM helices.

Summary: Residue-level detector for tryptophan (W) side chains, often firing on multiple W positions within a sequence and with a mild bias toward N‑terminal Ws; broadly applicable across taxa and protein classes, with frequent occurrences in short membrane/secreted proteins but also in diverse enzymes (e.g., ATP synthase ε, proteases) and mitochondrial proteins.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks centered on W; multiple independent peaks per protein; modest enrichment near N‑termini; occasional weak spillover to neighboring residues (C/E/Q/G/K/R) in W‑rich contexts.
Exemplars: - Viral small/accessory membrane proteins (e.g., viroporin-like): activation on Trp residues in short helices/interfacial segments.
- Bacteriocins and peptide toxins: activation on Trp-rich motifs that mediate membrane interaction/disruption.
- ATP synthase subunit ε (F1 epsilon): activation on conserved Trp residue(s) across bacteria/mitochondria.
- Proteases (serine, cysteine, metalloproteases): activation on Trp positions within the enzyme sequence.
- Secreted and transmembrane protein precursors: activation on interfacial/N‑terminal Trp residues around TM regions or signal-proximal segments.
- Mitochondrial proteins: activation on Trp residues, including in membrane-associated components.
- Eukaryotic micropeptides/antisense-encoded small proteins: activation on any Trp present, often near the N‑terminus due to short length.

Summary: Short low-complexity segments, frequently enriched in Gly with Ser/Asp/Glu and Pro and containing di-glycine or GP/GGS repeats; these disordered linker/tail or propeptide regions appear in diverse proteins (including viral proteins and secreted precursors) and likely act as flexible linkers or processing/targeting elements.
Activation pattern: Regional activation in short blocks (often a few to ~20 residues) with sharp peaks over Gly-Gly and Gly/Pro clusters; peaks occur in disordered N-terminal, internal, or C-terminal tail regions.
Exemplars:
- Viral envelope/capsid and small accessory proteins: activation on glycine/proline/serine-rich low-complexity segments.
- Secreted precursors from plants, fungi, and animals (defense proteins, glycan-processing enzymes): activation on signal peptide-adjacent regions and acidic/proline-rich propeptides containing Gly/GG motifs.
- Human testis/prostate-enriched microproteins and small uncharacterized/lncRNA-derived proteins: activation on short Gly/Ser/Pro-rich low-complexity segments.
- RNA/tRNA processing and modification factors (e.g., RNA-binding/helicase-associated proteins): activation on glycine-rich disordered tails and linkers.
- C2H2 zinc-finger/nucleic-acid-binding proteins: activation on glycine/proline-rich low-complexity regions flanking the DNA/RNA-binding domains.
- Bacterial/archaeal exported peptide and RiPP/bacteriocin precursors: activation on acidic/polar leaders with characteristic di-glycine-containing segments (double-Gly leader-like motifs).
- Large multidomain membrane/secreted proteins: activation on short glycine-rich flexible segments in disordered cytoplasmic tails or luminal regions.

Summary: Charge-dense or mixed disordered segments at protein termini that may serve as generic trafficking/interaction modules, with activation observed on terminal tails of metabolic enzymes and other proteins.
Activation pattern: Regional activation concentrated at a protein terminus, with residue-level peaks over contiguous tracts in the final tens of residues; activation length varies widely and the peak residues can include hydrophobic/aromatic as well as charged positions in low-complexity contexts.
Exemplars: - Serine hydroxymethyltransferase (SHMT): activation on its C-terminal tail.
- Tubulin-specific chaperone A (TBCA): activation on a disordered/charged terminal segment.
- Condensin complex subunit 2: activation on polybasic/NLS-like patches that mediate DNA/nuclear targeting.
- Autophagy-related protein 13 (ATG13): activation on an acidic, disordered cluster within its disordered tail.
- Aminoacyl‑tRNA synthetases and tRNA maturation/modification enzymes: activation on targeting peptides or basic, low-complexity extensions involved in RNA/organelle localization.
- Secreted/membrane proteins, including SRCR family and secreted hydrolases/proteases: activation on the basic region of Sec signal peptides preceding the hydrophobic core.
- Small viral accessory proteins and bacteriocins/toxins: activation on leader peptides for secretion or polybasic patches used for membrane/nucleic-acid association.
- Cytoskeleton/trafficking machinery (e.g., adaptors, motor/cargo linkers): activation on polybasic/disordered regions that bind acidic membranes or partner proteins.
- Nuclear/transcriptional and apoptosis regulators: activation on NLS-like basic runs within disordered tails.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity serine/threonine‑rich segments (often interspersed with glycine, acidic residues, and proline) that serve as flexible linkers or polar repeats, common in secreted/extracellular proteins and carbohydrate-active enzymes, and also appearing as short disordered patches in small viral or regulatory proteins.
Activation pattern: Primarily regional activation across long, contiguous S/T‑rich low‑complexity stretches (often mid‑to‑C‑terminal and outside catalytic cores); secondarily, sparse residue‑level peaks within short IDRs. Activated residues are enriched for S, T, G, D/E, and P and occur in coil/low‑pLDDT regions.
Exemplars: - Bacterial cellulases/endoglucanases: strong activation on C‑terminal serine‑rich disordered linkers connecting catalytic domains to carbohydrate‑binding modules.
- Carbohydrate‑active enzymes (glycosidases/lyases): mid/late‑sequence S/T‑rich low‑complexity linkers outside catalytic cores.
- Lipases/cutinases: activation on acidic/polar low‑complexity terminal segments.
- Viral immune‑modulatory proteins (e.g., ICP47): residue‑level peaks within central disordered regions.
- HTH‑type transcriptional regulators: isolated acidic residues in a flexible segment around positions 80–110.
- Mammalian membrane oxidases/peptidases: luminal/extracellular low‑complexity acidic/polar clusters.
- Dictyostelium secreted proteins: extensive S/T‑rich low‑complexity tracts.
- Mycobacterium proteins and Gram‑negative carbohydrate degraders: glycine‑rich GG‑motif linkers and S/T‑rich repeats in disordered regions.

Summary: Secreted, short cysteine-rich peptides and small extracellular cysteine-rich domains stabilized by multiple disulfide bonds (CRPs), spanning venom toxins, disintegrins, defensins/hepcidin, Kunitz/Kazal/hevein-like inhibitors/defense peptides, and related cystine‑knotted or cysteine‑stabilized folds. The feature captures the mature, proteolytically processed peptide/module characterized by clustered Cys (often CC motifs) and basic residues.
Activation pattern: Regional activation confined to short mature peptide segments (tens of residues) following the signal peptide and propeptides; minimal/absent on signal/pro-regions. Strong residue-level peaks on cysteines and frequent secondary peaks on Lys/Arg and Gly. Activation spans mixed secondary structure (β-strands, coils, short helices) and can include key functional loops (e.g., RGD in disintegrins).
Exemplars: - Plant cyclotides (cystine-knot cyclopeptides, e.g., chassatide): activation across the cyclic cystine‑knot core of the mature peptide after processing.
- Snake venom disintegrins: activation across the disintegrin domain, including the RGD integrin-binding loop and adjacent cysteine-dense core.
- Inhibitor cystine-knot (ICK) venom toxins from spiders, cone snails, centipedes, and sea anemones: activation on the disulfide‑knotted toxin core.
- Kunitz/BPTI- and Kazal-type serine protease inhibitors (including tick chemokine/complement inhibitors): activation on the small disulfide‑rich inhibitor domain.
- Hevein-like/seed defense peptides: activation on the cysteine-rich chitin‑binding hevein domain.
- Defensins (plant/fungal/animal CSαβ peptides) and vertebrate hepcidin: activation on the cysteine‑stabilized mature AMP region.
- Euplotes ciliate mating pheromones: activation on the secreted disulfide‑rich pheromone core.
- Cysteine-rich modules within large extracellular/mucin-like proteins: activation on the short, cysteine‑dense repeat/subdomain embedded in the larger precursor.

Summary: Classical cleavable N-terminal Sec signal peptides (type I) of secreted prepropeptides/proteins, especially venom toxins and antimicrobial/defense peptides; the feature captures the positively charged N-region and hydrophobic helical h‑region of the signal sequence, with activation tapering across the C-region/early propeptide and absent from the mature chain.
Activation pattern: Strong, contiguous regional activation confined to the extreme N-terminus (~20–40 residues), highest over a hydrophobic, alpha-helical block enriched in Leu/Ile/Val/Phe/Ala/Met with basic residues in the first few positions; activation drops near the signal peptidase cleavage site and may extend a few residues into the propeptide; negligible across the mature peptide; typically lower pLDDT in the activated segment.
Exemplars: - Scorpion kappa-KTx potassium channel toxin precursors: activation on the N-terminal signal peptide only.
- Conotoxin precursors (cone snail): activation confined to the signal peptide.
- Plant cyclotide/defensin-like precursors (e.g., chassatides): activation on the signal peptide with slight spillover into the propeptide.
- Insect diapause-specific peptide: activation on the signal peptide only.
- Sea anemone actitoxin precursors: activation across the signal peptide and diminishing in the adjacent propeptide.
- Scorpion chlorotoxin-like peptide precursors: activation on the signal peptide.
- Secreted serine protease inhibitor precursors: activation on the signal peptide, fading in early propeptide.
- Bacterial heat-stable enterotoxin: activation on the N-terminal signal peptide only.
- Secreted vanadium-binding protein: activation on the signal peptide and short propeptide.
- Tick evasin (chemokine-binding protein): activation across the N-terminal signal peptide only.

Summary: Detector for repetitive beta-architecture (parallel beta-helix/beta-solenoid and tandem beta-repeat modules such as gamma-CA-like domains) in secreted or surface-associated polysaccharide-active proteins and in carboxysome scaffold proteins; highlights per-repeat sheet/turn positions enriched in small/polar residues (G, N, D, T, S) that often coordinate metal ions/ligands.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks spread across long, repeat-rich beta domains (often C-terminal passengers) with periodic one-peak-per-repeat behavior; concentrated in beta-strands and the short turns linking them (e.g., X-D and T-x-T/T-A/G-X-T/N motifs) and at ion/substrate-binding residues; little activation in signal peptides or alpha-helices; occasionally extends into flexible coil-rich C-terminal appendages of spike/adhesin proteins.
Exemplars: 
- Phage capsular polysaccharide depolymerases/tailspikes: discrete peaks within the catalytic beta-helix domain on strand/loop residues; minimal signal in terminal lectin modules.
- Alginate mannuronan C5-epimerases (AlgE family): periodic single-residue peaks across PbH1 repeats; additional peaks in hemolysin-type calcium-binding repeats at the C-terminus.
- Carbohydrate-binding domains (pectin/polygalacturonan-binding): residues on beta-strands in Ca2+- and ligand-binding regions of the beta-helix groove.
- Autotransporter passengers (e.g., IgA1 protease passenger): scattered single-residue peaks across beta-solenoid strands of the large secreted passenger, not at the protease catalytic serine.
- S-layer/surface-layer proteins: residues in beta-turns showing an X-D pattern linking adjacent beta-strands of solenoid-like repeats.
- Cell-wall adhesins: isolated peaks within beta-strands of repeat-rich extracellular domains.
- Ice-binding/antifreeze beta-solenoids: residues within and around T-A/G-X-T/N ice-binding motifs on beta-sheet faces of the solenoid.
- Type VI secretion VgrG spikes: specific residues in the C-terminal, coil-rich extension appended to the spike.
- Carboxysome proteins (CcmM/gamma-CA-like repeat scaffolds): periodic peaks at conserved polar residues across tandem CA-like beta-repeat domains.

Summary: Cysteine-centered metal-binding/redox modules—especially [4Fe–4S] and Ni–Fe–S clusters and Cys–Zn (CXXC/di-Cys) motifs—and their scaffolding context; the feature emphasizes non-ligating residues in loops/turns flanking clustered cysteines, with reduced (though not always zero) activation on the coordinating cysteines themselves.
Activation pattern: In small Fe-S subunits, broad activation across the entire chain with peaks in coils, turns, and short strands flanking ligand Cys and lower activation at the coordinating cysteines. In larger multi-domain proteins, activation can extend diffusely throughout the chain while still showing the strongest peaks in sequence neighborhoods around the Cys-rich cluster-binding region.
Exemplars: - Fe–S enzyme small subunits (e.g., 4-hydroxyphenylacetate decarboxylase small subunit): broad activation across the Fe–S domain with reduced signal at several [4Fe–4S] ligand cysteines.
- Ni-Fe-S cluster enzymes (e.g., acetyl-CoA decarbonylase/synthase complex beta subunit): diffuse activation across the chain with top peaks in loops surrounding the cluster-binding region.
- WhiB/Wbl-type [4Fe–4S] transcription factors: strong activation in the N-terminal/early Wbl region with low or zero signal on the four cluster-binding Cys.
- Ion-translocating oxidoreductase complex subunit B with an N-terminal [4Fe–4S] domain: sharp peaks in the unstructured loop and short helix flanking the cluster site.
- CXXC-type CpG-island binding module (TET1): high activation across the CXXC Zn-binding domain and into the disordered C-terminal extension.
- Small RNA polymerase RPB6-like subunit: a short helix/coil patch is selectively activated, consistent with this feature's focus on localized scaffolding around cysteine-cluster metal-binding contexts.

Summary: Long, low-complexity intrinsically disordered regions enriched in acidic and polar residues with frequent FG dipeptides (G/S/T/P-biased LCDs), typified by nucleoporin FG-repeat domains and analogous scaffold/adaptor IDRs; anti-correlated with folded domains and short hydrophobic docking motifs.
Activation pattern: Domain- and regional-level activation spanning hundreds of residues across extended IDRs; strong troughs over structured modules (e.g., zinc fingers, coiled-coils). Sequence preferences include runs of Asp/Glu and enrichment for Gly/Ser/Thr/Pro with tolerance for FG dipeptides; localized negative spikes on bulky hydrophobics/aromatics, especially within short binding motifs such as WxxF.
Exemplars: - FG-nucleoporins: robust activation across FG-repeat domains; deactivation in embedded RanBP2-type zinc finger modules.
- Clathrin-associated endocytic adaptors (aftiphilin-like): broad activation over N-terminal low-complexity IDRs; sharp deactivation at phenylalanines in WxxF endocytic motifs and reduced signal in clathrin-binding elements.
- TACC family scaffolds: strong activation on the N-terminal disordered, acidic region; little to none on the structured C-terminal coiled-coil.
- Synaptonemal complex component SIX6OS1: activation concentrated in the disordered C-terminal half implicated in assembly/polycomplex formation.
- Also observed among activators: acidic C-terminal tails of ribosomal P proteins; replication/repair scaffolds with long acidic IDRs; viral proteins with compositionally biased low-complexity regions.

Summary: Short, intrinsically disordered C‑terminal tails of secreted or membrane‑associated proteins (from microproteins to larger multi‑pass enzymes) and viral accessory microproteins, typically low‑complexity and enriched in proline and basic residues, often immediately downstream of a hydrophobic signal/transmembrane segment; can include cysteine‑rich patches in secreted/toxin peptides.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over contiguous 10–30 aa windows, most frequently at the extreme C‑terminus; often spans a brief helix that transitions into coil with peak signal in the disordered coil; commonly adjacent to a hydrophobic (signal/TM) segment and characterized by low pLDDT; can also occur in short cytosolic juxtamembrane loops of larger multi‑pass proteins.
Exemplars:
- Oomycete RxLR secreted effectors: activation on the C‑terminal tail immediately following a predicted hydrophobic segment, in a low‑confidence helix/coil region.
- Human ST20 (apoptosis/stress‑related microprotein): activation on a short C‑terminal helix‑to‑coil, highly disordered stretch.
- Small uncharacterized microproteins: activation confined to the last ~10–15 residues forming a disordered coil tail.
- Viral accessory/viroporin‑like proteins: activation on basic/proline‑rich cytosolic C‑tails adjacent to a single‑pass TM helix; also applies to non‑TM viral accessory proteins with disordered C‑tails (e.g., Vif).
- Small secreted cysteine‑rich toxins/defensin‑like peptides: activation on short cationic/cysteine‑biased segments within the mature or processing tail.
- ATP synthase epsilon subunits: activation on a conserved, short, disordered C‑terminal regulatory segment in these small mitochondrial/bacterial proteins.
- Multi‑pass membrane enzymes (e.g., phytoene dehydrogenase): activation on short cytosolic C‑terminal or juxtamembrane tails adjacent to TM helices.

Summary: Cysteine-centered motifs (single conserved Cys or short CC/CXC/CXXC clusters), often—but not exclusively—found in oxidizing/extracellular or periplasmic contexts, used for disulfide bonding, redox catalysis, metal/Fe–S coordination, or regulatory thiol switches. The feature captures a generic “cysteine presence/cluster” signal near N-termini or in disordered loops across diverse proteins, including cytosolic and nuclear factors.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks centered on cysteines; strongest when two or more Cys occur within 0–2 residues (CC/CXC/CXXC) and frequently just after signal or transit peptide cleavage. Moderate peaks also occur at single conserved cysteines in disordered/low-complexity segments or coiled coils, regardless of subcellular location.
Exemplars:
- Chemokines (CC/CXC): activation on the signature N-terminal CC/CXC motif.
- Defensin-like antimicrobial peptides and disulfide-rich toxins (cystine-knot, conotoxins): activation across tightly clustered cysteines.
- Extracellular disulfide domains (Kazal/Kunitz, EGF-like): activation on paired disulfide-forming cysteines.
- Thiol–disulfide oxidoreductases (DsbA, PDI, thioredoxin): activation on catalytic CXXC motifs.
- Membrane proteins/transporters (ABC transporters, channels): activation on cysteines in luminal/extracytosolic/periplasmic loops or near processed N-termini.
- Fe–S/metal-binding proteins (rubredoxin, assembly factors): activation on closely spaced cysteines that coordinate cofactors.
- Cytosolic/nuclear regulators (e.g., BH3-only proteins like PUMA; viral early proteins such as adenovirus E4-ORF6): activation on a single Cys or short CC/CXC in disordered regions.
- Housekeeping enzymes and ribosomal/translation proteins (e.g., tRNA methyltransferases, FAD synthase, mitochondrial ribosomal proteins): activation on incidental CC/CXC or conserved single cysteines that may mediate local redox/metal interactions.

Summary: Residue-level detector for tryptophan (W) side chains, often firing on multiple W positions within a sequence and with a mild bias toward N‑terminal Ws; broadly applicable across taxa and protein classes, with frequent occurrences in short membrane/secreted proteins but also in diverse enzymes (e.g., ATP synthase ε, proteases) and mitochondrial proteins.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks centered on W; multiple independent peaks per protein; modest enrichment near N‑termini; occasional weak spillover to neighboring residues (C/E/Q/G/K/R) in W‑rich contexts.
Exemplars: - Viral small/accessory membrane proteins (e.g., viroporin-like): activation on Trp residues in short helices/interfacial segments.
- Bacteriocins and peptide toxins: activation on Trp-rich motifs that mediate membrane interaction/disruption.
- ATP synthase subunit ε (F1 epsilon): activation on conserved Trp residue(s) across bacteria/mitochondria.
- Proteases (serine, cysteine, metalloproteases): activation on Trp positions within the enzyme sequence.
- Secreted and transmembrane protein precursors: activation on interfacial/N‑terminal Trp residues around TM regions or signal-proximal segments.
- Mitochondrial proteins: activation on Trp residues, including in membrane-associated components.
- Eukaryotic micropeptides/antisense-encoded small proteins: activation on any Trp present, often near the N‑terminus due to short length.

Summary: Short hydrophobic targeting helices and cationic amphipathic motifs that mediate membrane/organellar targeting or unconventional secretion—encompassing classical N‑terminal signal peptides, internal signal‑anchor helices, C‑terminal tail‑anchors, mitochondrial targeting helices, and CPP‑like basic/aromatic motifs. Enriched for Leu/Phe with Tyr/Trp at helix boundaries; Arg/His frequent; acidic residues (D/E) scarce. In very small secreted/toxin-like proteins, activation can extend into cysteine/proline‑rich mature regions; in soluble enzymes/regulators it may mark short amphipathic or hydrophobic helices.

Activation pattern: Predominantly regional activation over 15–30 aa hydrophobic segments (whether N‑terminal signal peptides/signal anchors or C‑terminal tail‑anchors); in microproteins, activation can span most of the sequence; in large soluble proteins, limited residue‑level peaks over short amphipathic/basic or hydrophobic helices (e.g., DNA/RNA‑binding or coiled‑coil segments).

Exemplars:
- Viral envelope/accessory and regulatory proteins — activation on N‑terminal signal/signal‑anchor helices or on CPP‑like Arg/Trp‑enriched motifs (e.g., Tat‑like proteins) enabling leaderless export/cellular entry.
- Secreted peptide precursors (hormones, antimicrobial peptides, venom toxins, immune effectors) — activation on the signal peptide; in very short precursors, also across the cysteine/proline‑rich mature region.
- Oomycete RxLR effectors — activation on the N‑terminal signal peptide immediately upstream of the RxLR motif.
- Human microproteins/lncRNA‑derived peptides — activation across a single hydrophobic TM helix acting as a signal anchor or tail‑anchor, or short amphipathic targeting motifs.
- Mitochondrial nucleus‑encoded proteins (e.g., mitochondrial ribosomal proteins; ATP synthase-associated subunits) — activation on N‑terminal mitochondrial targeting helices or short hydrophobic segments.
- Bacterial/archaeal enzymes and phage integrases — isolated peaks over internal hydrophobic or amphipathic helices (e.g., helix‑turn‑helix/coiled‑coil regions) without spanning whole domains.
- Tail‑anchored SNAREs and other vesicle proteins — activation on the C‑terminal transmembrane tail‑anchor.

Summary: Small peptide/microprotein feature firing on short cationic and small-residue–enriched motifs in compact bioactive peptides, including mature bacteriocin-like cyclic peptides, neuropeptide/venom precursors, RxLR-like host-targeting motifs, and analogous cationic segments in small viral/accessory and microproteins
Activation pattern: Regional activation across short bioactive peptide segments, with residue-level peaks on basic clusters (KR, RR, RxLR) and adjacent small/polar residues; typically within compact peptides or short topogenic/leader motifs rather than broad domain coverage
Exemplars:
- Autophagy protein Atg2 family: activation on the basic, amphipathic N-terminal helix for membrane binding/tethering
- Oomycete RxLR effectors: activation on the RxLR motif and surrounding basic residues immediately downstream of the signal peptide
- Eukaryotic mitochondrial proteins (e.g., ATP synthase epsilon subunits): activation on N-terminal transit peptides (Arg/Ser/Thr/Ala-rich, acidic-poor)
- Secreted peptide/neuropeptide/venom precursors: activation on positively charged signal-peptide N-regions and nearby dibasic KR/RR processing sites
- Viral early/accessory and immune-modulatory proteins: activation on N-terminal polybasic/NLS-like segments for membrane association or nuclear import
- Gram-negative inner-membrane transporters (e.g., YeeO): activation on positive-inside N-termini/signal-anchor segments
- Bacterial secreted enzymes: activation on Sec signal-peptide N-regions
- Ribosomally synthesized bacteriocin-like peptides (e.g., sporulation killing factor SkfA): activation across the mature cyclic/bioactive peptide segment
- Small bioactive microproteins (e.g., Drosophila Stunted): activation across the short mature peptide including basic KR-containing motifs

Summary: Extended β-solenoid/β-helix repeat architectures (including right-handed pectate-lyase–like PBH1 repeats, RTX Ca2+-binding β-rolls, octa-/penta-peptide repeat β-solenoids, and left-handed β-helices) found predominantly in secreted/passenger domains of adhesins, tailspikes/depolymerases, and polysaccharide-modifying enzymes; also other β-strand–rich solenoids (e.g., LRR domains in type III effectors) and a minor class of small cysteine-rich metallothioneins; additionally, localized signals occur in certain cytosolic enzymes via conserved β-strand patches (e.g., LpxA/γ-CA and some sugar-nucleotide pyrophosphorylases such as UGPase).
Activation pattern: Domain-level activation across long, contiguous β-strand/loop repeat arrays with clear periodicity; residue-level peaks recur at small/polar residues typical of β-solenoid consensus positions (G, A, T, S, D/N). Activation often begins immediately after a signal peptide and spans the extracellular passenger/repeat domain, with little/no signal on N-terminal signal peptides, C-terminal autotransporter β-barrels, disordered tails, or α-helical regions. Strong signals also occur in Ca2+-binding RTX segments. In non-solenoidal cytosolic enzymes (e.g., UGPase), activation is restricted to short N- or internal β-strand patches; compact cysteine-rich metallothioneins can show global activation despite minimal regular secondary structure.
Exemplars:
- Type V autotransporter adhesins/invasins: strong activation across the extracellular passenger β-helix domain; absent on signal peptide and translocator β-barrel.
- Ice nucleation proteins: activation tracks the C-terminal octapeptide repeat β-solenoid with periodic peaks on G/A positions.
- Alginate mannuronan C5-epimerases/pectate-lyase–like enzymes: activation over PBH1 (pectate-lyase–type β-helix) repeats and is maximal in C-terminal hemolysin-type (RTX) Ca2+-binding β-roll repeats.
- Phage capsule depolymerases/tailspikes: continuous activation across the β-helix carbohydrate-binding/catalytic domain.
- Cytosolic enzymes: left-handed β-helix LpxA and γ-class carbonic anhydrase cores; UDP-glucose pyrophosphorylase shows localized β-strand patch activation.
- Type III–secreted effectors: internal solenoids including HECT-like SopA segments and LRR domains (e.g., IpaH).
- Fungal GPI-anchored adhesins: activation across long repeat-rich, β-strand–bearing passenger regions.
- Metallothioneins: small cysteine-rich proteins with broad activation despite low regular secondary structure.

Summary: Detector for repetitive beta-architecture (parallel beta-helix/beta-solenoid and tandem beta-repeat modules such as gamma-CA-like domains) in secreted or surface-associated polysaccharide-active proteins and in carboxysome scaffold proteins; highlights per-repeat sheet/turn positions enriched in small/polar residues (G, N, D, T, S) that often coordinate metal ions/ligands.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks spread across long, repeat-rich beta domains (often C-terminal passengers) with periodic one-peak-per-repeat behavior; concentrated in beta-strands and the short turns linking them (e.g., X-D and T-x-T/T-A/G-X-T/N motifs) and at ion/substrate-binding residues; little activation in signal peptides or alpha-helices; occasionally extends into flexible coil-rich C-terminal appendages of spike/adhesin proteins.
Exemplars: 
- Phage capsular polysaccharide depolymerases/tailspikes: discrete peaks within the catalytic beta-helix domain on strand/loop residues; minimal signal in terminal lectin modules.
- Alginate mannuronan C5-epimerases (AlgE family): periodic single-residue peaks across PbH1 repeats; additional peaks in hemolysin-type calcium-binding repeats at the C-terminus.
- Carbohydrate-binding domains (pectin/polygalacturonan-binding): residues on beta-strands in Ca2+- and ligand-binding regions of the beta-helix groove.
- Autotransporter passengers (e.g., IgA1 protease passenger): scattered single-residue peaks across beta-solenoid strands of the large secreted passenger, not at the protease catalytic serine.
- S-layer/surface-layer proteins: residues in beta-turns showing an X-D pattern linking adjacent beta-strands of solenoid-like repeats.
- Cell-wall adhesins: isolated peaks within beta-strands of repeat-rich extracellular domains.
- Ice-binding/antifreeze beta-solenoids: residues within and around T-A/G-X-T/N ice-binding motifs on beta-sheet faces of the solenoid.
- Type VI secretion VgrG spikes: specific residues in the C-terminal, coil-rich extension appended to the spike.
- Carboxysome proteins (CcmM/gamma-CA-like repeat scaffolds): periodic peaks at conserved polar residues across tandem CA-like beta-repeat domains.

Summary: Repetitive, compositionally biased segments used for assembly/scaffolding: (i) long, ordered alpha-helical repeat regions (coiled-coils, leucine zippers, and related helical repeats such as TPR/solenoids) and (ii) cysteine-dense small secreted peptides/prohormone segments and low-complexity acidic/Pro/Ser/Gly-rich tracts; the feature avoids compact globular catalytic cores.
Activation pattern: Domain-level/regional activation spanning continuous helical repeats; alternatively, strong activation over contiguous low-complexity runs (acidic/Pro/Ser/Gly) or Cys clusters in secreted precursors. Low in well-folded enzyme cores; disordered tails are weak unless they contain repeat-rich/low-complexity tracts.
Exemplars: - Mediator complex subunit (MED31; helical core), - MAP kinase kinase kinase (tandem leucine-zipper coiled-coils), - NIMA-related kinase (C-terminal coiled-coil), and additionally activation on TPR-repeat outer-envelope scaffolds, microtubule-associated low-complexity repeat regions (e.g., MAP4), metallothioneins and neuropeptide/prohormone precursors via cysteine/low-complexity segments.

Summary: Residue-level detector for the right‑handed parallel beta‑helix/beta‑solenoid scaffold, focusing on the short coil/turn and N‑cap positions that precede or initiate beta‑strands in repeat units; prevalent in secreted/surface polysaccharide‑active proteins (autotransporters, phage tailspikes/depolymerases, pectate/pectin lyases, ice‑nucleation repeats) and, more broadly, analogous coil→beta boundaries in other beta‑rich domains; often enriched for small/polar residues (Gly/Ser/Ala/Asn/Asp) and can include acidic residues that participate in Ca2+ binding or catalysis along the solenoid groove.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks, sparse but repeated across long beta‑rich repeat domains; strongest at glycine- and small/polar residues in coil turns that link repeats or at the first residue of a beta‑strand; frequently periodic in solenoids (e.g., 8‑residue repeats); largely absent from signal peptides and outer‑membrane translocator segments; mostly in well‑structured regions (high pLDDT) but can extend into glycine/Asn/Gln‑rich low‑complexity segments of secreted effectors.
Exemplars: - Autotransporter passenger (pertactin): sharp peaks at turns linking beta‑strands within the beta‑helix; no activation in the signal peptide or C‑terminal translocator.
- Fungal cell‑wall adhesin (AWP2): glycine‑rich coil turns connecting beta‑strands across the structured N‑terminal half; occasional proximity to glycosylation motifs.
- Phage capsule depolymerase catalytic domain: peaks within the pectate‑lyase–like beta‑helix core, including an active‑site Asp; noncatalytic lectin/carbohydrate‑binding appendages largely inactive.
- Pectate lyase A: residues at beta‑strand starts and loop turns within the right‑handed beta‑helix.
- Pectin/pectate‑interacting carbohydrate‑binding domain: turns preceding beta‑strands plus acidic Ca2+‑binding residues along the binding groove.
- Type VI secretion spike (VgrG): sparse peaks across a glycine/Asn/Gln‑rich C‑terminal effector segment predicted as disordered, consistent with repeat‑like coil regions.
- Ice nucleation protein: periodic activation every eight residues on serines in the octapeptide beta‑solenoid repeat, typically at coil positions just before beta‑strands.
- Formyltransferase/hydrolase complex subunit C: internal beta‑turns and strand starts in well‑ordered beta‑sheets, reflecting the same local coil→beta geometry outside classical solenoids.

Summary: Long, broadly active segments often spanning much of a protein chain, with strongest signals on compositionally biased tracts (low-complexity Gly/Pro/Ser/Thr- and charge-rich) including disordered C-terminal tails. These regions often function as flexible tails, linker/interaction segments, or isoform-variable extensions, and the concept is taxon-agnostic.
Activation pattern: Broad regional activation covering large fractions of the chain, with the highest peaks landing on compositionally biased disordered regions, frequently Pro-rich C-terminal tails. Weaker but still substantial activation occurs across much of the rest of the chain including some structured segments.
Exemplars: - EARLY STARVATION 1 (ESV1) family (rice, Arabidopsis, Marchantia): strongest peaks on the Pro-rich, disordered C-terminal tail; broad lower activation across the rest of the chain.
- Protein OCTOPUS and OCTOPUS-like (Arabidopsis): strong activation on internal Pro-rich disordered regions and adjacent stretches.
- Glutamate-rich protein 6 / 6B (human): broad activation across the chain with peaks in mid-protein regions.
- Uncharacterized protein C3orf20 (human): nearly chain-wide activation with peaks in central regions.
- Protein DIA1 (yeast): broad activation with peaks in a mid-chain Pro-containing segment.

Summary: Short, intrinsically disordered C‑terminal tails of secreted or membrane‑associated proteins (from microproteins to larger multi‑pass enzymes) and viral accessory microproteins, typically low‑complexity and enriched in proline and basic residues, often immediately downstream of a hydrophobic signal/transmembrane segment; can include cysteine‑rich patches in secreted/toxin peptides.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over contiguous 10–30 aa windows, most frequently at the extreme C‑terminus; often spans a brief helix that transitions into coil with peak signal in the disordered coil; commonly adjacent to a hydrophobic (signal/TM) segment and characterized by low pLDDT; can also occur in short cytosolic juxtamembrane loops of larger multi‑pass proteins.
Exemplars:
- Oomycete RxLR secreted effectors: activation on the C‑terminal tail immediately following a predicted hydrophobic segment, in a low‑confidence helix/coil region.
- Human ST20 (apoptosis/stress‑related microprotein): activation on a short C‑terminal helix‑to‑coil, highly disordered stretch.
- Small uncharacterized microproteins: activation confined to the last ~10–15 residues forming a disordered coil tail.
- Viral accessory/viroporin‑like proteins: activation on basic/proline‑rich cytosolic C‑tails adjacent to a single‑pass TM helix; also applies to non‑TM viral accessory proteins with disordered C‑tails (e.g., Vif).
- Small secreted cysteine‑rich toxins/defensin‑like peptides: activation on short cationic/cysteine‑biased segments within the mature or processing tail.
- ATP synthase epsilon subunits: activation on a conserved, short, disordered C‑terminal regulatory segment in these small mitochondrial/bacterial proteins.
- Multi‑pass membrane enzymes (e.g., phytoene dehydrogenase): activation on short cytosolic C‑terminal or juxtamembrane tails adjacent to TM helices.

Summary: Residue-level detector for tryptophan (W) side chains, often firing on multiple W positions within a sequence and with a mild bias toward N‑terminal Ws; broadly applicable across taxa and protein classes, with frequent occurrences in short membrane/secreted proteins but also in diverse enzymes (e.g., ATP synthase ε, proteases) and mitochondrial proteins.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks centered on W; multiple independent peaks per protein; modest enrichment near N‑termini; occasional weak spillover to neighboring residues (C/E/Q/G/K/R) in W‑rich contexts.
Exemplars: - Viral small/accessory membrane proteins (e.g., viroporin-like): activation on Trp residues in short helices/interfacial segments.
- Bacteriocins and peptide toxins: activation on Trp-rich motifs that mediate membrane interaction/disruption.
- ATP synthase subunit ε (F1 epsilon): activation on conserved Trp residue(s) across bacteria/mitochondria.
- Proteases (serine, cysteine, metalloproteases): activation on Trp positions within the enzyme sequence.
- Secreted and transmembrane protein precursors: activation on interfacial/N‑terminal Trp residues around TM regions or signal-proximal segments.
- Mitochondrial proteins: activation on Trp residues, including in membrane-associated components.
- Eukaryotic micropeptides/antisense-encoded small proteins: activation on any Trp present, often near the N‑terminus due to short length.

Summary: Short hydrophobic alpha-helical segments enriched in small aliphatic residues (A, V, I, L with frequent T/G), depleted of charged/aromatic residues—commonly the h‑region of Sec signal peptides, short transmembrane helices, and internal helix-forming hydrophobic patches in both membrane and soluble proteins; often N‑terminal but also internal/C‑terminal.
Activation pattern: Regional activation on contiguous hydrophobic clusters predicted as alpha‑helix, with sharp residue‑level peaks at A/V/I/L/T (often with G); observed in signal peptides, TM segments, and internal helices; occurs in both structured and disordered contexts (not restricted to low pLDDT).
Exemplars: Adenovirus E4‑ORF4 and HCV ARFP: internal hydrophobic helix‑prone stretches in small viral proteins; Oomycete RxLR effectors and yeast killer toxin precursors: strong activation on N‑terminal Sec signal peptides; Bacterial cytochrome c oxidase subunit 2 and DHHC palmitoyltransferases: activation on short transmembrane helices; Kdo transferase and OMA hydratase: activation on internal hydrophobic helices within soluble/peripheral membrane enzymes.

Summary: Glycine-biased, low-complexity coil/linker segments—often containing GG or small-residue motifs—that mark flexible junctions and proteolytic processing sites (leaders/propeptides, viral protease cuts), and that in NTPases coincide with the glycine-rich Walker A phosphate-binding loop
Activation pattern: - Predominantly regional activation across disordered, glycine/serine/threonine-rich stretches; enriched for G and R with interspersed E/D
- Sharp residue-level peaks at GG motifs and at helix–coil junctions
- Frequently near N-termini (leaders/propeptides and NBD/P-loop regions)
- In P-loop NTPases, concentrates on the glycine-rich Walker A (GxxxxGKT) loop
Exemplars: - Adenoviral structural proteins (e.g., hexon-linking protein VIII): GG motifs and adjacent residues in disordered regions flanking viral protease cleavage sites
- Viral capsid/tail proteins (including bacteriophage tape measure): glycines in flexible loops and helix–loop transitions
- Peptide hormone/neuropeptide precursors (e.g., KiSS-1): N-terminal disordered propeptides/leader regions around processing sites
- RiPP/bacteriocin precursors: N-terminal double-glycine leader cleavage motifs recognized by ABC transporter peptidases
- ABC transporter ATP-binding/NBD proteins (P-loop NTPases): glycine-rich Walker A phosphate-binding loop, often near the N-terminus of the domain
- Carbohydrate-active enzymes (glycoside hydrolases): glycine/threonine-rich interdomain linkers connecting catalytic and binding modules
- Sperm/protamine family proteins: arginine/glycine-rich low-complexity tracts
- Microtubule-associated Jupiter proteins: basic, low-complexity flexible segments
- Purine biosynthesis and tRNA/rRNA-modifying enzymes: glycine-rich loops/flexible hinges adjacent to functional motifs

Summary: Hydrophobic, low-acid, alpha-helix–prone terminal segments—primarily N-terminal signal peptides/signal anchors in secreted and viral proteins, and leucine/valine-rich low‑complexity helical/coiled‑coil regions (often oligomerization arms or tails) in large chromosome-structural and DNA/RNA repair/helicase proteins
Activation pattern: Regional activation in terminal low-pLDDT segments: strong clustering at N-termini of secreted/viral proteins (signal peptides) and at high sequence indices in very large SMC/repair/helicase proteins (long coiled-coil/low-complexity helices); residue-level peaks on hydrophobic/aliphatic positions (L/V/A/I/F) with frequent G/S/R/P and relative depletion of D/E; minimal activation within well-folded catalytic domains
Exemplars: - Oomycete RxLR effectors: activation on the N-terminal signal peptide helix and adjacent low-confidence helical/coil segments (including RxLR-dEER vicinity, favoring R/L over acidic residues).
- Bacterial BY-kinase (PtkA-like): activation confined to the disordered, low-pLDDT N-terminal leader preceding the structured kinase domain.
- SMC condensin/cohesin/Smc-like proteins: activation on leucine/isoleucine-rich coiled-coil arms located in distal/high-index regions that mediate oligomerization.
- DNA/RNA helicases and repair/scaffold proteins: activation on low-complexity helical linkers or basic/hydrophobic C-terminal tails used for interactions/assembly.
- Secreted peptide hormone and neuropeptide precursors: activation on N-terminal signal peptides and short hydrophobic prepro segments.
- Viral membrane/secreted proteins: activation on N-terminal signal peptides or single-pass signal-anchor helices.
- Small human micropeptides/alt-ORF products: activation across short hydrophobic helices consistent with membrane association or secretion.

Summary: Short segments within disordered and compositionally biased stretches of diverse proteins, particularly regions enriched in basic and acidic residues. Activations are also seen in non-disordered contexts across proteins of varied function, suggesting the feature captures a relatively broad local sequence pattern rather than a tight structural motif.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks with small clusters, distributed throughout the length of the protein. Peaks frequently overlap annotated disordered regions and basic/acidic compositionally biased segments, but also occur at isolated positions within structured chains; occurs in both helical and coil contexts.
Exemplars: - Oomycete RxLR secreted effectors: peaks within the mature effector chain, with occasional spikes in the signal peptide.
- Plant CLE peptide precursors: localized peaks within the C-terminal CLE motif corresponding to the mature signaling peptide.
- Cholecystokinin prohormone: peaks at or immediately adjacent to the N-termini of mature neuropeptides generated by proteolytic processing.
- Herpesvirus ICP47-like small accessory proteins: multiple peaks in the N-terminal active helical region and in polar, disordered C-terminal stretches.
- Keratin-associated proteins: activation across cysteine/proline/serine-rich, low-complexity repeat regions.
- Phosphodiesterase and fungal/bacterial enzymes with disordered N- or internal stretches: peaks within basic-and-acidic compositionally biased segments.

Summary: Short linear segments in intrinsically disordered or otherwise low-structure-confidence regions, often at N-termini and within signal peptides/propeptides of secreted and regulatory proteins (including viral accessory proteins and small ORF microproteins), enriched in small/basic residues (G, P, S, A, R; often with Cys), rather than in well-folded catalytic cores.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks scattered across IDRs and low-confidence coils/short helices; frequently clustered near the N-terminus, in signal peptides, propeptides, and disordered tails; little to no activation in well-structured domains; occasional activation in low-confidence transmembrane/signal-anchor helices.
Exemplars: - Viral accessory protein (HIV-1 Vif): peaks throughout low-pLDDT coils, especially the disordered N-terminal region.
- Neuropeptide precursor (Drosophila Amnesiac): activation in the N-terminal signal peptide and multiple mature peptide segments with very low pLDDT.
- Secreted serine carboxypeptidase: activation confined to disordered C-terminal tail, annotated disordered segment, the signal peptide, and a low-confidence C-terminal transmembrane helix; absent from the structured catalytic domain.
- Disordered human tumor-suppressor–associated protein (ST20): scattered peaks within predicted helices in a globally disordered chain, including the N-terminus.
- lncRNA/sORF-derived microprotein (IGF2 antisense protein): multiple peaks across annotated disordered regions rich in Arg/Pro/Gly.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low-complexity segments enriched in serine/threonine/proline/glycine and often basic (lysine/arginine), typically found in flexible N- or C-terminal tails and loops; highlights IDRs that may harbor short linear motifs (e.g., basic NLS patches) rather than structured domain cores.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long disordered stretches with additional sparse residue-level peaks in low-confidence loops; often N-terminal-biased in short/viral proteins; rarely within well-folded cores.
Exemplars: Retroviral accessory proteins (e.g., HTLV-1 p30): activation on central and C-terminal IDRs including a basic nuclear localization signal; p53-regulated apoptosis-inducing microprotein: widespread activation across a globally disordered protein; Bacterial DNA ligase: scattered activation in an annotated disordered linker and flexible loops within the ligase domain; Uncharacterized human microprotein: multiple peaks throughout a low-pLDDT, disordered sequence irrespective of predicted secondary structure.

Summary: Low-complexity, intrinsically disordered segments—often at protein N-termini—such as mucin-like/propeptide regions or flexible linkers adjacent to signal/transit peptides, common in small secreted or membrane-associated proteins and also as disordered extensions in diverse enzymes (broad taxonomic coverage, including viral, bacterial, and eukaryotic proteins).
Activation pattern: Regional activation over short to moderate stretches, frequently in disordered or polar/low-complexity segments; in longer proteins, multiple low-complexity patches can activate; in micropeptides, activation can span much of the sequence. Residue-level peaks can fall on Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly within polar-residue stretches but also on basic or hydrophobic residues within the same disordered context.
Exemplars:
- Viral envelope/accessory microproteins: activation on N-terminal Ser/Thr/Pro-rich disordered segments (often mucin-like or regulatory tails).
- Secreted eukaryotic effectors (e.g., oomycete RxLR effectors): activation on the low-complexity region flanking the signal peptide/RxLR motif.
- Human testis-biased and lncRNA-derived micropeptides: activation across intrinsically disordered peptide regions.
- Secreted precursors/propeptides: activation on N-terminal regions following the signal peptide.
- Membrane-associated single-pass proteins: activation on luminal or cytosolic tails flanking the transmembrane helix.
- Bacterial/archaeal metabolic enzymes: activation on disordered, low-complexity N-terminal extensions/linkers enriched in Ser/Thr/Gly/Pro.

Summary: Short, low‑complexity, intrinsically disordered proteins and modules that encode targeting/processing signals—often but not always secretory—combining hydrophobic signal peptides, double‑Gly bacteriocin leaders, or polybasic/NLS‑like segments, frequently adjacent to Ser/Thr/Pro‑rich stretches and basic clusters (e.g., RXLR, KR/RR)—common in micropeptides, toxins/secreted precursors, viral accessory proteins, keratin‑associated and testis‑specific low‑complexity proteins across taxa
Activation pattern: Regional activation across short proteins, spanning hydrophobic/targeting segments and Ser/Thr/Pro‑rich low‑complexity tracts with peaks on basic motifs such as RXLR, dibasic KR/RR, or double‑Gly leader junctions
Exemplars:
- Oomycete RxLR effectors: activation on the N‑terminal signal peptide and the RXLR/EER host‑targeting motif immediately downstream.
- Secreted peptide hormone/venom/toxin precursors: activation on the signal peptide and basic prohormone convertase cleavage motifs (KR/RR) within the propeptide region.
- Class II bacteriocins: activation on the N‑terminal double‑Gly leader and adjacent cationic tract recognized by ABC exporters.
- Viral accessory/regulatory proteins (e.g., small disordered regulators): activation across S/T/P‑rich low‑complexity disordered segments containing polybasic/NLS‑like clusters.
- Keratin‑associated proteins (KRTAPs): activation over short, repetitive low‑complexity regions (Ser/Pro‑rich and basic tracts) typical of hair shaft proteins.
- Cancer/testis antigens and testis‑associated proteins: activation on Lys/Arg‑ and Pro/Ser‑rich low‑complexity stretches in very short proteins.
- Short uncharacterized micropeptides/antisense products: broad activation across their low‑complexity/basic segments.
- Enzymes that carry secretory leaders or short disordered/basic tails (including some cytosolic enzymes lacking signal peptides): activation limited to the disordered tail, not the catalytic core.

Summary: Arg/Lys-rich, often Gly-containing low-complexity segments of ribosomal proteins—typically N- or C-terminal tails or internal loops—that form cationic rRNA-binding patches; the feature also picks up similar short cationic/disordered peptides outside the ribosome
Activation pattern: Regional activation across extended basic segments (usually disordered coils at termini or loops) with strong residue-level peaks on Lys/Arg; minimal activation in structured metal-binding/globular cores; occasionally extends to structured basic surface patches
Exemplars: - bL21: activates on a central basic beta-strand/coil patch (~75–105), consistent with an rRNA-contacting surface.
- uL4: activates on the long disordered, Lys/Arg-biased loop between helices (≈49–101) that threads into/contacts rRNA.
- uS13: activates on the Lys-rich disordered C-terminal tail (93–121) that binds rRNA.
- bL32: activates on the N-terminal basic tail (3–23); no activation on the C4 zinc-finger core.
- Secreted cationic peptide hormone (ELABELA/Toddler precursor): activates on the mature peptide region, not the signal peptide, reflecting recognition of short cationic low-complexity segments.

Summary: Compact, Lys/Arg-rich rRNA/RNP-binding cores from ribosome-related proteins—principally the smallest L/S ribosomal proteins across bacteria, archaea, eukaryotes, and organelles, plus select ribonucleoprotein and ribosome-biogenesis factors—capturing the mature, folded RNA-contacting domain rather than transit peptides or ubiquitin tags.
Activation pattern: Broad domain-level activation across the full mature chain, with residue-level peaks in the central RNA-contacting region; activation extends through structured elements (helices, strands, and connecting loops) and through C4-type Zn-finger segments where present.
Exemplars: - Small ribosomal subunit protein uS12m (mitochondrial S12): no activation on the N-terminal transit peptide; strong, continuous activation across the mature folded chain.
- Small L/S ribosomal proteins (e.g., L28–L37, L39, L41–L43; S17–S26, S28–S33, including organellar forms): activation spans most of the short, basic protein that binds rRNA, including C4-type Zn-finger regions in eL37/eL43-family members.
- Ubiquitin–ribosomal fusion proteins (e.g., eL40/Ub–L40): activation on the ribosomal L40 moiety, not on ubiquitin.
- RNase P protein component 4 (Rpp4): activation concentrated in the central beta/coil core that binds RNA.
- Ribosome biogenesis factor Nsa2: activation on the C-terminal beta-rich structured domain; low activation on the disordered N-terminal region with NLS.

Summary: Large ribosomal subunit (LSU) proteins, including tunnel/peptidyl‑transferase–proximal elements: the feature captures bacterial, chloroplastic, and mitochondrial LSU ribosomal proteins—prominently the bL17 family and the uL22/uL4 family along with their organellar orthologs—that dock to 23S/28S rRNA. The feature also extends to GGQ‑domain translation termination/rescue factors that insert into the PTC.
Activation pattern: Long, contiguous activation across structured rRNA‑contacting cores (β‑strands and helices) and basic/glycine‑rich extensions, often in N‑terminal portions; strong on rRNA‑binding helices and tunnel/PTC‑lining segments; minimal on long low‑complexity/disordered tails; in GGQ factors, high over the GGQ‑domain scaffold with a trough on the catalytic GGQ tripeptide itself.
Exemplars:
- Large‑subunit ribosomal protein bL17 (bacterial, chloroplastic bL17c, mitochondrial bL17m): activation across the N‑terminal helix‑strand‑helix core (e.g., the HELIX 38–55 segment) carrying the rRNA‑binding surface
- Large‑subunit ribosomal protein uL22 (bacterial/eukaryotic/organellar): activation on the long β‑hairpin and Lys/Arg‑rich loop that lines the exit tunnel
- Large‑subunit ribosomal protein uL4: activation on the glycine/lysine‑rich N‑terminal extension and extended loop forming the tunnel constriction
- Other tunnel‑proximal LSU proteins (e.g., uL23/uL24 and chloroplast/mitochondrial counterparts): activation on basic rRNA‑binding surfaces and extensions
- GGQ‑domain translation factors (class I release factors RF1/RF2/eRF1 and rescue factors ArfB/ICT1): activation on the structured GGQ domain that inserts into the PTC, with little/no signal on long C‑terminal basic tails and a dip over the GGQ motif itself
- Minor representation of small‑subunit proteins: activation on basic N‑terminal rRNA‑binding tails

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, Lys/Arg-rich N-terminal extensions and targeting peptides of nucleic-acid-associated proteins—especially ribosomal proteins and histone N-tails—that serve as rRNA/DNA-contacting basic tails, nuclear/organellar localization signals (e.g., NLS or transit peptides), and PTM-rich regulatory regions.
Activation pattern: Regional, N-terminally biased activation in long contiguous stretches (often starting at residue 1 and spanning tens of residues), with strongest peaks on basic low-complexity segments enriched in Lys/Arg with frequent Gly/Ser/Thr. In very small, highly basic ribosomal proteins, the activated region can cover essentially the entire chain, including the folded core. Also lights up NLSs and organellar transit peptides in precursor forms; occasionally includes Cys/His-containing motifs present in some small ribosomal proteins.
Exemplars: - Histones (e.g., H3): strong activation on the disordered, PTM-dense N-terminal tail; silent on the globular core.
- RNase P protein component: activation on the N-terminal low-complexity/disordered tail preceding the structured core; core largely off.
- Ribosome biogenesis factors (e.g., Nsa2): activation on a basic, NLS-containing N-terminal extension.
- Small ribosomal proteins across bacteria/archaea/eukaryotes (and organellar counterparts): broad activation on Lys/Arg-rich N-terminal tails and across the small basic chain, including in precursor entries on transit peptides.
- Ubiquitin-fusion ribosomal proteins: activation on the basic ribosomal protein segment following the ubiquitin moiety.

Summary: Terminal non‑globular linear segments: the feature marks contiguous, simple‑composition regions at protein ends, either (a) intrinsically disordered, charged/low‑complexity tails (acidic/basic, Pro/Ser/Gln‑rich) or (b) single isolated α‑helical tracts used for targeting/assembly (signal peptides, leucine‑rich NES/coiled‑coils, single‑pass transmembrane anchors). These segments often serve as trafficking, dimerization, or interaction modules rather than compact globular domains.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over continuous stretches, typically beginning at the onset of a terminal helix or tail and remaining high to the end of the segment; strong bias for N‑ or C‑terminal regions; minimal activation within compact folded domains; captures both charged low‑complexity IDRs and simple helical runs (hydrophobic or leucine‑rich) rather than residue‑specific peaks.
Exemplars: - Retroviral regulatory proteins (e.g., Rev): activation on the leucine‑rich nuclear export helix and the C‑terminal disordered tail.
- bZIP/coiled‑coil transcription factors: activation within the coiled‑coil/leucine‑zipper helix, especially toward the C‑terminal portion of the helix.
- Small ribosomal proteins (e.g., L32 family): activation on flexible C‑terminal halves/tails that contact rRNA.
- Single‑pass membrane proteins: activation across the transmembrane anchor helix.
- Secreted peptide/hormone precursors: activation on the N‑terminal signal peptide helix.
- HMGA/HMG architectural proteins: activation on the acidic, compositionally biased C‑terminal tail (and adjacent AT‑hook region).
- Transcriptional co‑factors with long IDRs (e.g., POU2AF1): activation across extended disordered regions C‑terminal to structured domains.
- EDRK‑rich SERF family: activation on the internal low‑complexity, charged/disordered segment.
- Plant TCP/TEOSINTE BRANCHED 1: activation on the C‑terminal intrinsically disordered tail, not in the structured DNA‑binding domain.

Summary: General zinc-binding finger modules coordinated by cysteine/histidine, with a strong bias toward tandem C2H2 DNA-binding zinc-finger arrays in eukaryotic transcription factors, but also activating on related Zn-finger families (RING, CCCH/TTP, LIM)
Activation pattern: Domain-level activation confined to structured zinc-finger regions, often spanning long contiguous blocks of adjacent repeats; strongest over the ββα core and basic linker segments, with reduced signal on the coordinating Cys/His themselves; peaks can extend slightly into immediate flanks (e.g., NLS-rich linkers); disordered regions and non–zinc-finger domains (e.g., homeobox) show little to no activation
Exemplars: - GLIS and Krüppel-like factors: strong activation across 3–5 C2H2 fingers at the C-terminus, highest in central fingers and adjacent basic linkers
- Fungal pH- and calcineurin-responsive C2H2 transcription factors (PacC/Rim101, CRZ1): activation over 2–3 C2H2 fingers, peaking in the first/second finger and linker
- Polycomb PHO: sustained activation across four tandem C2H2 fingers
- Proteasome regulator RPN4: activation centered on the single C2H2 finger and immediate C-terminal flank
- Plant GAF1 (C2H2 TF): maximal activation on the second C2H2 finger overlapping a nuclear localization signal; lower on a downstream degenerate/CCHC finger
- TTP/TIS11 family (CCCH RNA-binding zinc fingers): activation on the structural cores of both fingers, sparing many coordinating residues
- RING-type E3 ubiquitin ligase (Hakai): activation on the RING zinc-finger domain and short flanks
- LIM-homeobox proteins (e.g., Lhx3): activation on tandem LIM zinc-binding domains, with no activation on the adjacent homeobox domain

Summary: Segments enriched in small/polar residues (G/S/T/A; also tolerating Cys-rich arrays) within repeat-like or compositionally biased tracts, typically located in the mid-to-C-terminal regions of long viral/bacterial spike, fiber, and tail proteins, as well as eukaryotic low-complexity modules (e.g., nucleoporins, keratin-associated repeats; also consistent with cysteine-rich metallothioneins). Activation occurs both in flexible linker-like stretches and within short beta-strand elements embedded in receptor-binding/spike domains.
Activation pattern: - Broad regional activation across mid-to-C-terminal portions of very long phage tail/spike/fiber proteins, with strong residue-level peaks within short beta-strand segments and adjacent turns
- Patchy, repeated peaks within low-complexity arrays (e.g., selects Gly in FG repeats; terminal positions of 5-aa repeats) and dense clusters of small residues
- Rare residue-level peaks at Gly–Gly motifs marking beta-strand termini/turns
Exemplars: - Bacteriophage tail needle/spike/fiber proteins: strong activation over C-terminal regions including short beta-strand elements; reduced activation in central trimeric coiled-coil cores
