Summary: Low-complexity, intrinsically disordered segments—often at protein N-termini—such as mucin-like/propeptide regions or flexible linkers adjacent to signal/transit peptides, common in small secreted or membrane-associated proteins and also as disordered extensions in diverse enzymes (broad taxonomic coverage, including viral, bacterial, and eukaryotic proteins).
Activation pattern: Regional activation over short to moderate stretches, frequently in disordered or polar/low-complexity segments; in longer proteins, multiple low-complexity patches can activate; in micropeptides, activation can span much of the sequence. Residue-level peaks can fall on Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly within polar-residue stretches but also on basic or hydrophobic residues within the same disordered context.
Exemplars:
- Viral envelope/accessory microproteins: activation on N-terminal Ser/Thr/Pro-rich disordered segments (often mucin-like or regulatory tails).
- Secreted eukaryotic effectors (e.g., oomycete RxLR effectors): activation on the low-complexity region flanking the signal peptide/RxLR motif.
- Human testis-biased and lncRNA-derived micropeptides: activation across intrinsically disordered peptide regions.
- Secreted precursors/propeptides: activation on N-terminal regions following the signal peptide.
- Membrane-associated single-pass proteins: activation on luminal or cytosolic tails flanking the transmembrane helix.
- Bacterial/archaeal metabolic enzymes: activation on disordered, low-complexity N-terminal extensions/linkers enriched in Ser/Thr/Gly/Pro.

- La/La‑related (LARP) RNA‑binding proteins: activation on RG/RGG‑enriched disordered regions.
- DEAD‑box/DEAH RNA helicases and other RNA‑remodeling enzymes: activation on basic glycine‑rich tails.
- Bacterial RNase E/E‑like endoribonucleases: activation on extended low‑complexity C‑terminal scaffolds, including acidic subregions.
- Viral RNA‑binding/regulatory proteins: activation on RG‑rich, low‑complexity segments.

- Eukaryotic coiled‑coil proteins: activation along coiled‑coil helical segments constituting the stable structural core.

Summary: Low-complexity, intrinsically disordered segments—often at protein N-termini—such as mucin-like/propeptide regions or flexible linkers adjacent to signal/transit peptides, common in small secreted or membrane-associated proteins and also as disordered extensions in diverse enzymes (broad taxonomic coverage, including viral, bacterial, and eukaryotic proteins).
Activation pattern: Regional activation over short to moderate stretches, frequently in disordered or polar/low-complexity segments; in longer proteins, multiple low-complexity patches can activate; in micropeptides, activation can span much of the sequence. Residue-level peaks can fall on Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly within polar-residue stretches but also on basic or hydrophobic residues within the same disordered context.
Exemplars:
- Viral envelope/accessory microproteins: activation on N-terminal Ser/Thr/Pro-rich disordered segments (often mucin-like or regulatory tails).
- Secreted eukaryotic effectors (e.g., oomycete RxLR effectors): activation on the low-complexity region flanking the signal peptide/RxLR motif.
- Human testis-biased and lncRNA-derived micropeptides: activation across intrinsically disordered peptide regions.
- Secreted precursors/propeptides: activation on N-terminal regions following the signal peptide.
- Membrane-associated single-pass proteins: activation on luminal or cytosolic tails flanking the transmembrane helix.
- Bacterial/archaeal metabolic enzymes: activation on disordered, low-complexity N-terminal extensions/linkers enriched in Ser/Thr/Gly/Pro.

Summary: Arginine–glycine–rich low-complexity intrinsically disordered regions (RG/RGG-box–like basic tracts), typically as extended C‑terminal tails; prevalent in RNA‑associated proteins where they mediate RNA/RNP interactions and granule assembly, but also appearing as generic basic tails in non‑RNA proteins (often subject to arginine methylation).
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long contiguous stretches, usually in disordered/low‑pLDDT regions and often biased to C‑terminal tails; strongest on runs of RG/RGG (frequently with interspersed prolines), with occasional coverage of other low‑complexity repeats (including acidic patches in some bacterial RNase E–like C‑termini).

- Bacterial SecF (protein translocase subunit): activation confined to the basic, low‑complexity disordered C‑terminal tail.
- Ribosomal proteins (small and large subunits): activation on basic/RG‑rich low‑complexity extensions that contact rRNA.
- La/La‑related (LARP) RNA‑binding proteins: activation on RG/RGG‑enriched disordered regions.
- DEAD‑box/DEAH RNA helicases and other RNA‑remodeling enzymes: activation on basic glycine‑rich tails.
- Bacterial RNase E/E‑like endoribonucleases: activation on extended low‑complexity C‑terminal scaffolds, including acidic subregions.
- Viral RNA‑binding/regulatory proteins: activation on RG‑rich, low‑complexity segments.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity regions enriched in serine, threonine, proline and polar/charged residues—flexible regulatory linkers/tails and propeptide segments that often host short linear motifs (e.g., phosphorylation- and proline‑rich motifs) and proteolytic processing sites; signal is absent from well‑folded catalytic domains and is common across taxa
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long disordered stretches with many sparse residue‑level peaks; avoids structured domains; peaks biased toward S/T/P, glycine, and charged/polar residues; frequently concentrated in N‑ or C‑terminal IDRs and around cleavage/processing sites; can span hundreds of residues in large eukaryotic proteins
Exemplars: - PAK family serine/threonine kinases: activation on the N‑terminal regulatory IDR preceding the kinase domain (including low‑confidence helical propensities), not in the folded kinase domain.

- Centrosomal/kinetochore and chromosomal scaffold proteins: multiple low‑complexity, disordered tracts with scattered peaks.
- Transcriptional/chromatin regulators: activation on N‑terminal low‑complexity/activation domains and compositionally biased regions.
- Ribonucleotide reductase large subunit‑like proteins: activation on N‑terminal disordered tails, including proline‑rich segments.
- Neuropeptide/prohormone precursors: activation in disordered propeptides and at termini of amidated peptides, often adjacent to cleavage sites.

Summary: Compositionally biased low-complexity segments, especially N-terminal hydrophobic helices that form the hydrophobic core of signal peptides or membrane-anchoring amphipathic helices, and serine/threonine-rich intrinsically disordered tracts; the feature reflects sequence-composition bias rather than a specific fold or function and commonly occurs at protein termini across taxa

Summary: The feature represents extracellular/lumenal ectodomains of secretory‑pathway glycoproteins, most prominently viral envelope fusion/attachment spikes. It captures long, virion/extracellular‑exposed domains that are often disulfide‑bonded and N‑glycosylated (including heptad‑repeat coiled‑coil and membrane‑proximal external regions), while excluding signal peptides, transmembrane helices, and cytosolic tails.
Activation pattern: - Domain-level: Off on signal peptides; turns on at the start of the ectodomain; sustained high activation across long extracellular stretches; tapers near the membrane and collapses in transmembrane helices; absent in cytosolic tails.
- Proteolysis: Signal at internal cleavage sites (e.g., furin/host cleavages) is variable; activation tracks the mature extracellular subunits post-cleavage.
- Residue/region biases: Enrichment over cysteines involved in disulfides and at/near N‑glycosylation sequons; strong over heptad‑repeat coiled‑coil regions and membrane‑proximal external regions; not tied to any single short motif.
Exemplars: - Herpesvirus entry glycoproteins gB/gH: high across the virion‑surface ectodomain (including MPER), low in the TM and intravirion tails; may show reduced signal at some cleavage junctions.
- Paramyxovirus fusion protein F: strong over HRC/HRA/HRB heptad repeats and disulfide/glycosylation sites; variable signal at the furin site; off in TM and cytosolic tail.
- Arenavirus GP‑C (G1/G2): broad high activation across both ectodomains, including disulfide and glycan‑rich segments; off in the stable signal peptide, TM, and Zn‑binding cytosolic tail.
- Retroviral‑like Env (gp130): sustained activation across the SU/TM lumenal ectodomain (including the fusion peptide) and deactivation in the TM and ER‑retention tail.
- Diverse viral envelope glycoproteins: long, cysteine/glyco‑rich ectodomains strongly highlighted, termini/TM segments suppressed.
- Eukaryotic multi‑pass channels/transporters (Tweety/Ttyh3; CLIC‑like Cl− channels): selective activation of large extracellular loops (especially directly outside a TM helix), with low signal in transmembrane cores and cytosolic/disordered tails.

Summary: Low-complexity, compositionally biased segments in intrinsically disordered regions, typically enriched in Gly and/or Pro and frequently punctuated by aromatic residues (Tyr/Phe/Trp). YG/YGG/GYG motifs are common but not required. These tracts are common in secreted/extracellular proteins, antimicrobial/allergen precursors, and prion-like or reproductive IDRs.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across low-pLDDT coil-rich tracts with short Gly/Pro runs and intermittent aromatics; local peaks at Gly, Pro, and aromatic residues. Strongly off in well-structured helices/strands, transmembranes, and folded domains; activation often concentrates in N-terminal low-complexity leaders or propeptides.

- Plant HIPPs: activation on Pro/Tyr/Gly-rich low-complexity segments.
- Antimicrobial peptide precursors (e.g., clavanin) and allergens: activation on low-complexity signal/propeptides or IDRs that can be Pro/His-rich with occasional aromatics.
- Proline-rich salivary proteins (e.g., opiorphin/PRP1 precursors): activation on basic Pro-rich low-complexity stretches.
- Reproductive proteins including protamine/protamine-like: activation on simple Arg/Lys-rich low-complexity segments or cleaved propeptides when present.

Summary: Residue positions that mark polypeptide boundaries—especially the absolute N-terminus (position 1) and the terminal residue of sequence fragments—and, secondarily, isolated boundary-like sites within larger proteins (e.g., short linkers between secondary-structure elements or helix/turn cap-like positions), consistent with proteolytic processing junctions in pre/propeptides.
Activation pattern: Predominantly single-residue peaks at sequence extremities (most often the first residue; also the last residue of fragments); sparse internal single-residue peaks at boundary-like positions (short linkers or transitions between secondary structures). Often coincides with disordered/low-confidence termini; in secreted/toxin precursors a recurring window around residues ~50–70 is consistent with signal/propeptide cleavage. Per-protein activations are usually one or a few sites.
Exemplars: Snake venom serine protease: peaks at the N-terminal first residue and at the C-terminal end of the chain; Nuclear pore complex protein Nup155: isolated peaks on single residues within a helix and a low-confidence turn; U4/U6.U5 tri-snRNP–associated protein 1: single-residue peak at a glycine linker between β-strands; E4 ubiquitin-conjugation factor (UBE4): isolated methionine within a long α-helix; Reelin (fragment): strong activation at the fragment’s C-terminal residue in a disordered region; Glutamate dehydrogenase (fragment): activation marks the truncated C-terminal residue.

Summary: Detector of short, low‑complexity S/T/E/D/G/P–rich linear segments that nucleate or cap local secondary structure (helix/β‑turn/β‑hairpin ends), including transmembrane‑helix boundaries and short structured elements embedded in intrinsically disordered regions; occasionally collapses to a single residue that marks a turn/cap or specific helical register position
Activation pattern: - Mixed: (i) regional runs within IDRs (often N‑ or C‑terminal) enriched for Ser/Thr, acidic residues, Gly/Pro; and (ii) sharp, single‑residue peaks at secondary‑structure junctions (helix/coil, strand/loop) or characteristic cap/turn positions
- Selective at membrane-helix edges and adjacent loops; not all helices are marked—preference for segments showing capping/turn signatures
- Typically avoids catalytic cores and annotated active/ligand sites; bulky aromatics (especially Trp) and Cys are underrepresented

Summary: Single conserved residue—often hydrophobic/aromatic but variable (Phe/Tyr/Trp/Leu/Val/Ile, and sometimes His/Thr)—within nucleotide- or ligand-binding pockets and analogous buried sites across diverse folds; in non-nucleotide proteins it maps to an analogous internal pocket- or core-lining position.

Exemplars:

- tRNA (guanine-N7)-methyltransferases (class I SAM MTases): activation on the conserved aromatic that stacks with the SAM adenine and/or the target guanine in the active site.
- UDP-sugar glycosyltransferases for LPS/teichoic acid/lipid A biosynthesis (GT-B fold): activation on the aromatic that stacks with the UDP uracil ring in the donor-binding site.
- NAD(P)-dependent dehydrogenases (Rossmann fold): activation on an adenine-stacking Phe/Tyr in the dinucleotide-binding pocket.
- MurE (UDP-MurNAc-tripeptide synthetase; ATP-grasp ligase): activation on a buried hydrophobe that helps form the adenine-binding cleft for ATP.
- Carbonic anhydrases: activation on a conserved hydrophobic/aromatic residue lining the active-site hydrophobic pocket adjacent to the catalytic zinc.
- Small ribosomal subunit protein S8: activation on an aromatic residue that base-stacks with rRNA or stabilizes the RNA-binding surface.
- MICOS subunit Mic60 (mitofilin): activation on a buried aromatic within the coiled-coil/mitofilin scaffold that stabilizes the membrane-associated core.

Summary: Compositionally biased low-complexity segments, especially N-terminal hydrophobic helices that form the hydrophobic core of signal peptides or membrane-anchoring amphipathic helices, and serine/threonine-rich intrinsically disordered tracts; the feature reflects sequence-composition bias rather than a specific fold or function and commonly occurs at protein termini across taxa
Activation pattern: Regional activation over extended contiguous blocks (typically 8–20 residues), frequently at the N-terminus; strong peaks within hydrophobic cores of signal peptide–like helices or within S/T-rich low-complexity patches; minimal activation in structured catalytic/core domains
Exemplars: - Viral nonstructural/accessory proteins: activation on a short, flexible N-terminal hydrophobic helix (amphipathic/membrane-anchoring segment).
- Plant secreted signaling peptides (SCOOP family): activation on the N-terminal signal peptide hydrophobic core, not on the C-terminal functional motif.
- Eukaryotic transcriptional coactivator scaffolds (Mediator subunit 24): activation on multiple S/T- and Q-rich intrinsically disordered, low-complexity regions.

Summary: Amphipathic, hydrophobic secondary‑structure cores in small proteins—especially alpha‑helical segments and the juxtamembrane/N‑terminal half of signal‑anchor transmembrane helices with a positive‑inside (Lys/Arg) bias; in soluble proteins, the analogous β‑α/helix bundle core often at oligomerization interfaces—while avoiding disordered tails and catalytic/loop regions
Activation pattern: Regional activation over long, contiguous, high‑confidence secondary‑structure elements (helices and β‑α segments); strongest in ordered cores, weak/absent in disordered termini and peripheral loops; in bitopic membrane proteins, peaks at the cytosolic amphipathic helix and the N‑proximal half of the TM helix (positive‑inside), tapering toward the extracytosolic half
Exemplars: - Sec translocon subunit E (bitopic membrane protein): activation on the pre‑TM cytosolic amphipathic helix and the N‑terminal half of the TM helix, consistent with the positive‑inside rule; low on the periplasmic side.
- CRISPR Cas2 endoribonucleases: activation across the central β strands and adjoining α‑helix that form the homodimer core; catalytic Asp and flexible termini are not emphasized.
- Exodeoxyribonuclease VII small subunit: strong signal on the central ordered helix bundle, with little/no activation on disordered N/C‑terminal regions.
- ATP synthase and respiratory chain small membrane subunits: enrichment on N‑terminal amphipathic/juxtamembrane helices and the entry half of signal‑anchor TM segments.
- Small ribosomal proteins and other RNA/protein‑binding regulators: activation on amphipathic helical cores that present Lys/Arg‑rich faces, rather than on flexible/basic tails.
- Archaeal gas vesicle structural proteins: signal on extended hydrophobic/amphipathic helices forming the shell scaffold.
- Eukaryotic coiled‑coil proteins: activation along coiled‑coil helical segments constituting the stable structural core.

Summary: Basic polycationic patches enriched in arginine (often with lysine) within low-complexity/disordered regions, frequently N-terminal. These include classical monopartite NLSs, nucleic acid–binding basic tails, signal peptide n-regions and cytosolic juxtamembrane segments (positive-inside rule), and basic clusters in secreted precursors; typically depleted of acidic residues.
Activation pattern: Regional activation with strong residue-level peaks across contiguous basic runs; N-terminal bias; minimal Asp/Glu, Arg>Lys preference; predominantly in low-pLDDT segments and outside/adjacent to transmembranes on the cytosolic side; observed across viruses, bacteria, plants, and humans.
Exemplars:
- Viral regulators and capsid/accessory proteins: arginine-rich NLSs and nucleic acid–binding basic tails.
- Human regulators (e.g., ARF/Killin): arginine-rich disordered N-termini for targeting/interactions.
- Secreted zymogens and peptides (e.g., trypsinogen/PROPEPs): basic n-regions/dibasic clusters in pre/pro-sequences.
- Membrane proteins (transporters, respiratory chain subunits like ND2, ECF S-components): cytosolic basic patches consistent with the positive-inside rule.

Summary: Low-complexity, compositionally biased segments in intrinsically disordered regions, typically enriched in Gly and/or Pro and frequently punctuated by aromatic residues (Tyr/Phe/Trp). YG/YGG/GYG motifs are common but not required. These tracts are common in secreted/extracellular proteins, antimicrobial/allergen precursors, and prion-like or reproductive IDRs.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across low-pLDDT coil-rich tracts with short Gly/Pro runs and intermittent aromatics; local peaks at Gly, Pro, and aromatic residues. Strongly off in well-structured helices/strands, transmembranes, and folded domains; activation often concentrates in N-terminal low-complexity leaders or propeptides.
Exemplars:
- Peroxisomal membrane protein PEX13: N-terminal Gly/Pro- and Tyr/Phe-punctuated low-complexity coil; off in TM and SH3 domain.
- Small heat shock protein (Hsp42): N-terminal IDR with Y/F/G/P motifs; off over the alpha-crystallin domain.
- Keratin-associated proteins and other extracellular structural proteins (e.g., caseins, chorion components): activation on Gly/Pro/Tyr-rich repeats.
- Plant HIPPs: activation on Pro/Tyr/Gly-rich low-complexity segments.
- Antimicrobial peptide precursors (e.g., clavanin) and allergens: activation on low-complexity signal/propeptides or IDRs that can be Pro/His-rich with occasional aromatics.
- Proline-rich salivary proteins (e.g., opiorphin/PRP1 precursors): activation on basic Pro-rich low-complexity stretches.
- Reproductive proteins including protamine/protamine-like: activation on simple Arg/Lys-rich low-complexity segments or cleaved propeptides when present.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity regions enriched in serine, threonine, proline and polar/charged residues—flexible regulatory linkers/tails and propeptide segments that often host short linear motifs (e.g., phosphorylation- and proline‑rich motifs) and proteolytic processing sites; signal is absent from well‑folded catalytic domains and is common across taxa
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long disordered stretches with many sparse residue‑level peaks; avoids structured domains; peaks biased toward S/T/P, glycine, and charged/polar residues; frequently concentrated in N‑ or C‑terminal IDRs and around cleavage/processing sites; can span hundreds of residues in large eukaryotic proteins
Exemplars: - PAK family serine/threonine kinases: activation on the N‑terminal regulatory IDR preceding the kinase domain (including low‑confidence helical propensities), not in the folded kinase domain.
- Rap/Ras GTPase‑activating proteins: activation on disordered, low‑complexity linkers; absent from the structured GAP domain.
- CARMIL (actin/capping protein regulators): activation on a C‑terminal proline/basic‑rich disordered tail.
- Centrosomal/kinetochore and chromosomal scaffold proteins: multiple low‑complexity, disordered tracts with scattered peaks.
- Transcriptional/chromatin regulators: activation on N‑terminal low‑complexity/activation domains and compositionally biased regions.
- Ribonucleotide reductase large subunit‑like proteins: activation on N‑terminal disordered tails, including proline‑rich segments.
- Neuropeptide/prohormone precursors: activation in disordered propeptides and at termini of amidated peptides, often adjacent to cleavage sites.

Summary: Residue positions that mark polypeptide boundaries—especially the absolute N-terminus (position 1) and the terminal residue of sequence fragments—and, secondarily, isolated boundary-like sites within larger proteins (e.g., short linkers between secondary-structure elements or helix/turn cap-like positions), consistent with proteolytic processing junctions in pre/propeptides.
Activation pattern: Predominantly single-residue peaks at sequence extremities (most often the first residue; also the last residue of fragments); sparse internal single-residue peaks at boundary-like positions (short linkers or transitions between secondary structures). Often coincides with disordered/low-confidence termini; in secreted/toxin precursors a recurring window around residues ~50–70 is consistent with signal/propeptide cleavage. Per-protein activations are usually one or a few sites.
Exemplars: Snake venom serine protease: peaks at the N-terminal first residue and at the C-terminal end of the chain; Nuclear pore complex protein Nup155: isolated peaks on single residues within a helix and a low-confidence turn; U4/U6.U5 tri-snRNP–associated protein 1: single-residue peak at a glycine linker between β-strands; E4 ubiquitin-conjugation factor (UBE4): isolated methionine within a long α-helix; Reelin (fragment): strong activation at the fragment’s C-terminal residue in a disordered region; Glutamate dehydrogenase (fragment): activation marks the truncated C-terminal residue.

Summary: Low-complexity, intrinsically disordered segments—often at protein N-termini—such as mucin-like/propeptide regions or flexible linkers adjacent to signal/transit peptides, common in small secreted or membrane-associated proteins and also as disordered extensions in diverse enzymes (broad taxonomic coverage, including viral, bacterial, and eukaryotic proteins).
Activation pattern: Regional activation over short to moderate stretches, frequently in disordered or polar/low-complexity segments; in longer proteins, multiple low-complexity patches can activate; in micropeptides, activation can span much of the sequence. Residue-level peaks can fall on Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly within polar-residue stretches but also on basic or hydrophobic residues within the same disordered context.
Exemplars:
- Viral envelope/accessory microproteins: activation on N-terminal Ser/Thr/Pro-rich disordered segments (often mucin-like or regulatory tails).
- Secreted eukaryotic effectors (e.g., oomycete RxLR effectors): activation on the low-complexity region flanking the signal peptide/RxLR motif.
- Human testis-biased and lncRNA-derived micropeptides: activation across intrinsically disordered peptide regions.
- Secreted precursors/propeptides: activation on N-terminal regions following the signal peptide.
- Membrane-associated single-pass proteins: activation on luminal or cytosolic tails flanking the transmembrane helix.
- Bacterial/archaeal metabolic enzymes: activation on disordered, low-complexity N-terminal extensions/linkers enriched in Ser/Thr/Gly/Pro.

Summary: Long, low‑complexity Q/N‑rich tracts (poly‑asparagine and poly‑glutamine) in eukaryotic proteins—typically intrinsically disordered terminal or linker regions and compositionally biased coiled‑coil segments—lying outside structured catalytic/recognition domains; especially prevalent in Dictyostelium (and similar N‑rich proteomes).
Activation pattern: Regional activation across extended, compositionally biased blocks with dense N (and Q) runs; sustained high activation over tens of residues with residue‑level peaks on homopolymeric N/Q. Little to no activation in well‑folded domains (kinase cores, DNA‑binding folds, TM helices, ABC NBDs, zinc fingers); when present within a domain boundary, it coincides with a low‑confidence, low‑complexity insert. Often concentrated in N/C‑terminal tails and inter‑domain linkers; can include Q/N‑rich coiled‑coil segments.
Exemplars: - Alpha‑type protein kinase with Arf‑GAP regulator: strong activation on multiple polyQ and polyN tracts (including Q‑rich coiled‑coils) outside the Arf‑GAP and kinase domains.
- Hybrid histidine kinase (PAS–HisKA–RR two‑component‑like): activation on N‑ and Q‑rich disordered linkers; absent from PAS, HisKA, and response‑regulator domains.
- Homeobox transcription factor: activation confined to N‑rich low‑complexity segments; absent from the folded homeobox DNA‑binding domain.
- Rho GTPase‑activating protein (RhoGAP): activation on asparagine‑rich low‑complexity regions (notably a C‑terminal polyN tract); no activation in the MYND zinc finger or RhoGAP catalytic domain.
- Sirtuin (NAD‑dependent deacetylase): activation on extensive C‑terminal N‑rich disordered regions and a short N‑run insert with low structural confidence; not on the structured catalytic core.
- Diacylglycerol kinase: activation on asparagine‑rich disordered segments in the C‑terminus; not in C1 zinc fingers or the DAGK catalytic domain.
- ABC transporter (ABCB7‑like): activation on N‑rich disordered N‑ and C‑terminal tails; absent from transmembrane helices and the cytosolic ABC nucleotide‑binding domain.

Summary: Residue positions that mark polypeptide boundaries—especially the absolute N-terminus (position 1) and the terminal residue of sequence fragments—and, secondarily, isolated boundary-like sites within larger proteins (e.g., short linkers between secondary-structure elements or helix/turn cap-like positions), consistent with proteolytic processing junctions in pre/propeptides.

Summary: Low-complexity, compositionally biased segments in intrinsically disordered regions, typically enriched in Gly and/or Pro and frequently punctuated by aromatic residues (Tyr/Phe/Trp). Summary: Residue positions that mark polypeptide boundaries—especially the absolute N-terminus (position 1) and the terminal residue of sequence fragments—and, secondarily, isolated boundary-like sites within larger proteins (e.g., short linkers between secondary-structure elements or helix/turn cap-like positions), consistent with proteolytic processing junctions in pre/propeptides.
Activation pattern: Predominantly single-residue peaks at sequence extremities (most often the first residue; also the last residue of fragments); sparse internal single-residue peaks at boundary-like positions (short linkers or transitions between secondary structures). Often coincides with disordered/low-confidence termini; in secreted/toxin precursors a recurring window around residues ~50–70 is consistent with signal/propeptide cleavage. Per-protein activations are usually one or a few sites.
Exemplars: Snake venom serine protease: peaks at the N-terminal first residue and at the C-terminal end of the chain; Nuclear pore complex protein Nup155: isolated peaks on single residues within a helix and a low-confidence turn; U4/U6.U5 tri-snRNP–associated protein 1: single-residue peak at a glycine linker between β-strands; E4 ubiquitin-conjugation factor (UBE4): isolated methionine within a long α-helix; Reelin (fragment): strong activation at the fragment’s C-terminal residue in a disordered region; Glutamate dehydrogenase (fragment): activation marks the truncated C-terminal residue.

Summary: Detector of short, low‑complexity S/T/E/D/G/P–rich linear segments that nucleate or cap local secondary structure (helix/β‑turn/β‑hairpin ends), including transmembrane‑helix boundaries and short structured elements embedded in intrinsically disordered regions; occasionally collapses to a single residue that marks a turn/cap or specific helical register position
Activation pattern: - Mixed: (i) regional runs within IDRs (often N‑ or C‑terminal) enriched for Ser/Thr, acidic residues, Gly/Pro; and (ii) sharp, single‑residue peaks at secondary‑structure junctions (helix/coil, strand/loop) or characteristic cap/turn positions
- Selective at membrane-helix edges and adjacent loops; not all helices are marked—preference for segments showing capping/turn signatures
- Typically avoids catalytic cores and annotated active/ligand sites; bulky aromatics (especially Trp) and Cys are underrepresented
Exemplars:

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity regions enriched in serine, threonine, proline and polar/charged residues—flexible regulatory linkers/tails and propeptide segments that often host short linear motifs (e.g., phosphorylation- and proline‑rich motifs) and proteolytic processing sites; signal is absent from well‑folded catalytic domains and is common across taxa
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long disordered stretches with many sparse residue‑level peaks; avoids structured domains; peaks biased toward S/T/P, glycine, and charged/polar residues; frequently concentrated in N‑ or C‑terminal IDRs and around cleavage/processing sites; can span hundreds of residues in large eukaryotic proteins
Exemplars: - PAK family serine/threonine kinases: activation on the N‑terminal regulatory IDR preceding the kinase domain (including low‑confidence helical propensities), not in the folded kinase domain.

- Centrosomal/kinetochore and chromosomal scaffold proteins: multiple low‑complexity, disordered tracts with scattered peaks.
- Transcriptional/chromatin regulators: activation on N‑terminal low‑complexity/activation domains and compositionally biased regions.
- Ribonucleotide reductase large subunit‑like proteins: activation on N‑terminal disordered tails, including proline‑rich segments.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low-complexity segments enriched in small polar residues (Ser/Thr/Gly, often with Pro), typically found in N-terminal tails and flexible loops across diverse proteins (including viral proteins, secreted/effectors, membrane proteins, and transporter ATPase subunits), and largely absent from the well-folded cores of catalytic domains.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long, low-pLDDT stretches with residue-level peaks on S and G (secondarily T); frequently concentrated near N-termini but can occur throughout disordered regions; generally absent from well-folded cores yet can appear in short low-complexity termini or loop insertions within otherwise structured enzymes and ATPases; occasionally a single high peak on an isolated glycine in an otherwise structured protein.
Exemplars: Bacterial acetyl-CoA synthetase: strong activation on S/G/T within an N-terminal low-complexity, disordered segment, none in the structured enzyme core; Telomere-binding regulatory protein: scattered S/T activations confined to very low-confidence, coil-like regions; Viral non-structural/accessory protein: widespread activation on S and G across a globally disordered protein; Membrane/transport system components: S/G/T peaks in low-confidence extra-/intracellular loops and in flexible regions of soluble ATPase subunits; Cytosolic metabolic enzyme (e.g., HGPRT): localized activation limited to short disordered termini or low-complexity insertions.

Summary: Compositionally biased, low-complexity flexible segments (often terminal or in loops/propeptides), frequently enriched in Pro/Gly with a common—but not required—positive bias (Arg/Lys), and carrying simple repeats (e.g., RG/RGG, PG/GPG, PxxP or neutral/polar repeats); used for nucleic-acid contacts, SH3-mediated interactions, targeting peptides, or flexible linkers/tails.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long low-complexity tracts or shorter flexible loops/propeptides (avoiding structured catalytic or transmembrane cores), including mitochondrial transit peptides and serpin reactive center loops.
Exemplars: • Viral regulatory/tegument proteins: activation on basic low-complexity arms
• RNA-binding proteins (including bacterial RNase P protein): activation on short basic patches or disordered termini
• Proline-rich adaptor/scaffold regions: activation on PxxP/PG-rich segments
• Enzymes and transporters: activation on compositionally biased linkers, cytosolic/luminal loops, or targeting peptides, not on conserved cores
• Secreted proteases/serpins: activation on flexible propeptides or reactive center loops (not necessarily polybasic)

Summary: Amphipathic, hydrophobic secondary‑structure cores in small proteins—especially alpha‑helical segments and the juxtamembrane/N‑terminal half of signal‑anchor transmembrane helices with a positive‑inside (Lys/Arg) bias; in soluble proteins, the analogous β‑α/helix bundle core often at oligomerization interfaces—while avoiding disordered tails and catalytic/loop regions
Activation pattern: Regional activation over long, contiguous, high‑confidence secondary‑structure elements (helices and β‑α segments); strongest in ordered cores, weak/absent in disordered termini and peripheral loops; in bitopic membrane proteins, peaks at the cytosolic amphipathic helix and the N‑proximal half of the TM helix (positive‑inside), tapering toward the extracytosolic half
Exemplars: - Sec translocon subunit E (bitopic membrane protein): activation on the pre‑TM cytosolic amphipathic helix and the N‑terminal half of the TM helix, consistent with the positive‑inside rule; low on the periplasmic side.

- Archaeal gas vesicle structural proteins: signal on extended hydrophobic/amphipathic helices forming the shell scaffold.
- Eukaryotic coiled‑coil proteins: activation along coiled‑coil helical segments constituting the stable structural core.

Summary: Compositionally biased low-complexity segments, especially N-terminal hydrophobic helices that form the hydrophobic core of signal peptides or membrane-anchoring amphipathic helices, and serine/threonine-rich intrinsically disordered tracts; the feature reflects sequence-composition bias rather than a specific fold or function and commonly occurs at protein termini across taxa

Summary: Arg/Lys-rich, intrinsically disordered low‑complexity tails that mediate electrostatic binding and condensation of nucleic acids—found in histones (esp. Summary: Low-complexity, intrinsically disordered segments—often at protein N-termini—such as mucin-like/propeptide regions or flexible linkers adjacent to signal/transit peptides, common in small secreted or membrane-associated proteins and also as disordered extensions in diverse enzymes (broad taxonomic coverage, including viral, bacterial, and eukaryotic proteins).

Summary: Residue positions that mark polypeptide boundaries—especially the absolute N-terminus (position 1) and the terminal residue of sequence fragments—and, secondarily, isolated boundary-like sites within larger proteins (e.g., short linkers between secondary-structure elements or helix/turn cap-like positions), consistent with proteolytic processing junctions in pre/propeptides.

Summary: Low-complexity, intrinsically disordered segments—often at protein N-termini—such as mucin-like/propeptide regions or flexible linkers adjacent to signal/transit peptides, common in small secreted or membrane-associated proteins and also as disordered extensions in diverse enzymes (broad taxonomic coverage, including viral, bacterial, and eukaryotic proteins).

Summary: Residue positions that mark polypeptide boundaries—especially the absolute N-terminus (position 1) and the terminal residue of sequence fragments—and, secondarily, isolated boundary-like sites within larger proteins (e.g., short linkers between secondary-structure elements or helix/turn cap-like positions), consistent with proteolytic processing junctions in pre/propeptides.
Activation pattern: Predominantly single-residue peaks at sequence extremities (most often the first residue; also the last residue of fragments); sparse internal single-residue peaks at boundary-like positions (short linkers or transitions between secondary structures). Often coincides with disordered/low-confidence termini; in secreted/toxin precursors a recurring window around residues ~50–70 is consistent with signal/propeptide cleavage. Per-protein activations are usually one or a few sites.
Exemplars: Snake venom serine protease: peaks at the N-terminal first residue and at the C-terminal end of the chain; Nuclear pore complex protein Nup155: isolated peaks on single residues within a helix and a low-confidence turn; U4/U6.U5 tri-snRNP–associated protein 1: single-residue peak at a glycine linker between β-strands; E4 ubiquitin-conjugation factor (UBE4): isolated methionine within a long α-helix; Reelin (fragment): strong activation at the fragment’s C-terminal residue in a disordered region; Glutamate dehydrogenase (fragment): activation marks the truncated C-terminal residue.

Summary: Amphipathic, hydrophobic secondary‑structure cores in small proteins—especially alpha‑helical segments and the juxtamembrane/N‑terminal half of signal‑anchor transmembrane helices with a positive‑inside (Lys/Arg) bias; in soluble proteins, the analogous β‑α/helix bundle core often at oligomerization interfaces—while avoiding disordered tails and catalytic/loop regions

- Exodeoxyribonuclease VII small subunit: strong signal on the central ordered helix bundle, with little/no activation on disordered N/C‑terminal regions.
- ATP synthase and respiratory chain small membrane subunits: enrichment on N‑terminal amphipathic/juxtamembrane helices and the entry half of signal‑anchor TM segments.

- Archaeal gas vesicle structural proteins: signal on extended hydrophobic/amphipathic helices forming the shell scaffold.

Summary: Basic polycationic patches enriched in arginine (often with lysine) within low-complexity/disordered regions, frequently N-terminal. Exemplars:
- Viral regulators and capsid/accessory proteins: arginine-rich NLSs and nucleic acid–binding basic tails.
- Human regulators (e.g., ARF/Killin): arginine-rich disordered N-termini for targeting/interactions.
- Secreted zymogens and peptides (e.g., trypsinogen/PROPEPs): basic n-regions/dibasic clusters in pre/pro-sequences.

Summary: Low-complexity, intrinsically disordered segments—often at protein N-termini—such as mucin-like/propeptide regions or flexible linkers adjacent to signal/transit peptides, common in small secreted or membrane-associated proteins and also as disordered extensions in diverse enzymes (broad taxonomic coverage, including viral, bacterial, and eukaryotic proteins).

Residue-level peaks can fall on Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly within polar-residue stretches but also on basic or hydrophobic residues within the same disordered context.
Exemplars:
- Viral envelope/accessory microproteins: activation on N-terminal Ser/Thr/Pro-rich disordered segments (often mucin-like or regulatory tails).
- Secreted eukaryotic effectors (e.g., oomycete RxLR effectors): activation on the low-complexity region flanking the signal peptide/RxLR motif.
- Human testis-biased and lncRNA-derived micropeptides: activation across intrinsically disordered peptide regions.
- Secreted precursors/propeptides: activation on N-terminal regions following the signal peptide.
- Membrane-associated single-pass proteins: activation on luminal or cytosolic tails flanking the transmembrane helix.
- Bacterial/archaeal metabolic enzymes: activation on disordered, low-complexity N-terminal extensions/linkers enriched in Ser/Thr/Gly/Pro.

Summary: Low-complexity, compositionally biased segments in intrinsically disordered regions, typically enriched in Gly and/or Pro and frequently punctuated by aromatic residues (Tyr/Phe/Trp). Strongly off in well-structured helices/strands, transmembranes, and folded domains; activation often concentrates in N-terminal low-complexity leaders or propeptides.

- Selective at membrane-helix edges and adjacent loops; not all helices are marked—preference for segments showing capping/turn signatures

Exemplars: - Viral nonstructural/accessory proteins: activation on a short, flexible N-terminal hydrophobic helix (amphipathic/membrane-anchoring segment).
- Plant secreted signaling peptides (SCOOP family): activation on the N-terminal signal peptide hydrophobic core, not on the C-terminal functional motif.
- Eukaryotic transcriptional coactivator scaffolds (Mediator subunit 24): activation on multiple S/T- and Q-rich intrinsically disordered, low-complexity regions.

Summary: Amphipathic, hydrophobic secondary‑structure cores in small proteins—especially alpha‑helical segments and the juxtamembrane/N‑terminal half of signal‑anchor transmembrane helices with a positive‑inside (Lys/Arg) bias; in soluble proteins, the analogous β‑α/helix bundle core often at oligomerization interfaces—while avoiding disordered tails and catalytic/loop regions
Activation pattern: Regional activation over long, contiguous, high‑confidence secondary‑structure elements (helices and β‑α segments); strongest in ordered cores, weak/absent in disordered termini and peripheral loops; in bitopic membrane proteins, peaks at the cytosolic amphipathic helix and the N‑proximal half of the TM helix (positive‑inside), tapering toward the extracytosolic half
Exemplars: - Sec translocon subunit E (bitopic membrane protein): activation on the pre‑TM cytosolic amphipathic helix and the N‑terminal half of the TM helix, consistent with the positive‑inside rule; low on the periplasmic side.
- CRISPR Cas2 endoribonucleases: activation across the central β strands and adjoining α‑helix that form the homodimer core; catalytic Asp and flexible termini are not emphasized.
- Exodeoxyribonuclease VII small subunit: strong signal on the central ordered helix bundle, with little/no activation on disordered N/C‑terminal regions.
- ATP synthase and respiratory chain small membrane subunits: enrichment on N‑terminal amphipathic/juxtamembrane helices and the entry half of signal‑anchor TM segments.
- Small ribosomal proteins and other RNA/protein‑binding regulators: activation on amphipathic helical cores that present Lys/Arg‑rich faces, rather than on flexible/basic tails.
- Archaeal gas vesicle structural proteins: signal on extended hydrophobic/amphipathic helices forming the shell scaffold.
- Eukaryotic coiled‑coil proteins: activation along coiled‑coil helical segments constituting the stable structural core.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity regions enriched in serine, threonine, proline and polar/charged residues—flexible regulatory linkers/tails and propeptide segments that often host short linear motifs (e.g., phosphorylation- and proline‑rich motifs) and proteolytic processing sites; signal is absent from well‑folded catalytic domains and is common across taxa
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long disordered stretches with many sparse residue‑level peaks; avoids structured domains; peaks biased toward S/T/P, glycine, and charged/polar residues; frequently concentrated in N‑ or C‑terminal IDRs and around cleavage/processing sites; can span hundreds of residues in large eukaryotic proteins
Exemplars: - PAK family serine/threonine kinases: activation on the N‑terminal regulatory IDR preceding the kinase domain (including low‑confidence helical propensities), not in the folded kinase domain.
- Rap/Ras GTPase‑activating proteins: activation on disordered, low‑complexity linkers; absent from the structured GAP domain.
- CARMIL (actin/capping protein regulators): activation on a C‑terminal proline/basic‑rich disordered tail.
- Centrosomal/kinetochore and chromosomal scaffold proteins: multiple low‑complexity, disordered tracts with scattered peaks.
- Transcriptional/chromatin regulators: activation on N‑terminal low‑complexity/activation domains and compositionally biased regions.
- Ribonucleotide reductase large subunit‑like proteins: activation on N‑terminal disordered tails, including proline‑rich segments.
- Neuropeptide/prohormone precursors: activation in disordered propeptides and at termini of amidated peptides, often adjacent to cleavage sites.

Summary: Basic polycationic patches enriched in arginine (often with lysine) within low-complexity/disordered regions, frequently N-terminal. These include classical monopartite NLSs, nucleic acid–binding basic tails, signal peptide n-regions and cytosolic juxtamembrane segments (positive-inside rule), and basic clusters in secreted precursors; typically depleted of acidic residues.
Activation pattern: Regional activation with strong residue-level peaks across contiguous basic runs; N-terminal bias; minimal Asp/Glu, Arg>Lys preference; predominantly in low-pLDDT segments and outside/adjacent to transmembranes on the cytosolic side; observed across viruses, bacteria, plants, and humans.
Exemplars:
- Viral regulators and capsid/accessory proteins: arginine-rich NLSs and nucleic acid–binding basic tails.
- Human regulators (e.g., ARF/Killin): arginine-rich disordered N-termini for targeting/interactions.
- Secreted zymogens and peptides (e.g., trypsinogen/PROPEPs): basic n-regions/dibasic clusters in pre/pro-sequences.
- Membrane proteins (transporters, respiratory chain subunits like ND2, ECF S-components): cytosolic basic patches consistent with the positive-inside rule.

Summary: Low-complexity, compositionally biased segments in intrinsically disordered regions, typically enriched in Gly and/or Pro and frequently punctuated by aromatic residues (Tyr/Phe/Trp). YG/YGG/GYG motifs are common but not required. These tracts are common in secreted/extracellular proteins, antimicrobial/allergen precursors, and prion-like or reproductive IDRs.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across low-pLDDT coil-rich tracts with short Gly/Pro runs and intermittent aromatics; local peaks at Gly, Pro, and aromatic residues. Strongly off in well-structured helices/strands, transmembranes, and folded domains; activation often concentrates in N-terminal low-complexity leaders or propeptides.
Exemplars:
- Peroxisomal membrane protein PEX13: N-terminal Gly/Pro- and Tyr/Phe-punctuated low-complexity coil; off in TM and SH3 domain.
- Small heat shock protein (Hsp42): N-terminal IDR with Y/F/G/P motifs; off over the alpha-crystallin domain.
- Keratin-associated proteins and other extracellular structural proteins (e.g., caseins, chorion components): activation on Gly/Pro/Tyr-rich repeats.
- Plant HIPPs: activation on Pro/Tyr/Gly-rich low-complexity segments.
- Antimicrobial peptide precursors (e.g., clavanin) and allergens: activation on low-complexity signal/propeptides or IDRs that can be Pro/His-rich with occasional aromatics.
- Proline-rich salivary proteins (e.g., opiorphin/PRP1 precursors): activation on basic Pro-rich low-complexity stretches.
- Reproductive proteins including protamine/protamine-like: activation on simple Arg/Lys-rich low-complexity segments or cleaved propeptides when present.

Summary: Low-complexity, intrinsically disordered segments—often at protein N-termini—such as mucin-like/propeptide regions or flexible linkers adjacent to signal/transit peptides, common in small secreted or membrane-associated proteins and also as disordered extensions in diverse enzymes (broad taxonomic coverage, including viral, bacterial, and eukaryotic proteins).
Activation pattern: Regional activation over short to moderate stretches, frequently in disordered or polar/low-complexity segments; in longer proteins, multiple low-complexity patches can activate; in micropeptides, activation can span much of the sequence. Residue-level peaks can fall on Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly within polar-residue stretches but also on basic or hydrophobic residues within the same disordered context.
Exemplars:
- Viral envelope/accessory microproteins: activation on N-terminal Ser/Thr/Pro-rich disordered segments (often mucin-like or regulatory tails).
- Secreted eukaryotic effectors (e.g., oomycete RxLR effectors): activation on the low-complexity region flanking the signal peptide/RxLR motif.
- Human testis-biased and lncRNA-derived micropeptides: activation across intrinsically disordered peptide regions.
- Secreted precursors/propeptides: activation on N-terminal regions following the signal peptide.
- Membrane-associated single-pass proteins: activation on luminal or cytosolic tails flanking the transmembrane helix.
- Bacterial/archaeal metabolic enzymes: activation on disordered, low-complexity N-terminal extensions/linkers enriched in Ser/Thr/Gly/Pro.

Summary: Residue positions that mark polypeptide boundaries—especially the absolute N-terminus (position 1) and the terminal residue of sequence fragments—and, secondarily, isolated boundary-like sites within larger proteins (e.g., short linkers between secondary-structure elements or helix/turn cap-like positions), consistent with proteolytic processing junctions in pre/propeptides.
Activation pattern: Predominantly single-residue peaks at sequence extremities (most often the first residue; also the last residue of fragments); sparse internal single-residue peaks at boundary-like positions (short linkers or transitions between secondary structures). Often coincides with disordered/low-confidence termini; in secreted/toxin precursors a recurring window around residues ~50–70 is consistent with signal/propeptide cleavage. Per-protein activations are usually one or a few sites.
Exemplars: Snake venom serine protease: peaks at the N-terminal first residue and at the C-terminal end of the chain; Nuclear pore complex protein Nup155: isolated peaks on single residues within a helix and a low-confidence turn; U4/U6.U5 tri-snRNP–associated protein 1: single-residue peak at a glycine linker between β-strands; E4 ubiquitin-conjugation factor (UBE4): isolated methionine within a long α-helix; Reelin (fragment): strong activation at the fragment’s C-terminal residue in a disordered region; Glutamate dehydrogenase (fragment): activation marks the truncated C-terminal residue.

Summary: Detector of short, low‑complexity S/T/E/D/G/P–rich linear segments that nucleate or cap local secondary structure (helix/β‑turn/β‑hairpin ends), including transmembrane‑helix boundaries and short structured elements embedded in intrinsically disordered regions; occasionally collapses to a single residue that marks a turn/cap or specific helical register position
Activation pattern: - Mixed: (i) regional runs within IDRs (often N‑ or C‑terminal) enriched for Ser/Thr, acidic residues, Gly/Pro; and (ii) sharp, single‑residue peaks at secondary‑structure junctions (helix/coil, strand/loop) or characteristic cap/turn positions
- Selective at membrane-helix edges and adjacent loops; not all helices are marked—preference for segments showing capping/turn signatures
- Typically avoids catalytic cores and annotated active/ligand sites; bulky aromatics (especially Trp) and Cys are underrepresented

Summary: Residue-level detector for tryptophan (W) side chains, often firing on multiple W positions within a sequence and with a mild bias toward N‑terminal Ws; broadly applicable across taxa and protein classes, with frequent occurrences in short membrane/secreted proteins but also in diverse enzymes (e.g., ATP synthase ε, proteases) and mitochondrial proteins.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks centered on W; multiple independent peaks per protein; modest enrichment near N‑termini; occasional weak spillover to neighboring residues (C/E/Q/G/K/R) in W‑rich contexts.
Exemplars: - Viral small/accessory membrane proteins (e.g., viroporin-like): activation on Trp residues in short helices/interfacial segments.
- Bacteriocins and peptide toxins: activation on Trp-rich motifs that mediate membrane interaction/disruption.
- ATP synthase subunit ε (F1 epsilon): activation on conserved Trp residue(s) across bacteria/mitochondria.
- Proteases (serine, cysteine, metalloproteases): activation on Trp positions within the enzyme sequence.
- Secreted and transmembrane protein precursors: activation on interfacial/N‑terminal Trp residues around TM regions or signal-proximal segments.
- Mitochondrial proteins: activation on Trp residues, including in membrane-associated components.
- Eukaryotic micropeptides/antisense-encoded small proteins: activation on any Trp present, often near the N‑terminus due to short length.

Summary: Active-site diphosphate/adenylate–binding microenvironment: glycine‑rich, small/charged loop‑and‑helix segments that coordinate highly charged phosphoanhydride groups of cofactors or intermediates (especially ThDP diphosphate, but also AMP/NAD+/FAD and acyl‑adenylates), most prominently in ThDP‑dependent carboligases/decarboxylases and, by cross‑reactivity, other nucleotidyltransferase/adenylate‑forming enzymes; occasional single‑residue hits reflect similar helix/loop geometry rather than shared chemistry.

Exemplars: - ThDP‑dependent carboligases/lyases (e.g., 2‑hydroxyacyl‑CoA lyase): strong activation across the ThDP diphosphate‑binding loop and neighboring elements, also touching substrate‑binding arginines.
- Enzymes with annotated ThDP‑binding regions: continuous C‑terminal activation with maxima at the start of the “thiamine pyrophosphate binding” segment.
- NAD‑dependent DNA ligase (LigA): broad activation over the N‑terminal adenylation/catalytic core, including the catalytic lysine and NAD‑binding residues; no activation on the Zn module or BRCT domain.
- Archaeal 2‑oxoacid:ferredoxin oxidoreductase (E1‑like ThDP subunits): mid‑range activation on the ThDP PP‑binding domain.
- Acyl‑adenylate/CoA ligases (AMP‑forming): moderate activation on AMP‑binding/adenylation loops.
- Photolyase/cryptochrome FAD‑binding proteins: isolated activation in the dinucleotide (FAD‑ADP) pyrophosphate‑binding helix.
- Low‑level structural mimicry: single residues in unrelated proteins (e.g., a glycine at a transmembrane helix break in Na+/H+ antiporter, a lone alanine in an HDAC‑like fold, or a residue in a transglycosylase helix) matching the same loop/helix microenvironment without shared function.

Summary: Basic polycationic patches enriched in arginine (often with lysine) within low-complexity/disordered regions, frequently N-terminal. Exemplars:

- Secreted zymogens and peptides (e.g., trypsinogen/PROPEPs): basic n-regions/dibasic clusters in pre/pro-sequences.

Summary: Low-complexity, compositionally biased segments in intrinsically disordered regions, typically enriched in Gly and/or Pro and frequently punctuated by aromatic residues (Tyr/Phe/Trp). YG/YGG/GYG motifs are common but not required. These tracts are common in secreted/extracellular proteins, antimicrobial/allergen precursors, and prion-like or reproductive IDRs.

Summary: Long, low‑complexity Q/N‑rich tracts (poly‑asparagine and poly‑glutamine) in eukaryotic proteins—typically intrinsically disordered terminal or linker regions and compositionally biased coiled‑coil segments—lying outside structured catalytic/recognition domains; especially prevalent in Dictyostelium (and similar N‑rich proteomes).
Activation pattern: Regional activation across extended, compositionally biased blocks with dense N (and Q) runs; sustained high activation over tens of residues with residue‑level peaks on homopolymeric N/Q. Little to no activation in well‑folded domains (kinase cores, DNA‑binding folds, TM helices, ABC NBDs, zinc fingers); when present within a domain boundary, it coincides with a low‑confidence, low‑complexity insert. Often concentrated in N/C‑terminal tails and inter‑domain linkers; can include Q/N‑rich coiled‑coil segments.
Exemplars: - Alpha‑type protein kinase with Arf‑GAP regulator: strong activation on multiple polyQ and polyN tracts (including Q‑rich coiled‑coils) outside the Arf‑GAP and kinase domains.

- Homeobox transcription factor: activation confined to N‑rich low‑complexity segments; absent from the folded homeobox DNA‑binding domain.
- Rho GTPase‑activating protein (RhoGAP): activation on asparagine‑rich low‑complexity regions (notably a C‑terminal polyN tract); no activation in the MYND zinc finger or RhoGAP catalytic domain.
- Sirtuin (NAD‑dependent deacetylase): activation on extensive C‑terminal N‑rich disordered regions and a short N‑run insert with low structural confidence; not on the structured catalytic core.
- Diacylglycerol kinase: activation on asparagine‑rich disordered segments in the C‑terminus; not in C1 zinc fingers or the DAGK catalytic domain.
- ABC transporter (ABCB7‑like): activation on N‑rich disordered N‑ and C‑terminal tails; absent from transmembrane helices and the cytosolic ABC nucleotide‑binding domain.

Summary: Low‑complexity, simple‑sequence tandem‑repeat tracts enriched in small residues (especially A/T/S/P/G; e.g., AAT and TP/PT motifs), characteristic of mucin‑like PTS regions and antifreeze repeats, and more broadly of simple repeat LCRs across diverse proteins (including viral and reproductive proteins; occasionally extending to basic Arg‑rich LCRs such as protamines). Activation pattern: Predominantly regional/domain‑level activation across low‑complexity repeat segments, often with periodic residue‑level peaks aligned to specific positions within the repeat (e.g., the first Ala in AAT). Reduced in globular catalytic/zinc‑finger domains and transmembranes, but activation can occur in simple structured repeats (alanine‑rich helices) and appears as scattered peaks in basic Arg/Cys‑rich LCRs.
Exemplars: - Antifreeze/ice‑structuring proteins: strong periodic activation on AAT repeat tracts and on alanine‑rich type I AFP helices, with lower signal in nonrepetitive linkers.
- Mucin family extracellular glycoproteins: broad activation across disordered PTS‑rich tandem repeats with peaks on Ala/Ser/Thr; typically absent from transmembrane helix and cytosolic tail.
- Viral regulatory proteins (e.g., herpesvirus ICP0‑like RING E3s): activation confined to low‑complexity Pro/Ala- and Gly‑rich segments; reduced in the folded RING domain.
- Testis/sperm‑associated low‑complexity proteins (e.g., testis‑specific repeat proteins): continuous activation over annotated tandem‑repeat, low‑complexity regions.
- Protamines and cysteine‑rich basic sperm proteins: context‑dependent peaks on Arg (and some Cys/Lys/Pro) within Arg‑rich low‑complexity tracts.

Exemplars: Snake venom serine protease: peaks at the N-terminal first residue and at the C-terminal end of the chain; Nuclear pore complex protein Nup155: isolated peaks on single residues within a helix and a low-confidence turn; U4/U6.U5 tri-snRNP–associated protein 1: single-residue peak at a glycine linker between β-strands; E4 ubiquitin-conjugation factor (UBE4): isolated methionine within a long α-helix; Reelin (fragment): strong activation at the fragment’s C-terminal residue in a disordered region; Glutamate dehydrogenase (fragment): activation marks the truncated C-terminal residue.

Summary: Compositionally biased low-complexity segments, especially N-terminal hydrophobic helices that form the hydrophobic core of signal peptides or membrane-anchoring amphipathic helices, and serine/threonine-rich intrinsically disordered tracts; the feature reflects sequence-composition bias rather than a specific fold or function and commonly occurs at protein termini across taxa
Activation pattern: Regional activation over extended contiguous blocks (typically 8–20 residues), frequently at the N-terminus; strong peaks within hydrophobic cores of signal peptide–like helices or within S/T-rich low-complexity patches; minimal activation in structured catalytic/core domains
Exemplars: - Viral nonstructural/accessory proteins: activation on a short, flexible N-terminal hydrophobic helix (amphipathic/membrane-anchoring segment).
- Plant secreted signaling peptides (SCOOP family): activation on the N-terminal signal peptide hydrophobic core, not on the C-terminal functional motif.
- Eukaryotic transcriptional coactivator scaffolds (Mediator subunit 24): activation on multiple S/T- and Q-rich intrinsically disordered, low-complexity regions.

Summary: Amphipathic, hydrophobic secondary‑structure cores in small proteins—especially alpha‑helical segments and the juxtamembrane/N‑terminal half of signal‑anchor transmembrane helices with a positive‑inside (Lys/Arg) bias; in soluble proteins, the analogous β‑α/helix bundle core often at oligomerization interfaces—while avoiding disordered tails and catalytic/loop regions
Activation pattern: Regional activation over long, contiguous, high‑confidence secondary‑structure elements (helices and β‑α segments); strongest in ordered cores, weak/absent in disordered termini and peripheral loops; in bitopic membrane proteins, peaks at the cytosolic amphipathic helix and the N‑proximal half of the TM helix (positive‑inside), tapering toward the extracytosolic half
Exemplars: - Sec translocon subunit E (bitopic membrane protein): activation on the pre‑TM cytosolic amphipathic helix and the N‑terminal half of the TM helix, consistent with the positive‑inside rule; low on the periplasmic side.
- CRISPR Cas2 endoribonucleases: activation across the central β strands and adjoining α‑helix that form the homodimer core; catalytic Asp and flexible termini are not emphasized.
- Exodeoxyribonuclease VII small subunit: strong signal on the central ordered helix bundle, with little/no activation on disordered N/C‑terminal regions.
- ATP synthase and respiratory chain small membrane subunits: enrichment on N‑terminal amphipathic/juxtamembrane helices and the entry half of signal‑anchor TM segments.
- Small ribosomal proteins and other RNA/protein‑binding regulators: activation on amphipathic helical cores that present Lys/Arg‑rich faces, rather than on flexible/basic tails.
- Archaeal gas vesicle structural proteins: signal on extended hydrophobic/amphipathic helices forming the shell scaffold.
- Eukaryotic coiled‑coil proteins: activation along coiled‑coil helical segments constituting the stable structural core.

Summary: Low-complexity, compositionally biased segments in intrinsically disordered regions, typically enriched in Gly and/or Pro and frequently punctuated by aromatic residues (Tyr/Phe/Trp). YG/YGG/GYG motifs are common but not required. These tracts are common in secreted/extracellular proteins, antimicrobial/allergen precursors, and prion-like or reproductive IDRs.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across low-pLDDT coil-rich tracts with short Gly/Pro runs and intermittent aromatics; local peaks at Gly, Pro, and aromatic residues. Strongly off in well-structured helices/strands, transmembranes, and folded domains; activation often concentrates in N-terminal low-complexity leaders or propeptides.
Exemplars:
- Peroxisomal membrane protein PEX13: N-terminal Gly/Pro- and Tyr/Phe-punctuated low-complexity coil; off in TM and SH3 domain.
- Small heat shock protein (Hsp42): N-terminal IDR with Y/F/G/P motifs; off over the alpha-crystallin domain.
- Keratin-associated proteins and other extracellular structural proteins (e.g., caseins, chorion components): activation on Gly/Pro/Tyr-rich repeats.
- Plant HIPPs: activation on Pro/Tyr/Gly-rich low-complexity segments.
- Antimicrobial peptide precursors (e.g., clavanin) and allergens: activation on low-complexity signal/propeptides or IDRs that can be Pro/His-rich with occasional aromatics.
- Proline-rich salivary proteins (e.g., opiorphin/PRP1 precursors): activation on basic Pro-rich low-complexity stretches.
- Reproductive proteins including protamine/protamine-like: activation on simple Arg/Lys-rich low-complexity segments or cleaved propeptides when present.

Summary: Basic polycationic patches enriched in arginine (often with lysine) within low-complexity/disordered regions, frequently N-terminal. These include classical monopartite NLSs, nucleic acid–binding basic tails, signal peptide n-regions and cytosolic juxtamembrane segments (positive-inside rule), and basic clusters in secreted precursors; typically depleted of acidic residues.
Activation pattern: Regional activation with strong residue-level peaks across contiguous basic runs; N-terminal bias; minimal Asp/Glu, Arg>Lys preference; predominantly in low-pLDDT segments and outside/adjacent to transmembranes on the cytosolic side; observed across viruses, bacteria, plants, and humans.
Exemplars:
- Viral regulators and capsid/accessory proteins: arginine-rich NLSs and nucleic acid–binding basic tails.
- Human regulators (e.g., ARF/Killin): arginine-rich disordered N-termini for targeting/interactions.
- Secreted zymogens and peptides (e.g., trypsinogen/PROPEPs): basic n-regions/dibasic clusters in pre/pro-sequences.
- Membrane proteins (transporters, respiratory chain subunits like ND2, ECF S-components): cytosolic basic patches consistent with the positive-inside rule.

Summary: Residue positions that mark polypeptide boundaries—especially the absolute N-terminus (position 1) and the terminal residue of sequence fragments—and, secondarily, isolated boundary-like sites within larger proteins (e.g., short linkers between secondary-structure elements or helix/turn cap-like positions), consistent with proteolytic processing junctions in pre/propeptides.
Activation pattern: Predominantly single-residue peaks at sequence extremities (most often the first residue; also the last residue of fragments); sparse internal single-residue peaks at boundary-like positions (short linkers or transitions between secondary structures). Often coincides with disordered/low-confidence termini; in secreted/toxin precursors a recurring window around residues ~50–70 is consistent with signal/propeptide cleavage. Per-protein activations are usually one or a few sites.
Exemplars: Snake venom serine protease: peaks at the N-terminal first residue and at the C-terminal end of the chain; Nuclear pore complex protein Nup155: isolated peaks on single residues within a helix and a low-confidence turn; U4/U6.U5 tri-snRNP–associated protein 1: single-residue peak at a glycine linker between β-strands; E4 ubiquitin-conjugation factor (UBE4): isolated methionine within a long α-helix; Reelin (fragment): strong activation at the fragment’s C-terminal residue in a disordered region; Glutamate dehydrogenase (fragment): activation marks the truncated C-terminal residue.

Summary: Compositionally biased low-complexity segments, especially N-terminal hydrophobic helices that form the hydrophobic core of signal peptides or membrane-anchoring amphipathic helices, and serine/threonine-rich intrinsically disordered tracts; the feature reflects sequence-composition bias rather than a specific fold or function and commonly occurs at protein termini across taxa
Activation pattern: Regional activation over extended contiguous blocks (typically 8–20 residues), frequently at the N-terminus; strong peaks within hydrophobic cores of signal peptide–like helices or within S/T-rich low-complexity patches; minimal activation in structured catalytic/core domains
Exemplars: - Viral nonstructural/accessory proteins: activation on a short, flexible N-terminal hydrophobic helix (amphipathic/membrane-anchoring segment).

- Eukaryotic transcriptional coactivator scaffolds (Mediator subunit 24): activation on multiple S/T- and Q-rich intrinsically disordered, low-complexity regions.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity regions enriched in serine, threonine, proline and polar/charged residues—flexible regulatory linkers/tails and propeptide segments that often host short linear motifs (e.g., phosphorylation- and proline‑rich motifs) and proteolytic processing sites; signal is absent from well‑folded catalytic domains and is common across taxa
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long disordered stretches with many sparse residue‑level peaks; avoids structured domains; peaks biased toward S/T/P, glycine, and charged/polar residues; frequently concentrated in N‑ or C‑terminal IDRs and around cleavage/processing sites; can span hundreds of residues in large eukaryotic proteins
Exemplars: - PAK family serine/threonine kinases: activation on the N‑terminal regulatory IDR preceding the kinase domain (including low‑confidence helical propensities), not in the folded kinase domain.
- Rap/Ras GTPase‑activating proteins: activation on disordered, low‑complexity linkers; absent from the structured GAP domain.
- CARMIL (actin/capping protein regulators): activation on a C‑terminal proline/basic‑rich disordered tail.
- Centrosomal/kinetochore and chromosomal scaffold proteins: multiple low‑complexity, disordered tracts with scattered peaks.
- Transcriptional/chromatin regulators: activation on N‑terminal low‑complexity/activation domains and compositionally biased regions.
- Ribonucleotide reductase large subunit‑like proteins: activation on N‑terminal disordered tails, including proline‑rich segments.
- Neuropeptide/prohormone precursors: activation in disordered propeptides and at termini of amidated peptides, often adjacent to cleavage sites.

Summary: Amphipathic, hydrophobic secondary‑structure cores in small proteins—especially alpha‑helical segments and the juxtamembrane/N‑terminal half of signal‑anchor transmembrane helices with a positive‑inside (Lys/Arg) bias; in soluble proteins, the analogous β‑α/helix bundle core often at oligomerization interfaces—while avoiding disordered tails and catalytic/loop regions
Activation pattern: Regional activation over long, contiguous, high‑confidence secondary‑structure elements (helices and β‑α segments); strongest in ordered cores, weak/absent in disordered termini and peripheral loops; in bitopic membrane proteins, peaks at the cytosolic amphipathic helix and the N‑proximal half of the TM helix (positive‑inside), tapering toward the extracytosolic half

- Exodeoxyribonuclease VII small subunit: strong signal on the central ordered helix bundle, with little/no activation on disordered N/C‑terminal regions.
- ATP synthase and respiratory chain small membrane subunits: enrichment on N‑terminal amphipathic/juxtamembrane helices and the entry half of signal‑anchor TM segments.
- Small ribosomal proteins and other RNA/protein‑binding regulators: activation on amphipathic helical cores that present Lys/Arg‑rich faces, rather than on flexible/basic tails.

- Eukaryotic coiled‑coil proteins: activation along coiled‑coil helical segments constituting the stable structural core.

Activation pattern: Regional activation with strong residue-level peaks across contiguous basic runs; N-terminal bias; minimal Asp/Glu, Arg>Lys preference; predominantly in low-pLDDT segments and outside/adjacent to transmembranes on the cytosolic side; observed across viruses, bacteria, plants, and humans.
Exemplars:
- Viral regulators and capsid/accessory proteins: arginine-rich NLSs and nucleic acid–binding basic tails.

Summary: Long, low‑complexity Q/N‑rich tracts (poly‑asparagine and poly‑glutamine) in eukaryotic proteins—typically intrinsically disordered terminal or linker regions and compositionally biased coiled‑coil segments—lying outside structured catalytic/recognition domains; especially prevalent in Dictyostelium (and similar N‑rich proteomes).
Activation pattern: Regional activation across extended, compositionally biased blocks with dense N (and Q) runs; sustained high activation over tens of residues with residue‑level peaks on homopolymeric N/Q. Little to no activation in well‑folded domains (kinase cores, DNA‑binding folds, TM helices, ABC NBDs, zinc fingers); when present within a domain boundary, it coincides with a low‑confidence, low‑complexity insert. Often concentrated in N/C‑terminal tails and inter‑domain linkers; can include Q/N‑rich coiled‑coil segments.
Exemplars: - Alpha‑type protein kinase with Arf‑GAP regulator: strong activation on multiple polyQ and polyN tracts (including Q‑rich coiled‑coils) outside the Arf‑GAP and kinase domains.
- Hybrid histidine kinase (PAS–HisKA–RR two‑component‑like): activation on N‑ and Q‑rich disordered linkers; absent from PAS, HisKA, and response‑regulator domains.
- Homeobox transcription factor: activation confined to N‑rich low‑complexity segments; absent from the folded homeobox DNA‑binding domain.
- Rho GTPase‑activating protein (RhoGAP): activation on asparagine‑rich low‑complexity regions (notably a C‑terminal polyN tract); no activation in the MYND zinc finger or RhoGAP catalytic domain.
- Sirtuin (NAD‑dependent deacetylase): activation on extensive C‑terminal N‑rich disordered regions and a short N‑run insert with low structural confidence; not on the structured catalytic core.
- Diacylglycerol kinase: activation on asparagine‑rich disordered segments in the C‑terminus; not in C1 zinc fingers or the DAGK catalytic domain.
- ABC transporter (ABCB7‑like): activation on N‑rich disordered N‑ and C‑terminal tails; absent from transmembrane helices and the cytosolic ABC nucleotide‑binding domain.

Activation pattern: Predominantly single-residue peaks at sequence extremities (most often the first residue; also the last residue of fragments); sparse internal single-residue peaks at boundary-like positions (short linkers or transitions between secondary structures). Often coincides with disordered/low-confidence termini; in secreted/toxin precursors a recurring window around residues ~50–70 is consistent with signal/propeptide cleavage. Per-protein activations are usually one or a few sites.
