Summary: Extracellular/cell-surface secretome signature: the feature recognizes ectodomains of secreted or surface-presented proteins, especially cysteine-rich, disulfide-stabilized peptides and repeats (e.g., toxins, EGF/disintegrin/adhesion modules, lectins), C-terminal regions surrounding GPI-anchor attachment sites, and also short exofacial loops of multi-pass membrane proteins when these loops are cysteine- and/or glycan-rich; it captures appended extracellular carbohydrate-binding modules of secreted CAZymes
Activation pattern: Primarily regional/domain-level activation over long, contiguous stretches of extracellular sequence (often at protein termini), with residue-level peaks near Cys clusters and adjacent residues (aromatics/Pro/Ser/Thr); frequently highest around the GPI omega site and drops within cleaved C-terminal propeptides; can cover complete mature secreted peptide chains or selectively highlight appended extracellular modules (e.g., CBMs) rather than catalytic cores; additionally, can mark short exofacial loops (not necessarily at termini) in multi-pass transporters when they contain Cys–Cys/Cys-x(n)–Cys or NXS/T glycosylation motifs
Exemplars: Trypanosome variant surface glycoproteins (VSGs) – strong activation across the disordered C-terminal GPI-anchor region, peaking at the omega site and disappearing in the cleaved propeptide; Ciliate mating pheromones – activation across the mature secreted cystine-rich peptide with peaks at N-terminal aromatic residues and reduced signal on disulfide-bonded cysteines; Secreted carbohydrate-active enzymes – activation on C-terminal CBM10 carbohydrate-binding modules and adjacent helices, not on the catalytic cores; Disulfide-rich venom peptides and Kunitz/other protease inhibitors – extended activation across the mature, disulfide-stabilized chains; Viral envelope/entry glycoproteins – activation on cysteine-rich ectodomain loops; EGF-like/disintegrin/adhesion modules and lectins – activation on cysteine-constrained extracellular repeats/domains; SLC/GLUT-family transporters – activation on short extracellular loops bearing conserved disulfide-bonded cysteines and glycosylation sites

Summary: Extracellular cysteine‑rich, disulfide‑stabilized repeat modules—chiefly EGF/EGF‑like domains (including calcium‑binding variants) and related TNFR cysteine‑rich domains and LDLR class A (LA) repeats—recognized via their conserved disulfide framework and short beta‑strand cores in receptor ectodomains and secreted factors
Activation pattern: Domain/repeat‑module recognition with multiple short activated windows across tandem repeats; residue‑level peaks on disulfide‑forming cysteines and immediately adjacent positions (often beta‑strand and acidic residues characteristic of calcium‑coordinating motifs); minimal to none in signal peptides, transmembrane helices, cytosolic tails, and unrelated structured domains (e.g., YWTD beta‑propellers, catalytic metalloprotease cores)
Exemplars: - TNF receptor family: strong activation along extracellular TNFR cysteine‑rich repeats (CRDs); off in transmembrane and death domains
- LDL receptor family: sharp peaks in EGF‑like domains and moderate signal across LA repeats; off in the YWTD beta‑propeller, O‑glycosylated linker, transmembrane, and cytosolic tail
- ADAM/tolloid metalloproteases: activation confined to the ancillary EGF‑like domain; catalytic peptidase motifs silent
- Notch/Delta receptors: activation across tandem EGF‑like repeats in the ectodomain
- Complement and coagulation factors: activation on their EGF/EGF‑like modules within extracellular precursors
- Adhesion GPCRs: activation on long N‑terminal ectodomains containing EGF‑like/CRD modules
- Viral growth factors and EGF‑like toxins: activation on short cysteine‑clustered EGF‑like modules

Summary: Low-acidity, Ser/Thr- and Arg-rich intrinsically disordered low-complexity segments, most often at protein N-termini, that function as targeting leaders (mitochondrial/chloroplast transit peptides; host-/secretion-translocation motifs such as RxLR/PEXEL) or as non-export regulatory/processing modules (NLS-like/basic tails, phosphorylation/O-glycosylation hotspots), and that can also occur as internal acidic-poor LCRs.
Activation pattern: Predominant extended activation at the extreme N-terminus (20–100+ aa) with Ser/Thr/Arg enrichment and Asp/Glu depletion; activation may also occur at internal acidic-poor, Ser/Thr/Arg-rich low-complexity stretches; in secreted/viral proteins it can extend into cysteine-rich or mucin-like regions; includes type II membrane proteins with basic cytosolic N-termini lacking cleavable presequences.
Exemplars:
- Plant chloroplast-targeted proteins: activation on acidic-poor Ser/Thr-rich transit peptides.
- Eukaryotic mitochondrial proteins: activation on Arg/Ser/Thr-rich presequences; type II outer-membrane proteins (e.g., metaxin-like) show basic/Ser/Thr-rich cytosolic N-termini without a cleavable presequence.
- Oomycete RxLR effectors: activation on the secretory leader/host-translocation region after the signal peptide.
- Viral envelope/accessory, nuclear egress, and NSs proteins: activation on NLS-like/basic or mucin-like Ser/Thr-rich segments.
- Small secreted peptides/toxins/hormone precursors: activation near dibasic convertase sites and adjacent basic/Ser/Thr-rich tracks, even if the broader propeptide is acidic.
- Cytosolic/housekeeping enzymes: activation on short acidic-poor Ser/Thr-/Arg-rich N-terminal or internal disordered segments serving as PTM-rich regulatory regions.

Summary: Cysteine-centered motifs (single conserved Cys or short CC/CXC/CXXC clusters), often—but not exclusively—found in oxidizing/extracellular or periplasmic contexts, used for disulfide bonding, redox catalysis, metal/Fe–S coordination, or regulatory thiol switches. The feature captures a generic “cysteine presence/cluster” signal near N-termini or in disordered loops across diverse proteins, including cytosolic and nuclear factors.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks centered on cysteines; strongest when two or more Cys occur within 0–2 residues (CC/CXC/CXXC) and frequently just after signal or transit peptide cleavage. Moderate peaks also occur at single conserved cysteines in disordered/low-complexity segments or coiled coils, regardless of subcellular location.
Exemplars:
- Chemokines (CC/CXC): activation on the signature N-terminal CC/CXC motif.
- Defensin-like antimicrobial peptides and disulfide-rich toxins (cystine-knot, conotoxins): activation across tightly clustered cysteines.
- Extracellular disulfide domains (Kazal/Kunitz, EGF-like): activation on paired disulfide-forming cysteines.
- Thiol–disulfide oxidoreductases (DsbA, PDI, thioredoxin): activation on catalytic CXXC motifs.
- Membrane proteins/transporters (ABC transporters, channels): activation on cysteines in luminal/extracytosolic/periplasmic loops or near processed N-termini.
- Fe–S/metal-binding proteins (rubredoxin, assembly factors): activation on closely spaced cysteines that coordinate cofactors.
- Cytosolic/nuclear regulators (e.g., BH3-only proteins like PUMA; viral early proteins such as adenovirus E4-ORF6): activation on a single Cys or short CC/CXC in disordered regions.
- Housekeeping enzymes and ribosomal/translation proteins (e.g., tRNA methyltransferases, FAD synthase, mitochondrial ribosomal proteins): activation on incidental CC/CXC or conserved single cysteines that may mediate local redox/metal interactions.

Summary: Short, intrinsically disordered C‑terminal tails of secreted or membrane‑associated proteins (from microproteins to larger multi‑pass enzymes) and viral accessory microproteins, typically low‑complexity and enriched in proline and basic residues, often immediately downstream of a hydrophobic signal/transmembrane segment; can include cysteine‑rich patches in secreted/toxin peptides.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over contiguous 10–30 aa windows, most frequently at the extreme C‑terminus; often spans a brief helix that transitions into coil with peak signal in the disordered coil; commonly adjacent to a hydrophobic (signal/TM) segment and characterized by low pLDDT; can also occur in short cytosolic juxtamembrane loops of larger multi‑pass proteins.
Exemplars:
- Oomycete RxLR secreted effectors: activation on the C‑terminal tail immediately following a predicted hydrophobic segment, in a low‑confidence helix/coil region.
- Human ST20 (apoptosis/stress‑related microprotein): activation on a short C‑terminal helix‑to‑coil, highly disordered stretch.
- Small uncharacterized microproteins: activation confined to the last ~10–15 residues forming a disordered coil tail.
- Viral accessory/viroporin‑like proteins: activation on basic/proline‑rich cytosolic C‑tails adjacent to a single‑pass TM helix; also applies to non‑TM viral accessory proteins with disordered C‑tails (e.g., Vif).
- Small secreted cysteine‑rich toxins/defensin‑like peptides: activation on short cationic/cysteine‑biased segments within the mature or processing tail.
- ATP synthase epsilon subunits: activation on a conserved, short, disordered C‑terminal regulatory segment in these small mitochondrial/bacterial proteins.
- Multi‑pass membrane enzymes (e.g., phytoene dehydrogenase): activation on short cytosolic C‑terminal or juxtamembrane tails adjacent to TM helices.

Summary: Short hydrophobic alpha-helical segments enriched in small aliphatic residues (A, V, I, L with frequent T/G), depleted of charged/aromatic residues—commonly the h‑region of Sec signal peptides, short transmembrane helices, and internal helix-forming hydrophobic patches in both membrane and soluble proteins; often N‑terminal but also internal/C‑terminal.
Activation pattern: Regional activation on contiguous hydrophobic clusters predicted as alpha‑helix, with sharp residue‑level peaks at A/V/I/L/T (often with G); observed in signal peptides, TM segments, and internal helices; occurs in both structured and disordered contexts (not restricted to low pLDDT).
Exemplars: Adenovirus E4‑ORF4 and HCV ARFP: internal hydrophobic helix‑prone stretches in small viral proteins; Oomycete RxLR effectors and yeast killer toxin precursors: strong activation on N‑terminal Sec signal peptides; Bacterial cytochrome c oxidase subunit 2 and DHHC palmitoyltransferases: activation on short transmembrane helices; Kdo transferase and OMA hydratase: activation on internal hydrophobic helices within soluble/peripheral membrane enzymes.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low-complexity segments enriched in small polar residues (Ser/Thr/Gly, often with Pro), typically found in N-terminal tails and flexible loops across diverse proteins (including viral proteins, secreted/effectors, membrane proteins, and transporter ATPase subunits), and largely absent from the well-folded cores of catalytic domains.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long, low-pLDDT stretches with residue-level peaks on S and G (secondarily T); frequently concentrated near N-termini but can occur throughout disordered regions; generally absent from well-folded cores yet can appear in short low-complexity termini or loop insertions within otherwise structured enzymes and ATPases; occasionally a single high peak on an isolated glycine in an otherwise structured protein.
Exemplars: Bacterial acetyl-CoA synthetase: strong activation on S/G/T within an N-terminal low-complexity, disordered segment, none in the structured enzyme core; Telomere-binding regulatory protein: scattered S/T activations confined to very low-confidence, coil-like regions; Viral non-structural/accessory protein: widespread activation on S and G across a globally disordered protein; Membrane/transport system components: S/G/T peaks in low-confidence extra-/intracellular loops and in flexible regions of soluble ATPase subunits; Cytosolic metabolic enzyme (e.g., HGPRT): localized activation limited to short disordered termini or low-complexity insertions.

Summary: Secreted, propeptide‑processed cysteine‑rich mini‑domains: compact extracellular segments immediately downstream of a signal peptide that contain clustered cysteines forming multiple disulfide bonds (defensin/CSαβ, WAP four‑disulfide core, cystine‑knot/knottin, CHH‑like, evasin‑like, and related small CRP scaffolds), often flanked by dibasic convertase sites and enriched in Lys/Arg
Activation pattern: Regional activation on short segments (≈20–60 aa) right after the signal peptide; strong peaks on cysteines and nearby basic residues, frequently overlapping proprotein convertase (dibasic) processing motifs; may recur for multi‑domain or repeat CRP proteins
Exemplars: - WAP/four‑disulfide core protease inhibitors (SLPI/elafin/WFDC): activation on the WAP domain’s Cys framework following the signal/propeptide
- Plant defensin‑like peptides (DEFL/LURE/ESF) and thionins: activation on the mature antimicrobial CSαβ cysteine motif
- Venom cystine‑knot peptides (conotoxins/knottins, mini‑toxins): activation on the canonical Cys frameworks in the mature toxin region of prepropeptides
- Tick evasins (chemokine‑binding CRPs): activation on the Cys‑rich chemokine‑binding domain
- Crustacean CHH/MIH neuropeptide precursors: activation on the mature hormone core with conserved six‑Cys motif adjacent to dibasic cleavage
- Fungal GPI‑anchored cell‑wall adhesins/stress proteins: activation on extracellular Cys‑rich segments just after secretion signals
- Small plant CRP protease inhibitors: activation on the disulfide‑stabilized inhibitory mini‑domain

Summary: Extracellular/cell-surface secretome signature: the feature recognizes ectodomains of secreted or surface-presented proteins, especially cysteine-rich, disulfide-stabilized peptides and repeats (e.g., toxins, EGF/disintegrin/adhesion modules, lectins), C-terminal regions surrounding GPI-anchor attachment sites, and also short exofacial loops of multi-pass membrane proteins when these loops are cysteine- and/or glycan-rich; it captures appended extracellular carbohydrate-binding modules of secreted CAZymes
Activation pattern: Primarily regional/domain-level activation over long, contiguous stretches of extracellular sequence (often at protein termini), with residue-level peaks near Cys clusters and adjacent residues (aromatics/Pro/Ser/Thr); frequently highest around the GPI omega site and drops within cleaved C-terminal propeptides; can cover complete mature secreted peptide chains or selectively highlight appended extracellular modules (e.g., CBMs) rather than catalytic cores; additionally, can mark short exofacial loops (not necessarily at termini) in multi-pass transporters when they contain Cys–Cys/Cys-x(n)–Cys or NXS/T glycosylation motifs
Exemplars: Trypanosome variant surface glycoproteins (VSGs) – strong activation across the disordered C-terminal GPI-anchor region, peaking at the omega site and disappearing in the cleaved propeptide; Ciliate mating pheromones – activation across the mature secreted cystine-rich peptide with peaks at N-terminal aromatic residues and reduced signal on disulfide-bonded cysteines; Secreted carbohydrate-active enzymes – activation on C-terminal CBM10 carbohydrate-binding modules and adjacent helices, not on the catalytic cores; Disulfide-rich venom peptides and Kunitz/other protease inhibitors – extended activation across the mature, disulfide-stabilized chains; Viral envelope/entry glycoproteins – activation on cysteine-rich ectodomain loops; EGF-like/disintegrin/adhesion modules and lectins – activation on cysteine-constrained extracellular repeats/domains; SLC/GLUT-family transporters – activation on short extracellular loops bearing conserved disulfide-bonded cysteines and glycosylation sites

Summary: Secreted, short cysteine-rich peptides and small extracellular cysteine-rich domains stabilized by multiple disulfide bonds (CRPs), spanning venom toxins, disintegrins, defensins/hepcidin, Kunitz/Kazal/hevein-like inhibitors/defense peptides, and related cystine‑knotted or cysteine‑stabilized folds. The feature captures the mature, proteolytically processed peptide/module characterized by clustered Cys (often CC motifs) and basic residues.
Activation pattern: Regional activation confined to short mature peptide segments (tens of residues) following the signal peptide and propeptides; minimal/absent on signal/pro-regions. Strong residue-level peaks on cysteines and frequent secondary peaks on Lys/Arg and Gly. Activation spans mixed secondary structure (β-strands, coils, short helices) and can include key functional loops (e.g., RGD in disintegrins).
Exemplars: - Plant cyclotides (cystine-knot cyclopeptides, e.g., chassatide): activation across the cyclic cystine‑knot core of the mature peptide after processing.
- Snake venom disintegrins: activation across the disintegrin domain, including the RGD integrin-binding loop and adjacent cysteine-dense core.
- Inhibitor cystine-knot (ICK) venom toxins from spiders, cone snails, centipedes, and sea anemones: activation on the disulfide‑knotted toxin core.
- Kunitz/BPTI- and Kazal-type serine protease inhibitors (including tick chemokine/complement inhibitors): activation on the small disulfide‑rich inhibitor domain.
- Hevein-like/seed defense peptides: activation on the cysteine-rich chitin‑binding hevein domain.
- Defensins (plant/fungal/animal CSαβ peptides) and vertebrate hepcidin: activation on the cysteine‑stabilized mature AMP region.
- Euplotes ciliate mating pheromones: activation on the secreted disulfide‑rich pheromone core.
- Cysteine-rich modules within large extracellular/mucin-like proteins: activation on the short, cysteine‑dense repeat/subdomain embedded in the larger precursor.

Summary: Extracellular Cys–Trp (CW/CGW) disulfide‑loop signature common to secreted and single‑pass cell‑surface proteins and small cystine‑rich peptides; the feature highlights cysteine- and aromatic‑enriched ectodomain motifs used in adhesion, receptor–ligand/contact interfaces, and immune‑evasion coats (e.g., VSGs, semaphorins/plexins, integrins, RTKs, viral envelope glycoproteins)
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks centered on C…W (often CW/CGW with nearby Tyr/Phe) within disulfide‑stabilized loops; regional activation across extracellular, cysteine‑rich segments; extended, domain‑length activation in VSG ectodomains but short motif‑focused peaks in most other proteins; generally in secreted/ectodomain regions, not in transmembranes or cytosolic tails
Exemplars: - Trypanosoma variant surface glycoproteins (VSGs): strong, continuous activation across the disulfide‑rich GPI‑anchored coat domain with repeated C…W/Aromatic patches.
- Semaphorin and plexin receptors: peaks at conserved CW/CGW sites in Sema/PSI ectodomains.
- Viral envelope/spike glycoproteins: activation on disulfide‑stabilized surface loops containing Cys–Trp and nearby aromatics.
- Integrin beta subunits: activation within extracellular PSI/I‑EGF repeats at CW/CGW motifs.
- Receptor tyrosine kinases and related single‑pass receptors: peaks on extracellular cysteine‑rich segments bearing CGW/CW signatures.
- Disulfide‑rich secreted peptides (toxins, cyclotides, defensins‑like): localized peaks where Trp neighbors disulfide‑bonded cysteines.
- Kinetoplastid hexose transporters: activation in extracellular loops containing the conserved C…W motif.
- Adhesion/glycocalyx components (e.g., mucins/proteoglycan core proteins): activation on cysteine/aromatic‑rich ectodomain motifs.

Summary: Sequence contexts marking disulfide-bonded cysteines in secreted/extracellular proteins—cysteine pairs/clusters (often flanked by Gly/Pro) that form stabilizing disulfide frameworks typical of toxins, antimicrobial peptides, protease inhibitors, neuropeptide/hormone/pheromone peptides, and viral envelope ectodomains.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks at or immediately adjacent to disulfide-bonded cysteines; compact, contiguous activation across the cystine framework in short disulfide-rich peptides; multiple peaks scattered across ectodomains of large secreted glycoproteins; minimal activation in signal peptides, transmembranes, or cytosolic regions.
Exemplars: - AB toxins (pertussis toxin B subunit): peaks next to disulfide-forming cysteines within the mature chain.
- Venom disulfide-rich toxins (conotoxins; scorpion α/β-toxins; spider ω/κ-toxins): activation tracks the canonical Cys frameworks.
- Defensins and other CSαβ antimicrobial peptides: activation on the conserved disulfide pairs.
- Kunitz- and Kazal-type serine protease inhibitors: peaks around the conserved disulfide-bonded cysteines stabilizing the inhibitory fold.
- Neuropeptide hormones/pheromones with intrachain/interchain disulfides (e.g., insulin family, oxytocin/vasopressin): activation at the disulfide-forming Cys and neighboring Gly/Pro.
- Viral envelope glycoproteins: multiple peaks across ectodomain cysteine clusters and Cys–Gly/Pro motifs.
- Secreted nematode extracellular/ECM-associated cysteine-rich proteins: activation over disulfide-stabilized modules.

Summary: Non-LTR retrotransposon ORF2/Pol C-terminal RNA-binding regions, with additional firing in short N-terminal or internal low-complexity stretches of other proteins.
Activation pattern: Broad activation across the C-terminal RNA-binding segment of LINE-1 / R2-type retrotransposon ORF2 proteins, with strongest residue-level peaks landing on short helix/turn elements within that region; in unrelated proteins, sparse residue-level peaks appear in short N-terminal or low-complexity stretches.
Exemplars:
- Human and mouse LINE-1 ORF2p: dense activation throughout the carboxy-terminal RNA-binding segment, peaking on a short turn/helix cluster.
- Drosophila R2DM retrotransposon Pol polyprotein: peaks in a C-terminal Cys/His-containing stretch outside the reverse transcriptase domain.
- Mitochondrial transcription termination factor 1 (mTERF1): peaks in the N-terminal mitochondrial transit peptide.
- Cilia- and flagella-associated protein 61 (CFAP61): a short internal cluster of peaks in a low-complexity region.

Summary: Primary recognition of RNase H–like, Mg2+-dependent phosphodiesterase/nuclease domains (DEDD catalytic architecture) and their peri‑catalytic structural environment, with a secondary tendency to mark single-pass signal‑anchor/targeting helices in membranes
Activation pattern: Strong, contiguous domain-level activation over RNase H-type domains (often C‑terminal in viral Pol); in standalone RNase HI, heightened signal on adjacent loops/strands while catalytic acidic residues can be suppressed; in other hydrolase/metalloenzyme and protease domains, sharp residue-level peaks near catalytic or metal-binding motifs within well-structured elements; in membrane/secreted proteins, continuous peaks across a single transmembrane signal-anchor helix or the N‑terminal targeting peptide, with occasional isolated peaks elsewhere
Exemplars: - Retroviral Pol reverse transcriptase/RNase H: broad activation spanning the RNase H type‑1 domain, including the canonical metal-binding D/E residues, tapering into flanking linkers.
- Bacterial RNase HI: selective peaks on loops flanking the DEDD metal-binding site (e.g., K13–P15, A38–F42, K74), with the catalytic Asp/Glu themselves de-emphasized.
- EAL-type cyclic di‑GMP phosphodiesterases: localized peak within the EAL catalytic domain (coil between helices).
- Carbonic anhydrases: short, well-structured helical/coil segment in the C‑terminal portion of the catalytic domain.
- HtrA/Omi serine protease: single peak on a β‑strand immediately preceding a helix bearing active-site and zinc‑binding residues.
- MS4A/CD20 family multipass receptors: multiple peaks concentrated in TM3–TM4, including the highest signal within TM4.
- Ceramide synthase (TLC domain): single peak at a glycine within a predicted transmembrane helix of the catalytic region.
- Type II serine protease (TMPRSS family): strong, continuous activation across the N‑terminal signal‑anchor transmembrane helix and a sharp peak adjacent to the catalytic Asp in the S1 peptidase domain.
- Mitochondrial transcription termination factor: exclusive activation of the N‑terminal mitochondrial transit peptide starting at the initiator methionine, absent on the mature folded domain.

Summary: Short Cys/His-based metal-binding microdomains—especially Zn-coordinating fingers/ribbons (SWIM, ArfGAP C4, primase zinc-binding domain) and Cys4 Fe-S cluster sites—and their immediate flanking helix/strand context, most often in nucleic-acid–associated proteins
Activation pattern: Predominantly one localized stretch (tens of residues) per protein. Signal starts within the Cys/His motif and extends a few residues into the following helix/strand/loop, often peaking on non-ligating neighbors (e.g., Gly/Ser) or the first turn/strand after the motif; elsewhere only sparse single-residue peaks appear.
Exemplars: - SWIM zinc-finger proteins (ZSWIM family; plant FAR1-related sequence): strong, domain-length activation over the SWIM motif.
- DnaG-type primases and helicase–primases: N-terminal zinc-binding primase ZBD (around residues 47–85), with the peak just beyond the Cys/His-rich motif.
- WhiB/Wbl 4Fe-4S transcriptional regulators: activation across the Cys4 Fe-S–binding stretch and adjacent helices.
- ArfGAP GTPase-activating proteins: localized activation at the C-terminal C4 zinc finger within the ArfGAP domain.
- TnpB RNA-guided endonucleases: activation at a Cys-containing CPNC zinc-binding motif and residues surrounding the catalytic Asp.
- Additional weak/sparse matches: isolated residues in a tubulin glycylase loop, a single transmembrane-helix residue in an ABC transporter, and the C-terminal RNA-binding segment of LINE-1 ORF2.

Summary: A helix-boundary/hinge signal: the feature fires on single small or aromatic residues—most often glycine—that mark entry/exit or kinks of alpha helices (especially transmembrane helices) and other short structural junctions, and it also highlights N‑terminal organellar transit peptides as extended amphipathic-helical segments; analogous single-residue junctions at processing/splicing sites (e.g., intein boundaries) are likewise detected.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks at helix starts (N1–N2) or glycine kinks within helices (common in TM segments); occasional 1–2‑residue peaks immediately C‑terminal to the last TM; extended N‑terminal runs across mitochondrial/chloroplast transit peptides; sporadic peaks at short coil hinges between secondary-structure elements.
Exemplars: - Peptidase A1 aspartic proteases (secreted/vacuolar): single conserved glycine in a C‑lobe loop→helix junction (non-catalytic hinge).
- Formate–nitrite transporters (FNT): single glycine within a transmembrane helix consistent with a helix kink/packing site.
- Plant DETOX/MATE-family transporters: first residues at the N‑termini of TM helices.
- P‑type Cu‑transporting ATPases: small residue in a short coil between adjacent secondary-structure elements (local hinge).
- ZDHHC palmitoyltransferases: 1–2 residues immediately after the final TM helix in the flexible C‑terminal tail.
- Mitochondrial transcription termination factors and PPR RNA-processing proteins: strong, regional activation across the N‑terminal organellar transit peptide only.
- Undecaprenyl-diphosphatases (BacA/UppP): conserved glycine around positions 160–173 within the membrane domain.
- Intein-containing archaeal/bacterial enzymes: a single glycine at/near the intein–extein splice junction.
- Desumoylating isopeptidases (PPPDE family): small N‑terminal residues near the catalytic region/helix cap.
- Additional secondary transporters (e.g., SLC6): helix-boundary anchors (often Gly/Trp/Ile/Val) at membrane interfaces.
- Reverse transcriptases/retroelements/transposase-derived factors: small/aromatic hotspots (often W/G) in flexible or helical-boundary segments.

Summary: Broad, diffuse activation across long stretches of protein sequence, with the strongest peaks landing on individual residues within α-helical regions and adjacent loops. Peak residues are predominantly hydrophobic or aromatic (F, L, I, V, A, W, G) with occasional charged residues, often clustered near disordered or compositionally biased segments of the protein.
Activation pattern: The feature is broadly active, with a large fraction of residues showing nonzero activation in each protein. The highest-activation peaks tend to fall in α-helices and the residues flanking them, frequently in proteins containing reverse transcriptase domains or short disordered/charged segments.
Exemplars:
- LINE-1 and related retrotransposon ORF2 proteins: highest peaks on hydrophobic residues within α-helical regions C-terminal to the reverse transcriptase domain.
- ATP synthase F1 epsilon subunit: peaks on residues within the central α-helices of the small subunit.
- Anaphase-promoting complex subunit emb-1 (C. elegans): broad activation across the small chain with peaks on His and adjacent residues near the C-terminus.
- Influenza PB1-F2: activation through the C-terminal region overlapping the mitochondrial targeting sequence.

Exemplars: Trypanosome variant surface glycoproteins (VSGs) – strong activation across the disordered C-terminal GPI-anchor region, peaking at the omega site and disappearing in the cleaved propeptide; Ciliate mating pheromones – activation across the mature secreted cystine-rich peptide with peaks at N-terminal aromatic residues and reduced signal on disulfide-bonded cysteines; Secreted carbohydrate-active enzymes – activation on C-terminal CBM10 carbohydrate-binding modules and adjacent helices, not on the catalytic cores; Disulfide-rich venom peptides and Kunitz/other protease inhibitors – extended activation across the mature, disulfide-stabilized chains; Viral envelope/entry glycoproteins – activation on cysteine-rich ectodomain loops; EGF-like/disintegrin/adhesion modules and lectins – activation on cysteine-constrained extracellular repeats/domains; SLC/GLUT-family transporters – activation on short extracellular loops bearing conserved disulfide-bonded cysteines and glycosylation sites

Summary: Extracellular Cys–Trp (CW/CGW) disulfide‑loop signature common to secreted and single‑pass cell‑surface proteins and small cystine‑rich peptides; the feature highlights cysteine- and aromatic‑enriched ectodomain motifs used in adhesion, receptor–ligand/contact interfaces, and immune‑evasion coats (e.g., VSGs, semaphorins/plexins, integrins, RTKs, viral envelope glycoproteins)
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks centered on C…W (often CW/CGW with nearby Tyr/Phe) within disulfide‑stabilized loops; regional activation across extracellular, cysteine‑rich segments; extended, domain‑length activation in VSG ectodomains but short motif‑focused peaks in most other proteins; generally in secreted/ectodomain regions, not in transmembranes or cytosolic tails
Exemplars: - Trypanosoma variant surface glycoproteins (VSGs): strong, continuous activation across the disulfide‑rich GPI‑anchored coat domain with repeated C…W/Aromatic patches.
- Semaphorin and plexin receptors: peaks at conserved CW/CGW sites in Sema/PSI ectodomains.
- Viral envelope/spike glycoproteins: activation on disulfide‑stabilized surface loops containing Cys–Trp and nearby aromatics.
- Integrin beta subunits: activation within extracellular PSI/I‑EGF repeats at CW/CGW motifs.
- Receptor tyrosine kinases and related single‑pass receptors: peaks on extracellular cysteine‑rich segments bearing CGW/CW signatures.
- Disulfide‑rich secreted peptides (toxins, cyclotides, defensins‑like): localized peaks where Trp neighbors disulfide‑bonded cysteines.
- Kinetoplastid hexose transporters: activation in extracellular loops containing the conserved C…W motif.
- Adhesion/glycocalyx components (e.g., mucins/proteoglycan core proteins): activation on cysteine/aromatic‑rich ectodomain motifs.

Summary: Secreted, propeptide‑processed cysteine‑rich mini‑domains: compact extracellular segments immediately downstream of a signal peptide that contain clustered cysteines forming multiple disulfide bonds (defensin/CSαβ, WAP four‑disulfide core, cystine‑knot/knottin, CHH‑like, evasin‑like, and related small CRP scaffolds), often flanked by dibasic convertase sites and enriched in Lys/Arg
Activation pattern: Regional activation on short segments (≈20–60 aa) right after the signal peptide; strong peaks on cysteines and nearby basic residues, frequently overlapping proprotein convertase (dibasic) processing motifs; may recur for multi‑domain or repeat CRP proteins
Exemplars: - WAP/four‑disulfide core protease inhibitors (SLPI/elafin/WFDC): activation on the WAP domain’s Cys framework following the signal/propeptide
- Plant defensin‑like peptides (DEFL/LURE/ESF) and thionins: activation on the mature antimicrobial CSαβ cysteine motif
- Venom cystine‑knot peptides (conotoxins/knottins, mini‑toxins): activation on the canonical Cys frameworks in the mature toxin region of prepropeptides

Summary: Extracellular/cell-surface secretome signature: the feature recognizes ectodomains of secreted or surface-presented proteins, especially cysteine-rich, disulfide-stabilized peptides and repeats (e.g., toxins, EGF/disintegrin/adhesion modules, lectins), C-terminal regions surrounding GPI-anchor attachment sites, and also short exofacial loops of multi-pass membrane proteins when these loops are cysteine- and/or glycan-rich; it captures appended extracellular carbohydrate-binding modules of secreted CAZymes

Summary: Extracellular Cys–Trp (CW/CGW) disulfide‑loop signature common to secreted and single‑pass cell‑surface proteins and small cystine‑rich peptides; the feature highlights cysteine- and aromatic‑enriched ectodomain motifs used in adhesion, receptor–ligand/contact interfaces, and immune‑evasion coats (e.g., VSGs, semaphorins/plexins, integrins, RTKs, viral envelope glycoproteins)

- Viral envelope/spike glycoproteins: activation on disulfide‑stabilized surface loops containing Cys–Trp and nearby aromatics.
- Integrin beta subunits: activation within extracellular PSI/I‑EGF repeats at CW/CGW motifs.
- Receptor tyrosine kinases and related single‑pass receptors: peaks on extracellular cysteine‑rich segments bearing CGW/CW signatures.
- Disulfide‑rich secreted peptides (toxins, cyclotides, defensins‑like): localized peaks where Trp neighbors disulfide‑bonded cysteines.
- Kinetoplastid hexose transporters: activation in extracellular loops containing the conserved C…W motif.
- Adhesion/glycocalyx components (e.g., mucins/proteoglycan core proteins): activation on cysteine/aromatic‑rich ectodomain motifs.

Summary: Sequence contexts marking disulfide-bonded cysteines in secreted/extracellular proteins—cysteine pairs/clusters (often flanked by Gly/Pro) that form stabilizing disulfide frameworks typical of toxins, antimicrobial peptides, protease inhibitors, neuropeptide/hormone/pheromone peptides, and viral envelope ectodomains.

Summary: Mature secreted bioactive peptide module from preproproteins—especially cysteine‑rich, disulfide‑bonded and/or cyclic toxins, antimicrobial/defense peptides, and pheromone/inhibitory peptides. Activation pattern: Domain-level activation over a contiguous region that begins at or just after the signal/leader cleavage site and spans the entire mature peptide; minimal/absent on N‑terminal signal peptides and most propeptide segments. Activation is broad across secondary-structure types (helix, strand, coil) and present in both compact disulfide-stabilized folds and disordered bioactive tails; individual cysteines are not uniquely required or maximally peaked.
Exemplars: - Conotoxins (venom peptides): strong activation confined to the mature conotoxin; no activation on signal/propeptide.
- Plant cyclotides (defensin-like, head-to-tail cyclic): activation exactly across the cyclized mature peptide region.
- Fungal defensins (e.g., plectasin): activation across the mature defensin domain; absent on signal/propeptide.
- Bacterial heat-stable enterotoxin II: high activation on the mature toxin peptide; none on the signal peptide.
- Fungal/yeast killer toxins (KP4 family): activation across the mature secreted toxin chain; not on the signal peptide.
- Plant cyclopeptides (e.g., pumilarin precursor): activation restricted to the annotated cyclopeptide region.
- Gram-positive peptide pheromones/inhibitors (Rap phosphatase inhibitor propeptide): activation on the C‑terminal disordered bioactive peptide segment produced by processing.

Summary: Recognition of the N‑terminal signal peptide—specifically the hydrophobic h‑region and its C‑terminal boundary (h→c transition) around the signal peptidase cleavage site—in secreted and secretory‑pathway proteins (including soluble factors and single‑pass receptors)
Activation pattern: Regional activation confined to the extreme N‑terminus (~positions 10–40): strongest across the C‑terminal half of the signal peptide and often straddling just beyond the cleavage site into the first residues of the mature chain/propeptide; predicted helical/coil with low pLDDT; negligible activation elsewhere
Exemplars: - Serine protease (tissue‑type plasminogen activator): activation over the C‑terminal half of the signal peptide and into the propeptide.
- Kunitz‑type protease inhibitor: activation on the C‑terminal portion of the signal peptide, extending a few residues past the cleavage site.
- Mucin (MUC1): peak at the end of the signal peptide, coincident with the cleavage site.
- Wnt signaling modulator (Sclerostin): activation across the signal peptide; variants at the activated site affect secretion.
- Extracellular matrix glycoprotein (Tenascin): activation confined to the signal peptide, ending at chain start.
- Receptor‑like tyrosine kinase family member (PDGFR‑like): activation on the C‑terminal half of the signal peptide.
- Semaphorin: activation across the signal peptide with a sharp drop after cleavage.
- Glycoprotein hormone beta subunit (luteinizing hormone β): activation within the signal peptide, ending at cleavage.
- Adhesion GPCR (adhesion class): activation in the core and C‑terminal end of the signal peptide.
- Single‑pass receptor (secretory phospholipase A2 receptor): activation spanning the end of the signal peptide and the first residues of the mature ectodomain.

Summary: C-terminal helix/juxtamembrane-tail motif: the feature highlights the final helical segment of a polypeptide and the immediately following C-terminal tail—most prominently the cytosolic tail that follows a last transmembrane helix in membrane proteins, and the terminal helix of soluble secreted proteins. It prefers amphipathic, mildly hydrophobic/aromatic stretches and the helix-to-coil transition at the chain end.
Activation pattern: Regional activation concentrated in the last 10–40 residues, peaking at helix termini and in the extreme C-terminal residues (often extending into low-confidence/disordered tails). In multi-pass membrane proteins, activation extends modestly into the cytosolic end of the terminal transmembrane helix and strongly into the immediately adjacent cytosolic tail, with little to no signal in internal TMs or luminal/extracellular loops. In soluble/secreted proteins, the signal is largely silent on N-terminal signal peptides and catalytic cores, but rises on the final helix and last residues.
Exemplars: - Class I helical cytokines (e.g., interleukin-3): strong activation across the C-terminal long helix (helix D), highest at the last few residues.
- Plant CASP/CASPL multi-pass membrane proteins: moderate activation at the cytosolic end of the last transmembrane helix and strong activation in the adjacent C-terminal cytosolic tail; negligible signal in other TMs/loops.
- Secreted GDSL lipases: minimal signal on the signal peptide and catalytic machinery, with activation rising across the C-terminal region and peaking in the final low-confidence tail beyond the structured core.

Summary: Short, disulfide‑bonded extracellular cysteine‑rich repeat modules—especially EGF‑like (including cbEGF and laminin‑type LE) and LDL receptor class A (LDLa) domains, but also von Willebrand type C (CR) and other disulfide‑rich repeats—detected via acidic/polar loop motifs flanked by conserved cysteines (including Ca2+-binding Dx[D/N] motifs when present); broadly marks ectodomains of secreted proteins and single‑pass receptors.
Activation pattern:
- Strong activation confined to extracellular regions; absent in transmembrane helices and cytoplasmic tails.
- Repeated peaks aligning with tandem repeats; long activation tracts across multi‑repeat proteins.
- LDLa repeats: maxima over the central acidic DxSDE/DxD… segment; flanking cysteines variably engaged.
- EGF‑like repeats (cbEGF and LE): highest in the C‑terminal half containing the D/N‑x‑D/N‑x(4)‑Y/F motif when present, near the last cysteines.
- Also activates analogous acidic/polar loops in other cysteine‑rich repeats (e.g., VWC/CR, TIL/Kunitz, TSR); preference for D/E/S/T/N/Q/G and Y with nearby Cys; modest activation in short acidic linkers between repeats.
Exemplars:
- LDL receptor family (LDLR/LRP1/LRP4): LDLa repeat Ca2+-binding loops and cbEGF/LE segments across the ectodomain.
- Notch receptors and ligands (Notch, Delta/Jagged): tandem EGF‑like repeats with peaks at Ca2+-binding loops.
- Coagulation/complement components (e.g., Factors VII/IX/X, protein C/S, C1r/C1s modules): cbEGF domains.
- ECM scaffolds and glycoproteins (fibrillins, fibulins, LTBPs, laminins, tenascins, matrilins): arrays of EGF‑like/LE repeats.
- Chordin‑like/BMP modulators (BMPER/Crossveinless‑2, chordin): arrays of VWC/CR repeats.
- Cell‑adhesion receptors (selectins, integrin β I‑EGF modules) and extracellular metalloproteases/modulators (ADAM/ADAMTS): EGF‑like/cysteine‑rich repeats.
- Disulfide‑rich protease inhibitors and invertebrate toxins (e.g., Kunitz/TIL‑type).
- Plant receptor‑like proteins/kinases (e.g., WAKs, vacuolar sorting receptors): ectodomains with EGF‑like repeats.

Summary: Sequence contexts marking disulfide-bonded cysteines in secreted/extracellular proteins—cysteine pairs/clusters (often flanked by Gly/Pro) that form stabilizing disulfide frameworks typical of toxins, antimicrobial peptides, protease inhibitors, neuropeptide/hormone/pheromone peptides, and viral envelope ectodomains.

Summary: Short, intrinsically disordered C‑terminal tails of secreted or membrane‑associated proteins (from microproteins to larger multi‑pass enzymes) and viral accessory microproteins, typically low‑complexity and enriched in proline and basic residues, often immediately downstream of a hydrophobic signal/transmembrane segment; can include cysteine‑rich patches in secreted/toxin peptides.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over contiguous 10–30 aa windows, most frequently at the extreme C‑terminus; often spans a brief helix that transitions into coil with peak signal in the disordered coil; commonly adjacent to a hydrophobic (signal/TM) segment and characterized by low pLDDT; can also occur in short cytosolic juxtamembrane loops of larger multi‑pass proteins.
Exemplars:
- Oomycete RxLR secreted effectors: activation on the C‑terminal tail immediately following a predicted hydrophobic segment, in a low‑confidence helix/coil region.
- Human ST20 (apoptosis/stress‑related microprotein): activation on a short C‑terminal helix‑to‑coil, highly disordered stretch.
- Small uncharacterized microproteins: activation confined to the last ~10–15 residues forming a disordered coil tail.
- Viral accessory/viroporin‑like proteins: activation on basic/proline‑rich cytosolic C‑tails adjacent to a single‑pass TM helix; also applies to non‑TM viral accessory proteins with disordered C‑tails (e.g., Vif).
- Small secreted cysteine‑rich toxins/defensin‑like peptides: activation on short cationic/cysteine‑biased segments within the mature or processing tail.
- ATP synthase epsilon subunits: activation on a conserved, short, disordered C‑terminal regulatory segment in these small mitochondrial/bacterial proteins.
- Multi‑pass membrane enzymes (e.g., phytoene dehydrogenase): activation on short cytosolic C‑terminal or juxtamembrane tails adjacent to TM helices.

Summary: Intrinsic disorder/low-complexity segments enriched in small, polar and charged residues (S/T/N/G/A/E/D/R/K), especially N-terminal tails, C-terminal tails, and inter-domain regions that contain short repeating motifs; common in nucleic-acid-associated regulators and many viral proteins, and largely absent from structured domains
Activation pattern: Regional activation across low-pLDDT coil regions with dense stretches and periodic residue-level peaks (often on Ser/Asn within short repeats or in acidic/basic runs); frequent strong hotspots at extreme N-termini and flexible C-terminal tails; minimal activation within folded domain cores
Exemplars: - C2H2 zinc finger transcription factors: activation on disordered N- and C-terminal extensions flanking the zinc-finger array, not on the folded zinc-finger domains themselves.
- Meiosis regulator HED1: sharp activation on the disordered N-terminal segment (Asn/Ser-biased) and weaker activation in a disordered C-terminal tail; no activation on the central helical core.
- Viral regulatory/nucleic-acid-binding proteins: activation on low-complexity tails and charged tracts used for RNA/DNA binding or host-interaction.
- Small/uncharacterized human microproteins and pseudogene-derived proteins: activation on polar/charged low-complexity stretches characteristic of IDRs.

Activation pattern: Regional activation in short blocks (often a few to ~20 residues) with sharp peaks over Gly-Gly and Gly/Pro clusters; peaks occur in disordered N-terminal, internal, or C-terminal tail regions.
Exemplars:

- Repeated peaks aligning with tandem repeats; long activation tracts across multi‑repeat proteins.
- LDLa repeats: maxima over the central acidic DxSDE/DxD… segment; flanking cysteines variably engaged.
- EGF‑like repeats (cbEGF and LE): highest in the C‑terminal half containing the D/N‑x‑D/N‑x(4)‑Y/F motif when present, near the last cysteines.

- Notch receptors and ligands (Notch, Delta/Jagged): tandem EGF‑like repeats with peaks at Ca2+-binding loops.

- Venom disulfide-rich toxins (conotoxins; scorpion α/β-toxins; spider ω/κ-toxins): activation tracks the canonical Cys frameworks.
- Defensins and other CSαβ antimicrobial peptides: activation on the conserved disulfide pairs.
- Kunitz- and Kazal-type serine protease inhibitors: peaks around the conserved disulfide-bonded cysteines stabilizing the inhibitory fold.
- Neuropeptide hormones/pheromones with intrachain/interchain disulfides (e.g., insulin family, oxytocin/vasopressin): activation at the disulfide-forming Cys and neighboring Gly/Pro.
- Viral envelope glycoproteins: multiple peaks across ectodomain cysteine clusters and Cys–Gly/Pro motifs.
- Secreted nematode extracellular/ECM-associated cysteine-rich proteins: activation over disulfide-stabilized modules.

Summary: Extracellular secreted precursors and ectodomains with disulfide-bonded cysteine-rich loops/domains (cystine-stabilized scaffolds), and a subset of secreted neuropeptide precursors whose activation concentrates on flexible, processing-rich segments even without dense cysteine content. Common in proteins with signal peptides, glycosylation, and proteolytic processing.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks on cysteines and adjacent positions (often Gly/Pro and basic Lys/Arg) within extracellular regions; regional activation over cysteine-rich loops or repeats; also highlights Gly/Pro and Lys/Arg flanking propeptide cleavage motifs in cysteine-poor neuropeptide precursors; absent in transmembrane helices and cytosolic tails; strongest in low-to-moderate order ectodomain segments, sometimes near N-glycosylation and cleavage sites.
Exemplars:
- Chemokines (especially CXC): activation on conserved disulfide-forming cysteine motifs.
- Defensins/plant CRPs and knottin-like/trypsin inhibitor peptides (CSαβ/ICK scaffolds): activation across disulfide-bonded loops.
- WFDC, Kunitz, and Kazal protease inhibitors: activation on disulfide-stabilized inhibitor domains.
- Venom toxins (e.g., Kunitz-type, ShK, disintegrins): activation on clustered cysteines defining the scaffold.
- Viral envelope glycoproteins (class I/II/III): activation in cysteine-rich ectodomains near disulfide networks and glycosylation sites.
- Extracellular receptor/adhesion and metalloprotease proteins: activation on EGF-like, disintegrin, and other cysteine-rich modules.
- DEG/ENaC family channels: activation in the extracellular cysteine-rich loop.
- Neuropeptide hormone precursors (e.g., small cardioactive peptides): activation around flexible, dibasic cleavage-rich segments even with low cysteine content.
- Apicomplexan AMA1 invasion protein: activation confined to ectodomain cysteine-rich segments, absent from TM/cytosolic regions.

Summary: Extracellular/cell-surface secretome signature: the feature recognizes ectodomains of secreted or surface-presented proteins, especially cysteine-rich, disulfide-stabilized peptides and repeats (e.g., toxins, EGF/disintegrin/adhesion modules, lectins), C-terminal regions surrounding GPI-anchor attachment sites, and also short exofacial loops of multi-pass membrane proteins when these loops are cysteine- and/or glycan-rich; it captures appended extracellular carbohydrate-binding modules of secreted CAZymes
Activation pattern: Primarily regional/domain-level activation over long, contiguous stretches of extracellular sequence (often at protein termini), with residue-level peaks near Cys clusters and adjacent residues (aromatics/Pro/Ser/Thr); frequently highest around the GPI omega site and drops within cleaved C-terminal propeptides; can cover complete mature secreted peptide chains or selectively highlight appended extracellular modules (e.g., CBMs) rather than catalytic cores; additionally, can mark short exofacial loops (not necessarily at termini) in multi-pass transporters when they contain Cys–Cys/Cys-x(n)–Cys or NXS/T glycosylation motifs
Exemplars: Trypanosome variant surface glycoproteins (VSGs) – strong activation across the disordered C-terminal GPI-anchor region, peaking at the omega site and disappearing in the cleaved propeptide; Ciliate mating pheromones – activation across the mature secreted cystine-rich peptide with peaks at N-terminal aromatic residues and reduced signal on disulfide-bonded cysteines; Secreted carbohydrate-active enzymes – activation on C-terminal CBM10 carbohydrate-binding modules and adjacent helices, not on the catalytic cores; Disulfide-rich venom peptides and Kunitz/other protease inhibitors – extended activation across the mature, disulfide-stabilized chains; Viral envelope/entry glycoproteins – activation on cysteine-rich ectodomain loops; EGF-like/disintegrin/adhesion modules and lectins – activation on cysteine-constrained extracellular repeats/domains; SLC/GLUT-family transporters – activation on short extracellular loops bearing conserved disulfide-bonded cysteines and glycosylation sites

Summary: Secreted, short cysteine-rich peptides and small extracellular cysteine-rich domains stabilized by multiple disulfide bonds (CRPs), spanning venom toxins, disintegrins, defensins/hepcidin, Kunitz/Kazal/hevein-like inhibitors/defense peptides, and related cystine‑knotted or cysteine‑stabilized folds. The feature captures the mature, proteolytically processed peptide/module characterized by clustered Cys (often CC motifs) and basic residues.
Activation pattern: Regional activation confined to short mature peptide segments (tens of residues) following the signal peptide and propeptides; minimal/absent on signal/pro-regions. Strong residue-level peaks on cysteines and frequent secondary peaks on Lys/Arg and Gly. Activation spans mixed secondary structure (β-strands, coils, short helices) and can include key functional loops (e.g., RGD in disintegrins).
Exemplars: - Plant cyclotides (cystine-knot cyclopeptides, e.g., chassatide): activation across the cyclic cystine‑knot core of the mature peptide after processing.
- Snake venom disintegrins: activation across the disintegrin domain, including the RGD integrin-binding loop and adjacent cysteine-dense core.
- Inhibitor cystine-knot (ICK) venom toxins from spiders, cone snails, centipedes, and sea anemones: activation on the disulfide‑knotted toxin core.
- Kunitz/BPTI- and Kazal-type serine protease inhibitors (including tick chemokine/complement inhibitors): activation on the small disulfide‑rich inhibitor domain.
- Hevein-like/seed defense peptides: activation on the cysteine-rich chitin‑binding hevein domain.
- Defensins (plant/fungal/animal CSαβ peptides) and vertebrate hepcidin: activation on the cysteine‑stabilized mature AMP region.
- Euplotes ciliate mating pheromones: activation on the secreted disulfide‑rich pheromone core.
- Cysteine-rich modules within large extracellular/mucin-like proteins: activation on the short, cysteine‑dense repeat/subdomain embedded in the larger precursor.

Summary: Extracellular Cys–Trp (CW/CGW) disulfide‑loop signature common to secreted and single‑pass cell‑surface proteins and small cystine‑rich peptides; the feature highlights cysteine- and aromatic‑enriched ectodomain motifs used in adhesion, receptor–ligand/contact interfaces, and immune‑evasion coats (e.g., VSGs, semaphorins/plexins, integrins, RTKs, viral envelope glycoproteins)
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks centered on C…W (often CW/CGW with nearby Tyr/Phe) within disulfide‑stabilized loops; regional activation across extracellular, cysteine‑rich segments; extended, domain‑length activation in VSG ectodomains but short motif‑focused peaks in most other proteins; generally in secreted/ectodomain regions, not in transmembranes or cytosolic tails
Exemplars: - Trypanosoma variant surface glycoproteins (VSGs): strong, continuous activation across the disulfide‑rich GPI‑anchored coat domain with repeated C…W/Aromatic patches.
- Semaphorin and plexin receptors: peaks at conserved CW/CGW sites in Sema/PSI ectodomains.
- Viral envelope/spike glycoproteins: activation on disulfide‑stabilized surface loops containing Cys–Trp and nearby aromatics.
- Integrin beta subunits: activation within extracellular PSI/I‑EGF repeats at CW/CGW motifs.
- Receptor tyrosine kinases and related single‑pass receptors: peaks on extracellular cysteine‑rich segments bearing CGW/CW signatures.
- Disulfide‑rich secreted peptides (toxins, cyclotides, defensins‑like): localized peaks where Trp neighbors disulfide‑bonded cysteines.
- Kinetoplastid hexose transporters: activation in extracellular loops containing the conserved C…W motif.
- Adhesion/glycocalyx components (e.g., mucins/proteoglycan core proteins): activation on cysteine/aromatic‑rich ectodomain motifs.

Summary: Secreted, propeptide‑processed cysteine‑rich mini‑domains: compact extracellular segments immediately downstream of a signal peptide that contain clustered cysteines forming multiple disulfide bonds (defensin/CSαβ, WAP four‑disulfide core, cystine‑knot/knottin, CHH‑like, evasin‑like, and related small CRP scaffolds), often flanked by dibasic convertase sites and enriched in Lys/Arg
Activation pattern: Regional activation on short segments (≈20–60 aa) right after the signal peptide; strong peaks on cysteines and nearby basic residues, frequently overlapping proprotein convertase (dibasic) processing motifs; may recur for multi‑domain or repeat CRP proteins
Exemplars: - WAP/four‑disulfide core protease inhibitors (SLPI/elafin/WFDC): activation on the WAP domain’s Cys framework following the signal/propeptide
- Plant defensin‑like peptides (DEFL/LURE/ESF) and thionins: activation on the mature antimicrobial CSαβ cysteine motif
- Venom cystine‑knot peptides (conotoxins/knottins, mini‑toxins): activation on the canonical Cys frameworks in the mature toxin region of prepropeptides
- Tick evasins (chemokine‑binding CRPs): activation on the Cys‑rich chemokine‑binding domain
- Crustacean CHH/MIH neuropeptide precursors: activation on the mature hormone core with conserved six‑Cys motif adjacent to dibasic cleavage
- Fungal GPI‑anchored cell‑wall adhesins/stress proteins: activation on extracellular Cys‑rich segments just after secretion signals
- Small plant CRP protease inhibitors: activation on the disulfide‑stabilized inhibitory mini‑domain

Summary: Short, disulfide‑bonded extracellular cysteine‑rich repeat modules—especially EGF‑like (including cbEGF and laminin‑type LE) and LDL receptor class A (LDLa) domains, but also von Willebrand type C (CR) and other disulfide‑rich repeats—detected via acidic/polar loop motifs flanked by conserved cysteines (including Ca2+-binding Dx[D/N] motifs when present); broadly marks ectodomains of secreted proteins and single‑pass receptors.
Activation pattern:
- Strong activation confined to extracellular regions; absent in transmembrane helices and cytoplasmic tails.
- Repeated peaks aligning with tandem repeats; long activation tracts across multi‑repeat proteins.
- LDLa repeats: maxima over the central acidic DxSDE/DxD… segment; flanking cysteines variably engaged.
- EGF‑like repeats (cbEGF and LE): highest in the C‑terminal half containing the D/N‑x‑D/N‑x(4)‑Y/F motif when present, near the last cysteines.
- Also activates analogous acidic/polar loops in other cysteine‑rich repeats (e.g., VWC/CR, TIL/Kunitz, TSR); preference for D/E/S/T/N/Q/G and Y with nearby Cys; modest activation in short acidic linkers between repeats.
Exemplars:
- LDL receptor family (LDLR/LRP1/LRP4): LDLa repeat Ca2+-binding loops and cbEGF/LE segments across the ectodomain.
- Notch receptors and ligands (Notch, Delta/Jagged): tandem EGF‑like repeats with peaks at Ca2+-binding loops.
- Coagulation/complement components (e.g., Factors VII/IX/X, protein C/S, C1r/C1s modules): cbEGF domains.
- ECM scaffolds and glycoproteins (fibrillins, fibulins, LTBPs, laminins, tenascins, matrilins): arrays of EGF‑like/LE repeats.
- Chordin‑like/BMP modulators (BMPER/Crossveinless‑2, chordin): arrays of VWC/CR repeats.
- Cell‑adhesion receptors (selectins, integrin β I‑EGF modules) and extracellular metalloproteases/modulators (ADAM/ADAMTS): EGF‑like/cysteine‑rich repeats.
- Disulfide‑rich protease inhibitors and invertebrate toxins (e.g., Kunitz/TIL‑type).
- Plant receptor‑like proteins/kinases (e.g., WAKs, vacuolar sorting receptors): ectodomains with EGF‑like repeats.

Summary: Disulfide‑stabilized extracellular ectodomain repeats and their linkers—especially EGF‑like repeats and TNFR cysteine‑rich domains—across secreted proteins and the N‑terminal/luminal regions of cell‑surface receptors and transporters
Activation pattern: Regionally confined to extracellular/N‑terminal ectodomains; sparse residue‑level peaks centered on cysteines that form disulfides and nearby glycine/acidic residues; frequent signal in flexible/low‑pLDDT loops flanking structured repeats; negligible in signal peptides, transmembrane helices, and cytosolic tails
Exemplars: • Adhesion GPCRs (latrophilins): activation in EGF‑like repeats and adjacent flexible segments of the ectodomain
• Viral TNFR‑like immunomodulators (e.g., UL144): strong peaks on cysteines within TNFR cysteine‑rich domains
• Cell‑adhesion glycoproteins with EGF‑like modules: peaks within the EGF‑like repeat and its flanking unstructured regions
• Venom/toxin EGF‑like microproteins: sparse peaks across the disulfide‑rich EGF‑like fold
• ABCG family membrane transporters: activation restricted to the long N‑terminal luminal region before the first transmembrane helix, absent from TM and cytosolic domains

Summary: Classical cleavable N-terminal Sec signal peptides (type I) of secreted prepropeptides/proteins, especially venom toxins and antimicrobial/defense peptides; the feature captures the positively charged N-region and hydrophobic helical h‑region of the signal sequence, with activation tapering across the C-region/early propeptide and absent from the mature chain.
Activation pattern: Strong, contiguous regional activation confined to the extreme N-terminus (~20–40 residues), highest over a hydrophobic, alpha-helical block enriched in Leu/Ile/Val/Phe/Ala/Met with basic residues in the first few positions; activation drops near the signal peptidase cleavage site and may extend a few residues into the propeptide; negligible across the mature peptide; typically lower pLDDT in the activated segment.
Exemplars: - Scorpion kappa-KTx potassium channel toxin precursors: activation on the N-terminal signal peptide only.
- Conotoxin precursors (cone snail): activation confined to the signal peptide.
- Plant cyclotide/defensin-like precursors (e.g., chassatides): activation on the signal peptide with slight spillover into the propeptide.
- Insect diapause-specific peptide: activation on the signal peptide only.
- Sea anemone actitoxin precursors: activation across the signal peptide and diminishing in the adjacent propeptide.
- Scorpion chlorotoxin-like peptide precursors: activation on the signal peptide.
- Secreted serine protease inhibitor precursors: activation on the signal peptide, fading in early propeptide.
- Bacterial heat-stable enterotoxin: activation on the N-terminal signal peptide only.
- Secreted vanadium-binding protein: activation on the signal peptide and short propeptide.
- Tick evasin (chemokine-binding protein): activation across the N-terminal signal peptide only.

- Disulfide‑rich secreted peptides (toxins, cyclotides, defensins‑like): localized peaks where Trp neighbors disulfide‑bonded cysteines.
- Kinetoplastid hexose transporters: activation in extracellular loops containing the conserved C…W motif.
- Adhesion/glycocalyx components (e.g., mucins/proteoglycan core proteins): activation on cysteine/aromatic‑rich ectodomain motifs.

Summary: Extracellular/cell-surface secretome signature: the feature recognizes ectodomains of secreted or surface-presented proteins, especially cysteine-rich, disulfide-stabilized peptides and repeats (e.g., toxins, EGF/disintegrin/adhesion modules, lectins), C-terminal regions surrounding GPI-anchor attachment sites, and also short exofacial loops of multi-pass membrane proteins when these loops are cysteine- and/or glycan-rich; it captures appended extracellular carbohydrate-binding modules of secreted CAZymes
Activation pattern: Primarily regional/domain-level activation over long, contiguous stretches of extracellular sequence (often at protein termini), with residue-level peaks near Cys clusters and adjacent residues (aromatics/Pro/Ser/Thr); frequently highest around the GPI omega site and drops within cleaved C-terminal propeptides; can cover complete mature secreted peptide chains or selectively highlight appended extracellular modules (e.g., CBMs) rather than catalytic cores; additionally, can mark short exofacial loops (not necessarily at termini) in multi-pass transporters when they contain Cys–Cys/Cys-x(n)–Cys or NXS/T glycosylation motifs
Exemplars: Trypanosome variant surface glycoproteins (VSGs) – strong activation across the disordered C-terminal GPI-anchor region, peaking at the omega site and disappearing in the cleaved propeptide; Ciliate mating pheromones – activation across the mature secreted cystine-rich peptide with peaks at N-terminal aromatic residues and reduced signal on disulfide-bonded cysteines; Secreted carbohydrate-active enzymes – activation on C-terminal CBM10 carbohydrate-binding modules and adjacent helices, not on the catalytic cores; Disulfide-rich venom peptides and Kunitz/other protease inhibitors – extended activation across the mature, disulfide-stabilized chains; Viral envelope/entry glycoproteins – activation on cysteine-rich ectodomain loops; EGF-like/disintegrin/adhesion modules and lectins – activation on cysteine-constrained extracellular repeats/domains; SLC/GLUT-family transporters – activation on short extracellular loops bearing conserved disulfide-bonded cysteines and glycosylation sites

Summary: Secreted, propeptide‑processed cysteine‑rich mini‑domains: compact extracellular segments immediately downstream of a signal peptide that contain clustered cysteines forming multiple disulfide bonds (defensin/CSαβ, WAP four‑disulfide core, cystine‑knot/knottin, CHH‑like, evasin‑like, and related small CRP scaffolds), often flanked by dibasic convertase sites and enriched in Lys/Arg
Activation pattern: Regional activation on short segments (≈20–60 aa) right after the signal peptide; strong peaks on cysteines and nearby basic residues, frequently overlapping proprotein convertase (dibasic) processing motifs; may recur for multi‑domain or repeat CRP proteins
Exemplars: - WAP/four‑disulfide core protease inhibitors (SLPI/elafin/WFDC): activation on the WAP domain’s Cys framework following the signal/propeptide
- Plant defensin‑like peptides (DEFL/LURE/ESF) and thionins: activation on the mature antimicrobial CSαβ cysteine motif
- Venom cystine‑knot peptides (conotoxins/knottins, mini‑toxins): activation on the canonical Cys frameworks in the mature toxin region of prepropeptides
- Tick evasins (chemokine‑binding CRPs): activation on the Cys‑rich chemokine‑binding domain
- Crustacean CHH/MIH neuropeptide precursors: activation on the mature hormone core with conserved six‑Cys motif adjacent to dibasic cleavage
- Fungal GPI‑anchored cell‑wall adhesins/stress proteins: activation on extracellular Cys‑rich segments just after secretion signals
- Small plant CRP protease inhibitors: activation on the disulfide‑stabilized inhibitory mini‑domain

Summary: Sequence contexts marking disulfide-bonded cysteines in secreted/extracellular proteins—cysteine pairs/clusters (often flanked by Gly/Pro) that form stabilizing disulfide frameworks typical of toxins, antimicrobial peptides, protease inhibitors, neuropeptide/hormone/pheromone peptides, and viral envelope ectodomains.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks at or immediately adjacent to disulfide-bonded cysteines; compact, contiguous activation across the cystine framework in short disulfide-rich peptides; multiple peaks scattered across ectodomains of large secreted glycoproteins; minimal activation in signal peptides, transmembranes, or cytosolic regions.
Exemplars: - AB toxins (pertussis toxin B subunit): peaks next to disulfide-forming cysteines within the mature chain.
- Venom disulfide-rich toxins (conotoxins; scorpion α/β-toxins; spider ω/κ-toxins): activation tracks the canonical Cys frameworks.
- Defensins and other CSαβ antimicrobial peptides: activation on the conserved disulfide pairs.
- Kunitz- and Kazal-type serine protease inhibitors: peaks around the conserved disulfide-bonded cysteines stabilizing the inhibitory fold.
- Neuropeptide hormones/pheromones with intrachain/interchain disulfides (e.g., insulin family, oxytocin/vasopressin): activation at the disulfide-forming Cys and neighboring Gly/Pro.
- Viral envelope glycoproteins: multiple peaks across ectodomain cysteine clusters and Cys–Gly/Pro motifs.
- Secreted nematode extracellular/ECM-associated cysteine-rich proteins: activation over disulfide-stabilized modules.

Summary: Short linear segments in intrinsically disordered or otherwise low-structure-confidence regions, often at N-termini and within signal peptides/propeptides of secreted and regulatory proteins (including viral accessory proteins and small ORF microproteins), enriched in small/basic residues (G, P, S, A, R; often with Cys), rather than in well-folded catalytic cores.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks scattered across IDRs and low-confidence coils/short helices; frequently clustered near the N-terminus, in signal peptides, propeptides, and disordered tails; little to no activation in well-structured domains; occasional activation in low-confidence transmembrane/signal-anchor helices.
Exemplars: - Viral accessory protein (HIV-1 Vif): peaks throughout low-pLDDT coils, especially the disordered N-terminal region.
- Neuropeptide precursor (Drosophila Amnesiac): activation in the N-terminal signal peptide and multiple mature peptide segments with very low pLDDT.
- Secreted serine carboxypeptidase: activation confined to disordered C-terminal tail, annotated disordered segment, the signal peptide, and a low-confidence C-terminal transmembrane helix; absent from the structured catalytic domain.
- Disordered human tumor-suppressor–associated protein (ST20): scattered peaks within predicted helices in a globally disordered chain, including the N-terminus.
- lncRNA/sORF-derived microprotein (IGF2 antisense protein): multiple peaks across annotated disordered regions rich in Arg/Pro/Gly.

Summary: Short segments within disordered and compositionally biased stretches of diverse proteins, particularly regions enriched in basic and acidic residues. Activations are also seen in non-disordered contexts across proteins of varied function, suggesting the feature captures a relatively broad local sequence pattern rather than a tight structural motif.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks with small clusters, distributed throughout the length of the protein. Peaks frequently overlap annotated disordered regions and basic/acidic compositionally biased segments, but also occur at isolated positions within structured chains; occurs in both helical and coil contexts.
Exemplars: - Oomycete RxLR secreted effectors: peaks within the mature effector chain, with occasional spikes in the signal peptide.
- Plant CLE peptide precursors: localized peaks within the C-terminal CLE motif corresponding to the mature signaling peptide.
- Cholecystokinin prohormone: peaks at or immediately adjacent to the N-termini of mature neuropeptides generated by proteolytic processing.
- Herpesvirus ICP47-like small accessory proteins: multiple peaks in the N-terminal active helical region and in polar, disordered C-terminal stretches.
- Keratin-associated proteins: activation across cysteine/proline/serine-rich, low-complexity repeat regions.
- Phosphodiesterase and fungal/bacterial enzymes with disordered N- or internal stretches: peaks within basic-and-acidic compositionally biased segments.

Summary: Low-complexity, intrinsically disordered segments with a bias for serine/threonine (often with proline and nearby basic/acidic residues) that encode short linear motifs for regulation or targeting (e.g., phosphosite motifs, RxLR-dEER), found in flexible regulatory tails, disordered viral protein regions, and short secreted peptide precursors.
Activation pattern: Predominantly regional activation across disordered, low-pLDDT stretches with many sites per segment; superimposed residue-level peaks on S/T and adjacent charged/proline residues. Also active in short, low-complexity transmembrane/peptide precursors; minimal in well-folded globular domains.
Exemplars: - Coronavirus nucleocapsid proteins: central low-complexity, disordered regions enriched in Ser/Thr with known phosphosites, plus disordered C-terminal tails.
- Viral disordered regulatory proteins (e.g., hepadnavirus protein X, HIV Vif): disordered internal regions and flexible linkers with peaks on S/E/P/R.
- Oomycete RxLR effectors: flexible N-terminal/mature regions around the RxLR-dEER host-targeting motif, with peaks on E/S/R within low-confidence structure.
- Secreted antimicrobial peptide precursors: activation on the N-terminal signal peptide and on flexible residues within the mature peptide region.
- Disordered human regulatory proteins (e.g., PRAS40, p311, NoBody): scattered activation across intrinsically disordered segments, often overlapping known phosphosites.

Summary: Detector of compositionally biased, low‑complexity segments—predominantly intrinsically disordered Ser/Thr‑rich (often RS-/Pro‑containing) tracts—with a strong N‑terminal bias; it also flags the extreme N‑terminus including signal peptides of secreted precursors.
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks clustered within long disordered/low‑complexity regions (often spanning tens to hundreds of residues), with strongest peaks on Ser/Thr and nearby polar/basic residues; broad regional activation across such IDRs and minimal signal in well‑folded domains or transmembranes; additional discrete peaks frequently occur at residues 1–10, including within N‑terminal signal peptides.
Exemplars: - Transcriptional regulator (CROC-4): multiple peaks across a central low‑complexity disordered segment (S/T/R/P‑rich), with minor N‑terminal peaks.
- Mechanosensory receptor (Stum): numerous high peaks on serines dispersed through annotated disordered, low‑complexity/polar regions.
- Yeast RNA/chromatin‑associated factor (REF2‑interacting protein): peaks within disordered, compositionally biased tracts; strongest at a threonine in an S/T‑rich context, near (but not exactly on) annotated phosphosites.
- Secreted antimicrobial peptide precursor (lumbricin): strongest activation on the N‑terminal signal peptide helix; weaker peaks just after the signal peptide preceding a long disordered pro‑region.
- Yeast HPH2 regulatory protein: activation confined to disordered, low‑complexity regions in the N‑terminal two‑thirds; absent from the structured C‑terminal domain and its transmembrane helix.

Summary: Often fires within intrinsic disorder/low-complexity segments—especially terminal or propeptide regions enriched in Pro/Ser/Thr/Gly—that serve as flexible carriers of short linear motifs; the feature highlights unstructured tails/loops across diverse proteins (including secreted precursors, viral regulators, membrane-protein tails, and micropeptides), sometimes coinciding with proteolytic processing and PTM sites, but also produces residue-level peaks within some short folded enzymes/fragments.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks within annotated/predicted disordered coils and low-complexity tracts, frequently enriched toward N-termini; additional scattered peaks can occur within short folded chains.
Exemplars: - Secreted peptide hormone precursors (e.g., cholecystokinin/prohormones): peaks in unstructured propeptide segments at sulfotyrosine, amidation sites, and cleavage boundaries.
- Herpesviral nuclear egress proteins: activation on N-terminal disordered, polar-biased regions; not on the structured zinc-finger domain.
- Integrase-family proteins: peaks include very low-pLDDT loops and annotated disordered segments, with additional scattered peaks elsewhere in the chain.
- Mycobacterial cell-envelope–associated proteins: single-residue/short-segment peaks within UniProt-annotated disordered coil regions.
- p53-inducible regulatory proteins: sparse peaks across N-terminal and central intrinsically disordered regions, including isoform-variable segments.
- Alternative reading frame micropeptides: activation across low-complexity, disordered coils.

Summary: Short linear segments in intrinsically disordered or otherwise low-structure-confidence regions, often at N-termini and within signal peptides/propeptides of secreted and regulatory proteins (including viral accessory proteins and small ORF microproteins), enriched in small/basic residues (G, P, S, A, R; often with Cys), rather than in well-folded catalytic cores.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks scattered across IDRs and low-confidence coils/short helices; frequently clustered near the N-terminus, in signal peptides, propeptides, and disordered tails; little to no activation in well-structured domains; occasional activation in low-confidence transmembrane/signal-anchor helices.
Exemplars: - Viral accessory protein (HIV-1 Vif): peaks throughout low-pLDDT coils, especially the disordered N-terminal region.
- Neuropeptide precursor (Drosophila Amnesiac): activation in the N-terminal signal peptide and multiple mature peptide segments with very low pLDDT.
- Secreted serine carboxypeptidase: activation confined to disordered C-terminal tail, annotated disordered segment, the signal peptide, and a low-confidence C-terminal transmembrane helix; absent from the structured catalytic domain.
- Disordered human tumor-suppressor–associated protein (ST20): scattered peaks within predicted helices in a globally disordered chain, including the N-terminus.
- lncRNA/sORF-derived microprotein (IGF2 antisense protein): multiple peaks across annotated disordered regions rich in Arg/Pro/Gly.

Summary: Low-complexity, intrinsically disordered segments—often at protein N-termini—such as mucin-like/propeptide regions or flexible linkers adjacent to signal/transit peptides, common in small secreted or membrane-associated proteins and also as disordered extensions in diverse enzymes (broad taxonomic coverage, including viral, bacterial, and eukaryotic proteins).
Activation pattern: Regional activation over short to moderate stretches, frequently in disordered or polar/low-complexity segments; in longer proteins, multiple low-complexity patches can activate; in micropeptides, activation can span much of the sequence. Residue-level peaks can fall on Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly within polar-residue stretches but also on basic or hydrophobic residues within the same disordered context.
Exemplars:
- Viral envelope/accessory microproteins: activation on N-terminal Ser/Thr/Pro-rich disordered segments (often mucin-like or regulatory tails).
- Secreted eukaryotic effectors (e.g., oomycete RxLR effectors): activation on the low-complexity region flanking the signal peptide/RxLR motif.
- Human testis-biased and lncRNA-derived micropeptides: activation across intrinsically disordered peptide regions.
- Secreted precursors/propeptides: activation on N-terminal regions following the signal peptide.
- Membrane-associated single-pass proteins: activation on luminal or cytosolic tails flanking the transmembrane helix.
- Bacterial/archaeal metabolic enzymes: activation on disordered, low-complexity N-terminal extensions/linkers enriched in Ser/Thr/Gly/Pro.

Summary: N‑terminal start and proteolytic maturation junction detector: activates on the initiator methionine or the first residue of a newly formed mature peptide after signal peptide/propeptide cleavage, typically within low‑complexity, disordered segments enriched in Ser/Pro/Gly/Arg; most prominent in secreted and membrane precursors and small peptides, but also marking N‑termini of diverse proteins (including many viral proteins) across taxa.
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks at the exact boundary (the first residue of the mature peptide and/or the immediately preceding residue), with short flanking N‑terminal stretches in low‑complexity IDRs; occasional weaker N‑terminal peaks elsewhere; broad, low‑specificity activation across taxa.
Exemplars: Plant PROPEP/Pep danger‑peptide precursors: strong peak at the N‑terminal boundary of the mature Pep within a disordered, acidic/basic‑biased prodomain; Viral envelope glycoproteins (e.g., class I fusion proteins): activation at signal peptide cleavage and/or polybasic convertase junctions, and at the extreme N‑terminus; Secreted hormone/neuropeptide and growth factor precursors: activation at propeptide removal sites that define the N‑terminus of the active peptide; Type I membrane receptors and secretory pathway glycoproteins: initiator Met and signal peptide region/cleavage site highlighted; lncRNA‑encoded micropeptides/smORFs: activation at Met1 and adjacent low‑complexity N‑terminal residues; Sperm/testis secreted or acrosomal proteins: activation on N‑terminal signal/pro‑region cleavage junctions; Bacterial/archaeal metabolic enzymes: weaker, generic N‑terminal activation at the start of disordered/low‑complexity tails; p53/apoptosis‑related proteins: N‑terminal disordered domains (e.g., transactivation/pro‑segments) show start‑proximal peaks.
