- Membrane-anchored secretory peptide-like precursor (e.g., Frey): inactive on the N‑terminal transmembrane helix; strong activation on the disordered luminal C‑terminal region consistent with a processed propeptide segment.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity/prion‑like regions enriched in G, Y, P, Q (often poly‑Q/N), S and T—frequently containing YG/GY/GYG patterns—commonly found in eukaryotic RNA‑binding proteins and transcription factors; these LCDs serve as modular interaction/activation segments and can include transportin‑1–recognized PY‑NLS motifs.
Activation pattern: Long, contiguous activation across intrinsically disordered segments (often C‑terminal tails) with multiple sub‑peaks; little to no activation within adjacent folded domains. Strong sequence preference for Q/N‑rich, P/Y/G/S/T‑rich low‑complexity runs and YG repeats; activation tracks regions with low pLDDT.
Exemplars: - Heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoproteins (hnRNPs): activation confined to the disordered C‑terminal tail harboring the transportin‑1 (PY‑NLS)–dependent nuclear import/export region; no activation in RRM domains.
- Homeobox transcription factors (e.g., bicoid‑like): activation on disordered C‑terminal low‑complexity activation domains; no activation in the structured homeodomain.
- Heavy metal‑associated isoprenylated plant proteins (HIPP): activation on the C‑terminal intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity tail; not in the N‑terminal HMA domain.
- RNA polymerase II degradation factor Def1‑like proteins: broad activation across the C‑terminal Q/G/P/S/Y‑rich disordered region; not in the N‑terminal CUE domain.

Summary: Small, often poorly characterized or compositionally biased proteins, including viral accessory proteins, cancer/testis and germline-associated proteins, antisense-ORF microproteins, and short secreted/surface peptides; activation is broadly distributed across the polypeptide rather than focused on a single structured domain
Activation pattern: Regional/distributed activation spread across much of the protein with sparse residue-level peaks; often includes early N-terminal residues and disordered segments; variable coverage from short patches to most of the protein
Exemplars:
- Viral non-structural/accessory proteins: activation distributed through the protein, including basic/Arg-rich motifs such as nuclear localization signals.
- Cancer/testis antigens and germline-associated proteins: activation on long disordered low-complexity regions, often at N-termini.
- Small uncharacterized microproteins/antisense ORFs: activation spanning most of the polypeptide.
- Short secreted peptides and toxin precursors: activation across both signal/propeptide and mature regions.
- Compact cytosolic proteins with disordered N- or C-terminal extensions: activation enriched on the disordered tails.

Summary: Low-complexity, intrinsically disordered segments—often at protein N-termini—such as mucin-like/propeptide regions or flexible linkers adjacent to signal/transit peptides, common in small secreted or membrane-associated proteins and also as disordered extensions in diverse enzymes (broad taxonomic coverage, including viral, bacterial, and eukaryotic proteins).
Activation pattern: Regional activation over short to moderate stretches, frequently in disordered or polar/low-complexity segments; in longer proteins, multiple low-complexity patches can activate; in micropeptides, activation can span much of the sequence. Residue-level peaks can fall on Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly within polar-residue stretches but also on basic or hydrophobic residues within the same disordered context.
Exemplars:
- Viral envelope/accessory microproteins: activation on N-terminal Ser/Thr/Pro-rich disordered segments (often mucin-like or regulatory tails).
- Secreted eukaryotic effectors (e.g., oomycete RxLR effectors): activation on the low-complexity region flanking the signal peptide/RxLR motif.
- Human testis-biased and lncRNA-derived micropeptides: activation across intrinsically disordered peptide regions.
- Secreted precursors/propeptides: activation on N-terminal regions following the signal peptide.
- Membrane-associated single-pass proteins: activation on luminal or cytosolic tails flanking the transmembrane helix.
- Bacterial/archaeal metabolic enzymes: activation on disordered, low-complexity N-terminal extensions/linkers enriched in Ser/Thr/Gly/Pro.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low-complexity segments enriched in serine/threonine/proline/glycine and often basic (lysine/arginine), typically found in flexible N- or C-terminal tails and loops; highlights IDRs that may harbor short linear motifs (e.g., basic NLS patches) rather than structured domain cores.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long disordered stretches with additional sparse residue-level peaks in low-confidence loops; often N-terminal-biased in short/viral proteins; rarely within well-folded cores.
Exemplars: Retroviral accessory proteins (e.g., HTLV-1 p30): activation on central and C-terminal IDRs including a basic nuclear localization signal; p53-regulated apoptosis-inducing microprotein: widespread activation across a globally disordered protein; Bacterial DNA ligase: scattered activation in an annotated disordered linker and flexible loops within the ligase domain; Uncharacterized human microprotein: multiple peaks throughout a low-pLDDT, disordered sequence irrespective of predicted secondary structure.

Summary: Short segments within disordered and compositionally biased stretches of diverse proteins, particularly regions enriched in basic and acidic residues. Activations are also seen in non-disordered contexts across proteins of varied function, suggesting the feature captures a relatively broad local sequence pattern rather than a tight structural motif.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks with small clusters, distributed throughout the length of the protein. Peaks frequently overlap annotated disordered regions and basic/acidic compositionally biased segments, but also occur at isolated positions within structured chains; occurs in both helical and coil contexts.
Exemplars: - Oomycete RxLR secreted effectors: peaks within the mature effector chain, with occasional spikes in the signal peptide.
- Plant CLE peptide precursors: localized peaks within the C-terminal CLE motif corresponding to the mature signaling peptide.
- Cholecystokinin prohormone: peaks at or immediately adjacent to the N-termini of mature neuropeptides generated by proteolytic processing.
- Herpesvirus ICP47-like small accessory proteins: multiple peaks in the N-terminal active helical region and in polar, disordered C-terminal stretches.
- Keratin-associated proteins: activation across cysteine/proline/serine-rich, low-complexity repeat regions.
- Phosphodiesterase and fungal/bacterial enzymes with disordered N- or internal stretches: peaks within basic-and-acidic compositionally biased segments.

Summary: Small, often poorly characterized or compositionally biased proteins, including viral accessory proteins, cancer/testis and germline-associated proteins, antisense-ORF microproteins, and short secreted/surface peptides; activation is broadly distributed across the polypeptide rather than focused on a single structured domain
Activation pattern: Regional/distributed activation spread across much of the protein with sparse residue-level peaks; often includes early N-terminal residues and disordered segments; variable coverage from short patches to most of the protein
Exemplars:
- Viral non-structural/accessory proteins: activation distributed through the protein, including basic/Arg-rich motifs such as nuclear localization signals.
- Cancer/testis antigens and germline-associated proteins: activation on long disordered low-complexity regions, often at N-termini.
- Small uncharacterized microproteins/antisense ORFs: activation spanning most of the polypeptide.
- Short secreted peptides and toxin precursors: activation across both signal/propeptide and mature regions.
- Compact cytosolic proteins with disordered N- or C-terminal extensions: activation enriched on the disordered tails.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity/prion‑like regions enriched in G, Y, P, Q (often poly‑Q/N), S and T—frequently containing YG/GY/GYG patterns—commonly found in eukaryotic RNA‑binding proteins and transcription factors; these LCDs serve as modular interaction/activation segments and can include transportin‑1–recognized PY‑NLS motifs.
Activation pattern: Long, contiguous activation across intrinsically disordered segments (often C‑terminal tails) with multiple sub‑peaks; little to no activation within adjacent folded domains. Strong sequence preference for Q/N‑rich, P/Y/G/S/T‑rich low‑complexity runs and YG repeats; activation tracks regions with low pLDDT.
Exemplars: - Heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoproteins (hnRNPs): activation confined to the disordered C‑terminal tail harboring the transportin‑1 (PY‑NLS)–dependent nuclear import/export region; no activation in RRM domains.
- Homeobox transcription factors (e.g., bicoid‑like): activation on disordered C‑terminal low‑complexity activation domains; no activation in the structured homeodomain.
- Heavy metal‑associated isoprenylated plant proteins (HIPP): activation on the C‑terminal intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity tail; not in the N‑terminal HMA domain.
- RNA polymerase II degradation factor Def1‑like proteins: broad activation across the C‑terminal Q/G/P/S/Y‑rich disordered region; not in the N‑terminal CUE domain.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low-complexity segments enriched in serine/threonine/proline/glycine and often basic (lysine/arginine), typically found in flexible N- or C-terminal tails and loops; highlights IDRs that may harbor short linear motifs (e.g., basic NLS patches) rather than structured domain cores.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long disordered stretches with additional sparse residue-level peaks in low-confidence loops; often N-terminal-biased in short/viral proteins; rarely within well-folded cores.
Exemplars: Retroviral accessory proteins (e.g., HTLV-1 p30): activation on central and C-terminal IDRs including a basic nuclear localization signal; p53-regulated apoptosis-inducing microprotein: widespread activation across a globally disordered protein; Bacterial DNA ligase: scattered activation in an annotated disordered linker and flexible loops within the ligase domain; Uncharacterized human microprotein: multiple peaks throughout a low-pLDDT, disordered sequence irrespective of predicted secondary structure.

Summary: Short, low‑complexity, intrinsically disordered proteins and modules that encode targeting/processing signals—often but not always secretory—combining hydrophobic signal peptides, double‑Gly bacteriocin leaders, or polybasic/NLS‑like segments, frequently adjacent to Ser/Thr/Pro‑rich stretches and basic clusters (e.g., RXLR, KR/RR)—common in micropeptides, toxins/secreted precursors, viral accessory proteins, keratin‑associated and testis‑specific low‑complexity proteins across taxa
Activation pattern: Regional activation across short proteins, spanning hydrophobic/targeting segments and Ser/Thr/Pro‑rich low‑complexity tracts with peaks on basic motifs such as RXLR, dibasic KR/RR, or double‑Gly leader junctions
Exemplars:
- Oomycete RxLR effectors: activation on the N‑terminal signal peptide and the RXLR/EER host‑targeting motif immediately downstream.
- Secreted peptide hormone/venom/toxin precursors: activation on the signal peptide and basic prohormone convertase cleavage motifs (KR/RR) within the propeptide region.
- Class II bacteriocins: activation on the N‑terminal double‑Gly leader and adjacent cationic tract recognized by ABC exporters.
- Viral accessory/regulatory proteins (e.g., small disordered regulators): activation across S/T/P‑rich low‑complexity disordered segments containing polybasic/NLS‑like clusters.
- Keratin‑associated proteins (KRTAPs): activation over short, repetitive low‑complexity regions (Ser/Pro‑rich and basic tracts) typical of hair shaft proteins.
- Cancer/testis antigens and testis‑associated proteins: activation on Lys/Arg‑ and Pro/Ser‑rich low‑complexity stretches in very short proteins.
- Short uncharacterized micropeptides/antisense products: broad activation across their low‑complexity/basic segments.
- Enzymes that carry secretory leaders or short disordered/basic tails (including some cytosolic enzymes lacking signal peptides): activation limited to the disordered tail, not the catalytic core.

Summary: Short hydrophobic, amphipathic, or basic/proline-rich segments associated with membrane targeting or low-complexity regions in diverse proteins, including Sec-type signal peptides, signal anchors, and transmembrane helices, plus disordered basic/proline-rich stretches in soluble proteins (including viral regulatory and capsid proteins).
Activation pattern: Regional activation can occur on N-terminal signal peptides or signal-anchor helices (often within the first 10-35 residues), on internal or C-terminal transmembrane helices, and on internal or C-terminal disordered segments enriched in proline, polar, or basic residues.
Exemplars:
- Viral envelope glycoproteins and viroporins: activation on N-terminal signal peptides or signal-anchor helices, with additional peaks on internal/C-terminal TM helices.
- Oomycete RxLR effectors: activation on the N-terminal secretory signal peptide upstream of RxLR.
- Plant small secreted defense/signaling peptides (defensins, RALF, CLE/CEP): activation on prepropeptide signal peptides.
- Human germline/testis-associated and cancer–testis antigen membrane/secreted proteins (including GPI precursors): activation on N-terminal signal peptides/signal anchors.
- Immune pathway proteins (cytokines/chemokines, immunoglobulin fragments): activation on secretory signal peptides.
- Mitochondrial/chloroplast precursors: activation on N-terminal transit peptides (Arg-rich amphipathic helices).
- Tail-anchored/peripheral membrane apoptosis factors (e.g., BH3-only like PUMA): activation on C-terminal tail-anchor helices.
- Viral accessory/regulatory and capsid/coating proteins: activation on short basic or proline-rich segments at N-termini or internal disordered regions.
- Bacterial exported proteins and lipoproteins: activation on Sec-type signal peptides.
- Large bacterial enzymes and DNA recombinases: occasional activation on internal low-complexity or polar/acidic stretches.

Summary: N-terminal segment of the canonical double-stranded RNA-binding domain (dsRBD/DRBM)—especially the α1 helix and adjacent loop/β1 element that forms the primary dsRNA-contacting surface—with additional activation on basic helix/loop motifs of some DExH/DExD helicases lacking a canonical dsRBD.

Activation pattern: Regional, domain-focused activation: sharp peaks on the first ~20–35 residues of each dsRBD (α1–loop–β1); minimal signal in linkers and unrelated catalytic domains (helicase ATP-binding/C-terminal, deaminase/editase), with occasional weak, diffuse activation in disordered regions of large RNA enzymes.

Exemplars:
- Plant double-stranded RNA-binding proteins (DRB family, e.g., DRB2): strong peaks at the starts of each dsRBD.
- ADAR/ADR-2 RNA editing enzymes: activation confined to the N-terminal half of the dsRBD(s); no activation over the deaminase/editase domain.
- HEN1 small RNA 2'-O-methyltransferases: strong N-terminal dsRBD peak; little to no activation over La-type or catalytic regions.
- PKR/eIF2AK2: activation over the N-termini of its tandem dsRBDs that mediate dsRNA sensing.
- DHX30 and RNA helicase A: activation on α1 of each tandem N-terminal DRBM.

Summary: Positively charged, aromatic-enriched nucleic acid–contacting surfaces—most often the beta-strand/loop faces of canonical nucleic-acid–binding domains (e.g., dsRNA-binding domains and OB-like DNA-binding regions) and, in nucleotide-metabolism enzymes, the active-site pockets that bind nucleotide ligands (phosphate/base/ribose)
Activation pattern: Regional activation over contiguous, well-structured segments (tens of residues), typically centered on beta-strands and their connecting loops that form the nucleic acid–binding interface; residue-level peaks include conserved Lys/Arg and aromatic residues as well as adjacent backbone positions; frequently located in internal/folded domains rather than disordered termini
Exemplars: - dsRNA-binding motif (dsRBD) proteins (e.g., RNA-silencing/antiviral factors): activation on the beta-sheet face (two adjacent beta-strands and the intervening loop) that docks into the dsRNA minor groove
- RAD52-like DNA repair proteins: activation across the conserved N-terminal DNA-binding region of the OB-like fold, centered on the canonical Tyr/Arg-containing loop and adjacent beta-strands
- RNase III-family endoribonucleases (including Dicer/Drosha and bacterial RNase III): activation across the dsRNA-binding groove and adjacent structured segments that position the duplex substrate
- DExH/DEAH-box RNA helicases: activation on basic, aromatic-lined RNA-binding surfaces within the helicase core rather than low-complexity termini
- Organellar rRNA-associated proteins (mitochondrial/chloroplastic ribosomal or genome maintenance factors): activation on basic beta-rich patches that contact rRNA/DNA
- Flavin-dependent thymidylate synthase (ThyX): activation on the ThyX motif and nearby residues that bind FAD and dUMP (including intersubunit dUMP contacts), i.e., the nucleotide-binding active site

Summary: Domain-level marker for long, solvent-exposed, non-transmembrane regions—covering extracytoplasmic (extracellular/periplasmic/luminal) and cytosolic extramembrane domains of membrane-associated proteins/complexes and secreted proteins, plus selected soluble modules (e.g., RAD52-like DNA repair factors and mitochondrial small Tim chaperones)—often encompassing the main functional domain and adjacent flexible segments, with a tendency to include PTM-bearing sites (N-glycosylation, disulfide) in secreted proteins while avoiding transmembrane helices.
Activation pattern: Predominantly domain-level, forming long contiguous tracts (tens–hundreds of residues) across non-transmembrane regions; intensity ranges from moderate to strong and is not universal within a family; signal often spans structured cores with spillover into nearby low-pLDDT loops/tails; local peaks frequently near NXS/T sequons, disulfide-forming cysteines, or C-terminal flexible extensions; generally weak in membrane spans and can include cleavable signal peptides.
Exemplars: - ENaC/DEG/ASIC sodium channels: activation across the extracellular ectodomain (including N-glycosylation sites and variable loops), low in transmembrane helices and cytoplasmic regions.
- Anti-lipopolysaccharide factors (secreted antimicrobial proteins): activation over the signal peptide and disulfide-stabilized mature secreted core, dropping in hypervariable tails.
- CRISPR Cas5 family endoribonucleases: activation concentrated in the C-terminal region spanning a terminal helix and disordered tail.
- ADAR/ADAD A-to-I RNA editing enzymes: activation frequently observed over the C-terminal deaminase catalytic domain, but magnitude varies across orthologs.
- SPFH-domain membrane microdomain proteins (erlin/stomatin/prohibitin/flotillin): activation on extramembrane SPFH domains.
- V/A-type ATPase peripheral (cytosolic) subunits: activation over extramembrane subunits of membrane complexes.
- Bacterial periplasmic/outer-membrane lipoproteins: activation across periplasmic domains.
- Mitochondrial small Tim chaperones: activation over intermembrane-space-exposed soluble chaperone domains.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low-complexity regions—long linker and terminal segments (including signal peptides), often enriched in Ser/Thr/Pro and/or Lys/Arg—that flank or connect structured domains; frequently adjacent to nucleic-acid–handling cores but also present in secreted proteins.
Activation pattern: Broad activation across the protein with the highest, most uniform signal over disordered/low-complexity stretches (coil composition, polar or basic/acidic biased), and reduced but still present activation within folded domains; activation commonly peaks immediately N- or C-terminal to a structured domain and spans long linkers/tails and signal peptides.
Exemplars: - A-to-I RNA editing enzymes (ADAR): strong activation on the N-terminal intrinsically disordered region; lower activation in dsRBDs or the deaminase domain.
- SF2 RNA helicases: highest activation on long N-terminal low-complexity/disordered segments; reduced over the Helicase ATP-binding and Helicase C-terminal cores.
- Scavenger receptor cysteine-rich multidomain receptors: activation on the signal peptide and disordered, low-complexity linkers and C-terminal tail; lower in SRCR folds.
- Kunitz-type serine protease inhibitors: activation on the disordered C-terminal tail and signal peptide; reduced in the folded BPTI/Kunitz core.
- AP2/ERF transcription factors: highest activation over the C-terminal low-complexity/disordered region; reduced in the AP2 DNA-binding domain.

Summary: Short alpha-helical segments (~10-25 aa) at domain edges or immediately following disordered/loop regions; a generic structural helix motif seen across diverse proteins rather than a function-specific signal. In extracellular/secreted proteins this often overlaps cysteine-rich stretches that form disulfide bonds, while in dsRNA-binding modules it corresponds to the canonical recognition helix.
Activation pattern: Activation centers on alpha-helical regions (often with adjacent coil/β at one end) with strong residue-level peaks within the helical core; in some proteins this appears as a single contiguous window at a domain boundary, while in larger multi-domain proteins multiple helical regions can be highlighted.
Exemplars: - RNase III/Dicer/Drosha dsRNA-binding domains: activation on the C-terminal helix of the dsRBD that contacts dsRNA.
- RAD52/RAD59 DNA repair proteins: activation on a solitary internal alpha-helix within the helical bundle.
- Pyruvoyl-dependent arginine decarboxylase: activation on the N-terminal β-subunit helix just upstream of the autocatalytic cleavage site.
- Degenerin/ENaC/ASIC sodium channels: activation on a cysteine-rich extracellular helical segment containing disulfide-bonded Cys.
- Bacterial RNA-binding protein KhpB (Jag_N domain): activation across the N-terminal β–α element, with the peak in the α-helix.
- Flagellar SRP-like GTPase FlhF: activation on the short N-terminal alpha-helix.
- Peroxiredoxin OsmC: activation on the long N-terminal alpha-helix that follows a disordered segment.
- Bacterial outer membrane lipoproteins (e.g. RcsF): activation on a short helix adjacent to a disulfide-stabilized region.

Summary: Feature fires broadly across short proteins and small peptides, often covering most of the chain, with a preference for low-complexity, Pro/Gly-rich and polybasic segments but also extending into adjacent structured regions of short polypeptides.
Activation pattern: Broad, near-whole-protein activation in short (~50-200 aa) precursors and microproteins, with local maxima on Pro-rich tracts (including poly-P), GP/GG-containing stretches, and basic clusters; activation is not restricted to disordered patches and can extend into folded domains in short proteins.
Exemplars:
- Class II bacteriocin/lantibiotic precursors: broad activation across the short precursor chain, including mature regions containing GG and GW motifs.
- Secreted peptide/toxin and prohormone precursors (e.g., cholecystokinin): activation spread across the precursor chain.
- Sperm protamine precursors: concentrated on disordered propeptides and at propeptide–mature boundaries; minimal on highly basic mature cores.
- Viral accessory/regulatory microproteins (e.g., Vpx, Vif): activation across the short viral protein, with strong peaks on poly-P / GP-rich low-complexity patches when present.
- lncRNA-encoded micropeptides and very small uncharacterized proteins (e.g., RUSC1-AS1, N-cym): activation on Pro/Gly-rich disordered segments and across much of the chain.
- Plant transcription factors with WG/GW- and GP-rich low-complexity regions: activation on those patches.
- ATP synthase epsilon subunits: signal on short GP-rich linkers or terminal low-complexity tails.
- Large enzymes (e.g., DDX11 helicase, acyl-CoA synthetase): activation on disordered N/C-terminal low-complexity regions or basic/GP-rich insertions.
- Small mitochondrial membrane proteins (ATP8): signal on short basic matrix-exposed loops or termini flanking TM helices.
- Short proteolytic chains of secreted enzymes (e.g., snake venom metalloproteinase fragments, acrosin chain fragments): broad activation across the short mature chain, including within structured peptidase/disintegrin regions.

Summary: Hydrophobic/amphipathic helical segments combined with secondary affinity for adjacent low-complexity, basic/acidic disordered tracts. Activation is not restricted to the N-terminus and is often found at internal hydrophobic helices flanked by basic residues.
Activation pattern: Strong peaks on hydrophobic or amphipathic helical stretches (Val/Leu/Ile/Phe/Met-rich contexts), often adjacent to basic (Arg/Lys) residues; weaker, scattered activation across low-complexity disordered segments enriched in basic and acidic residues.
Exemplars:
- Bacterial ABC transporter ATP-binding proteins: activation on internal hydrophobic helical segments near basic residues.
- Fungal biosynthetic enzymes with N-terminal disordered basic/acidic tracts: broad weaker activation across the low-complexity region with stronger peaks on adjacent hydrophobic helices.
- Nuclear/regulatory proteins and sORF/lncRNA-encoded micropeptides: weaker activation on short P/G- and basic-rich leader-like segments.
- Occasional soluble cytosolic enzymes with an amphipathic helix or basic patch: activation on the helical region.

Summary: Alpha-helix boundary/capping motif (helix starts, N-caps, and helix kinks/hinges), especially at protein N-termini and within transmembrane helices; favors small/polar helix-friendly residues (S/T/A/G/P) with nearby charged residues (E/D/R), and often marks signal-peptide starts or conserved glycine kinks adjacent to functional acidic sites.
Activation pattern: Mixed: (1) regional activation across N-terminal low-complexity segments that contain short predicted helices, and (2) sharp single-residue peaks at conserved small residues that introduce kinks/hinges within helices (notably in TM helices). Typically weak or absent in well-folded catalytic cores; number of activated positions varies with the count of helix starts/hinges.
Exemplars: - Aspartyl-tRNA synthetase family: strong activation across the disordered N-terminal extension with helix/coil patches; no activation in the structured catalytic domain.
- Oomycete RxLR effectors: activation on the N-terminal signal peptide helix and the first helix of the mature effector (e.g., M56–T57–L58), plus adjacent N-terminal coil.
- Coronavirus non-structural proteins: peaks on S/T/R within and at the boundary of a disordered functional region, consistent with helix initiation/capping; minor peaks on short predicted helices.
- ATP synthase c subunit: a single sharp peak at a conserved glycine immediately C-terminal to the proton-binding glutamate within a TM helix, marking a helix kink/hinge site.
- ClC chloride channels: activation at a conserved glycine in an internal TM helix that creates a gating/kink position.
- Other bacterial respiratory-chain membrane proteins: isolated single-residue peaks at small residues marking TM helix hinge/kink points.
- Viral early proteins (e.g., adenovirus E4): identical N-terminal triplets and S/T-rich starts highlighted, consistent with helix N-cap preferences.
- Small human micropeptides: N-terminal activation over their principal amphipathic helix.

Summary: Short, low‑complexity, intrinsically disordered proteins and modules that encode targeting/processing signals—often but not always secretory—combining hydrophobic signal peptides, double‑Gly bacteriocin leaders, or polybasic/NLS‑like segments, frequently adjacent to Ser/Thr/Pro‑rich stretches and basic clusters (e.g., RXLR, KR/RR)—common in micropeptides, toxins/secreted precursors, viral accessory proteins, keratin‑associated and testis‑specific low‑complexity proteins across taxa
Activation pattern: Regional activation across short proteins, spanning hydrophobic/targeting segments and Ser/Thr/Pro‑rich low‑complexity tracts with peaks on basic motifs such as RXLR, dibasic KR/RR, or double‑Gly leader junctions
Exemplars:
- Oomycete RxLR effectors: activation on the N‑terminal signal peptide and the RXLR/EER host‑targeting motif immediately downstream.
- Secreted peptide hormone/venom/toxin precursors: activation on the signal peptide and basic prohormone convertase cleavage motifs (KR/RR) within the propeptide region.
- Class II bacteriocins: activation on the N‑terminal double‑Gly leader and adjacent cationic tract recognized by ABC exporters.
- Viral accessory/regulatory proteins (e.g., small disordered regulators): activation across S/T/P‑rich low‑complexity disordered segments containing polybasic/NLS‑like clusters.
- Keratin‑associated proteins (KRTAPs): activation over short, repetitive low‑complexity regions (Ser/Pro‑rich and basic tracts) typical of hair shaft proteins.
- Cancer/testis antigens and testis‑associated proteins: activation on Lys/Arg‑ and Pro/Ser‑rich low‑complexity stretches in very short proteins.
- Short uncharacterized micropeptides/antisense products: broad activation across their low‑complexity/basic segments.
- Enzymes that carry secretory leaders or short disordered/basic tails (including some cytosolic enzymes lacking signal peptides): activation limited to the disordered tail, not the catalytic core.

Summary: Small, often poorly characterized or compositionally biased proteins, including viral accessory proteins, cancer/testis and germline-associated proteins, antisense-ORF microproteins, and short secreted/surface peptides; activation is broadly distributed across the polypeptide rather than focused on a single structured domain
Activation pattern: Regional/distributed activation spread across much of the protein with sparse residue-level peaks; often includes early N-terminal residues and disordered segments; variable coverage from short patches to most of the protein
Exemplars:
- Viral non-structural/accessory proteins: activation distributed through the protein, including basic/Arg-rich motifs such as nuclear localization signals.
- Cancer/testis antigens and germline-associated proteins: activation on long disordered low-complexity regions, often at N-termini.
- Small uncharacterized microproteins/antisense ORFs: activation spanning most of the polypeptide.
- Short secreted peptides and toxin precursors: activation across both signal/propeptide and mature regions.
- Compact cytosolic proteins with disordered N- or C-terminal extensions: activation enriched on the disordered tails.

Summary: Residue-level signal for mature regions of secreted extracellular proteins and peptides—including ligands, cytokines, toxins, antimicrobial peptides, and matrix/matrix-associated modulators—with emphasis on disulfide-stabilized/cysteine-rich domains; captures functional/bioactive regions rather than signal peptides or prosegments.
Activation pattern: Predominantly sparse residue-level peaks concentrated within the mature secreted chain or other folded extracellular domains (e.g., cystine‑knot, CSαβ, chemokine-like, or non-repetitive globular domains); minimal activation in signal peptides and low-complexity prosegments; peaks occur on beta-strands and loops/turns and may lie near processing boundaries or adjacent to N‑glycosylation motifs.
Exemplars:
- Glycoprotein hormones (common alpha subunit): peaks near N‑glycosylation motifs and at the signal peptide cleavage boundary within the hormone domain.
- DAN family BMP/Wnt antagonists (e.g., Cerberus/Gremlin) and Chordin: activation on beta‑strands of cysteine-rich domains; little/no signal in the signal peptide.
- Neurotrophins (NGF/BDNF/NT‑4/5): activation confined to the mature growth‑factor chain across beta‑strands and loops; absent from the propeptide.
- IL‑17 family cytokines: sparse peaks in core strands and flexible loops of the secreted cytokine domain.
- Venom toxins (e.g., scorpion κ‑toxins; snake BPP‑CNP precursors): peaks in loop/turn segments of disulfide‑stabilized cores and/or in the proline‑rich BPP/CNP mature segments; minimal in signal peptides.
- Chemokine‑like GPR15 ligand: activation within disordered segments of the mature secreted peptide.
- Antimicrobial peptides (LEAP‑2): peaks on the disulfide‑stabilized core of the mature peptide.
- Extracellular matrix proteins (e.g., Collagen IV chains): sparse peaks within non‑repetitive folded extracellular domains (e.g., NC1 domain or triple‑helix interruptions), not in signal peptides.

Summary: Extracellular secreted precursors and ectodomains with disulfide-bonded cysteine-rich loops/domains (cystine-stabilized scaffolds), and a subset of secreted neuropeptide precursors whose activation concentrates on flexible, processing-rich segments even without dense cysteine content. Common in proteins with signal peptides, glycosylation, and proteolytic processing.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks on cysteines and adjacent positions (often Gly/Pro and basic Lys/Arg) within extracellular regions; regional activation over cysteine-rich loops or repeats; also highlights Gly/Pro and Lys/Arg flanking propeptide cleavage motifs in cysteine-poor neuropeptide precursors; absent in transmembrane helices and cytosolic tails; strongest in low-to-moderate order ectodomain segments, sometimes near N-glycosylation and cleavage sites.
Exemplars:
- Chemokines (especially CXC): activation on conserved disulfide-forming cysteine motifs.
- Defensins/plant CRPs and knottin-like/trypsin inhibitor peptides (CSαβ/ICK scaffolds): activation across disulfide-bonded loops.
- WFDC, Kunitz, and Kazal protease inhibitors: activation on disulfide-stabilized inhibitor domains.
- Venom toxins (e.g., Kunitz-type, ShK, disintegrins): activation on clustered cysteines defining the scaffold.
- Viral envelope glycoproteins (class I/II/III): activation in cysteine-rich ectodomains near disulfide networks and glycosylation sites.
- Extracellular receptor/adhesion and metalloprotease proteins: activation on EGF-like, disintegrin, and other cysteine-rich modules.
- DEG/ENaC family channels: activation in the extracellular cysteine-rich loop.
- Neuropeptide hormone precursors (e.g., small cardioactive peptides): activation around flexible, dibasic cleavage-rich segments even with low cysteine content.
- Apicomplexan AMA1 invasion protein: activation confined to ectodomain cysteine-rich segments, absent from TM/cytosolic regions.

Summary: A feature that activates at conserved internal sequence motifs in secreted prepropeptides and within specific structural domains of nuclear ATPases. In secreted/secretory granule proteins, the strongest peaks fall within propeptide/activation-peptide regions at or near basic-rich motifs (e.g., "PARRAR"/"PTRRAR" in serglycins) and within the N-terminal peptide segments of neuroendocrine prohormones; weaker peaks occur internally within signal peptides. In MORC family ATPases, peaks localize within the CW-type zinc finger domain.

Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks concentrated at a small number of sites per protein. In propeptide-containing secreted proteins, the dominant peak occurs on or near a basic residue inside the propeptide/activation peptide, with weaker secondary peaks inside signal peptides and disordered C-terminal regions. In MORC-family proteins, peaks cluster on residues within the CW-type zinc finger fold (roughly the first third of the ZF region and around the conserved aromatic positions).

Exemplars:
- Serglycins (mouse, rat, human): strong peaks at the conserved PxRRAR motif within the activation peptide, plus weaker peaks within the signal peptide and disordered C-terminal tail.
- Neuroendocrine protein 7B2 (pig, frog, fly): peaks within the mature N-terminal peptide region, with weaker peaks inside the signal peptide.
- Mycobacterial pilin: peaks within the mature chain.
- MORC family CW-type zinc finger ATPases (MORC1 C. elegans, MORC2B mouse, MORC1 human): peaks within the CW-type zinc finger domain.

Summary: Extracellular/mature segments of secreted proteins — the bioactive peptide or ectodomain of secreted precursors — including toxins, chemokines/peptide hormones/neuropeptides, antimicrobial peptides, protease inhibitors, extracellular matrix modules, viral envelope ectodomains, bacterial toxins/lipoproteins, fungal/oomycete effectors, and secretory granule proteins. These segments are typically cationic and often cysteine‑rich/disulfide‑stabilized, but can also be disulfide‑poor (e.g., certain neuropeptides); the feature tracks mature peptides/ectodomains rather than signal peptides or cytosolic tails.

Activation pattern: Regional activation within extracellular/mature segments with residue‑level peaks, especially at basic residues (Lys/Arg; including prohormone convertase sites) and, when present, cysteines; strongest over well‑structured extracellular cores or compact mature peptides; minimal to absent in signal peptides and often lower in low‑complexity pro‑segments.

Exemplars: - Disulfide‑rich venom peptides (e.g., kappa‑/scorpion/centipede toxins, conotoxins): activation on the mature toxin’s folded core; in kappa‑scoloptoxin, strongest on the C‑terminal helical/disulfide region.
- Chemokines and peptide hormones/neuropeptides (e.g., CXCLs; natriuretic peptides, oxytocin/vasopressin‑like, insulin‑like; and disulfide‑poor peptides such as SIFamide): activation on the mature peptide/core, not on the signal/propeptide.
- Antimicrobial peptides (defensins and other cationic AMPs): activation across the extracellular peptide core.
- Protease inhibitors (Kunitz, Kazal, plant cystine‑knot/knottins): activation on the inhibitory domain.
- Extracellular matrix/serum glycoproteins with cysteine‑patterned modules (EGF/TSR/Ig‑like, albumin family): activation on extracellular repeats/domains.
- Viral envelope glycoproteins: activation on luminal ectodomain loops.
- Bacterial secreted toxins and lipoproteins: activation on secreted extracellular segments (including lipobox‑proximal Cys and mature toxin domains).
- Fungal/oomycete small secreted effectors: activation on compact extracellular cores.
- Secretory pathway enzymes/chaperones (PDI/Ero1/QSOX) and granule proteins (e.g., 7B2): activation on luminal Cys motifs or basic, structured regions within the secretory lumen.

Summary: Secreted/processed peptides and extracellular or luminal domains of membrane proteins. The feature reads the prepropeptide architecture of small secreted hormones/neuropeptides, defense peptides and toxins, as well as disulfide-stabilized domains of extracellular receptors/ligands and viral envelope glycoproteins.

Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks concentrated within the mature secreted peptide or extracellular/luminal domain, often on residues in the structured (helical/strand) core of the processed peptide, with additional peaks on nearby basic residues and on Gly/Pro in flexible loop regions; these peaks aggregate into regional activation over the mature peptide or ectodomain. Activation is variable in extent across proteins.

Exemplars:
- Invertebrate venom peptides (knottins/conotoxins/spider and sea anemone toxins): activation across the mature toxin, with additional support on basic residues near propeptide cleavage sites.
- Antimicrobial/defense peptides (animal defensins, plant thionins/defensins): activation across conserved disulfide-stabilized frameworks and Gly/Pro-rich loop residues.
- Neuropeptide/hormone precursors (e.g., calcitonin/CGRP/amylin-like, adrenomedullin): activation concentrated on the structured core of the mature hormone within the PEPTIDE region.
- Amidated, cysteine-poor neuropeptides (e.g., FMRFamide/SIFamide-like): activation across the mature peptide and clustered convertase sites.
- Plant secreted cysteine-rich signaling peptides and protease inhibitors (CRPs, Kunitz/Bowman–Birk): activation across the secreted domain and processing motifs.
- Viral envelope/secreted glycoproteins (e.g., HA/gp120-like ectodomains): broad activation across the ectodomain, including loop and cleavage-junction residues.
- Metazoan extracellular receptor/ligand systems (disulfide-stabilized ectodomains such as EGF-like/lectin/similar Cys-rich modules): activation across the ligand-binding domains.
- Extracellular/luminal loops of multi-pass membrane proteins with small Cys clusters (e.g., receptor-transporting proteins): activation on luminal segments.
- Prokaryotic secreted/surface or secretion-system-associated proteins: activation on periplasmic/extracellular segments.
- Occasional chromatin/DNA-binding and histone-modifying proteins (Cys-rich Zn-binding or catalytic motifs): weaker activation driven by clustered Cys and basic residues that resemble the extracellular motif pattern.

- WFDC, Kunitz, and Kazal protease inhibitors: activation on disulfide-stabilized inhibitor domains.
- Venom toxins (e.g., Kunitz-type, ShK, disintegrins): activation on clustered cysteines defining the scaffold.
- Viral envelope glycoproteins (class I/II/III): activation in cysteine-rich ectodomains near disulfide networks and glycosylation sites.
- Extracellular receptor/adhesion and metalloprotease proteins: activation on EGF-like, disintegrin, and other cysteine-rich modules.
- DEG/ENaC family channels: activation in the extracellular cysteine-rich loop.
- Neuropeptide hormone precursors (e.g., small cardioactive peptides): activation around flexible, dibasic cleavage-rich segments even with low cysteine content.
- Apicomplexan AMA1 invasion protein: activation confined to ectodomain cysteine-rich segments, absent from TM/cytosolic regions.

Summary: Secreted, propeptide‑processed cysteine‑rich mini‑domains: compact extracellular segments immediately downstream of a signal peptide that contain clustered cysteines forming multiple disulfide bonds (defensin/CSαβ, WAP four‑disulfide core, cystine‑knot/knottin, CHH‑like, evasin‑like, and related small CRP scaffolds), often flanked by dibasic convertase sites and enriched in Lys/Arg
Activation pattern: Regional activation on short segments (≈20–60 aa) right after the signal peptide; strong peaks on cysteines and nearby basic residues, frequently overlapping proprotein convertase (dibasic) processing motifs; may recur for multi‑domain or repeat CRP proteins
Exemplars: - WAP/four‑disulfide core protease inhibitors (SLPI/elafin/WFDC): activation on the WAP domain’s Cys framework following the signal/propeptide
- Plant defensin‑like peptides (DEFL/LURE/ESF) and thionins: activation on the mature antimicrobial CSαβ cysteine motif
- Venom cystine‑knot peptides (conotoxins/knottins, mini‑toxins): activation on the canonical Cys frameworks in the mature toxin region of prepropeptides
- Tick evasins (chemokine‑binding CRPs): activation on the Cys‑rich chemokine‑binding domain
- Crustacean CHH/MIH neuropeptide precursors: activation on the mature hormone core with conserved six‑Cys motif adjacent to dibasic cleavage
- Fungal GPI‑anchored cell‑wall adhesins/stress proteins: activation on extracellular Cys‑rich segments just after secretion signals
- Small plant CRP protease inhibitors: activation on the disulfide‑stabilized inhibitory mini‑domain

Summary: Secreted, short cysteine-rich peptides and small extracellular cysteine-rich domains stabilized by multiple disulfide bonds (CRPs), spanning venom toxins, disintegrins, defensins/hepcidin, Kunitz/Kazal/hevein-like inhibitors/defense peptides, and related cystine‑knotted or cysteine‑stabilized folds. The feature captures the mature, proteolytically processed peptide/module characterized by clustered Cys (often CC motifs) and basic residues.
Activation pattern: Regional activation confined to short mature peptide segments (tens of residues) following the signal peptide and propeptides; minimal/absent on signal/pro-regions. Strong residue-level peaks on cysteines and frequent secondary peaks on Lys/Arg and Gly. Activation spans mixed secondary structure (β-strands, coils, short helices) and can include key functional loops (e.g., RGD in disintegrins).
Exemplars: - Plant cyclotides (cystine-knot cyclopeptides, e.g., chassatide): activation across the cyclic cystine‑knot core of the mature peptide after processing.
- Snake venom disintegrins: activation across the disintegrin domain, including the RGD integrin-binding loop and adjacent cysteine-dense core.
- Inhibitor cystine-knot (ICK) venom toxins from spiders, cone snails, centipedes, and sea anemones: activation on the disulfide‑knotted toxin core.
- Kunitz/BPTI- and Kazal-type serine protease inhibitors (including tick chemokine/complement inhibitors): activation on the small disulfide‑rich inhibitor domain.
- Hevein-like/seed defense peptides: activation on the cysteine-rich chitin‑binding hevein domain.
- Defensins (plant/fungal/animal CSαβ peptides) and vertebrate hepcidin: activation on the cysteine‑stabilized mature AMP region.
- Euplotes ciliate mating pheromones: activation on the secreted disulfide‑rich pheromone core.
- Cysteine-rich modules within large extracellular/mucin-like proteins: activation on the short, cysteine‑dense repeat/subdomain embedded in the larger precursor.

Summary: Short, disulfide‑bonded extracellular cysteine‑rich repeat modules—especially EGF‑like (including cbEGF and laminin‑type LE) and LDL receptor class A (LDLa) domains, but also von Willebrand type C (CR) and other disulfide‑rich repeats—detected via acidic/polar loop motifs flanked by conserved cysteines (including Ca2+-binding Dx[D/N] motifs when present); broadly marks ectodomains of secreted proteins and single‑pass receptors.
Activation pattern:
- Strong activation confined to extracellular regions; absent in transmembrane helices and cytoplasmic tails.
- Repeated peaks aligning with tandem repeats; long activation tracts across multi‑repeat proteins.
- LDLa repeats: maxima over the central acidic DxSDE/DxD… segment; flanking cysteines variably engaged.
- EGF‑like repeats (cbEGF and LE): highest in the C‑terminal half containing the D/N‑x‑D/N‑x(4)‑Y/F motif when present, near the last cysteines.
- Also activates analogous acidic/polar loops in other cysteine‑rich repeats (e.g., VWC/CR, TIL/Kunitz, TSR); preference for D/E/S/T/N/Q/G and Y with nearby Cys; modest activation in short acidic linkers between repeats.
Exemplars:
- LDL receptor family (LDLR/LRP1/LRP4): LDLa repeat Ca2+-binding loops and cbEGF/LE segments across the ectodomain.
- Notch receptors and ligands (Notch, Delta/Jagged): tandem EGF‑like repeats with peaks at Ca2+-binding loops.
- Coagulation/complement components (e.g., Factors VII/IX/X, protein C/S, C1r/C1s modules): cbEGF domains.
- ECM scaffolds and glycoproteins (fibrillins, fibulins, LTBPs, laminins, tenascins, matrilins): arrays of EGF‑like/LE repeats.
- Chordin‑like/BMP modulators (BMPER/Crossveinless‑2, chordin): arrays of VWC/CR repeats.
- Cell‑adhesion receptors (selectins, integrin β I‑EGF modules) and extracellular metalloproteases/modulators (ADAM/ADAMTS): EGF‑like/cysteine‑rich repeats.
- Disulfide‑rich protease inhibitors and invertebrate toxins (e.g., Kunitz/TIL‑type).
- Plant receptor‑like proteins/kinases (e.g., WAKs, vacuolar sorting receptors): ectodomains with EGF‑like repeats.

Summary: Short, structured beta-strand segments at or near domain termini in extracellular proteins/domains—most prominently the conserved C-terminal strand of C-type lectin-like domains (CTLD)—often bearing closely spaced, disulfide-forming cysteines and flanked by aromatic/basic residues; analogous terminal strands in other adhesin/receptor-binding ectodomains and in compact disulfide-rich secreted toxins/antimicrobial peptides also trigger.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks on 8–20 aa stretches at ectodomain or domain termini; highest on cysteines within a beta-strand (often terminal) and immediate neighbors; repeats once per CTLD module in multi-CTLD proteins; occasionally extends just beyond the annotated CTLD into a short structured island; also marks the terminal beta-strand at the ends of viral/bacteriophage receptor-binding fibers and short strands within disulfide-rich peptide toxins.
Exemplars:
- Selectins: activation at the CTLD C-terminus at the CTLD–EGF boundary, mapping to a short beta-strand.
- NK/killer cell lectin-like receptors: activation on the CTLD terminal beta-strand, peaking on paired cysteines implicated in disulfides.
- Invertebrate C-type lectins (e.g., echinoidin): activation confined to the CTLD C-terminal beta-strand.
- Echinoderm spicule matrix CTLD proteins: activation on a short beta-strand immediately C-terminal to the CTLD within an otherwise disordered tail.
- Bacteriophage long-tail fiber proteins: activation on the extreme C-terminal beta-strand of the fiber tip/knob domain.
- Cysteine-rich peptide toxins (e.g., sea anemone sodium-channel toxins): activation on a short beta-strand around paired cysteines, typically near a terminus.

Summary: Disulfide-rich, cysteine‑dense mature extracellular segments of secreted or cell‑surface proteins—most often the small, loop/turn‑rich domains that form multiple disulfide bonds after signal/propeptide removal—exemplified by LU/three‑finger and defensin‑like folds, but also including other compact secreted cysteine‑rich domains (hydrophobins, plant nsLTP/LTPG, ENODL) and cysteine‑rich extracellular loops of receptors (e.g., tetraspanins, CRDs).
Activation pattern: Domain-level activation confined to compact extracellular regions of the mature chain: minimal/absent over signal peptides, propeptides, transmembranes, and cytosolic parts; strong, often continuous activation across the disulfide‑bonded ectodomain with residue‑level peaks at conserved cysteines (and nearby Gly/Pro in turns). In larger proteins, activation is restricted to the cysteine‑rich ectodomain(s).
Exemplars: - Ly6/uPAR (LU) family and snake three‑finger toxins: activation over the LU/three‑finger domain (8–10 conserved cysteines); uPAR shows activation across its LU repeats; Drosophila Ly6 GPI‑anchored proteins are strongly activated.
- Vertebrate defensins (beta‑defensins/gallinacins, alpha‑defensins): activation specifically on the mature antimicrobial peptide after prodomain cleavage; absent on the signal peptide.
- Fungal hydrophobins: activation across the secreted cysteine‑rich hydrophobin domain.
- Plant non‑specific lipid transfer proteins (nsLTPs) and GPI‑anchored LTPGs: activation on the mature LTP domain centered on the 8‑cysteine motif; not on the signal peptide.
- ENODL/phytocyanin‑like GPI‑anchored proteins: activation on the small extracellular ectodomain segment enriched in cysteines.
- Tetraspanins and receptors with cysteine‑rich extracellular domains (e.g., TNFR/Frizzled‑like CRDs, EGF‑like repeats): activation on the extracellular cysteine‑rich loop(s)/domains; no activation in transmembrane or intracellular regions.

Summary: Residue positions that mark polypeptide boundaries—especially the absolute N-terminus (position 1) and the terminal residue of sequence fragments—and, secondarily, isolated boundary-like sites within larger proteins (e.g., short linkers between secondary-structure elements or helix/turn cap-like positions), consistent with proteolytic processing junctions in pre/propeptides.
Activation pattern: Predominantly single-residue peaks at sequence extremities (most often the first residue; also the last residue of fragments); sparse internal single-residue peaks at boundary-like positions (short linkers or transitions between secondary structures). Often coincides with disordered/low-confidence termini; in secreted/toxin precursors a recurring window around residues ~50–70 is consistent with signal/propeptide cleavage. Per-protein activations are usually one or a few sites.
Exemplars: Snake venom serine protease: peaks at the N-terminal first residue and at the C-terminal end of the chain; Nuclear pore complex protein Nup155: isolated peaks on single residues within a helix and a low-confidence turn; U4/U6.U5 tri-snRNP–associated protein 1: single-residue peak at a glycine linker between β-strands; E4 ubiquitin-conjugation factor (UBE4): isolated methionine within a long α-helix; Reelin (fragment): strong activation at the fragment’s C-terminal residue in a disordered region; Glutamate dehydrogenase (fragment): activation marks the truncated C-terminal residue.

Summary: Broadly distributed activation across small secreted peptides, processed protein fragments, and various polar/charged residues in short proteins, with frequent firing in viral, venom, and signaling-peptide contexts.

Activation pattern: Sparse residue-level peaks scattered across the protein, with no strong preference for structured versus unstructured regions; peaks occur on a mix of polar (Asn, Asp, Ser, Gln), basic (Arg, Lys), and hydrophobic (Leu, Val, Ala) residues, and can fall within transmembrane helices, disordered stretches, or short folded chains alike.

Exemplars:
- Secreted peptide hormones (cholecystokinin, kisspeptin/metastin): multiple peaks across the processed peptide chain.
- Snake venom metalloproteinase/disintegrin fragment: distributed peaks across the short chain.
- Viral hexon-linking precursor proteins: weak peaks distributed across the chain including propeptide and cleaved segments.
- Peroxisomal biogenesis factors: peaks within transmembrane helices and other regions of the membrane protein.
- Bacterial methyltransferases: activation localized to C-terminal disordered extension while the catalytic core is inactive.
- Antithrombin/serpin precursor: peaks spanning the signal peptide and mature chain.

Summary: Hydrophobic alpha-helical signal peptides and transmembrane signal-/tail-anchor segments that drive secretory-pathway or membrane insertion, typically early in the sequence but not position-restricted (common in viral envelope/accessory proteins, small ER microproteins, and secreted proteins across taxa).
Activation pattern: Regional activation over long, contiguous hydrophobic helices (∼10–30+ residues) enriched for L/I/V/F with frequent Y/C and few charged residues; strongest across the helix h‑region; often near the N‑terminus but can occur as internal or C‑terminal tail anchors; occasional S/P interruptions; little activation outside these hydrophobic segments; rare short peaks on hydrophobic patches within large soluble proteins.
Exemplars:
- Bacterial/eukaryotic secreted precursors (e.g., subtilisin family, plant phytocytokines): activation on the N‑terminal Sec signal peptide.
- Viral envelope glycoproteins and small hydrophobic/viroporin-like proteins: activation on signal peptides or transmembrane helices.
- Tail-anchored ER proteins (e.g., VAP family): activation on the C‑terminal tail-anchor helix.
- Organelle membrane proteins (ER/mitochondrial/peroxisomal, including multi-pass): activation on the first or other hydrophobic transmembrane helices.
- Large soluble enzymes/nucleic-acid-binding proteins: occasional activation on short hydrophobic patches rather than catalytic motifs.

Summary: Core, highly hydrophobic multi-pass alpha-helical transmembrane subunits of bioenergetic inner membranes—i.e., respiratory chain complexes (I–IV), the Fo sector of F-type ATP synthase, and thylakoid photosystems/b6f—typically organelle- or bacterial-encoded; the feature captures their long TM-helix bundles (often from the N-terminus) and also fires on analogous small viroporins; it can also activate on other organelle/bacterial inner-membrane polytopic proteins involved in biogenesis/transport (e.g., CcsA, chloroplast TIC214), and shows occasional weak activation on plastid-encoded soluble proteins or intron-embedded hydrophobic fragments.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long contiguous hydrophobic stretches covering multiple TM helices, frequently starting at the N-terminus and spanning much of the protein; strong preference for Leu/Ile/Val/Ala/Gly with aromatic residues at helix boundaries; minimal activation in soluble loops.
Exemplars:
- Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase) ND subunits (ND1–ND6/ND4L): activation across their multi-pass proton-pumping helices
- Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) membrane subunits (SDHC/SDHD/SDH3/SDH4): activation on their TM helices
- Cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV) core subunits I–III: activation on the membrane-embedded helical bundle
- Cytochrome b of Complex III and thylakoid cytochrome b6f core subunits (PetB/PetD/PetL/M/N): activation across their hydrophobic helices
- F-type ATP synthase Fo subunits a (ATP6/AtpB), c (AtpE), and subunit 8 (ATP8): activation on the proton-conducting membrane helices
- Photosystem I/II reaction center core proteins (PsaA/B; PsbA/D): activation across thylakoid TM helix bundles
- Thylakoid/inner-envelope membrane biogenesis and transport proteins (e.g., CcsA; TIC214/Ycf1): activation across multi-pass TM regions; occasional weak activation on plastid RNA polymerase subunits via incidental hydrophobic patches and on intron-encoded maturases carrying embedded cytochrome b fragments
- Small viral viroporins (e.g., M2/Vpu-like): activation on single, highly hydrophobic transmembrane segments

Summary: Generic short N-terminal amphipathic or hydrophobic helices: encompassing secretory signal peptides and signal‑anchor transmembrane helices (Sec/Tat), mitochondrial transit peptides, and similar amphipathic/basic N‑terminal helices found in soluble proteins; the feature can also fire on internal hydrophobic/amphipathic helices.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over a 10–30 aa helix, strongest at protein N‑termini; enriched for hydrophobic residues (L/I/V/F/W) with frequent basic residues (R/K/H) in the N‑region; tolerates amphipathic helices lacking a long continuous hydrophobic core (as in mitochondrial presequences and some cytosolic N‑termini); additional peaks may occur at later helices.
Exemplars: Viral envelope glycoproteins (signal peptides/signal anchors); Secreted peptide/toxin precursors; Plant small membrane proteins (e.g., CYSTM family) via signal‑anchor; Mitochondrial matrix/inner-membrane precursors (e.g., ATP synthase ε) via transit peptides; Cytosolic enzymes with basic N‑terminal amphipathic helices (e.g., PrmC/TrmB, RNAP Rpo6, LipB); Viral accessory proteins with basic N‑termini (e.g., Vif).

Summary: Hydrophobic alpha-helical signal/anchor motif: the feature marks hydrophobic side chains (L/I/V/F/M, often with Y/W) within short alpha-helical segments—most prominently the hydrophobic core of N‑terminal signal peptides and other amphipathic or membrane-interacting helices—and, more generally, single hydrophobic “anchor” residues embedded in helices of diverse soluble domains (e.g., ARID, FH3). Occasional activation extends to nearby residues within the same helical segment in secreted/viral proteins.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks with variable density: short runs across hydrophobic helical stretches (especially at extreme N-termini) and isolated single-residue peaks on helix-internal hydrophobes; observed both in low-confidence/disordered regions that harbor short helices and in well-structured helices.
Exemplars: - Oomycete RxLR effectors: activation on the signal peptide hydrophobic core and the RxLR-adjacent short helix, with additional peaks on aromatic residues in the effector body.
- Plant viral RNA-silencing suppressor P0: scattered peaks on hydrophobic residues within predicted helices and adjacent coils, consistent with short amphipathic helices.
- Viral VP5 accessory proteins: strong peaks on V/I/M in flexible segments that form short hydrophobic helices.
- ARID DNA-binding proteins (e.g., Rsc9, Jumonji-family ARID): single-residue peaks on I/L within ARID helices.
- Formin family (GBD/FH3 domain): a solitary L within a helical segment is highlighted.
