- Wnt signaling modulator (Sclerostin): activation across the signal peptide; variants at the activated site affect secretion.
- Extracellular matrix glycoprotein (Tenascin): activation confined to the signal peptide, ending at chain start.
- Receptor‑like tyrosine kinase family member (PDGFR‑like): activation on the C‑terminal half of the signal peptide.
- Semaphorin: activation across the signal peptide with a sharp drop after cleavage.
- Glycoprotein hormone beta subunit (luteinizing hormone β): activation within the signal peptide, ending at cleavage.
- Adhesion GPCR (adhesion class): activation in the core and C‑terminal end of the signal peptide.
- Single‑pass receptor (secretory phospholipase A2 receptor): activation spanning the end of the signal peptide and the first residues of the mature ectodomain.

Summary: Classical cleaved secretory signal peptides (Sec/SPI) at the extreme N-terminus, with the feature specifically recognizing the hydrophobic, alpha-helical h‑region (preceded by a short Lys/Arg-rich n‑region) that targets proteins to the ER and is removed upon secretion.
Activation pattern: Regional activation restricted to the first ~15–25 residues at the N-terminus; strong, continuous signal across the hydrophobic helical core with residue-level peaks on Leu/Val/Ile/Phe/Ala; often preceded by one or more positively charged residues; activation tapers across the c‑region and drops sharply at/just after the signal peptidase cleavage site; essentially no activation in the mature/disordered propeptide or downstream domains, with only rare weak distal residues.
Exemplars: - Arthropod antimicrobial peptide precursors (e.g., ctenidins): activation on the N-terminal signal-peptide helix.
- Kininogen/bradykinin peptide precursors: activation confined to the signal peptide, absent from propeptide/peptide regions.
- Invertebrate neuropeptide/decapeptide precursors: activation on the N-terminal signal helix only.
- Plant small secreted peptide precursors (e.g., SCOOP-family) and cell-wall proteins: activation on the signal peptide preceding low-complexity regions.
- Oomycete RxLR effector precursors: activation on the signal peptide, not on RxLR/dEER motifs or disordered regions.
- Salivary proline-rich proteins/mucins: activation on the N-terminal secretion signal, not on the proline-rich mature chain.
- Milk caseins: activation on the cleaved signal peptide at the N-terminus.
- Seminal vesicle secreted proteins: activation on the N-terminal signal peptide with sharp loss at the mature chain start.

Summary: Hydrophobic/amphipathic helical segments combined with secondary affinity for adjacent low-complexity, basic/acidic disordered tracts. Activation is not restricted to the N-terminus and is often found at internal hydrophobic helices flanked by basic residues.
Activation pattern: Strong peaks on hydrophobic or amphipathic helical stretches (Val/Leu/Ile/Phe/Met-rich contexts), often adjacent to basic (Arg/Lys) residues; weaker, scattered activation across low-complexity disordered segments enriched in basic and acidic residues.
Exemplars:
- Bacterial ABC transporter ATP-binding proteins: activation on internal hydrophobic helical segments near basic residues.
- Fungal biosynthetic enzymes with N-terminal disordered basic/acidic tracts: broad weaker activation across the low-complexity region with stronger peaks on adjacent hydrophobic helices.
- Nuclear/regulatory proteins and sORF/lncRNA-encoded micropeptides: weaker activation on short P/G- and basic-rich leader-like segments.
- Occasional soluble cytosolic enzymes with an amphipathic helix or basic patch: activation on the helical region.

Summary: Short, charge-rich patches in intrinsically disordered regions, enriched in Lys/Arg with interspersed Gln/Gly/Ser/Thr and mixed acidic residues, typically of low structural order.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks in very short windows (2–10 aa), tightly clustered around basic K/R-Q-R motifs within disordered segments; multiple short peaks can occur in one protein; peaks coincide with low‑pLDDT, compositionally biased basic-and-acidic patches; activation is largely absent from structured domains.
Exemplars:
- HIV/SIV Virion infectivity factor (Vif): activation on a conserved K-Q-R-G basic patch in the C-terminal disordered region (~190–193).
- Bacterial ABC transporter ATP-binding proteins (e.g., ModC): activation on a polybasic K/R-rich patch within a C-terminal disordered, basic-and-acidic compositionally biased segment.
- Bacterial membrane-insertion sensor proteins (e.g., MifM): activation on an internal short basic K-S-K-R patch.
- Conotoxin precursors: activation on a basic/mixed-charge K-G-Q-R patch within the disordered propeptide region, not on the signal peptide.
- Transcriptional regulators and E3 ubiquitin ligases: activation on short polybasic or mixed-charge patches (NLS-like/basic clusters) in low-complexity disordered regions.
- IMPase/FBPase superfamily phosphatases: occasional internal peaks at conserved Ser/Thr-containing short loops (~85–110), reflecting the feature’s sensitivity to brief polar/charged motifs.

Summary: Short hydrophobic alpha-helical segments enriched in small aliphatic residues (A, V, I, L with frequent T/G), depleted of charged/aromatic residues—commonly the h‑region of Sec signal peptides, short transmembrane helices, and internal helix-forming hydrophobic patches in both membrane and soluble proteins; often N‑terminal but also internal/C‑terminal.
Activation pattern: Regional activation on contiguous hydrophobic clusters predicted as alpha‑helix, with sharp residue‑level peaks at A/V/I/L/T (often with G); observed in signal peptides, TM segments, and internal helices; occurs in both structured and disordered contexts (not restricted to low pLDDT).
Exemplars: Adenovirus E4‑ORF4 and HCV ARFP: internal hydrophobic helix‑prone stretches in small viral proteins; Oomycete RxLR effectors and yeast killer toxin precursors: strong activation on N‑terminal Sec signal peptides; Bacterial cytochrome c oxidase subunit 2 and DHHC palmitoyltransferases: activation on short transmembrane helices; Kdo transferase and OMA hydratase: activation on internal hydrophobic helices within soluble/peripheral membrane enzymes.

Summary: Polybasic, lysine‑rich low‑complexity intrinsically disordered segments (acidic‑poor and often N/T/S‑rich), frequently located near protein N‑termini; the feature highlights short basic patches/tracts rather than structured domains
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks on Lys that coalesce into short regional activation across disordered/basic patches; strongest in low‑pLDDT coils or low‑confidence helices, often near the N‑terminus, with neighboring N/T/S also elevated
Exemplars: - Viral accessory proteins (e.g., agnoproteins): strong peaks at terminal K and adjacent N in unstructured tails.
- Antimicrobial peptide precursors (e.g., Ixosin): activation within the mature cationic peptide on K/N, with weaker signals in the propeptide.
- ABC transporters: concentrated activation in an N‑terminal disordered, lysine‑rich segment immediately preceding the structured transporter domain.
- Telomere‑associated proteins: scattered peaks on K/N within low‑pLDDT coils across the sequence.
- Human intrinsically disordered regulatory proteins: multiple K‑centered peaks distributed across low‑confidence helices/coils.

Summary: Cysteine-centered motifs (single conserved Cys or short CC/CXC/CXXC clusters), often—but not exclusively—found in oxidizing/extracellular or periplasmic contexts, used for disulfide bonding, redox catalysis, metal/Fe–S coordination, or regulatory thiol switches. The feature captures a generic “cysteine presence/cluster” signal near N-termini or in disordered loops across diverse proteins, including cytosolic and nuclear factors.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks centered on cysteines; strongest when two or more Cys occur within 0–2 residues (CC/CXC/CXXC) and frequently just after signal or transit peptide cleavage. Moderate peaks also occur at single conserved cysteines in disordered/low-complexity segments or coiled coils, regardless of subcellular location.
Exemplars:
- Chemokines (CC/CXC): activation on the signature N-terminal CC/CXC motif.
- Defensin-like antimicrobial peptides and disulfide-rich toxins (cystine-knot, conotoxins): activation across tightly clustered cysteines.
- Extracellular disulfide domains (Kazal/Kunitz, EGF-like): activation on paired disulfide-forming cysteines.
- Thiol–disulfide oxidoreductases (DsbA, PDI, thioredoxin): activation on catalytic CXXC motifs.
- Membrane proteins/transporters (ABC transporters, channels): activation on cysteines in luminal/extracytosolic/periplasmic loops or near processed N-termini.
- Fe–S/metal-binding proteins (rubredoxin, assembly factors): activation on closely spaced cysteines that coordinate cofactors.
- Cytosolic/nuclear regulators (e.g., BH3-only proteins like PUMA; viral early proteins such as adenovirus E4-ORF6): activation on a single Cys or short CC/CXC in disordered regions.
- Housekeeping enzymes and ribosomal/translation proteins (e.g., tRNA methyltransferases, FAD synthase, mitochondrial ribosomal proteins): activation on incidental CC/CXC or conserved single cysteines that may mediate local redox/metal interactions.

Summary: Sec-dependent N-terminal signal peptides—the hydrophobic h-region and adjoining c-region/cleavage site—of exported proteins, especially in bacteria; captures both canonical SPase I signals (small residues S/T/A/G near the end) and SPase II lipoprotein signals (lipobox with a Cys at +1), i.e., generic secretory leader peptides for periplasm/outer-membrane/secreted proteins
Activation pattern: Regional activation confined to the extreme N-terminus (~residues 2–17) as a short, contiguous hydrophobic run; strong residue-level peaks in the hydrophobic core; sharp drop at the predicted signal peptidase cleavage boundary; no activation in the mature chain; often helical propensity and low structure-confidence typical of signal peptides
Exemplars: Secreted glycoside hydrolase (beta-porphyranase/GH16) — activation on its N-terminal signal peptide; AB-type toxin component (cytolethal distending toxin C) — N-terminal signal peptide; secreted metalloprotease (Karilysin) — N-terminal signal peptide; periplasmic disulfide isomerase (DsbG) — N-terminal signal peptide; periplasmic binding protein (TupA) — N-terminal signal peptide; surface adhesin — N-terminal signal peptide; outer membrane protein (OmpA-like beta-barrel) — N-terminal signal peptide; periplasmic c-type cytochrome (cytochrome c-552) — N-terminal signal peptide; phage exported protein (Spackle) — N-terminal signal peptide; periplasmic peptidase (D-Ala-D-Ala endopeptidase) — N-terminal signal peptide

Summary: Boundary at the C-terminal end of the N-terminal hydrophobic targeting segment—either a cleaved Sec/SPI signal peptide or an uncleaved signal-anchor transmembrane helix—marking the transition into the mature/structured domain across taxa.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks around positions ~15–35 at the hydrophobic-to-polar junction; for SPI signals, strongest at -1 with flanking -3/+1; for signal-anchors (no cleavage), peaks at the last 1–3 residues of the first TM helix and immediate downstream residues. Prefers small/hydrophobic residues in short local clusters; signal vanishes in the structured core.
Exemplars: - Secreted/periplasmic/outer-membrane proteins (TonB-dependent receptors, autotransporters, SBPs, secreted enzymes, toxins, cytochromes, photosynthetic lumenal proteins): activation at the Sec/SPI cleavage site.
- Inner-membrane proteins with N-terminal signal-anchor helices (e.g., F-type ATP synthase subunit b, some channels/transporters): activation at the end of the signal-anchor/first TM helix.

Summary: Positively charged n‑region of N‑terminal signal peptides that target proteins for export (primarily bacterial Sec, with some Tat), characterized by an M–K/R–K/R start immediately preceding the hydrophobic h‑region; this marks secreted/periplasmic/outer‑membrane/lipoprotein precursors across diverse taxa
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks confined to the extreme N-terminus: strongest at positions 2–3 (Lys/Arg), with minor activation at Met1 and a hydrophobic residue at position 4; limited to the first 3–5 residues of annotated signal peptides, often in low-confidence coil to short-helix transition; no activation in the mature chain
Exemplars: - Periplasmic ABC transporter substrate-binding proteins: activation on the M-KK/M-KR n-region of the Sec signal peptide.
- Outer-membrane/surface proteins (e.g., SLH-associated or OmpA-like): activation on Lys/Arg at positions 2–3 within the signal peptide n-region.
- Periplasmic c-type cytochromes and other redox/metalloproteins: activation on the positively charged n-region of Sec/Tat signal peptides (including RR/KR variants).
- Secreted carbohydrate-active enzymes (e.g., endoglucanases): activation on the n-region preceding the hydrophobic core of the signal peptide.
- Extracellular metalloproteases (fervidolysin/thermolysin-like): activation on the n-region of the export signal peptide.
- Secreted toxins (heat-stable enterotoxins): activation on the basic n-region of the signal peptide.
- Bacterial lipoproteins: activation on the n-region immediately upstream of the lipobox-containing signal peptide.
- Adhesins and surface-interaction factors (fimbrial/surface adhesins): activation on the n-region of the signal peptide directing export.
- Phage secreted/virion-associated proteins (e.g., spackle): activation on the basic n-region at the start of the signal peptide.
- Uncharacterized exported/periplasmic proteins: activation restricted to the N-terminal n-region of the annotated signal peptide.

Summary: Sec-dependent signal peptide recognition, specifically the positively charged N-region followed immediately by the hydrophobic, helical h-region at the extreme N terminus of secreted/periplasmic/outer-membrane precursors (including some lipoproteins) across bacteria and eukaryotes
Activation pattern: Short, residue-level activation restricted to the first ~2–10 residues after M1, peaking on Lys/Arg in positions 2–3 and adjacent hydrophobic residues (L/I/V/F/A) within an N-terminal helix; acidic residues are disfavored; activation falls to ~0 before the C-region/cleavage motif and remains off across the mature domain; M1 often inactive; occasionally includes a cysteine when present in lipoprotein-type leaders
Exemplars: - Arylsulfatase precursor (secreted enzyme): activation on a basic/hydrophobic helical segment within the signal peptide (early h-region).
- Periplasmic aliphatic sulfonate–binding protein (ABC transporter SBP): activation on R2–A10 in the N/h-region of the signal peptide; silent on the mature periplasmic domain.
- Cytochrome c′ (periplasmic c-type cytochrome family): activation confined to M1–A11 signal peptide helix; no signal at heme-binding residues.
- Heat-labile enterotoxin B subunit (AB5 toxin): activation on residues 4–12 of the N-terminal signal peptide helix; no activation in the β-sandwich of the mature chain.
- Secreted proteinase inhibitor precursor (eukaryotic): activation on M1–A7 within the signal peptide; absent over disulfide-rich inhibitor domain.
- Venom/peptide hormone precursor (Hypotensin): activation on residues 2–10 in the signal peptide’s initial helix; no activation in propeptide/bioactive regions.

Summary: Recognition of the N‑terminal signal peptide—specifically the hydrophobic h‑region and its C‑terminal boundary (h→c transition) around the signal peptidase cleavage site—in secreted and secretory‑pathway proteins (including soluble factors and single‑pass receptors)
Activation pattern: Regional activation confined to the extreme N‑terminus (~positions 10–40): strongest across the C‑terminal half of the signal peptide and often straddling just beyond the cleavage site into the first residues of the mature chain/propeptide; predicted helical/coil with low pLDDT; negligible activation elsewhere
Exemplars: - Serine protease (tissue‑type plasminogen activator): activation over the C‑terminal half of the signal peptide and into the propeptide.
- Kunitz‑type protease inhibitor: activation on the C‑terminal portion of the signal peptide, extending a few residues past the cleavage site.
- Mucin (MUC1): peak at the end of the signal peptide, coincident with the cleavage site.
- Wnt signaling modulator (Sclerostin): activation across the signal peptide; variants at the activated site affect secretion.
- Extracellular matrix glycoprotein (Tenascin): activation confined to the signal peptide, ending at chain start.
- Receptor‑like tyrosine kinase family member (PDGFR‑like): activation on the C‑terminal half of the signal peptide.
- Semaphorin: activation across the signal peptide with a sharp drop after cleavage.
- Glycoprotein hormone beta subunit (luteinizing hormone β): activation within the signal peptide, ending at cleavage.
- Adhesion GPCR (adhesion class): activation in the core and C‑terminal end of the signal peptide.
- Single‑pass receptor (secretory phospholipase A2 receptor): activation spanning the end of the signal peptide and the first residues of the mature ectodomain.

Summary: Residue positions that mark polypeptide boundaries—especially the absolute N-terminus (position 1) and the terminal residue of sequence fragments—and, secondarily, isolated boundary-like sites within larger proteins (e.g., short linkers between secondary-structure elements or helix/turn cap-like positions), consistent with proteolytic processing junctions in pre/propeptides.
Activation pattern: Predominantly single-residue peaks at sequence extremities (most often the first residue; also the last residue of fragments); sparse internal single-residue peaks at boundary-like positions (short linkers or transitions between secondary structures). Often coincides with disordered/low-confidence termini; in secreted/toxin precursors a recurring window around residues ~50–70 is consistent with signal/propeptide cleavage. Per-protein activations are usually one or a few sites.
Exemplars: Snake venom serine protease: peaks at the N-terminal first residue and at the C-terminal end of the chain; Nuclear pore complex protein Nup155: isolated peaks on single residues within a helix and a low-confidence turn; U4/U6.U5 tri-snRNP–associated protein 1: single-residue peak at a glycine linker between β-strands; E4 ubiquitin-conjugation factor (UBE4): isolated methionine within a long α-helix; Reelin (fragment): strong activation at the fragment’s C-terminal residue in a disordered region; Glutamate dehydrogenase (fragment): activation marks the truncated C-terminal residue.

Summary: Short linear segments in intrinsically disordered or otherwise low-structure-confidence regions, often at N-termini and within signal peptides/propeptides of secreted and regulatory proteins (including viral accessory proteins and small ORF microproteins), enriched in small/basic residues (G, P, S, A, R; often with Cys), rather than in well-folded catalytic cores.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks scattered across IDRs and low-confidence coils/short helices; frequently clustered near the N-terminus, in signal peptides, propeptides, and disordered tails; little to no activation in well-structured domains; occasional activation in low-confidence transmembrane/signal-anchor helices.
Exemplars: - Viral accessory protein (HIV-1 Vif): peaks throughout low-pLDDT coils, especially the disordered N-terminal region.
- Neuropeptide precursor (Drosophila Amnesiac): activation in the N-terminal signal peptide and multiple mature peptide segments with very low pLDDT.
- Secreted serine carboxypeptidase: activation confined to disordered C-terminal tail, annotated disordered segment, the signal peptide, and a low-confidence C-terminal transmembrane helix; absent from the structured catalytic domain.
- Disordered human tumor-suppressor–associated protein (ST20): scattered peaks within predicted helices in a globally disordered chain, including the N-terminus.
- lncRNA/sORF-derived microprotein (IGF2 antisense protein): multiple peaks across annotated disordered regions rich in Arg/Pro/Gly.

Summary: Broadly distributed activation across small secreted peptides, processed protein fragments, and various polar/charged residues in short proteins, with frequent firing in viral, venom, and signaling-peptide contexts.

Activation pattern: Sparse residue-level peaks scattered across the protein, with no strong preference for structured versus unstructured regions; peaks occur on a mix of polar (Asn, Asp, Ser, Gln), basic (Arg, Lys), and hydrophobic (Leu, Val, Ala) residues, and can fall within transmembrane helices, disordered stretches, or short folded chains alike.

Exemplars:
- Secreted peptide hormones (cholecystokinin, kisspeptin/metastin): multiple peaks across the processed peptide chain.
- Snake venom metalloproteinase/disintegrin fragment: distributed peaks across the short chain.
- Viral hexon-linking precursor proteins: weak peaks distributed across the chain including propeptide and cleaved segments.
- Peroxisomal biogenesis factors: peaks within transmembrane helices and other regions of the membrane protein.
- Bacterial methyltransferases: activation localized to C-terminal disordered extension while the catalytic core is inactive.
- Antithrombin/serpin precursor: peaks spanning the signal peptide and mature chain.

Summary: Short basic (Lys/Arg-rich) cationic motifs used for protein routing, processing, and nucleic-acid/host targeting — including secretory signal-peptide regions, organellar transit peptides, dibasic propeptide cleavage sites, and NLS-like basic clusters.
Activation pattern: Regional activation centered on Lys/Arg-rich clusters, often flanked by small residues (Ala/Ser/Gly) around processing/cleavage positions. Peaks frequently occur at N-termini but also within internal basic clusters (NLS-like motifs, propeptide processing sites, basic cytoplasmic tails). In very short proteins the activation can span much of the sequence.
Exemplars:
- Secreted hormone/neuropeptide precursors: activation over signal peptide and at dibasic KR/RR processing sites within the propeptide and mature peptide.
- Viral envelope glycoproteins: activation on signal peptide or signal-anchor with a positively charged n-region; can highlight proximal basic proprotein-convertase motifs.
- Viral accessory/regulatory proteins: activation on Lys/Arg-rich basic clusters and NLS-like motifs used for host targeting (often internal, e.g. lentiviral Tat NLS, polyomavirus agnoprotein basic cluster).
- ATP synthase epsilon (mitochondrial forms): activation on the N-terminal mitochondrial targeting presequence.
- tRNA/rRNA m7G methyltransferases and TilS: activation on N-terminal organellar transit peptides in eukaryotes (mitochondria/plastids) or on basic RNA-binding N-terminal tails in prokaryotes.
- Lipoate biosynthesis/lipoylation enzymes: activation on mitochondrial/chloroplast transit peptides directing enzymes to the organelle where lipoylation occurs.
- Membrane transporters and other membrane-associated proteins: activation on signal anchors with positively charged n-regions.
- Plant proteins and plant-pathogen effectors: activation on secretory signal peptides and basic host-targeting motifs (e.g., RxLR-like) located just after the signal peptide.
- Proteases and protease-related secreted proteins: activation on the secretory signal peptide and basic propeptide processing motifs.
- Ribosome-related proteins/modifiers: activation on short basic segments (often nucleic acid-binding/NLS-like).
- Uncharacterized micropeptides/lncRNA-encoded peptides: activation across short basic regions consistent with leader/targeting-like segments.

Summary: Hydrophobic alpha-helical signal/anchor motif: the feature marks hydrophobic side chains (L/I/V/F/M, often with Y/W) within short alpha-helical segments—most prominently the hydrophobic core of N‑terminal signal peptides and other amphipathic or membrane-interacting helices—and, more generally, single hydrophobic “anchor” residues embedded in helices of diverse soluble domains (e.g., ARID, FH3). Occasional activation extends to nearby residues within the same helical segment in secreted/viral proteins.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks with variable density: short runs across hydrophobic helical stretches (especially at extreme N-termini) and isolated single-residue peaks on helix-internal hydrophobes; observed both in low-confidence/disordered regions that harbor short helices and in well-structured helices.
Exemplars: - Oomycete RxLR effectors: activation on the signal peptide hydrophobic core and the RxLR-adjacent short helix, with additional peaks on aromatic residues in the effector body.
- Plant viral RNA-silencing suppressor P0: scattered peaks on hydrophobic residues within predicted helices and adjacent coils, consistent with short amphipathic helices.
- Viral VP5 accessory proteins: strong peaks on V/I/M in flexible segments that form short hydrophobic helices.
- ARID DNA-binding proteins (e.g., Rsc9, Jumonji-family ARID): single-residue peaks on I/L within ARID helices.
- Formin family (GBD/FH3 domain): a solitary L within a helical segment is highlighted.

Summary: Secreted, short cysteine-rich peptides and small extracellular cysteine-rich domains stabilized by multiple disulfide bonds (CRPs), spanning venom toxins, disintegrins, defensins/hepcidin, Kunitz/Kazal/hevein-like inhibitors/defense peptides, and related cystine‑knotted or cysteine‑stabilized folds. The feature captures the mature, proteolytically processed peptide/module characterized by clustered Cys (often CC motifs) and basic residues.
Activation pattern: Regional activation confined to short mature peptide segments (tens of residues) following the signal peptide and propeptides; minimal/absent on signal/pro-regions. Strong residue-level peaks on cysteines and frequent secondary peaks on Lys/Arg and Gly. Activation spans mixed secondary structure (β-strands, coils, short helices) and can include key functional loops (e.g., RGD in disintegrins).
Exemplars: - Plant cyclotides (cystine-knot cyclopeptides, e.g., chassatide): activation across the cyclic cystine‑knot core of the mature peptide after processing.
- Snake venom disintegrins: activation across the disintegrin domain, including the RGD integrin-binding loop and adjacent cysteine-dense core.
- Inhibitor cystine-knot (ICK) venom toxins from spiders, cone snails, centipedes, and sea anemones: activation on the disulfide‑knotted toxin core.
- Kunitz/BPTI- and Kazal-type serine protease inhibitors (including tick chemokine/complement inhibitors): activation on the small disulfide‑rich inhibitor domain.
- Hevein-like/seed defense peptides: activation on the cysteine-rich chitin‑binding hevein domain.
- Defensins (plant/fungal/animal CSαβ peptides) and vertebrate hepcidin: activation on the cysteine‑stabilized mature AMP region.
- Euplotes ciliate mating pheromones: activation on the secreted disulfide‑rich pheromone core.
- Cysteine-rich modules within large extracellular/mucin-like proteins: activation on the short, cysteine‑dense repeat/subdomain embedded in the larger precursor.

Summary: Secreted, propeptide‑processed cysteine‑rich mini‑domains: compact extracellular segments immediately downstream of a signal peptide that contain clustered cysteines forming multiple disulfide bonds (defensin/CSαβ, WAP four‑disulfide core, cystine‑knot/knottin, CHH‑like, evasin‑like, and related small CRP scaffolds), often flanked by dibasic convertase sites and enriched in Lys/Arg
Activation pattern: Regional activation on short segments (≈20–60 aa) right after the signal peptide; strong peaks on cysteines and nearby basic residues, frequently overlapping proprotein convertase (dibasic) processing motifs; may recur for multi‑domain or repeat CRP proteins
Exemplars: - WAP/four‑disulfide core protease inhibitors (SLPI/elafin/WFDC): activation on the WAP domain’s Cys framework following the signal/propeptide
- Plant defensin‑like peptides (DEFL/LURE/ESF) and thionins: activation on the mature antimicrobial CSαβ cysteine motif
- Venom cystine‑knot peptides (conotoxins/knottins, mini‑toxins): activation on the canonical Cys frameworks in the mature toxin region of prepropeptides
- Tick evasins (chemokine‑binding CRPs): activation on the Cys‑rich chemokine‑binding domain
- Crustacean CHH/MIH neuropeptide precursors: activation on the mature hormone core with conserved six‑Cys motif adjacent to dibasic cleavage
- Fungal GPI‑anchored cell‑wall adhesins/stress proteins: activation on extracellular Cys‑rich segments just after secretion signals
- Small plant CRP protease inhibitors: activation on the disulfide‑stabilized inhibitory mini‑domain

Summary: Sequence contexts marking disulfide-bonded cysteines in secreted/extracellular proteins—cysteine pairs/clusters (often flanked by Gly/Pro) that form stabilizing disulfide frameworks typical of toxins, antimicrobial peptides, protease inhibitors, neuropeptide/hormone/pheromone peptides, and viral envelope ectodomains.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks at or immediately adjacent to disulfide-bonded cysteines; compact, contiguous activation across the cystine framework in short disulfide-rich peptides; multiple peaks scattered across ectodomains of large secreted glycoproteins; minimal activation in signal peptides, transmembranes, or cytosolic regions.
Exemplars: - AB toxins (pertussis toxin B subunit): peaks next to disulfide-forming cysteines within the mature chain.
- Venom disulfide-rich toxins (conotoxins; scorpion α/β-toxins; spider ω/κ-toxins): activation tracks the canonical Cys frameworks.
- Defensins and other CSαβ antimicrobial peptides: activation on the conserved disulfide pairs.
- Kunitz- and Kazal-type serine protease inhibitors: peaks around the conserved disulfide-bonded cysteines stabilizing the inhibitory fold.
- Neuropeptide hormones/pheromones with intrachain/interchain disulfides (e.g., insulin family, oxytocin/vasopressin): activation at the disulfide-forming Cys and neighboring Gly/Pro.
- Viral envelope glycoproteins: multiple peaks across ectodomain cysteine clusters and Cys–Gly/Pro motifs.
- Secreted nematode extracellular/ECM-associated cysteine-rich proteins: activation over disulfide-stabilized modules.

Summary: Extracellular/cell-surface secretome signature: the feature recognizes ectodomains of secreted or surface-presented proteins, especially cysteine-rich, disulfide-stabilized peptides and repeats (e.g., toxins, EGF/disintegrin/adhesion modules, lectins), C-terminal regions surrounding GPI-anchor attachment sites, and also short exofacial loops of multi-pass membrane proteins when these loops are cysteine- and/or glycan-rich; it captures appended extracellular carbohydrate-binding modules of secreted CAZymes
Activation pattern: Primarily regional/domain-level activation over long, contiguous stretches of extracellular sequence (often at protein termini), with residue-level peaks near Cys clusters and adjacent residues (aromatics/Pro/Ser/Thr); frequently highest around the GPI omega site and drops within cleaved C-terminal propeptides; can cover complete mature secreted peptide chains or selectively highlight appended extracellular modules (e.g., CBMs) rather than catalytic cores; additionally, can mark short exofacial loops (not necessarily at termini) in multi-pass transporters when they contain Cys–Cys/Cys-x(n)–Cys or NXS/T glycosylation motifs
Exemplars: Trypanosome variant surface glycoproteins (VSGs) – strong activation across the disordered C-terminal GPI-anchor region, peaking at the omega site and disappearing in the cleaved propeptide; Ciliate mating pheromones – activation across the mature secreted cystine-rich peptide with peaks at N-terminal aromatic residues and reduced signal on disulfide-bonded cysteines; Secreted carbohydrate-active enzymes – activation on C-terminal CBM10 carbohydrate-binding modules and adjacent helices, not on the catalytic cores; Disulfide-rich venom peptides and Kunitz/other protease inhibitors – extended activation across the mature, disulfide-stabilized chains; Viral envelope/entry glycoproteins – activation on cysteine-rich ectodomain loops; EGF-like/disintegrin/adhesion modules and lectins – activation on cysteine-constrained extracellular repeats/domains; SLC/GLUT-family transporters – activation on short extracellular loops bearing conserved disulfide-bonded cysteines and glycosylation sites

Summary: Disulfide‑stabilized extracellular ectodomain repeats and their linkers—especially EGF‑like repeats and TNFR cysteine‑rich domains—across secreted proteins and the N‑terminal/luminal regions of cell‑surface receptors and transporters
Activation pattern: Regionally confined to extracellular/N‑terminal ectodomains; sparse residue‑level peaks centered on cysteines that form disulfides and nearby glycine/acidic residues; frequent signal in flexible/low‑pLDDT loops flanking structured repeats; negligible in signal peptides, transmembrane helices, and cytosolic tails
Exemplars: • Adhesion GPCRs (latrophilins): activation in EGF‑like repeats and adjacent flexible segments of the ectodomain
• Viral TNFR‑like immunomodulators (e.g., UL144): strong peaks on cysteines within TNFR cysteine‑rich domains
• Cell‑adhesion glycoproteins with EGF‑like modules: peaks within the EGF‑like repeat and its flanking unstructured regions
• Venom/toxin EGF‑like microproteins: sparse peaks across the disulfide‑rich EGF‑like fold
• ABCG family membrane transporters: activation restricted to the long N‑terminal luminal region before the first transmembrane helix, absent from TM and cytosolic domains

Summary: Intrinsically disordered post-signal/TM prohormone regions of secreted short-peptide precursors—i.e., the segments that encode mature neuropeptides/hormones or toxin/antimicrobial peptides and their flanking propeptides—characterized by Lys/Arg-rich convertase cleavage motifs and frequent support for C‑terminal amidation
Activation pattern: Domain-level: inactive on signal peptides and transmembrane helices; strongly active across the luminal propeptide from signal/TM cleavage to the C-terminus. Regional: sustained high activation over mature peptide blocks and adjacent propeptides, often spanning multiple peptides in one precursor; activation typically drops immediately after the last processed peptide. Residue-level: peaks over peptide cores and nearby linkers; selective dips at the second residue of dibasic Lys/Arg cleavage pairs; enrichment around basic clusters and glycine positions associated with amidation.
Exemplars: - Dermaseptin antimicrobial peptide precursor: high on the mature dermaseptin and both flanking propeptides; off on the N‑terminal signal peptide; all activated regions are disordered.
- Insect prokineticin/hugin precursor: strong activation across the region containing Hug‑gamma and PK‑2 peptides and linker/C‑terminal propeptide; inactive on the signal peptide; disordered.
- Tachykinin/protachykinin (neurokinin family): activated across the neurokinin peptide (e.g., Neurokinin‑B) and propeptide segments; sharp local drop at a dibasic cleavage Arg; disordered.
- Neuropeptide F precursor: moderate to strong activation on the mature NPF and the C‑terminal propeptide; signal peptide unactivated; disordered.
- Insect diuretic hormone class 2 precursor: maximal activation across the mature diuretic hormone peptide; off on the signal peptide; disordered.
- Proenkephalin (opioid peptide precursor): broadly activated over enkephalin copies and intervening prosegments; recurrent dip at the second basic residue of dibasic cleavage motifs; disordered.
- Gonadoliberin (GnRH) precursor: high activation across the GnRH peptide and the associated peptide; inactive on the signal peptide; disordered.
- Gastrin prohormone: strong activation over “Big gastrin”/“Gastrin” region and C‑terminal propeptide where amidation/cleavage motifs occur; off on the signal peptide; disordered.
- Pigment-dispersing factor (PDF) precursor: activated on the mature PDF chain; signal peptide not activated; disordered.
- Membrane-anchored secretory peptide-like precursor (e.g., Frey): inactive on the N‑terminal transmembrane helix; strong activation on the disordered luminal C‑terminal region consistent with a processed propeptide segment.

Summary: N-terminal, signal-peptide–adjacent pro-regions of secreted proteins that encode processing/targeting information—especially prohormone/neuropeptide propeptides and analogous effector pre-sequences—characteristically disordered; the feature de-emphasizes the structured, cysteine/PTM-rich mature peptide cores.
Activation pattern: - Low-to-moderate in the signal peptide, then a sharp rise at the signal peptide/pro-region junction.
- Strong, continuous activation across long, disordered N-terminal stretches of the propeptide/pre-sequence.
- Gradual decline across more structured regions; minima in mature hormone/peptide domains, disulfide-bonded cysteines, and PTM endpoints (e.g., sulfotyrosine, amidated residues).
- In effectors, highest immediately upstream of the RxLR motif and reduced across the motif and the structured C-terminal core.
Exemplars: - Gastrin/cholecystokinin-family prohormones: activates on the disordered N-terminal propeptide; low in the modified hormone core.
- Urotensin-2 precursor: high in the propeptide after the signal peptide; absent over the cystine-stabilized mature peptide.
- RFamide and other amidated neuropeptide precursors (including insect families): emphasizes prosegments flanking multiple peptide products.
- Class-B (glucagon/secretin family) peptide hormone precursors: highlights signal-proximal prodomains rather than the mature hormone regions.
- Oomycete secreted RxLR effectors: peaks in the low-complexity N-terminus immediately before the RxLR host-targeting motif; drops on the motif and the structured core.

Summary: Short low-complexity intrinsically disordered linear motifs used for protein–protein interactions—including acidic D/E-rich tracts as well as other short linear motifs (e.g., PIP boxes, viral late-domain motifs, and the conserved acidic C-terminal tail of ribosomal P-stalk proteins, …GFGLFD-like)
Activation pattern: Regional activation with sharp residue-level peaks confined to short (≈10–30 aa) windows in IDRs/low-complexity regions; frequently terminus-biased (especially extreme C-termini for P-stalk tails and PIP boxes); peaks fall in clustered acidic patches or in short hydrophobic/aromatic-anchored linear motifs (e.g., LxLxL-like, GFGLFD, QxxLxF-type PIP cores); minimal signal in structured cores but can show multiple peaks across extended low-complexity regions
Exemplars: Ribosomal P-stalk proteins (uL10/P0, P1/P2, P3): activation on the conserved acidic C-terminal tail with E/D runs and GFGLFD core; Eukaryotic transcription factors (homeobox, forkhead, T-box, DMRT, zinc-finger): activation on acidic/proline- or Ser/Thr-rich activation/repression segments; Plant auxin/EAR-type repressors (Aux/IAA, ERF/ARF co-repressors, TOPLESS-associated): activation on EAR motifs (LxLxL, DLNxxP) within acidic LCRs; Spliceosome tri-snRNP–associated proteins: activation on acidic/S/T-rich disordered tracts; DNA replication/repair factors: short IDR linear motifs (including PIP boxes) for partner recruitment; Viral Gag/late-domain and transactivator proteins: short linear motifs within disordered C-terminal segments (e.g., LYPX(n)L late domain, SLFGND); Zinc-finger E3 ligases: acidic low-complexity linkers/tails; Cytosolic tails of some membrane proteins: proline-rich, acidic PRD segments

Summary: N-terminal non-globular segments: broadly activating on early low-complexity/intrinsically disordered regions enriched in S/P/E/D (often regulatory/targeting regions) and, in secreted precursors, on the N-terminal signal peptide helix
Activation pattern: Single broad regional activation largely confined to the first ~30–200 residues, peaking over coils/IDRs with low pLDDT and sometimes encompassing short helices; little to no activation on folded C‑terminal domains. In secreted precursors, the activation collapses onto the hydrophobic signal peptide at the extreme N-terminus.
Exemplars: - Plant LAZY/TAC/DRO gravity-signaling proteins: strongest on a central early low-structure coil segment adjacent to, but not centered on, the IGT/TAC motif.
- Secreted peptide hormone/neuropeptide precursors (e.g., apelin, natriuretic/urotensin families): focused on the N-terminal signal peptide alpha-helix.
- BRI1 kinase inhibitor (BKI1): broad activation across a long N-terminal intrinsically disordered, low-complexity region.
- Calmodulin-binding nuclear proteins: activation over an N-terminal IDR that includes a disordered patch and extends through a bipartite NLS.
- Plant oxidative stress-associated regulators: activation across an N-terminal acidic/Ser/Pro‑rich low-complexity disordered segment.

Summary: Long, low-complexity intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), typically enriched in S/P/Q/E/A/G and frequently occupying extended N‑terminal segments that serve as propeptides, transcriptional activation domains, flexible linkers, or receptor tails/stalks; activation drops sharply in adjacent folded motifs (coiled-coils, globular domains, zinc-finger/Ig-like modules, BH3 helix).
Activation pattern: Broad regional activation across extended IDRs—often starting near the initiator methionine and continuing for hundreds of residues—with minimal activation in structured domains; occasional local boosts around dibasic KR/RR clusters in secretory precursors.
Exemplars: - BH3-only Bcl-2 family: strong activation on long N-terminal disordered regions; low over the structured BH3 alpha-helix.
- NBPF/Olduvai repeat proteins: high activation across C-terminal, low-confidence, compositionally biased repeat-rich segments; reduced within ordered coiled-coil regions.
- Neuropeptide/prohormone and venom/natriuretic peptide precursors: activation over extended disordered propeptides (often encompassing the N-terminal region) with KR/RR convertase cleavage clusters.
- TNF ligands and TNFR-like receptors: activation on low-complexity prodomains/flexible stalks; low on the folded TNF domain and cysteine-rich repeat cores.
- Immunoreceptors/C-type lectins: activation on disordered cytoplasmic tails and extracellular stalks; minimal on Ig-like or lectin folds.
- Zinc-finger/SCAN/RING/THAP and homeobox/bHLH transcription factors: activation on acidic/Q/P-rich activation domains and terminal low-complexity regions; low on the DNA-binding folds.
- Testis/spermatogenesis/acrosomal proteins: activation across very long low-complexity stretches and repeats; diminished in any structured/coiled-coil modules.
- KASH-domain nuclear envelope proteins: activation on giant disordered linkers outside coiled-coils and the transmembrane KASH segment.

Summary: Short residue windows in mixed-composition regions of diverse proteins, frequently in N-terminal or non-catalytic portions of enzymes, transmembrane-adjacent stretches, and small secreted peptides.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks concentrated in short 3–7 residue windows, often clustered with several nearby peaks. Activated residues are chemically diverse (including hydrophobic, polar, and charged residues) and can occur in helical transmembrane segments, disordered linkers, or globular regions outside annotated catalytic/binding sites.
Exemplars:
- Bacterial DNA ligase: clusters of peaks in the N-terminal region upstream of the catalytic and BRCT domains.
- Viral integrase homolog: short peaks within the chain including a GPAYGRP-containing segment.
- Peroxisomal biogenesis factor 9 (Pex9): peaks overlapping helical transmembrane segments and an adjacent disordered/polar region.
- Small secreted peptides (e.g., Califin-B large subunit): short peaks within the mature peptide.

Summary: Residue-level detector that activates broadly at sparse positions across diverse protein contexts, with notable preference for disordered/low-complexity regions, mature secreted peptides, and short helical segments (including transmembrane helices and helix-prone regions inside intrinsically disordered stretches). It does not appear to track a single specific motif.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks, typically one to a few strong peaks per protein with additional weaker peaks scattered along the sequence. Strong activation is observed within intrinsically disordered regions (including Gly-rich and polar/charged compositionally biased segments), within short transmembrane helices, and within mature processed peptides. Activation is also seen scattered within globular enzyme domains.
Exemplars:
- Small integral membrane proteins: single strong peak within a short transmembrane helix.
- Secretory preprohormones (e.g., cholecystokinin): multiple peaks within the mature processed peptide regions.
- Homeobox/disordered regulators (e.g., Rhox5): multiple peaks throughout disordered Gly-rich and basic/acidic compositionally biased segments.
- CaMKII inhibitor peptides: peaks at the start of the inhibitory domain and at Pro-rich positions.
- Viral accessory/integrase-like proteins: multiple short peaks scattered across the chain, including disordered C-terminal segments.
- Bacterial/yeast enzymes (e.g., beta-lactamase, aspartyl-tRNA synthetase, imidazolonepropionase, peroxin-9): scattered peaks within N-terminal or globular regions.

Summary: Broad, regional recognition of helical and hydrophobic/amphipathic segments, including contiguous hydrophobic alpha-helical transmembrane segments and proline/glycine-rich low-complexity stretches; the feature also fires across large internal regions of soluble enzymes and effector proteins, with a bias toward hydrophobic and helix-favoring residues and proline/glycine context.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over stretches: contiguous activation across single-pass or multi-pass transmembrane alpha-helices and amphipathic helical motifs; broad, distributed activation across internal regions of soluble proteins; sparser peaks within short secreted, low-complexity segments; overall bias toward hydrophobic and helix-favoring residues with enrichment for proline and glycine context.
Exemplars:
- Fibrillar collagens: strong activation along the triple-helical G–X–Y domain, peaking at X/Y positions (especially proline/hydroxyproline-like Y), with minimal signal on G.
- Light-harvesting complex alpha subunits (photosynthetic bacteria): activation along their single transmembrane alpha-helix.
- YhhN/TMEM86 lysoplasmalogenases: activation across multiple transmembrane segments.
- Viral accessory proteins (including non-membrane factors like replication enhancers), envelope proteins, and viroporins: activation on short hydrophobic or amphipathic helical motifs (membrane-anchored or not).
- Single-pass small integral membrane proteins: activation on the transmembrane helix.
- Plant CLE/CLAVATA/ESR peptide precursors: activation on the conserved proline-rich mature peptide region and adjacent low-complexity stretches.
- Oomycete RxLR effectors: activation across the mature effector region including the RxLR-dEER motif and adjacent low-complexity repeats.
- Fungal secreted/surface-associated effectors (e.g., hydrophobin-like): activation on hydrophobic, repetitive patches outside core cystine motifs.
- Small cysteine-rich toxins/defensin-like peptides: activation on hydrophobic patches within or adjacent to the disulfide-stabilized core.
- Soluble cytosolic enzymes/regulators: broad, distributed activation across internal regions, including disordered and low-complexity stretches.

Summary: Short segments within disordered and compositionally biased stretches of diverse proteins, particularly regions enriched in basic and acidic residues. Activations are also seen in non-disordered contexts across proteins of varied function, suggesting the feature captures a relatively broad local sequence pattern rather than a tight structural motif.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks with small clusters, distributed throughout the length of the protein. Peaks frequently overlap annotated disordered regions and basic/acidic compositionally biased segments, but also occur at isolated positions within structured chains; occurs in both helical and coil contexts.
Exemplars: - Oomycete RxLR secreted effectors: peaks within the mature effector chain, with occasional spikes in the signal peptide.
- Plant CLE peptide precursors: localized peaks within the C-terminal CLE motif corresponding to the mature signaling peptide.
- Cholecystokinin prohormone: peaks at or immediately adjacent to the N-termini of mature neuropeptides generated by proteolytic processing.
- Herpesvirus ICP47-like small accessory proteins: multiple peaks in the N-terminal active helical region and in polar, disordered C-terminal stretches.
- Keratin-associated proteins: activation across cysteine/proline/serine-rich, low-complexity repeat regions.
- Phosphodiesterase and fungal/bacterial enzymes with disordered N- or internal stretches: peaks within basic-and-acidic compositionally biased segments.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity, serine/threonine- and charge‑rich segments (flexible linkers, targeting regions, and cytosolic/luminal tails), often containing P/G and K/R/E/D, and frequently forming transient/low‑confidence helices; largely absent from well‑folded domain cores and transmembrane helices
Activation pattern: Regional activation across extended IDRs with many residue‑level peaks on S/T and adjacent polar/charged residues; sparse or absent over structured globular domains, coiled‑coils of high confidence, and transmembrane spans; occasional activation on low‑pLDDT helical segments embedded within disordered regions and juxtamembrane basic clusters
Exemplars: - Eisosome/cortical membrane protein (yeast Sle1 family): activation on disordered, polar eisosome‑targeting region and other low‑complexity coils, with strongest peaks in long IDRs.
- 12‑TM solute carrier–type sodium transporter: activation confined to disordered N‑terminal tail and large extramembranous loops; silent across all transmembrane helices.
- ArfGAP regulator with PH and ankyrin repeats (AGAP family): activation on long disordered linkers between domains and basic low‑complexity blocks after the PH domain; off in GLD/PH cores, C4 zinc‑finger catalytic region, and ankyrin repeats.
- TORC1 scaffold subunit (Tco89‑like): strong hotspots in low‑complexity, disordered basic/acidic segments with sporadic peaks at helix edges; does not uniformly track annotated phosphosites.
- Inner nuclear membrane SUN‑domain protein: activation on low‑confidence helical stretches and basic clusters in the post‑TM luminal tail and juxtamembrane region; absent in the coiled‑coil, transmembrane helix, and structured SUN domain.

Summary: Low-complexity, intrinsically disordered segments—often at protein N-termini—such as mucin-like/propeptide regions or flexible linkers adjacent to signal/transit peptides, common in small secreted or membrane-associated proteins and also as disordered extensions in diverse enzymes (broad taxonomic coverage, including viral, bacterial, and eukaryotic proteins).
Activation pattern: Regional activation over short to moderate stretches, frequently in disordered or polar/low-complexity segments; in longer proteins, multiple low-complexity patches can activate; in micropeptides, activation can span much of the sequence. Residue-level peaks can fall on Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly within polar-residue stretches but also on basic or hydrophobic residues within the same disordered context.
Exemplars:
- Viral envelope/accessory microproteins: activation on N-terminal Ser/Thr/Pro-rich disordered segments (often mucin-like or regulatory tails).
- Secreted eukaryotic effectors (e.g., oomycete RxLR effectors): activation on the low-complexity region flanking the signal peptide/RxLR motif.
- Human testis-biased and lncRNA-derived micropeptides: activation across intrinsically disordered peptide regions.
- Secreted precursors/propeptides: activation on N-terminal regions following the signal peptide.
- Membrane-associated single-pass proteins: activation on luminal or cytosolic tails flanking the transmembrane helix.
- Bacterial/archaeal metabolic enzymes: activation on disordered, low-complexity N-terminal extensions/linkers enriched in Ser/Thr/Gly/Pro.

Summary: Short segments within disordered and compositionally biased stretches of diverse proteins, particularly regions enriched in basic and acidic residues. Activations are also seen in non-disordered contexts across proteins of varied function, suggesting the feature captures a relatively broad local sequence pattern rather than a tight structural motif.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks with small clusters, distributed throughout the length of the protein. Peaks frequently overlap annotated disordered regions and basic/acidic compositionally biased segments, but also occur at isolated positions within structured chains; occurs in both helical and coil contexts.
Exemplars: - Oomycete RxLR secreted effectors: peaks within the mature effector chain, with occasional spikes in the signal peptide.
- Plant CLE peptide precursors: localized peaks within the C-terminal CLE motif corresponding to the mature signaling peptide.
- Cholecystokinin prohormone: peaks at or immediately adjacent to the N-termini of mature neuropeptides generated by proteolytic processing.
- Herpesvirus ICP47-like small accessory proteins: multiple peaks in the N-terminal active helical region and in polar, disordered C-terminal stretches.
- Keratin-associated proteins: activation across cysteine/proline/serine-rich, low-complexity repeat regions.
- Phosphodiesterase and fungal/bacterial enzymes with disordered N- or internal stretches: peaks within basic-and-acidic compositionally biased segments.

Summary: The feature recognizes cationic, amphipathic, low-complexity segments that mediate targeting or membrane/lipid association—classically N‑terminal signal/transit/leader-like regions of secreted, mitochondrial, and viral proteins—and frequently the propeptide/mature regions of toxin and neuropeptide precursors; it can also highlight short basic/hydrophobic helices or redox-active motifs within structured domains.
Activation pattern: Predominantly long, continuous activation over N‑terminal, low‑pLDDT leader/propeptide regions enriched in Lys/Arg, Ser/Pro and hydrophobic/aromatic residues; with occasional residue-level peaks within well-structured helices (e.g., specific positions in thioredoxin CGHC motifs or matrix-exposed helices of membrane proteins).
Exemplars: 
- Venom phospholipase A2 precursors (activation on signal/propeptide segments and conserved cationic patches).
- Apolipoproteins (N‑terminal signal peptide and amphipathic helical stretches).
- Protein kinases with disordered/basic N‑termini (e.g., cyclin-dependent and PRK family N‑tails).
- Thioredoxin-fold protein disulfide-isomerases (peak at the CGHC active-site helix).
- Mitochondrial calcium uniporter (selected residues in a matrix-exposed helix).
- Conotoxin and other secreted toxin precursors; neuropeptide prepropeptides (activation across pro/mature peptide regions).
- Viral silencing suppressors and small membrane/morphogenesis proteins (basic, hydrophobic leader-like segments).
- Kinetochore coiled-coil scaffold proteins (basic low-complexity regions).
- FYVE-domain endosomal adaptors (basic, membrane/PIP-interacting low-complexity segments).
- RNA-modifying enzymes with basic N‑terminal tails (e.g., tRNA methyltransferases).

Summary: Hydrophobic alpha-helical signal/anchor motif: the feature marks hydrophobic side chains (L/I/V/F/M, often with Y/W) within short alpha-helical segments—most prominently the hydrophobic core of N‑terminal signal peptides and other amphipathic or membrane-interacting helices—and, more generally, single hydrophobic “anchor” residues embedded in helices of diverse soluble domains (e.g., ARID, FH3). Occasional activation extends to nearby residues within the same helical segment in secreted/viral proteins.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks with variable density: short runs across hydrophobic helical stretches (especially at extreme N-termini) and isolated single-residue peaks on helix-internal hydrophobes; observed both in low-confidence/disordered regions that harbor short helices and in well-structured helices.
Exemplars: - Oomycete RxLR effectors: activation on the signal peptide hydrophobic core and the RxLR-adjacent short helix, with additional peaks on aromatic residues in the effector body.
- Plant viral RNA-silencing suppressor P0: scattered peaks on hydrophobic residues within predicted helices and adjacent coils, consistent with short amphipathic helices.
- Viral VP5 accessory proteins: strong peaks on V/I/M in flexible segments that form short hydrophobic helices.
- ARID DNA-binding proteins (e.g., Rsc9, Jumonji-family ARID): single-residue peaks on I/L within ARID helices.
- Formin family (GBD/FH3 domain): a solitary L within a helical segment is highlighted.

Summary: Short, low‑complexity, intrinsically disordered proteins and modules that encode targeting/processing signals—often but not always secretory—combining hydrophobic signal peptides, double‑Gly bacteriocin leaders, or polybasic/NLS‑like segments, frequently adjacent to Ser/Thr/Pro‑rich stretches and basic clusters (e.g., RXLR, KR/RR)—common in micropeptides, toxins/secreted precursors, viral accessory proteins, keratin‑associated and testis‑specific low‑complexity proteins across taxa
Activation pattern: Regional activation across short proteins, spanning hydrophobic/targeting segments and Ser/Thr/Pro‑rich low‑complexity tracts with peaks on basic motifs such as RXLR, dibasic KR/RR, or double‑Gly leader junctions
Exemplars:
- Oomycete RxLR effectors: activation on the N‑terminal signal peptide and the RXLR/EER host‑targeting motif immediately downstream.
- Secreted peptide hormone/venom/toxin precursors: activation on the signal peptide and basic prohormone convertase cleavage motifs (KR/RR) within the propeptide region.
- Class II bacteriocins: activation on the N‑terminal double‑Gly leader and adjacent cationic tract recognized by ABC exporters.
- Viral accessory/regulatory proteins (e.g., small disordered regulators): activation across S/T/P‑rich low‑complexity disordered segments containing polybasic/NLS‑like clusters.
- Keratin‑associated proteins (KRTAPs): activation over short, repetitive low‑complexity regions (Ser/Pro‑rich and basic tracts) typical of hair shaft proteins.
- Cancer/testis antigens and testis‑associated proteins: activation on Lys/Arg‑ and Pro/Ser‑rich low‑complexity stretches in very short proteins.
- Short uncharacterized micropeptides/antisense products: broad activation across their low‑complexity/basic segments.
- Enzymes that carry secretory leaders or short disordered/basic tails (including some cytosolic enzymes lacking signal peptides): activation limited to the disordered tail, not the catalytic core.

Summary: Small, often poorly characterized or compositionally biased proteins, including viral accessory proteins, cancer/testis and germline-associated proteins, antisense-ORF microproteins, and short secreted/surface peptides; activation is broadly distributed across the polypeptide rather than focused on a single structured domain
Activation pattern: Regional/distributed activation spread across much of the protein with sparse residue-level peaks; often includes early N-terminal residues and disordered segments; variable coverage from short patches to most of the protein
Exemplars:
- Viral non-structural/accessory proteins: activation distributed through the protein, including basic/Arg-rich motifs such as nuclear localization signals.
- Cancer/testis antigens and germline-associated proteins: activation on long disordered low-complexity regions, often at N-termini.
- Small uncharacterized microproteins/antisense ORFs: activation spanning most of the polypeptide.
- Short secreted peptides and toxin precursors: activation across both signal/propeptide and mature regions.
- Compact cytosolic proteins with disordered N- or C-terminal extensions: activation enriched on the disordered tails.

Summary: Compositionally biased intrinsically disordered low‑complexity regions (LCD/IDRs) enriched in Ser/Pro/Gly with mixed charged residues (Glu/Asp and Lys/Arg), often containing poly‑Q/E/K or RS/S‑rich tracts; these correspond to regulatory tails, activation/linker segments, and isoform‑variable regions in nuclear transcription/chromatin and RNA‑processing proteins, and analogous acidic low‑complexity tails in some bacterial factors; signal is depleted in well‑folded domains (e.g., BTB, C2H2 zinc fingers)
Activation pattern: Regional activation spanning long disordered, low‑complexity stretches with multiple adjacent residues high; pronounced local peaks within short, low‑confidence sub‑segments and alternative/isoform‑variable exons; tolerates transient helix inside IDRs but avoids stable, structured domains; strongest over S/P/G/T‑rich and mixed acidic/basic patches, including repetitive poly‑Q/E/K tracts
Exemplars: - BTB/POZ zinc‑finger transcription factors (e.g., fruitless, ZBTB family): activation on low‑complexity disordered linkers and isoform‑variable regions; little to no signal over the BTB domain or C2H2 fingers.
- HMG/AT‑hook DNA‑binding proteins: activation over Gly/Pro/Lys/Arg‑rich AT‑hook motifs and flanking low‑complexity acidic/basic stretches.
- Mediator complex subunits: activation on acidic, Q/E/K‑rich IDRs that mediate multivalent interactions.
- Histone‑modifying enzymes (HATs, HMTs, demethylases): activation on long disordered N/C‑terminal tails and Ser/Pro/Glu‑rich linkers/activation regions.
- Spliceosomal and other RNA‑binding factors: activation on RS/S‑rich low‑complexity domains and disordered linkers.
- Ubiquitin system components (E3 ligases, deubiquitinases): activation on flexible regulatory IDRs and acidic/basic low‑complexity segments.
- Shugoshin/centromere‑associated proteins and TACC coiled‑coil proteins: activation on low‑complexity acidic/basic tails and coiled‑coil–flanking IDRs (and sometimes E/K‑biased heptad regions).
- DNA repair and general transcription machinery: activation on disordered activation/linker regions rather than catalytic cores.
- Bacterial RNase E and RNAP delta subunit: activation on long acidic low‑complexity tails/scaffolding regions analogous to eukaryotic IDRs.

Summary: Detector of compositionally biased, low‑complexity segments—predominantly intrinsically disordered Ser/Thr‑rich (often RS-/Pro‑containing) tracts—with a strong N‑terminal bias; it also flags the extreme N‑terminus including signal peptides of secreted precursors.
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks clustered within long disordered/low‑complexity regions (often spanning tens to hundreds of residues), with strongest peaks on Ser/Thr and nearby polar/basic residues; broad regional activation across such IDRs and minimal signal in well‑folded domains or transmembranes; additional discrete peaks frequently occur at residues 1–10, including within N‑terminal signal peptides.
Exemplars: - Transcriptional regulator (CROC-4): multiple peaks across a central low‑complexity disordered segment (S/T/R/P‑rich), with minor N‑terminal peaks.
- Mechanosensory receptor (Stum): numerous high peaks on serines dispersed through annotated disordered, low‑complexity/polar regions.
- Yeast RNA/chromatin‑associated factor (REF2‑interacting protein): peaks within disordered, compositionally biased tracts; strongest at a threonine in an S/T‑rich context, near (but not exactly on) annotated phosphosites.
- Secreted antimicrobial peptide precursor (lumbricin): strongest activation on the N‑terminal signal peptide helix; weaker peaks just after the signal peptide preceding a long disordered pro‑region.
- Yeast HPH2 regulatory protein: activation confined to disordered, low‑complexity regions in the N‑terminal two‑thirds; absent from the structured C‑terminal domain and its transmembrane helix.

Summary: Short, non-transmembrane α‑helical segments in secretory‑pathway proteins, with a strong bias toward N‑terminal propeptides of secreted precursors and early extracellular/lumenal regions; often amphipathic/charged and, in disulfide‑rich peptides, may include cysteines; excludes signal peptides and catalytic cores
Activation pattern: Regional activation in contiguous 10–25 aa blocks that map to α‑helices (often multiple blocks per protein); peaks centered within the helix and taper into adjacent coils; strongest near the N‑terminus just after the signal peptide (commonly within propeptides) or in lumenal/extracellular helices; minimal/no activation in signal peptides or mature catalytic domains
Exemplars: - Metalloprotease zymogens (e.g., Vibrio M4 gelatinase): two α‑helical segments within the propeptide.
- Papain‑family cysteine protease zymogens (e.g., staphopains): dominant α‑helix in the propeptide, with a secondary propeptide segment.
- Cystatin family protease inhibitors: the N‑terminal helix (helix 1) within the cystatin domain.
- Disulfide‑rich arthropod toxins (CSαβ/defensin‑like peptides, e.g., scoloptoxins): the central α‑helix that includes cysteines.
- Type II glycosyltransferases (e.g., chondroitin sulfate synthase/mig‑22): a lumenal domain α‑helix.
- Secreted/periplasmic copper amine oxidases: α‑helical segments at the N‑terminus of the mature chain and a second helix in the N‑terminal region, with no activation in the catalytic core.

Summary: Short, cysteine-centered beta-strand–loop–beta hairpins and adjacent loop/turn segments enriched in charged/polar residues, often forming one side of a disulfide bond; typified by ETxC/KTTC/CP sequence contexts in cystatin/cathelin-like domains but occurring in analogous exposed loops of diverse secreted/periplasmic and some intracellular proteins.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks confined to short (≈10–20 aa) segments, strongest at a cysteine (and sometimes the immediately following Pro) within a loop connecting beta-strands; frequently the disulfide partner in the structured strand shows little/no activation. Secondary peaks can occur at strand–helix junctions or in flexible, charged/disordered tails lacking clear secondary structure.
Exemplars: Cathelicidin/cathelin antimicrobial precursors: loop in the cathelin (cystatin-like) propeptide with ETxC/CP, peaking on the disulfide-bonded cysteine; Cystatin/cystatin-like protease inhibitors (including kininogen domains): conserved KTTC-centered hairpin with paired cysteines ~9–12 residues apart; Type IV secretion protein VirB8: periplasmic beta-strand–loop–beta hairpin centered on the loop; Chloroplast division factor ARC6: C-terminal PDV2-interaction region spanning a beta-strand–loop–beta segment with a central cysteine; NTF2-like export proteins: short loop linking beta-strands within the NTF2 fold; Vitellogenins (lipovitellin N-terminus): strand–loop or strand–helix junctions in the LV-1N chain; Other secreted/periplasmic families (BPI/PLUNC/latherin, PsbP/extrinsic PSII proteins) and viral capsids: short, exposed, charged loops often containing a cysteine; Mitochondrial m-AAA protease-interacting proteins: acidic, low-structure C-terminal segments that mimic the short charged loop signature.

Summary: A short, surface‑exposed β‑strand/turn (β‑hairpin/edge‑strand) motif characteristic of cystatin‑like domains and widely reused in small β‑rich extracellular/periplasmic proteins; often includes the cystatin L2 Pro–Trp hairpin and basic/aromatic residues, serving as a protease‑binding/inhibitory loop in cystatins and propeptides and as an analogous interaction loop in other β‑sandwich–type folds.
Activation pattern: Regional activation on 20–40 aa windows centered on a β‑strand and its immediately flanking loop/turn (frequently a strand→coil→strand block); sharp residue‑level peaks on the strand and adjacent turn; low on long helices, intrinsically disordered segments, and transmembrane helices; commonly in secreted/periplasmic portions and near disulfide‑bonded cysteines; enriched for Pro/Trp and Lys/Arg alongside Gly/Pro motifs.
Exemplars: - Cathelicidin precursors (cathelin/cystatin‑like proregions): activation over the central β‑sheet core and flanking loops of the cathelin domain, including disulfide‑proximal residues.
- Papain‑family cysteine protease zymogens (e.g., streptopain/SpeB): a single hotspot within the ordered propeptide β‑strand/coil segment that occludes the active site; catalytic domain remains inactive.
- Cell‑wall–associated secreted/periplasmic regulators with a single transmembrane helix: selective activation on extracellular β‑strands and adjacent turns near the C‑terminus; absent in the TM and cytosolic regions.
- Gas vesicle structural proteins (GvpO): activation confined to a C‑terminal helix–strand–turn–strand block centered on an edge β‑strand, with earlier β‑strands and disordered N‑termini remaining off.

Summary: Extracellular juxtamembrane regions of single-pass and multi-pass transmembrane proteins, with strong preference for SEA domains in type II transmembrane serine proteases and related receptors, and analogous extended extracellular stretches in soluble extracellular proteins; typically long contiguous regions frequently glycosylated or disulfide-bonded that serve in ectodomain presentation and proteolytic shedding.
Activation pattern:
- Regional activation on long, contiguous extracellular stretches, with strongest signal centered on SEA domains
- Sharp peaks frequently overlap N-linked glycosylation sites within the SEA domain
- In soluble extracellular proteins, activation spans extended Ser/Thr- and/or cysteine-rich segments or compact disulfide-bonded modules rather than short linear motifs

Summary: Exposed β-strand–loop–β-strand “reactive/processing” segments of non-cytosolic proteins—i.e., short hairpins in secreted/periplasmic proteins and in organellar lumen- or membrane-exposed domains (e.g., mitochondrial IMS, gas vesicle proteins)—that harbor protease activation/autolysis sites in zymogen propeptides and the reactive-site loops of protease inhibitors; the feature also fires on closely similar hairpins in other non-cytosolic proteins.
Activation pattern: Regional activation: a single contiguous block (≈20–60 aa) typically immediately after the signal or targeting sequence (signal peptide, Sec/Tat, organellar presequence) or at the start of the first extracytoplasmic/lumenal domain, aligning to a β-strand–loop–β-strand hairpin. Residue-level peaks occur at or flanking annotated scissile/reactive-bond or processing sites. Signal/targeting peptides, catalytic residues, and most of the mature catalytic domains are silent; other nearby β-strands are usually not activated unless they form the same exposed hairpin geometry.
Exemplars:
- Secreted bacterial cysteine proteases (streptopain/SpeB): activation confined to a propeptide β-hairpin with autolysis/processing sites; mature core is off.
- Secreted trypsin-like serine proteases (streptogrisin): short β-strand/loop stretch within the propeptide highlighted; mature enzyme off.
- Kazal-type serine protease inhibitors (trypsin inhibitor 1): strong signal on the reactive-site loop around the P1–P1′ bond with flanking β-strands; other disulfide-stabilized regions off.
- Cathelicidin precursors (cathelin-like/cystatin-like domain): β-strand–loop–β-strand inhibitory wedge in the CLD is activated; antimicrobial peptide region and distal CLD β-sheet not.
- Gas vesicle protein O: a central exposed β-hairpin within a β-sheet is selected, consistent with the motif preference outside protease/inhibitor contexts.
- Mitochondrial inner-membrane protein TIM29: activation on an IMS-exposed β-hairpin within the lumenal domain, consistent with non-cytosolic hairpin targeting.

Summary: Low-complexity, compositionally biased segments in intrinsically disordered regions, typically enriched in Gly and/or Pro and frequently punctuated by aromatic residues (Tyr/Phe/Trp). YG/YGG/GYG motifs are common but not required. These tracts are common in secreted/extracellular proteins, antimicrobial/allergen precursors, and prion-like or reproductive IDRs.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across low-pLDDT coil-rich tracts with short Gly/Pro runs and intermittent aromatics; local peaks at Gly, Pro, and aromatic residues. Strongly off in well-structured helices/strands, transmembranes, and folded domains; activation often concentrates in N-terminal low-complexity leaders or propeptides.
Exemplars:
- Peroxisomal membrane protein PEX13: N-terminal Gly/Pro- and Tyr/Phe-punctuated low-complexity coil; off in TM and SH3 domain.
- Small heat shock protein (Hsp42): N-terminal IDR with Y/F/G/P motifs; off over the alpha-crystallin domain.
- Keratin-associated proteins and other extracellular structural proteins (e.g., caseins, chorion components): activation on Gly/Pro/Tyr-rich repeats.
- Plant HIPPs: activation on Pro/Tyr/Gly-rich low-complexity segments.
- Antimicrobial peptide precursors (e.g., clavanin) and allergens: activation on low-complexity signal/propeptides or IDRs that can be Pro/His-rich with occasional aromatics.

Summary: Glycine-rich low‑complexity, intrinsically disordered repeat segments, especially those containing glycine–aromatic dipeptides (FG, GY) and related small‑residue motifs (G/S/P with optional C enrichment), as found in FG‑nucleoporins and in structural/adhesive proteins of metazoan integuments (keratin‑associated, cuticle/eggshell, epidermal) and other glycine‑rich biomaterials
Activation pattern: Long, contiguous activation across disordered low‑complexity regions; strongest residue‑level peaks on glycine and aromatic positions within FG/GY repeats; tolerates S/P/C within G‑rich tracts; little to no activation in folded helical/strand domains
Exemplars: - FG‑nucleoporins (e.g., Nup54/Nup62/Nup98): activation on the FG‑repeat IDRs (e.g., N‑terminal FG blocks), absent from structured C‑terminal domains.

- Arthropod cuticle/eggshell structural proteins: activation on glycine‑ and aromatic‑rich repetitive low‑complexity segments involved in exoskeletal matrices.
- Extracellular adhesive/biomaterial proteins (silk‑like, mussel/barnacle/caddisfly adhesives): activation on G/Y‑rich repetitive blocks in secreted biomaterials.
- Short secreted peptides (neuropeptides, toxins, antimicrobial peptides): activation on short repetitive G/Y‑motif segments (often low complexity).

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity repeat regions enriched in Pro/Gln/Gly/Tyr—especially FG, YG, PG (and GGY) repeats and Q/P‑rich tracts—typically found in long N‑ or C‑terminal tails and linkers of diverse proteins (e.g., FG‑nucleoporins, prion‑like RNA‑binding/regulatory proteins, proline‑rich secreted proteins, plant prolamins, and bacterial spore‑coat/adhesin repeats).

Exemplars: - FG‑nucleoporins: activation on N‑terminal FG‑repeat low‑complexity segments (e.g., NUP54 FG region).
- DEAD‑box RNA helicases and prion‑like regulators: activation on disordered Q/P‑rich C‑terminal tails beyond the helicase core (e.g., Dhh1‑like).
- Bacterial spore coat/adhesin proteins: activation on central PG/GGY/YG repeat blocks in low‑complexity regions.
- Salivary proline‑rich proteins: activation across long proline/tyrosine‑rich repeat segments.
- Plant cereal storage proteins (prolamins/glutamine‑rich): activation across Q/P‑rich repetitive domains.
- ESCRT/endocytosis and actin adaptors: activation on proline‑rich disordered regions (including PxxP‑rich stretches).
- Mediator complex subunits and transcriptional regulators: activation on Q/N‑rich low‑complexity activation domains.
- Annexins/PEF/EF‑hand proteins: activation limited to flexible N‑terminal tails/linkers, not the structured Ca2+‑binding cores.

Summary: Glycine-rich, low-complexity intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs)—often long terminal/linker tracts enriched for RG/RGG (RGG/GAR boxes) and GY/GYG repeats—serving as flexible nucleic-acid–associated tails or interaction modules across diverse proteins
Activation pattern: Regional activation over long contiguous IDRs with low pLDDT/coil propensity, typically at N/C termini or between domains; minimal/absent in folded domains (e.g., RRMs, helicase cores, zinc fingers). Residue-level peaks center on glycine runs with interspersed arginine and/or tyrosine (RG/RGG, GY/GYG), sometimes extending to adjacent basic/serine/proline residues.
Exemplars: - Bacterial single-stranded DNA-binding proteins (SSB): disordered C-terminal glycine-rich tails.
- Cold-shock proteins with CCHC zinc fingers: glycine-rich disordered C-terminal segments, including the linker between zinc fingers.
- Plant glycine-rich RNA-binding proteins: gly/tyr-rich C-terminal tails following an RRM domain.
- TFIID subunit (RanBP2-type zinc finger + RRM): glycine-biased disordered N-terminus, central linker, and C-terminus flanking structured domains.
- SR splicing factor (SRSF1): short glycine-rich disordered linker between RRM1 and RRM2; minor activation in the C-terminal SR-rich IDR.
- DEAD-box RNA helicase (DBP2): disordered termini, with strongest activation in the C-terminal RGG-box.
- Nucleolin: C-terminal GAR (RGG) domain with repeated RG/RGG motifs subject to arginine methylation.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity/prion‑like regions enriched in G, Y, P, Q (often poly‑Q/N), S and T—frequently containing YG/GY/GYG patterns—commonly found in eukaryotic RNA‑binding proteins and transcription factors; these LCDs serve as modular interaction/activation segments and can include transportin‑1–recognized PY‑NLS motifs.
Activation pattern: Long, contiguous activation across intrinsically disordered segments (often C‑terminal tails) with multiple sub‑peaks; little to no activation within adjacent folded domains. Strong sequence preference for Q/N‑rich, P/Y/G/S/T‑rich low‑complexity runs and YG repeats; activation tracks regions with low pLDDT.
Exemplars: - Heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoproteins (hnRNPs): activation confined to the disordered C‑terminal tail harboring the transportin‑1 (PY‑NLS)–dependent nuclear import/export region; no activation in RRM domains.
- Homeobox transcription factors (e.g., bicoid‑like): activation on disordered C‑terminal low‑complexity activation domains; no activation in the structured homeodomain.
- Heavy metal‑associated isoprenylated plant proteins (HIPP): activation on the C‑terminal intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity tail; not in the N‑terminal HMA domain.
- RNA polymerase II degradation factor Def1‑like proteins: broad activation across the C‑terminal Q/G/P/S/Y‑rich disordered region; not in the N‑terminal CUE domain.
