Summary: Low-complexity, compositionally biased segments in intrinsically disordered regions, typically enriched in Gly and/or Pro and frequently punctuated by aromatic residues (Tyr/Phe/Trp). YG/YGG/GYG motifs are common but not required. These tracts are common in secreted/extracellular proteins, antimicrobial/allergen precursors, and prion-like or reproductive IDRs.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across low-pLDDT coil-rich tracts with short Gly/Pro runs and intermittent aromatics; local peaks at Gly, Pro, and aromatic residues. Strongly off in well-structured helices/strands, transmembranes, and folded domains; activation often concentrates in N-terminal low-complexity leaders or propeptides.
Exemplars:

Summary: Short N-terminal signal/leader/propeptide segments of secreted precursors, plus some internal helical/disordered segments in select intracellular proteins.
Activation pattern: Strong, localized activation within the first ~1–25 residues of secreted precursors, with a sharp peak across the hydrophobic h-region of the signal peptide that drops at the cleavage site into the mature chain; in some intracellular proteins, activation peaks over an internal α-helical or loop segment rather than the very termini.
Exemplars:
- Secreted peptide precursors: RiPP/bacteriocin leaders (e.g., microcin B17); antimicrobial peptide and neuropeptide precursors (e.g., C. elegans NLP family, holotricin); salivary/gland proline-rich proteins
- Intracellular proteins: periplasmic/secreted bacterial proteins like ZraP (internal helix); J-domain/Hsp40 co-chaperones; bacterial SSB; urease accessory UreE; keratin-associated/repetitive structural proteins

Summary: Nucleic‑acid replication/junction‑processing catalytic cores, centered on SF3/P‑loop helicase ATPase modules in viral replication proteins (and the homologous helicase regions of ssDNA rolling‑circle Reps), with secondary recognition of structure‑specific nuclease cores that resolve branched DNA (Holliday junction resolvases). The feature homes in on Walker A/B and adjacent helicase motifs and, in ssDNA virus Reps, a conserved mid‑protein Trp‑anchored segment characteristic of their helicase region.
Activation pattern: - Domain-level activation across superfamily 3/P-loop helicase cores: long contiguous bands spanning the ATPase module with strong peaks on Walker A (P-loop), Walker B, nearby arginine finger/motif VI, and flanking nucleic‑acid–engaging loops.
- In ssDNA virus Rep proteins (Circoviridae/Geminiviridae/alphasatellites), strong regional activation in a mid‑protein segment (~190–240) often marked by tandem Trp followed by acidic/glycine residues, extending into the C‑terminal helicase domain.
- In large DNA virus helicases (e.g., herpesvirus origin‑binding proteins, poxvirus A18‑like), broad activation over the ATPase/helicase core.
- In (+)RNA virus replicase polyproteins, concentrated activation in the NTPase/SF3 helicase region with residue‑level peaks at annotated ATP‑binding positions; protease and most polymerase regions remain low.
- In Holliday junction resolvases (RecU/Hjc families), strong activation across the compact metal‑dependent nuclease core, with peaks at catalytic residues (often near the N‑terminus) and associated metal‑binding/transition‑state–stabilizing sites.
- Generally low/no signal in unrelated domains (membrane segments, disordered linkers, proteases, most polymerase cores).
Exemplars: - Rolling‑circle Rep proteins of Circoviridae/Geminiviridae/alphasatellites: activation at the conserved mid‑region Trp‑anchored motif and across the C‑terminal SF3 helicase/ATPase module.
- Positive‑strand RNA virus replicase polyproteins (caliciviruses, dicistroviruses): strong activation within the SF3 helicase with peaks over Walker A/B and adjacent helicase motifs; little activation in 3C‑like protease or RdRp.
- Herpesvirus UL9‑like origin‑binding proteins: activation over the P‑loop NTPase/helicase core used for origin DNA unwinding.
- Poxvirus A18‑like termination/helicase factors: domain‑level activation across the helicase ATPase region.
- Bacterial/archaeal Holliday junction resolvases (RecU/Hjc): broad activation across the small catalytic core, with peaks at the catalytic residues and metal‑binding sites that cleave DNA junctions.
- Phage nucleotide‑processing enzymes (helicases/kinases/nucleases): activation on P‑loop NTPase elements of helicases/kinases and on nuclease catalytic cores when present.

Summary: Small, compact proteins (~70-170 residues) showing near whole-protein activation, enriched for viral/phage host-defense antagonists and nucleic-acid–associated factors, alongside small bacterial accessory subunits with similar size and fold characteristics.
Activation pattern: Broad, domain-level activation spanning the majority of each protein (typically 70-85% of residues active), with peaks distributed across both structured (helical/strand) and loop regions; activation often covers essentially the entire chain in short proteins.
Exemplars:
- Phage anti-restriction/host-defense antagonists (Ocr, lambda Gam): activation across the full protein used to bind and inhibit host nuclease/restriction systems
- Phage proteins involved in resistance/replication (phi29 gp17 DNA replication protein; Lactococcus phage gp38 anti-AbiQ): broad activation across the small protein body
- Viral nucleic-acid-associated factors (HIV-1 Vif RNA-binding region; plant virus P15 RNA silencing suppressor): activation over the RNA-binding/effector region
- Bacterial nitrogenase iron-iron protein delta chains (Clostridium, Azotobacter, Azomonas): broad activation across the small subunit with peaks centered on a conserved Cys/Tyr/Trp-containing helix
- Small eukaryotic regulatory proteins (Ataxin-7-like 3B): activation over the structured N-terminal region

Summary: Amphipathic α-helical packing elements—short helix or helix–turn–helix (helical hairpin/coiled-coil–like) segments enriched in hydrophobic (Leu/Phe/Ile) and basic (Lys/Arg) residues that form generic helical interaction/packing modules within structured domains across diverse proteins
Activation pattern: Regional activation over single contiguous 20–50 residue stretches that map to one or two adjacent α-helices (often a helix–loop–helix), with strongest signal on helical cores and basic/hydrophobic positions and dips at intervening coil residues; repeats multiple times within large proteins; largely absent from disordered/transit peptides
Exemplars: - Rab3-GAP catalytic subunit: activation on a C-terminal helical bundle segment
- Glycyl radical enzymes (pyruvate formate lyase/formate acetyltransferase): activation on the C‑terminal helix–loop–helix bordering the glycyl radical site and on a separate helical patch in the N‑terminal domain
- D‑ornithine 4,5‑aminomutase α‑subunit: activation on an N‑terminal twin‑helix packing element
- Holocytochrome c–type synthase: activation across a structured core β–α segment, peaking on the α‑helix
- Ferredoxin‑dependent bilin reductase (phytochromobilin:ferredoxin oxidoreductase/PcyA): activation on a short helical hairpin in the core
- ESCRT‑I subunit TSG101/Vps23: activation within the C‑terminal “steadiness box” helical region
- RGS domain proteins: activation on internal α‑helical segments of the all‑α RGS fold
- Chromatin remodeler/corepressor scaffolds and ubiquitin/AAA‑associated adaptors: activation on coiled‑coil–like helical segments used for assembly/interaction

Summary: Short loop–β-strand–α-helix(–α) "wing"/hairpin motif recurring in accessory subdomains of nucleic-acid-associated enzymes and transcription factors, including helicases, type IA topoisomerases (incl. reverse gyrase), TFIIH p52/TFB2 subunits, and certain restriction enzymes; the SAE chiefly tracks this β→α structural element, which is also occasionally mimicked in unrelated enzymes.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks at β→α junctions and within small helical hairpins; in helicases the activation is narrow and concentrated in C-terminal accessory regions outside the motor core, whereas in TFIIH p52/TFB2 subunits the feature fires broadly across multiple disjoint β-strand/α-helix elements covering a large fraction of the protein; sometimes multiple disjoint regions per protein.
Exemplars: - Ski2-like RNA helicases (SKI2, MTR4, and related DExH-box helicases): strong activation on a C-terminal helical segment outside the helicase core (arch/arm region).
- MER3 DNA helicase: activation at the N-terminus of the Sec63-like accessory domain, centered on a β-strand followed by an α-helix.
- DNA polymerase theta (N-terminal helicase-like module): activation immediately C-terminal to the annotated Helicase C-terminal domain on an accessory helical segment.
- Type IA topoisomerases (Topo I/III) and reverse gyrase: activation across late C-terminal accessory ssDNA-binding modules (e.g., zinc-ribbon/HRDC/winged-helix-like elements), often over longer stretches.
- TFIIH subunit p52/TFB2 (across human, yeast, plants): broad, strong activation over multiple β-strand/α-helix elements in the central region of the subunit.
- Type II restriction enzyme FokI: activation at internal β→α junctions, consistent with structural rather than functional similarity.
- Viral SF1/SF2 helicases: strong activation on basic C-terminal helical patches adjacent to the motor core.
- Ribosomal proteins/biogenesis factors: shorter, weaker hits on small helical/wing elements.
- SAM-dependent O-methyltransferases: low-score matches to a local loop–β–α motif within the Rossmann-like fold, consistent with structural (not functional) similarity.

Summary: N-terminal alpha-helix of small accessory proteins and peptide precursors used as a docking/processing module, mediating partner/chaperone engagement, complex assembly, or export recognition across diverse systems.
Activation pattern: Strong regional activation confined to the first ~10–30 residues; peaks typically coincide with a predicted N‑terminal alpha-helix or the entry of a coiled‑coil; little/no activation in downstream folded cores or in the processed mature peptide after leader removal.
Exemplars: - Double‑glycine bacteriocin and quorum‑sensing pheromone precursors (e.g., ComX/ComC/class II bacteriocins): activation on the N‑terminal propeptide/leader helix, absent on the mature peptide.
- Dam1/DASH outer kinetochore subunits: activation on N‑terminal segments at the start of coiled‑coils that nucleate assembly and interface with partner subunits.
- Small RNA polymerase–associated factors (e.g., DksA/Gre/TFIIS‑like and small RNAP subunits): activation on N‑terminal helix/hairpin regions that dock to RNAP.
- Type III/VI secretion chaperones and toxin immunity proteins: activation on N‑terminal helices that present cargo or neutralize cognate toxins via chaperone/partner binding.
- Viral/phage small accessory proteins: activation on N‑terminal helical stretches used to recruit/antagonize host machineries.
- Halophilic gas vesicle proteins (e.g., GvpC‑like): activation on N‑terminal repeat/helix segments that bind vesicle surfaces.
- Metallothioneins and other small cysteine‑rich proteins: activation on short N‑terminal segments adjacent to Cys‑rich cores.
- Mitochondrial respiratory chain assembly factors and other small assembly cofactors: activation on N‑terminal helices that act as assembly/docking elements.
- Nucleoid‑associated/regulatory small proteins: activation on N‑terminal tails that modulate interactions with DNA/RNA‑binding partners rather than DNA contact itself.

Summary: Structural boundary micro-motifs: helix caps and adjacent coil/turn loops (often Gly/Pro- and polar-enriched), marking flexible linkers at secondary-structure transitions and, more rarely, isolated hallmark residues within compact helical domains.
Activation pattern: Mostly residue-level peaks at helix termini or loop/turn positions; sometimes short regional runs across gly/pro-rich or low-complexity segments; occasionally extended activation over disordered stretches; rare single-residue hits within continuous helices that border such loops.
Exemplars: - ATP synthase F0 subunit a: single glutamine immediately C-terminal to a transmembrane helix (helix C-cap/periplasmic loop entry).
- Myosin motor proteins: isolated glycine in a flexible loop within the motor domain core.
- PX-domain scaffolding proteins (e.g., p47phox/NCF1): a specific residue within a well-ordered PX-domain helix, consistent with a conserved local helix-cap/turn micro-environment.
- Carbohydrate-active hydrolases (e.g., isopullulanase/pullulanase): short loop/turn-rich segment between brief helices with glycine peaks, including an NXS/T glycosylation motif.
- Bacillus thuringiensis Cry toxins: broad activation over a low-pLDDT disordered region, with secondary weaker activation on a helical bundle.
- Polyketide synthase acyltransferase domains: single-residue landmark within the AT subdomain of a megasynthase.

Summary: Short linear segments in intrinsically disordered or otherwise low-structure-confidence regions, often at N-termini and within signal peptides/propeptides of secreted and regulatory proteins (including viral accessory proteins and small ORF microproteins), enriched in small/basic residues (G, P, S, A, R; often with Cys), rather than in well-folded catalytic cores.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks scattered across IDRs and low-confidence coils/short helices; frequently clustered near the N-terminus, in signal peptides, propeptides, and disordered tails; little to no activation in well-structured domains; occasional activation in low-confidence transmembrane/signal-anchor helices.
Exemplars: - Viral accessory protein (HIV-1 Vif): peaks throughout low-pLDDT coils, especially the disordered N-terminal region.
- Neuropeptide precursor (Drosophila Amnesiac): activation in the N-terminal signal peptide and multiple mature peptide segments with very low pLDDT.
- Secreted serine carboxypeptidase: activation confined to disordered C-terminal tail, annotated disordered segment, the signal peptide, and a low-confidence C-terminal transmembrane helix; absent from the structured catalytic domain.
- Disordered human tumor-suppressor–associated protein (ST20): scattered peaks within predicted helices in a globally disordered chain, including the N-terminus.
- lncRNA/sORF-derived microprotein (IGF2 antisense protein): multiple peaks across annotated disordered regions rich in Arg/Pro/Gly.

Summary: Broad, regional recognition of helical and hydrophobic/amphipathic segments, including contiguous hydrophobic alpha-helical transmembrane segments and proline/glycine-rich low-complexity stretches; the feature also fires across large internal regions of soluble enzymes and effector proteins, with a bias toward hydrophobic and helix-favoring residues and proline/glycine context.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over stretches: contiguous activation across single-pass or multi-pass transmembrane alpha-helices and amphipathic helical motifs; broad, distributed activation across internal regions of soluble proteins; sparser peaks within short secreted, low-complexity segments; overall bias toward hydrophobic and helix-favoring residues with enrichment for proline and glycine context.
Exemplars:
- Fibrillar collagens: strong activation along the triple-helical G–X–Y domain, peaking at X/Y positions (especially proline/hydroxyproline-like Y), with minimal signal on G.
- Light-harvesting complex alpha subunits (photosynthetic bacteria): activation along their single transmembrane alpha-helix.
- YhhN/TMEM86 lysoplasmalogenases: activation across multiple transmembrane segments.
- Viral accessory proteins (including non-membrane factors like replication enhancers), envelope proteins, and viroporins: activation on short hydrophobic or amphipathic helical motifs (membrane-anchored or not).
- Single-pass small integral membrane proteins: activation on the transmembrane helix.
- Plant CLE/CLAVATA/ESR peptide precursors: activation on the conserved proline-rich mature peptide region and adjacent low-complexity stretches.
- Oomycete RxLR effectors: activation across the mature effector region including the RxLR-dEER motif and adjacent low-complexity repeats.
- Fungal secreted/surface-associated effectors (e.g., hydrophobin-like): activation on hydrophobic, repetitive patches outside core cystine motifs.
- Small cysteine-rich toxins/defensin-like peptides: activation on hydrophobic patches within or adjacent to the disulfide-stabilized core.
- Soluble cytosolic enzymes/regulators: broad, distributed activation across internal regions, including disordered and low-complexity stretches.

Summary: Small, often poorly characterized or compositionally biased proteins, including viral accessory proteins, cancer/testis and germline-associated proteins, antisense-ORF microproteins, and short secreted/surface peptides; activation is broadly distributed across the polypeptide rather than focused on a single structured domain
Activation pattern: Regional/distributed activation spread across much of the protein with sparse residue-level peaks; often includes early N-terminal residues and disordered segments; variable coverage from short patches to most of the protein
Exemplars:
- Viral non-structural/accessory proteins: activation distributed through the protein, including basic/Arg-rich motifs such as nuclear localization signals.
- Cancer/testis antigens and germline-associated proteins: activation on long disordered low-complexity regions, often at N-termini.
- Small uncharacterized microproteins/antisense ORFs: activation spanning most of the polypeptide.
- Short secreted peptides and toxin precursors: activation across both signal/propeptide and mature regions.
- Compact cytosolic proteins with disordered N- or C-terminal extensions: activation enriched on the disordered tails.

Summary: Compositionally biased intrinsically disordered low‑complexity regions (LCD/IDRs) enriched in Ser/Pro/Gly with mixed charged residues (Glu/Asp and Lys/Arg), often containing poly‑Q/E/K or RS/S‑rich tracts; these correspond to regulatory tails, activation/linker segments, and isoform‑variable regions in nuclear transcription/chromatin and RNA‑processing proteins, and analogous acidic low‑complexity tails in some bacterial factors; signal is depleted in well‑folded domains (e.g., BTB, C2H2 zinc fingers)
Activation pattern: Regional activation spanning long disordered, low‑complexity stretches with multiple adjacent residues high; pronounced local peaks within short, low‑confidence sub‑segments and alternative/isoform‑variable exons; tolerates transient helix inside IDRs but avoids stable, structured domains; strongest over S/P/G/T‑rich and mixed acidic/basic patches, including repetitive poly‑Q/E/K tracts
Exemplars: - BTB/POZ zinc‑finger transcription factors (e.g., fruitless, ZBTB family): activation on low‑complexity disordered linkers and isoform‑variable regions; little to no signal over the BTB domain or C2H2 fingers.
- HMG/AT‑hook DNA‑binding proteins: activation over Gly/Pro/Lys/Arg‑rich AT‑hook motifs and flanking low‑complexity acidic/basic stretches.
- Mediator complex subunits: activation on acidic, Q/E/K‑rich IDRs that mediate multivalent interactions.
- Histone‑modifying enzymes (HATs, HMTs, demethylases): activation on long disordered N/C‑terminal tails and Ser/Pro/Glu‑rich linkers/activation regions.
- Spliceosomal and other RNA‑binding factors: activation on RS/S‑rich low‑complexity domains and disordered linkers.
- Ubiquitin system components (E3 ligases, deubiquitinases): activation on flexible regulatory IDRs and acidic/basic low‑complexity segments.
- Shugoshin/centromere‑associated proteins and TACC coiled‑coil proteins: activation on low‑complexity acidic/basic tails and coiled‑coil–flanking IDRs (and sometimes E/K‑biased heptad regions).
- DNA repair and general transcription machinery: activation on disordered activation/linker regions rather than catalytic cores.
- Bacterial RNase E and RNAP delta subunit: activation on long acidic low‑complexity tails/scaffolding regions analogous to eukaryotic IDRs.

Summary: Short segments within disordered and compositionally biased stretches of diverse proteins, particularly regions enriched in basic and acidic residues. Activations are also seen in non-disordered contexts across proteins of varied function, suggesting the feature captures a relatively broad local sequence pattern rather than a tight structural motif.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks with small clusters, distributed throughout the length of the protein. Peaks frequently overlap annotated disordered regions and basic/acidic compositionally biased segments, but also occur at isolated positions within structured chains; occurs in both helical and coil contexts.
Exemplars: - Oomycete RxLR secreted effectors: peaks within the mature effector chain, with occasional spikes in the signal peptide.
- Plant CLE peptide precursors: localized peaks within the C-terminal CLE motif corresponding to the mature signaling peptide.
- Cholecystokinin prohormone: peaks at or immediately adjacent to the N-termini of mature neuropeptides generated by proteolytic processing.
- Herpesvirus ICP47-like small accessory proteins: multiple peaks in the N-terminal active helical region and in polar, disordered C-terminal stretches.
- Keratin-associated proteins: activation across cysteine/proline/serine-rich, low-complexity repeat regions.
- Phosphodiesterase and fungal/bacterial enzymes with disordered N- or internal stretches: peaks within basic-and-acidic compositionally biased segments.

Summary: Residue positions that mark polypeptide boundaries—especially the absolute N-terminus (position 1) and the terminal residue of sequence fragments—and, secondarily, isolated boundary-like sites within larger proteins (e.g., short linkers between secondary-structure elements or helix/turn cap-like positions), consistent with proteolytic processing junctions in pre/propeptides.
Activation pattern: Predominantly single-residue peaks at sequence extremities (most often the first residue; also the last residue of fragments); sparse internal single-residue peaks at boundary-like positions (short linkers or transitions between secondary structures). Often coincides with disordered/low-confidence termini; in secreted/toxin precursors a recurring window around residues ~50–70 is consistent with signal/propeptide cleavage. Per-protein activations are usually one or a few sites.
Exemplars: Snake venom serine protease: peaks at the N-terminal first residue and at the C-terminal end of the chain; Nuclear pore complex protein Nup155: isolated peaks on single residues within a helix and a low-confidence turn; U4/U6.U5 tri-snRNP–associated protein 1: single-residue peak at a glycine linker between β-strands; E4 ubiquitin-conjugation factor (UBE4): isolated methionine within a long α-helix; Reelin (fragment): strong activation at the fragment’s C-terminal residue in a disordered region; Glutamate dehydrogenase (fragment): activation marks the truncated C-terminal residue.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity regions enriched in serine, threonine, proline and polar/charged residues—flexible regulatory linkers/tails and propeptide segments that often host short linear motifs (e.g., phosphorylation- and proline‑rich motifs) and proteolytic processing sites; signal is absent from well‑folded catalytic domains and is common across taxa
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long disordered stretches with many sparse residue‑level peaks; avoids structured domains; peaks biased toward S/T/P, glycine, and charged/polar residues; frequently concentrated in N‑ or C‑terminal IDRs and around cleavage/processing sites; can span hundreds of residues in large eukaryotic proteins
Exemplars: - PAK family serine/threonine kinases: activation on the N‑terminal regulatory IDR preceding the kinase domain (including low‑confidence helical propensities), not in the folded kinase domain.
- Rap/Ras GTPase‑activating proteins: activation on disordered, low‑complexity linkers; absent from the structured GAP domain.
- CARMIL (actin/capping protein regulators): activation on a C‑terminal proline/basic‑rich disordered tail.
- Centrosomal/kinetochore and chromosomal scaffold proteins: multiple low‑complexity, disordered tracts with scattered peaks.
- Transcriptional/chromatin regulators: activation on N‑terminal low‑complexity/activation domains and compositionally biased regions.
- Ribonucleotide reductase large subunit‑like proteins: activation on N‑terminal disordered tails, including proline‑rich segments.
- Neuropeptide/prohormone precursors: activation in disordered propeptides and at termini of amidated peptides, often adjacent to cleavage sites.

Summary: Broadly distributed activation across small secreted peptides, processed protein fragments, and various polar/charged residues in short proteins, with frequent firing in viral, venom, and signaling-peptide contexts.

Activation pattern: Sparse residue-level peaks scattered across the protein, with no strong preference for structured versus unstructured regions; peaks occur on a mix of polar (Asn, Asp, Ser, Gln), basic (Arg, Lys), and hydrophobic (Leu, Val, Ala) residues, and can fall within transmembrane helices, disordered stretches, or short folded chains alike.

Exemplars:
- Secreted peptide hormones (cholecystokinin, kisspeptin/metastin): multiple peaks across the processed peptide chain.
- Snake venom metalloproteinase/disintegrin fragment: distributed peaks across the short chain.
- Viral hexon-linking precursor proteins: weak peaks distributed across the chain including propeptide and cleaved segments.
- Peroxisomal biogenesis factors: peaks within transmembrane helices and other regions of the membrane protein.
- Bacterial methyltransferases: activation localized to C-terminal disordered extension while the catalytic core is inactive.
- Antithrombin/serpin precursor: peaks spanning the signal peptide and mature chain.

Summary: Short G/S/P-rich low-complexity motifs (often containing a "GSSP"/"GSNP" core) frequently located near the N-terminus, appearing across diverse bacterial, archaeal, and viral proteins
Activation pattern: A single sharp residue-level peak (commonly on a glycine) within a short 3–10 aa G/S/P-rich cluster, most often within the first ~20 residues; occasionally additional peaks distributed across longer disordered low-complexity stretches or internal linkers
Exemplars:
- Bacterial PLP-dependent aminotransferases (e.g., acetylornithine aminotransferase across cyanobacteria): peak on a conserved N-terminal GSSP-like motif
- Archaeal tRNA-modifying enzymes (e.g., tRNA(Met) cytidine acetyltransferase TmcA): peak on an N-terminal "MIPGSNPGG" motif
- Bacterial cell-wall ligases (e.g., MurE-family): peak on the very N-terminal G of an "MGSNPTP"-like motif
- Bacterial extracellular proteases: peak on an internal G/S/P-rich segment
- Archaeal viral integrases (SSV1): peaks within a disordered N-proximal region containing G-rich and basic stretches

Summary: Ala/Val/Gly–enriched low‑complexity segments, often within intrinsically disordered or low‑confidence regions of small/unstructured proteins (signal peptides, pro‑peptide extensions, regulatory tails, microproteins), characterized by small aliphatic residues interspersed with sparse acidic residues; composition- rather than function-specific.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks land predominantly on V (and A/D/E) residues within low-complexity or disordered tracts; multiple peaks can be distributed across a stretch (regional LCR activation), with reduced signal in well-folded globular domains.
Exemplars: - Oomycete RxLR effectors: activation on alanines/valines and acidic residues flanking the RxLR motif and within adjacent disordered N‑terminal regions (including non-helical segments of annotated signal/TM zones).
- OmpR/PhoB-type response regulators (e.g., PfeR): activation confined to the N‑terminal intrinsically disordered extension; absent from the structured receiver and HTH DNA‑binding domains.
- Conotoxin precursors: peaks in the N‑terminal signal peptide (A/V/E sites) and scattered across the low‑confidence mature toxin region.
- Mammalian unstructured microproteins (e.g., testis-specific proteins) and ST20-like regulators: sparse peaks on V/A residues distributed throughout globally disordered sequences.
- Small viral accessory proteins (e.g., agnoprotein, PB1‑F2): scattered V/D/E peaks across short, largely disordered chains.

Summary: Extended amphipathic alpha‑helical bundle segments that form the ordered cores of C‑terminal catalytic/regulatory domains in large eukaryotic signaling and scaffold proteins (e.g., FH2, SEC7, HECT, PAP‑associated, plexin cytoplasmic modules, and cullin helical scaffolds).
Activation pattern: Domain-level, long continuous activation over tens to hundreds of residues, predominantly in high-index/C‑terminal regions. Signal tracks along ordered alpha‑helices and helical bundles (often amphipathic; enriched in K/E/R/D and L/V/I/F), with little emphasis on catalytic residues themselves (e.g., not centered on HECT catalytic Cys or SEC7 catalytic Glu). Peaks occur within helices; weaker in loops/disordered segments.
Exemplars: - Formins: strong activation across the FH2 domain core (with secondary, weaker signal in the helical GBD/FH3 region).
- ARF guanine nucleotide exchange factors: activation within the C‑terminal portion of the SEC7 catalytic domain.
- HECT E3 ubiquitin ligases: activation on the helical lobe/hinge of the HECT domain, excluding the catalytic cysteine site.
- Cytoplasmic poly(A) polymerase complexes (GLD‑2): activation at the start of the C‑terminal PAP‑associated helical region.
- Plexin receptors: activation on intracellular helical modules (GAP/RBD-containing cytoplasmic region).
- Cullin scaffold proteins: activation along the elongated alpha‑helical scaffold repeats.
- Ras/Rap/Ral GEFs: activation on CDC25-like all‑alpha helical catalytic domains.
- Large translation/RNA-binding scaffolds: activation on HEAT/ARM-like alpha‑helical solenoids in C‑terminal regions.

Summary: Folded alpha-helical core of the formin FH2 (Formin Homology 2) domain in large eukaryotic actin-nucleating/cytoskeletal regulator proteins. The feature favors the contiguous helical FH2 fold and avoids the adjacent proline-rich FH1 tracts and disordered linkers/tails typical of formins.
Activation pattern: - Domain-level, contiguous activation across the FH2 helical core with peaks in central helices; sharp drop at domain termini
- Turns on at disorder-to-helix boundaries; near-zero in low-complexity/disordered regions (including FH1 proline-rich tracts and the C-terminal DAD/disordered tail)
- Selective within proteins: strongly engages the FH2 domain while showing much weaker activation over the also-helical GBD/FH3 region and other coiled-coil segments
Exemplars: - Yeast/fungal formins (Bni1, Bnr1, Fus1, Cdc12, sepA, Formin-A, Formin-3): strong contiguous activation throughout the FH2 domain; reduced over GBD/FH3; off in FH1 Pro-rich segments and disordered linkers
- Plant formins (AtFH5): activation confined to the FH2 domain; off across the N-terminal disordered region and transmembrane segments

Summary: Long all-alpha helical scaffold domains—primarily alpha-solenoids/HEAT-like repeats (including MIF4G/ACE1) and related helical-rod bundles—that mediate protein-protein interactions in large eukaryotic assemblies
Activation pattern: Domain-level activation over long, contiguous blocks, typically in central/C-terminal regions; multiple internal peaks aligned with successive alpha-helices; minimal activation in disordered N-termini, sometimes extending into adjacent coil segments
Exemplars: - Y-complex nucleoporins (e.g., Nup85): activation on the central ACE1 alpha-solenoid scaffold region
- Gamma-tubulin ring complex components (GCP3): activation across the C-terminal helical scaffold domain
- Formins (FH2-containing): strong activation spanning the FH2 all-alpha helical bundle
- Cap-binding/translation factor scaffolds (CBP80/NCBP1): peak activation within the MIF4G (HEAT-repeat) domain with moderate activation across downstream helical segments

Summary: Extended alpha-helical scaffold/assembly modules in large eukaryotic proteins—prototypically the formin FH2 domain—and similar long coiled-coil or helical connector/bundle regions that mediate oligomerization and organization of cytoskeletal, ciliary/axonemal, nuclear-pore, and trafficking complexes
Activation pattern: Broad regional/domain-level activation over long, contiguous blocks (often 100–400+ aa) that are enriched in helix-favoring residues (E/K/L/A); strongest in C-terminal FH2 regions of formins, but also in other extended helical segments (coiled-coils, alpha-helical bundles/solenoids). Activation forms a plateau with modest local peaks; generally avoids catalytic/beta-rich domains. Common in eukaryotes across diverse lineages.
Exemplars: - Formins (FH2 domain): very strong, continuous activation across the C-terminal FH2 helical domain.
- Rho GEFs: activation on a long accessory helix-rich block adjacent to but outside the DH catalytic core.
- MICOS Mic60: activation over a C-terminal helix/coil segment implicated in mitochondrial scaffold assembly.
- MutS family (Msh2): activation across the helical Connector (domain V) that links subdomains within the mismatch repair clamp.
- Ciliary/axonemal scaffold proteins: long coiled-coil regions supporting axoneme assembly show strong regional activation.
- Nuclear pore scaffolds (nucleoporins): alpha-helical scaffold/solenoid regions activate, not FG-repeat segments.
- Endosomal trafficking/BAR/ESCRT adaptors: BAR/coiled-coil assembly regions and related helical scaffolds activate.

Summary: Extended alpha‑helical domain cores of large, multidomain eukaryotic proteins—most often the major C‑terminal catalytic/regulatory module—such as helical bundles and coiled‑coils (e.g., FH2, Cdc25/Ras‑GEF, myosin DIL, DUB helical cores), while ignoring N‑terminal low‑complexity/proline‑rich and disordered regions.
Activation pattern: Turns on sharply at the boundary of a long structured domain (typically mid‑to‑C‑terminal), remains continuously high across its contiguous alpha‑helices and adjacent short coils, and peaks in the central helical core; depressed at isolated catalytic residues/short β segments and in flexible/disordered loops. Activation requires domain‑length helical continuity (not single helices), yielding long, dense bands spanning hundreds of residues; N‑terminal, low‑complexity, and disordered stretches remain near zero.
Exemplars: - Formins: selectively marks the FH2 domain, with strongest signal over its central/C‑terminal helical core; ignores the disordered, proline‑rich FH1 and other N‑terminal regions.
- Ras/Rap/Ral GEFs: highlights the C‑terminal Cdc25/Ras‑GEF catalytic domain (helical bundle), with weak signal in the disordered N‑terminus.
- Deubiquitinases (MINDY family): activates across the C‑terminal structured catalytic module’s helical/β core, with a trough at the catalytic His and no signal in long disordered regions.
- Myosins: strongly marks the C‑terminal Dilute (DIL) globular tail (helical bundle), with only minor, scattered signal elsewhere in the motor.
- Coiled‑coil scaffolds (e.g., tubulin epsilon/delta complex protein 1): continuous activation across the long central coiled‑coil/helical region, absent in flanking disordered or isolated helical segments.

Summary: Residue positions that mark polypeptide boundaries—especially the absolute N-terminus (position 1) and the terminal residue of sequence fragments—and, secondarily, isolated boundary-like sites within larger proteins (e.g., short linkers between secondary-structure elements or helix/turn cap-like positions), consistent with proteolytic processing junctions in pre/propeptides.
Activation pattern: Predominantly single-residue peaks at sequence extremities (most often the first residue; also the last residue of fragments); sparse internal single-residue peaks at boundary-like positions (short linkers or transitions between secondary structures). Often coincides with disordered/low-confidence termini; in secreted/toxin precursors a recurring window around residues ~50–70 is consistent with signal/propeptide cleavage. Per-protein activations are usually one or a few sites.
Exemplars: Snake venom serine protease: peaks at the N-terminal first residue and at the C-terminal end of the chain; Nuclear pore complex protein Nup155: isolated peaks on single residues within a helix and a low-confidence turn; U4/U6.U5 tri-snRNP–associated protein 1: single-residue peak at a glycine linker between β-strands; E4 ubiquitin-conjugation factor (UBE4): isolated methionine within a long α-helix; Reelin (fragment): strong activation at the fragment’s C-terminal residue in a disordered region; Glutamate dehydrogenase (fragment): activation marks the truncated C-terminal residue.

Summary: Broadly distributed activation across small secreted peptides, processed protein fragments, and various polar/charged residues in short proteins, with frequent firing in viral, venom, and signaling-peptide contexts.

Activation pattern: Sparse residue-level peaks scattered across the protein, with no strong preference for structured versus unstructured regions; peaks occur on a mix of polar (Asn, Asp, Ser, Gln), basic (Arg, Lys), and hydrophobic (Leu, Val, Ala) residues, and can fall within transmembrane helices, disordered stretches, or short folded chains alike.

Exemplars:
- Secreted peptide hormones (cholecystokinin, kisspeptin/metastin): multiple peaks across the processed peptide chain.
- Snake venom metalloproteinase/disintegrin fragment: distributed peaks across the short chain.
- Viral hexon-linking precursor proteins: weak peaks distributed across the chain including propeptide and cleaved segments.
- Peroxisomal biogenesis factors: peaks within transmembrane helices and other regions of the membrane protein.
- Bacterial methyltransferases: activation localized to C-terminal disordered extension while the catalytic core is inactive.
- Antithrombin/serpin precursor: peaks spanning the signal peptide and mature chain.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity regions enriched in serine, threonine, proline and polar/charged residues—flexible regulatory linkers/tails and propeptide segments that often host short linear motifs (e.g., phosphorylation- and proline‑rich motifs) and proteolytic processing sites; signal is absent from well‑folded catalytic domains and is common across taxa
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long disordered stretches with many sparse residue‑level peaks; avoids structured domains; peaks biased toward S/T/P, glycine, and charged/polar residues; frequently concentrated in N‑ or C‑terminal IDRs and around cleavage/processing sites; can span hundreds of residues in large eukaryotic proteins
Exemplars: - PAK family serine/threonine kinases: activation on the N‑terminal regulatory IDR preceding the kinase domain (including low‑confidence helical propensities), not in the folded kinase domain.
- Rap/Ras GTPase‑activating proteins: activation on disordered, low‑complexity linkers; absent from the structured GAP domain.
- CARMIL (actin/capping protein regulators): activation on a C‑terminal proline/basic‑rich disordered tail.
- Centrosomal/kinetochore and chromosomal scaffold proteins: multiple low‑complexity, disordered tracts with scattered peaks.
- Transcriptional/chromatin regulators: activation on N‑terminal low‑complexity/activation domains and compositionally biased regions.
- Ribonucleotide reductase large subunit‑like proteins: activation on N‑terminal disordered tails, including proline‑rich segments.
- Neuropeptide/prohormone precursors: activation in disordered propeptides and at termini of amidated peptides, often adjacent to cleavage sites.

Summary: Single conserved residue—often hydrophobic/aromatic but variable (Phe/Tyr/Trp/Leu/Val/Ile, and sometimes His/Thr)—within nucleotide- or ligand-binding pockets and analogous buried sites across diverse folds; in non-nucleotide proteins it maps to an analogous internal pocket- or core-lining position.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks at an internal pocket-lining residue, occasionally with short adjacent clusters; position varies widely with the fold.
Exemplars:
- Protein kinases (including viral/atypical): activation within the kinase domain at a residue near the ATP-binding cleft.
- tRNA (guanine-N7)-methyltransferases (class I SAM MTases): activation on the conserved aromatic that stacks with the SAM adenine and/or the target guanine in the active site.
- UDP-sugar glycosyltransferases for LPS/teichoic acid/lipid A biosynthesis (GT-B fold): activation on the aromatic that stacks with the UDP uracil ring in the donor-binding site.
- NAD(P)-dependent dehydrogenases (Rossmann fold): activation on an adenine-stacking Phe/Tyr in the dinucleotide-binding pocket.
- MurE (UDP-MurNAc-tripeptide synthetase; ATP-grasp ligase): activation on a buried hydrophobe that helps form the adenine-binding cleft for ATP.
- Carbonic anhydrases: activation on a conserved hydrophobic/aromatic residue lining the active-site hydrophobic pocket adjacent to the catalytic zinc.
- Small ribosomal subunit protein S8: activation on an aromatic residue that base-stacks with rRNA or stabilizes the RNA-binding surface.
- MICOS subunit Mic60 (mitofilin): activation on a buried aromatic within the coiled-coil/mitofilin scaffold that stabilizes the membrane-associated core.

Summary: Generic short N-terminal amphipathic or hydrophobic helices: encompassing secretory signal peptides and signal‑anchor transmembrane helices (Sec/Tat), mitochondrial transit peptides, and similar amphipathic/basic N‑terminal helices found in soluble proteins; the feature can also fire on internal hydrophobic/amphipathic helices.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over a 10–30 aa helix, strongest at protein N‑termini; enriched for hydrophobic residues (L/I/V/F/W) with frequent basic residues (R/K/H) in the N‑region; tolerates amphipathic helices lacking a long continuous hydrophobic core (as in mitochondrial presequences and some cytosolic N‑termini); additional peaks may occur at later helices.
Exemplars: Viral envelope glycoproteins (signal peptides/signal anchors); Secreted peptide/toxin precursors; Plant small membrane proteins (e.g., CYSTM family) via signal‑anchor; Mitochondrial matrix/inner-membrane precursors (e.g., ATP synthase ε) via transit peptides; Cytosolic enzymes with basic N‑terminal amphipathic helices (e.g., PrmC/TrmB, RNAP Rpo6, LipB); Viral accessory proteins with basic N‑termini (e.g., Vif).

Summary: Short, cationic, amphipathic peptide segments—typically the mature cores of secreted antimicrobial/cytolytic peptides and analogous AMP‑like helices embedded in larger proteins. These regions are Lys/Arg‑rich with interspersed hydrophobes, often form (or have propensity for) an amphipathic α‑helix, and are used for membrane interaction/disruption or other bioactive signaling; they are usually produced by proteolytic processing from precursor proteins and can include RiPP cores despite post‑translational crosslinks.
Activation pattern: Regional activation on short contiguous blocks (∼15–40 aa, sometimes shorter), with sharp on/off at the boundaries of mature peptide segments; minimal activation in signal peptides and propeptides. Peaks often coincide with hydrophobic residues along an amphipathic face and clusters of Lys/Arg. Frequently at N‑ or C‑terminal helices or short internal helices with low-to-moderate pLDDT.
Exemplars: - Amphibian helical antimicrobial peptides (e.g., aureins): activation precisely on the mature AMP helix, not on signal/propeptide.
- Hymenopteran venom cytolysins (e.g., myrmeciitoxins): strong activation across the mature toxin’s amphipathic α‑helix.
- Lantibiotic RiPPs (e.g., lacticin 3147 A2): activation on the modified mature lantibiotic core despite lanthionine/beta‑methyllanthionine crosslinks.
- Phage/bacterial holins: activation on the N‑terminal amphipathic helix adjacent to the first transmembrane segment; little/no activation in TM or periplasmic domains.
- Crustacean anti‑lipopolysaccharide factors (ALFs): activation on the N‑terminal cationic LPS‑binding helix of the mature peptide.
- Plant NLR immune receptors (coiled‑coil N‑termini): activation on the N‑terminal CC helix implicated in membrane permeabilization/channel activity.
- Insect stress-response secreted proteins (Turandot family): activation on a C‑terminal amphipathic α‑helix of the mature chain.
- Outer membrane polysaccharide export proteins (CtrA family): activation on a short periplasmic C‑terminal helical tail with amphipathic character.
- Kininogen‑derived peptides (bradykinin variants): activation on the short, basic bioactive peptide released from a disordered region.

Summary: Membrane‑active amphipathic α‑helices enriched in small hydrophobic residues (A/V/L/I/G) that insert into, line, or associate with lipid bilayers—i.e., the pore‑forming/translocation helices of toxins and translocons and analogous lipid‑binding/stress‑sensing helices in other membrane proteins
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long, contiguous helical segments (often single helices or helical hairpins), with sparse charges and frequent Gly/Ala runs; peaks track α‑helical stretches that often fold upon membrane contact (low pLDDT in isolation). Activation typically avoids catalytic motifs and generic signal peptides/TM anchors, instead favoring amphipathic or pore‑lining helices (including lipid‑binding helices) within toxin, antimicrobial, and membrane‑associated domains.
Exemplars: - Pore-forming colicins: strong activation on the C‑terminal pore‑forming transmembrane/helical hairpin region.
- Bacillus thuringiensis Cry (δ‑endotoxins): activation on the N‑terminal pore‑forming helical bundle (domain I) with peaks in membrane‑inserting helices.
- Cationic antimicrobial peptides (e.g., Styelin‑D): activation confined to the mature amphipathic α‑helix; absent on the signal peptide and propeptide.
- Mitochondrial inner‑membrane protease OMA1: activation on amphipathic helices within the peptidase domain, including a cardiolipin‑binding/stress‑sensor region; little to no activation on the N‑terminal propeptide or the single‑pass TM anchor.

Summary: Membrane-interacting helical modules: cationic, Gly/Ala-rich amphipathic α-helices and short transmembrane hairpins/fusogenic segments that mediate lipid binding, insertion, or pore formation in toxins, secretion/translocation factors, and viral/secreted proteins; typically low-confidence/disordered in isolation and become helical upon membrane contact.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long, contiguous helical stretches; strongest over amphipathic or hydrophobic helices (including TM segments), with peaks on small hydrophobics (A/V/L/I/G) and frequent Lys/Arg; tends to avoid structured catalytic cores, instead marking N- or C‑terminal delivery/membrane-interaction regions; often coincides with low pLDDT and predicted helices or annotated transmembranes; in peptides, activates on the mature membrane-active helix rather than the signal peptide.
Exemplars: - Cry-family insecticidal δ-endotoxins: activation on the N‑terminal pore-forming helical bundle (domain I) of Cry13Aa.
- Cationic antimicrobial peptide (moricin): activation across the mature α‑helical AMP, not the signal peptide.
- Type VI secretion effector VasX: activation over the C‑terminal membrane-inserting module comprising multiple transmembrane helices.
- LXG polymorphic toxin (YqcG): activation on a long C‑terminal, low‑pLDDT disordered segment following the LXG export domain (a membrane/translocation-prone tail-like region).
- T6SS ADP‑ribosyltransferase (mART) effector (Tre1): activation on N‑terminal glycine‑rich, low‑confidence helical regions flanking PAAR and outside the catalytic core, consistent with delivery/membrane-targeting helices.

Summary: Low-complexity, intrinsically disordered, cysteine-poor segments enriched in small/polar and charged residues (G, A, S, T, K, E, D) that act as surface‑active, lipid‑interface–binding regions (amphipathic/helix‑forming “hydrophilin/apolipoprotein‑like” tracts). These occur broadly across taxa, often at N‑termini or luminal/cytosolic tails of secreted or membrane‑associated proteins, including stress‑protective hydrophilins/LEA proteins, apolipoproteins, ATG2 lipid‑transfer tethers, and cationic antimicrobial/venom peptides.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over long low‑complexity stretches (frequently N‑terminal), with diffuse highlighting and occasional peaks on glycine/threonine repeats or short amphipathic helix motifs; spans entire sequence for small AMPs/venom peptides; in large proteins (e.g., ATG2) covers extended acidic/polar IDRs flanking or preceding hydrophobic cores but not the transmembrane segments.
Exemplars: - Apolipoproteins (e.g., ApoC/ApoA/ApoE families): activation on amphipathic helix repeats and adjacent polar low‑complexity segments that coat lipid particles.
- Plant LEA/hydrophilin proteins (LEA4/LEA5, dehydrins, Hsp12‑like): activation across glycine/threonine/serine‑rich, charged repeats conferring stress‑protective, membrane‑associating properties.
- Autophagy‑related protein 2 (ATG2 family): activation over long acidic/polar IDRs and N‑terminal amphipathic membrane‑tethering segments used at ER–mitochondria/phagophore contact sites.
- Lipid‑droplet/oil‑body scaffolds (oleosins, perilipins, apolipoprotein‑like droplet proteins): activation on low‑complexity polar tails and amphipathic segments surrounding the hydrophobic hairpin/core.
- Cationic antimicrobial and venom peptides (melittin/cecropin/magainin/mastoparan‑like): activation across the whole cationic amphipathic segment that binds membranes.
- Membrane proteins with long disordered N‑ or luminal regions (mitochondrial/ER/PM): activation on polar/charged low‑complexity tails used as flexible linkers or membrane‑proximal surface‑binders.
- Viral matrix/core/viroporin‑associated proteins: activation on low‑complexity, amphipathic, membrane‑interacting stretches.
- Bacterial low‑complexity scaffold/toxin repeats: activation on glycine/threonine‑rich polar segments used for surface association or scaffolding.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered post-signal/TM prohormone regions of secreted short-peptide precursors—i.e., the segments that encode mature neuropeptides/hormones or toxin/antimicrobial peptides and their flanking propeptides—characterized by Lys/Arg-rich convertase cleavage motifs and frequent support for C‑terminal amidation
Activation pattern: Domain-level: inactive on signal peptides and transmembrane helices; strongly active across the luminal propeptide from signal/TM cleavage to the C-terminus. Regional: sustained high activation over mature peptide blocks and adjacent propeptides, often spanning multiple peptides in one precursor; activation typically drops immediately after the last processed peptide. Residue-level: peaks over peptide cores and nearby linkers; selective dips at the second residue of dibasic Lys/Arg cleavage pairs; enrichment around basic clusters and glycine positions associated with amidation.
Exemplars: - Dermaseptin antimicrobial peptide precursor: high on the mature dermaseptin and both flanking propeptides; off on the N‑terminal signal peptide; all activated regions are disordered.
- Insect prokineticin/hugin precursor: strong activation across the region containing Hug‑gamma and PK‑2 peptides and linker/C‑terminal propeptide; inactive on the signal peptide; disordered.
- Tachykinin/protachykinin (neurokinin family): activated across the neurokinin peptide (e.g., Neurokinin‑B) and propeptide segments; sharp local drop at a dibasic cleavage Arg; disordered.
- Neuropeptide F precursor: moderate to strong activation on the mature NPF and the C‑terminal propeptide; signal peptide unactivated; disordered.
- Insect diuretic hormone class 2 precursor: maximal activation across the mature diuretic hormone peptide; off on the signal peptide; disordered.
- Proenkephalin (opioid peptide precursor): broadly activated over enkephalin copies and intervening prosegments; recurrent dip at the second basic residue of dibasic cleavage motifs; disordered.
- Gonadoliberin (GnRH) precursor: high activation across the GnRH peptide and the associated peptide; inactive on the signal peptide; disordered.
- Gastrin prohormone: strong activation over “Big gastrin”/“Gastrin” region and C‑terminal propeptide where amidation/cleavage motifs occur; off on the signal peptide; disordered.
- Pigment-dispersing factor (PDF) precursor: activated on the mature PDF chain; signal peptide not activated; disordered.
- Membrane-anchored secretory peptide-like precursor (e.g., Frey): inactive on the N‑terminal transmembrane helix; strong activation on the disordered luminal C‑terminal region consistent with a processed propeptide segment.

Summary: Short segments within disordered and compositionally biased stretches of diverse proteins, particularly regions enriched in basic and acidic residues. Activations are also seen in non-disordered contexts across proteins of varied function, suggesting the feature captures a relatively broad local sequence pattern rather than a tight structural motif.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks with small clusters, distributed throughout the length of the protein. Peaks frequently overlap annotated disordered regions and basic/acidic compositionally biased segments, but also occur at isolated positions within structured chains; occurs in both helical and coil contexts.
Exemplars: - Oomycete RxLR secreted effectors: peaks within the mature effector chain, with occasional spikes in the signal peptide.
- Plant CLE peptide precursors: localized peaks within the C-terminal CLE motif corresponding to the mature signaling peptide.
- Cholecystokinin prohormone: peaks at or immediately adjacent to the N-termini of mature neuropeptides generated by proteolytic processing.
- Herpesvirus ICP47-like small accessory proteins: multiple peaks in the N-terminal active helical region and in polar, disordered C-terminal stretches.
- Keratin-associated proteins: activation across cysteine/proline/serine-rich, low-complexity repeat regions.
- Phosphodiesterase and fungal/bacterial enzymes with disordered N- or internal stretches: peaks within basic-and-acidic compositionally biased segments.

Summary: Short, low‑complexity, intrinsically disordered proteins and modules that encode targeting/processing signals—often but not always secretory—combining hydrophobic signal peptides, double‑Gly bacteriocin leaders, or polybasic/NLS‑like segments, frequently adjacent to Ser/Thr/Pro‑rich stretches and basic clusters (e.g., RXLR, KR/RR)—common in micropeptides, toxins/secreted precursors, viral accessory proteins, keratin‑associated and testis‑specific low‑complexity proteins across taxa
Activation pattern: Regional activation across short proteins, spanning hydrophobic/targeting segments and Ser/Thr/Pro‑rich low‑complexity tracts with peaks on basic motifs such as RXLR, dibasic KR/RR, or double‑Gly leader junctions
Exemplars:
- Oomycete RxLR effectors: activation on the N‑terminal signal peptide and the RXLR/EER host‑targeting motif immediately downstream.
- Secreted peptide hormone/venom/toxin precursors: activation on the signal peptide and basic prohormone convertase cleavage motifs (KR/RR) within the propeptide region.
- Class II bacteriocins: activation on the N‑terminal double‑Gly leader and adjacent cationic tract recognized by ABC exporters.
- Viral accessory/regulatory proteins (e.g., small disordered regulators): activation across S/T/P‑rich low‑complexity disordered segments containing polybasic/NLS‑like clusters.
- Keratin‑associated proteins (KRTAPs): activation over short, repetitive low‑complexity regions (Ser/Pro‑rich and basic tracts) typical of hair shaft proteins.
- Cancer/testis antigens and testis‑associated proteins: activation on Lys/Arg‑ and Pro/Ser‑rich low‑complexity stretches in very short proteins.
- Short uncharacterized micropeptides/antisense products: broad activation across their low‑complexity/basic segments.
- Enzymes that carry secretory leaders or short disordered/basic tails (including some cytosolic enzymes lacking signal peptides): activation limited to the disordered tail, not the catalytic core.

Summary: Low-complexity, intrinsically disordered segments with a bias for serine/threonine (often with proline and nearby basic/acidic residues) that encode short linear motifs for regulation or targeting (e.g., phosphosite motifs, RxLR-dEER), found in flexible regulatory tails, disordered viral protein regions, and short secreted peptide precursors.
Activation pattern: Predominantly regional activation across disordered, low-pLDDT stretches with many sites per segment; superimposed residue-level peaks on S/T and adjacent charged/proline residues. Also active in short, low-complexity transmembrane/peptide precursors; minimal in well-folded globular domains.
Exemplars: - Coronavirus nucleocapsid proteins: central low-complexity, disordered regions enriched in Ser/Thr with known phosphosites, plus disordered C-terminal tails.
- Viral disordered regulatory proteins (e.g., hepadnavirus protein X, HIV Vif): disordered internal regions and flexible linkers with peaks on S/E/P/R.
- Oomycete RxLR effectors: flexible N-terminal/mature regions around the RxLR-dEER host-targeting motif, with peaks on E/S/R within low-confidence structure.
- Secreted antimicrobial peptide precursors: activation on the N-terminal signal peptide and on flexible residues within the mature peptide region.
- Disordered human regulatory proteins (e.g., PRAS40, p311, NoBody): scattered activation across intrinsically disordered segments, often overlapping known phosphosites.

Summary: Residue-level signal for mature regions of secreted extracellular proteins and peptides—including ligands, cytokines, toxins, antimicrobial peptides, and matrix/matrix-associated modulators—with emphasis on disulfide-stabilized/cysteine-rich domains; captures functional/bioactive regions rather than signal peptides or prosegments.
Activation pattern: Predominantly sparse residue-level peaks concentrated within the mature secreted chain or other folded extracellular domains (e.g., cystine‑knot, CSαβ, chemokine-like, or non-repetitive globular domains); minimal activation in signal peptides and low-complexity prosegments; peaks occur on beta-strands and loops/turns and may lie near processing boundaries or adjacent to N‑glycosylation motifs.
Exemplars:
- Glycoprotein hormones (common alpha subunit): peaks near N‑glycosylation motifs and at the signal peptide cleavage boundary within the hormone domain.
- DAN family BMP/Wnt antagonists (e.g., Cerberus/Gremlin) and Chordin: activation on beta‑strands of cysteine-rich domains; little/no signal in the signal peptide.
- Neurotrophins (NGF/BDNF/NT‑4/5): activation confined to the mature growth‑factor chain across beta‑strands and loops; absent from the propeptide.
- IL‑17 family cytokines: sparse peaks in core strands and flexible loops of the secreted cytokine domain.
- Venom toxins (e.g., scorpion κ‑toxins; snake BPP‑CNP precursors): peaks in loop/turn segments of disulfide‑stabilized cores and/or in the proline‑rich BPP/CNP mature segments; minimal in signal peptides.
- Chemokine‑like GPR15 ligand: activation within disordered segments of the mature secreted peptide.
- Antimicrobial peptides (LEAP‑2): peaks on the disulfide‑stabilized core of the mature peptide.
- Extracellular matrix proteins (e.g., Collagen IV chains): sparse peaks within non‑repetitive folded extracellular domains (e.g., NC1 domain or triple‑helix interruptions), not in signal peptides.

Summary: Cysteine-rich mature secreted peptide/protein feature: the feature activates within the mature chains of secretory-pathway precursors (secreted/extracellular peptides, virion-surface glycoproteins, outer-membrane proteins, and ER/Golgi lumenal residents), preferentially at and near cysteine residues participating in disulfide-bonded cores.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks fall inside mature CHAIN/PEPTIDE regions, typically on or immediately adjacent to cysteines that form intramolecular disulfides, often within compact cysteine-rich folds of the secreted product. Signal/leader peptides themselves are generally not activated. Small, variable number of activated residues per protein.
Exemplars: - Venom peptide precursors (three-finger toxins, conotoxins, Kunitz inhibitors): activation across the conserved cysteine-rich mature toxin core.
- Antimicrobial peptides/defensins and bacteriocins (plant/fungal defensins, hepcidins; class II bacteriocins; lantibiotics): activation across cysteine-rich mature peptide segments.
- Neuropeptide/prohormone precursors (POMC, proenkephalin, neuropeptide Y, insulin/IGF): activation within mature peptide segments.
- Viral envelope glycoproteins (influenza HA, coronavirus spike, retroviral Env): activation within cysteine-rich extracellular/ectodomain regions.
- Bacterial secreted toxins and secretory/outer-membrane proteins, including lipoproteins: activation within mature, disulfide-containing secreted segments.
- Plant/fungal pathogen effectors: activation within cysteine-rich effector cores of secreted effectors.
- ER/Golgi lumenal secretory pathway residents (e.g., ERO1/ERO1-like): activation within mature lumenal regions.

Summary: Low-complexity, intrinsically disordered segments with a bias for serine/threonine (often with proline and nearby basic/acidic residues) that encode short linear motifs for regulation or targeting (e.g., phosphosite motifs, RxLR-dEER), found in flexible regulatory tails, disordered viral protein regions, and short secreted peptide precursors.
Activation pattern: Predominantly regional activation across disordered, low-pLDDT stretches with many sites per segment; superimposed residue-level peaks on S/T and adjacent charged/proline residues. Exemplars: - Coronavirus nucleocapsid proteins: central low-complexity, disordered regions enriched in Ser/Thr with known phosphosites, plus disordered C-terminal tails.

- Oomycete RxLR effectors: flexible N-terminal/mature regions around the RxLR-dEER host-targeting motif, with peaks on E/S/R within low-confidence structure.
- Secreted antimicrobial peptide precursors: activation on the N-terminal signal peptide and on flexible residues within the mature peptide region.
- Disordered human regulatory proteins (e.g., PRAS40, p311, NoBody): scattered activation across intrinsically disordered segments, often overlapping known phosphosites.

Summary: Small, often poorly characterized or compositionally biased proteins, including viral accessory proteins, cancer/testis and germline-associated proteins, antisense-ORF microproteins, and short secreted/surface peptides; activation is broadly distributed across the polypeptide rather than focused on a single structured domain
Activation pattern: Regional/distributed activation spread across much of the protein with sparse residue-level peaks; often includes early N-terminal residues and disordered segments; variable coverage from short patches to most of the protein
Exemplars:
- Viral non-structural/accessory proteins: activation distributed through the protein, including basic/Arg-rich motifs such as nuclear localization signals.
- Cancer/testis antigens and germline-associated proteins: activation on long disordered low-complexity regions, often at N-termini.
- Small uncharacterized microproteins/antisense ORFs: activation spanning most of the polypeptide.
- Short secreted peptides and toxin precursors: activation across both signal/propeptide and mature regions.
- Compact cytosolic proteins with disordered N- or C-terminal extensions: activation enriched on the disordered tails.

Summary: Detector of compositionally biased, low‑complexity segments—predominantly intrinsically disordered Ser/Thr‑rich (often RS-/Pro‑containing) tracts—with a strong N‑terminal bias; it also flags the extreme N‑terminus including signal peptides of secreted precursors.
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks clustered within long disordered/low‑complexity regions (often spanning tens to hundreds of residues), with strongest peaks on Ser/Thr and nearby polar/basic residues; broad regional activation across such IDRs and minimal signal in well‑folded domains or transmembranes; additional discrete peaks frequently occur at residues 1–10, including within N‑terminal signal peptides.
Exemplars: - Transcriptional regulator (CROC-4): multiple peaks across a central low‑complexity disordered segment (S/T/R/P‑rich), with minor N‑terminal peaks.
- Mechanosensory receptor (Stum): numerous high peaks on serines dispersed through annotated disordered, low‑complexity/polar regions.
- Yeast RNA/chromatin‑associated factor (REF2‑interacting protein): peaks within disordered, compositionally biased tracts; strongest at a threonine in an S/T‑rich context, near (but not exactly on) annotated phosphosites.
- Secreted antimicrobial peptide precursor (lumbricin): strongest activation on the N‑terminal signal peptide helix; weaker peaks just after the signal peptide preceding a long disordered pro‑region.
- Yeast HPH2 regulatory protein: activation confined to disordered, low‑complexity regions in the N‑terminal two‑thirds; absent from the structured C‑terminal domain and its transmembrane helix.

Summary: Short linear segments in intrinsically disordered or otherwise low-structure-confidence regions, often at N-termini and within signal peptides/propeptides of secreted and regulatory proteins (including viral accessory proteins and small ORF microproteins), enriched in small/basic residues (G, P, S, A, R; often with Cys), rather than in well-folded catalytic cores.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks scattered across IDRs and low-confidence coils/short helices; frequently clustered near the N-terminus, in signal peptides, propeptides, and disordered tails; little to no activation in well-structured domains; occasional activation in low-confidence transmembrane/signal-anchor helices.
Exemplars: - Viral accessory protein (HIV-1 Vif): peaks throughout low-pLDDT coils, especially the disordered N-terminal region.
- Neuropeptide precursor (Drosophila Amnesiac): activation in the N-terminal signal peptide and multiple mature peptide segments with very low pLDDT.
- Secreted serine carboxypeptidase: activation confined to disordered C-terminal tail, annotated disordered segment, the signal peptide, and a low-confidence C-terminal transmembrane helix; absent from the structured catalytic domain.
- Disordered human tumor-suppressor–associated protein (ST20): scattered peaks within predicted helices in a globally disordered chain, including the N-terminus.
- lncRNA/sORF-derived microprotein (IGF2 antisense protein): multiple peaks across annotated disordered regions rich in Arg/Pro/Gly.

Summary: Often fires within intrinsic disorder/low-complexity segments—especially terminal or propeptide regions enriched in Pro/Ser/Thr/Gly—that serve as flexible carriers of short linear motifs; the feature highlights unstructured tails/loops across diverse proteins (including secreted precursors, viral regulators, membrane-protein tails, and micropeptides), sometimes coinciding with proteolytic processing and PTM sites, but also produces residue-level peaks within some short folded enzymes/fragments.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks within annotated/predicted disordered coils and low-complexity tracts, frequently enriched toward N-termini; additional scattered peaks can occur within short folded chains.
Exemplars: - Secreted peptide hormone precursors (e.g., cholecystokinin/prohormones): peaks in unstructured propeptide segments at sulfotyrosine, amidation sites, and cleavage boundaries.
- Herpesviral nuclear egress proteins: activation on N-terminal disordered, polar-biased regions; not on the structured zinc-finger domain.
- Integrase-family proteins: peaks include very low-pLDDT loops and annotated disordered segments, with additional scattered peaks elsewhere in the chain.
- Mycobacterial cell-envelope–associated proteins: single-residue/short-segment peaks within UniProt-annotated disordered coil regions.
- p53-inducible regulatory proteins: sparse peaks across N-terminal and central intrinsically disordered regions, including isoform-variable segments.
- Alternative reading frame micropeptides: activation across low-complexity, disordered coils.

Summary: Hydrophobic alpha-helical signal/anchor motif: the feature marks hydrophobic side chains (L/I/V/F/M, often with Y/W) within short alpha-helical segments—most prominently the hydrophobic core of N‑terminal signal peptides and other amphipathic or membrane-interacting helices—and, more generally, single hydrophobic “anchor” residues embedded in helices of diverse soluble domains (e.g., ARID, FH3). Occasional activation extends to nearby residues within the same helical segment in secreted/viral proteins.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks with variable density: short runs across hydrophobic helical stretches (especially at extreme N-termini) and isolated single-residue peaks on helix-internal hydrophobes; observed both in low-confidence/disordered regions that harbor short helices and in well-structured helices.
Exemplars: - Oomycete RxLR effectors: activation on the signal peptide hydrophobic core and the RxLR-adjacent short helix, with additional peaks on aromatic residues in the effector body.
- Plant viral RNA-silencing suppressor P0: scattered peaks on hydrophobic residues within predicted helices and adjacent coils, consistent with short amphipathic helices.
- Viral VP5 accessory proteins: strong peaks on V/I/M in flexible segments that form short hydrophobic helices.
- ARID DNA-binding proteins (e.g., Rsc9, Jumonji-family ARID): single-residue peaks on I/L within ARID helices.
- Formin family (GBD/FH3 domain): a solitary L within a helical segment is highlighted.
